titres.titre: In the beginning: the creation of the world
The creation of man and woman

versets.t: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was formless and empty; darkness covered the deep, and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters.
God said, "Let there be light!" And there was light.
God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness.
God called the light "day," and the darkness "night." There was evening, and there was morning: the first day.
God said, "Let there be a vault in the midst of the waters, to separate the waters from the waters."
God made the vault and separated the waters below it from the waters above it. And so it was.
God called the vault "sky." There was evening, and there was morning: the second day.
God said, "Let the waters below the sky be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear." And so it was.
God called the dry land "earth," and the gathered waters "seas." And God saw that it was good.
God said, "Let the earth be covered with greenery: plants bearing their seed, and fruit trees each yielding, according to its kind, fruit that contains its seed." And so it was.
The earth brought forth greenery: plants bearing their seed according to their kind, and trees yielding fruit that contains its seed according to their kind. And God saw that it was good.
There was evening, and there was morning: the third day.
God said, "Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to separate the day from the night; let them serve as signs to mark the feasts, the days, and the years,
and let them shine in the vault of the sky to give light upon the earth." And so it was.
God made the two great lights: the greater one to govern the day, the lesser one to govern the night; he made the stars as well.
God set them in the vault of the sky to give light upon the earth,
to govern the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.
There was evening, and there was morning: the fourth day.
God said, "Let the waters teem with a multitude of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth, beneath the vault of the sky."

God created the great sea monsters, all the living creatures that move about and teem in the waters, according to their kind, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply, fill the waters of the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth."
There was evening, and there was morning: the fifth day.
God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kind: livestock, creatures that crawl, and wild animals, each according to its kind." And so it was.
God made the wild animals according to their kind, the livestock according to their kind, and all the small creatures that crawl on the ground according to their kind. And God saw that it was good.
God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. Let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the livestock, all the earth, and every creature that crawls on the ground."
God created man in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
God blessed them and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every creature that moves about on the earth."
God said further, "See, I give you every plant bearing its seed on the whole face of the earth, and every tree that bears fruit containing its seed: this will be your food.
And to every animal of the earth, to every bird of the sky, to everything that crawls on the ground and has in it the breath of life, I give every green plant for food." And so it was.
And God saw all that he had made: it was very good. There was evening, and there was morning: the sixth day.

titres.titre: The rest of the seventh day

versets.t: Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, with all their array.
On the seventh day God had finished the work he had done; on that seventh day he rested from all the work he had done.
God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, for on that day he rested from all the work he had created.
Such is the story of the heavens and the earth at their creation. On the day the Lord God made the earth and the heavens,
there was as yet no shrub of the field on the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprung up, for the Lord God had not made it rain upon the earth, and there was no one to till the ground.
But a spring rose from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground.
Then the Lord God shaped man from the dust of the ground; he breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living being.
Then the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he placed the man he had shaped.
The Lord God made grow out of the ground every kind of tree pleasing to look at and good to eat, with, in the middle of the garden, the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden; from there it divided into four branches.
The first is called the Pishon: it is the one that winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold,
and the gold of that land is good. There too are found bdellium (a precious resin) and onyx stone.
The second river is called the Gihon: it is the one that winds through the whole land of Cush.
The third river is called the Tigris: it flows east of Asshur. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
The Lord God took the man and placed him in the garden of Eden to serve it and to keep it.
The Lord God gave the man this command: "You may eat from all the trees of the garden;
but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; for on the day you eat from it, you shall surely die."
The Lord God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper who suits him."

Out of the earth the Lord God shaped all the animals of the field and all the birds of the sky, and he brought them to the man to see what he would call them: each living creature was to bear the name the man would give it.
So the man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to all the animals of the field; but he found no helper who suited him.
Then the Lord God made a deep sleep fall upon the man. While he slept, he took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place.
With the rib he had taken from the man, the Lord God shaped a woman, and he brought her to the man.
The man exclaimed, "This time, here is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh! She shall be called woman, for she was taken from man."
That is why a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Both of them were naked, the man and his wife, and felt no shame.
The serpent was the most cunning of all the animals of the field that the Lord God had made. It said to the woman, "So, has God really told you: You shall not eat from any tree of the garden?"
The woman answered the serpent, "We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden.
But of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the garden, God has said: You shall not eat from it, you shall not touch it, or you will die."
The serpent said to the woman, "Not at all! You will not die.
But God knows that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."

The woman saw that the fruit of the tree was good to eat, that it was beautiful to look at and desirable for gaining wisdom. She took some and ate it; she also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate.
Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.
They heard the Lord God moving about in the garden at the hour when the breeze of the day blows; and the man and his wife hid from the Lord God among the trees of the garden.
But the Lord God called to the man, "Where are you?"
He answered, "I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid."
The Lord God said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I forbade you to eat from?"
The man answered, "The woman you put here with me, she is the one who gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate."
The Lord God said to the woman, "What have you done?" The woman answered, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."

Then the Lord God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, you are cursed above all the livestock and all the animals of the field. You shall crawl on your belly and eat dust all the days of your life.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your offspring and hers: he will crush your head, and you will strike his heel."
To the woman he said, "I will multiply the pains of your pregnancies: in pain you shall bring forth sons. Your desire will be for your husband, but he will rule over you."

To the man he said, "Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree I forbade you to eat from, the ground is cursed because of you. In toil you shall draw your food from it, all the days of your life.
It will produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the ground, since it was from it that you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return."
The man called his wife Eve, that is, the living one, because she is the mother of all the living.
The Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and he clothed them.
Then the Lord God said, "See, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now let him not reach out his hand to take also from the tree of life, eat, and live forever!"
And the Lord God sent him out of the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he had been taken.
He drove the man out, and east of the garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim and the flame of the whirling sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.
Adam knew Eve, his wife; she conceived and gave birth to Cain. Then she said, "I have gained a man, with the help of the Lord!"
She also gave birth to his brother, Abel. Abel kept the flocks, and Cain tilled the ground.
After some time, Cain brought the Lord an offering from the produce of the ground.
Abel, for his part, offered the firstborn of his flock and their fat. The Lord looked with favor on Abel and his offering,
but he did not look on Cain and his. Cain was very angry, and his face fell.
The Lord said to Cain, "Why are you angry? Why has your face fallen?
If you do well, will you not hold your head high? But if you do not do well, sin is crouching at your door: it desires you, but you must master it."
Cain said to his brother Abel, "Let us go out to the fields." And once they were in the fields, Cain set upon his brother Abel and killed him.
The Lord said to Cain, "Where is your brother Abel?" He answered, "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?"
The Lord said, "What have you done? Your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground.
Now you are cursed and driven far from this ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.
When you till it, the ground will no longer yield anything to you. You will be a restless wanderer, a fugitive on the earth."
Cain said to the Lord, "My punishment is too heavy to bear.
See, today you drive me from this land; I must hide far from your face, I will be a restless wanderer, a fugitive on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me."
The Lord said to him, "Then whoever kills Cain will suffer vengeance seven times over." And the Lord put a mark on Cain, so that no one who met him would strike him down.
Then Cain went away from the presence of the Lord and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Cain knew his wife; she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. As Cain was building a city, he named it after his son, Enoch.
Enoch had a son, Irad; Irad fathered Mehujael, Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech.
Lamech took two wives: one was called Adah, the other Zillah.
Adah gave birth to Jabal: he was the ancestor of those who live in tents, among the herds.
His brother was called Jubal: he was the ancestor of all who play the harp and the flute.
Zillah, for her part, gave birth to Tubal-cain, who forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron. Tubal-cain had a sister, Naamah.
Lamech said to his wives, "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for a wound, a young man for a mere bruise.
If Cain is avenged seven times, Lamech will be avenged seventy-seven times."
Adam knew his wife again; she gave birth to a son whom she named Seth, "for," she said, "God has granted me other offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed."
Seth too had a son, whom he named Enosh. It was then that people began to call on the name of the Lord.
This is the book of the family of Adam. On the day God created man, he made him in the likeness of God.
He created them male and female, he blessed them and called them "man," on the day of their creation.
Adam was a hundred and thirty years old when he fathered a son in his likeness, after his image, and he named him Seth.
After the birth of Seth, Adam lived another eight hundred years, and he had sons and daughters.
Adam lived nine hundred and thirty years in all, and then he died.
Seth was a hundred and five years old when he fathered Enosh.
After the birth of Enosh, Seth lived another eight hundred and seven years, and he had sons and daughters.
Seth lived nine hundred and twelve years in all, and then he died.
Enosh was ninety years old when he fathered Kenan.
After the birth of Kenan, Enosh lived another eight hundred and fifteen years, and he had sons and daughters.
Enosh lived nine hundred and five years in all, and then he died.
Kenan was seventy years old when he fathered Mahalalel.
After the birth of Mahalalel, Kenan lived another eight hundred and forty years, and he had sons and daughters.
Kenan lived nine hundred and ten years in all, and then he died.
Mahalalel was sixty-five years old when he fathered Jared.
After the birth of Jared, Mahalalel lived another eight hundred and thirty years, and he had sons and daughters.
Mahalalel lived eight hundred and ninety-five years in all, and then he died.
Jared was a hundred and sixty-two years old when he fathered Enoch.
After the birth of Enoch, Jared lived another eight hundred years, and he had sons and daughters.
Jared lived nine hundred and sixty-two years in all, and then he died.
Enoch was sixty-five years old when he fathered Methuselah.
After the birth of Methuselah, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and he had sons and daughters.
Enoch lived three hundred and sixty-five years in all.
Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, for God had taken him.
Methuselah was a hundred and eighty-seven years old when he fathered Lamech.
After the birth of Lamech, Methuselah lived another seven hundred and eighty-two years, and he had sons and daughters.
Methuselah lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years in all, and then he died.
Lamech was a hundred and eighty-two years old when he fathered a son.
He named him Noah, saying, "This one will bring us comfort in our labor and in the toil of our hands, on this ground that the Lord has cursed."
After the birth of Noah, Lamech lived another five hundred and ninety-five years, and he had sons and daughters.
Lamech lived seven hundred and seventy-seven years in all, and then he died.
At the age of five hundred years, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

titres.titre: God decides on the flood; Noah finds favor

versets.t: When human beings began to multiply on the face of the earth and daughters were born to them,
the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives any they chose.
Then the Lord said, "My breath will not remain in man forever, for he is only flesh; his life will not exceed a hundred and twenty years."
In those days the Nephilim were on the earth, and also afterward, when the sons of God united with the daughters of men and they bore them children. These are the famous heroes of ancient times.
The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that his heart conceived nothing but evil, all day long.
The Lord regretted having made man on the earth, and his heart was grieved.
He said, "I will wipe from the face of the earth man, whom I have created, and with him the animals, the creatures that crawl, and the birds of the sky, for I regret having made them."
But Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.
This is the story of Noah. Noah was a righteous and blameless man among his contemporaries; Noah walked with God.
Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Now the earth had become corrupt before God; it had become filled with violence.
God looked at the earth: it was corrupt, for all living things on the earth followed a corrupt way.
Then God said to Noah, "The end of all living things has come; I have decided it, for because of them the earth is full of violence. See, I am going to destroy them, along with the earth.
Make yourself an ark of resinous wood; you will fit it out with compartments and coat it with pitch inside and out.
This is how you shall make it: a hundred and fifty metres long, twenty-five metres wide, and fifteen metres high.
You will make an opening for light, half a metre from the top; you will set a door in the side of the ark, and you will make a first, a second, and a third deck.
And I, I am going to bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, to destroy under the sky every creature that has in it the breath of life: everything on the earth will perish.
But with you I will establish my covenant. You will enter the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.
Of every living thing, of all flesh, you will bring into the ark two of each kind, to keep them alive with you: they will be male and female.

Of the birds according to their kind, the livestock according to their kind, all the creatures that crawl on the ground according to their kind, two of each kind will come to you, so that you may keep them alive.
And you, take some of every kind of food and store it up: it will serve as food, for you and for them."
Noah set to work: he did everything God had commanded him.
The Lord said to Noah, "Enter the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me among this generation.
Of all the clean animals, you will take seven pairs, the male and its female; of the unclean animals, you will take one pair, the male and its female;
and of the birds of the sky, seven pairs as well, the male and the female, so that their kind may be preserved on all the earth.
For in seven days I will send rain upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe from the face of the ground every creature I have made."
Noah did everything the Lord had commanded him.
Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came upon the earth.
To escape the waters of the flood, he entered the ark with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives.
Of the clean and unclean animals, the birds, and all the creatures that crawl on the ground,
a pair, male and female, came to Noah in the ark, as God had commanded him.
And after seven days, the waters of the flood spread over the earth.

In the year of Noah's six hundredth year, on the seventeenth day of the second month (around April-May), on that day, all the springs of the great deep burst forth and the floodgates of the sky opened.
The rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.
On that very day, Noah entered the ark, with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, his wife, and the three wives of his sons,

and with them all the wild animals according to their kind, all the livestock according to their kind, all the creatures that crawl on the earth according to their kind, and all the birds according to their kind, everything that flies and has wings.
They came to Noah in the ark, two by two, of every creature having in it the breath of life.
Those that entered were a male and a female of each kind, as God had commanded him. And the Lord shut the door behind him.
The flood lasted forty days on the earth. The waters rose and lifted the ark, which floated above the earth.
The waters rose and swelled enormously on the earth, and the ark floated on their surface.
The waters rose higher and higher on the earth, until they covered all the high mountains under the sky.
The waters rose about seven and a half metres above the mountains they covered.
Then perished all the creatures that moved on the earth: birds, livestock, wild animals, everything that swarms on the earth, and all human beings.
Everything that had in its nostrils the breath of life, everything that lived on the dry land, died.

The Lord wiped out all the creatures that were on the face of the ground, from man to livestock, to the creatures that crawl and to the birds of the sky: they were wiped from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark.
The waters prevailed over the earth for a hundred and fifty days.
God remembered Noah, and all the wild animals and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters subsided.
The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the sky closed, and the rain stopped falling.
Little by little, the waters withdrew from the earth; after a hundred and fifty days, they had gone down.
On the seventeenth day of the seventh month (around September-October), the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
The waters kept going down until the tenth month (around December-January); on the first day of that month, the tops of the mountains appeared.
After forty days, Noah opened the window he had made in the ark
and let out the raven, which flew off, going back and forth, until the waters had dried up on the earth.
Then he let out the dove, to see whether the waters had gone down on the face of the ground.
But the dove found no place to set its feet and returned to him in the ark, for the waters still covered the whole earth. Noah reached out his hand, took it, and brought it back to him.
He waited another seven days and again let the dove out of the ark.
Toward evening, it came back to him, and there in its beak it held a fresh olive leaf. Noah then knew that the waters had gone down on the earth.
He waited another seven days and let the dove out; this time, it did not come back to him.

In the year of Noah's six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month (around March-April), the waters had dried up on the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark, looked out, and saw that the surface of the ground was dry.
On the twenty-seventh day of the second month (around April-May), the earth was dry.
Then God said to Noah:
"Come out of the ark, you, your wife, your sons, and your sons' wives with you.

Bring out with you all the animals that are with you, all living things, the birds, the livestock, and all the creatures that crawl on the earth. Let them spread over the earth, be fruitful, and multiply upon it."
Noah came out, with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives.
All the wild animals, all the crawling creatures, all the birds, everything that moves on the earth, came out of the ark, each kind apart.
Noah built an altar to the Lord; he took some of all the clean animals and all the clean birds, and he offered burnt offerings on the altar.

The Lord breathed in the soothing fragrance of the offering, and he said to himself, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man, for the heart of man is inclined to evil from his youth; never again will I strike down all living things, as I have done.
As long as the earth lasts, sowing and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never cease."
God blessed Noah and his sons, and he said to them, "Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth.
You will be feared and dreaded by all the animals of the earth, by all the birds of the sky, by everything that crawls on the ground, and by all the fish of the sea: they are handed over to you.
Everything that lives and moves will serve you as food; I give you all this, just as I had given you the green plants.
However, you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, with its blood.

And your own blood, the blood of your life, I will require an account of it: I will require it of every animal and of every man; of whoever kills his brother, I will require an account of the life of the man.
Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man will his own blood be shed; for God made man in his image.
As for you, be fruitful and multiply, spread over the earth and multiply upon it."
God said further to Noah and his sons:
"See, I am establishing my covenant with you, with your offspring after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, all the animals of the earth, all those that came out of the ark, down to the last animal of the earth.
I establish my covenant with you: never again will any creature be destroyed by the waters of a flood, and never again will a flood ravage the earth."
God said further, "Here is the sign of the covenant that I establish between me and you, and every living creature that is with you, for all generations to come:
I set my bow in the clouds, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
When I gather clouds over the earth and the bow appears in the clouds,
I will remember my covenant between me and you and every living creature; and never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all that lives.
The bow will be in the clouds, and seeing it, I will remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature that is on the earth."
God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all living things that are on the earth."
The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth; Ham was the father of Canaan.
These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth was peopled.
Noah, who was a farmer, was the first to plant a vineyard.
Having drunk some wine, he became drunk and lay naked inside his tent.
Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and he went out and told his two brothers.
Then Shem and Japheth took Noah's cloak, laid it on both their shoulders, and walking backward, they covered their father's nakedness.
Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father's nakedness. When Noah awoke from his drunkenness, he learned what his youngest son had done to him,
and he said, "Cursed be Canaan! May he be the lowest of slaves to his brothers!"
Then he said, "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem, and may Canaan be his slave!
May God give room to Japheth, may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his slave!"
After the flood, Noah lived another three hundred and fifty years.
Noah lived nine hundred and fifty years in all, and then he died.
This is the line of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth: sons were born to them after the flood.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
The sons of Javan: Elishah and Tarshish, the Kittim and the Dodanim.
From these the peoples of the coastlands spread out, each in its own land, according to its language, its clans, and its nations.
The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
Cush also fathered Nimrod, who was the first potentate on the earth.
He was a mighty hunter before the Lord; hence the saying, "Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord."
His kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.
From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah,
and Resen, between Nineveh and Calah: that is the great city.
Mizraim fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim,
the Pathrusim, the Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines, and the Caphtorim.
Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, then Heth,
as well as the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,
the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,
the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Later, the clans of the Canaanites scattered.
The territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon toward Gerar, as far as Gaza, then toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.
These are the sons of Ham, according to their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.
Shem too had sons. He is the ancestor of all the sons of Eber and the elder brother of Japheth.
The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.
The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.
Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber.
To Eber were born two sons: one was called Peleg, for in his time the earth was divided, and his brother was called Joktan.
Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,
Obal, Abimael, Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.
The land they inhabited stretched from Mesha toward Sephar, the mountain of the east.
These are the sons of Shem, according to their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.
These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their lines and their nations. From them the nations spread over the earth after the flood.
The whole earth had one language and the same words.
Now, as they moved eastward, people found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.
They said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and bake them in the fire." Brick served them as stone, and pitch as mortar.
Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city, with a tower whose top touches the sky. Thus we will make a name for ourselves, and we will not be scattered over the whole face of the earth."
The Lord came down to see the city and the tower that the people were building.
And the Lord said, "See, they are one people, with one language for all; and this is only the beginning of their undertakings. From now on, nothing they plan to do will be impossible for them.
Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they no longer understand one another."
From there the Lord scattered them over the whole face of the earth, and they stopped building the city.
That is why it was called Babel, for it was there that the Lord confused the language of the whole earth, and it was from there that he scattered them over the whole face of the earth.
This is the line of Shem. At the age of a hundred years, two years after the flood, Shem fathered Arpachshad.
After the birth of Arpachshad, Shem lived another five hundred years, and he had sons and daughters.
Arpachshad, at thirty-five years, fathered Shelah.
After the birth of Shelah, Arpachshad lived another four hundred and three years, and he had sons and daughters.
Shelah, at thirty years, fathered Eber.
After the birth of Eber, Shelah lived another four hundred and three years, and he had sons and daughters.
Eber, at thirty-four years, fathered Peleg.
After the birth of Peleg, Eber lived another four hundred and thirty years, and he had sons and daughters.
Peleg, at thirty years, fathered Reu.
After the birth of Reu, Peleg lived another two hundred and nine years, and he had sons and daughters.
Reu, at thirty-two years, fathered Serug.
After the birth of Serug, Reu lived another two hundred and seven years, and he had sons and daughters.
Serug, at thirty years, fathered Nahor.
After the birth of Nahor, Serug lived another two hundred years, and he had sons and daughters.
Nahor, at twenty-nine years, fathered Terah.
After the birth of Terah, Nahor lived another hundred and nineteen years, and he had sons and daughters.
Terah, at seventy years, fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
This is the line of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.
Haran died during the lifetime of his father Terah, in his native land, at Ur of the Chaldeans.
Abram and Nahor took wives: the wife of Abram was called Sarai, and that of Nahor, Milcah, daughter of Haran, himself the father of Milcah and Iscah.
Now Sarai was barren: she had no child.

Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot, son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, the wife of his son Abram. Together they left Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. But when they reached Haran, they settled there.
Terah lived two hundred and five years in all, and then he died at Haran.
The Lord said to Abram, "Leave your country, your kindred, and your father's house, for the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation, I will bless you, I will make your name so great that it will become a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse anyone who curses you. In you all the families of the earth will be blessed."
Abram set out, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

Abram took Sarai, his wife, Lot, his brother's son, all the possessions they had gathered and the people they had acquired at Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan. When they reached the land of Canaan,
Abram passed through it as far as the place of Shechem, as far as the oak of Moreh. At that time, the Canaanites inhabited the land.
The Lord appeared to Abram and said to him, "It is to your offspring that I will give this land." Abram built there an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him.
From there he moved on to the mountain east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. There again he built an altar to the Lord and called on his name.
Then Abram continued his journey, from camp to camp, toward the Negeb.
There was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to stay there, for the famine was severe.
As he was approaching Egypt, he said to Sarai, his wife, "See, I know that you are a beautiful woman.
When the Egyptians see you, they will say: This is his wife! They will kill me and let you live.
Say, then, that you are my sister, so that I may be treated well because of you and my life spared for your sake."
When Abram arrived in Egypt, the Egyptians saw that his wife was very beautiful.
Pharaoh's officials noticed her and praised her to him; and the woman was taken to Pharaoh's palace.
Because of her, Pharaoh treated Abram well: he received sheep, oxen, donkeys, male and female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
But the Lord struck Pharaoh and his household with great plagues, because of Sarai, the wife of Abram.
Pharaoh summoned Abram and said to him, "What have you done to me? Why did you not tell me she was your wife?
Why did you claim: She is my sister? So I took her as my wife! Now, here is your wife: take her and go."
Pharaoh gave orders to his men concerning Abram, and they sent him away, with his wife and all that he had.
From Egypt, Abram went back up to the Negeb, with his wife, all that he had, and Lot with him.
Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold.
By stages, he went from the Negeb as far as Bethel, to the place where he had first pitched his tent, between Bethel and Ai,
to the place where he had built his first altar. And there Abram called on the name of the Lord.
Lot, who was traveling with Abram, also had sheep, oxen, and tents,
and the land could not support them dwelling together, for they had too many possessions to remain side by side.
A quarrel broke out between Abram's herdsmen and Lot's. At that time, the Canaanites and the Perizzites inhabited the land.
Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no dispute between you and me, nor between my herdsmen and yours, for we are brothers.
Is not the whole land before you? Part from me, then: if you take the left, I will go to the right; if you take the right, I will go to the left."

Lot looked up and saw the whole plain of the Jordan, well watered throughout. This was before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah; it was like the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt, in the direction of Zoar.
Lot chose for himself the whole plain of the Jordan and set out eastward. And so they parted from each other.
Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the plain and pitched his tents as far as Sodom.
Now the people of Sodom were very wicked and great sinners against the Lord.
The Lord said to Abram, after Lot had parted from him, "Look up and, from where you are, gaze to the north and the south, to the east and the west:
all the land that you see, I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
I will make your offspring as numerous as the dust of the earth: if one could count the dust of the earth, then one could also count your offspring.
Rise! Walk through the land in its length and breadth, for it is to you that I give it."
Abram moved his tents and came to settle by the oaks of Mamre, at Hebron, where he built an altar to the Lord.

titres.titre: The war of the kings; Lot taken captive

versets.t: In those days, Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goiim,
made war on Bera, king of Sodom, Birsha, king of Gomorrah, Shinab, king of Admah, Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar.
These latter joined forces in the Valley of Siddim, which is now the Salt Sea.
For twelve years they had been subject to Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they had rebelled.
In the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him set out. They defeated the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim at Ham, the Emim in the plain of Kiriathaim,
and the Horites in their mountains of Seir, as far as El-paran, on the edge of the desert.
Then, turning back, they came to En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh, and ravaged the whole country of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorites settled at Hazazon-tamar.
Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar, marched out and drew up in battle in the Valley of Siddim
against Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, Tidal, king of Goiim, Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Ellasar: four kings against five.
Now the Valley of Siddim was full of pits of pitch. In their flight, the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah fell into them, and the survivors fled to the mountains.
The victors seized all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, all their provisions, and went off.
They also carried off Lot, Abram's nephew, with his possessions, for he was living in Sodom.
A survivor came to report this to Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and Aner; these were Abram's allies.
When Abram learned that his kinsman had been carried off captive, he mustered his most seasoned men, born in his household, three hundred and eighteen in number, and pursued the kings as far as Dan.
There, in the dead of night, he divided his forces, attacked them with his servants, defeated them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus.
He brought back all the possessions, and he also brought back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, along with the women and the people.
As Abram was returning, victorious over Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him, the king of Sodom came out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King's Valley.
Then Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High,
and he blessed Abram, saying, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who made heaven and earth!
And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hands!" And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
The king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the people and keep the possessions for yourself."
But Abram answered the king of Sodom, "I raise my hand to the Lord, God Most High, who made heaven and earth:
from a thread to a sandal strap, I will take nothing that is yours! So you will not be able to say: It was I who made Abram rich.
Nothing for me, except what my men have eaten. As for my companions, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, let them take their share."
After these events, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision: "Do not be afraid, Abram: I am your shield, and your reward will be very great."
Abram answered, "Lord God, what will you give me? I am going on without a child, and the heir of my house will be Eliezer of Damascus."
And Abram added, "You have given me no offspring, and a servant of my house will be my heir."
Then the word of the Lord came to him: "No, this man will not be your heir, but a son, born of you, will be your heir."
Then he led him outside and said to him, "Look up to the sky and count the stars, if you can." And he added, "So shall your offspring be."
Abram had faith in the Lord, and the Lord counted it to him as righteousness.
Then he said to him, "I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land as a possession."
Abram answered, "Lord God, how will I know that I will possess it?"
The Lord said to him, "Take a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."
Abram brought him all these animals, split them down the middle, and set each half opposite the other; but he did not split the birds.
Birds of prey swooped down on the dead animals, and Abram drove them away.
At sunset, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and there a terror, a thick darkness, came over him.
The Lord said to Abram, "Know this well: your descendants will be immigrants in a land that is not their own; there they will be slaves and oppressed for four hundred years.
But the nation that enslaved them, I will judge; and afterward they will come out with great possessions.
As for you, you will go to your fathers in peace, and you will be buried after a happy old age.
It is in the fourth generation that they will return here, for the sin of the Amorites has not yet reached its full measure."
When the sun had set, in the thick darkness, a smoking oven and a flaming torch passed between the divided animals.
On that day, the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates:
the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites."

titres.titre: Hagar and the birth of Ishmael
The Angel of the Lord comforts Hagar

versets.t: Sarai, the wife of Abram, had given him no child. She had an Egyptian servant, named Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, "See, the Lord has kept me from having children. Go, then, to my servant: through her, perhaps, I will have a son." Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
So, after ten years of Abram's stay in the land of Canaan, Sarai, his wife, took her Egyptian servant Hagar and gave her as a wife to Abram, her husband.
He went to Hagar, and she conceived. Seeing herself pregnant, she began to look on her mistress with contempt.

Sarai said to Abram, "The wrong I suffer is your fault! It was I who put my servant in your arms, and now that she sees herself pregnant, she looks on me with contempt. May the Lord judge between you and me!"
Abram answered Sarai, "Your servant is in your power: do to her whatever seems good to you." Then Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar fled from her.
The Angel of the Lord found her near a spring, in the desert, the spring that is on the way to Shur.
He said to her, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She answered, "I am fleeing from Sarai, my mistress."
The Angel of the Lord said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."
He added, "I will make your offspring so numerous that they cannot be counted."
Then the Angel of the Lord said to her, "You are pregnant, and you will give birth to a son; you will name him Ishmael, for the Lord has heard your distress.
He will be an untamable man, like a wild donkey: his hand will be against all, and the hand of all against him; he will pitch his tent facing all his brothers."
Hagar gave a name to the Lord who had spoken to her: "You are the God who sees me." For she said, "Have I not seen here the very one who sees me?"
That is why the well was called "the well of the Living One who sees me." It lies between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore a son for Abram, and Abram named the son that Hagar had given him Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore him Ishmael.

titres.titre: The covenant and Abraham's new name
Circumcision, the sign of the covenant

versets.t: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said, "I am God Almighty. Walk in my presence and be blameless.
I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will make you exceedingly numerous."
Abram fell face down on the ground, and God spoke to him thus:
"Here is my covenant with you: you will become the father of a multitude of nations.
You will no longer be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I make you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you exceedingly fruitful, I will make nations of you, and kings will come forth from you.
I establish my covenant between me and you, and with your offspring after you, from generation to generation: an everlasting covenant, to be your God and the God of your offspring after you.
I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land where you now stay as an immigrant, all the land of Canaan, as a possession forever; and I will be their God."
God said to Abraham, "And you, you will keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you, from generation to generation.
This is the covenant that you will keep between me and you, and your offspring after you: every male among you will be circumcised.
You will circumcise your flesh, and this will be the sign of the covenant between me and you.
At the age of eight days, every male among you will be circumcised, from generation to generation: whether born in the household or bought with money from a foreigner who is not of your offspring.
Yes, he must be circumcised, the one born in your household as well as the one bought; so my covenant will be marked in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.
The uncircumcised male, the one whose flesh has not been circumcised, will be cut off from his people: he will have broken my covenant."
God said to Abraham, "Your wife Sarai, you will no longer call her Sarai: her name will be Sarah.
I will bless her, and I will even give you a son by her. I will bless her: she will become nations, and kings of peoples will come forth from her."
Abraham fell face down on the ground; he began to laugh and said to himself, "Can a son be born to a man of a hundred years? And Sarah, at ninety, is she to give birth?"
And Abraham said to God, "If only Ishmael might live before you!"
God answered, "No: it is Sarah, your wife, who will give you a son, and you will name him Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him, an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you: I bless him, I will make him fruitful and multiply him exceedingly. He will be the father of twelve princes, and I will make of him a great nation.
But my covenant, I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you next year, at this same season."
When he had finished speaking with Abraham, God went up and left him.
Then Abraham took his son Ishmael, all the servants born in his household, all those he had bought, all the males of his household, and he circumcised them that very day, as God had told him.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in his flesh,
and his son Ishmael was thirteen years old when he was circumcised.
On that same day were circumcised Abraham and his son Ishmael,
as well as all the men of his household, those born in it and those bought from foreigners: all were circumcised with him.

titres.titre: The promise of a son; Sarah's laughter

versets.t: The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he was sitting at the entrance of his tent in the hottest part of the day.
Looking up, Abraham saw three men standing near him. As soon as he saw them, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bowed to the ground.
He said, "My lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant.
Let a little water be brought, so you may wash your feet and rest under this tree.
I will fetch a morsel of bread to refresh you before you continue on your way, since you have come near your servant." They answered, "Do as you have said."
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Take about twenty litres of fine flour, knead it, and make loaves."
Then Abraham ran to the herd, took a tender, choice calf, and gave it to a servant, who hurried to prepare it.
He took curds and fresh milk, along with the calf that had been prepared, and set it all before them; he himself stood by them under the tree while they ate.
They said to him, "Where is Sarah, your wife?" He answered, "There, in the tent."
One of them said, "I will return to you at this same time next year, and Sarah, your wife, will have a son." Now Sarah was listening at the entrance of the tent, behind him.
Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in years, and Sarah was past the age of childbearing.
So Sarah laughed to herself, thinking, "Old as I am, am I to know pleasure again? And my husband too is old!"
The Lord said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh, saying, 'Am I really to bear a child, old as I am?'
Is anything impossible for the Lord? At this same time next year I will return to you, and Sarah will have a son."
Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. But he replied, "Yes, you did laugh."
The men rose and set out toward Sodom; Abraham walked with them to see them on their way.
The Lord said to himself, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?
Abraham is to become a great and mighty nation, and through him all the nations of the earth will be blessed.

For I have chosen him, so that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord by doing what is right and just; then the Lord will bring about for Abraham what he has promised him."
Then the Lord said, "The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is immense, and their sin is very grave.
I will go down and see whether they have acted altogether according to the outcry that has reached me. I want to know."
The men turned away and went toward Sodom, while Abraham still stood before the Lord.
Abraham came forward and said, "Will you really sweep away the righteous with the guilty?
Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city: will you sweep them away? Will you not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous who are in it?

Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the guilty, treating the righteous like the guilty! Far be it from you! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?"
The Lord answered, "If I find fifty righteous within the city of Sodom, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
Abraham spoke again, "I have dared to speak to my Lord, I who am but dust and ashes.
Suppose the fifty righteous lack five: will you destroy the whole city for those five?" He answered, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there."
Abraham pressed him again, "Suppose there are only forty." He answered, "For the sake of those forty, I will not do it."
Abraham said, "Do not let my Lord be angry if I speak again: suppose there are only thirty." He answered, "I will not do it if I find thirty there."
Abraham said, "I have dared to speak to my Lord: suppose there are only twenty." He answered, "For the sake of those twenty, I will not destroy it."
Abraham said, "Do not let my Lord be angry if I speak just once more: suppose there are only ten." He answered, "For the sake of those ten, I will not destroy it."
When he had finished speaking with Abraham, the Lord went away, and Abraham returned home.

titres.titre: The angels at Lot's house; the sin of Sodom
The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

versets.t: The two angels reached Sodom in the evening. Lot was sitting at the city gate. When he saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed to the ground.

He said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house; spend the night and wash your feet, and in the morning you may go on your way." They answered, "No, we will spend the night in the square."
But he pressed them so strongly that they came with him and entered his house. He prepared a meal for them, baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
Before they had lain down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, young and old, the whole population, from every quarter.
They called out to Lot and said, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, so we can have sex with them!"
Lot went out to them at the entrance, shutting the door behind him,
and said, "No, my brothers, I beg you, do not do this wicked thing!
I have two daughters who have never known a man; let me bring them out to you, and do with them as you please. But do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."

They retorted, "Get out of the way!" And they added, "This fellow came here as a foreigner, and now he plays the judge! We will treat you worse than them!" They pressed hard against Lot and moved in to break down the door.
But the two men reached out, pulled Lot inside the house with them, and shut the door.
Then they struck the men at the entrance with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they wore themselves out trying to find the door.
The two men said to Lot, "Whom else do you have here? A son-in-law, sons, daughters, all who are yours in the city: get them out of this place.
We are about to destroy this place, for the outcry against its people is immense before the Lord, and the Lord has sent us to destroy it."
So Lot went out to speak to his sons-in-law, the men who were to marry his daughters: "Get up! Leave this place, for the Lord is about to destroy the city!" But his sons-in-law thought he was joking.
At dawn the angels urged Lot on, saying, "Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away in the punishment of the city."
When he hesitated, the men took him, his wife, and his two daughters by the hand, for the Lord meant to spare him; they led him out and set him down outside the city.
Once they were outside, one of them said, "Flee for your life! Do not look back, do not stop anywhere in the plain; escape to the hills, or you will be swept away."
Lot said to them, "No, my lord, I beg you!
Your servant has found favor in your eyes, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot reach the hills; disaster would overtake me and I would die.
Look, that town is near enough to flee to, and it is so small: let me escape there. Is it not small? Then I will live."
He answered him, "I grant you this favor too: I will not destroy the town you speak of.
Hurry, escape there, for I can do nothing until you have arrived." That is why the town was named Zoar, which means the Little One.
The sun was rising over the land when Lot entered Zoar.
Then the Lord rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah; it came from the Lord, out of the heavens.
He destroyed those cities and the whole plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and everything that grew from the ground.
But Lot's wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
Early the next morning, Abraham went to the place where he had stood before the Lord.
He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and over the whole expanse of the plain, and he saw smoke rising from the land like the smoke of a furnace.
So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, he remembered Abraham, and he brought Lot safely out of the catastrophe that overthrew the cities where Lot had lived.
Lot left Zoar and settled in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to stay in Zoar. He lived in a cave, he and his two daughters.
The elder said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to be with us, as is the custom everywhere.
Come, let us make our father drink wine and lie with him, so that we may preserve his line."
That night they made their father drink wine. The elder went in and lay with him, and he was not aware of it, neither when she lay down nor when she rose.
The next day, the elder said to the younger, "Last night I lay with my father. Let us make him drink wine again tonight, and you go and lie with him, so that we may preserve his line."
That night too they made their father drink wine. The younger went and lay with him, and he was not aware of it, neither when she lay down nor when she rose.
So both of Lot's daughters became pregnant by their father.
The elder gave birth to a son and named him Moab: he is the ancestor of the Moabites, who still exist today.
The younger also had a son, and she named him Ben-Ammi: he is the ancestor of the Ammonites, who still exist today.
Abraham set out from there toward the region of the Negev and settled between Kadesh and Shur; then he stayed in Gerar.
There Abraham said of his wife Sarah, "She is my sister." So Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for Sarah and took her.
But during the night God came to Abimelech in a dream and said, "You are about to die because of the woman you have taken: she is married."
Now Abimelech had not approached her, and he answered, "Lord, would you destroy even the innocent?
Did he not tell me himself, 'She is my sister'? And she too said, 'He is my brother.' I acted with a clear conscience and clean hands."
God said to him in the dream, "I know that you acted with a clear conscience, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me; that is why I did not let you touch her.
Now give the man's wife back, for he is a prophet: he will pray for you, and you will live. But if you do not give her back, know this: you will surely die, you and all who are yours."
Abimelech rose early in the morning, summoned all his servants, and told them the whole matter; and these men were seized with great fear.

Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? How have I wronged you, that you should bring such a great sin upon me and my kingdom? You have done to me what should never be done."
And Abimelech added, "What were you thinking, to act like this?"
Abraham answered, "I thought to myself, 'Surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.'
Besides, she really is my sister: she is my father's daughter, though not my mother's, and she became my wife.
So when God made me leave my father's house to wander, I said to Sarah, 'This is the kindness you must show me: wherever we go, say of me that I am your brother.'"
Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, male and female servants, and gave them to Abraham; and he returned his wife Sarah to him.
Abimelech said, "See, my land is before you: settle wherever you please."
And to Sarah he said, "I am giving your brother about eleven kilograms of silver: this will be, in the eyes of all who are with you, the proof of your innocence; you are fully vindicated."
Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his slave women, so that they could bear children again.
For because of Sarah, Abraham's wife, the Lord had made every womb in Abimelech's household barren.

titres.titre: The covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba

versets.t: The Lord visited Sarah as he had said; he did for her what he had promised.
Sarah became pregnant and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the time God had appointed.
Abraham named the son who was born to him, the one Sarah had borne him, Isaac.
And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born.
Sarah said, "God has given me cause to laugh, and everyone who hears of it will laugh with me."
She added, "Who would ever have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."
The child grew and was weaned. On the day Isaac was weaned, Abraham held a great feast.
But Sarah saw the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham mocking,
and she said to Abraham, "Drive out this slave woman and her son, for the son of this slave woman must not share the inheritance with my son, with Isaac."
This distressed Abraham deeply, on account of his son Ishmael.
But God said to him, "Do not be troubled about the boy and your slave woman. Listen to everything Sarah asks of you, for it is through Isaac that you will have descendants who bear your name.
But I will also make a nation of the slave woman's son, for he too is your offspring."
Abraham rose early in the morning, took bread and a skin of water, put them on Hagar's shoulder, gave her the child, and sent her away. She left and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
When the water in the skin was gone, she left the child under a bush
and went and sat down apart, about a bowshot away, saying, "I cannot watch the child die." Sitting there facing him, she broke into sobs.
God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, "What is the matter, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies.
Get up! Lift the boy and take him by the hand, for I will make him a great nation."
God opened her eyes, and she saw a well. She went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy. He grew up, lived in the wilderness, and became an archer.
He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother chose a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
At that time Abimelech, together with Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham, "God is with you in everything you do.

Swear to me here, by the name of God, that you will never deal falsely with me, with my children, or with my descendants; show to me and to this land where you are staying the same kindness I have shown to you."
Abraham answered, "I swear it."
But Abraham reproached Abimelech about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized by force.
Abimelech answered, "I do not know who did this. You yourself never told me, and I hear of it only today."
Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant.
Then Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs from the flock.
Abimelech asked him, "What are these seven ewe lambs you have set apart?"
He answered, "You are to accept these seven lambs from my hand, as a witness that I am the one who dug this well."
That is why the place was called Beersheba, for it was there that the two of them swore an oath.
After they had made their covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, returned to the land of the Philistines.
Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beersheba and there called on the name of the Lord, the Eternal God.
And Abraham stayed a long time in the land of the Philistines.
After these events, God put Abraham to the test. He called to him, "Abraham!" He answered, "Here I am."
God said, "Take your son, your only son, the one you love, Isaac; go to the land of Moriah, and there offer him as a burnt offering on the mountain I will show you."
Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took with him two of his servants and his son Isaac. He split the wood for the burnt offering and set out for the place God had shown him.
On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance.
He said to his servants, "Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will come back to you."
Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac; he himself carried the fire and the knife. And the two of them went on together.
Isaac said to his father, "My father!" Abraham answered, "Here I am, my son." Isaac said, "Here are the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?"
Abraham answered, "God himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son." And the two of them went on together.
When they reached the place God had shown him, Abraham built the altar there, arranged the wood, bound his son Isaac, and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.
Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slay his son.
But the Angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, "Abraham! Abraham!" He answered, "Here I am."
The angel said, "Do not lay a hand on the boy; do nothing to him! Now I know that you fear God: you have not withheld from me your son, your only son."
Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He went and took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.
Abraham named that place "The Lord Provides," and so the saying goes today: "On the mountain the Lord provides."
From heaven the Angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time
and said, "I swear by myself, declares the Lord: because you have done this, because you have not withheld your son, your only son,
I will fill you with blessings and make your descendants as numerous as the stars of the sky and the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will conquer the cities of their enemies,
and through them all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice."
Abraham returned to his servants, and together they set out again for Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.
After these events, Abraham was told, "Milcah too has borne sons to your brother Nahor:
Uz, his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."
Bethuel became the father of Rebekah. These are the eight sons Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.
His concubine, named Reumah, also had children: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

titres.titre: The purchase of the tomb at Machpelah

versets.t: Sarah lived a hundred and twenty-seven years: such was the length of her life.
She died at Kiriath-Arba, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
Then Abraham rose from beside his dead wife and spoke to the Hittites:
"Among you I am only a foreigner, a passing guest. Grant me a burial site among you, so that I may bury my dead."
The Hittites answered Abraham:
"Listen to us, my lord: you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the finest of our tombs; none of us will refuse you his tomb for the burial of your dead."
Then Abraham rose and bowed before the people of the land, the Hittites,
and said to them, "If you are willing to let me bury my dead, listen to me: intercede for me with Ephron son of Zohar,
so that he may sell me the cave of Machpelah, which belongs to him, at the edge of his field. Let him sell it to me in your presence, at its full price, as a burial site."
Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites. He answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, before all who passed through the gate of his city:
"No, my lord, listen to me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. I give it to you in the presence of my people: bury your dead."
Abraham bowed before the people of the land
and said to Ephron in their hearing, "You, please listen to me. I will pay the price of the field: accept it from me, and I will bury my dead there."
Ephron answered Abraham:
"My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth about four and a half kilograms of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead."
Abraham agreed with Ephron, and he weighed out for him the amount he had named in the hearing of the Hittites: about four and a half kilograms of silver, according to the weight used by merchants.
So Ephron's field at Machpelah, facing Mamre, the field, the cave in it, and all the trees within its borders,
became Abraham's property, before the eyes of the Hittites and all who passed through the city gate.
After that, Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
Thus the field and the cave in it passed from the Hittites to Abraham as a burial site.

titres.titre: Abraham seeks a wife for Isaac
The servant and Rebekah at the well

versets.t: Abraham was old, well advanced in years, and the Lord had blessed him in everything.
Abraham said to the oldest servant of his household, the one who managed all he owned, "Put your hand under my thigh,
and swear to me by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I live.
You will go to my country, to my kindred, to take a wife for my son Isaac."
The servant answered him, "Perhaps the woman will not want to follow me here. Should I then take your son back to the land you came from?"
Abraham said to him, "Be careful never to take my son back there!

The Lord, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and my native land, who spoke to me and swore to give this land to my descendants, will himself send his angel ahead of you, and there you will take a wife for my son.
If the woman will not follow you, you will be released from the oath I ask of you; but never take my son back there."
So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.
Then he took ten of his master's camels and set out, taking with him all sorts of precious goods belonging to his master. He journeyed to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.
In the evening, at the time when the women go out to draw water, he had the camels kneel by a well outside the city.
And he said, "Lord, God of my master Abraham, grant me a fortunate meeting today, and show your kindness to my master Abraham.
Here I stand by the spring, and the daughters of the townsfolk are coming out to draw water.

The young woman to whom I say, 'Tip your jar so I may drink,' and who answers, 'Drink, and I will draw for your camels too,' let her be the one you have chosen for your servant Isaac. By this I will know that you have shown your kindness to my master."
He had not yet finished speaking when Rebekah came out, her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother.
The young woman was very beautiful; she was a virgin, and no man had known her. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came back up.
The servant ran to meet her and said, "Let me drink a little water from your jar."
"Drink, my lord," she answered; and quickly she lowered her jar onto her hand and gave him a drink.
When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will also draw for your camels, until they have all had enough."
She quickly emptied her jar into the trough, ran back to the well to draw more, and drew for all the camels.
The man watched her in silence, wondering whether the Lord had made his journey a success or not.
When the camels had finished drinking, he took a gold ring weighing about six grams and two gold bracelets weighing about a hundred and ten grams,
and asked, "Whose daughter are you? Tell me, please. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?"
She answered, "I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son whom Milcah bore to Nahor."
And she added, "We have plenty of straw and fodder, and room to spend the night."
Then the man bowed and worshiped before the Lord,
saying, "Blessed be the Lord, the God of my master Abraham, who has not ceased to show his kindness and faithfulness to my master. The Lord has led me straight to the house of my master's kinsmen."
The young woman ran to tell all this at her mother's house.
Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban. Laban ran out to the man at the spring.
He had seen the ring and the bracelets on his sister's wrists, and he had heard Rebekah report the man's words. So he came to him and found him standing by the camels at the spring.
He said to him, "Come, blessed of the Lord! Why do you stay outside? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels."
The man entered the house. Laban unloaded the camels, gave them straw and fodder, and brought water to wash the feet of the man and his companions.
Then food was set before him. But he said, "I will not eat until I have said what I have to say." "Speak," Laban answered.
He said, "I am Abraham's servant.
The Lord has richly blessed my master, and he has become powerful: he has given him sheep and oxen, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys.
Sarah, my master's wife, bore him a son in her old age, and my master has given him all he owns.
He made me swear this: 'You will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I live.
Instead, you will go to my father's house, to my kindred, to take a wife for my son.'
I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not want to follow me.'
He answered, 'The Lord, before whom I walk, will send his angel with you and make your journey a success; you will take for my son a wife from my kindred, from my father's house.
You will be released from my oath only if, once you have come to my kindred, they refuse to grant her to you: then you will be released from the oath I ask of you.'
So today, when I came to the spring, I said, 'Lord, God of my master Abraham, if you are willing to make the journey I am undertaking a success,
here I stand by the spring. Let the young woman who comes out to draw water, to whom I say, "Give me a little water to drink from your jar,"
and who answers me, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels too," be the woman the Lord has chosen for my master's son.'
Before I had finished speaking in my heart, Rebekah came out, her jar on her shoulder; she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, 'Give me a drink, please.'
At once she lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will give your camels water too.' I drank, and she watered the camels.
I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She answered, 'The daughter of Bethuel, the son whom Milcah bore to Nahor.' Then I put the ring in her nose and the bracelets on her wrists.
Then I bowed and worshiped before the Lord, and I blessed the Lord, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me by the right road to take the daughter of my master's kinsman for his son.
Now, if you are willing to show kindness and faithfulness to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me that too, so that I may turn to the right or to the left."
Laban and Bethuel answered, "This matter comes from the Lord; we can say nothing to you, either good or bad.
Here is Rebekah before you: take her and go, and let her become the wife of your master's son, as the Lord has said."
When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed to the ground before the Lord.
Then he brought out objects of silver and gold and garments, and gave them to Rebekah; he also gave rich gifts to her brother and her mother.
Then he and his companions ate and drank and spent the night there. In the morning, when they rose, the servant said, "Let me return to my master."
Rebekah's brother and her mother said, "Let the young woman stay with us a few days, about ten; then she will go."
He answered them, "Do not delay me, since the Lord has made my journey a success. Let me go, so that I may return to my master."
They said, "Let us call the young woman and ask what she thinks."
So they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" She answered, "I will go."
So they let their sister Rebekah go, with her nurse, along with Abraham's servant and his men.
They blessed Rebekah, saying, "O our sister, may you become the mother of countless thousands! May your descendants conquer the cities of their enemies!"
Rebekah rose with her maids; they mounted the camels and followed the man. So the servant took Rebekah and departed.
Isaac had come back from the well of the Living One who sees me, for he was living in the Negev.
One evening he had gone out into the fields to meditate; looking up, he saw camels approaching.
Rebekah in turn looked up and, when she saw Isaac, she quickly got down from her camel.
She asked the servant, "Who is that man coming through the fields to meet us?" "He is my master," he answered. Then she took her veil and covered herself.
The servant told Isaac all that he had done.
Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent of his mother Sarah; he took her as his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.

titres.titre: The birth of Jacob and Esau

versets.t: Abraham took another wife, named Keturah.
She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan; the sons of Dedan were the Asshurim, the Letushim, and the Leummim.
The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.
Abraham gave all he owned to Isaac.
As for the sons of his concubines, he gave them gifts and, while he was still alive, sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward, to the land of the East.
Abraham lived a hundred and seventy-five years in all.
Then he breathed his last: he died at a good old age, aged and full of years, and he was gathered to his people.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, facing Mamre,
the field Abraham had bought from the Hittites. There Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried.
After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac, who was living near the well of the Living One who sees me.
These are the descendants of Ishmael, the son whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's slave, had borne to Abraham.
These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, in order of their birth: Nebaioth, Ishmael's firstborn, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, according to their villages and their camps: twelve tribal chiefs.
Ishmael lived a hundred and thirty-seven years in all; then he breathed his last and died, and he was gathered to his people.
His descendants lived from Havilah to Shur, near the border of Egypt, in the direction of Assyria. So he settled facing all his kinsmen.
This is the story of Isaac, the son of Abraham. Abraham had fathered Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he took as his wife Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean and sister of Laban the Aramean, from Paddan-Aram.
Isaac pleaded with the Lord on behalf of his wife, for she was barren. The Lord answered him, and Rebekah his wife became pregnant.
But the children struggled within her, and she said, "If it is to be like this, why go on living?" So she went to consult the Lord,
and the Lord answered her, "Two nations are in your womb, two peoples will part from your very birth; one will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger."
When the time came for her to give birth, there were indeed twins in her womb.
The first came out red, all covered with hair like a coat of fur, and they named him Esau.
Then his brother came out, his hand gripping Esau's heel, and they named him Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old at their birth.
The boys grew up. Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the open country, while Jacob, a quiet man, stayed among the tents.
Isaac preferred Esau, because he had a taste for game; but Rebekah preferred Jacob.
