One day, while Jacob was cooking a stew, Esau came in from the country, worn out.
He said to Jacob, "Let me gulp down some of that red stuff, that red stew, for I am worn out." That is why he was called Edom.
Jacob answered, "Sell me your birthright first."
Esau said, "Here I am about to die; what use is my birthright to me?"
Jacob said, "Swear it to me first." So Esau swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. Esau ate and drank, then got up and went away. So Esau despised his birthright.
There was a famine in the land, different from the earlier one in the time of Abraham, and Isaac went to Gerar, to Abimelech, king of the Philistines.
The Lord appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt, but stay in the land I will show you.
Stay in this land: I will be with you and bless you, for it is to you and your descendants that I will give all these lands, and I will keep the oath I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars of the sky, I will give them all these lands, and through them all the nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my decrees, and my laws."
So Isaac settled in Gerar.
When the people of the place asked about his wife, he would answer, "She is my sister," for he was afraid to say "my wife," thinking they might kill him because of Rebekah, who was very beautiful.
As his stay in Gerar lengthened, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked out of a window one day and saw Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.
Abimelech summoned Isaac and said, "She must surely be your wife! How could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac answered him, "I thought I might die because of her."
Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of us might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."
So Abimelech gave this command to all the people: "Whoever touches this man or his wife will be put to death."
Isaac sowed seed in that land, and that year he reaped a hundredfold, for the Lord blessed him.
The man grew rich, and his wealth kept increasing until it became very great.
He had flocks and herds and a large body of servants, so that the Philistines grew jealous of him.
All the wells his father's servants had dug in the time of Abraham, the Philistines stopped up, filling them with earth.
And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you have become far more powerful than we are."
So Isaac left, pitched his camp in the valley of Gerar, and settled there.

He dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the time of his father Abraham and that the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death, and he gave them the names his father had given them.
Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of fresh, running water.
But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with those of Isaac, saying, "The water is ours!" So Isaac named the well Esek, that is, Dispute, because they had disputed with him.
His servants dug another well, which brought on another quarrel, and he named it Sitnah, that is, Hostility.
He moved on from there and dug another well, which caused no quarrel; he named it Rehoboth, that is, Broad Places, saying, "Now the Lord has given us room, and we will prosper in the land."
From there he went up to Beersheba.

The Lord appeared to him that night and said, "I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bless you and make your descendants numerous, for the sake of Abraham my servant."
Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the Lord; he pitched his tent there, and his servants dug a well.
Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
Isaac said to them, "Why do you come to me, you who hate me and drove me away from you?"
They answered, "We have clearly seen that the Lord is with you, and we thought, 'Let there be an oath between us, between you and us. We want to make a covenant with you:
swear that you will do us no harm, just as we never wronged you, but did you only good and let you go in peace. Now you are the blessed of the Lord.'"
Isaac gave them a feast, and they ate and drank.
Early the next morning, they swore an oath to each other. Then Isaac sent them off, and they left him in peace.
That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug, saying, "We have found water!"
He named it Shibah, that is, Oath. That is why the city is called Beersheba to this day.
At the age of forty, Esau took as wives Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon the Hittite.
They were a source of bitterness to Isaac and Rebekah.
Isaac had grown old, and his eyes had failed so that he could no longer see. He called Esau, his elder son, "My son!" He answered, "Here I am."
Isaac said, "See, I am old and I do not know the day of my death.
So take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, go out into the country, and hunt some game for me.
Prepare me a tasty dish, the kind I love, and bring it to me; I will eat, and I will bless you with all my soul before I die."
Now Rebekah was listening while Isaac spoke to his son Esau. When Esau set off to hunt game in the country and bring it back,
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I have just heard your father say to your brother Esau,
'Bring me some game and prepare me a tasty dish; I will eat, and I will bless you before the Lord before I die.'
Now, my son, listen to me and do what I command you.
Go to the flock, bring me two fine young goats, and I will prepare from them a tasty dish for your father, the kind he loves.
You will bring it to your father, he will eat it, and so he will bless you before he dies."
Jacob answered his mother Rebekah, "But my brother Esau is hairy, and my skin is smooth.
If my father touches me, I will seem to him an impostor, and I will bring on myself a curse instead of a blessing."
His mother said to him, "Let your curse fall on me, my son! Only listen to me: go and get me the goats."
He went to get them and brought them to his mother, who prepared a tasty dish, the kind his father loved.
Then Rebekah took the finest clothes of her elder son Esau, which she kept in the house, and put them on Jacob, her younger son.
With the skins of the young goats she covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck.
And she handed her son Jacob the tasty dish and the bread she had prepared.
Jacob went in to his father and said, "My father!" "Here I am," answered Isaac; "who are you, my son?"
Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you asked me. Please get up, sit and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me with all your soul."
Isaac said to his son, "How did you find it so quickly, my son?" Jacob answered, "Because the Lord your God brought it my way."
Isaac said to Jacob, "Come closer, my son, so I may touch you, to know whether you are really my son Esau."
Jacob went closer to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
He did not recognize him, for his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau; and he blessed him.
He asked once more, "Are you really my son Esau?" "I am," answered Jacob.
Isaac said, "Serve me, so I may eat some of my son's game and bless you with all my soul." Jacob served him, and Isaac ate; he also brought him wine, and he drank.
Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come near, my son, and kiss me."
Jacob came near and kissed him. Isaac smelled the scent of his clothes, and he blessed him, saying, "Yes, the scent of my son is like the scent of a field the Lord has blessed.
May God give you the dew of heaven and the riches of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine!

May peoples serve you, may nations bow down before you! Be master over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down before you! Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you!"
Isaac had barely finished blessing Jacob, who had just left his father, when his brother Esau came back from the hunt.
He too prepared a tasty dish, brought it to his father, and said to him, "Let my father get up and eat some of his son's game, so that you may bless me with all your soul."
His father Isaac asked him, "Who are you?" "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau," he answered.
Isaac was seized with violent trembling and said, "Who was it, then, that hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him; and he will remain blessed!"
When Esau heard his father's words, he let out a loud and bitter cry and pleaded, "Bless me too, my father!"
Isaac answered, "Your brother came by trickery and took your blessing."

Esau said, "Is he called Jacob, the one who grasps the heel, because he has now supplanted me twice? He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing!" And he added, "Have you not kept a blessing for me?"
Isaac answered Esau, "See, I have made him your master, I have given him all his brothers as servants, I have provided him with grain and wine. What can I still do for you, my son?"
Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, my father!" And Esau broke into sobs.
His father Isaac answered him, "Your dwelling will be far from the riches of the earth, far from the dew that falls from heaven above.
You will live by your sword and you will serve your brother. But when you rise up in revolt, you will break his yoke from your neck."
Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him, and he said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are near; then I will kill my brother Jacob."
Rebekah was told the words of her elder son Esau. She sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, "Your brother Esau means to take revenge on you by killing you.
Now, my son, listen to me: get up and flee to my brother Laban, at Haran.
Stay with him for a while, until your brother's fury subsides,
until his anger turns away from you and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send for you to come back. Why should I lose you both on the same day?"
Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am sick of my life because of these daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth like these, a woman of this land, what is my life worth?"
Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and gave him this command: "Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
Get up, go to Paddan-Aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and there take a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.
May God Almighty bless you, make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you become a company of peoples!
May he give you and your descendants the blessing of Abraham, so that you may possess the land where you are now a stranger, the land God gave to Abraham!"
Then Isaac sent Jacob on his way, and he went to Paddan-Aram, to Laban, son of Bethuel the Aramean and brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-Aram to take a wife there, and that in blessing him he had commanded him, "Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan."
He saw too that Jacob, obeying his father and mother, had set out for Paddan-Aram.
So Esau understood that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing to his father Isaac.
He therefore went to Ishmael and, besides the wives he already had, married Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham and sister of Nebaioth.
Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran.
He came to a certain place and spent the night there, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, made it a pillow, and lay down there.
He had a dream: there was a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven; and angels of God were going up and coming down on it.
At the top stood the Lord, who said, "I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land on which you are lying I will give to you and your descendants.

Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth; you will spread out to the west and the east, to the north and the south, and all the families of the earth will be blessed in you and in your descendants.
I am with you; I will keep you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. No, I will not abandon you until I have done what I have promised you."
Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, "Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it!"
Seized with awe, he added, "How awesome is this place! This is the house of God, this is the gate of heaven."
Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone he had used as a pillow, set it up as a standing stone, and poured oil on top of it.
He named that place Bethel, that is, House of God; the city had previously been called Luz.
Then Jacob made this vow: "If God is with me and keeps me all along the way I am traveling, if he gives me bread to eat and clothes to wear,
and if I return safely to my father's house, then the Lord will be my God.
This stone that I have set up as a standing stone will be a house of God, and of all that you give me, I will faithfully offer you a tenth."

titres.titre: Jacob meets Rachel at the well

versets.t: Jacob continued on his way and came to the land of the people of the East.
He looked, and there in the open country was a well, beside which three flocks of sheep were lying, for it was at this well that the animals were watered. A large stone covered the mouth of the well.
When all the flocks were gathered there, they would roll the stone away from the mouth of the well, water the animals, and then put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
Jacob said to the shepherds, "My brothers, where are you from?" "We are from Haran," they answered.
He asked them, "Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?" "We know him," they said.
"Is he well?" he asked. "He is well," they answered, "and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep."
He said, "It is still broad daylight; it is not time to bring the flocks in. Water the sheep, then go and let them graze."
They answered, "We cannot, until all the flocks are gathered; then the stone is rolled away from the mouth of the well, and we water the animals."
He was still speaking with them when Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.

As soon as Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban, he went up, rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well, and watered the sheep of Laban his mother's brother.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and, raising his voice, he wept.
He told Rachel that he was a relative of her father, a son of Rebekah; and she ran to tell her father.
As soon as Laban heard the news of Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Jacob told Laban all that had happened,
and Laban said to him, "Yes, you are indeed my own bone and flesh." Jacob stayed with him a full month.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "Just because you are my relative, are you to serve me for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be."
Now Laban had two daughters: the elder was named Leah, and the younger Rachel.
Leah had dull eyes, while Rachel was beautiful in form and face.
Since Jacob loved Rachel, he said, "I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter."
Laban answered, "It is better to give her to you than to another man; stay with me."
So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like a few days, so much did he love her.
Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my time is completed, and I wish to be with her."
Laban gathered all the people of the place and gave a feast.
But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, who slept with her.
Laban gave his slave Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant.
In the morning, there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, "What have you done to me? Was it not for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?"
Laban answered, "It is not the custom here to marry off the younger before the elder.
Finish this one's wedding week, and we will give you the other as well, in return for seven more years of service with me."
Jacob agreed: he finished Leah's week, and then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban gave his slave Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
Jacob also slept with Rachel, and he loved her more than Leah. He served Laban for another seven years.
The Lord saw that Leah was unloved, and he made her fruitful, while Rachel remained barren.
Leah became pregnant and gave birth to a son, whom she named Reuben, for she said, "The Lord has seen my humiliation; now my husband will love me."
She became pregnant again and had a son. She said, "The Lord has heard that I was unloved, and he has given me this one too." And she named him Simeon.
She became pregnant again and had a son. She said, "This time my husband will become attached to me, for I have given him three sons." That is why he was named Levi.
She became pregnant again and had a son. She said, "This time I will praise the Lord." That is why she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing children.

titres.titre: The rivalry of Rachel and Leah
The agreement between Jacob and Laban

versets.t: When Rachel saw that she was bearing Jacob no children, she became jealous of her sister and said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!"
Jacob grew angry with Rachel and answered, "Am I in the place of God, who has denied you children?"
She said, "Here is my slave Bilhah; sleep with her. Let her give birth on my knees, and through her I too will have children."
So she gave him her slave Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah became pregnant and bore Jacob a son.
Then Rachel said, "God has judged in my favor; he has heard my voice and given me a son." That is why she named him Dan.
Bilhah, Rachel's slave, became pregnant again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, "I have waged the struggles of God against my sister, and I have prevailed." And she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, she took her slave Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah, Leah's slave, bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, "What good fortune!" and she named him Gad.
Zilpah, Leah's slave, bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, "What happiness for me! Women will call me blessed." And she named him Asher.
At the time of the wheat harvest, Reuben went out into the fields, found some mandrakes, and brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."

Leah answered her, "Is it not enough that you have taken my husband? Do you want my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel said, "Very well, let him sleep with you tonight, in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
In the evening, as Jacob was coming in from the fields, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You are to come to me, for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So that night he slept with her.
God answered Leah: she became pregnant and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has given me my wages, because I gave my slave to my husband." And she named him Issachar.
Leah became pregnant again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
She said, "God has given me a fine gift; this time my husband will stay with me, for I have given him six sons." And she named him Zebulun.
Later she had a daughter, whom she named Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel; he answered her and made her fruitful.
She became pregnant, had a son, and said, "God has taken away my disgrace."
She named him Joseph, saying, "May the Lord add me another son!"
After Joseph was born, Jacob said to Laban, "Let me go, so that I may return to my own home, to my own country.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, and I will go; for you yourself know how well I have served you."
Laban answered him, "If I have found favor in your eyes, listen: I have seen clearly that the Lord has blessed me because of you.
Name me your wages," he added, "and I will give them to you."
Jacob said to him, "You yourself know how I have served you, and what has become of your livestock in my care.
The little you had before me has increased enormously, and the Lord has blessed you wherever I set foot. But now, when will I ever provide for my own household?"
Laban asked, "What should I give you?" Jacob answered, "You will give me nothing at all. If you grant me what I am about to say, I will go on pasturing and keeping your flock.
Today I will go through your whole flock: set aside every speckled or spotted animal, all the dark lambs, and all the spotted or speckled goats. That will be my wages.
So my honesty will testify for me in time to come: when you come to check my wages, every goat that is not speckled or spotted, and every lamb that is not dark, will count as stolen by me."
Laban said, "Good! Let it be as you have said."
That very day, Laban set aside the striped or spotted male goats, all the speckled or spotted she-goats, all that had any white on them, and all the dark lambs, and he handed them over to his sons.
Then he put a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob went on pasturing the rest of Laban's flock.
Then Jacob took fresh branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees, and peeled white strips in them, laying bare the white of the branches.
He set these peeled branches in full view of the animals, in the troughs and watering places where they came to drink; and it was there that they came into heat.
The animals mated in front of the branches, and they gave birth to young that were striped, spotted, or speckled.
Jacob set these lambs apart and turned the rest of the flock toward what was striped and dark among Laban's animals. So he built up flocks of his own, which he did not mix with Laban's.
Whenever the strong animals came into heat, Jacob would set the branches before their eyes in the troughs, so that they would mate in front of them.
But when the animals were feeble, he did not set them out: so the feeble young went to Laban, and the strong ones to Jacob.
The man grew exceedingly rich: he had large flocks, male and female servants, camels and donkeys.
Jacob heard the sons of Laban saying, "Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and it is at our father's expense that he has amassed all this wealth."
Jacob also observed Laban's face: it was no longer the same toward him as before.
Then the Lord said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers, to your homeland, and I will be with you."
Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah to come to the fields where his flock was,
and he said to them, "I see that your father's face is no longer the same toward me as before. But the God of my father has been with me.
You yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength,
and that your father has cheated me, changing my wages ten times; but God did not let him harm me.
When he said, 'The speckled ones will be your wages,' the whole flock bore speckled young; and when he said, 'The striped ones will be your wages,' the whole flock bore striped young.
So God has taken your father's livestock and given it to me.
At the time when the animals came into heat, I looked up and saw in a dream that the rams mounting the ewes were striped, speckled, or spotted.
The Angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob!' I answered, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Look up and see: all the rams mounting the ewes are striped, speckled, or spotted, for I have seen all that Laban is doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you consecrated a standing stone and made me a vow. Now get up, leave this land, and return to your homeland.'"
Rachel and Leah answered him, "Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father's house?
Has he not treated us like strangers? He sold us and has even spent our money.
All the wealth God has taken from our father is now ours and our children's. So do everything God has told you."
Jacob rose, put his children and his wives on the camels,
and drove off all his livestock and all the possessions he had gathered, the flock he had acquired in Paddan-Aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
While Laban had gone to shear his sheep, Rachel stole her father's household idols.
And Jacob outwitted Laban the Aramean, not telling him that he was fleeing.
So he fled with all that he had; he set out, crossed the Euphrates, and headed for the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day, Laban was told that Jacob had fled.
He took his kinsmen with him, pursued Jacob for seven days' journey, and caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
But during the night, God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream and said to him, "Take care not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad."
So Laban overtook Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban pitched his, with his kinsmen, on that same hill country of Gilead.
Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You have deceived me and carried off my daughters like prisoners of war!
Why did you flee in secret and deceive me, without telling me anything? I would have sent you off with joy, with songs, to the sound of the tambourine and the harp.
You did not even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters! You have acted foolishly.
I have it in my power to do you harm, but the God of your father spoke to me last night: 'Take care not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.'
Now, you have gone because you longed for your father's house; but why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "I was afraid; I thought you would take your daughters from me by force.

But as for the one with whom you find your gods, let him not live! In the presence of our kinsmen, examine what belongs to you here with me, and take it back." Now Jacob did not know that it was Rachel who had stolen them.
Laban went into Jacob's tent, into Leah's, and into that of the two slave women, without finding anything. Coming out of Leah's tent, he went into Rachel's.
Now Rachel had taken the idols, hidden them in the camel's saddle, and sat on them. Laban searched the whole tent without finding anything.
Rachel said to her father, "Let my lord not be angry that I cannot rise before you: I am having what regularly happens to women." He searched, but did not find the idols.
Then Jacob grew angry and reproached Laban. He said to him, "What is my crime, what is my sin, that you should pursue me so relentlessly?
You have searched through all my belongings: what have you found that belongs to you? Set it here before my kinsmen and yours, and let them judge between the two of us!
For twenty years now I have been with you. Your ewes and your goats have never miscarried, and I have never eaten the rams of your flock.
The animals torn by wild beasts I did not bring back to you: I bore the loss myself, for you demanded payment from me, whether they were stolen by day or by night.
By day I was worn down by the heat, and by night by the cold, and sleep fled from my eyes.
For twenty years now I have been in your household: I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your livestock, and you have changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, you would have sent me away empty-handed. But God has seen my misery and the toil of my hands, and last night he gave his verdict."

Laban answered Jacob, "These daughters are my daughters, these children are my children, these flocks are my flocks: everything you see is mine. But what can I do today for my daughters and for the children they have borne?
Come, then, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between us."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a standing stone.
Then he said to his kinsmen, "Gather stones." They took stones, made a heap of them, and ate there on the heap.
Laban named it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob named it Galeed, two names that both mean the Heap of Witness.
Laban declared, "This heap is a witness today between you and me." That is why it was called Galeed,
and also Mizpah, that is, the Watchpost, for Laban said, "May the Lord keep watch between us both when we are out of each other's sight.
If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives besides them, remember that, even if no one else is there, God is a witness between you and me."
Laban said further to Jacob, "See this heap, and see this standing stone that I have set up between you and me.
This heap is a witness, and this standing stone is a witness, that I will not go past this heap to you, and that you will not go past this heap or this standing stone to me with evil intent.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their fathers, judge between us!" And Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Then Jacob offered a sacrifice on the hill and invited his kinsmen to the meal. They ate and spent the night on the hill.

titres.titre: Laban's departure; the angels of God
The struggle at the ford of the Jabbok

versets.t: Early the next morning, Laban rose, kissed his grandchildren and his daughters, and blessed them; then he departed and returned home.
Jacob went on his way, and angels of God met him.
When he saw them, he said, "This is God's camp!" And he named that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau, in the land of Seir, in the country of Edom.
He gave them this order: "You will say this to my lord Esau: This is what your servant Jacob says. I have been staying with Laban, where I have remained until now.
I have oxen, donkeys, sheep, male and female servants; and I send word of this to my lord, in the hope of finding favor in your eyes."
The messengers came back to Jacob and said, "We went to your brother Esau: he is coming to meet you, with four hundred men."
Jacob was terrified and seized with anguish. He divided the people who were with him, along with the sheep, the oxen, and the camels, into two camps.
He thought, "If Esau attacks one camp and destroys it, the camp that is left may escape."
Then Jacob said, "God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, Lord, you who told me, 'Return to your country, to your kindred, and I will do you good'!
I am too small for all the kindnesses and all the faithfulness you have shown to your servant: I had only my staff when I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.
Deliver me, I beg you, from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid he may come and strike me down, mothers and children alike.
You yourself said, 'I will do you good and make your descendants as numerous as the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted, there is so much of it.'"
Jacob spent the night in that place. Then he took, from what he had, a gift to offer his brother Esau:
two hundred she-goats and twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He entrusted them to his servants, each herd separately, and said to them, "Go on ahead of me, leaving a space between each herd."
He gave this order to the first: "When my brother Esau meets you and asks, 'Whose servant are you? Where are you going? To whom does this herd ahead of you belong?'
you will answer, 'They belong to your servant Jacob; it is a gift he is sending to my lord Esau, and he himself is coming behind us.'"
He gave the same order to the second, to the third, and to all who followed the herds: "This is what you will say to Esau when you meet him.

You will add, 'Your servant Jacob is coming behind us himself.'" For he thought, "I will appease him with this gift that goes ahead of me; then I will see his face: perhaps he will receive me kindly."
The gift went on ahead of him, while he himself spent the night in the camp.
That night he got up, took his two wives, his two slave women, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, and he sent across all that he had.
Jacob was left alone. And a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When he saw that he could not overcome him, the man struck Jacob at the socket of his hip, and Jacob's hip was dislocated as he wrestled with him.
The man said, "Let me go, for dawn is breaking." Jacob answered, "I will not let you go until you bless me."
The man asked him, "What is your name?" He answered, "Jacob."
The man said, "You will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed."
Jacob asked him, "Tell me your name, I beg you." He answered, "Why do you ask my name?" And he blessed him there.
Jacob named that place Peniel, for, he said, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared."
The sun was rising as he passed Peniel; he was limping because of his hip.
That is why, to this day, the children of Israel do not eat the great tendon attached to the socket of the hip: for it was there that God had touched Jacob's hip, at the great tendon.
Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming, with four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two slave women.
He placed the slave women with their children in front, behind them Leah with her children, and last of all Rachel with Joseph.
He himself went ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times, until he was close to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.
Then, looking up, Esau saw the women and children and asked, "Who are these with you?" Jacob answered, "They are the children God has graciously given your servant."
The slave women came forward with their children and bowed down.
Leah too came forward with her children, and they bowed down. Last of all, Joseph and Rachel came forward and bowed down.
Esau asked, "What did you mean by all that camp I met?" Jacob answered, "It was to find favor in the eyes of my lord."
Esau said, "I have all I need, my brother; keep what is yours."
But Jacob answered, "No, please! If I have found favor in your eyes, accept this gift from my hand; for I have seen your face as one sees the face of God, and you have received me kindly.
Please accept the gift that has been brought to you, for God has been generous to me and I lack nothing." He pressed him so hard that Esau accepted.
Esau said, "Let us set out and be on our way; I will go ahead of you."
Jacob answered, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that I have with me nursing ewes and cows; if they are driven hard for even a single day, the whole flock will die.
Let my lord go on ahead of his servant; I will follow slowly, at the pace of the herd before me and at the pace of the children, until I reach my lord at Seir."
Esau said, "Let me at least leave some of my men with you." Jacob answered, "Why do that? Only let me find favor in the eyes of my lord."
That day Esau set out again on the road to Seir,
while Jacob set out for Succoth. There he built himself a house and made shelters for his livestock; that is why the place was called Succoth.
On his return from Paddan-Aram, Jacob arrived safely at the city of Shechem, in the land of Canaan, and he camped in front of the city.
He bought from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred pieces of silver, the plot of ground where he had pitched his tent.
There he set up an altar, which he named "God, the God of Israel."

titres.titre: The revenge of Simeon and Levi

versets.t: Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to see the women of the land.
Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the land, saw her, seized her, and lay with her, violating her.
Then he became attached with all his soul to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob; he loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, "Get me this young woman for a wife."
Jacob learned that Shechem had dishonored his daughter Dinah; but since his sons were in the fields with the livestock, he kept silent until they returned.
Hamor, the father of Shechem, went out to Jacob to speak with him.

Jacob's sons, coming in from the fields, heard the news. These men were outraged and seized with fierce anger, for Shechem had committed an outrage against Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter: such a thing should never be done.
Hamor spoke to them, saying, "My son Shechem has set his heart on your daughter; please give her to him as a wife.
Join with us by marriage: give us your daughters and take ours.
You will live among us, and the land will be open to you; you may live in it, trade in it, and acquire property in it."
Shechem said to Dinah's father and brothers, "Let me find favor in your eyes, and I will give whatever you ask of me.
Set the bride-price as high as you wish, along with rich gifts: I will give whatever you tell me, only give me the young woman as a wife."
Jacob's sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor with cunning, because Shechem had dishonored their sister Dinah.
They said to them, "We cannot do this: to give our sister to an uncircumcised man would be a disgrace to us.
We will agree only on one condition: that you become like us, by circumcising every male among you.
Then we will give you our daughters and take yours; we will live among you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our sister and go."
Their words pleased Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man did not delay in acting, for he desired Jacob's daughter; and he was the most respected of his whole father's house.
Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and spoke to their fellow citizens:
"These people are well disposed toward us. Let them settle in the land and trade in it: the land is surely large enough for them. We will take their daughters as wives and give them ours.
But these men will consent to live with us and become one people only on one condition: that every male among us be circumcised, as they themselves are.
Will not their flocks, their goods, and all their livestock become ours? Let us only agree to their request, and they will settle among us."
All who passed through the gate of the city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who passed through the gate of the city.
On the third day, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his sword, entered the city unopposed, and killed every male.
They also put Hamor and his son Shechem to the sword, took Dinah from Shechem's house, and left.
The other sons of Jacob fell upon the slain and plundered the city, because their sister had been dishonored.
They took the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, everything that was in the city and in the fields.
They carried off as plunder all their wealth, all their children and their wives, and everything that was in the houses.

Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me, making me hateful to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I have only a few men; if they band together against me and attack me, I will be destroyed, I and my household."
They answered, "Should our sister have been treated like a prostitute?"

titres.titre: The death of Rachel; the twelve sons of Jacob

versets.t: God said to Jacob, "Arise! Go up to Bethel and settle there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau."
Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Get rid of the foreign gods among you, purify yourselves, and change your clothes.
We are going to set out and go up to Bethel; there I will build an altar to the God who answered me in the day of my distress and who has been with me all along the way I have gone."
They handed over to Jacob all the foreign gods they had, and the rings that were in their ears; and Jacob buried them under the terebinth near Shechem.
Then they set out. The terror of God fell upon the surrounding towns, and no one pursued the sons of Jacob.
Jacob came, with all who were with him, to Luz, that is, Bethel, in the land of Canaan.
There he built an altar and named the place El-Bethel, because it was there that God had revealed himself to him when he was fleeing from his brother.
It was then that Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died; she was buried below Bethel, at the foot of the oak, which was called the Oak of Weeping.
God appeared again to Jacob, on his return from Paddan-Aram, and blessed him.
God said to him, "Your name is Jacob; but you will no longer be called Jacob: your name will be Israel." So he named him Israel.
God said to him, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply: a nation, an assembly of nations will come from you, and kings will spring from you.
The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I give to you; and after you, I will give it to your descendants."
Then God went up from him, at the place where he had spoken with him.
At that very place where God had spoken with him, Jacob set up a stone pillar, poured out on it a drink offering of wine, and poured oil over it.
And Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They set out from Bethel. There was still some distance to go before reaching Ephrath, when Rachel went into labor; her delivery was hard.
As she suffered greatly, the midwife said to her, "Do not be afraid: you have another son."
As she breathed her last, for she was dying, she named the child Ben-oni, "son of my sorrow"; but his father called him Benjamin, "son of the right hand."
Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave; it is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which still stands today.
Israel set out again and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine; and Israel heard of it. The sons of Jacob were twelve.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan-Aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived.
Isaac lived a hundred and eighty years.
Then he breathed his last and died: he was gathered to his people, old and full of years. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

titres.titre: The wives and sons of Esau
The sons of Seir the Horite

versets.t: This is the descent of Esau, that is, Edom.
Esau took his wives from among the daughters of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite;
and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore Esau a son, Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel;
and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau, who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, all the members of his household, his flocks, all his livestock, and all the possessions he had acquired in the land of Canaan, and he went to another land, away from his brother Jacob.
For their possessions were too great for them to live together, and the land where they were staying could not support their flocks.
So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
This is the descent of Esau, father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, son of Adah, Esau's wife; Reuel, son of Basemath, Esau's wife.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna, concubine of Eliphaz son of Esau, bore him Amalek. These are the descendants of Adah, Esau's wife.
These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the descendants of Basemath, Esau's wife.
These are the sons of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
These are the clan chiefs descended from Esau's sons. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz,
Korah, Gatam, and Amalek. These are the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom; they are the descendants of Adah.
The sons of Reuel son of Esau: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom; they are the descendants of Basemath, Esau's wife.
The sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the chiefs descended from Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and Esau's wife.
These are the sons of Esau and these are their chiefs. That is Edom.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; Timna was Lotan's sister.
These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who discovered the hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah, Anah's daughter.
These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, according to their clans, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the sons of Israel.
Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom; the name of his city was Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah, reigned in his place.
When Jobab died, Husham, from the land of the Temanites, reigned in his place.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad reigned in his place; it was he who defeated Midian in the country of Moab. The name of his city was Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah, from Masrekah, reigned in his place.
When Samlah died, Shaul, from Rehoboth on the River, reigned in his place.
When Shaul died, Baal-Hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.
When Baal-Hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar reigned in his place; the name of his city was Pau, and the name of his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of the chiefs descended from Esau, according to their clans, their territories, and their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
Magdiel, and Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, according to their settlements in the land they possessed. That is Esau, the father of Edom.

titres.titre: Joseph and his brothers; the dreams

versets.t: Jacob settled in the land of Canaan, where his father had lived.

This is the history of Jacob's family. Joseph, seventeen years old, was tending the sheep with his brothers. Since he was still young, he stayed with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives; and Joseph brought their father the bad reports that were circulating about them.
Israel loved Joseph more than all his other sons, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a long tunic of many colors.
His brothers, seeing that their father loved him more than all of them, began to hate him and could no longer speak to him on friendly terms.
Now Joseph had a dream, and he told it to his brothers, who hated him all the more.
He said to them, "Listen to the dream I had.
We were binding sheaves out in the fields, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down before it."
His brothers said to him, "Are you going to reign over us, then? Are you going to rule over us?" And they hated him all the more, because of his dreams and his words.
He had yet another dream, which he told to his brothers: "I have had another dream: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down before me."
He told it to his father and his brothers. His father rebuked him, "What is this dream you have had? Are we really to come, I, your mother, and your brothers, and bow to the ground before you?"
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in his heart.
Joseph's brothers went to pasture their father's flocks at Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, "Are your brothers not tending the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." Joseph answered, "Here I am."
Israel said to him, "Go and see whether all is well with your brothers and with the flock, then bring me back word." So he sent him from the valley of Hebron, and Joseph came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the countryside and asked him, "What are you looking for?"
Joseph answered, "I am looking for my brothers; please tell me where they are pasturing the flock."
The man said, "They have moved on from here; I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
They saw him from a distance, and before he reached them, they plotted to kill him.
They said to one another, "Here comes the dreamer.
Come now, let us kill him and throw him into a cistern; we will say that a wild beast devoured him. Then we will see what becomes of his dreams!"
Reuben heard this and tried to save him from their hands. He said, "Let us not take his life."
Reuben added, "Do not shed blood! Throw him into this cistern in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him." He said this in order to rescue him from their hands and bring him back to his father.
As soon as Joseph reached his brothers, they stripped him of his tunic, the long tunic of many colors that he was wearing,
and they seized him and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty, without water.
Then they sat down to eat. Looking up, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead; their camels were loaded with spices, balm, and fragrant resin, which they were carrying down to Egypt.
Then Judah said to his brothers, "What will we gain by killing our brother and covering up his blood?
Let us rather sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not lay a hand on him: after all, he is our brother, our own flesh." His brothers listened to him.
When the Midianite traders passed by, they pulled Joseph up out of the cistern and sold him for twenty pieces of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.
When Reuben came back to the cistern, Joseph was no longer there. He tore his clothes,
returned to his brothers, and said, "The boy is gone! And I, where can I go now?"
Then they took Joseph's tunic, slaughtered a goat, and dipped the tunic in the blood.
They had the long tunic carried to their father with this message: "This is what we found. Look closely: is it your son's tunic or not?"
Jacob recognized it and cried out, "It is my son's tunic! A wild beast has devoured him! Joseph has been torn to pieces!"
Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned his son for many days.
All his sons and daughters came to comfort him, but he refused all comfort. He said, "No, I will go down to my son in mourning, to the realm of the dead." And he kept weeping for him.
As for the Midianites, they sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.

titres.titre: The birth of Perez and Zerah

versets.t: About that time, Judah left his brothers and went down to stay with a man of Adullam named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua; he took her as his wife and slept with her.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son, whom he named Er.
She conceived again and had a son, whom she named Onan.
She had yet another son, whom she named Shelah; Judah was at Chezib when she gave birth to him.
Judah chose for Er, his firstborn, a wife named Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was displeasing to the Lord, and the Lord put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, "Go to your brother's wife, do your duty as a brother-in-law toward her, and so raise up offspring for your brother."
But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his; so whenever he slept with his brother's wife, he let his seed spill on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.
What he did was displeasing to the Lord, who put him to death as well.

Then Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow in your father's house, until my son Shelah has grown up." For he thought, "He must not die too, like his brothers." So Tamar went to live in her father's house.
Many days passed, and Shua's daughter, Judah's wife, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he went up to Timnah, to those who were shearing his sheep, with his friend Hirah of Adullam.
Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep."

Then she took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil to make herself unrecognizable, and sat down at the entrance to Enaim, on the road to Timnah. For she saw clearly that Shelah had grown up and that she had not been given to him as his wife.
When Judah saw her, he took her for a prostitute, because she had her face covered.
He turned toward her at the side of the road and said, "Let me come to you." He did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She asked, "What will you give me to come to me?"
He answered, "I will send you a young goat from my flock." She said, "Only if you leave me a pledge until you send it."
He asked, "What pledge should I give you?" She answered, "Your seal, its cord, and the staff in your hand." He gave them to her, slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
Then she got up and left; she took off her veil and put her widow's clothes back on.
Judah sent the young goat by his friend from Adullam, to recover the pledge from the woman's hands; but he could not find her.
He asked the people of the place, "Where is the prostitute who was at Enaim, by the roadside?" They answered, "There has never been a prostitute here."
He went back to Judah and said, "I could not find her, and even the people of the place told me there had never been a prostitute there."
Judah said, "Let her keep the pledge, then! Let us not make ourselves a laughingstock. After all, I did send this young goat, and you could not find her."

About three months later, Judah was told, "Your daughter-in-law Tamar has prostituted herself, and now she is even pregnant from her immorality." Judah ordered, "Bring her out, and let her be burned!"
As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, "I am pregnant by the man to whom these things belong. See if you recognize whose seal, cord, and staff these are."
Judah recognized them and declared, "She is more righteous than I, for I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he had no further relations with her.
When the time came for her to give birth, it turned out that she was carrying twins.
As she was giving birth, one of them put out a hand; the midwife took it and tied a scarlet thread on it, saying, "This one came out first."
But he drew back his hand, and it was his brother who came out. The midwife exclaimed, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" So he was named Perez.
Then his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand; and he was named Zerah.

titres.titre: Potiphar's wife and the false accusation

versets.t: Joseph was taken down to Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him there.
The Lord was with Joseph, and everything he did prospered; he lived in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the Lord was with him and made everything he undertook succeed in his hands.
Joseph found favor in his master's eyes and entered his service; his master put him in charge of his household and entrusted to him everything he owned.

From the moment he put him in charge of his household and all his possessions, the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house because of Joseph; the Lord's blessing rested on all that he owned, in the house and in the fields.
So he left everything he had in Joseph's hands and no longer concerned himself with anything except the food he ate. Now Joseph was well built and handsome.
After some time, his master's wife looked at Joseph and said, "Sleep with me."
He refused and said to his master's wife, "Look: my master no longer concerns himself with anything in the house and has entrusted to me all that he owns.
He himself is no greater than I am in this house; he has forbidden me nothing except you, because you are his wife. How could I commit such a great evil and sin against God?"
Although she spoke to Joseph about it every day, he refused to sleep with her or to be with her.
Now, one day when he had gone into the house to do his work, with none of the household present,
she caught hold of him by his garment and said, "Sleep with me." But he left his garment in her hands and fled outside.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hands and had fled outside,
she called the people of her household and said to them, "Look! A Hebrew has been brought to us to make sport of us. He came to me to sleep with me, but I screamed loudly.
When he heard me raise my voice and cry out, he left his garment beside me and fled outside."
She kept Joseph's garment beside her until his master came home,
and she told him the same story: "The Hebrew servant you brought us came to me to make sport of me.
But when I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled outside."
When his master heard his wife say, "This is how your servant treated me," he became very angry.
He had Joseph seized and thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners were held. And Joseph remained there, in prison.
But the Lord was with Joseph: he extended his kindness to him and made him find favor in the eyes of the chief jailer.
The chief jailer put all the prisoners in the prison in Joseph's charge, and nothing was done there without him.
The jailer no longer concerned himself with anything that was in Joseph's charge, for the Lord was with him and made everything he undertook succeed.

titres.titre: The dreams of the cupbearer and the baker

versets.t: Some time later, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt offended their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker,
and he had them confined in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was held.
The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of them, and Joseph waited on them. They remained in custody for some time.
One night, both the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, held in the prison, each had a dream, each with its own meaning.
In the morning, when Joseph came to see them, he found them troubled.
So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were confined with him in his master's house, "Why do you look so downcast this morning?"
They answered, "We have had a dream, and there is no one to explain it." Joseph said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams, then."
The chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream: "In my dream, there was a vine before me,
with three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms opened, and its clusters produced ripe grapes.
I had Pharaoh's cup in my hand; I took the grapes, pressed their juice into the cup, and put it in Pharaoh's hand."
Joseph said to him, "This is what it means: the three branches are three days.
Within three days, Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office: you will put the cup in Pharaoh's hand, as you used to do when you were his cupbearer.
But remember me when all goes well for you, and do me the kindness of speaking about me to Pharaoh, to get me out of this house.
For I was carried off by force from the land of the Hebrews, and here too I have done nothing for which they should throw me into this pit."
Seeing that Joseph had given a favorable interpretation, the chief baker said to him, "I too, in my dream, was carrying three baskets of white bread on my head.
In the top basket there were all kinds of pastries for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head."
Joseph answered, "This is what it means: the three baskets are three days.
Within three days, Pharaoh will lift off your head, he will hang you on a tree, and the birds will devour your flesh."
Now, on the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, he gave a feast for all his servants, and he brought out the chief cupbearer and the chief baker before them.
He restored the chief cupbearer to his office, and he put the cup in Pharaoh's hand;
but he had the chief baker hanged, just as Joseph had foretold in his interpretation.
Yet the chief cupbearer did not think of Joseph again: he forgot him.

titres.titre: Joseph raised to rule over Egypt
The years of plenty; Joseph's sons

versets.t: Two years later, Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing by the Nile,
when seven fine, fat cows came up out of the river and began grazing among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up out of the Nile, ugly and gaunt, and stood beside the first ones on the bank of the river.
Then the ugly, gaunt cows devoured the seven fine, fat cows. At that Pharaoh woke up.
He fell asleep again and had a second dream: seven ears of grain, plump and good, were growing on a single stalk.
Then seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, sprouted up after them.
And the thin ears swallowed the seven plump and full ears. Pharaoh woke up: it was a dream.
In the morning, his mind troubled, he sent for all the magicians and all the wise men of Egypt and told them his dreams; but no one could explain them to him.
Then the chief cupbearer spoke up and said to Pharaoh, "Today I must acknowledge my faults.
Once, Pharaoh was angry with his servants and had me confined in the house of the captain of the guard, me and the chief baker.
One night, we each had a dream, each with its own meaning.
There was with us a young Hebrew, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he interpreted them for us, each according to his own.
And it all happened just as he had foretold: I was restored to my office, and the other was hanged."
Then Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and he was hurriedly brought out of the prison. He shaved, changed his clothes, and presented himself before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have had a dream, and no one can explain it. But I have heard it said of you that you need only hear a dream to interpret it."
Joseph answered Pharaoh, "It is not I: it is God who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream, I was standing on the bank of the Nile,
when seven fat, fine cows came up out of the river and began grazing among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up, scrawny, very ugly and gaunt; I have never seen any so ugly in all the land of Egypt.
These thin, ugly cows devoured the first seven, the fat ones;
they swallowed them, but no one could tell: they looked just as ugly as before. Then I woke up.
I saw again in my dream seven full and fine ears growing on a single stalk,
then seven dry ears, thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouting after them.
And the thin ears swallowed the seven fine ears. I told this to the magicians, but none could explain it to me."
Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's two dreams are one and the same: God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven fine cows are seven years, and the seven fine ears are seven years: it is one and the same dream.
The seven thin, ugly cows that came up afterward are seven years, and the seven empty ears, scorched by the east wind, will be seven years of famine.
This is what I meant when I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
Behold: seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the land of Egypt.
Then will come seven years of famine, which will make all this abundance in Egypt be forgotten; the famine will exhaust the land.
The abundance will no longer be remembered, so terrible will the famine be that follows.
And the fact that the dream was repeated twice to Pharaoh means that the matter has been firmly decided by God, and that he will soon carry it out.
Let Pharaoh therefore choose an intelligent and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh also appoint overseers throughout the land, to take a fifth of Egypt's harvests during the seven years of plenty.
Let them gather all the produce of these good years to come, let them store up the grain at Pharaoh's disposal as a reserve in the cities, and let them keep it.
These provisions will serve as a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine that will strike Egypt; thus the land will not be destroyed by the famine."
This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find a man like this, in whom the spirit of God dwells?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, no one is as intelligent and wise as you.
You shall govern my house, and all my people will submit to your orders; only by the throne will I be greater than you."
Pharaoh said further to Joseph, "See: I set you over all the land of Egypt."
Pharaoh took his ring off his own hand and put it on Joseph's; he clothed him in garments of fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck.
He had him ride in the second of his chariots, and men cried out before him, "Kneel!" So he set him over all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, but without your order no one will lift a hand or a foot in all the land of Egypt."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah and gave him as wife Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. And Joseph traveled throughout the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he presented himself before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Having left Pharaoh, he traveled throughout the whole land of Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty, the land produced abundantly.
Joseph gathered all the food of these seven good years in Egypt and stored it in the cities: in each city he put the harvest of the surrounding fields.
He amassed grain as abundant as the sand of the sea, in such quantity that they stopped counting, for it was beyond all measure.
Before the years of famine came, Joseph had two sons, whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore him.
Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, "for," he said, "God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's household."
He named the second Ephraim, "for," he said, "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."
The seven years of plenty that Egypt had known came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began, as Joseph had foretold. There was famine in all the lands, but throughout Egypt there was bread.
Then all the land of Egypt was famished in turn, and the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph, do whatever he tells you."
The famine spread over the whole land. Then Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians; but the famine grew worse in Egypt.
From every land, people came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, for the famine had grown severe over all the earth.

titres.titre: Joseph's brothers go down to Egypt

versets.t: Seeing that there was grain in Egypt, Jacob said to his sons, "Why do you keep looking at one another?
I have heard," he added, "that there is grain in Egypt. Go down and buy some for us there, so that we may stay alive and not die."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, with the others, for he thought, "Something might happen to him."
So the sons of Israel came to buy grain, among others who were also coming, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.
Joseph was the ruler of the land, and it was he who sold grain to everyone. His brothers, on arriving, bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.
As soon as he saw them, Joseph recognized his brothers, but he pretended to be a stranger and spoke harshly to them, "Where do you come from?" They answered, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food."
Joseph had recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Then Joseph remembered the dreams he had had about them, and he said to them, "You are spies! You have come to find out the weak points of the land."
They answered him, "No, my lord! Your servants have come to buy food.
We are all sons of one man; we are honest men, your servants are not spies."
He insisted, "No! You have come to find out the weak points of the land."
They answered, "Your servants were twelve brothers, sons of one man, in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more."
Joseph said to them, "It is just as I said: you are spies.
This is how you will be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you will not leave here unless your youngest brother comes!

Send one of you to fetch your brother; the rest of you will stay as prisoners. Thus your words will be tested, to see whether you are telling the truth. Otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies!"
And he had them all put in prison for three days.
On the third day, Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one of you, your brother, stay confined in your prison; the rest of you, go, take grain for your starving families,
then bring your youngest brother to me. Thus your words will be confirmed and you will not die." They agreed.
And they said to one another, "Truly, we are paying for our brother! We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen; that is why this trouble has come upon us."
Reuben said to them, "Did I not tell you, 'Do not harm the boy'? But you would not listen, and now his blood is being demanded of us."
They did not know that Joseph understood them, for he was speaking to them through an interpreter.
Joseph turned away from them to weep. Then he came back, spoke to them, and took Simeon from among them, whom he had bound before their eyes.
Joseph gave orders to fill their sacks with grain, to put each man's money back in his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. So it was done.
They loaded the grain on their donkeys and set out.
At the place where they spent the night, one of them opened his sack to give fodder to his donkey, and he saw his money, there at the mouth of the sack.
He said to his brothers, "My money has been returned! Here it is in my sack!" Their hearts failed them, and trembling they said to one another, "What is this that God has done to us?"
When they reached their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they told him all that had happened to them:
"The man who is master of the land spoke harshly to us and took us for spies.
We told him, 'We are honest men, we are not spies.
We are twelve brothers, sons of one father. One is no more, and the youngest is with our father in the land of Canaan.'
Then the man, the master of the land, said to us, 'This is how I will know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, take enough to feed your starving families, and go.
Then bring me your youngest brother: so I will know that you are not spies but honest men. Then I will give you back your brother, and you may move about freely in the land.'"
As they were emptying their sacks, each man found his pouch of money in his own. When they saw the pouches of money, they and their father were seized with fear.
Jacob, their father, said to them, "You are robbing me of my children! Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and now you want to take Benjamin! It all falls on me."
Reuben said to his father, "You may put my two sons to death if I do not bring Benjamin back to you. Entrust him to me, and I will return him to you."

But Jacob answered, "My son will not go down with you! His brother is dead, and he alone is left. If harm should come to him on the journey, you would bring down my gray hairs in sorrow to the realm of the dead."
The famine weighed more and more heavily on the land.
When they had finished eating the grain brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go back and buy us a little food."
Judah answered him, "The man solemnly warned us, 'You will not be admitted into my presence unless your brother is with you.'
If you let our brother come with us, we will go down and buy you food.
But if you do not let him come, we will not go down; for the man told us, 'You will not be admitted into my presence unless your brother is with you.'"
Israel said, "Why did you do me this wrong, by telling the man that you had another brother?"

They answered, "The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family: 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' And we answered his questions. How could we have guessed that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"
Then Judah said to his father Israel, "Let the boy go with me. Let us get up and set out; then we will live instead of dying, we, you, and our little ones.
I will be his guarantor: you may hold me responsible for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, I will be guilty before you forever.
If we had not delayed so long, we would already have been back twice."

Their father Israel said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: take in your baggage the best products of the land and bring them to the man as a gift: a little balm and a little honey, gum, fragrant resin, pistachios, and almonds.
Take twice as much money with you, and bring back the money that was put back at the mouths of your sacks: perhaps it was a mistake.
Take your brother, get up, and go back to the man.
May God Almighty grant you mercy before him, so that he will let your other brother come back with you, along with Benjamin. As for me, if I must lose my children, then let me lose them!"
The men took the gift, twice as much money, and Benjamin; they set out, went down to Egypt, and presented themselves before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to his steward, "Bring these men into my house, slaughter an animal, and prepare a meal, for they will eat with me at noon."
The steward did as Joseph had ordered and led them to Joseph's house.

When they saw that they were being taken to Joseph's house, the men were afraid and said, "It is because of the money put back in our sacks the last time that we are being brought here! They are going to fall upon us, make us slaves, and take our donkeys."
They approached Joseph's steward and spoke to him at the entrance of the house:
"Please, my lord! We came down once before to buy food.
But at the place where we spent the night, when we opened our sacks, we found each man's money at the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight. We have brought it back with us,
and we have brought additional money to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks."
He answered them, "Peace be with you, do not be afraid! It is your God, the God of your father, who put a treasure in your sacks; your money reached me safely." And he brought Simeon out to them.
The steward brought them into Joseph's house, gave them water to wash their feet, and gave fodder to their donkeys.
They prepared their gift, awaiting Joseph's arrival at noon, for they had been told they would eat there.
When Joseph came home, they presented him with the gift they had brought and bowed down before him to the ground.
He asked how they were, then said, "Is your old father, of whom you spoke to me, well? Is he still alive?"
They answered, "Your servant, our father, is well; he is still alive." And they bowed low in homage.
Looking up, Joseph saw Benjamin, his brother, the son of his own mother, and he asked, "Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me?" Then he added, "May God be gracious to you, my son!"
Overcome at the sight of his brother, Joseph, his throat tight, quickly sought a place to weep; he went into his room and wept there.
Then he washed his face and came out again; controlling himself, he ordered, "Serve the meal."
He was served apart, his brothers apart, and apart too the Egyptians who ate with him, for the Egyptians cannot share a meal with the Hebrews: it is loathsome to them.
The brothers were seated facing him, from the eldest to the youngest, each according to his rank, and they looked at one another in astonishment.
Joseph had portions carried to them from his own table, and Benjamin's portion was five times larger than the others'. They drank and made merry with him.

titres.titre: The cup hidden in Benjamin's sack

versets.t: Joseph gave this order to his steward, "Fill the men's sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man's money at the mouth of his sack.
You shall also place my cup, the silver cup, at the mouth of the youngest one's sack, along with the money for his grain." The steward did as Joseph had ordered.
At dawn, as soon as it was light, the men were sent off with their donkeys.
They had just left the city, not yet far off, when Joseph said to his steward, "Get up! Pursue those men, and when you overtake them, say to them, 'Why have you returned evil for good?
Is this not the cup my master drinks from, and which he uses for divination? You have done wrong.'"
The steward overtook them and repeated these words to them.
They answered him, "Why does my lord speak like this? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing!
See: the money we found at the mouths of our sacks, we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your master's house?
If any of your servants is found with the cup, let him die, and we ourselves will be my lord's slaves."
He said, "Very well, let it be as you say! The one with whom the cup is found will be my slave; the rest of you will be blameless."
Each one quickly lowered his sack to the ground and opened it.
The steward searched, from the oldest to the youngest; and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
They tore their clothes and, each reloading his donkey, returned to the city.
Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, where he still was, and they threw themselves to the ground before him.
Joseph said to them, "What is this you have done? Did you not know that a man like me can practice divination?"

Judah answered, "What can we say to my lord? How can we speak? How can we justify ourselves? God has uncovered the guilt of your servants. Here we are, slaves of my lord, we and the one with whom the cup was found."
But Joseph said, "God forbid! Only the one with whom the cup was found will be my slave; the rest of you, go back in peace to your father."
Then Judah approached him and said, "Please, my lord, let your servant say a word to my lord, and do not let your anger blaze against him, for you are the equal of Pharaoh.
My lord had asked his servants, 'Do you have a father, or a brother?'
And we answered my lord, 'We have an old father and a young brother, born in his old age; this boy's brother is dead, he is the only son of his mother left, and his father cherishes him.'
Then you said to your servants, 'Bring him to me, that I may set eyes on him.'
We answered, 'The boy cannot leave his father; if he leaves him, his father will die.'
But you insisted, 'If your youngest brother does not come down with you, you will no longer be admitted into my presence.'
When we went back up to your servant, our father, we reported to him the words of my lord.
