Then our father said, 'Go back and buy us a little food.'
We answered, 'We cannot go down; we will go only if our youngest brother is with us, for we cannot appear before the man without him.'
Your servant, our father, said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two sons.
One left me, and I said, "A beast has surely torn him to pieces"; and I have not seen him since.
If you take this one from me too and harm comes to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in sorrow to the realm of the dead.'
Now, if I return to your servant, my father, without the boy to whom he is bound with all his soul,
as soon as he sees that the boy is not there, he will die; and your servants will have brought down the gray hairs of your servant, our father, in sorrow to the realm of the dead.
For I, your servant, went guarantor for the boy to my father: 'If I do not bring him back to you,' I said, 'I will be guilty before my father forever.'
So let your servant remain as my lord's slave in place of the boy, and let the boy go back up with his brothers.
How could I go back up to my father without the boy? No! I could not bear to see the grief that would overwhelm my father."

titres.titre: Joseph makes himself known to his brothers

versets.t: Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all those around him. He cried out, "Send everyone out!" So no one was with him when he made himself known to his brothers.
He wept aloud, so loudly that the Egyptians heard, and the news reached Pharaoh's household.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" But his brothers, dumbfounded, could not answer him.
Joseph said to them, "Come closer to me." They came closer, and he said, "I am Joseph, your brother, the one you sold into Egypt.
Now, do not be distressed and do not reproach yourselves for having sold me to be brought here: it was to save your lives that God sent me ahead of you.
For two years now the famine has been in the land, and for five more years there will be neither plowing nor harvest.
God sent me ahead of you to ensure your survival in the land and to preserve your lives by a great deliverance.
So it was not you who sent me here, but God. It is he who made me Pharaoh's counselor, master of all his household, and governor of all Egypt.
Go back up quickly to my father and tell him, 'This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me master of all Egypt. Come down to me without delay.
You will live in the land of Goshen, close to me, you, your sons and grandsons, your sheep, your cattle, and all that you have.
There I will provide for you, for there are still five years of famine to come; so you will lack nothing, you, your household, and all who are yours.'
You see with your own eyes, and Benjamin, my brother, sees too: it is indeed I who am speaking to you.
Tell my father of all my glory in Egypt and all that you have seen, and bring him down here as quickly as you can."
Then he threw his arms around his brother Benjamin's neck and wept; and Benjamin wept on his shoulder.
He also kissed all his brothers, holding them close and weeping; then his brothers began to talk with him.
The news reached Pharaoh's palace: "Joseph's brothers have come!" This pleased Pharaoh and his servants.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Tell your brothers, 'This is what you shall do: load your animals and return to the land of Canaan.
Take your father and your families, and come back to me. I will give you the best of Egypt, and you will eat the fat of the land.'
Here too are my orders: 'Take carts from Egypt for your children and your wives, put your father in them, and come.
Do not regret the possessions you leave behind, for the best of all Egypt will be yours.'"
The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them carts, as Pharaoh had ordered, and provisions for the journey.
He gave each of them a change of clothes, and to Benjamin about three and a half kilos of silver with five changes of clothes.
To his father he sent ten donkeys loaded with the best products of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provisions for the journey.
Then he sent his brothers off, telling them, "Do not quarrel on the way."
They went up from Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, to their father Jacob.
They told him, "Joseph is still alive, and it is even he who governs all Egypt!" But Jacob was unmoved, for he did not believe them.
Then they reported to him all the words Joseph had spoken; and when he saw the carts Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived.
Israel said, "Enough! Joseph, my son, is still alive! I will go and see him before I die."

titres.titre: God speaks to Jacob at Beersheba
Jacob's family that came to Egypt

versets.t: Israel set out with all that he had. Arriving at Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
God spoke to Israel in a vision at night, "Jacob! Jacob!" He answered, "Here I am."
God said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you a great nation.
I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I myself will bring you back up; and Joseph will close your eyes with his hand."
Jacob left Beersheba. The sons of Israel set their father Jacob, their wives, and their children on the carts Pharaoh had sent to carry them.
They also took their flocks and the possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan. So Jacob went to Egypt with all his descendants:
his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters, all his descendants, he brought with him to Egypt.
These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Jacob's firstborn was Reuben.
The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of the Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan had died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Job, and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the sons Leah bore to Jacob in Paddan-Aram, along with his daughter Dinah: his sons and daughters were thirty-three persons in all.
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah their sister. The sons of Beriah were Heber and Malchiel.
These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban had given to his daughter Leah: she bore these to Jacob, sixteen persons in all.
The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin.
In Egypt, Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These are the sons Rachel bore to Jacob, fourteen persons in all.
The son of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban had given to his daughter Rachel: she bore these to Jacob, seven persons in all.
The total number of persons descended from Jacob who came with him to Egypt, not counting his sons' wives, was sixty-six.
Counting the two sons born to Joseph in Egypt, the household of Jacob that came to Egypt numbered seventy persons in all.
Jacob had sent Judah ahead to Joseph, to prepare for his arrival at Goshen. When they had reached there,
Joseph had his chariot harnessed and went up to Goshen to meet his father Israel. As soon as he saw him, he threw his arms around his neck and wept a long while on his shoulder.
Israel said to Joseph, "Now I can die, since I have seen your face and you are still alive!"
Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go and tell Pharaoh and say to him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who lived in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
They are shepherds, keepers of livestock; they have brought their sheep, their cattle, and all that they own.'
When Pharaoh calls you and asks your occupation,

answer, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth until now, as our fathers were before us.' Thus you will be able to live in the land of Goshen, for the Egyptians abhor all shepherds."

titres.titre: Settling in the land of Goshen
Joseph and the administration of the famine

versets.t: Joseph went to announce the news to Pharaoh, "My father and my brothers have come from the land of Canaan with their sheep, their cattle, and all that they own, and here they are in the land of Goshen."
He had taken five of his brothers, whom he presented to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked them, "What is your occupation?" They answered, "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were before us."

They added, "We have come to stay in the land, for there is no longer any pasture for your servants' flocks, so heavily does the famine weigh on the land of Canaan. Allow your servants, then, to live in the land of Goshen."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.

Egypt is at your disposal: settle your father and your brothers in the best region of the land. Let them live in the land of Goshen. And if you know of any capable men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock."
Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him to Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked him, "How old are you?"

Jacob answered, "The years of my pilgrimage are a hundred and thirty. Few and hard have been the years of my life, and they have not reached the number of the years my fathers lived during their own pilgrimage."
Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh again and withdrew.
Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a holding in the best region of Egypt, the region of Rameses, as Pharaoh had ordered.
And Joseph provided bread for his father, his brothers, and all his father's household, according to the number of the children.
There was no more bread in all the land, for the famine was crushing; Egypt and the land of Canaan were worn out by hunger.
Joseph collected all the money to be found in Egypt and Canaan, in exchange for the grain that was bought, and he brought it to Pharaoh's palace.
When there was no more money in Egypt and Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, "Give us bread! Why should we die before your eyes? We have no more money."
Joseph answered, "Bring your livestock, and I will give you bread in exchange, since you have no more money."
They brought their livestock to Joseph, who gave them bread in exchange for their horses, sheep, cattle, and donkeys. That year he fed them thus in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year was over, they came to him the following year and said, "We will not hide it from my lord: the money is gone, and our livestock already belongs to my lord. Nothing is left before my lord but our bodies and our lands.

Why should we perish before your eyes, we and our lands? Buy us and our lands in exchange for bread, and we will be Pharaoh's slaves, with our lands. Give us seed, so that we may live instead of dying and the land may not become a desert."
So Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh: the Egyptians each sold their field, so pressing was the famine, and the land became Pharaoh's property.
As for the people, Joseph moved them into the cities, from one end of Egypt to the other.
Only the priests' lands were not acquired: the priests received a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the income he assigned them; that is why they did not sell their lands.
Joseph said to the people, "Today I have bought you and your lands for Pharaoh. Here is seed: sow the land.
At harvest, you will give a fifth to Pharaoh, and you will keep the other four parts to sow your fields and to feed yourselves, your families, and your children."
They answered, "You have saved our lives! May we find favor in the eyes of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh's slaves."
Joseph made it a law, which stands to this day: a fifth of Egypt's harvests goes to Pharaoh. Only the priests' lands are exempt from this rule.
Israel settled in Egypt, in the land of Goshen; there they acquired holdings, were fruitful, and became very numerous.
Jacob lived seventeen years in Egypt, and the total span of his life was a hundred and forty-seven years.

When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand under my thigh and swear to me your kindness and faithfulness: do not bury me in Egypt.
When I rest with my fathers, you will carry me out of Egypt to bury me in their tomb." Joseph answered, "I will do as you say."
Jacob went on, "Swear it to me." Joseph swore it to him, and Israel bowed down, leaning on the top of his staff.
After this, Joseph was told, "Your father is ill." He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, with him.
Jacob was told, "Here is your son Joseph, coming to see you." Israel gathered his strength and sat up on his bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz, in the land of Canaan, and blessed me,
saying, 'I will make you fruitful, I will multiply you, I will make of you an assembly of peoples, and I will give this land to your descendants after you, as an everlasting possession.'
Now, the two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you will be mine: Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, like Reuben and Simeon.
But the children born to you after them will be yours; they will be recorded under the names of their brothers for their share of the inheritance.
For, on my return from Paddan, Rachel died on the way, in the land of Canaan, a short distance from Ephrath, and I buried her there, on the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem."
Then Israel saw Joseph's sons and asked, "Who are these?"
Joseph answered his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." Israel said, "Bring them to me, that I may bless them."
Israel's eyes were dim with age, and he could no longer see well. Joseph brought his sons close, and Israel kissed them and held them against himself.
Israel said to Joseph, "I never thought to see your face again, and now God has let me see even your descendants!"
Joseph took his sons from between his father's knees and bowed down with his face to the ground.
Then he took the two of them, Ephraim with his right hand, to Israel's left, and Manasseh with his left hand, to Israel's right, and brought them close to him.

But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh: he thus crossed his hands deliberately, even though Manasseh was the firstborn.
He blessed Joseph, saying, "May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,

the Angel who delivered me from all evil, bless these boys! Through them may my name and the name of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac, be carried on, and may they grow into a great multitude in the midst of the land!"
Joseph, seeing that his father was laying his right hand on Ephraim's head, was displeased; he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's,
and he said to his father, "Not so, my father! This one is the firstborn: lay your right hand on his head."

But his father refused, "I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, he too will be great; but his younger brother will be greater than he, and his descendants will become a multitude of nations."
That day he blessed them, saying, "By you will Israel pronounce its blessings, saying, 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh!'" And so he placed Ephraim before Manasseh.
Israel said to Joseph, "See, I am about to die. But God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers.
And I give to you, more than to your brothers, one portion of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow."
Jacob called his sons and said, "Gather round, that I may tell you what will happen to you in the days to come.
Gather round and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel, your father.
Reuben, you are my firstborn, my strength, the firstfruits of my vigor, first in dignity and first in power.
Turbulent as water, you will no longer hold the first place, for you climbed onto your father's bed and defiled it by climbing there.
Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are instruments of violence.
Let me not enter their secrets, let me not join their assembly! For in their anger they killed men, and on a whim they maimed bulls.
Cursed be their anger, so fierce, and their fury, so cruel! I will divide them in Jacob, I will scatter them in Israel.
You, Judah, your brothers will praise you; your hand will press on the neck of your enemies, and your father's sons will bow down before you.
Judah is a young lion. You return from the kill, my son! He crouched down, lay like a lion, like a lioness: who will dare to rouse him?
The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs, the one whom the peoples will obey.
He ties his donkey to the vine, the colt of his she-donkey to the choicest branch; he washes his garment in wine, his cloak in the blood of grapes.
His eyes are darker than wine, his teeth whiter than milk.
Zebulun dwells by the sea; he is on the shore where the ships come in, and his flank stretches toward Sidon.
Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down among its pens.
He saw that rest was good and the land pleasant; so he bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to forced labor.
Dan will govern his people, like one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a serpent on the road, a viper on the path, biting the horse's heel so that the rider falls backward.
I wait for your salvation, Lord!
Gad, raiders assail him, but he presses on their heels and drives them back.
From Asher comes savory food; he provides delicacies fit for a king.
Naphtali is a doe set free, who speaks beautiful words.
Joseph is the shoot of a fruitful tree, the shoot of a fruitful tree beside a spring; his branches climb over the wall.
Archers harass him, riddle him with arrows, and attack him,
but his bow stays firm, and his arms keep their suppleness, by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, by the one who is the Shepherd and the Rock of Israel,

by the God of your father, who comes to your help, by the Almighty, who blesses you. Yours are the blessings of heaven above, the blessings of the deep lying below, the blessings of the breasts and of the womb!

Your father's blessings surpass the blessings of the ancient mountains and the treasures of the everlasting hills. May they rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the one set apart among his brothers!
Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he devours his prey; in the evening he divides the spoil."
These are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them as he blessed them: he blessed each one with the blessing suited to him.
Then he gave them this order, "I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers, in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre, in the land of Canaan, the one Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, along with the field, as a burial place.
There Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried, there Isaac and his wife Rebekah were buried, and there I buried Leah.
The field and the cave in it had been bought from the sons of Heth."
When Jacob had finished giving orders to his sons, he drew his feet up into the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people.

titres.titre: The mourning and burial of Jacob

versets.t: Joseph threw himself on his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him.
Then he ordered the physicians in his service to embalm his father, and the physicians embalmed Israel.
It took forty days, the time required for embalming, and the Egyptians mourned him seventy days.
When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph said to the household of Pharaoh, "If I have found favor in your eyes, convey this to Pharaoh:
My father made me swear, saying, 'I am about to die; you will bury me in the tomb I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.' Let me go up, then, to bury my father, and I will return."
Pharaoh answered, "Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear."
Joseph went up to bury his father, and with him went up all Pharaoh's servants, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,
all Joseph's household, his brothers, and his father's household; they left in the land of Goshen only their children, their sheep, and their cattle.
Chariots and horsemen also went up with him: the procession was immense.
When they reached the threshing floor of Atad, beyond the Jordan, they raised loud and deep lamentations, and Joseph observed seven days of mourning for his father.

Seeing this mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, the Canaanites who inhabited the land said, "This is a great mourning among the Egyptians!" That is why the place beyond the Jordan was named Abel-mizraim, that is, the mourning of Egypt.
Jacob's sons did for him what he had commanded them:
they carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre, the field that Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
After burying his father, Joseph returned to Egypt, with his brothers and all who had accompanied him.
Seeing that their father was dead, Joseph's brothers said, "What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and repays us for all the wrong we did him?"
So they sent word to Joseph, "Before he died, your father gave this order:

'You shall say to Joseph: Please forgive your brothers their crime and their sin, all the wrong they did you.' Forgive, then, we beg you, the offense of the servants of your father's God." On hearing these words, Joseph wept.
His brothers themselves came and threw themselves at his feet and said, "Here we are, we are your slaves."
Joseph answered them, "Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God?
You meant to do me harm; but God turned it into good, to bring about what is happening today: the saving of the lives of a great many people.
So do not be afraid: I will provide for you and your children." Thus he comforted them and spoke to their hearts.
Joseph stayed in Egypt, he and his father's household. He lived a hundred and ten years.
He saw Ephraim's children to the third generation, and the sons of Machir, son of Manasseh, were also born on his knees.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am about to die; but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the one he swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."
And Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, "When God visits you, you will carry my bones up from here."
Joseph died at the age of a hundred and ten. He was embalmed and laid in a coffin, in Egypt.

titres.titre: The sons of Israel in Egypt

versets.t: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all; Joseph was already in Egypt.
Then Joseph died, and so did all his brothers and that whole generation.
But the sons of Israel were fruitful; they swarmed and multiplied and grew so numerous and so strong that the land was filled with them.
A new king, who had never known Joseph, came to the throne of Egypt.
He said to his people, "Look, the people of the sons of Israel are more numerous and stronger than we are.
Let us deal shrewdly with them, then, so that they stop increasing. Otherwise, if war breaks out, they will join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country."
So they set taskmasters over Israel to crush them under forced labor, and the people built the store cities of Pithom and Rameses for Pharaoh.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, until the Egyptians came to dread the sons of Israel.
So the Egyptians reduced the sons of Israel to harsh slavery.
They made their lives bitter with hard labor, at mortar and bricks and every kind of work in the fields; all this work they imposed on them brutally.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah.
He said, "When you deliver the Hebrew women, watch the child closely: if it is a boy, put him to death; if it is a girl, let her live."
But the midwives feared God; they did not do what the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they let the boys live.
The king of Egypt summoned the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this and let the boys live?"
The midwives answered Pharaoh, "The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; they are full of life, and they give birth before the midwife reaches them."
God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very strong.
Because the midwives had feared God, he gave them families of their own.
Then Pharaoh gave this order to all his people: "Every boy that is born, throw into the Nile; but every girl, let her live."
A man of the house of Levi went and married a daughter of Levi.
She conceived and bore a son. Seeing that he was beautiful, she hid him for three months.
When she could hide him no longer, she took a basket of papyrus, coated it with tar and pitch, placed the child in it, and set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.
The child's sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him.
Now Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe in the Nile, while her attendants walked along the bank. She noticed the basket among the reeds and sent her servant to fetch it.
She opened it and saw the child: it was a little boy, and he was crying. Moved with compassion, she said, "This is one of the Hebrew children."
Then the child's sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and find you a nurse from among the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?"
"Go," Pharaoh's daughter answered her. So the girl went and called the child's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child and nurse him for me; I will pay you." So the woman took the child and nursed him.
When the child had grown, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, for, she said, "I drew him out of the water."
In those days, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and saw their forced labor. He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his own people.
Looking this way and that and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
The next day he went out again, and there were two Hebrews fighting. He said to the one in the wrong, "Why are you striking your companion?"
The man retorted, "Who made you ruler and judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Moses was afraid and thought, "Surely the thing is known."
Pharaoh heard of the matter and sought to put Moses to death. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, where he sat down by a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father's flock.
Some shepherds came and drove them off, but Moses got up, came to their defense, and watered their flock.
When they returned to their father Reuel, he said to them, "Why have you come back so early today?"
They answered, "An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds; he even drew water for us and watered the flock."
"And where is he?" he said to his daughters. "Why did you leave the man behind? Call him, so that he may eat."
Moses agreed to stay with the man, who gave him his daughter Zipporah in marriage.
She bore a son, and he named him Gershom, for, he said, "I am a stranger in a foreign land."
Many days passed, and the king of Egypt died. The sons of Israel still groaned under their slavery; they cried out, and from the depths of their bondage their plea rose up to God.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
God looked upon the sons of Israel, and God took notice of them.
Moses was tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock beyond the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush. Moses looked: the bush was on fire, yet it was not consumed.
He thought, "I must turn aside to see this great sight: why is the bush not burning up?"
When the Lord saw that he had turned aside to look, God called to him from the midst of the bush, "Moses! Moses!" He answered, "Here I am."
God said, "Do not come any closer. Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground."
Then he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
The Lord said, "I have seen, yes, I have seen the misery of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry against their oppressors; yes, I know their sufferings.

I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey, the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
Now the cry of the sons of Israel has reached me, and I have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians crush them.
Go now: I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people, the sons of Israel, out of Egypt."
Moses said to God, "Who am I, to go to Pharaoh and bring the sons of Israel out of Egypt?"
God answered, "I will be with you, and this will be the sign that it is I who send you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain."
Moses said to God, "Suppose I go to the sons of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' What shall I tell them?"
God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." Then he added, "This is what you will say to the sons of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"

God said further to Moses, "You will say this to the sons of Israel: 'The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be invoked from age to age.

Go, gather the elders of Israel and say to them: 'The Lord, the God of your fathers, has appeared to me, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, and he said: I have watched over you and seen what is being done to you in Egypt,

and I have resolved to bring you up out of the misery of Egypt to the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, a land flowing with milk and honey.'

They will listen to you. Then you and the elders of Israel will go to the king of Egypt and say to him: 'The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. So let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, to offer a sacrifice to the Lord our God.'
But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless a mighty hand forces him.
So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders I will perform in its midst; after that, he will let you go.
And I will make this people find favor with the Egyptians, so that when you leave, you will not go empty-handed:
each woman will ask her neighbor and the woman staying in her house for objects of silver, objects of gold, and clothing. You will put them on your sons and daughters, and so you will plunder Egypt."
Moses spoke up again, "But what if they do not believe me or listen to me, and say, 'The Lord did not appear to you'?"
The Lord said to him, "What is that in your hand?" "A staff," he answered.
"Throw it on the ground," said the Lord. He threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and Moses fled from it.
The Lord said to Moses, "Reach out your hand and seize it by the tail." He reached out his hand and grasped it, and in his hand the snake became a staff again.
"This is so that they may believe that the Lord, the God of their fathers, has appeared to you, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob."
The Lord said to him again, "Put your hand inside your cloak." He put his hand inside his cloak, then drew it out: his hand was covered with a skin disease, white as snow.
"Put your hand back inside your cloak," said the Lord. He put it back, then drew it out: it had become like the rest of his body again.
"So," said the Lord, "if they do not believe you or heed the first sign, they will believe because of the second.

And if they do not believe even these two signs or listen to you, you will take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground; the water you have drawn from the Nile will become blood on the ground."
Moses said to the Lord, "Please, my Lord, I am not a man of words; I never was, and I am not now that you have spoken to your servant: I am slow of speech and slow of tongue."
The Lord said to him, "Who gave man his mouth? Who makes him mute or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, the Lord?
Go now: I will be with your mouth and will teach you what to say."
Moses answered, "Please, my Lord, send whomever you will."

Then the Lord's anger blazed against Moses, and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he speaks well. He is even now coming to meet you, and when he sees you, he will rejoice in his heart.
You will speak to him and put the words in his mouth; I will be with your mouth and with his, and I will teach you both what to do.
He will speak to the people for you: he will be your mouth, and you will be like a god to him.
And take this staff in your hand, with which you will perform the signs."
Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, "Let me go, I pray, and return to my own people in Egypt, to see whether they are still alive." Jethro said to him, "Go in peace."
The Lord said to Moses, in Midian, "Go, return to Egypt, for all those who sought your life are dead."
So Moses took his wife and his sons, put them on a donkey, and set out for Egypt, holding in his hand the staff of God.
The Lord said to Moses, "As you go back to Egypt, be sure to perform before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.
Then you will say to Pharaoh: 'Thus says the Lord: Israel is my son, my firstborn.
I said to you: Let my son go, so that he may worship me. But you refused to let him go: so now I will put your son to death, your firstborn.'"
On the way, at the place where they spent the night, the Lord came to meet Moses and sought to put him to death.
Zipporah took a flint, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched Moses' feet with it, saying, "You are a bridegroom of blood to me."
Then the Lord let him alone. She had said "bridegroom of blood" because of the circumcision.
The Lord said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he set out, met him at the mountain of God, and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord who had sent him, and all the signs he had commanded him to perform.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the sons of Israel.
Aaron repeated all the words the Lord had spoken to Moses, and he performed the signs in the sight of the people.
The people believed; they understood that the Lord had watched over the sons of Israel and had seen their misery, and they bowed down and worshiped.
After this, Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let my people go, so that they may hold a feast for me in the wilderness."
Pharaoh answered, "Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go."

They said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. So let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness to offer a sacrifice to the Lord our God, or he may strike us with plague or with the sword."
The king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your labor!"
And Pharaoh added, "Look, the people are now numerous in the land, and you would have them stop their labor!"
That same day Pharaoh gave this order to the overseers of the people and to their foremen:
"You will no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks, as before; let them go and gather straw for themselves.
But you will require of them the same quota of bricks as they made before; do not reduce it at all. They are lazy; that is why they cry out, 'Let us go and offer a sacrifice to our God.'
Make the work heavier for these people, so that they labor at it and pay no attention to lying words!"
So the overseers of the people and their foremen went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh: I will supply you with straw no longer.
Go and get straw for yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced at all."
So the people scattered throughout Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
The overseers pressed them, saying, "Finish your daily task, just as when there was straw."
And the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh's overseers had set over them, were beaten and asked, "Why have you not finished your quota of bricks yesterday and today, as before?"
The Israelite foremen went and complained to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants this way?
No straw is given to your servants, yet we are told, 'Make bricks!' And now your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people."
Pharaoh retorted, "Lazy, that is what you are, lazy! That is why you say, 'Let us go and offer a sacrifice to the Lord.'
Now get to work. No straw will be given you, but you will deliver the same quota of bricks."
The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when they were told, "You will not reduce your daily quota of bricks at all."
As they left Pharaoh, they came upon Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them.
They said to them, "May the Lord see you and judge! You have made us reek in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants; you have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
Moses turned back to the Lord and said, "Lord, why have you brought harm on this people? Why did you ever send me?
Ever since I came to speak to Pharaoh in your name, he has mistreated this people, and you have done nothing to rescue your people."

titres.titre: The genealogy of Moses and Aaron

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses, "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh: forced by a mighty hand, he will let them go; forced by a mighty hand, he will even drive them out of his land."
God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the Lord.
I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name, the Lord, I did not make myself known to them.
I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they had lived as strangers.
And I have heard the groaning of the sons of Israel, whom the Egyptians hold in slavery, and I have remembered my covenant.

Therefore say to the sons of Israel: 'I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt, I will free you from their slavery, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment.
I will take you as my people, and I will be your God; and you will know that I am the Lord your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.
I will bring you into the land I swore with uplifted hand to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob; I will give it to you as a possession. I am the Lord.'"
Moses reported this to the sons of Israel, but they did not listen to him, for they were worn down by their harsh slavery.
The Lord said to Moses,
"Go and tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to let the sons of Israel go out of his land."
But Moses said to the Lord, "See, the sons of Israel have not listened to me; how then will Pharaoh listen to me, since I am a man of faltering lips?"
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them his commands for the sons of Israel and for Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so as to bring the sons of Israel out of Egypt.
These are the heads of their families. The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their lines of descent: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived a hundred and thirty-three years.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of Levi according to their lines of descent.
Amram married Jochebed, his aunt, who bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon; she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites.
Eleazar, son of Aaron, married one of the daughters of Putiel; she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the Levite families, by their clans.
It was this Aaron and this Moses to whom the Lord said, "Bring the sons of Israel out of Egypt by their divisions."
It was they who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the sons of Israel out of Egypt: this same Moses and Aaron.
Now on the day the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
the Lord said to Moses, "I am the Lord. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything I tell you."
But Moses said before the Lord, "See, I am a man of faltering lips; how will Pharaoh listen to me?"

titres.titre: The first plague: water turned to blood

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses, "See, I make you like a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet.
You are to say everything I command you, and Aaron your brother is to tell Pharaoh to let the sons of Israel go out of his land.
But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and I will multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you; then I will lay my hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring my divisions, my people, the sons of Israel, out of the land of Egypt.
And the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring the sons of Israel out from among them."
Moses and Aaron did exactly as the Lord had commanded them.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron,
"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Perform a wonder,' you will say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh, and let it become a snake.'"
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did as the Lord had commanded: Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a snake.
Pharaoh in turn summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did the same thing by their secret arts:
each one threw down his staff, and they became snakes. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.
Yet Pharaoh's heart grew hard, and he would not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is unyielding: he refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning, at the hour when he goes out to the water; station yourself to meet him on the bank of the Nile, holding in your hand the staff that turned into a snake.
Say to him: 'The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you to say: Let my people go, so that they may worship me in the wilderness. But until now you have not listened.
Thus says the Lord: By this you will know that I am the Lord. See, with the staff in my hand I will strike the waters of the Nile, and they will turn to blood.
The fish in the Nile will die, the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will no longer be able to drink its water.'"

The Lord said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over its rivers, its canals, its ponds, and all its reservoirs, and they will become blood. There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in the vessels of wood and stone."
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded: Aaron raised the staff and struck the waters of the Nile in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and all the water of the Nile turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile died, the Nile stank, and the Egyptians could no longer drink its water; there was blood throughout the land of Egypt.
But the magicians of Egypt did the same thing by their secret arts; so Pharaoh's heart grew hard, and he would not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug along the banks of the Nile for water to drink, because they could no longer drink the water of the river.
Seven full days passed after the Lord struck the Nile.
The Lord said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.
If you refuse to let them go, I will strike your whole territory with a plague of frogs.
The Nile will teem with frogs; they will come up and enter your house, your bedroom and your bed, the houses of your servants and among your people, even into your ovens and your kneading bowls.
The frogs will come up on you, on your people, and on all your servants."
The Lord said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, the canals, and the ponds, and make frogs come up over the land of Egypt."
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.
But the magicians did the same thing by their secret arts: they made frogs come up over the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Pray to the Lord to take the frogs away from me and my people, and I will let the people go to offer a sacrifice to the Lord."

Moses said to Pharaoh, "The honor is yours to set the time when I am to pray for you, for your servants, and for your people, that the frogs may be removed from you and your houses and remain only in the Nile."
"Tomorrow," he answered. Moses replied, "It will be as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the Lord our God.
The frogs will leave you, your houses, your servants, and your people; they will remain only in the Nile."
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the Lord about the frogs he had brought upon Pharaoh.
The Lord did what Moses asked: the frogs died in the houses, in the courtyards, and in the fields.
They were piled up in heaps, and the land reeked with them.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he made his heart unyielding and would not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the ground, and it will become gnats throughout the land of Egypt."

So they did: Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the ground, and gnats swarmed over the people and the animals. All the dust of the ground became gnats throughout the land of Egypt.
The magicians tried to do the same, to produce gnats by their secret arts, but they could not. And the gnats were on the people and the animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God!" But Pharaoh's heart grew hard, and he would not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.

The Lord said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning and station yourself before Pharaoh at the hour when he goes out to the water. Say to him: Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.

If you do not let my people go, I will send swarms of flies against you, your servants, your people, and your houses; the houses of the Egyptians will be full of flies, and even the ground where they stand.
But on that day I will set apart the region of Goshen, where my people live: there will be no flies there, so that you may know that I, the Lord, am in the midst of the land.
I will make a distinction between my people and yours. This sign will take place tomorrow."
And the Lord did so: dense swarms of flies invaded Pharaoh's house, the houses of his servants, and all the land of Egypt; the land was ravaged by the flies.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, offer a sacrifice to your God, but within the land."

Moses answered, "It would not be right to do so, for what we sacrifice to the Lord our God is an abomination to the Egyptians. If we offer, before their eyes, a sacrifice that is an abomination to them, will they not stone us?
We must go a three days' journey into the wilderness to offer a sacrifice to the Lord our God, as he has told us."
Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to offer a sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness; only, do not go very far. Pray for me."

Moses said, "As soon as I leave you, I will pray to the Lord; tomorrow the flies will leave Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. But let Pharaoh stop toying with us by not letting the people go to offer a sacrifice to the Lord."
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord.
The Lord did what Moses asked: he removed the flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people; not one was left.
But this time too Pharaoh made his heart unyielding and did not let the people go.

titres.titre: The fifth plague: the death of the livestock

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.
If you refuse to let them go and hold them back any longer,
the hand of the Lord will strike your livestock in the fields, the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds and the flocks: a very severe plague.
But the Lord will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt: nothing belonging to the sons of Israel will die."
The Lord set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the Lord will do this in the land."
The next day the Lord did it: all the livestock of Egypt died, but of the livestock of the sons of Israel not one animal died.
Pharaoh sent to inquire, and behold, not one animal of the livestock of Israel had died. Yet Pharaoh's heart remained unyielding, and he did not let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from a furnace, and have Moses toss it toward the sky in the sight of Pharaoh.
It will become a fine dust over the whole land of Egypt, and on people and animals throughout the land of Egypt it will produce boils breaking out in sores."
So they took soot from a furnace and stood before Pharaoh; Moses tossed it toward the sky, and it produced boils breaking out in sores on people and animals.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils had struck the magicians as well as all the Egyptians.
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the Lord had told Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning, station yourself before Pharaoh, and say to him: Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.
For this time I will send all my plagues against your very heart, against your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
If I had stretched out my hand to strike you and your people with plague, you would already have vanished from the earth.
But this is why I have let you stand: to show you my power, and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth.
You still set yourself against my people by refusing to let them go:
so tomorrow, at this hour, I will send down hail so violent that there has never been its like in Egypt from the day of its founding until now.

Now then, have your livestock and everything you have in the fields brought to safety: on every person and animal that is in the fields and has not been brought home, the hail will fall, and they will die."
Among Pharaoh's servants, whoever feared the word of the Lord brought his servants and his livestock to safety in the houses;
but whoever did not take the word of the Lord to heart left his servants and his livestock in the fields.
The Lord said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and let hail fall on all the land of Egypt, on people, on animals, and on every plant of the field, throughout the land of Egypt."
Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and the Lord sent thunder and hail; lightning struck the earth, and the Lord rained hail on the land of Egypt.
There was hail, and in the midst of the hail, fire flashing back and forth, of a violence without equal in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.
Throughout the land of Egypt the hail struck everything that was in the fields, people and animals; it struck every plant of the field and shattered every tree of the field.
Only the region of Goshen, where the sons of Israel lived, was spared the hail.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned. The Lord is just; it is I and my people who are guilty.
Pray to the Lord: enough of God's thunder and hail! I will let you go, and you will stay no longer."

Moses said to him, "As soon as I have left the city, I will spread out my hands to the Lord; the thunder will stop and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord.
But you and your servants, I know, do not yet fear the Lord God."
The flax and the barley were struck, for the barley was in the ear and the flax in bud;
but the wheat and the spelt were not, because they ripen later.
Moses left the city and Pharaoh, and spread out his hands to the Lord: the thunder and the hail stopped, and the rain no longer poured down on the earth.
But when Pharaoh saw that the rain, the hail, and the thunder had stopped, he sinned again and made his heart unyielding, he and his servants.
Pharaoh's heart grew hard, and he did not let the sons of Israel go, just as the Lord had said through Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh, for I have made his heart unyielding, and the hearts of his servants, so that I may perform these signs of mine among them,
and so that you may tell your children and grandchildren how I made a mockery of Egypt, and what signs I performed among them: thus you will know that I am the Lord."
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, so that they may worship me.
If you refuse to let my people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your territory.

They will cover the face of the land, so that no one will be able to see the ground; they will devour the remnant that escaped, what the hail has left you, and they will devour every tree that grows in your fields.

They will fill your houses, the houses of your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians, such as neither your fathers nor your fathers' fathers have ever seen from the day they came into the land until today." Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long will this man be a snare to us? Let these people go, so that they may worship the Lord their God. Do you not yet see that Egypt is ruined?"
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, who said to them, "Go, worship the Lord your God. But who exactly are the ones to go?"
Moses answered, "We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and our daughters, with our flocks and our herds, for it is a feast of the Lord for us."
Pharaoh said to them, "May the Lord be with you the same way I let you go, along with your little ones! Look, you have evil intentions.
No! Go, you men, and worship the Lord, since that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.
The Lord said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts; let them come up over the land of Egypt and devour every plant of the land, all that the hail has left."
Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the Lord made an east wind blow over the land all that day and all that night. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts.
The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled over the whole territory, in vast swarms; never before had there been so many, and never again will there be.

They covered the face of the whole land, and the land was darkened; they devoured every plant of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left; nothing green was left on the trees or on the plants of the field, throughout the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hurriedly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you.
Now forgive my sin, this once more, and pray to the Lord your God to take only this deadly plague away from me."
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord.
The Lord changed the wind into a very strong west wind, which carried the locusts off and drove them into the Red Sea; not a single locust was left in all the territory of Egypt.
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the sons of Israel go.
The Lord said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and let darkness cover the land of Egypt, darkness that can be felt."
Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and thick darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else, and no one moved from his place for three days; but for all the sons of Israel there was light in their dwellings.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, "Go, worship the Lord; only your flocks and your herds are to stay behind. Even your little ones may go with you."
Moses answered, "You yourself must provide us with sacrifices and burnt offerings to present to the Lord our God.

Our livestock too must go with us: not a hoof is to be left behind, for from them we will take what we need to worship the Lord our God; and we ourselves do not know what we will offer to the Lord until we arrive there."
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he was unwilling to let them go.
Pharaoh said to Moses, "Get away from me! Take care never to appear before me again: the day you see my face, you will die."
"You have said it," Moses answered. "I will never appear before you again."

titres.titre: The announcement of the death of the firstborn

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses, "I will bring one more plague on Pharaoh and on Egypt; after that, he will let you go from here. And when he finally lets you go, he will drive you out of here altogether.
So speak to the people: let every man ask his neighbor, and every woman hers, for objects of silver and objects of gold."
And the Lord made the people find favor with the Egyptians. Moses himself was a very great man in the land of Egypt, in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants and in the eyes of the people.
Moses said, "Thus says the Lord: About midnight I will pass through the midst of Egypt,
and every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the servant girl at the mill, and every firstborn of the livestock.
A great cry will rise throughout the land of Egypt, such as there has never been and never will be again.
But among all the sons of Israel not even a dog will bark against a person or an animal, so that you may know what a distinction the Lord makes between Egypt and Israel.

Then all these servants of yours will come down to me, bow before me, and say: 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you!' After that, I will leave." And Moses, burning with anger, left Pharaoh.
The Lord said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt."
Moses and Aaron performed all these wonders before Pharaoh; but the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the sons of Israel go out of his land.

titres.titre: Moses passes on the command to the people
The death of the firstborn and the departure

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,
"This month is to be for you the first of months; it is to be for you the first month of the year.
Speak to the whole community of Israel: On the tenth of this month, let each man take a lamb for his family, one lamb for each household.
If the household is too small for a lamb, they are to share one with the nearest neighbor, according to the number of persons; you will count for the lamb according to what each can eat.
Your lamb is to be without blemish, a male a year old; you may take it from the sheep or the goats.
You are to keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and then the whole assembly of the community of Israel is to slaughter it at twilight.
They are to take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses where they eat it.
That night they are to eat its meat, roasted over the fire; they are to eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over the fire, the head, the legs, and the inner parts.
You are to leave none of it until morning; whatever is left until morning you are to burn in the fire.
This is how you are to eat it: your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, your staff in your hand; you are to eat it in haste. It is the Passover of the Lord.

That night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both people and animals; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments. I am the Lord.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are: I will see the blood and pass over you, and no destroying plague will touch you when I strike the land of Egypt.
This day is to be a memorial for you: you are to celebrate it as a feast to the Lord, from age to age; you are to keep it as a lasting ordinance.

For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses; for whoever eats anything leavened, from the first day to the seventh, will be cut off from Israel.
On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly, and likewise on the seventh day; no work is to be done on these days, except the preparing of food for each person: that is all you may do.
You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for it was on this very day that I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt. You are to keep this day from age to age, as a lasting ordinance.
In the first month, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day, you are to eat unleavened bread.
For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses; for whoever eats anything leavened will be cut off from the community of Israel, whether a stranger or native-born.
You are to eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you are to eat unleavened bread."
Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and take lambs for your families, and slaughter the Passover.

You are to take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood collected in a basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood from the basin. None of you is to go out the door of his house until morning.
The Lord will pass through to strike Egypt; he will see the blood on the lintel and the two doorposts, and the Lord will pass over the door: he will not let the destroyer enter your houses to strike.
You are to keep this command as an ordinance for you and your children forever.
And when you enter the land that the Lord will give you, as he has promised, you are to keep this rite.
And when your children ask you, 'What does this rite mean to you?'

you are to answer, 'It is the Passover sacrifice to the Lord, who passed over the houses of the sons of Israel in Egypt when he struck Egypt and spared our houses.'" Then the people bowed down and worshiped.
The sons of Israel went and did just as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did.

At midnight the Lord struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon, and every firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh got up that night, he and all his servants and all Egypt, and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was no house without someone dead.
That night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Get up, leave the midst of my people, you and the sons of Israel. Go, worship the Lord, as you have said.
Take your flocks and your herds too, as you have said; go, and bless me also."
The Egyptians pressed the people, in their haste to send them out of the land, for they said, "We are all going to die!"
So the people carried off their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks on their shoulders.
The sons of Israel had done as Moses had said: they had asked the Egyptians for objects of silver, objects of gold, and clothing.
The Lord had made the people find favor with the Egyptians, who granted their request. So they plundered Egypt.
The sons of Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides the children.
A mixed multitude went up with them as well, along with flocks and herds, a great many animals.
From the dough they had brought out of Egypt they baked unleavened cakes, for it had not risen: driven out of Egypt, they could not linger or prepare provisions for themselves.
The stay of the sons of Israel in Egypt had lasted four hundred and thirty years.
At the end of these four hundred and thirty years, on that very day, all the divisions of the Lord went out of the land of Egypt.
It was a night of vigil for the Lord, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This same night belongs to the Lord, a vigil for all the sons of Israel, from age to age.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the law of the Passover: no foreigner is to eat of it.
Any slave bought for money you are to circumcise, and then he may eat of it.
A temporary resident and a hired worker are not to eat of it.
It is to be eaten in a single house; you are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you are not to break any of its bones.
The whole community of Israel is to celebrate it.

If a stranger living among you wishes to celebrate the Passover of the Lord, every male in his household is to be circumcised; then he may draw near to celebrate it, and he will be like the native-born. But no uncircumcised person is to eat of it.
There is to be one law for the native-born and for the stranger who lives among you."
All the sons of Israel did just as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did.
And on that very day the Lord brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt, by their divisions.

titres.titre: The pillar of cloud and fire

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses,
"Consecrate to me every firstborn, the first to open every womb among the sons of Israel, both of people and of animals: it belongs to me."

Moses said to the people, "Remember this day, on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for it was by the strength of his hand that the Lord brought you out: no leavened bread is to be eaten.
You are going out today, in the month of Abib.

When the Lord has brought you into the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you are to keep this rite in this month.
For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there is to be a feast to the Lord.
Unleavened bread is to be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread or leaven is to be seen anywhere in your territory.
On that day you are to explain to your son, 'It is because of what the Lord did for me when I came out of Egypt.'
It will be for you like a sign on your hand and a memorial on your forehead, so that the law of the Lord may be on your lips; for it was with a mighty hand that the Lord brought you out of Egypt.
You are to keep this rite at the appointed time, year after year.
When the Lord has brought you into the land of the Canaanite, as he swore to you and to your fathers, and has given it to you,
you are to set apart for the Lord every first to open the womb. Every firstborn male of your livestock will belong to the Lord.
Every firstborn of a donkey you are to redeem with a lamb; if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you are to redeem.
And when your son asks you in time to come, 'What does this mean?' you are to tell him, 'It was by the strength of his hand that the Lord brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the Lord put to death every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of animals. That is why I sacrifice to the Lord every male that first opens the womb, and why I redeem every firstborn of my sons.'
It will be like a sign on your hand and a band on your forehead, for it was by the strength of his hand that the Lord brought us out of Egypt."

Now when Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was the shortest; for God said, "The people might change their minds at the sight of war and return to Egypt."
So God led the people around by the desert road toward the Red Sea. The sons of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt in good order.
Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear an oath, saying, "God will surely watch over you, and you must carry my bones up from here with you."
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etam, on the edge of the wilderness.
The Lord went ahead of them, by day in a pillar of cloud to guide them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so that they could travel by day and by night.
The pillar of cloud did not depart from before the people by day, nor the pillar of fire by night.

titres.titre: The crossing of the Red Sea

versets.t: The Lord said to Moses,
"Tell the sons of Israel to turn back and camp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you are to camp facing that place, by the sea.
Pharaoh will say of the sons of Israel, 'They are wandering, lost in the land; the wilderness has closed in on them.'
I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them; but I will gain glory over Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord." So they did.

When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the hearts of Pharaoh and his servants turned against the people, and they said, "What have we done, letting Israel go and giving up their service?"
So Pharaoh had his chariot harnessed and took his people with him.
He took six hundred of the best chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt, each with its officers.
The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who pursued the sons of Israel; but the sons of Israel were going out boldly.
The Egyptians pursued them and overtook them as they camped by the sea, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots, his horsemen and his army, near Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.
Pharaoh drew near. The sons of Israel looked up, and there were the Egyptians on the march behind them. Seized with great fear, the sons of Israel cried out to the Lord.
They said to Moses, "Were there no graves in Egypt, that you have brought us out to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt?
Is this not what we told you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone to serve the Egyptians'? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness."
Moses answered the people, "Do not be afraid! Stand firm, and you will see the deliverance the Lord will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.
The Lord will fight for you; you have only to keep still."
The Lord said to Moses, "Why do you cry out to me? Tell the sons of Israel to move on.
As for you, raise your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the sons of Israel may go through the midst of the sea on dry ground.
And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians, so that they go in after them; then I will gain glory over Pharaoh and all his army, his chariots and his horsemen.
The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord, when I have gained glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen."
Then the angel of God, who had been going ahead of the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them; the pillar of cloud, which had been in front of them, moved and stood behind them.
It came to stand between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. The cloud was dark to the one side, and to the other it lit up the night; all night long neither camp drew near the other.
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord, by a strong east wind that blew all night, drove the sea back and turned it into dry land; the waters divided.
The sons of Israel went through the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall to their right and to their left.
The Egyptians pursued them, and all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen went in after them into the midst of the sea.
In the morning watch the Lord, from the pillar of fire and cloud, looked down on the camp of the Egyptians and threw it into panic.
He jammed the wheels of their chariots, so that they could barely move. The Egyptians said, "Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord is fighting for them against Egypt!"
The Lord said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians, over their chariots and their horsemen."
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its usual place. The Egyptians were fleeing toward it, and the Lord swept them into the midst of the sea.
The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and the horsemen, the whole army of Pharaoh that had gone into the sea in pursuit of Israel; not one of them was left.
But the sons of Israel had walked on dry ground through the midst of the sea, the waters forming a wall to their right and to their left.
That day the Lord saved Israel from the hand of Egypt, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore of the sea.
Israel saw the mighty hand that the Lord had wielded against Egypt; the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord and in Moses his servant.
Then Moses and the sons of Israel sang this song to the Lord; they said: "I will sing to the Lord, for his glory shines out: horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.
My strength and my song is the Lord; he has become my salvation. He is my God, and I praise him; the God of my father, and I exalt him.
The Lord is a warrior; the Lord is his name.
Pharaoh's chariots and his army he has cast into the sea; the finest of his officers have sunk in the Red Sea.
The depths have covered them; they went down to the bottom like a stone.
Your right hand, Lord, is glorious in power; your right hand, Lord, shatters the enemy.
In the greatness of your majesty you cast down those who rise against you; you unleash your fury, and it devours them like stubble.
At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up, the floods stood up like a wall, the depths congealed in the heart of the sea.
The enemy said: 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil; my desire will be satisfied on them; I will draw my sword, my hand will destroy them.'
You blew with your breath, the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like you among the gods, Lord? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, awesome in your deeds, working wonders?
You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.
In your love you have led this people whom you redeemed; by your power you have guided them to your holy dwelling.
The peoples have heard, they tremble; anguish has gripped the inhabitants of Philistia.
Now the chiefs of Edom are terrified, trembling seizes the leaders of Moab, all the inhabitants of Canaan melt away.
Terror and dread fall upon them; before the greatness of your arm they stand still as stone, while your people pass by, Lord, while this people you have won pass by.
You bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, the place, Lord, that you have made your dwelling, the sanctuary, Lord, that your hands have established.
The Lord will reign forever and ever."

For Pharaoh's horses, with his chariots and his horsemen, had gone into the sea, and the Lord had brought the waters of the sea back over them; but the sons of Israel had walked on dry ground through the midst of the sea.
Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines, dancing.
Miriam sang to them in response: "Sing to the Lord, for his glory shines out: horse and rider he has thrown into the sea."
Moses led Israel on from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; they walked for three days in the wilderness without finding water.
They came to Marah, but they could not drink the water of Marah, for it was bitter; that is why it was named Marah, that is, Bitter.
The people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What are we to drink?"

Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood; he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the Lord gave him a decree and a rule, and there he put him to the test.

He said, "If you truly listen to the voice of the Lord your God, if you do what is right in his eyes, if you give ear to his commandments and keep all his decrees, I will not inflict on you any of the diseases I inflicted on Egypt; for I, the Lord, am the one who heals you."
Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees; and they camped there by the water.

The whole community of the children of Israel set out from Elim and came to the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left the land of Egypt.
In the wilderness the whole community of the children of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron.

The children of Israel said to them, "If only we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate our fill of bread! But you have brought us out into this wilderness to starve this whole assembly to death."

The Lord said to Moses, "I am going to rain down bread on you from heaven. Each day the people will go out and gather their portion for the day, so that I may test them: will they follow my law or not?
On the sixth day, when they prepare what they have brought in, it will be twice as much as they gather each day."
So Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, "This evening you will know that it was the Lord who brought you out of the land of Egypt,
and in the morning you will see the glory of the Lord, for he has heard your grumbling against the Lord. As for us, what are we, that you should grumble against us?"

Moses added, "You will know it when the Lord gives you meat to eat this evening and bread to your fill in the morning, for the Lord has heard the grumbling you raise against him. As for us, what are we? Your grumbling is not against us, but against the Lord."
