The men of Israel said to Gideon: "Rule over us, you, then your son and your son's son, for you have delivered us from the hand of Midian."
But Gideon answered them: "I will not rule over you, nor will my son: the Lord will rule over you."
Then he added: "I have only one request: give me each a ring from your plunder." The vanquished, in fact, wore gold rings, for they were Ishmaelites.
"We will gladly give them to you," they answered. They spread out a cloak, and each threw onto it a ring from his plunder.

The weight of the gold rings Gideon had asked for came to about nineteen kilograms, not counting the crescents, the pendants, and the purple garments the kings of Midian wore, nor the collars from their camels' necks.
With this gold Gideon made an ephod, which he set up in his town, at Ophrah. There all Israel prostituted itself before this object, which became a snare for Gideon and his family.
Midian was brought low before the sons of Israel and lifted its head no more; and the land had rest for forty years, as long as Gideon lived.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went back to live in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons, for he had many wives.
His concubine at Shechem also bore him a son, whom he named Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died after a happy old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash, at Ophrah of Abiezer.
After the death of Gideon, the sons of Israel began again to prostitute themselves to the Baals and took Baal-berith as their god.
They no longer remembered the Lord their God, who had delivered them from all their enemies around them,
and they showed no gratitude to the house of Jerubbaal, that is, of Gideon, for all the good he had done for Israel.

titres.titre: Abimelech makes himself king of Shechem

versets.t: Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem, to his mother's brothers, and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother:
"Ask all the citizens of Shechem: Which is better for you, that all seventy sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one man rule? Remember that I am your own flesh and bone."
His mother's brothers repeated all this to the citizens of Shechem, whose hearts inclined toward Abimelech, for they said: "He is our brother."
They gave him about eight hundred grams of silver, taken from the temple of Baal-berith, and Abimelech used it to hire a band of worthless and reckless men.

He went to Ophrah, to his father's house, and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on a single stone. Only Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, escaped, because he had hidden himself.
Then all the citizens of Shechem and all the house of Millo gathered together and proclaimed Abimelech king, by the terebinth of the monument at Shechem.
When Jotham was told of it, he went up to the top of Mount Gerizim and cried out at the top of his voice: "Listen to me, citizens of Shechem, that God may listen to you!
One day the trees set out to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree: Reign over us.
The olive tree answered: Should I give up my oil, by which God and men are honored, to go and sway above the other trees?
Then the trees said to the fig tree: Come, you reign over us.
The fig tree answered: Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit, to go and sway above the other trees?
The trees said to the vine: Come, you reign over us.
The vine answered: Should I give up my wine, which gladdens God and men, to go and sway above the other trees?
Finally all the trees said to the thornbush: Come, you reign over us.

The thornbush answered the trees: If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, come and take shelter in my shade; but if not, let fire come out of the thornbush and devour the cedars of Lebanon!
Now then, have you acted loyally and honorably in making Abimelech king? Have you dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house? Have you repaid him as he deserved?
For my father fought for you: he risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian.

And you, today, have risen up against my father's house, you have killed his sons, seventy men, on a single stone, and you have made Abimelech, the son of his servant girl, king of Shechem, because he is your brother!
If, then, you have acted loyally and honorably toward Jerubbaal and his house this day, rejoice in Abimelech, and let him rejoice in you!

But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the citizens of Shechem and the house of Millo, and let fire come out from the citizens of Shechem and the house of Millo and devour Abimelech!"
Then Jotham fled; he took refuge at Beer, where he settled, for fear of his brother Abimelech.
Abimelech held sway over Israel for three years.
Then God sent a spirit of discord between Abimelech and the citizens of Shechem, who became unfaithful to Abimelech.

Thus the crime committed against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal was to be avenged, and their blood to fall back on Abimelech, their brother, who had killed them, and on the citizens of Shechem, who had helped him kill his brothers.
The citizens of Shechem set men against him on the mountaintops, who robbed everyone who passed by; and Abimelech was informed of it.
Now Gaal son of Ebed arrived at Shechem with his brothers, and the citizens of Shechem put their trust in him.
They went out into the fields, harvested their vineyards, trod the grapes, and held a festival; then, going into the temple of their god, they ate, drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed then said: "Who is Abimelech, and what is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, with Zebul as his lieutenant? Serve rather the descendants of Hamor, the father of Shechem! Why should we serve Abimelech?
Ah, if only this people were under my command, I would drive Abimelech out!" Then he flung at Abimelech: "Strengthen your army and come out to fight!"
When Zebul, the governor of the town, heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed, he flew into a rage.
He secretly sent messengers to Abimelech: "Gaal son of Ebed has arrived at Shechem with his brothers, and they are stirring up the town against you.
Get up this night, with your troops, and lie in ambush in the countryside.
In the morning, at sunrise, sweep down on the town. When Gaal and his troops come out against you, deal with him as best you can."
Abimelech and all his troops got up by night and lay in ambush near Shechem, in four companies.
Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the town gate; at that moment Abimelech and his troops sprang from their ambush.
Seeing them, Gaal said to Zebul: "Here are people coming down from the mountaintops." Zebul answered: "It is the shadow of the mountains that you take for men."
Gaal went on: "Look: a company is coming down from the center of the land, and another is coming by the road of the diviners' oak."
Zebul retorted: "Where now is your big mouth, you who said: Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? Are these not the people you despised? Go out now and fight them!"
Gaal went out at the head of the citizens of Shechem and gave battle to Abimelech.
But Abimelech put him to flight and pursued him; many of his men fell, dead, right up to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech settled at Arumah, while Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers, who could no longer remain at Shechem.
The next day the people went out into the countryside. Abimelech was informed of it:
he took his troops, divided them into three companies, and lay in ambush in the countryside. As soon as he saw the people coming out of the town, he fell upon them and struck them down.
With his own company, Abimelech rushed forward and took position at the entrance of the gate, while the other two companies fell upon all those in the countryside and slaughtered them.
All that day Abimelech assaulted the town; he captured it, killed its inhabitants, razed it, and sowed it with salt.
At this news, all the men of the tower of Shechem took refuge in the crypt of the temple of the god Berith.
When Abimelech was told that they had all gathered there,
he went up to Mount Zalmon with all his troops. He took an axe, cut off a tree branch, lifted it, and set it on his shoulder, saying to his troops: "What you have seen me do, do quickly as I have."

So each man cut his branch and followed Abimelech; they piled the branches against the crypt and set it on fire over those inside. So all the people of the tower of Shechem also perished, about a thousand men and women.
From there Abimelech marched on Thebez, which he besieged and captured.
In the middle of the town there was a strong tower; all the inhabitants, men and women, took refuge in it, shut the door behind them, and went up onto the roof.
Abimelech reached the tower, attacked it, and approached the door to set it on fire.
But a woman threw a millstone down on his head and shattered his skull.
At once he called the young man who carried his weapons: "Draw your sword and finish me off, so that no one can say of me: A woman killed him." The young man ran him through, and he died.
Seeing Abimelech dead, the men of Israel went back, each to his own home.
Thus God brought back upon Abimelech the evil he had done to his father, in killing his seventy brothers.
And God brought back upon the men of Shechem all their wickedness. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal was fulfilled upon them.
After Abimelech, it was Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, who arose to save Israel. He lived at Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim.
He was judge in Israel for twenty-three years, then he died and was buried at Shamir.
After him arose Jair of Gilead, who was judge in Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons, who rode thirty young donkeys and owned thirty towns; these are still called the Encampments of Jair today, in the land of Gilead.
Jair died and was buried at Kamon.

Once again the sons of Israel did what is evil in the eyes of the Lord: they served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Aram, of Sidon, of Moab, of the Ammonites, and of the Philistines; they forsook the Lord and no longer served him.
The anger of the Lord blazed against Israel, and he sold them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites.
That year they oppressed and crushed the sons of Israel; and for eighteen years they afflicted all the sons of Israel settled beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites, in Gilead.
The Ammonites even crossed the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim as well, and Israel was reduced to great distress.
The sons of Israel then cried out to the Lord: "We have sinned against you, for we have forsaken our God to serve the Baals."
The Lord answered the sons of Israel: "Did I not deliver you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines?
And when the Sidonians, Amalek, and Maon oppressed you, and you cried out to me, did I not save you from their hands?
But you, you have forsaken me to serve other gods. That is why I will deliver you no more.
Go then and cry out to the gods you have chosen: let them deliver you in your time of distress!"
The sons of Israel said to the Lord: "We have sinned. Deal with us as you please, but, we beg you, deliver us today."
They removed the foreign gods from their midst and served the Lord; and the Lord could no longer bear the suffering of Israel.
The Ammonites gathered and camped in Gilead, while the sons of Israel assembled and camped at Mizpah.
The people and the leaders of Gilead said to one another: "Who is the man who will open the attack against the Ammonites? He shall become the head of all the inhabitants of Gilead."

titres.titre: Jephthah negotiates with the king of Ammon

versets.t: Jephthah of Gilead was a mighty warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and it was Gilead who had fathered him.
But Gilead's wife bore him other sons; and when they had grown up, they drove Jephthah out, saying to him: "You shall have no inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."
So Jephthah fled far from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob. Worthless men gathered around him and went out on raids with him.
Some time later, the Ammonites made war on Israel.
As the Ammonites were attacking Israel, the elders of Gilead went to fetch Jephthah from the land of Tob.
They said to him: "Come, be our commander in war, and we will fight the Ammonites."
Jephthah answered them: "Did you not hate me and drive me from my father's house? Why do you come to me now, now that you are in distress?"
The elders of Gilead replied: "It is for this very reason that we come back to you: come with us to fight the Ammonites, and you shall be our head, over all of us, the inhabitants of Gilead."
Jephthah said to them: "If you bring me back to fight the Ammonites and the Lord gives them to me, I will be your head."
The elders of Gilead answered: "The Lord is witness between us: we will do exactly as you say."
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead. The people set him at their head as chief and commander, and Jephthah restated all his terms before the Lord, at Mizpah.
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites: "What is there between you and me, that you come to attack my land?"

The king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah: "It is because Israel, when it came up from Egypt, seized my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Give it back to me now, willingly."
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites
to tell him: "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not seize the land of Moab or that of the Ammonites.
When it came up from Egypt, Israel marched through the wilderness to the Red Sea, then arrived at Kadesh.

From there Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom: Let me pass through your land, I beg you. But the king of Edom refused. It sent them also to the king of Moab, who likewise refused. And Israel stayed at Kadesh.
Then, through the wilderness, it went around the lands of Edom and Moab, arrived east of Moab, and camped beyond the Arnon, without entering the territory of Moab, for the Arnon marks its border.
Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who reigned at Heshbon: Let us pass through your land to our own, I beg you.
But Sihon distrusted Israel too much to let it pass through his territory. He gathered his whole army, camped at Jahaz, and gave battle to Israel.
The Lord, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and his whole army into the hands of Israel, which defeated them and took possession of all the land of the Amorites who lived there.
Israel thus seized all their territory, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Since it is the Lord, the God of Israel, who drove out the Amorites before his people, would you now dispossess us?
What your god Chemosh gives you to possess, do you not possess it? Well then, all that the Lord our God has given us, we possess it too.
Are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel, or make war on it?
For three hundred years now Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during all that time?
I have done you no wrong; it is you who act wickedly toward me by making war on me. May the Lord, the supreme judge, decide today between the sons of Israel and the Ammonites."
But the king of the Ammonites took no account of the message from Jephthah.
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh, went by Mizpah of Gilead, and from there marched against the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the Lord:

"If you give the Ammonites into my hands, the first to come out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return victorious from the Ammonites, will belong to the Lord: I will offer it up as a sacrifice."
Jephthah advanced against the Ammonites, and the Lord gave them into his hands.

He struck them from Aroer to the outskirts of Minnith, taking twenty towns from them, and as far as Abel-keramim. It was a very heavy defeat, and the Ammonites were brought low before the sons of Israel.
When Jephthah came home, to Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him, with tambourines and dancing. She was his only child: he had no other son or daughter.
When he saw her, he tore his clothes and cried out: "Ah, my daughter, you have brought me down, you have made my ruin! I have given my word to the Lord, and I cannot take it back."
She answered him: "My father, you have given your word to the Lord: do to me according to the word that came from your mouth, since the Lord has avenged you on your enemies, the Ammonites."
Then she added: "Grant me only this: let me have two months, that I may go into the mountains and weep over my virginity with my companions."
"Go," he said, and he let her leave for two months. She went off with her companions to weep over her virginity on the mountains.
At the end of the two months, she came back to her father, and he carried out on her the vow he had made; she had never known a man. From this comes that custom in Israel:
every year the daughters of Israel go off, for four days, to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah of Gilead.

titres.titre: The war against Ephraim and the password

versets.t: The men of Ephraim gathered, crossed over toward Zaphon, and said to Jephthah, "Why did you go to fight the Ammonites without calling us to march with you? We are going to burn your house down over you!"
Jephthah answered them, "My people and I were locked in a bitter conflict with the Ammonites. I called you, but you did not deliver me from their hands.
When I saw that you would not come to my aid, I risked my life and marched against the Ammonites, and the Lord delivered them into my hands. So why have you come up today to attack me?"

Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and gave battle to Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck down the Ephraimites, for these had said, "You Gileadites are nothing but fugitives from Ephraim, lost between Ephraim and Manasseh!"
Gilead seized the fords of the Jordan on the side toward Ephraim. Whenever a fugitive of Ephraim asked to cross over, the men of Gilead would ask him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" If he answered, "No,"

they would say to him, "Very well, say: Shibboleth." He would say, "Sibboleth," unable to pronounce it correctly. Then they would seize him and cut his throat by the fords of the Jordan. At that time forty-two thousand men of Ephraim fell.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years; then he died and was buried in one of the towns of Gilead.
After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He married his daughters off to men outside his clan and brought in thirty wives from outside for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years;
then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
After him, Elon of Zebulun judged Israel; he judged it for ten years;
then Elon of Zebulun died and was buried at Aijalon, in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Abdon son of Hillel, of Pirathon, judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy young donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years;
then Abdon son of Hillel, of Pirathon, died and was buried at Pirathon, in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
Once again, the sons of Israel did what is evil in the eyes of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
There was at Zorah a man of the clan of Dan named Manoah. His wife was barren and had borne no children.
The angel of the Lord appeared to this woman and said to her, "You are barren and have borne no children; but you shall conceive and give birth to a son.
From now on, be very careful: drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean,

for you shall conceive and give birth to a son. No razor shall touch his head, for the boy shall be consecrated to God as a Nazirite from his mother's womb; he is the one who will begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines."

The woman went to her husband and said to him, "A man of God came to me; his appearance was as awe-inspiring as that of an angel of God. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

He said to me, 'You shall conceive and give birth to a son. From now on, drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the boy shall be consecrated to God as a Nazirite from his mother's womb until the day of his death.'"
Then Manoah prayed to the Lord, "Please, Lord, let the man of God you sent come to us again and teach us what we must do for the boy who is to be born."
God heard Manoah's prayer, and the angel of God came again to the woman while she was sitting in a field; her husband Manoah was not with her.
She ran at once to tell her husband, "Look, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me again."
Manoah got up, followed his wife, approached the man, and asked him, "Are you the one who spoke to this woman?" He answered, "I am."
Manoah went on, "When your word comes true, what rule of life and what conduct shall the boy follow?"
The angel of the Lord answered Manoah, "The woman must abstain from everything I told her:
she shall eat nothing that comes from the vine, drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean. She shall observe all that I have commanded her."
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, "Allow us to detain you and prepare a young goat for you."
The angel of the Lord replied, "Even if you detain me, I will not eat your food; but if you wish to offer a sacrifice, offer it to the Lord." Manoah did not know that this was the angel of the Lord.
Manoah asked the angel of the Lord further, "What is your name? So that, when your word comes true, we may honor you."
The angel of the Lord answered him, "Why do you ask my name? It is Wonderful."
Manoah took the young goat and the offering and offered them to the Lord on the rock. Then the Lord did a wondrous thing, before the eyes of Manoah and his wife:
as the flame went up from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame. At this sight, Manoah and his wife fell on their faces to the ground.
The angel of the Lord did not appear to them again. Manoah then understood that it was the angel of the Lord,
and he said to his wife, "We are going to die, for we have seen God!"

His wife answered him, "If the Lord had wanted to put us to death, he would not have accepted the sacrifice and the offering from our hands, he would not have shown us all this, nor announced to us such things."
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
Then the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him to action, at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and noticed there a woman, a Philistine.
On his return, he spoke of it to his father and mother, "I have noticed at Timnah a Philistine woman; get her for me as my wife."

His father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among the daughters of your kinsmen and in all our people, that you should go to take a wife from the Philistines, those uncircumcised men?" But Samson answered his father, "Get her for me, for she is the one who pleases me."
His father and mother did not know that this came from the Lord, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When he reached the vineyards of Timnah, suddenly a young lion came roaring at him.
The Spirit of the Lord seized Samson: with nothing in his hands, he tore the lion apart as one tears apart a young goat. But he did not tell his parents what he had done.
He continued on his way, spoke with the woman, and she pleased him.
Some time later, coming back to marry her, he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion: and there was a swarm of bees in the body of the animal, and honey.

He scooped some into his hands and ate it as he went along. Rejoining his father and mother, he gave them some, and they ate it; but he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the body of the lion.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson gave a feast there, as the young men were accustomed to do.
As soon as they saw him, they assigned him thirty companions.
Samson said to them, "Let me propose a riddle to you. If you can explain it to me during the seven days of the feast, if you guess it, I will give you thirty tunics and thirty changes of clothing.
But if you cannot, then you shall give me thirty tunics and thirty changes of clothing." They said to him, "Propose your riddle; let us hear it."
He said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came the sweet." For three days they were unable to solve the riddle.
On the seventh day, they said to Samson's wife, "Coax your husband into explaining the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father's house. Did you invite us here to rob us?"

Samson's wife wept before him, "You only hate me, you do not love me! You have proposed a riddle to the sons of my people, and you have not explained it to me." He answered her, "I have not explained it to my father or my mother, and am I to explain it to you?"
She wept before him thus during the seven days of the feast. On the seventh day, as she pressed him, he finally explained the riddle to her, and she revealed it to the sons of her people.

On the seventh day, before sunset, the men of the town said to Samson, "What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?" He retorted to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have guessed my riddle."

The Spirit of the Lord seized him: he went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty men there, took their spoils, and gave the changes of clothing to those who had guessed the riddle. Then, burning with anger, he went back up to his father's house.
As for Samson's wife, she was given to the companion who had served as his best man.

titres.titre: Samson takes revenge on the Philistines

versets.t: Some time later, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife, bringing a young goat. He said, "I want to go into my wife's room." But her father refused to let him in.
"I was convinced that you hated her," he said, "so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Take her instead."
Samson retorted to them, "This time no one can blame me if I do harm to the Philistines."
Samson went off, caught three hundred foxes, took torches, tied the foxes tail to tail in pairs, and fastened a torch between each pair of tails.
He lit the torches and let the foxes loose in the standing grain of the Philistines: he burned up the stacked sheaves as well as the standing grain, and even the vineyards and olive groves.

The Philistines asked, "Who did this?" They were told, "It was Samson, the son-in-law of the man of Timnah, because the man took back his wife and gave her to his companion." Then the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
Samson said to them, "Since you act like this, I will not rest until I have taken my revenge on you."
And he struck them hard, cutting them to pieces. Then he went down to live in the cave of the rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah, deploying near Lehi.
The men of Judah asked, "Why have you come up against us?" They answered, "We have come up to bind Samson and to do to him what he did to us."

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are our masters? What is this you have done to us?" He answered, "I did to them what they had done to me."
They went on, "We have come down to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves."
"No," they answered, "we only want to bind you and hand you over to them; we will not put you to death." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

When he reached Lehi, the Philistines came to meet him with shouts of joy. Then the Spirit of the Lord seized him: the ropes binding his arms became like flax scorched by fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.
Finding a fresh donkey's jawbone, he picked it up and struck down a thousand men with it.
Then Samson said, "With a donkey's jawbone, heaps upon heaps! With a donkey's jawbone I have struck down a thousand men."
When he had said this, he threw the jawbone away and named that place Ramath-lehi.

Consumed by thirst, he called on the Lord, "You are the one who granted this great victory by the hand of your servant; and now, must I die of thirst and fall into the hands of these uncircumcised men?"

Then God split open the hollow of the rock at Lehi, and water gushed from it. Samson drank, his strength returned, and he revived. That is why the spring was named En-hakkore; it is still at Lehi today.
Samson judged Israel, in the days of the Philistines, for twenty years.
Samson went to Gaza; there he saw a prostitute and went in to her.

The people of Gaza were warned, "Samson has come here." They surrounded the place and lay in wait all night at the town gate, staying still, saying to themselves, "Let us wait for daybreak, and then we will kill him."

But Samson lay there until midnight. At midnight he got up, seized the two doors of the town gate and the two doorposts, tore them out along with the bar, hoisted them onto his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron.
After this, he fell in love with a woman of the Valley of Sorek, named Delilah.

The lords of the Philistines went up to her and said, "Coax him and find out where his immense strength comes from, and how we might overpower him to bind and subdue him. Each of us will give you about twelve and a half kilograms of silver."
Delilah said to Samson, "Tell me, I beg you, where your immense strength comes from, and with what you would have to be bound to be subdued."
Samson answered her, "If I were bound with seven fresh bowstrings, not yet dried, I would lose my strength and become like anyone else."
The lords of the Philistines brought Delilah seven fresh bowstrings, not yet dried, and she bound him with them.

She had posted men in ambush in the room. She cried out to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings as a strand of tow snaps when it touches fire; and the secret of his strength remained hidden.
Delilah said to Samson, "You have mocked me and lied to me. Now tell me, please, with what you must be bound."
He answered her, "If I were bound with new ropes that have never been used, I would lose my strength and become like anyone else."

Delilah took new ropes, bound him with them, and cried out to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" Men were lying in ambush in the room. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a mere thread.

Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and lied to me. Tell me with what you must be bound." He answered her, "You need only weave the seven locks of my head into the web of your loom."
She fastened them with the pin of the loom, then cried out to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" He woke up and tore away the pin, the loom, and the web all at once.
She said to him, "How can you say that you love me, when your heart is not with me? Three times now you have mocked me, without telling me where your immense strength comes from."
As she pressed him like this day after day and wore him out with her nagging, he grew so exasperated that he could have died,

and at last he opened his whole heart to her, "No razor has ever touched my head, for I am consecrated to God as a Nazirite from my mother's womb. If I were shaved, my strength would leave me: I would become weak, like anyone else."

Delilah realized that he had opened his whole heart to her. She sent for the lords of the Philistines, "Come up this time, for he has opened his whole heart to me." They came up to her, the silver in hand.
She lulled Samson to sleep on her knees, called a man, and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to master him, for his strength had left him.

She cried out, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" He woke up, saying to himself, "I will get out of it as I did the other times, I will shake myself free." He did not know that the Lord had withdrawn from him.
The Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, and took him down to Gaza. There they bound him with a double chain of bronze, and he turned the mill in the prison.
But his hair, once shaved off, began to grow again.
The lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to rejoice. They said, "Our god has delivered Samson, our enemy, into our hands."
When they saw him, the people too praised their god, "Our god has delivered into our hands our enemy, the one who laid waste our land and killed so many of us."
In high spirits, they cried out, "Bring Samson out, let him amuse us!" Samson was brought out of the prison, and he had to make sport before them. They had placed him between the pillars.
Samson said to the young man who was holding him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars that support the building, so that I may lean on them."
Now the building was full of men and women; all the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof were about three thousand people, men and women, watching Samson make sport.

Then Samson called on the Lord, "Lord God, remember me, I beg you! Give me back my strength just this once more, O God, that with a single blow I may avenge myself on the Philistines for my two eyes."
Then Samson grasped the two central pillars that supported the building and braced himself against them, the right one with one hand and the left with the other.

"Let me die with the Philistines!" he said. He pushed with all his might, and the building collapsed on the lords and on all the people present. So those he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his whole life.

His brothers and all his father's household came down, took him up, and, having gone back home, buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
There was in the hill country of Ephraim a man named Micah.

He said to his mother, "That silver that was taken from you, about twelve and a half kilograms, over which you pronounced a curse that I myself heard you speak, here it is: I am the one who took it." His mother answered, "May my son be blessed by the Lord!"

He returned the silver to his mother, about twelve and a half kilograms. His mother declared, "I solemnly consecrate this silver to the Lord, from my own hand, on behalf of my son, to make from it a carved image and a cast idol. So I give it back to you."

When he had returned the silver to his mother, she took about two and a half kilograms of it and gave them to the silversmith, who made from it a carved image and a cast idol; they remained in Micah's house.
This Micah had a sanctuary at his house; he made an ephod and household idols, and he installed one of his sons as priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel: everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem of Judah, of the clan of Judah; he was a Levite and was staying there.
This man left the town of Bethlehem of Judah to look for a place to settle. On his way, he came into the hill country of Ephraim, as far as the house of Micah.
Micah asked him, "Where do you come from?" He answered, "I am a Levite, from Bethlehem of Judah, and I am looking for a place to settle."
Micah said to him, "Stay with me; be a father and a priest to me. I will give you about a hundred grams of silver a year, along with clothing and food." And the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to stay with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his own sons.
Micah installed him, and the young Levite served him as priest, living in his house.
Then Micah said, "Now I know that the Lord will do me good, since I have this Levite as my priest."

titres.titre: The migration of the tribe of Dan

versets.t: In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of Dan was looking for a territory to settle in, for it had not yet received an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites chose from among themselves five valiant men, from Zorah and Eshtaol, and sent them to explore and reconnoiter the land. "Go, reconnoiter the land," they told them. The five men reached the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah, where they spent the night.
As they were near Micah's house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. They approached and asked him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing here, and what is your business here?"
He answered them, "Micah does such and such for me: he pays me, and I serve him as priest."
They said to him, "Then inquire of God, so that we may know whether our journey will succeed."
The priest answered them, "Go in peace: the journey you are making is under the eyes of the Lord."

The five men set out and came to Laish. They saw that the people of the town lived in security, in the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and confident; no one in the land held authority to trouble them; they were far from the Sidonians and had no ties with anyone.
They returned to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, who asked them, "What do you report?"
They answered, "Up, let us go up and attack them! We have seen the land: it is excellent. And you, are you going to stay there doing nothing? Do not delay to set out and go take possession of it.
When you arrive, you will find a confident people and a spacious land. God has delivered it into your hands: it is a place where nothing is lacking of all that is on the earth."
So six hundred men of the clan of Dan set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed for war.
They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim, in Judah; that is why the place is still called Mahaneh-dan to this day, west of Kiriath-jearim.
From there they passed into the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah.

Then the five men who had explored the land of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household idols, a carved image, and a cast idol? Now consider what you are to do."
They turned aside there, entered the house of the young Levite, at Micah's, and greeted him.
The six hundred Danites, armed for war, stood at the entrance of the gate.

The five explorers went up, entered the sanctuary, and took the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast idol, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men.
When they had gone into Micah's house and taken the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast idol, the priest asked them, "What are you doing?"

They answered him, "Be quiet! Put your hand over your mouth and come with us: you shall be a father and a priest to us. Is it better to be the priest of one man, or the priest of a whole tribe, of a clan of Israel?"
The priest was glad. He took the ephod, the household idols, and the carved image, and joined the troop.
They set out again, placing the children, the livestock, and the precious goods ahead of them.
They were already far from Micah's house when the men of the neighboring houses gathered and set off in pursuit of the Danites.
They shouted after them; the Danites turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you have mustered all these men?"
He answered, "You have taken away the gods I made for myself, and the priest along with them, and off you go: what is left for me? How dare you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'"
The Danites said to him, "Let us hear your voice no more, or furious men will fall upon you, and you will lose your life and the lives of your household."
Then the Danites went on their way. Seeing that they were stronger than he, Micah turned back and went home.
So the Danites carried off what Micah had made, along with his priest. They marched against Laish, against a peaceful and confident people, put them to the sword, and burned the town.
No one came to its rescue, for it was far from Sidon and had no ties with anyone; it lay in the valley that stretches toward Beth-rehob. The Danites rebuilt the town and settled in it.
They named it Dan, after their ancestor Dan, son of Israel; but the town had previously been called Laish.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves; and Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses, and then his descendants, were priests of the tribe of Dan until the day the land went into exile.
They kept the carved image that Micah had made set up the whole time that the house of God remained at Shiloh.

titres.titre: The Levite and the crime of Gibeah

versets.t: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite who lived deep in the hill country of Ephraim took as his concubine a woman from Bethlehem of Judah.
But his concubine was unfaithful to him and left him to return to her father's house, at Bethlehem of Judah; she stayed there four months.

Her husband set out to go to her, to speak tenderly to her and bring her back; he had with him his servant and two donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and when the young woman's father saw him, he welcomed him with joy.
His father-in-law detained him, and he stayed with him three days; they ate, drank, and spent the nights there.
On the fourth day they rose early, and the Levite prepared to leave. But the young woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Have a morsel of bread first to strengthen yourself, and then you can go."
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the young woman's father said to the husband, "Please agree to stay one more night, and enjoy yourself."
The husband got up to leave, but his father-in-law urged him so much that he came back to spend the night there again.
On the fifth day he rose early to leave. The young woman's father said, "Strengthen yourself first, please, and linger until the day declines." And the two of them ate.

The husband was getting up to leave with his concubine and his servant when his father-in-law said to him, "See, the day is fading, evening is near: spend the night here. The day is drawing to a close; stay here tonight and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can rise early for your journey, and go home."
But the husband refused to stay; he got up and left. He came opposite Jebus, that is, Jerusalem, with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine.
When they were near Jebus, the day was far gone. The servant said to his master, "Come, please, let us stop at this town of the Jebusites and spend the night there."
His master answered, "No, we will not go into a foreign town that does not belong to Israel; we will push on to Gibeah."
He added, "Come, let us try to reach Gibeah or Ramah to spend the night there."
So they continued on their way, and the sun set as they approached Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They stopped there to spend the night. The Levite went in and sat down in the town square, but no one took them into his home for the night.
Now in the evening an old man was coming back from the fields, from his work. He was a man of the hill country of Ephraim who was living at Gibeah; the people of the place were Benjaminites.
Looking up, he saw the traveler in the town square and asked him, "Where are you going? Where do you come from?"

The Levite answered, "We are coming from Bethlehem of Judah and going deep into the hill country of Ephraim, where I am from. I had gone to Bethlehem of Judah, and now I am on my way to the house of the Lord; but no one takes me into his home.
Yet we have straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, for your maidservant, and for the servant who is with me: we lack nothing."
"You are welcome," said the old man. "I will provide for all your needs; only do not spend the night in the square."
He brought him into his house and gave the donkeys fodder. The travelers washed their feet, then ate and drank.

They were enjoying themselves when men of the town, scoundrels, surrounded the house. Beating on the door, they said to the old man, the master of the house, "Bring out the man who has come into your house: we want to abuse him."
The master of the house went out to them and said, "No, my brothers, I beg you, do not do this evil. This man has come into my house: do not commit such an outrage.
Here is my daughter, still a virgin, and this man's concubine. Let me bring them out to you; abuse them and do to them what you will. But do not commit such an outrage against this man."
But the men would not listen to him. Then the Levite seized his concubine and brought her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, then let her go at daybreak.
At dawn the woman came and collapsed at the entrance of the house where her husband was, and she lay there until full daylight.
In the morning her husband got up, opened the door of the house, and went out to continue on his way: his concubine lay at the entrance, her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, "Get up, let us go." But there was no answer: she was dead. Then he lifted her onto his donkey and set out for home.
When he reached home, he took a knife, took hold of his concubine, and cut her up, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, which he sent throughout the territory of Israel.
And all who saw this said, "Never has anything like this happened or been seen since the sons of Israel came up out of Egypt to this day. Think it over, take counsel, and speak."
All the sons of Israel set out, from Dan to Beersheba, including the land of Gilead, and the assembly gathered as one man before the Lord at Mizpah.
The leaders of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God: four hundred thousand foot soldiers armed with the sword.
The Benjaminites heard that the sons of Israel had gone up to Mizpah. The sons of Israel said, "Tell us: how was this crime committed?"
The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, spoke up, "I had come to Gibeah of Benjamin, with my concubine, to spend the night there.
The men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house during the night. They meant to kill me; they raped my concubine, and she died of it.
So I took her body, cut it into pieces, and sent it throughout the territory of Israel, for they have committed a criminal and shameful act in Israel.
Here you all are, sons of Israel: consult together and reach a decision, here and now."
All the people rose as one man, "None of us will go back to his tent, none will return home.
Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will march against it as the lot designates.

In all the tribes of Israel, we will take ten men out of a hundred, a hundred out of a thousand, a thousand out of ten thousand, to fetch provisions for the army, so that when it arrives, Gibeah of Benjamin may be dealt with according to all the outrage it has committed in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered against the town, united as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men throughout the clan of Benjamin to say, "What is this crime that has been committed among you?
Now hand over the scoundrels of Gibeah: we will put them to death and remove the evil from the midst of Israel." But the Benjaminites refused to listen to their brothers, the sons of Israel.
Leaving their towns, they gathered at Gibeah to go to war against the sons of Israel.
That day, twenty-six thousand Benjaminites armed with the sword were counted, coming from the towns, not counting the inhabitants of Gibeah, who made up seven hundred picked men.
Among all this people were seven hundred left-handed picked men, each able to sling a stone at a hair without missing.
On Israel's side, not counting Benjamin, four hundred thousand men armed with the sword were counted, all men of war.
The sons of Israel went up to Bethel and inquired of God, "Which of us shall go up first to fight the Benjaminites?" The Lord answered, "Let Judah go up first."
In the morning the sons of Israel set out and camped facing Gibeah.
They advanced to battle against Benjamin and drew up in battle line before Gibeah.
But the Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and laid low on the ground that day twenty-two thousand men of Israel.
The people of Israel took courage again and drew up once more in battle line, at the same place as the day before.
The sons of Israel went up and wept before the Lord until evening, then inquired of him, "Shall I go again to fight the Benjaminites, my brothers?" The Lord answered, "Go up against them."
On the second day, the sons of Israel advanced again against the Benjaminites,
and that second day Benjamin came out of Gibeah to meet them and again laid low on the ground eighteen thousand of the sons of Israel, all armed with the sword.

Then all the sons of Israel, the whole people, went up to Bethel. They wept there, sitting before the Lord; that day they fasted until evening and offered to the Lord sacrifices, including peace offerings.
Then the sons of Israel inquired of the Lord. In those days the ark of the covenant of God was at Bethel,

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, stood before it. They asked, "Shall I go out yet again to fight the Benjaminites, my brothers, or shall I stop?" The Lord answered, "Go up, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hands."
Then Israel set men in ambush all around Gibeah.
On the third day, the sons of Israel went up against Benjamin and drew up in battle line before Gibeah, as on the previous occasions.

The Benjaminites came out to meet the people and let themselves be drawn away from the town. As on the previous occasions, they began to strike and kill, on the roads, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, in the open country: about thirty men of Israel.
The Benjaminites said to themselves, "There they are, beaten before us as before." But the sons of Israel had planned, "Let us flee, to draw them away from the town, toward the roads."
All the men of Israel left their position and drew up at Baal-tamar, while the ambush of Israel burst from its post, west of Gibeah.
Ten thousand picked men from all Israel came thus facing Gibeah. The fighting was fierce, and the Benjaminites did not suspect the disaster about to strike them.
The Lord struck down Benjamin before Israel, and that day the sons of Israel killed twenty-five thousand one hundred Benjaminites, all armed with the sword.
The Benjaminites saw then that they were beaten. In fact, the men of Israel had given ground before Benjamin only because they were counting on the ambush set near Gibeah.
The men of the ambush rushed swiftly upon Gibeah; they spread out and put the whole town to the sword.
Now there was an agreed signal between the sons of Israel and the ambush: the latter would send up from the town a thick column of smoke.
When the men of Israel turned about in the battle, Benjamin had already killed about thirty of their men and was saying, "There they are, thoroughly beaten before us, as in the first battle."
But the signal, a column of smoke, began to rise from the town. The Benjaminites, turning around, saw the whole town going up in flames toward the sky.
Then the men of Israel turned about, and the Benjaminites were struck with terror when they saw the disaster falling upon them.
They turned their backs on the men of Israel and fled toward the wilderness, but the fighters pressed them hard, and those coming out of the towns cut them down as they passed.
They surrounded Benjamin, pursued him without respite, and crushed him as far as opposite Gibeah, to the east.
Eighteen thousand Benjaminites fell, all valiant men.

The survivors turned their backs and fled toward the wilderness, toward the rock of Rimmon. The men of Israel struck down five thousand of them on the roads, chased them hard as far as Gidom, and killed two thousand more.
The total number of Benjaminites who fell that day was twenty-five thousand men armed with the sword, all valiant men.
Only six hundred men, having turned their backs and fled into the wilderness, reached the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed four months.
The men of Israel then turned back on the Benjaminites and put to the sword the towns, the inhabitants, and the livestock, everything they found; and they set fire to all the towns they came upon.

titres.titre: Wives for the survivors of Benjamin

versets.t: At Mizpah, the sons of Israel had sworn, "None of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjaminite."
The people came to Bethel and stayed there before God until evening. Raising their voices, they wept bitterly
and said, "Why, Lord, God of Israel, has it come about that one tribe is missing today from Israel?"
The next day, the people rose early, built an altar there, and offered sacrifices, including peace offerings.

Then the sons of Israel said, "Among all the tribes of Israel, which one did not come up to the assembly before the Lord?" For a solemn oath had threatened with death anyone who had not come up to the Lord at Mizpah.
The sons of Israel were moved with pity for Benjamin, their brother, "Today," they said, "one tribe has been cut off from Israel!
How can we provide wives for those who remain, since we have sworn by the Lord not to give them our daughters in marriage?"
They asked, "Among the tribes of Israel, which one did not come up to the Lord at Mizpah?" Now no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp, to the assembly.
The people were counted: indeed, not one inhabitant of Jabesh-gilead was present.
So the assembly sent twelve thousand valiant men there, with this order, "Go, put to the sword the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead, including the women and children.
This is what you shall do: you shall devote to destruction every male, and every woman who has already lain with a man."
Among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead, they found four hundred young virgins who had never lain with a man, and they brought them to the camp, at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole assembly sent messengers to the Benjaminites who had taken refuge at the rock of Rimmon, to offer them peace.
The Benjaminites returned, and they were given the women of Jabesh-gilead who had been left alive; but there were not enough for them all.
The people were moved with pity for Benjamin, for the Lord had opened a breach in the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the assembly said, "How can we provide wives for those who remain, since the women of Benjamin have been wiped out?"
And they added, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe may not be blotted out of Israel.
But we cannot give them our daughters in marriage, for the sons of Israel have sworn: Cursed be anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin!"
They went on, "There is, as it happens, the annual feast of the Lord at Shiloh, a town located north of Bethel, east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."
So they gave this order to the Benjaminites, "Go, lie in wait in the vineyards.

Watch; and when the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the choruses, come out from the vineyards, each of you seize a wife from among the daughters of Shiloh, and go back to the land of Benjamin.

If their fathers or brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them: Do us the favor of leaving them to them, for we did not bring back a wife for each of them in the war; and you did not give them to them, which would have made you guilty."
The Benjaminites did so: each took a wife from among the dancers whom they carried off, then they went back to their inheritance, rebuilt their towns, and settled in them.
At that time, each of the sons of Israel returned to his tribe, his clan, and his inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel: everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.

titres.titre: Naomi in the land of Moab
The return of Naomi and the loyalty of Ruth

versets.t: In the days when the Judges ruled, a famine came upon the land. A man of Bethlehem in Judah set out to settle for a time in the country of Moab, he, his wife, and his two sons.

The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and his two sons were named Mahlon and Chilion; they were Ephrathites, from Bethlehem in Judah. They came into the country of Moab and settled there.
Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
These married Moabite women: one was named Orpah, the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years,
and then Mahlon and Chilion also died, both of them, and Naomi was left alone, bereft of her two children and of her husband.
Then she set out, with her daughters-in-law, to leave the country of Moab, for there she had heard that the Lord had visited his people and given them bread.
So she left the place where she had been living, her two daughters-in-law with her, and they set out on the road to return to the land of Judah.
Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, each of you return to your mother's house. May the Lord show you his faithful love, as you have shown it to those who have died and to me.
May he grant each of you to find rest in the house of a husband!" Then she kissed them. But they began to weep aloud
and said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people."
Naomi answered, "Turn back, my daughters! Why would you come with me? Do I still have sons in my womb who could become your husbands?
Turn back, my daughters, go! I am too old to belong to a husband. And even if I said, 'I still have hope,' even if I were to belong to a man this very night and bear sons,

would you wait for them to grow up? Would you keep yourselves from marrying a husband on that account? No, my daughters! My bitterness is greater than yours, for the hand of the Lord has been raised against me."
Again they wept aloud. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and went back, but Ruth clung to her.
Naomi said to her, "See, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her god; go back, you also, after your sister-in-law."
Ruth answered, "Do not press me to leave you, to turn away from you. Where you go, I will go; where you spend the night, I will spend it; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the Lord deal with me in all severity if anything but death separates me from you!"
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.
So the two of them walked on until they came to Bethlehem. When they entered it, the whole town was stirred on their account, and the women said, "Is this not Naomi?"
She answered them, "Do not call me Naomi, the sweet one; call me Mara, the bitter one, for the Almighty has filled me with bitterness.
I went away with my hands full, and the Lord brings me back with my hands empty. Why call me Naomi, when the Lord has testified against me and the Almighty has brought me low?"
So Naomi came back, and with her Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, who was returning from the country of Moab. They arrived at Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

titres.titre: Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz

versets.t: Naomi had, on her husband's side, a kinsman named Boaz, a man of worth and wealth, of the clan of Elimelech.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go out to the fields to glean ears of grain behind anyone who will show me favor." She answered her, "Go, my daughter."
So she went out to glean in a field, behind the harvesters. As it happened, it was the plot belonging to Boaz, of the clan of Elimelech.
And Boaz arrived from Bethlehem. He said to the harvesters, "The Lord be with you!" They answered him, "The Lord bless you!"
Boaz asked the servant who was in charge of the harvesters, "Whose young woman is this?"
The servant answered, "She is a young Moabite woman, the one who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.
She asked, 'Let me glean and gather ears of grain among the sheaves, behind the harvesters.' She came, and she has stayed on her feet from morning until now; she has hardly rested for a moment."
Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen well, my daughter: do not go to glean in another field, do not go far from here, but stay with my servant girls.
Keep your eyes on the field they are harvesting and follow them. I have ordered the servants not to touch you. If you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink from what the servants have drawn."
Then she threw herself face to the ground, bowed low, and said to him, "How is it that I have found favor with you, that you take care of me, a foreigner?"

Boaz answered her, "I have been told all that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband: you left your father, your mother, and your native land, and you came to a people you did not know until yesterday.
May the Lord repay you for what you have done! May your reward be full, from the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!"
She said, "May I always find favor in your eyes, my lord! For you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your servant, though I am not even one of your servant girls."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here, eat some of this bread and dip your piece in the vinegar." She sat down beside the harvesters; he held out roasted grain to her. She ate her fill and kept what was left.
Then she got up to glean. Boaz gave this order to his servants, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her.
You shall even pull out some ears from the bundles for her and leave them on the ground for her to gather, without scolding her."
She gleaned in the field until evening, then she beat out what she had gathered: it came to about twenty-two liters of barley.
She carried it and went back to the town, and her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. Ruth also brought out what she had kept from her meal, once she was full, and gave it to her.

Her mother-in-law asked her, "Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Blessed be the one who took notice of you!" Then Ruth told her mother-in-law with whom she had worked: "The man with whom I worked today is named Boaz."

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the Lord, who has not withdrawn his faithful love from the living or from the dead!" And she added, "This man is a close relative of ours: he is one of those who have the right of redemption over us."
Ruth the Moabite went on, "He even said to me, 'Stay with my servants until they have finished all my harvest.'"
Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It is better, my daughter, that you go out with his servant girls; that way no one will mistreat you in another field."
So she stayed with the servant girls of Boaz to glean, until the end of the barley harvest and of the wheat harvest. And she lived with her mother-in-law.

titres.titre: Ruth at the feet of Boaz, on the threshing floor

versets.t: Naomi, her mother-in-law, said to her, "My daughter, should I not seek a home for you where you will be happy?
Now Boaz, with whose servant girls you have worked, is he not our kinsman? This very night he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor.
Wash yourself, put on perfume, wrap your cloak around you, and go down to the threshing floor; but do not make yourself known to him until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, mark well the place where he stretches out; then go, uncover his feet, and lie down there. He himself will tell you what you must do."
Ruth answered her, "I will do everything you tell me."
She went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had commanded her.
Boaz ate and drank, and his heart grew merry. He went to lie down at the end of the pile of sheaves. Then Ruth came quietly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.
In the middle of the night the man shivered; he turned over, and there was a woman lying at his feet.
He asked, "Who are you?" She answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread the corner of your cloak over your servant, for you have the right of redemption over us."
He said, "May you be blessed by the Lord, my daughter! Your latest kindness surpasses the first, for you have not run after the young men, whether poor or rich.
Now, my daughter, do not be afraid: everything you ask of me I will do for you, for everyone at the town gate knows that you are a woman of worth.
It is true that I have the right of redemption; but there is a kinsman closer than I.

Spend the night here. In the morning, if he wishes to exercise his right over you, well and good, let him do it; but if he does not want to, then I will redeem you, as the Lord lives! Stay lying down until morning."

So she stayed lying at his feet until morning, then got up before the hour when one person can be recognized by another, for Boaz had said to himself, "Let no one know that this woman came to the threshing floor!"
He said further, "Give me the cloak you are wearing and hold it firmly." She held it, and he measured out six measures of barley into it, which he loaded onto her. Then he went back to town.
Ruth came back to her mother-in-law, who asked her, "How did it go, my daughter?" And Ruth told her all that the man had done for her.
She added, "He gave me these six measures of barley, saying to me, 'You must not go back to your mother-in-law with your hands empty.'"
Naomi said to her, "Stay here, my daughter, until you know how the matter will turn out; for this man will have no rest until he has settled it this very day."

titres.titre: The redemption at the town gate
The birth of Obed, ancestor of David

versets.t: Boaz went up to the town gate and sat down there. And there was the man with the right of redemption passing by, the one of whom Boaz had spoken. Boaz said to him, "You there, come over, come sit here." The man came over and sat down.
Then Boaz took ten men from among the elders of the town and said to them, "Sit down here." They sat down.
He said to the man with the right of redemption, "The plot of field that belonged to our brother Elimelech, Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is putting up for sale.

I thought I should inform you and say to you: Buy it, before those seated here and before the elders of my people. If you wish to exercise your right of redemption, do so; if not, tell me, so that I may know, for no one can redeem before you, and I come after you." The man answered, "I will redeem it."
Boaz went on, "On the day you acquire the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the wife of the dead man, to raise up the name of the dead man over his inheritance."
The man with the right of redemption answered, "Then I cannot redeem it for myself, or I would ruin my own inheritance. Exercise my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot do it."
In former times in Israel, to confirm a redemption or an exchange, the custom was this: one man took off his sandal and gave it to the other. This was the manner of attesting a matter in Israel.
So the man with the right of redemption said to Boaz, "Make the purchase for yourself." And he took off his sandal.
Then Boaz said to the elders and to all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have acquired from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, and to Chilion and to Mahlon.

And at the same time I have acquired as my wife Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, to raise up the name of the dead man over his inheritance, so that this name may not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his town. You are witnesses to this today."

All the people who were at the gate, and the elders, said, "We are witnesses! May the Lord make the woman who is coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel! Become powerful in Ephrathah, and make a name for yourself in Bethlehem!
May your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, through the offspring that the Lord will give you by this young woman!"
Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He united with her, and the Lord granted her to conceive: she gave birth to a son.
The women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the Lord, who has not left you today without a redeemer! May his name be celebrated in Israel!
He will restore your life and be the support of your old age, since he is born of your daughter-in-law, the one who loves you and who is worth more to you than seven sons."
Naomi took the child, laid him on her breast, and became his nurse.
The neighbor women gave him a name, saying, "A son is born to Naomi!" They called him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
This is the line of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron;
Hezron fathered Ram; Ram fathered Amminadab;
Amminadab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon;
Salmon fathered Boaz; Boaz fathered Obed;
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.

titres.titre: Hannah and the birth of Samuel

versets.t: There was a man from Ramathaim-zophim, in the hill country of Ephraim, named Elkanah. He was the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph; he was an Ephraimite.
He had two wives: one was named Hannah, the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Every year this man went up from his town to worship the Lord of hosts and to offer him sacrifices at Shiloh. There the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the Lord.
On the day when Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters;
but to Hannah he gave a special portion, for he loved her, though the Lord had made her barren.
Her rival kept wounding her, seeking to humiliate her because the Lord had left her childless.
So it went year after year: whenever Hannah went up to the house of the Lord, Peninnah wounded her in this way. Then Hannah would weep and would not eat.
Elkanah her husband said to her: "Hannah, why are you weeping? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad? Am I not worth more to you than ten sons?"
One day at Shiloh, after they had eaten and drunk, Hannah rose. The priest Eli was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of the temple of the Lord.
Her soul filled with bitterness, she prayed to the Lord, weeping many tears,

and she made this vow: "Lord of hosts, if you will only look upon the misery of your servant, if you remember me and do not forget your servant, if you give your servant a son, then I will give him to the Lord for all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."
As she prayed long before the Lord, Eli watched her mouth.
Now Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice could not be heard. Eli thought she was drunk
and said to her: "How long will you stay drunk? Put away your wine!"
Hannah answered: "No, my lord! I am a woman weighed down; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I was pouring out my soul before the Lord.
Do not take your servant for a worthless woman: it is out of the depth of my grief and sorrow that I have spoken until now."
Eli replied: "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant you what you have asked of him!"
She said: "May your servant find favour in your eyes!" Then she went away; she ate, and her face was no longer the same.
The next morning they rose early, worshipped before the Lord, and returned home to Ramah. Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her.
In due time Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, for, she said, I asked him of the Lord.
Elkanah her husband went up with all his household to offer the Lord the yearly sacrifice and to fulfil his vow.
But Hannah did not go up; she said to her husband: "When the child is weaned, I will bring him to appear before the Lord and to remain there for ever."
Elkanah her husband said to her: "Do what seems good to you. Stay until you have weaned him; only may the Lord fulfil his word!" So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.

When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, bringing three bulls, about twenty-two litres of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the Lord at Shiloh. The child was still very young.
They slaughtered the bull and brought the child to Eli.
Hannah said: "Pardon, my lord! As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you, praying to the Lord.
It was for this child that I prayed, and the Lord has granted me what I asked of him.
In turn, I give him to the Lord: for all the days of his life he is given to the Lord." And they worshipped the Lord there.

titres.titre: The oracle against the house of Eli

versets.t: Hannah prayed this prayer: "My heart exults in the Lord, the Lord lifts up my strength; my mouth laughs at my enemies, for I rejoice in your salvation.
No one is holy like the Lord, there is no God but you; there is no Rock like our God.
Do not multiply proud words, let no arrogance come out of your mouth: the Lord is a God who knows all things, and it is he who weighs our deeds.
The bow of the mighty is broken, but the weak are girded with strength.
The well-fed hire themselves out for bread, and the hungry hunger no more; the barren woman bears seven times, and the mother of many sons withers away.
The Lord kills and gives life, he brings down to the realm of the dead and raises up.
The Lord makes poor and makes rich, he humbles and he exalts.

From the dust he lifts the weak, from the ash heap he raises the poor, to seat them among princes and give them a throne of glory as their portion. For the pillars of the earth belong to the Lord, and on them he has set the world.
He watches over the steps of his faithful, but the wicked vanish in darkness; for it is not by his own strength that a man prevails.

The Lord! his adversaries will be shattered; against them he will thunder from the heights of heaven. The Lord will judge to the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and lift up the strength of his anointed."
Then Elkanah returned home to Ramah, while the child stayed in the service of the Lord, under the eyes of the priest Eli.
Now the sons of Eli were worthless men: they did not know the Lord.
This is how these priests treated the people: when a man offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come, while the meat was cooking, with a three-pronged fork in his hand;
he would thrust it into the cauldron, the pot, or the kettle, and whatever the fork brought up, the priest took for himself. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh.

Even worse, before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man offering the sacrifice: "Give the priest meat to roast; he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw."
If the man answered: "Let the fat be burned first, then take whatever you want," the servant would reply: "No, give it now, or I will take it by force!"
The sin of these young men was very great before the Lord, for they treated the Lord's offering with contempt.
Meanwhile Samuel ministered before the Lord; this small child was clothed in a linen ephod.
Each year his mother made him a little robe and brought it to him when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying: "May the Lord give you children by this woman in place of the one she asked for the Lord!" Then they would return home.
The Lord visited Hannah: she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the Lord.
Eli was very old. He heard all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
He said to them: "Why do you do such things? I hear from all the people about your evil deeds.
No, my sons! The report I hear is not good: you are making the people of the Lord sin.

If a man sins against another, God is there to arbitrate; but if he sins against the Lord, who will intercede for him?" But they did not listen to their father's voice, for the Lord meant to put them to death.
Meanwhile the boy Samuel kept growing, and he found favour with the Lord and with men.
A man of God came to Eli and said to him: "Thus says the Lord: Did I not reveal myself plainly to the house of your father when they were in Egypt, slaves of Pharaoh's house?

I chose it out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense and to carry the ephod before me; and I gave to the house of your father a share of all the offerings by fire of the sons of Israel.

Why then do you trample on my sacrifices and my offerings, which I commanded for my dwelling? Why do you honour your sons more than me, fattening yourselves on the best of all the offerings of Israel my people?

Therefore, oracle of the Lord, the God of Israel: I did indeed say that your house and the house of your father would walk before me for ever. But now, oracle of the Lord, far be it from me! For I honour those who honour me, and those who despise me will be covered with shame.
Behold, days are coming when I will break your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will be no old man in your house.
You will see the distress of my dwelling, while the Lord fills Israel with good things; and never again will there be an old man in your house.
I will not cut off from my altar every one of yours, only to let your eyes waste away and your soul languish; but all the descendants of your house will die in the prime of life.
And this will be the sign to you: what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas. On the same day both of them will die.
Then I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will act according to my heart and my desire; I will build him a lasting house, and he will walk before my anointed always.

Then whoever is left of your house will come to bow down before him for a little money and a piece of bread, and will say: Admit me, I beg you, to some priestly office, so that I may have a piece of bread to eat."
The boy Samuel ministered to the Lord under the eyes of Eli. In those days the word of the Lord was rare, and visions were infrequent.
Now that night Eli was lying in his place. His eyes had begun to grow dim, and he could no longer see.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.
The Lord called Samuel. He answered: "Here I am!"
He ran to Eli and said: "Here I am, since you called me." Eli answered: "I did not call you; go back and lie down." And he went and lay down.
Again the Lord called: "Samuel!" Samuel rose, went to Eli, and said: "Here I am, since you called me." Eli answered: "I did not call you, my son; go back and lie down."
Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.
A third time the Lord called Samuel. He rose, went to Eli, and said: "Here I am, since you called me." Then Eli understood that it was the Lord who was calling the boy.
He said to Samuel: "Go and lie down, and if you are called again, you shall say: Speak, Lord, your servant is listening." So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The Lord came, stood there, and called as before: "Samuel! Samuel!" Samuel answered: "Speak, your servant is listening."
The Lord said to Samuel: "Behold, I am about to do something in Israel that will make the ears of everyone who hears of it tingle.
