On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end.
I have told him: I am going to judge his house for ever, because of the guilt he knew about; for his sons were bringing a curse upon themselves, and he did not restrain them.
Therefore I swear to the house of Eli: never will the guilt of the house of Eli be wiped away, by sacrifice or by offering."
Samuel lay down until morning, then opened the doors of the house of the Lord. He was afraid to report the vision to Eli.
But Eli called Samuel: "Samuel, my son!" He answered: "Here I am."
Eli asked: "What word did he speak to you? Hide nothing from me, I beg you. May the Lord deal with you with the utmost severity if you hide from me a single word of all that he told you!"
Samuel reported everything to him, hiding nothing. And Eli said: "It is the Lord: let him do what seems good to him."
Samuel grew up; the Lord was with him, and he let none of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, recognized that Samuel was a true prophet of the Lord.
The Lord continued to appear at Shiloh, for it was at Shiloh that the Lord revealed himself to Samuel through his word.

titres.titre: The ark captured by the Philistines

versets.t: The word of Samuel came to all Israel. In those days Israel went out to war against the Philistines. They camped near Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up in battle line facing Israel; the fighting spread, and Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the open field.

When the people returned to camp, the elders of Israel said: "Why has the Lord let us be defeated today by the Philistines? Let us fetch from Shiloh the ark of the covenant of the Lord: let it come among us and save us from the hand of our enemies!"

So the people sent to Shiloh, and they brought back from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the covenant of the Lord entered the camp, all Israel raised a mighty shout, and the earth resounded with it.
Hearing this shout, the Philistines asked: "What is this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?" And they learned that the ark of the Lord had come to the camp.
The Philistines were afraid, for they said: "God has come into the camp!" And they added: "Woe to us! Nothing like this has ever happened before.
Woe to us! Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck Egypt with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Take courage! Be men, Philistines, or you will become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been slaves to you. Be men and fight!"
The Philistines gave battle. Israel was defeated, and everyone fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great: thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.
The ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A man of Benjamin escaped from the front and reached Shiloh that same day, his clothes torn and his head covered with dust.
When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat beside the road, watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. The man entered the town to bring the news, and the whole town began to cry out.
Hearing these cries, Eli asked: "What is this great uproar?" The man hurried over to tell Eli.
Now Eli was ninety-eight years old; his eyes were fixed, and he could no longer see.
The man said to Eli: "I have come from the front; it was from there that I fled today." Eli asked: "What happened, my son?"
The messenger answered: "Israel fled before the Philistines; the people suffered a heavy defeat; your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are also dead, and the ark of God has been captured."
As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat, against the doorpost: he broke his neck and died, for he was an old and heavy man. He had judged Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant, about to give birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she doubled over and gave birth, for the pains had seized her.
As she was dying, the women around her said: "Do not be afraid, you have given birth to a son!" But she did not answer or pay attention.
She named the child Ichabod, "No-glory," saying: "The glory has departed from Israel," because of the capture of the ark of God and the death of her father-in-law and her husband.
She repeated: "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
The Philistines, having seized the ark of God, carried it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
They took the ark of God, brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon.
The next morning the people of Ashdod rose early: there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the Lord. They lifted Dagon up and put him back in his place.

The following day, early in the morning, there was Dagon again, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the Lord; his head and both his hands, cut off, lay on the threshold: only Dagon's trunk was left to him.
That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon at Ashdod do not step on the threshold.
The hand of the Lord lay heavy on the people of Ashdod: he spread terror and struck them with tumours, in Ashdod and its territory.
Seeing this, the people of Ashdod said: "The ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, for his hand lies hard on us and on Dagon our god."

So they summoned to them all the rulers of the Philistines and asked: "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" The rulers answered: "Let the ark of the God of Israel be moved to Gath." And they moved it there.
But after this move, the hand of the Lord fell upon the town and threw it into very great panic: he struck the people of the town, from the least to the greatest, and tumours broke out on them.
So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But when the ark of God entered Ekron, the people of Ekron began to cry out: "They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people!"
They summoned all the rulers of the Philistines and said: "Send away the ark of the God of Israel! Let it return to its own place and stop killing us and our people."
For a deadly terror reigned throughout the town: the hand of God lay very heavy there. Those who did not die were struck with tumours, and the town's cry of distress went up to heaven.

titres.titre: The return of the ark to Israel

versets.t: The ark of the Lord stayed seven months in the land of the Philistines.
The Philistines called the priests and the diviners and asked: "What shall we do with the ark of the Lord? Tell us how to send it back to its place."

They answered: "If you send back the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty: you must by all means offer him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand had not withdrawn from you."

The Philistines asked: "What guilt offering should we offer him?" They answered: "Five gold tumours and five gold mice, according to the number of the rulers of the Philistines, for one and the same plague struck you and your rulers.
So make images of your tumours and images of the mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel: perhaps he will stop pressing his hand on you, on your gods, and on your land.
Why harden your hearts as Egypt and Pharaoh hardened theirs? After God had dealt harshly with them, did they not have to let the sons of Israel go?
Now then, prepare a new cart and take two nursing cows that have never borne a yoke. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves back to the barn, away from them.
Take the ark of the Lord, place it on the cart, and set beside it, in a box, the gold objects you are offering him as a guilt offering. Then let it go.

Watch it: if it goes up toward its own territory, in the direction of Beth-shemesh, then it is the Lord who has brought this great disaster upon us; if not, we will know that it was not his hand that struck us, but that this happened to us by chance."
The people did so: they took two nursing cows, hitched them to the cart, and shut their calves in the barn.
They placed on the cart the ark of the Lord, along with the box containing the gold mice and the images of their tumours.

The cows went straight along the road to Beth-shemesh, keeping to the one highway; they went along lowing, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left. The rulers of the Philistines walked behind them as far as the outskirts of Beth-shemesh.
The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they looked up, they saw the ark and rejoiced to see it.
The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. There was a large stone there. They split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the Lord.

The Levites had taken down the ark of the Lord and the box that went with it, containing the gold objects, and had set them all on the large stone. That day the people of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord.
After seeing this, the five rulers of the Philistines returned that same day to Ekron.
These are the gold tumours that the Philistines offered to the Lord as a guilt offering: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron.

And the gold mice matched the number of all the Philistine towns of the five rulers, both the fortified towns and the open villages. Witness the large stone on which they set the ark of the Lord: it is still today in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.

But the Lord struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh, because they had looked into the ark of the Lord: he struck down seventy of them. And the people mourned, for the Lord had struck them a great blow.
The people of Beth-shemesh said: "Who can stand before the Lord, this holy God? And to whom will the ark go up when it leaves us?"
They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying: "The Philistines have returned the ark of the Lord; come down and take it up to your place."
The people of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the Lord; they brought it into the house of Abinadab, on the hill, and consecrated his son Eleazar to guard it.
From the day the ark settled at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, twenty years, and the whole house of Israel longed for the Lord.

Then Samuel said to the whole house of Israel: "If it is with all your heart that you are returning to the Lord, remove from among you the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth, turn your hearts firmly to the Lord and serve him alone: then he will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines."
So the sons of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and served the Lord alone.
Samuel said: "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the Lord for you."

They gathered at Mizpah. They drew water and poured it out before the Lord, they fasted that day and confessed: "We have sinned against the Lord." And Samuel administered justice for the sons of Israel at Mizpah.
The Philistines heard that the sons of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, and their rulers went up against Israel. When they heard of it, the sons of Israel were afraid of the Philistines
and said to Samuel: "Do not stop crying out for us to the Lord our God, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines."
Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it whole as a burnt offering to the Lord; he cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines advanced to attack Israel. But that day the Lord thundered a great crash upon them, threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel.
Coming out from Mizpah, the men of Israel pursued the Philistines and cut them down as far as below Beth-car.
Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen, and named it Ebenezer, "the stone of help," saying: "Thus far the Lord has helped us."
So humbled, the Philistines came no more into the territory of Israel, and the hand of the Lord was against them all the days of Samuel.

The towns that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to it, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel wrested their territory from the hand of the Philistines. And there was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel administered justice in Israel all the days of his life.
Each year he went on a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and he rendered justice to Israel in all these places.
Then he would return to Ramah, where his home was; there too he judged Israel, and there he built an altar to the Lord.
When Samuel had grown old, he appointed his sons as judges of Israel.
His firstborn son was named Joel, the second Abijah; they rendered justice at Beersheba.
But Samuel's sons did not walk in his ways: they let themselves be corrupted by gain, took bribes, and perverted justice.
All the elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him: "You are old now, and your sons do not walk in your ways. So appoint over us a king to govern us, like all the nations have."
This word displeased Samuel, because they had said: "Give us a king to govern us." And Samuel prayed to the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel: "Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you; for it is not you they are rejecting, it is me they are rejecting, refusing to have me reign over them.
As they have acted from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until now, abandoning me to serve other gods, so they are acting toward you as well.
Now then, listen to their voice; but warn them solemnly and make known to them the ways of the king who will reign over them."
Samuel reported all the words of the Lord to the people who were asking him for a king.
He said: "These are the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and assign them to his chariots and his cavalry, and they will run before his chariot.
He will make them commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties; he will have them plough his fields, reap his harvest, and make his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters as perfumers, cooks, and bakers.
He will take your fields, your vineyards, and your best olive trees, and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your crops and your vineyards, and give it to his courtiers and his servants.
He will take your male and female servants, your best oxen and your donkeys, and put them to his service.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of the king you have chosen for yourselves, but on that day the Lord will not answer you."
The people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel. They said: "No! There shall be a king over us.
We too will be like all the nations: our king will govern us, he will go out at our head and fight our battles."
Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the ears of the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel: "Listen to their voice, and give them a king." Then Samuel said to the men of Israel: "Return, each of you, to your own town."

titres.titre: Saul in search of the donkeys

versets.t: There was a man of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah; he was a Benjaminite, a man of standing.
He had a son named Saul, young and handsome: no man of Israel was more handsome than he, and he stood a head taller than all the people.
Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, had strayed. Kish said to his son Saul: "Take one of the servants and go look for the donkeys."

They crossed the hill country of Ephraim, then the land of Shalishah, without finding anything; they crossed the land of Shaalim: the donkeys were not there; they crossed the land of Benjamin, without finding them.
When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul said to the servant who was with him: "Come, let us turn back, or my father may stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us."
The servant answered him: "Look, there is in this town a man of God, a man greatly respected: everything he says comes true without fail. Let us go there; perhaps he will tell us the way to take."
Saul said to his servant: "If we go, what shall we bring the man? There is no more bread in our bags, and we have no gift to offer the man of God. What do we have?"
The servant answered: "I still have with me a quarter of a piece of silver; I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way."
(Formerly in Israel, when someone went to inquire of God, he would say: Come, let us go to the seer. For the one now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.)
Saul said to his servant: "Well said! Come, let us go." And they went to the town where the man of God was.
As they were climbing the ascent to the town, they met young women coming out to draw water, and they asked them: "Is the seer here?"
They answered: "Yes, he is right there ahead of you! Hurry: he has come to town today, for the people are offering a sacrifice today on the high place.

As soon as you enter the town, you will find him before he goes up to eat at the high place; the people will not eat until he arrives, for it is he who blesses the sacrifice, and afterward the guests eat. So go up: you will find him now."
They went up to the town. They had just entered when Samuel came out toward them, on his way up to the high place.
Now the day before Saul's arrival, the Lord had made this revelation to Samuel:

"Tomorrow, at this same hour, I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin; you shall anoint him as ruler over my people Israel, and he will save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen the misery of my people, and their cry has come up to me."
As soon as Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him: "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you; he is the one who will govern my people."
Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gateway and said: "Tell me, please, where the seer's house is."
Samuel answered Saul: "I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place: you shall eat with me today, and tomorrow morning I will let you go, after I have told you all that is on your heart.
As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them: they have been found. And to whom does all that Israel treasures belong, if not to you and to all your father's house?"
Saul answered: "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the smallest of the tribes of Israel? Is not my clan the least of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why do you speak to me like this?"
Samuel then took Saul and his servant, brought them into the hall, and gave them the chief place among the guests, who numbered about thirty.
Samuel said to the cook: "Bring the portion I gave you, the one I told you to set aside."

The cook lifted up the leg with what goes with it and set it before Saul. Samuel said: "Here is what was reserved: help yourself and eat, for it was kept for you for this occasion when I summoned the people." So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
Then they went down from the high place to the town, and Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof.
The next day they rose early. At dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof: "Get up, and I will send you on your way." Saul rose, and the two of them, he and Samuel, went out.

As they were going down to the edge of the town, Samuel said to Saul: "Tell the servant to go on ahead of us." The servant went on ahead. "You, stay here a moment," Samuel added, "and I will let you hear the word of God."
Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul's head, and kissed him, then said: "Has not the Lord anointed you as ruler over his heritage?

When you leave me today, you will find near Rachel's tomb, at Zelzah, in the territory of Benjamin, two men who will tell you: The donkeys you went to look for have been found; your father is no longer thinking about the donkeys, but is worried about you and wondering: What shall I do about my son?

From there, going on your way, you will come to the oak of Tabor. There you will meet three men going up to God at Bethel: one carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, the third a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves, which you will take from their hand.

Then you will come to Gibeah of God, where there is a Philistine garrison. As you enter the town, you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place, preceded by the harp, the tambourine, the flute, and the lyre, and they will be prophesying.
Then the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you; you will prophesy with them and be changed into another man.
When these signs have come to pass for you, do whatever the occasion calls for, for God is with you.
You will go down ahead of me to Gilgal, and I will come down to join you there to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. You will wait seven days, until I come to tell you what you are to do."
As soon as Saul turned his back to leave Samuel, God changed his heart, and all these signs came to pass that same day.
When they reached Gibeah, a band of prophets came to meet him; the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.
Seeing that he was prophesying with the prophets, all who had known him before said to one another: "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"
A man from the place retorted: "And who is their father?" This is how the saying arose: Is Saul also among the prophets?
When he had finished prophesying, he went to the high place.
Saul's uncle asked him and his servant: "Where did you go?" Saul answered: "To look for the donkeys; but finding them nowhere, we went to see Samuel."
Saul's uncle said: "Tell me, then, what Samuel said to you."
Saul answered his uncle: "He assured us that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingship, of which Samuel had spoken, he told him nothing.
Samuel summoned the people before the Lord at Mizpah,

and he said to the sons of Israel: "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: It was I who brought Israel up from Egypt and delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.

But today you are rejecting your God, the one who saves you from all your troubles and all your distress, and you say to him: Give us a king! Well then, present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes and your clans."
Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen by lot.
He had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by clans, and the clan of Matri was chosen; then Saul, son of Kish, was chosen. They looked for him, but could not find him.
They inquired of the Lord again: "Has the man come here?" The Lord answered: "There he is, hidden among the baggage."
They ran and pulled him out; he stood in the midst of the people, taller than everyone by a head.
Samuel said to all the people: "Look at the one the Lord has chosen: there is no one like him in all the people!" And all the people shouted: "Long live the king!"
Samuel then set forth to the people the laws of the kingship, wrote them in a book that he laid before the Lord, and then he sent all the people away, each to his home.
Saul too went home to Gibeah, accompanied by the brave men whose hearts God had touched.
But some worthless men said: "How can this fellow save us?" They despised him and brought him no gift. But Saul acted as if he heard nothing.
Nahash the Ammonite went up and camped against Jabesh-gilead. All the inhabitants of Jabesh said to Nahash: "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."
But Nahash the Ammonite answered them: "I will make a treaty with you on one condition only: that I gouge out everyone's right eye, to bring disgrace on all Israel."
The elders of Jabesh said to him: "Grant us seven days' respite, so that we may send messengers throughout the territory of Israel; if no one comes to save us, we will surrender to you."
The messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and reported these words in the ears of the people; then all the people wept aloud.
Just then Saul was coming in from the fields, behind his oxen. He asked: "What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?" They reported to him the words of the men of Jabesh.
When he heard these words, the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul, and his anger blazed up violently.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them in pieces, and sent them by the messengers throughout the territory of Israel, with this message: "This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march out behind Saul and Samuel!" The terror of the Lord fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.
Saul mustered them at Bezek: there were three hundred thousand men of Israel and thirty thousand men of Judah.

They said to the messengers who had come from Jabesh: "Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be rescued." The messengers went back and reported it to the men of Jabesh, who were filled with joy.
Then the men of Jabesh said to the Ammonites: "Tomorrow we will surrender to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you."

The next day Saul divided the people into three companies. They entered the enemy camp during the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. The survivors were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
Then the people said to Samuel: "Who was it that said: Shall Saul reign over us? Hand over these men, that we may put them to death!"
But Saul said: "No one shall be put to death today, for today the Lord has saved Israel."
Samuel said to the people: "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingship."

All the people went to Gilgal, and there, before the Lord, they made Saul king. They offered peace offerings before the Lord, and Saul and all the men of Israel gave themselves over to great rejoicing there.
Samuel said to all Israel: "I have listened to your voice in all that you asked of me, and I have set a king over you.
From now on, it is the king who will walk before you; as for me, I am old, my hair has turned white, and my sons are among you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.

Here I am. Testify against me before the Lord and before his anointed: Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I wronged? Whom have I oppressed? From whom have I taken a bribe to close my eyes? I will restore it to you."
They answered: "You have not wronged us, you have not oppressed us, you have taken nothing from anyone."
He said to them: "The Lord is witness against you, and his anointed is witness today, that you have found nothing in my hands." They answered: "He is witness."
Samuel said to the people: "Yes, it is the Lord who made Moses and Aaron and who brought your fathers up from the land of Egypt.
Now then, take your stand: I am going to call you to judgment before the Lord, reminding you of all the good deeds he has done for you and for your fathers.
When Jacob had come to Egypt and your fathers cried out to the Lord, the Lord sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.
But they forgot the Lord their God; so he handed them over to Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, to the Philistines, and to the king of Moab, who made war on them.
They cried out to the Lord: We have sinned, for we have abandoned the Lord to serve the Baals and the Ashtaroth; now deliver us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you.
Then the Lord sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and he delivered you from the hand of the enemies around you, so that you lived in safety.
But when you saw Nahash, king of the Ammonites, marching against you, you said to me: No, a king shall reign over us! though the Lord your God was your king.
Well, here is the king you have chosen, the one you asked for: behold, the Lord has given you a king.
If you fear the Lord, if you serve him and listen to his voice, if you do not rebel against his command, then you and the king who reigns over you will follow the Lord your God, and all will be well.
But if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord, if you rebel against his command, then the hand of the Lord will be against you as it was against your fathers.
Now once again, take your stand and see the great thing that the Lord is about to do before your eyes.

Is it not the wheat harvest today? I am going to call upon the Lord: he will send thunder and rain. Then you will know, you will see how grave the Lord considers the evil you have done in asking for a king for yourselves."
Samuel called upon the Lord, and that day the Lord sent thunder and rain; and all the people were seized with a great fear of the Lord and of Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel: "Pray to the Lord your God for your servants, that we may not die; for we have added to all our sins the wrong of asking for a king."
Samuel answered the people: "Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil; yet do not turn away from the Lord, serve the Lord with all your heart.
Do not turn away to follow empty things, unable to profit or to save, for they are nothing but emptiness.
For the Lord will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name; it is the Lord who was pleased to make you his people.
As for me, far be it from me to sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you! I will teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the Lord and serve him faithfully, with all your heart; see what great things he has done for you.
But if you persist in evil, you will perish, you and your king."

titres.titre: The Philistine war and the fault of Saul

versets.t: Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty-two years over Israel.

Saul chose for himself three thousand men of Israel: two thousand were with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people away, each to his tent.
Jonathan struck down the Philistine garrison that was at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. Saul had the horn sounded throughout the land, saying: "Let the Hebrews hear!"
All Israel heard the news: Saul has struck down the Philistine garrison, and Israel has made itself odious to the Philistines. The people were summoned behind Saul at Gilgal.
The Philistines gathered to fight Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.
Seeing themselves in great distress, for they were hard pressed, the men of Israel hid in caves, thickets, rocks, tunnels, and cisterns.
Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan, into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people behind him were trembling.
He waited seven days, the time set by Samuel; but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering away from Saul.
Then Saul said: "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.
He had scarcely finished offering the burnt offering when Samuel arrived. Saul went out to meet him and greet him.

Samuel asked: "What have you done?" Saul answered: "I saw that the people were scattering away from me, that you were not coming at the appointed time, and that the Philistines were gathering at Michmash.
I said to myself: The Philistines are going to come down on me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favour of the Lord! So I forced myself and offered the burnt offering."
Samuel said to Saul: "You have acted foolishly! You have not kept the command that the Lord your God gave you. Otherwise the Lord would have established your kingship over Israel for ever.
But now your kingship will not endure: the Lord has sought out a man after his own heart, and has appointed him ruler over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded you."
Samuel rose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul reviewed the people who remained with him: about six hundred men.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the people who remained with them were stationed at Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash.
From the Philistine camp came out a raiding party in three companies: one took the direction of Ophrah, toward the land of Shual;
another took the direction of Beth-horon; the third took the direction of the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim, toward the wilderness.
Now in all the land of Israel no blacksmith could be found, for the Philistines had said: The Hebrews must not make swords or spears.
So all Israel would go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plough tips, their picks, their axes, or their sickles.
The charge was two-thirds of a piece of silver for the plough tips and the picks, and a third for sharpening the axes and straightening the goads.
So on the day of battle, neither sword nor spear was to be found in the hands of all the people who were with Saul and Jonathan; only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
A Philistine garrison advanced toward the pass of Michmash.

One day Jonathan, son of Saul, said to the young man who carried his armour: "Come, let us cross over to the Philistine garrison, over there on the other side." But he said nothing of it to his father.
Saul was staying at the edge of Gibeah, under the pomegranate tree of Migron; the people with him numbered about six hundred men.
Ahijah, son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, priest of the Lord at Shiloh, was wearing the ephod. The people did not know that Jonathan had gone.
In the passes that Jonathan was trying to cross to reach the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other: one was called Bozez, the other Seneh.
One of these crags rises to the north, facing Michmash, the other to the south, facing Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armour: "Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the Lord will act for us, for nothing prevents the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few."
His armour-bearer answered him: "Do all that is on your heart; go, here I am with you, heart and soul."
Jonathan said: "Look, we are going to cross over toward these men and let them see us.
If they say to us: Wait until we reach you! then we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say: Come up to us! then we will go up, for the Lord will have delivered them into our hands. This will be the sign for us."
So the two of them showed themselves to the Philistine garrison, who cried out: "Here come the Hebrews out of the holes where they had hidden!"

The men of the garrison called out to Jonathan and his armour-bearer: "Come up to us, we have something to tell you!" Jonathan said to his armour-bearer: "Come up behind me, for the Lord has delivered them into the hand of Israel."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, his armour-bearer behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and the armour-bearer finished them off behind him.
This first blow struck by Jonathan and his armour-bearer left about twenty dead, over an area of about two thousand square metres.
Panic spread through the camp, through the countryside, and among all the people; the garrison and the raiders themselves were seized with terror, the earth trembled: it was a terror from God.
Saul's watchmen at Gibeah of Benjamin saw the multitude of Philistines scattering and running in every direction.
Saul said to the people who were with him: "Call the roll and see who has left us." They called the roll: Jonathan and his armour-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah: "Bring the ark of God near." For the ark of God was that day among the sons of Israel.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp kept growing. So Saul said to the priest: "Withdraw your hand."
Saul and all the people with him assembled and came to the battle: the Philistines were turning their swords against one another, in utter confusion.
The Hebrews who, the day before, had been on the Philistines' side and had gone up with them to the camp, now went over as well to the side of Israel, with Saul and Jonathan.
Likewise, all the men of Israel who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim, hearing of the flight of the Philistines, threw themselves into the pursuit to fight.
So that day the Lord saved Israel, and the fighting continued beyond Beth-aven.

The men of Israel were exhausted that day. Now Saul had bound the people by this oath: "Cursed be anyone who takes food before evening, before I have avenged myself on my enemies!" So no one among the people tasted any food.
The whole land was covered with woods, and there was honey on the surface of the ground.
When the people came into the woods, they saw the honey flowing, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.
Now Jonathan had not heard his father put the people under oath. He reached out the end of the staff he was holding, dipped it into a honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth: his eyes brightened.
Then someone from the people said to him: "Your father bound the people with an oath: Cursed be anyone who takes food today! And the people are worn out."
Jonathan answered: "My father brings trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened for having tasted a little of this honey!
If only the people had eaten today from the plunder taken from the enemy, would not the defeat of the Philistines have been even greater?"
That day they struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were exhausted.
Then the people rushed on the plunder: they took sheep, oxen, and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate them with the blood.
It was reported to Saul: "Behold, the people are sinning against the Lord by eating meat with the blood." Saul said: "You are traitors! Roll a large stone over to me at once."

Then he added: "Spread out among the people and tell them: Let everyone bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter it here, and eat it; that way you will not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood." That night everyone brought his ox by his own hand and slaughtered it there.
Saul built an altar to the Lord: this was the first altar he raised to the Lord.

Saul said: "Let us go down by night after the Philistines; let us plunder them until dawn, and let us not leave a single one alive." They answered: "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said: "Let us draw near to God here."
Saul inquired of God: "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into the hand of Israel?" But that day he did not answer him.
Saul said: "Come here, all you leaders of the people; search and see how this sin was committed today.
For as surely as the Lord, the saviour of Israel, lives, even if this fault is on my son Jonathan, he shall die!" But no one among all the people answered him.
He said to all Israel: "Stand on one side; my son Jonathan and I will be on the other." The people answered Saul: "Do what seems good to you."
Saul said to the Lord, the God of Israel: "Give a clear answer!" The lot fell on Jonathan and Saul, and the people were cleared.
Saul said: "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken.
Saul said to Jonathan: "Tell me what you have done." Jonathan confessed: "I tasted a little honey with the end of the staff I was holding. Here I am, I am ready to die."
Saul said: "May God deal with me with the utmost severity! Yes, you shall die, Jonathan."

But the people said to Saul: "Shall Jonathan die, he who has won this great victory in Israel? Never! As surely as the Lord lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for it was with God that he acted today." So the people ransomed Jonathan, and he did not die.
Saul stopped pursuing the Philistines, who returned to their own land.
When Saul had secured his kingship over Israel, he made war on all his enemies around him: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines; wherever he turned, he prevailed.
He showed his valour, struck down Amalek, and delivered Israel from the hand of those who plundered it.
The sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His two daughters were named: the elder Merab, the younger Michal.
Saul's wife was named Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army was named Abner, son of Ner, Saul's uncle.
Kish, Saul's father, and Ner, Abner's father, were sons of Abiel.
The war was fierce against the Philistines all the days of Saul; and whenever Saul noticed a strong and valiant man, he attached him to his service.
Samuel said to Saul: "It was I whom the Lord sent to anoint you as king over his people Israel; so listen now to the words of the Lord.
Thus says the Lord of hosts: I am going to call Amalek to account for what he did to Israel, when he barred his way as he came up from Egypt.
Go now, strike down Amalek, devote to destruction all that belongs to him; show him no pity, put to death man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey."
Saul summoned the people and reviewed them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul advanced as far as the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley.

Saul said to the Kenites: "Go, withdraw, come down from among the Amalekites, or I may destroy you along with them; for you showed kindness to all the sons of Israel when they came up from Egypt." So the Kenites withdrew from among the Amalekites.
Saul struck down Amalek from Havilah as far as Shur, on the borders of Egypt.
He took alive Agag, king of Amalek, and devoted all the people to destruction, putting them to the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, along with the best of the flocks and herds, the fat animals and the lambs, everything that was good; they were unwilling to devote them to destruction. They devoted to destruction only what was poor and worthless.
The word of the Lord came to Samuel in these terms:
"I regret having made Saul king, for he has turned away from me and has not carried out my words." Samuel was deeply troubled and cried out to the Lord all night.
The next morning Samuel rose early to go meet Saul. He was told: "Saul went to Carmel, where he set up a monument for himself; then he turned around and went down to Gilgal."
Samuel came to Saul, who said to him: "May you be blessed by the Lord! I have carried out the word of the Lord."
But Samuel asked: "What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and this lowing of oxen that I hear?"
Saul answered: "They were brought from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the flocks and herds to sacrifice to the Lord your God; the rest we devoted to destruction."
Samuel said to Saul: "Enough! I will tell you what the Lord said to me last night." Saul said: "Speak."
Samuel went on: "Small as you were in your own eyes, have you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The Lord anointed you king over Israel.
The Lord sent you on a mission: Go, devote to destruction those sinners, the Amalekites, and fight them until they are wiped out.
Why did you not listen to the voice of the Lord? Why did you pounce on the plunder and do what is evil in the eyes of the Lord?"
Saul said to Samuel: "But I did listen to the voice of the Lord! I went on the mission where the Lord sent me, I brought back Agag, king of Amalek, and I devoted Amalek to destruction.
The people only took, from the plunder, flocks and herds, the best of what was devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the Lord your God at Gilgal."
Samuel said: "Does the Lord take as much pleasure in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obedience to his voice? To obey is better than to sacrifice, to be attentive is better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is a sin of divination, and stubbornness a crime of idolatry. Since you have rejected the word of the Lord, he rejects you as king."
Saul said to Samuel: "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the command of the Lord and your words: I was afraid of the people and listened to their voice.
Now, I beg you, pardon my sin, come back with me, and I will worship before the Lord."
But Samuel said to Saul: "I will not come back with you, for you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord rejects you: you shall no longer be king over Israel."
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul seized the hem of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him: "The Lord has torn the kingship of Israel from you today, and has given it to another, better than you.
The Glory of Israel does not lie and does not change his mind, for he is not a man, that he should change his mind."
Saul said: "I have sinned! But honour me, I beg you, before the elders of my people and before Israel: come back with me, and I will worship before the Lord your God."
So Samuel went back, following Saul, and Saul worshipped before the Lord.
Then Samuel said: "Bring me Agag, king of Amalek." Agag came to him confidently, saying to himself: Surely the bitterness of death has passed.
But Samuel said: "As your sword has left women childless, so among women shall your mother be left childless." And Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.
Samuel went away to Ramah, and Saul went up to his home at Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but he mourned for Saul; and the Lord regretted having made Saul king of Israel.

The Lord said to Samuel, "How long will you go on grieving over Saul, when I have rejected him and he is no longer to reign over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and set out; I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for among his sons I have chosen myself a king."
Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears of it, he will kill me." The Lord answered, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to offer a sacrifice to the Lord.'
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will let you know what you are to do; you shall anoint for me the one I point out to you."
Samuel did what the Lord had told him and went to Bethlehem. The elders of the town came anxiously to meet him and asked, "Do you come in peace?"
He answered, "In peace! I have come to offer a sacrifice to the Lord. Sanctify yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice." Then he sanctified Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said to himself, "Surely the Lord's anointed stands here before him."

But the Lord said to Samuel, "Do not look at his appearance or his great height, for I have rejected him. God does not see as man sees: man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."
Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass before Samuel, who said, "This is not the one the Lord has chosen either."
Jesse had Shammah pass by; Samuel said, "This is not the one the Lord has chosen either."
So Jesse had seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel said to Jesse, "The Lord has not chosen any of these."

Then Samuel asked Jesse, "Are these all the boys you have?" He answered, "There is still the youngest, but he is tending the sheep." Samuel said to Jesse, "Send for him, for we will not sit down to eat until he arrives."
Jesse sent for him. He was ruddy, with fine eyes and a handsome face. The Lord said, "Rise and anoint him; this is the one!"
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. From that day on, the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon David and never left him again. Then Samuel rose and returned to Ramah.
The Spirit of the Lord had withdrawn from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him.
Saul's servants said to him, "See, an evil spirit from God is tormenting you.
Let our lord command, and your servants here will look for a man who knows how to play the harp; when the evil spirit from God comes upon you, he will play, and you will feel better."
Saul said to his servants, "Find me a good musician, then, and bring him to me."
One of the servants spoke up, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play; he is a brave man, a warrior, wise in speech and of fine bearing, and the Lord is with him."
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse to say, "Send me your son David, the one who is with the sheep."
Jesse took a donkey laden with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them to Saul by his son David.
David came to Saul and entered his service; Saul loved him greatly and made him his armor-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse, "Let David remain in my service, I beg you, for he has found favor in my eyes."
So whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would take the harp and play; Saul would grow calm and feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their troops for war. They assembled at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and camped between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel also gathered and camped in the Valley of Elah; they drew up in battle line facing the Philistines.
The Philistines held the hill on one side, Israel the hill on the other, with the valley between them.
Then from the ranks of the Philistines came out a champion named Goliath, from Gath. He stood about three and a quarter metres tall.
A bronze helmet covered his head; he wore a coat of scale armor weighing about fifty-seven kilos of bronze,
bronze greaves on his legs, and a bronze javelin slung across his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and its iron point weighed nearly seven kilos. His shield-bearer walked ahead of him.

Goliath stopped and shouted toward the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not the Philistine, and are you not the slaves of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down against me.
If he is able to fight me and kill me, we will become your slaves; but if I overcome him and kill him, you will become our slaves and serve us."
The Philistine added, "Today I defy the ranks of Israel: give me a man, and let us fight together!"
When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and seized with great fear.
Now David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse, who had eight sons. In the days of Saul this man was already old, advanced in years.
Jesse's three eldest sons had gone off to war behind Saul. These three sons were named Eliab, the firstborn; Abinadab, the second; and Shammah, the third.
David was the youngest. The three eldest had followed Saul,
but David went back and forth between Saul and Bethlehem, to tend his father's sheep.
The Philistine came forward morning and evening, and he presented himself like this for forty days.
Jesse said to his son David, "Take for your brothers about twenty-two litres of roasted grain and these ten loaves, and hurry them to the camp, to your brothers.
As for these ten cheeses, give them to the commander of their unit. See how your brothers are and bring me back a token from them.
They are with Saul and all the men of Israel in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines."

David rose early in the morning, left the sheep with a keeper, took the provisions, and set out as Jesse had commanded him. He reached the camp just as the army was going out to its battle line, raising the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines drew up line against line.
David left his baggage in the hands of the keeper of the supplies and ran to the ranks; when he got there, he greeted his brothers.
While he was speaking with them, the champion, the Philistine of Gath named Goliath, came forward out of the Philistine ranks and spoke the same words as before. David heard him.
At the sight of the man, all the Israelites drew back, seized with great fear.

Each man said, "Do you see this man coming forward? He comes to defy Israel. The one who kills him, the king will make him rich, give him his daughter, and free his father's house from all obligation in Israel."

David said to the men standing near him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and wipes away this disgrace from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised man, to defy the ranks of the living God?"
The people repeated the same words to him, "This is what will be done for the man who kills him."

Eliab, his eldest brother, heard him speaking with the men and grew angry with David, "Why have you come down? And with whom did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart: you have come down to watch the battle!"
David answered, "What have I done now? Was it not just a word?"
Then he turned away from him toward another and asked the same question, and the people answered him as before.
David's words were reported, and Saul had him brought in.
David said to Saul, "Let no one lose heart because of him! Your servant will go and fight this Philistine."
Saul said to David, "You cannot face this Philistine to fight him: you are only a boy, and he has been a warrior since his youth."
David said to Saul, "When your servant was tending his father's sheep, and a lion or a bear came and carried off an animal from the flock,
I would go after it, strike it, and rescue the animal from its mouth; and if it turned on me, I would seize it by the mane and strike it dead.
Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, for he has defied the ranks of the living God."
David added, "The Lord, who rescued me from the claw of the lion and the bear, will also rescue me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said to David, "Go, and may the Lord be with you!"
Saul dressed David in his own garments, set a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him in a coat of armor.
Over it David buckled Saul's sword and tried to walk, for he was not used to it. Then David said to Saul, "I cannot walk in these, for I am not used to them." And he took them off.
He took his staff in hand, chose five smooth stones from the wadi, put them in his shepherd's bag, and, sling in hand, went toward the Philistine.
The Philistine too drew nearer and nearer to David, preceded by his shield-bearer.
When he saw David, he despised him, for he was only a boy, ruddy and handsome of face.
The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" And he cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David again, "Come here, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the field!"
David answered the Philistine, "You come at me with sword and spear and javelin; but I come at you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

This very day the Lord will hand you over to me: I will strike you down, cut off your head, and today I will give the corpses of the Philistine army to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth. Then all the earth will know that there is a God in Israel,
and all this assembly will know that the Lord saves neither by sword nor by spear: for the battle belongs to the Lord, and he will hand you over to us."
Then the Philistine set out and came forward to meet David; and David ran quickly toward the line, to meet the Philistine.
He plunged his hand into his bag, took out a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell face down to the ground.
So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone: he struck the Philistine down and killed him, without even a sword in his hand.
David ran and stood over the Philistine, seized his sword, drew it from its sheath, and finished him off by cutting off his head.

Seeing their champion dead, the Philistines fled. The men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued them as far as the approach to Gath and the gates of Ekron. The Philistines fell, strewn along the road of Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron.
Then the sons of Israel came back from their fierce pursuit and plundered the Philistine camp.
David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem; as for Goliath's weapons, he placed them in his tent.

When Saul had seen David going out to meet the Philistine, he had asked Abner, the commander of the army, "Whose son is this boy, Abner?" Abner answered, "As surely as you live, O king, I do not know."
The king said, "Then find out whose son this young man is."
When David came back after killing the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul; David was holding the Philistine's head in his hand.
Saul asked him, "Whose son are you, young man?" David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse, of Bethlehem."
When David had finished speaking with Saul, the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David: Jonathan loved him as himself.
That day Saul kept David and would not let him return to his father's house.
Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan stripped off the cloak he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his garments, even his sword, his bow, and his belt.
Wherever Saul sent him, David succeeded. Saul put him in command of the men of war, and he was pleasing to all the people, even to the king's servants.

Now on their return, when David came back after striking down the Philistine, the women came out of all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul, singing and dancing with joy, to the sound of tambourines and lyres.
And the women, as they danced, sang to one another, "Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands!"
Saul was greatly annoyed; these words displeased him, and he said, "They give David tens of thousands, and to me only thousands! All he lacks now is the kingship."
From that day on, Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house. David was playing the harp, as on other days, and Saul had his spear in hand.
Saul brandished the spear, saying to himself, "I will pin David to the wall!" But David eluded him twice.
Saul became afraid of David, for the Lord was with David and had withdrawn from Saul.
So Saul removed him from his presence and made him commander of a thousand men; David went out on campaign and came back at the head of the people.
David succeeded in all his undertakings, for the Lord was with him.
Seeing how well he succeeded, Saul was afraid of him.
But all Israel and all Judah loved David, because he marched at their head into battle.

Saul said to David, "Here is my eldest daughter, Merab; I will give her to you as wife. Only be valiant in my service and fight the Lord's battles." For Saul said to himself, Let it not be my hand that strikes him, but the hand of the Philistines!
David answered Saul, "Who am I, and what is my kindred, my father's family in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
But when the time came to give Merab, Saul's daughter, to David, she was given as wife to Adriel of Meholah.
But Michal, Saul's daughter, loved David. It was reported to Saul, and it pleased him.

Saul said to himself, I will give her to him, so that she may be a snare to him and the hand of the Philistines may fall upon him. So Saul said to David a second time, "Today you shall become my son-in-law."
Then Saul ordered his servants, "Speak privately to David and say, 'The king is fond of you, and all his servants love you; become the king's son-in-law, then.'"
Saul's servants repeated these words to David, but David said, "Do you think it a small thing to become the king's son-in-law, I who am poor and of humble station?"
Saul's servants reported to him, "This is what David said."

Saul said, "You shall say this to David: 'The king asks no other bride-price than a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to take revenge on his enemies.'" Saul was counting on making David fall into the hands of the Philistines.
The servants repeated these words to David, and it pleased him to become the king's son-in-law. Before the appointed time was up,

David rose and went out with his men; he killed two hundred Philistines, brought back their foreskins, and counted out the full number to the king, to become his son-in-law. Then Saul gave him his daughter Michal as wife.
Saul saw clearly and understood that the Lord was with David, and that Michal, his daughter, loved him.
Saul was more and more afraid of David, and he remained his enemy for the rest of his life.
The Philistine chiefs kept making raids; and every time, David succeeded better than all of Saul's servants, and his name became very famous.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to put David to death. But Jonathan, Saul's son, was very fond of David.
Jonathan warned David, "My father Saul is seeking to put you to death. Be on your guard, then, tomorrow morning: stay out of sight and hide.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are; I will speak to him about you, and when I see how things stand, I will let you know."
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul, "Let the king not sin against his servant David, for he has not sinned against you; on the contrary, what he has done has served you well.

He risked his life, he struck down the Philistine, and the Lord won a great victory for all Israel. You saw it, you rejoiced; why then would you make yourself guilty of innocent blood by putting David to death without cause?"
Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan and swore this oath, "As surely as the Lord lives, David shall not be put to death!"
Jonathan called David and told him all this; then he brought him back to Saul, and David stood in his presence as before.
War broke out again, and David went out to fight the Philistines; he inflicted a great defeat on them, and they fled before him.
Then an evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul as he was sitting in his house with his spear in hand; David was playing the harp.
Saul tried to pin David to the wall with his spear, but David eluded him, and the spear stuck in the wall. David fled and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him and put him to death in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, warned him, "If you do not save yourself tonight, tomorrow you will be put to death."
Michal let David down through the window; he went off, fled, and was saved.
Then Michal took the household idol, laid it in the bed, put a goat's-hair cushion at its head, and covered it with a garment.
When Saul sent messengers to seize David, she said, "He is sick."
Saul sent the messengers back to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in his bed, so that I may put him to death."
The messengers went in, and there in the bed was the household idol, with a goat's-hair cushion at its head.
Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me like this, letting my enemy escape?" Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go, or I will kill you!'"
So David fled and was saved. He went to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. Then David and Samuel went to stay at Naioth.
It was reported to Saul, "David is at Naioth, near Ramah."

Saul sent messengers to seize David. But when they saw the band of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing at their head, the Spirit of God came upon Saul's messengers, and they too began to prophesy.
This was reported to Saul, who sent other messengers; they too prophesied. A third time Saul sent messengers, and they too prophesied.
Then he himself set out for Ramah. When he came to the great cistern at Secu, he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" He was told, "At Naioth, near Ramah."
He made his way toward Naioth, near Ramah; the Spirit of God came upon him too, and he went along prophesying until he arrived at Naioth.
There he too stripped off his garments and prophesied before Samuel; he lay on the ground, naked, all that day and all that night. That is why people say, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

titres.titre: The covenant of David and Jonathan

versets.t: David fled from Naioth, near Ramah, and came and said to Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my guilt, what is my sin against your father, that he seeks my life?"
Jonathan said to him, "Far from it! You shall not die. See, my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me; why would he hide this from me? It is not so."

But David answered, with an oath, "Your father knows very well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said to himself, 'Let Jonathan not know this, or he will be grieved.' But as surely as the Lord lives and as you live, there is only a step between me and death."
Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you desire, I will do for you."
David said to Jonathan, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and I ought to sit at table with the king. Let me go instead: I will hide in the fields until the evening of the day after tomorrow.
If your father notices my absence, you will say, 'David begged me insistently to hurry to Bethlehem, his town, for the yearly sacrifice of his whole clan.'
If he says, 'Very well,' your servant is safe; but if he flies into a rage, know that the harm is fully decided on his part.

Deal kindly, then, with your servant, since you have bound him to yourself by a covenant in the name of the Lord. And if there is any guilt in me, put me to death yourself; why bring me to your father?"
Jonathan said, "Far be that thought from you! If I truly learn that harm is decided by my father against you, would I not tell you?"
David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?"
Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the fields." And the two of them went out into the fields.
Jonathan said to David, "By the Lord, the God of Israel! Tomorrow or the day after, at this hour, I will sound out my father. If all is well for David, and I do not send someone to tell you,

may the Lord deal with me ever so severely! But if my father intends to harm you, I will tell you and send you away, so that you may go in peace; and may the Lord be with you as he has been with my father.
If I am still alive, show me the faithful love of the Lord; and if I die,
never withdraw your kindness from my house, not even when the Lord has wiped every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, "May the Lord call David's enemies to account!"
And Jonathan made David swear again, by the love he bore him, for he loved him as himself.
Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon; your absence will be noticed, for your place will be empty.
The day after tomorrow, go down quickly to the place where you hid on the day of the affair, and stay beside the stone Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows to that side, as if aiming at a target.

Then I will send the boy: 'Go and find the arrows.' If I say plainly to him, 'The arrows are on this side of you, pick them up!' then come, for you are safe, there is nothing to fear, as surely as the Lord lives.
But if I say to the boy, 'The arrows are beyond you!' then go, for the Lord is sending you away.
As for the word we have exchanged, you and I, the Lord is witness between you and me forever."
So David hid in the fields. When the new moon came, the king sat down to the meal.
He sat in his usual place, against the wall; Jonathan sat opposite, Abner beside Saul, and David's place remained empty.
That day Saul said nothing, for he thought, Something has happened to him, he is not clean; surely he is not clean.
But the next day, the second day of the new moon, David's place was still empty. Saul said to his son Jonathan, "Why has the son of Jesse come to the meal neither yesterday nor today?"
Jonathan answered Saul, "David begged me insistently for leave to go to Bethlehem.

He said to me, 'Let me go, I beg you, for we have a family sacrifice in the town, and my brother has asked for me. If I have found favor in your eyes, let me go and see my brothers.' That is why he has not come to the king's table."
Then Saul's anger blazed against Jonathan, "Son of a rebellious, wayward woman! Do I not know that you side with the son of Jesse, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother who bore you?
As long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, there will be no security for you or for your kingship. Send for him, then, and bring him to me, for he is a man doomed to death."
Jonathan answered his father Saul, "Why put him to death? What has he done?"
But Saul brandished his spear at him to strike him. Then Jonathan understood that his father was set on David's death.
In a burning rage, Jonathan rose from the table and, on this second day of the new moon, he ate nothing, so grieved was he for David, whom his father had insulted.
The next morning Jonathan went out to the fields at the time set with David, accompanied by a young boy.
He said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows I am going to shoot." The boy ran, and Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy reached the place of the arrow Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called out to him, "Is the arrow not beyond you?"
Then Jonathan called out again, "Quick, hurry, do not stop!" The boy picked up the arrow and came back to his master.
The boy knew nothing; only Jonathan and David were in on the secret.
Jonathan handed his weapons to the boy who was with him, "Go, carry them back to town."
When the boy had gone, David rose from the south side, threw himself face down to the ground, and bowed three times. Then they kissed each other and wept over each other, David the more.
Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace! For the two of us have sworn in the name of the Lord: 'May the Lord be between you and me, between your descendants and mine, forever.'"
David rose and set out, while Jonathan went back into town.
David went to Nob, to the priest Ahimelech. Ahimelech came trembling to meet him and asked, "Why are you alone, with no one with you?"

David answered the priest Ahimelech, "The king has charged me with a mission and told me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter for which I am sending you and with which I have charged you.' As for my men, I have appointed a meeting place for them.
Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves, or whatever you can find."
The priest answered David, "I have no ordinary bread on hand, only consecrated bread; but only if your men have kept themselves from women."

David answered the priest, "Of course, women have been kept from us, as always when I set out on campaign: the persons of my men are holy. This journey itself is unhallowed, yet today it will be all the more consecrated."
So the priest gave him consecrated bread, for there was no bread there except the bread of the offering, which was taken from before the Lord to be replaced, that very day, with fresh bread.
Now that day one of Saul's servants was there, detained before the Lord: his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chief of Saul's shepherds.
David said to Ahimelech, "Do you not have here, on hand, a spear or a sword? I brought neither my sword nor my weapons, so urgent was the king's order."

The priest answered, "There is the sword of Goliath, the Philistine you struck down in the Valley of Elah: here it is, wrapped in a cloak, behind the ephod. Take it if you like, there is no other here." David said, "There is none like it: give it to me."
David rose and fled that day from Saul; he went to Achish, king of Gath.
But the servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the king of the land? Is this not the one they sang of in the dances, 'Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"
David took these words to heart and was seized with great fear of Achish, king of Gath.
So, before their eyes, he changed his behavior and acted like a madman in their hands: he drummed on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, "You can see the man is mad. Why bring him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you bring me this one to carry on his madness in front of me? Should such a man enter my house?"

titres.titre: David in the cave of Adullam
The massacre of the priests of Nob

versets.t: David left there and took refuge in the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and all his father's house heard of it, they went down to join him there.
All those who were in distress, in debt, or bitter of soul gathered around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were thus with him.
From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab and said to the king of Moab, "Let my father and mother withdraw to your land, until I know what God will do with me."
He presented them to the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in his stronghold.
But the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not stay in this stronghold; go and enter the land of Judah." So David set out and came to the forest of Hereth.
Saul heard that David and his men had been spotted. He was then sitting at Gibeah, under the tamarisk on the height, his spear in hand, all his servants standing before him.

Saul said to his servants standing before him, "Listen, Benjaminites! Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds,

that you have all conspired against me? No one told me that my son had made a covenant with the son of Jesse; none of you cared about me or revealed to me that my son had set my servant against me, to lie in wait for me, as he does today."
Doeg the Edomite, who was standing among Saul's servants, answered, "I saw the son of Jesse come to Nob, to Ahimelech son of Ahitub.
He consulted the Lord for him, gave him provisions, and handed him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."
The king summoned the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests of Nob.
They all came to the king, and Saul said, "Listen, son of Ahitub!" He answered, "Here I am, my lord."

Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse? You gave him bread and a sword and consulted God for him, so that he might rise against me and lie in wait for me, as he does today."
Ahimelech answered the king, "Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king's son-in-law, captain of your guard and honored in your house?

Is it today that I began to consult God for him? Far be it from me! Let the king lay nothing to the charge of his servant or of all my father's house, for your servant knew nothing of all this, little or much."
But the king said, "You shall die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house."

And the king ordered the guards around him, "Turn and put the priests of the Lord to death, for they have sided with David: they knew he was fleeing and did not warn me." But the king's servants refused to raise their hand to strike the priests of the Lord.
Then the king said to Doeg, "You, turn and strike the priests." Doeg the Edomite turned and struck the priests himself: that day he put to death eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
Then Saul put Nob, the town of the priests, to the sword: men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep, all were put to the sword.
One son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the Lord.
David said to Abiathar, "That day, when Doeg the Edomite was present, I knew he would report everything to Saul. I am responsible for the death of all your father's house.
Stay with me, do not be afraid: the one who seeks my life seeks yours; with me you will be safe."

titres.titre: David hunted in the wilderness of Ziph

versets.t: Word came to David, "The Philistines are attacking Keilah and looting the threshing floors."
David consulted the Lord, "Shall I go and strike these Philistines?" The Lord answered David, "Go, you will strike the Philistines and deliver Keilah."
But David's men said to him, "Here in Judah we are already afraid; how much more if we go to Keilah, against the Philistine army!"
David consulted the Lord again, and he answered, "Rise, go down to Keilah, for I am handing the Philistines over to you."
So David went with his men to Keilah, attacked the Philistines, drove off their livestock, and inflicted a heavy defeat on them. Thus David delivered the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech had fled to David at Keilah, he had come down with the ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had entered Keilah, and Saul said, "God has handed him over to me, for he has shut himself in by entering a town with gates and bars."
Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah and besiege David and his men there.
Knowing that Saul was plotting his ruin, David said to the priest Abiathar, "Bring the ephod."
Then David said, "Lord, God of Israel, your servant has heard that Saul is seeking to come to Keilah to destroy the town because of me.
Will the citizens of Keilah hand me over to him? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? Lord, God of Israel, tell your servant, I beg you." The Lord answered, "He will come down."
David went on, "Will the citizens of Keilah hand me and my men over to Saul?" The Lord answered, "They will hand you over."
So David rose with his men, about six hundred, left Keilah, and wandered wherever they could. When Saul learned that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up going there.
David stayed in the wilderness, in the strongholds; he remained in the hill country, in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every day, but God did not hand him over to him.
David realized that Saul had set out to take his life. He was then in the wilderness of Ziph, at Horesh.
Jonathan, Saul's son, went to David at Horesh and strengthened his hand in God.
He said to him, "Do not be afraid: the hand of my father Saul will not reach you. It is you who will reign over Israel, and I will be your second; my father Saul himself knows it well."
The two of them made a covenant before the Lord. David stayed at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.
The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Is David not hiding among us, in the strongholds of Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, south of the wasteland?
Now then, O king, come down, since you so desire, and it will be for us to hand him over to the king."
Saul answered, "May you be blessed by the Lord for having taken pity on me!
Go, I beg you, make further inquiry; observe and mark the place where he sets foot and who has seen him there, for I am told he is very cunning.

Observe and mark all the hiding places where he takes refuge, then come back to me with reliable information, and I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will track him down among all the clans of Judah."
So they set out for Ziph, ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain, south of the wasteland.

Saul went with his men to search for David. David was told of it, and he went down to the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. Hearing this, Saul set out in pursuit of him into the wilderness of Maon.
Saul was moving along one side of the mountain, David and his men along the other; David was hurrying to flee before Saul, while Saul and his men were trying to encircle them to capture them.
But a messenger came to Saul, "Come quickly! The Philistines have invaded the land!"
So Saul stopped pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place was called the Rock of Escape.

titres.titre: David spares Saul in the cave
