versets.t: David went up from there and settled in the strongholds of En-gedi.
When Saul returned from pursuing the Philistines, he was told, "David is in the wilderness of En-gedi."
Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and set out to search for David and his men on the Rocks of the Wild Goats.
He came to the sheepfolds beside the road. There was a cave there, which Saul entered to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting at the back of the cave.
David's men said to him, "This is the day of which the Lord said to you, 'I am handing your enemy over to you; do to him as you please.'" David rose and stealthily cut off the corner of Saul's cloak.
But afterward David's heart began to pound because he had cut off the corner of Saul's cloak,
and he said to his men, "The Lord keep me from doing such a thing to my lord, the Lord's anointed, and from laying my hand on him, for he is the Lord's anointed!"
By these words David restrained his men and did not let them fall upon Saul. Saul left the cave and went on his way.
Then David too came out of the cave and called after Saul, "My lord the king!" Saul looked behind him, and David bowed with his face to the ground and prostrated himself.
David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to those who say, 'David is seeking to harm you'?

This very day your own eyes have seen how the Lord handed you over to me in the cave. They urged me to kill you, but I spared you, saying to myself, 'I will not lay my hand on my lord, for he is the Lord's anointed.'

Look, my father, look at the corner of your cloak in my hand! I cut off this corner without killing you: acknowledge, then, that there is no malice or rebellion in me, and that I have not sinned against you. Yet you hunt me down to take my life.
May the Lord judge between you and me, and may the Lord avenge me on you! But my hand will not be raised against you.
As the old proverb says, 'From the wicked comes wickedness.' So my hand will not be raised against you.
After whom has the king of Israel set out? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog, a single flea!
May the Lord be judge and decide between you and me! May he examine and defend my cause and grant me justice by delivering me from your hand."
When David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is that your voice, my son David?" And Saul wept aloud.
He said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have done me good, while I have done you harm.
You have shown today the goodness of your conduct toward me: the Lord had handed me over to you, and you did not kill me.
When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go away safe and sound? May the Lord reward you for what you have done for me today!
Now I know that you will reign, and that the kingship of Israel will remain firm in your hands.
Swear to me, then, by the Lord that you will not wipe out my descendants after me and will not blot out my name from my father's house."
David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, and David and his men went back up to the stronghold.
Samuel died. All Israel gathered to mourn him, and they buried him at his home, in Ramah. Then David rose and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
There was at Maon a man whose property was at Carmel. He was a very rich man: he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. He was at Carmel for the shearing of his sheep.
This man was named Nabal, and his wife Abigail. She was full of good sense and beautiful, but he was harsh and brutal in his dealings; he was a Calebite.
David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
He sent ten young men and said to them, "Go up to Carmel, go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.
You shall say to him, 'Long life to you! Peace to you, peace to your house, peace to all that is yours!
I hear that you have the shearers. Now your shepherds have been with us; we did not mistreat them, and nothing of their flock went missing during their whole stay at Carmel.
Ask your servants, and they will tell you. Let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a feast day. Give, I beg you, to your servants and to your son David whatever you have on hand.'"
David's young men arrived and repeated all these words to Nabal in David's name; then they waited.
But Nabal retorted to David's servants, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who break away from their masters!
Am I to take my bread, my water, and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, to give to men who come from I know not where?"
David's young men turned back and, on their return, reported all this to him.
Then David said to his men, "Let every man buckle on his sword!" Each buckled on his sword, David too, and about four hundred men went up behind David, while two hundred stayed with the baggage.
Now one of the servants warned Abigail, Nabal's wife, "David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he flew at them.
Yet these men were very good to us: they did not mistreat us, and we lacked nothing all the time we were near their camp in the open country.
Night and day they were like a wall around us, all the time we were with them tending the flocks.
Consider, then, and see what you must do, for harm is decided against our master and all his house; but he is such a scoundrel that no one can speak to him."

At once Abigail took two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, about thirty-six litres of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and loaded them on donkeys.
Then she said to her servants, "Go on ahead of me; I am coming behind you." But she said nothing to her husband Nabal.
As she was riding down on her donkey, under cover of the mountain, David and his men were coming down toward her, and she came upon them.
Now David had just been saying, "It was all in vain that I protected this man's whole property in the wilderness, so that nothing of his was missing: he repays me evil for good!
May God do so to David, and worse, if by morning I leave a single male of all that belongs to Nabal!"
As soon as Abigail saw David, she hurried down from her donkey and fell on her face before David, bowing to the ground.
Throwing herself at his feet, she said, "On me be the guilt, my lord, on me alone! Let your servant speak to you, and hear the words of your servant.
Let my lord pay no attention to this scoundrel Nabal, for he is well named: he is called Nabal, the Fool, and folly is with him. As for me, your servant, I did not see the men my lord sent.

Now, my lord, as surely as the Lord lives and as you live, the Lord has held you back from shedding blood and from taking vengeance with your own hand. May your enemies, and all who seek to harm my lord, become like Nabal!
Accept this present that your servant brings to my lord, and let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.

Forgive, I beg you, the offense of your servant. For the Lord will surely make my lord a lasting house, since my lord fights the Lord's battles, and no wrong will be found in you throughout your life.

If anyone rises to pursue you and seek your life, the life of my lord will be bound up in the bundle of the living with the Lord your God; but the lives of your enemies he will hurl away, as from the hollow of a sling.
And when the Lord has done for my lord all the good he has promised concerning you, and has appointed you ruler over Israel,

you will not have this remorse, this weight on your heart, of having shed blood without cause and having taken vengeance yourself. And when the Lord has dealt well with my lord, remember your servant."
David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me! Blessed be your good sense,
and blessed be you, who have kept me today from shedding blood and from taking vengeance with my own hand!

For as surely as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, who has held me back from harming you: if you had not come quickly to meet me, there would not have been left to Nabal, by morning, a single male."
David received from her hand what she had brought him and said to her, "Go up in peace to your house. See, I have listened to your voice and granted your request."
Abigail went back to Nabal. He was holding a feast in his house, a feast fit for a king; his heart was merry, and he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until morning.
In the morning, when Nabal had sobered up, his wife told him everything: his heart died within him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later, the Lord struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the Lord, who has defended my cause against the insult I suffered from Nabal and has kept his servant from doing wrong! The Lord has brought Nabal's wickedness down on his own head." Then David sent to ask Abigail in marriage.
David's servants came to Abigail at Carmel and said to her, "David has sent us to you to take you as his wife."
She rose, bowed with her face to the ground, and said, "Your servant is only a slave, ready to wash the feet of my lord's servants."
Then Abigail rose in haste, mounted a donkey, and, followed by her five maids, went off behind David's messengers, and she became his wife.
David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel: the two of them were his wives.
As for Saul, he had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, of Gallim.

titres.titre: David spares Saul in the wilderness of Ziph

versets.t: The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Is David not hiding on the hill of Hachilah, opposite the wasteland?"
Saul rose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, with three thousand chosen men of Israel, to search for David there.
Saul camped on the hill of Hachilah, opposite the wasteland, beside the road. David, who was staying in the wilderness, realized that Saul had come there in search of him.
He sent out spies and learned for certain that Saul had arrived.

David rose and came to the place where Saul was camped. He saw the spot where Saul lay, with Abner son of Ner, the commander of his army: Saul lay in the center of the camp, the troops camped around him.
David spoke to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, "Who will go down with me into the camp, to Saul?" Abishai answered, "I will go down with you."
David and Abishai came to the troops by night: Saul was asleep, lying in the center of the camp, his spear thrust into the ground at his head; Abner and the troops lay around him.
Abishai said to David, "Today God has handed your enemy over to you. Let me pin him to the ground with a single thrust of the spear, without a second blow."
But David said to Abishai, "Do not kill him! Who could lay a hand on the Lord's anointed and go unpunished?"
And David added, "As surely as the Lord lives, the Lord himself will strike him: either his day will come and he will die, or he will go down into battle and perish there.
The Lord keep me from laying my hand on his anointed! Take only the spear at his head, and the water jug, and let us go."
So David took the spear and the water jug from Saul's head, and they went off. No one saw, no one knew, no one woke: they were all asleep, for the Lord had brought a deep sleep upon them.
David crossed to the other side and stood far off, on the top of the mountain; a wide space separated them.
David called out to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, "Will you not answer, Abner?" Abner answered, "Who are you, who calls out to the king?"
David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is your equal in Israel? Why then did you not keep watch over the king, your lord? Someone from the people came to kill the king, your lord!

What you have done is not right. As surely as the Lord lives, you deserve to die for not keeping watch over your master, the Lord's anointed. Look now: where are the king's spear and the water jug that were at his head?"
Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is that your voice, my son David?" David answered, "It is my voice, O king, my lord."
He added, "Why does my lord pursue his servant? What have I done, what wrong has my hand committed?

Now let the king my lord listen to the words of his servant. If it is the Lord who has stirred you up against me, may he savor the fragrance of an offering; but if it is men, may they be cursed before the Lord, for they have driven me out today, shutting me off from the Lord's heritage, as if to say, 'Go, serve other gods!'
Let my blood not fall to the ground far from the face of the Lord! For the king of Israel has set out to look for a single flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains."
Saul said, "I have sinned. Come back, my son David: I will not harm you again, since today my life was precious in your eyes. Yes, I have acted foolishly and gone badly astray."
David answered, "Here is the king's spear! Let one of the young men come and take it.
The Lord will repay each one according to his righteousness and faithfulness: today he had handed you over to me, but I would not lay my hand on the Lord's anointed.
As your life counted much in my eyes today, so may my life count in the eyes of the Lord, and may he deliver me from every distress."
Saul said to David, "Blessed are you, my son David! You will accomplish great things and prevail." Then David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

titres.titre: David in the service of Achish

versets.t: David said to himself, One day I will perish by the hand of Saul. The best thing for me is to take refuge in the land of the Philistines: Saul will give up hunting me throughout the territory of Israel, and I will escape his hand.
So David rose and crossed over, with the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David stayed with Achish at Gath, he and his men, each with his family, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.
Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, and he stopped pursuing him.
David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let me be given a place in one of the country towns, so that I may settle there; why should your servant live with you in the royal city?"
That day Achish gave him Ziklag; that is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.
David lived in the land of the Philistines for a year and four months.
David and his men would go up and raid the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites; for these peoples had inhabited the land from ancient times, in the direction of Shur and as far as Egypt.
David would ravage the region, leaving neither man nor woman alive, carrying off sheep, oxen, donkeys, camels, and garments; then he would return to Achish.
Achish would ask, "Where did you raid today?" David would answer, "In the Negev of Judah, in the Negev of the Jerahmeelites, in the Negev of the Kenites."

David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring back to Gath, thinking, They might denounce us and say, 'This is what David did.' Such was his practice all the time he lived in the land of the Philistines.
Achish trusted David and said to himself, He has made himself utterly hated by his own people, Israel; he will be my servant forever.

titres.titre: Saul and the medium of Endor

versets.t: In those days the Philistines gathered their troops into a single army to make war on Israel. Achish said to David, "Understand clearly that you will go out with me to the camp, you and your men."
David answered Achish, "Very well, you will see what your servant can do." Achish said to David, "Then I will make you my bodyguard for life."
Now Samuel was dead; all Israel had mourned him and buried him at Ramah, in his own town. And Saul had driven the mediums and the diviners out of the land.
The Philistines assembled and came and camped at Shunem; Saul gathered all Israel, and they camped at Mount Gilboa.
At the sight of the Philistine camp, Saul was afraid, and his heart trembled violently.
Saul consulted the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by the Urim, nor by the prophets.
Then Saul said to his servants, "Find me a medium, that I may go and consult her." His servants answered him, "There is in fact a medium at Endor."

Saul disguised himself, put on other clothes, and set out, accompanied by two men. They came to the woman by night, and he said to her, "Foretell the future for me by consulting the dead, and bring up for me the one I name to you."
The woman answered him, "You know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the diviners from the land. Why are you setting a trap for me, to have me put to death?"
Saul swore to her by the Lord, "As surely as the Lord lives, no punishment will come upon you for this!"
The woman asked, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He answered, "Bring up Samuel for me."
When she saw Samuel, the woman gave a loud cry and said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!"
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" The woman answered Saul, "I see a divine being coming up from the earth."
He asked, "What does he look like?" She answered, "It is an old man coming up, wrapped in a cloak." Saul knew it was Samuel; he bowed with his face to the ground and prostrated himself.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed my rest by bringing me up?" Saul answered, "I am in great distress: the Philistines are making war on me, and God has withdrawn from me; he no longer answers me, neither by the prophets nor by dreams. I have called on you to let me know what I must do."
Samuel said, "Why consult me, since the Lord has withdrawn from you and has become your adversary?
The Lord has done as he foretold through me: he has torn the kingship from your hand and given it to another, to David.
Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out the fury of his anger against Amalek, this is why the Lord is treating you thus today.

What is more, the Lord will hand Israel over with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me; and the camp of Israel, the Lord will hand it over into the hands of the Philistines."
At once Saul fell full length on the ground, chilled with terror at Samuel's words; his strength was gone, for he had eaten nothing all that day and all that night.
The woman came to Saul and, seeing him so shaken, said to him, "Your servant has obeyed you: I risked my life in listening to the words you spoke to me.
Now, in turn, listen to the voice of your servant: let me set before you a morsel of bread. Eat, so as to regain your strength before you go on your way."
He refused, "I will not eat." But his servants and the woman pressed him, and he gave in. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf at her house; she hurried to kill it, took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread.
She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went off that same night.
The Philistines gathered all their troops at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring of Jezreel.
The princes of the Philistines advanced at the head of their hundreds and thousands, and David and his men marched in the rear guard, with Achish.

The chiefs of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish answered the chiefs of the Philistines, "But this is David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel! He has been with me for a year or two, and I have found nothing to hold against him from the day he came over to me until now."

But the chiefs of the Philistines were angry with him and said to him, "Send this man back, let him return to the place you assigned him! Let him not go down with us into battle, lest he turn against us in the thick of the fight: how better could he win back his master's favor than with the heads of our men?
Is this not the David of whom they sang in the dances, 'Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"

Achish called David and said to him, "As surely as the Lord lives, you are an upright man, and I would be glad to have you go out and come in with me in the camp, for I have found nothing bad in you from the day you came until now. But you do not please the princes.
Go back, then, and go in peace, so as to do nothing that would displease the princes of the Philistines."

David said to Achish, "But what have I done, and what have you found to hold against your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight the enemies of my lord the king?"
Achish answered David, "I know that you have been as precious to me as an angel of God; but the chiefs of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up into battle with us.'
So rise early, you and your master's servants who came with you; rise early in the morning and leave as soon as it is light."
David and his men rose early to set out at daybreak and return to the land of the Philistines, while the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

titres.titre: David recovers Ziklag from the Amalekites

versets.t: When David and his men reached Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid into the Negev and against Ziklag; they had taken Ziklag and burned it.
They had carried off captive the women and all who were there, small and great, without killing anyone, and had taken them away, continuing on their route.
When David and his men came to the town, they found it burned, and their wives, their sons, and their daughters carried off into captivity.
Then David and the people with him wept aloud, until they had no strength left to weep.
David's two wives had been carried off captive as well: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.
David was in great anguish, for the people spoke of stoning him: each man's soul was full of bitterness over his sons and daughters. But David took courage in the Lord his God.
David said to the priest Abiathar son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David consulted the Lord, "Shall I pursue this band? Will I overtake it?" The Lord answered, "Pursue, for you will surely overtake it and rescue the captives."
David set out with the six hundred men who were with him. When they reached the Wadi Besor, the stragglers halted.
David continued the pursuit with four hundred men; two hundred had stopped, too exhausted to cross the Wadi Besor.
They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. They gave him bread, which he ate, and water to drink;
they also gave him a piece of fig cake and two cakes of raisins. When he had eaten, his strength returned, for he had not eaten or drunk for three days and three nights.
David asked him, "To whom do you belong, and where do you come from?" He answered, "I am a young Egyptian, the slave of an Amalekite; three days ago my master abandoned me because I was sick.
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag."
David said to him, "Can you lead me to this band?" He answered, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will lead you to this band."

He led him there: the Amalekites were scattered over the whole region, eating, drinking, and feasting because of all the great plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah.
David struck them down from dawn until the evening of the next day, and none escaped, except four hundred young men who fled on camels.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, and he rescued his two wives.
Nothing was missing, neither small nor great, neither son nor daughter, neither plunder nor anything they had taken: David brought it all back.
David also took all the flocks and herds; these were driven ahead of him, and people said, "This is David's plunder!"

David came back to the two hundred men too exhausted to have followed him, who had been left at the Wadi Besor. They came forward to meet David and his troops; approaching them, David greeted them warmly.

But all the wicked men, the scoundrels among those who had gone with David, spoke up, "Since they did not go with us, we will give them nothing of the plunder we have recovered, except that each may take his wife and children; let them take them and go!"
But David said, "Do not act like this, my brothers, with what the Lord has given us: he has protected us and handed over to us the band that attacked us.
Who would listen to you in this matter? The share will be the same for the one who goes down into battle and for the one who stays with the baggage: they will share alike."
And so it was, from that day onward; David made it a statute and a rule for Israel, which stands to this day.
Back at Ziklag, David sent a portion of the plunder to the elders of Judah, his friends, saying, "Here is a gift for you, from the plunder of the Lord's enemies."
He sent some to those of Bethel, to those of Ramoth of the Negev, to those of Jattir,
to those of Aroer, to those of Siphmoth, to those of Eshtemoa,
to those of Racal, to those of the towns of the Jerahmeelites, to those of the towns of the Kenites,
to those of Hormah, to those of Bor-ashan, to those of Athach,
to those of Hebron, and to all the places where David and his men had roamed.

titres.titre: The death of Saul at Gilboa

versets.t: The Philistines fought against Israel. The men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell, slain, on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines pressed hard on Saul and his sons, and they killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul's sons.
The weight of the battle bore down on Saul: the archers found him, and he was seized with great fear before them.

Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and run me through, so that these uncircumcised men do not come and run me through and abuse me." But the armor-bearer refused, seized with great fear. Then Saul took his own sword and fell on it.
Seeing Saul dead, the armor-bearer too fell on his own sword and died with him.
So they perished together that day: Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men.

When the men of Israel on the other side of the valley and on the other side of the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and fled, and the Philistines came and settled in them.
The next day the Philistines came to strip the dead and found Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head, stripped off his weapons, and sent word throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among the people.
They put Saul's weapons in the temple of the Ashtaroth and nailed his body to the walls of Beth-shan.
But the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul.
All the valiant men rose and, after marching all night, they took the body of Saul and those of his sons down from the walls of Beth-shan, then returned to Jabesh, where they burned them.
They gathered their bones and buried them under the tamarisk of Jabesh; then they fasted seven days.

titres.titre: David learns of the death of Saul
David's lament over Saul and Jonathan

versets.t: After the death of Saul, David, having returned from his victory over the Amalekites, had been at Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul's camp, his clothes torn and dust on his head. When he reached David, he threw himself to the ground and bowed low.
David said to him, 'Where do you come from?' He answered, 'I have escaped from the camp of Israel.'
David went on, 'What has happened? Tell me.' He said, 'The people fled from the battle; many fell and died; Saul himself and his son Jonathan are dead.'
David asked the young messenger, 'How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?'
The young messenger answered, 'I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, while the chariots and horsemen were closing in on him.
Turning around, he caught sight of me and called to me. I answered, "Here I am."
He asked me, "Who are you?" I said to him, "I am an Amalekite."
He said to me, "Come here and finish me off, for a dizziness has seized me, though my life is still whole within me."
So I went over to him and finished him off, for I knew he could not survive his fall. Then I took the crown from his head and the armlet from his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.'
David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and all the men with him did the same.
They mourned, weeping and fasting until evening for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young messenger, 'Where are you from?' He answered, 'I am the son of a resident alien, an Amalekite.'
David said to him, 'How is it you were not afraid to raise your hand to finish off the Lord's anointed?'
Then David called one of his young men, 'Come here and strike him down!' The man struck him, and he died.
David said to him, 'Your blood be on your own head! For your own mouth accused you when you said, "I am the one who finished off the Lord's anointed."'
David sang this lament over Saul and over his son Jonathan,
and he ordered that it be taught to the sons of Judah; it is the Song of the Bow, which is written in the Book of Jashar:
The splendor of Israel lies slain upon your heights! How the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath, do not proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.
Mountains of Gilboa, let there be on you no more dew or rain, no fields of offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil,
but which drank the blood of the slain and the fat of the valiant. The bow of Jonathan never turned back, and the sword of Saul never returned empty.
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and gracious in their life, in their death were not parted. Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions!
Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in purple and delights, who adorned your garments with ornaments of gold.
How the mighty have fallen in the heat of battle! Jonathan lies slain upon your heights!
I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother! You were so dear to me: your love was more wonderful to me than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!

titres.titre: David king of Judah at Hebron
Ish-bosheth made king; the battle of Gibeon

versets.t: After this, David consulted the Lord, 'Shall I go up into one of the towns of Judah?' The Lord answered, 'Go up.' David asked, 'Where shall I go up?' He answered, 'To Hebron.'
So David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, the widow of Nabal.
He also brought up his men, each with his family, and they settled in the towns around Hebron.
The men of Judah came and there anointed David king over the house of Judah. David was told that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul.
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead to say to them, 'May you be blessed by the Lord, you who fulfilled this duty of faithfulness toward your lord Saul by burying him.
May the Lord now show you his faithful love and his faithfulness! I too will do you good, because you have acted in this way.
And now, take courage, be valiant: your lord Saul is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me to be its king.'
But Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul, brought him over to Mahanaim,
and made him king over Gilead, over the Ashurites, over Jezreel, over Ephraim, over Benjamin, over all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king of Israel, and he reigned two years. Only the house of Judah followed David.
David reigned over the house of Judah, at Hebron, for seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul set out from Mahanaim to march on Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out to meet them near the pool of Gibeon. They halted, the one group on one side of the pool, the other on the other side.
Abner said to Joab, 'Let the young men get up and fight before us!' Joab answered, 'Let them get up!'
They got up and came forward in equal numbers: twelve for Benjamin and for Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve from the servants of David.
Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side; they all fell together. So that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, the Field of Swords; it is near Gibeon.
The fighting was very fierce that day, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was light of foot like a gazelle of the field.
Asahel set out in pursuit of Abner, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left of him.
Abner turned around and said, 'Is that you, Asahel?' He answered, 'It is I.'
Abner said to him, 'Turn aside to your right or your left, seize one of the young men and take his spoil.' But Asahel would not let go of him.
Abner insisted, 'Stop chasing me! Why should I strike you down? How could I then look your brother Joab in the face?'

When Asahel refused to turn aside, Abner struck him in the belly with the butt of his spear, so that it came out behind him. He fell there and died on the spot. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen dead stopped there.
Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. At sunset they came to the hill of Ammah, opposite Giah, on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The sons of Benjamin rallied behind Abner and, forming a single body, took their stand on the top of a hill.
Abner called out to Joab, 'Will the sword devour forever? Do you not know that bitterness will come in the end? How long before you tell the people to stop pursuing their brothers?'
Joab answered, 'As surely as God lives, if you had not spoken, the people would not have given up pursuing their brothers until morning.'
Joab sounded the horn, and all the people halted: they stopped pursuing Israel and fought no more.
Abner and his men marched all night through the plain of the Jordan, crossed it, went through the whole Bithron, and came to Mahanaim.
When Joab had given up pursuing Abner, he gathered all the people: nineteen men of David's servants were missing, besides Asahel.
But the servants of David had struck down three hundred and sixty men of Benjamin, of Abner's followers.
They carried Asahel away and buried him in his father's tomb, at Bethlehem. Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
The war between the house of Saul and the house of David dragged on; David kept growing stronger, and the house of Saul weaker.
Sons were born to David at Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel;
the second, Chileab, by Abigail, the widow of Nabal, of Carmel; the third, Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital;
the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah, David's wife. These were the sons born to David at Hebron.
During the war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was gaining more and more power in the house of Saul.
Now Saul had had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner,

'Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?' Furious at Ish-bosheth's words, Abner replied, 'Am I a dog's head, on Judah's side? To this very day I deal faithfully with the house of Saul your father, with his brothers and his friends, and I have not handed you over to David; and now you charge me with an offense over this woman!
May God deal with Abner with the utmost severity if I do not bring about for David what the Lord swore to him:
to take the kingship away from the house of Saul and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba!'
Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner a single word, so afraid of him was he.
Abner sent messengers on his own behalf to say to David, 'To whom does the land belong? Make a covenant with me, and my hand will help you bring all Israel over to you.'
David answered, 'Good! I will make a covenant with you. But I demand one thing: you shall not appear before me unless you bring Michal, daughter of Saul, when you come to see me.'
Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, 'Give me back my wife Michal, whom I acquired for a hundred Philistine foreskins.'
Ish-bosheth had her taken from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband went with her, walking and weeping behind her as far as Bahurim. There Abner said to him, 'Go, go back home!' And he went back.
Abner spoke with the elders of Israel, 'For a long time now you have wanted David as your king.
Act now, then, for the Lord has said of David: By the hand of David my servant I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from all their enemies.'
Abner also spoke to the people of Benjamin, then went to report to David at Hebron all that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin.
So Abner came to David at Hebron, with twenty men, and David gave them a feast.

Abner said to David, 'Let me set out to gather all Israel to my lord the king; they will make a covenant with you, and you will reign over all that you desire.' David dismissed Abner, and he went away in peace.

Now just then the servants of David and Joab came back from a raid, bringing much plunder with them. Abner was no longer with David at Hebron, for David had dismissed him, and he had gone away in peace.
When Joab and all his troops arrived, he was told, 'Abner son of Ner came to the king, who dismissed him, and he has gone away in peace.'
Joab went to the king, 'What have you done? Abner came to you: why did you let him go free?
You know Abner son of Ner: he came to deceive you, to spy out your comings and goings and to learn everything you are doing.'
When he had left David, Joab sent messengers after Abner; they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah, without David's knowledge.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab drew him aside inside the gateway, as if to speak with him quietly; there he struck him in the belly, and Abner died, because of the blood of his brother Asahel.
David heard of it afterward and said, 'I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the Lord of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May that blood fall on the head of Joab and on all his father's house! May the house of Joab never be without a man suffering from a discharge or leprosy, a man who handles the spindle, who falls by the sword, or who lacks bread!'
So Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel in battle, at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and to all the people with him, 'Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner!' And King David walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner at Hebron; the king wept aloud at Abner's grave, and all the people wept.
The king sang a lament over Abner: Should Abner have died as a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound, your feet were not put in chains: you fell as one falls before scoundrels. And all the people wept over him again.

Then all the people came to David to make him eat while it was still day, but David took this oath, 'May the Lord deal with me with the utmost severity if I taste bread or anything else before sunset!'
All the people noticed it and approved, just as they approved of everything the king did.
That day all the people and all Israel understood that the king had no part in the death of Abner son of Ner.
The king said to his servants, 'Do you not know that a leader, a great man, has fallen today in Israel?
And I, king though I am by anointing, remain weak; these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. May the Lord repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!'
When Saul's son heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his hands went limp, and all Israel was dismayed.
Saul's son had two captains of raiding bands: one was named Baanah, the other Rechab, both sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, of the tribe of Benjamin, for Beeroth is reckoned as part of Benjamin,
and the people of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim, where they live to this day.

Jonathan son of Saul had a son crippled in both feet. He was five years old when the news of the death of Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel: his nurse had picked him up to flee, but in her haste the child had fallen and been left lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Now the sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, Rechab and Baanah, came to the house of Ish-bosheth in the heat of the day, while he was taking his midday rest.
They came into the middle of the house, as if to fetch wheat, and struck him in the belly. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah slipped away.
They had entered the house while Ish-bosheth was lying on his bed in his room; they struck him dead, cut off his head, and carried it away, marching all night through the plain of the Jordan.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, 'Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. Today the Lord has avenged my lord the king on Saul and on his offspring.'
But David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, 'As surely as the Lord lives, who has delivered me from every distress:
the man who came to tell me of Saul's death, thinking he brought good news, I had seized and put to death at Ziklag, as the only reward for his news.
How much more, when scoundrels have murdered an innocent man in his own house, on his bed: shall I not now require his blood at your hands and rid the earth of you?'
At David's command, his young men killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung them up beside the pool of Hebron. As for the head of Ish-bosheth, they buried it in Abner's tomb, at Hebron.
All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, 'Here we are: we are your own bone and flesh.

In the past, even when Saul was our king, it was you who led Israel out on campaign and brought it home. And the Lord said to you: You shall shepherd my people Israel, you shall be ruler over Israel.'
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron; there King David made a covenant with them before the Lord, and they anointed David king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years.
At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months; at Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

The king marched with his men on Jerusalem, against the Jebusites who inhabited the land. They said to David, 'You will not get in here: the blind and the lame will drive you back!' Meaning: David will never get in here.
But David captured the fortress of Zion: this is the City of David.

That day David said, 'Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him reach through the water shaft these lame and these blind, whom David hates!' That is why it is said: The blind and the lame shall not enter the House.
David settled in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built up the area all around, from the Millo inward.
David kept growing greater, and the Lord, the God of hosts, was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, with cedar wood, carpenters, and stonemasons, who built him a palace.
David then knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingship for the sake of his people Israel.
After leaving Hebron, David took still more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of those born to him at Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg,
Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all came up in search of him. David heard of it and went down to the fortress.
The Philistines came and deployed in the Valley of Rephaim.
David consulted the Lord, 'Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hands?' The Lord answered, 'Go up, for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hands.'

David came to Baal-perazim and defeated them there. He said, 'The Lord has broken through my enemies before me, like a breach made by waters.' That is why that place was called Baal-perazim, the Lord of Breaches.
The Philistines abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them off.
The Philistines came up again and deployed in the Valley of Rephaim.
David consulted the Lord, who answered, 'Do not go up to meet them head-on; circle around behind them and attack them opposite the balsam trees.
When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then move quickly, for the Lord will have gone out before you to strike the army of the Philistines.'
David did as the Lord had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.

titres.titre: The ark brought up to Jerusalem

versets.t: David again gathered all the picked men of Israel, thirty thousand.

Then, with all the people assembled around him, David set out from Baale-judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, the ark that bears the Name, the name of the Lord of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim.
They loaded the ark of God onto a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart;
they brought it, with the ark of God, out of the house of Abinadab on the hill, and Ahio walked in front of the ark.
David and all the house of Israel danced before the Lord with all their might, to the sound of songs, harps, lyres, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals.
When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out his hand toward the ark of God and held it, for the oxen had stumbled.
The Lord's anger blazed against Uzzah: God struck him down there for this fault, and he died there, beside the ark of God.
David was distressed that the Lord had broken out in anger against Uzzah; and that place has been called, to this day, Perez-uzzah, the Breach of Uzzah.
That day David was afraid of the Lord and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'
David was unwilling to take the ark of the Lord home with him, into the City of David; he had it taken to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the Lord stayed three months in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household.

King David was told, 'The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God.' So David set out and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the City of David, with rejoicing.
When those carrying the ark of the Lord had gone six steps, he offered a bull and a fattened calf in sacrifice.
David danced with all his might before the Lord, girded with a linen ephod.
David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord amid shouts of joy and the sound of the horn.
As the ark of the Lord entered the City of David, Michal daughter of Saul looked out the window; seeing King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of the Lord and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it; then David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord.
When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts.

Then he distributed to all the people, to the whole multitude of Israel, men and women alike, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a raisin cake. And all the people went away, each to his own home.

As David was returning to bless his household, Michal daughter of Saul came out to meet him and said, 'What honor for the king of Israel today, to have exposed himself before the eyes of his servants' maidservants, as any worthless fellow might expose himself!'
David answered Michal, 'It was before the Lord, who chose me in preference to your father and all his house, to appoint me ruler over his people Israel; it was before the Lord that I danced!
I will humble myself even more and make myself small in my own eyes; but among the maidservants you speak of, by them I will be held in honor.'
And Michal daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
When the king was settled in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies around him,
the king said to the prophet Nathan, 'Look: here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God dwells in a tent!'
Nathan answered the king, 'Go, do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you.'
But that night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying:
'Go and tell my servant David: Thus says the Lord: Are you the one to build me a house to dwell in?
I have never lived in a house, from the day I brought the sons of Israel up from Egypt to this day: I was moving about in a tent, in the Dwelling.
In all my journeying among the sons of Israel, did I ever say to any of the leaders of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel: Why have you not built me a house of cedar?
Now then, you shall say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people Israel;
I have been with you wherever you went, I have cut off all your enemies before you, and I will make you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.
I will fix a place for my people Israel, I will plant them there, and they will dwell in their own home and be disturbed no more; the sons of iniquity will oppress them no longer as they did before,
in the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. And the Lord announces to you that it is he, the Lord, who will make you a house.
When your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, the one who will come from your own body, and I will make his kingship secure.
It is he who will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. If he does wrong, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men,
but my faithful love will not turn away from him, as I turned it away from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
Your house and your kingship will stand firm forever before me; your throne will be established forever.'
Nathan reported to David all these words and all this vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the Lord; he said, 'Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
And even this was a small thing in your eyes, Lord God: now you speak also of the house of your servant for a distant future! Is this the law you give to man, Lord God?
What more can David say to you? You yourself know your servant, Lord God!
For the sake of your word and according to your own heart you have done all this great thing, to make it known to your servant.
How great you are, Lord God! There is none like you, and there is no God but you, according to all that we have heard with our own ears.

And what nation is like your people Israel, the only one on earth whom a God came to redeem as his own people, to make himself a name by doing for it great things and wonders, driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, the nations and their gods?
You firmly bound your people Israel to yourself to be your people forever; and you, Lord, became their God.
Now then, Lord God, the word you have spoken concerning your servant and his house, keep it forever and act as you have said:
may your name be glorified forever, and may it be said: The Lord of hosts is God over Israel! And may the house of your servant David be established before you.
For it is you, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, who have revealed this to your servant: I will build you a house. That is why your servant has found the courage to offer you this prayer.
Now, Lord God, it is you who are God, and your words are true. You have made your servant this good promise:

be pleased, then, to bless the house of your servant, that it may endure forever before you. For it is you, Lord God, who have spoken, and by your blessing the house of your servant will be blessed forever.'
After this, David defeated the Philistines and subdued them; he wrested from the Philistines the control of their capital.

He also defeated the Moabites: making them lie on the ground, he measured them off with a cord, two cord-lengths for death and one full cord-length for life. So the Moabites became David's tributary slaves.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he was going to restore his rule over the river Euphrates.
David took from him one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers; he hamstrung all the chariot horses, keeping only a hundred of them.
The Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, but David struck down twenty-two thousand of them.
David placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became David's tributary slaves. The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's servants and brought them to Jerusalem.
King David also took a great quantity of bronze from Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer.
When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer,

he sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and to congratulate him on having fought and defeated Hadadezer, for Toi was constantly at war with him. Joram brought objects of gold, silver, and bronze,
which King David also consecrated to the Lord, along with the silver and gold he had consecrated from the plunder of all the nations he had subdued:
from Aram, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David made a name for himself on returning from defeating the Edomites in the Valley of Salt: eighteen thousand men.
He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all Edom was subject to David. The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.
David reigned over all Israel, and he administered right and justice to all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder;
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was secretary;
Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were foremost at the king's side.
David asked, 'Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, to whom I may show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?'
Now there was a servant of Saul's household named Ziba. He was brought to David, and the king asked him, 'Are you Ziba?' He answered, 'Your servant!'

The king went on, 'Is there no one at all left of the house of Saul, to whom I may show a kindness that comes from God?' Ziba answered the king, 'There is still a son of Jonathan, crippled in both feet.'
The king asked, 'Where is he?' Ziba answered, 'He is at the house of Machir son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.'
King David sent for him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.
When Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David, he fell on his face to the ground and bowed low. David said, 'Mephibosheth!' He answered, 'Here is your servant.'

David said to him, 'Do not be afraid, for I mean to show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I am restoring to you all the lands of your grandfather Saul, and you yourself shall always eat at my table.'
Mephibosheth bowed low and said, 'What is your servant, that you should turn to a dead dog like me?'
The king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, 'All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I give to your master's son.

You shall farm the land for him, you, your sons, and your servants, and you shall bring in the harvest, so that your master's son may have food to eat; but Mephibosheth, your master's son, will always eat at my table.' Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, 'Your servant will do all that my lord the king commands his servant.' And Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house were in Mephibosheth's service.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he always ate at the king's table; and he was lame in both feet.
After this, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place.

David said, 'I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.' So David sent his servants to console him over his father. But when David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites,

the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their master, 'Do you think it is to honor your father that David sends you consolers? Is it not rather to reconnoiter the city, to spy it out and destroy it, that David has sent you his servants?'
So Hanun seized David's servants, shaved off half their beards, cut off their garments at the middle, up to the buttocks, and sent them away.
David was told, and he sent people to meet them, for the men were covered with shame. The king had them told, 'Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown back, then return.'

The Ammonites saw that they had made themselves odious to David; so they sent to hire the Arameans of Beth-rehob and of Zobah, twenty thousand foot soldiers, the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and the men of Tob, twelve thousand men.
At this news, David sent Joab and the whole army against them, the valiant warriors.
The Ammonites came out and drew up in battle order at the entrance of the gate, while the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob, the men of Tob and of Maacah, stood apart in the open country.
Seeing that he faced a battle line in front of him and behind him, Joab chose some of the picked men of Israel and drew them up facing the Arameans;
he entrusted the rest of the people to his brother Abishai, who drew them up facing the Ammonites.
Joab said, 'If the Arameans get the better of me, you will come to my aid; and if the Ammonites get the better of you, I will come to your rescue.
Be strong! Let us show ourselves valiant for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the Lord do what seems good to him!'
Joab advanced with his troops to attack the Arameans, and they fled before him.
Seeing the Arameans in flight, the Ammonites too fled before Abishai and withdrew into the city. Then Joab broke off the war against the Ammonites and returned to Jerusalem.
Seeing themselves defeated by Israel, the Arameans regrouped.
Hadadezer sent for the Arameans from beyond the river; they came to Helam, under the command of Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army.
David was told, and he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. The Arameans drew up in battle order against David and fought him,
but they fled before Israel. David killed among the Arameans the crews of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen; he also struck down Shobach, the commander of their army, who died there.

All the kings who were vassals of Hadadezer, seeing themselves defeated by Israel, made peace with Israel and became subject to it. And the Arameans dared no longer to come to the aid of the Ammonites.

At the turn of the year, at the time when kings go out to war, David sent Joab with his servants and all Israel; they ravaged the land of the Ammonites and laid siege to Rabbah. But David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening, David, having risen from his bed, was strolling on the roof terrace of the palace. From there he caught sight of a woman bathing; she was very beautiful.
David had inquiries made about her, and he was told, 'Is this not Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?'
David sent people to fetch her; she came to him and he lay with her, at the very time she had purified herself from her uncleanness. Then she returned home.
The woman conceived and sent word to David, 'I am pregnant.'
Then David sent word to Joab, 'Send me Uriah the Hittite.' And Joab sent him to David.
When Uriah had arrived, David asked him about Joab, about the army, and about the fighting.
Then David said to Uriah, 'Go down to your house and wash your feet.' Uriah left the palace, followed by a gift from the king's table;
but Uriah slept at the palace gate, with all his master's servants, and did not go down to his house.
David was told, 'Uriah did not go down to his house.' So David said to Uriah, 'Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?'

Uriah answered David, 'The ark, Israel, and Judah are lodged in tents, my master Joab and my lord's servants are camped in the open field, and am I to go to my house to eat, drink, and lie with my wife? By your life and by your own life, I will do no such thing!'
David said to Uriah, 'Stay here today as well, and tomorrow I will let you go back.' So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him to eat and drink in his presence and made him drunk; but in the evening Uriah went out to sleep with his master's servants, and did not go down to his house.
The next morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and had Uriah carry it.
In the letter he wrote, 'Put Uriah in the front line of the fiercest fighting, then draw back from behind him, so that he may be struck down and die.'
Joab, who was besieging the city, therefore placed Uriah at the spot where he knew the fiercest defenders were.
The men of the city made a sortie against Joab; some of the people fell, among David's servants, and Uriah the Hittite died as well.
Joab sent word to David of all that had happened in the fighting;
he gave this order to the messenger, 'When you have finished telling the king all that happened in the fighting,
if the king becomes angry and asks you: Why did you go so close to the city to fight? Did you not know that they shoot from the top of the wall?

Who struck down Abimelech son of Jerubbaal? Was it not a woman who, from the top of the wall, threw a piece of millstone down on him, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so close to the wall? Then you shall say: Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.'
The messenger set out and, when he came to David, he reported everything Joab had ordered him to say.
The messenger said to David, 'Those men got the better of us; they made a sortie against us in the open field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.
Then the archers shot from the top of the wall at your servants; several of the king's servants died, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.'

David said to the messenger, 'This is what you shall say to Joab: Do not be troubled over this matter, for the sword devours now one, now another. Press your assault harder against the city and destroy it. And you, encourage him.'
Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead and mourned for her husband.
When the mourning was over, David sent for her and took her into his house; she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Lord.
The Lord sent Nathan to David. Nathan came to him and said, 'There were two men in a town, one rich, the other poor.
The rich man had sheep and cattle in great abundance.

The poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb that he had bought. He fed it, and it grew up with him and his children, eating his bread, drinking from his cup, sleeping on his lap: it was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man; but he, unwilling to take one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare a meal for the traveler who had come to him, took the poor man's ewe lamb and prepared it for his guest.'
David's anger blazed fiercely against that man, and he said to Nathan, 'As surely as the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
And he shall restore the lamb fourfold, for having done such a thing and for having shown no pity.'
Then Nathan said to David, 'You are the man! Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: I anointed you king over Israel, I delivered you from the hand of Saul;
I gave you your master's house and put his wives in your arms, I gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that had been too little, I would have added this and that besides.

Why have you despised the word of the Lord, by doing what is evil in his eyes? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword, you took his wife to make her your own, and him you killed with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now, therefore, the sword will never again depart from your house, because you have despised me and taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to make her your own.
Thus says the Lord: I am going to raise up evil against you out of your own house. Before your very eyes I will take your wives and give them to another, who will lie with them in broad daylight.
You acted in secret; but I will do this before all Israel, in broad daylight.'
David said to Nathan, 'I have sinned against the Lord.' Nathan answered David, 'The Lord, for his part, has forgiven your sin: you shall not die.
But since by this deed you have made the Lord utterly despised, the son who has been born to you shall die.'
Then Nathan went home. The Lord struck the child that Uriah's wife had borne to David, and he fell gravely ill.
David pleaded with God for the child; he fasted and, going home, spent the night lying on the ground.
The elders of his household stood by him to raise him from the ground, but he refused and would not eat anything with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him of its death, for they said to themselves, 'While the child was still alive, we spoke to him and he would not listen to us; how can we tell him the child is dead? He might do something desperate!'
But David, seeing his servants whispering among themselves, understood that the child was dead. He asked them, 'Is the child dead?' They answered, 'He is dead.'
Then David rose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, changed his clothes, entered the house of the Lord, and worshiped. Returning home, he asked to be served food, and he ate.
His servants said to him, 'What are you doing? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept; and now that he is dead, you get up and eat!'
He answered, 'While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said to myself: Who knows? Perhaps the Lord will have pity on me and the child will live.
But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back? It is I who will go to him; he will not come back to me.'
David consoled Bathsheba his wife; he went to her and lay with her. She gave birth to a son, whom he named Solomon. The Lord loved him
and made it known through the prophet Nathan, who gave him the name Jedidiah, the Beloved of the Lord, for the sake of the Lord.
Joab attacked Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
He sent messengers to say to David, 'I have attacked Rabbah, and I have already captured the water supply.
Now gather the rest of the people, come and camp against the city, and take it yourself, lest I be the one to take it and it be named after me.'
David gathered all the people, marched on Rabbah, attacked it, and captured it.

He took from the head of their king his crown, which weighed about thirty-four kilograms of gold and held a precious stone; it was placed on David's head. He carried off a great deal of plunder from the city.

As for its population, he took them away and set them to work with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, and made them labor at the brick molds; he did the same to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After this, it happened as follows. Absalom, son of David, had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon, son of David, fell in love with her.
Amnon was so tormented over his sister Tamar that he made himself ill, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.
Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, son of Shimeah, David's brother; Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He said to him, "Son of the king, why are you so downcast morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon answered him, "I love Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom."

Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him: Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat; let her prepare the food in my sight, so that I may watch, and I will eat from her hand."
So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. The king came to see him, and Amnon said to him, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, and I will eat from her hand."
David sent word to Tamar at her house, "Go now to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked them;
then she took the pan and emptied it out before him. But he refused to eat and said, "Send everyone out from me." When they had all gone out,
Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the bedroom, so that I may eat from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.
As she was offering them to him, he seized her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister!"
She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me! Such a thing is not done in Israel; do not commit this outrage.
And I, where would I carry my shame? And you, you would be like one of the fools in Israel. Speak rather to the king: he will not refuse to give me to you."
But he would not listen to her; being stronger than she, he forced her and lay with her.
Then at once Amnon felt a violent loathing for her, greater even than the love he had felt for her. Amnon said to her, "Get up, go away!"
She answered him, "No! Sending me away would be a greater wrong than the one you have already done me." But he refused to listen to her.
He called the young man who served him and said, "Throw this woman out of my presence, and bolt the door behind her."
Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for this was how the king's virgin daughters used to dress. The servant put her out and bolted the door behind her.
Tamar put ashes on her head, tore the long robe with sleeves that she was wearing, laid her hand on her head, and went away crying aloud.

Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has your brother Amnon been with you? For now, my sister, keep quiet: he is your brother; do not take this matter to heart." So Tamar remained, desolate, in her brother Absalom's house.
When King David heard about all this, he was very angry; but he would not hurt his son Amnon, for he loved him, since he was his firstborn.
Absalom said nothing to Amnon, either good or bad, for he hated Amnon for having dishonored his sister Tamar.
Two years later, Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said, "Your servant has sheepshearers; may the king and his servants come along with your servant."
The king answered Absalom, "No, my son, we should not all go, lest we be a burden to you." Absalom pressed him, but he refused to go; however, he blessed him.
Then Absalom said, "If you will not come, please let my brother Amnon go with us." The king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"
But Absalom pressed him, so he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.

Absalom gave this order to his servants: "Watch closely! When Amnon's heart is merry with wine and I say to you: Strike Amnon! then kill him. Do not be afraid: is it not I who command you? Be strong and show yourselves brave!"
Absalom's servants did to Amnon as Absalom had ordered. Then all the king's sons rose, each mounted his mule, and fled.
While they were still on the way, this rumor reached David: "Absalom has killed all the king's sons; not one of them is left!"
The king rose, tore his garments, and lay down on the ground; and all his servants stood by with their garments torn.

But Jonadab, son of Shimeah, David's brother, spoke up: "Let my lord not think that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons: Amnon alone is dead. This has been determined by Absalom ever since the day Amnon dishonored his sister Tamar.
So let the king my lord not take it to heart, thinking that all the king's sons are dead: Amnon alone is dead."
Meanwhile Absalom had fled. The young man on watch looked up and saw a large crowd coming down the road along the hillside.
Jonadab said to the king, "There, the king's sons are coming; it is just as your servant said."
As he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived, and they wept aloud; the king too and all his servants wept very bitterly.
Absalom had fled and gone to Talmai, son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day.
Absalom, having fled to Geshur, stayed there three years.
King David gave up pursuing Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon's death.
Joab, son of Zeruiah, perceived that the king's heart was turning toward Absalom.

He sent to Tekoa for a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be in mourning, put on mourning garments, do not anoint yourself with oil, and behave like a woman who has been mourning a long time for the dead.
You will go to the king and speak these words to him." And Joab put in her mouth what she was to say.
The woman of Tekoa went to speak to the king. Falling on her face to the ground, she prostrated herself and said, "Help, O king!"
The king said to her, "What is the matter?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.
Your servant had two sons; they quarreled in the field, and since there was no one to separate them, one struck the other and killed him.

And now the whole family has risen against your servant, saying: Hand over the one who struck down his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed, and so destroy the heir as well! In this way they would quench the last ember left to me, leaving my husband neither name nor survivor on the face of the earth."
The king said to the woman, "Go home; I will give orders concerning you."
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, O king my lord, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be innocent."
The king replied, "If anyone troubles you again, bring him to me, and he will never touch you again."

She said, "Let the king invoke the Lord your God, so that the avenger of blood may not add to the ruin and my son not be destroyed." He answered, "As the Lord lives, not one hair of your son will fall to the ground!"
The woman said, "Let your servant say one more word to my lord the king." He answered, "Speak."
The woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? In pronouncing this sentence, the king condemns himself, since he does not bring back the one he has banished.

We must all die: we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. Yet God does not take away life; he devises plans so that the banished one may not remain excluded from his presence.

If I have come to speak these words to my lord the king, it is because the people frightened me; your servant said to herself: I will speak to the king; perhaps the king will do what his servant asks.
Yes, the king will listen, to deliver his servant from the hand of the man who wants to cut off both me and my son from God's inheritance.
Your servant said to herself: May the word of my lord the king bring me rest! For my lord the king is like an angel of God, to discern good and evil. May the Lord your God be with you!"
The king answered the woman, "Hide nothing from me of what I am about to ask you." The woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."

The king asked, "Is not the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered, "As surely as you live, O king my lord, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king says! Yes, it was your servant Joab who gave me these orders and who put all these words in the mouth of your servant.
It was to present the matter differently that your servant Joab acted in this way; but my lord is wise, like an angel of God, knowing all that happens on the earth."
The king said to Joab, "Very well, I grant this; go now and bring back young Absalom."

Joab fell on his face to the ground, prostrated himself, and blessed the king; then he said, "Today your servant knows that he has found favor in your eyes, O king my lord, since the king has done what his servant asked."
Joab rose, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the king said, "Let him withdraw to his own house; he shall not see my face." So Absalom withdrew to his house and did not see the king's face.
In all Israel there was no man so praised for his beauty as Absalom: from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.
When he shaved his head, which he did every year because his hair grew heavy on him, the weight of his hair was about two kilograms three hundred grams by the royal weight.
To Absalom were born three sons and one daughter, named Tamar: she was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived two years in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face.
He sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab refused to come. He sent for him a second time, and again Joab refused.
Then Absalom said to his servants, "Look: Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley in it; go and set it on fire." And Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Joab rose, came to Absalom at his house, and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom answered Joab, "I had sent word to you: Come here, so that I may send you to the king to say: Why have I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now I want to see the king's face; and if there is any guilt in me, let him put me to death!"
Joab went to the king and reported these words. The king summoned Absalom, who came and prostrated himself on his face to the ground before him; and the king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom procured a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run before him.

He would rise early and stand beside the road leading to the gate. Whenever a man with a lawsuit came to the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and ask, "What city are you from?" He would answer, "Your servant is from such and such a tribe of Israel."
Then Absalom would say to him, "Look, your case is good and just, but there is no one from the king to hear you."
And he would add, "Ah, if only I were made judge in the land! Then everyone with a lawsuit or a case would come to me, and I would give them justice."
And whenever someone approached to bow down before him, he would stretch out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him.
Absalom acted in this way toward all the Israelites who came to the king for justice; and he stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
At the end of four years, Absalom said to the king, "Let me go to Hebron to fulfill the vow I made to the Lord.
For your servant, while living at Geshur in Aram, made this vow: If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will serve him."
The king said to him, "Go in peace." So Absalom rose and went to Hebron.
