Absalom sent messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the ram's horn, you shall say: Absalom is king at Hebron!"
With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem, invited guests who went in all innocence, suspecting nothing.

While he was offering the sacrifices, Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city of Giloh. The conspiracy grew strong, and the people who rallied to Absalom kept increasing.
Word came to David: "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone over to Absalom."

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, "Get up, let us flee, for there is no other escape for us from Absalom! Hurry and go, lest he overtake us, bring disaster upon us, and put the city to the sword."
The king's servants said to him, "Whatever my lord the king chooses, here are your servants."
The king set out on foot with his whole household; he left ten concubines to keep the palace.
The king went out, with all the people following him, and they halted at the last house.
All his servants marched at his side; all the Cherethites, all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men who had come from Gath in his train, filed past before the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why should you also come with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner, and even an exile far from your homeland.

You came only yesterday, and today should I make you wander with us, when I myself am going I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you; may the Lord show you his faithful love and his faithfulness!"
Ittai answered the king, "As surely as the Lord lives and my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be!"
David said to Ittai, "Go, cross over then." So Ittai the Gittite crossed over, with all his men and all the children who were with him.
The whole countryside wept aloud as the people passed by. The king crossed the Wadi Kidron, and all the people crossed over, heading toward the wilderness.

And there was Zadok too, with all the Levites, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until all the people had finished leaving the city.
The king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and let me see it again, and its dwelling place.
But if he says: I take no pleasure in you, here I am: let him do to me whatever seems good to him."
The king also said to the priest Zadok, "Are you not a seer? Return in peace to the city, with your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan, son of Abiathar: your two sons with you.
Look: I will wait near the fords of the wilderness, until word comes from you to inform me."
So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and remained there.
David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, his head veiled and his feet bare; and all the people with him went up too, their heads covered, weeping as they went.
David was told, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O Lord, turn the counsel of Ahithophel to foolishness, I pray!"
As David reached the summit, where God is worshiped, Hushai the Archite came to meet him, his tunic torn and dust on his head.
David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me.
But if you return to the city and say to Absalom: O king, I will be your servant; as I was once your father's servant, so now I will be yours, then you can frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel for me.
The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be there with you; everything you hear from the king's palace, you shall report to them.
Their two sons are there with them, Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, and Jonathan, son of Abiathar: through them you shall send me word of everything you hear."
So Hushai, David's friend, returned to the city just as Absalom was making his entry into Jerusalem.

David had gone a little beyond the summit when Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, came to meet him with a pair of saddled donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, "What do you mean to do with these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride; the bread and the fruit are food for the young men; the wine is to refresh those who grow weary in the wilderness."
The king asked, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba answered the king, "He has stayed in Jerusalem, for he said to himself: Today the house of Israel will give me back my father's kingship."
The king said to Ziba, "Look, everything that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba said, "I bow down; may I find favor in your eyes, O king my lord!"
As King David came to Bahurim, out came a man of the clan of Saul's house, named Shimei, son of Gera. He came forward cursing
and throwing stones at David and at all King David's servants, while all the people and all the warriors marched at his right and his left.
Shimei said as he cursed him, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you scoundrel!

The Lord is bringing back upon you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you made yourself king; the Lord has handed over the kingship into the hand of your son Absalom, and here you are, caught in your own ruin, for you are a man of blood!"
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me cross over and cut off his head."
But the king answered, "What business is this of yours, sons of Zeruiah? If he curses, it is because the Lord has said to him: Curse David. Who then may ask: Why do you do this?"

David said further to Abishai and to all his servants, "Look, my own son, who came from my own body, seeks my life: how much more, then, this Benjaminite! Let him curse, for the Lord has told him to do so.
Perhaps the Lord will look on my misery and repay me with good in place of the curse laid on me today."
So David and his men went on their way, while Shimei kept pace with him along the hillside, cursing him without ceasing, throwing stones at him and flinging up dust.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted at their destination, and there they refreshed themselves.
Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, entered Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, he said to him, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"
Absalom said to Hushai, "So this is your loyalty to your friend! Why did you not go with him?"
Hushai answered Absalom, "No! The one whom the Lord has chosen, along with all this people and all the men of Israel, to him I will belong, and with him I will stay.
Besides, whom should I serve, if not his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you."
Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Take counsel among yourselves: what should we do?"

Ahithophel answered Absalom, "Go in to the concubines your father left to keep the palace; then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself odious to your father, and all who follow you will be strengthened."
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days, a counsel given by Ahithophel was like an oracle sought from God: such was every counsel of Ahithophel, both for David and for Absalom.

titres.titre: The Counsels of Ahithophel and Hushai

versets.t: Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men; I will set out and pursue David this very night.
I will fall upon him while he is weary and weak, I will terrify him, and all the people with him will flee. Then I will strike down the king alone,
and I will bring back all the people to you: the man you seek is worth the return of all, and all the people will be at peace."
This proposal pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
But Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite as well, and let us hear what he too has to say."
Hushai came to Absalom, who said to him, "This is how Ahithophel has spoken; should we follow his counsel? If not, speak up."
Hushai answered Absalom, "This time the counsel Ahithophel has given is not good."

And he added, "You know that your father and his men are warriors, and that they are as enraged as a bear robbed of her cubs in the wild. Your father is a man of war: he will not spend the night with the people.

Even now he is surely hidden in some cave or some other place. If some of your men fall at the first assault, whoever hears of it will say: There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.
Then even the bravest man, with a heart like a lion's, will lose courage; for all Israel knows that your father is a hero and that his companions are warriors.
This, then, is my counsel: let all Israel gather to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as numerous as the sand by the sea, and go into battle in person.
We will reach him wherever he may be, we will fall upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and not one will be left, neither he nor any of his men.
And if he withdraws into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down to the wadi, until not even a pebble can be found there."

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel." For the Lord had determined to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel, in order to bring disaster upon Absalom.
Hushai said to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, "Ahithophel gave such and such counsel to Absalom and the elders of Israel, and I gave such other counsel.
Now send quickly and warn David: Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but cross over at once, lest the king and all the people with him be swallowed up."
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel; a servant girl would come and inform them, and they would go and tell King David, for they could not be seen entering the city.
But a young man spotted them and reported it to Absalom. So the two of them left in haste and came to Bahurim, to the house of a man who had a cistern in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
The woman took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the cistern, and scattered crushed grain over it, so that nothing could be noticed.

Absalom's servants came to the woman's house and asked, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman answered them, "They have crossed the brook." They searched, found nothing, and returned to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the two men climbed up out of the cistern and went to warn King David: "Get up and hurry across the water, for this is the counsel Ahithophel has given against you."
So David and all the people with him rose and crossed the Jordan; by daybreak not one was left who had not crossed over.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, he saddled his donkey and went home to his own city; after setting his house in order, he hanged himself and died. He was buried in his father's tomb.
David came to Mahanaim, while Absalom crossed the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him.

Absalom had put Amasa in command of the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had gone in to Abigail, daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi, son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir, son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, bowls, and earthenware vessels, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils,

honey, curds, sheep, and cheese from cows' milk. They offered all this to David and to the people with him, for they said, "These people have suffered hunger, weariness, and thirst in the wilderness."
David reviewed the people who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.

He arranged the people in three divisions: a third under the command of Joab, a third under Abishai, son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. The king said to the people, "I too will go out with you."

But the people answered, "You shall not go out! For if we had to flee, no one would care; even if half of us fell, no one would care. But you are worth ten thousand of us; it is better that you be ready to help us from the city."
The king answered them, "I will do what seems best to you." So the king stood beside the gate, while all the people went out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king gave this order to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with young Absalom!" And all the people heard the order the king gave to all the commanders concerning Absalom.
The people went out into the open country to meet Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.
There the army of Israel was defeated by the servants of David; the slaughter that day was great: twenty thousand men.
The battle spread over the whole region, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.

Now Absalom came face to face with the servants of David. He was riding a mule, and the mule went in under the thick branches of a great terebinth; Absalom's head caught fast in the terebinth, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule that carried him went on.
A man saw it and came to report it to Joab: "I saw Absalom hanging in a terebinth!"
Joab said to the man who had told him, "You saw him! Why did you not strike him down on the spot? I would gladly have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."

The man answered Joab, "Even if I could weigh out a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I would not lay a hand on the king's son; for in our hearing the king gave this order to you, to Abishai, and to Ittai: Protect young Absalom for me, each of you!
Had I treacherously taken his life, nothing would have escaped the king, and you yourself would have stood aloof."
Joab said, "I will not waste my time like this with you!" He took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into Absalom's heart, while he was still alive in the middle of the terebinth.
Then ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom, struck him, and finished him off.
Joab sounded the ram's horn, and the people stopped pursuing Israel, for Joab held the people back.
They took Absalom, threw him into a great pit in the middle of the forest, and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each to his own tent.

During his lifetime, Absalom had set up a pillar for himself in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name alive." He gave the pillar his own name, and it is called Absalom's Monument to this day.
Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, said, "Let me run and bring the king the good news that the Lord has vindicated him by delivering him from the hand of his enemies."
Joab said to him, "You are not the one to carry the news today; you shall carry it another day, but not today, for the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to a Cushite, "Go and report to the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed down before Joab and set off running.
Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, pressed Joab again, "Come what may, let me also run behind the Cushite." Joab said, "Why run, my son? This news will bring you no reward."
He replied, "Come what may, I will run." Joab said to him, "Run." So Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof of the gate, above the wall; raising his eyes, he saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out to inform the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he brings good news." The man kept coming closer.
The watchman saw another man running and called out to the gatekeeper, "Here is a second man running alone!" The king said, "He too brings good news."
The watchman added, "By the running of the first, I recognize Ahimaaz, son of Zadok." The king said, "He is a good man, he comes with good news."

Ahimaaz called out to the king, "All is well!" Then he prostrated himself before the king, his face to the ground, and said, "Blessed be the Lord your God, who has handed over the men who lifted their hands against my lord the king!"
The king asked, "Is all well with young Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "I saw a great commotion when Joab sent off the king's servant and me, your servant, but I do not know what it was."
The king said, "Step aside and stand there." He stepped aside and waited.
Then the Cushite arrived and said, "Let my lord the king hear good news! Today the Lord has vindicated you against all who rose up against you."
The king asked the Cushite, "Is all well with young Absalom?" The Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you become like that young man!"
The king shuddered, went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept. As he went he said, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died in your place! Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab was told, "The king is weeping and mourning for his son."
That day the victory turned to mourning for all the people, for the people heard it said, "The king is grieving for his son."
That day the people stole back into the city, as troops steal back when they are ashamed of having fled in battle.
The king had covered his face and was crying out in a loud voice, "My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"

Joab came to the king and said to him, "Today you cover with shame the faces of all your servants, who have just saved your life, and the lives of your sons and daughters, of your wives and your concubines.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you! Today you show that commanders and servants are nothing to you; yes, I see clearly that if Absalom were alive and all of us dead today, that would please you.

Now get up, go out, and speak to the hearts of your servants! For I swear by the Lord, if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you tonight; and that will be a worse disaster for you than any that has befallen you from your youth until now."
So the king rose and sat at the gate. All the people were told, "The king is sitting at the gate." And all the people came before the king. Meanwhile Israel had fled, each to his own tent.

Throughout all the tribes of Israel, all the people were arguing, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies, it was he who saved us from the hand of the Philistines; and now he has had to flee the land before Absalom.
But Absalom, whom we had anointed to reign over us, has died in battle. Why then do you delay in bringing back the king?"

King David sent word to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, "Speak to the elders of Judah: Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house? For what all Israel was saying had reached the king at his residence.
You are my brothers, you are my own bone and my own flesh: why should you be the last to bring back the king?"
And say to Amasa: "Are you not my own bone and my own flesh? May God do so to me and more, if you do not become the commander of my army before me, in place of Joab, for all time!"
So David won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as one man; they sent word to the king, "Return, you and all your servants."
The king came back and reached the Jordan. Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei, son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
He had with him a thousand men of Benjamin, as well as Ziba, the servant of Saul's house, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants; they rushed to the Jordan ahead of the king.
The ferry kept crossing to bring over the king's household and to do whatever he desired. Shimei, son of Gera, threw himself at the king's feet as he was about to cross the Jordan
and said to him, "Let my lord not hold me guilty; do not remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem; let the king not take it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned; but here I am, come today, the first of all the house of Joseph, to meet my lord the king."
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, spoke up, "Does not Shimei deserve death for having cursed the Lord's anointed?"

But David said, "What business is this of yours, sons of Zeruiah, that you should become my adversaries today? Should anyone be put to death today in Israel? Do I not know that today I am again king over Israel?"
And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king swore it to him.

Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, also came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet, nor trimmed his mustache, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king left until the day he returned in peace.
When he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"
He answered, "My lord the king, my servant deceived me. Your servant had said: I will saddle my donkey, ride on it, and go with the king, for your servant is lame.
But he slandered your servant to my lord the king. Yet my lord the king is like an angel of God: do what seems good to you.
The whole house of my father deserved nothing from my lord the king but death; and yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What right have I still to cry out to the king?"
The king said to him, "Why say anything more? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the lands."
Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him even take it all, since my lord the king has come home in peace!"
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king to escort him beyond the river.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age; he had provided for the king during his stay at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem."
But Barzillai answered the king, "How many years of life do I have left, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am now eighty years old. Can I still tell good from bad? Can your servant taste what he eats and drinks? Can I still enjoy the voice of male and female singers? Why should your servant be one more burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will cross a little way beyond the Jordan with the king; but why should the king grant me such a reward?

Let your servant return, that I may die in my own city, near the tomb of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham: let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what seems good to you."
The king said, "Let Chimham cross over with me! I will do for him whatever pleases you, and whatever you ask of me, I will grant you."
All the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed too. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned to his home.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed over with him. All the people of Judah were escorting the king, along with half the people of Israel.

But then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, carried you off and brought you and your household across the Jordan, along with all David's men?"
All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is near of kin to us; why are you angry about this? Have we eaten at the king's expense, or received any gift?"

The men of Israel replied, "I have ten shares in the king, and even in David I have more claim than you! Why have you despised me? Was I not the first to speak of bringing back my king?" But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than those of the men of Israel.

Now there happened to be there a scoundrel named Sheba, son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He sounded the ram's horn and said, "We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse! Each to your tents, Israel!"
So all the men of Israel abandoned David to follow Sheba, son of Bichri; but the men of Judah stayed loyal to their king, from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David went back into his palace at Jerusalem. He took the ten concubines he had left to keep the palace and put them under guard; he provided for their upkeep but did not go in to them again. They remained shut away until the day of their death, living as widows.
The king said to Amasa, "Summon the men of Judah to me within three days, and be present here yourself."
Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the time the king had set.
So David said to Abishai, "Sheba, son of Bichri, will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your master's servants and pursue him, lest he reach fortified cities and escape us."
Behind Abishai went out Joab's men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the warriors; they left Jerusalem to pursue Sheba, son of Bichri.

They were near the great stone at Gibeon when Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his battle dress, girded with a sword fastened at his waist in its sheath; as he stepped forward, the sword fell out.
Joab said to Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" and with his right hand he took hold of Amasa's beard to kiss him.

Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab's other hand; Joab struck him in the belly with it and spilled his entrails on the ground. Without needing a second blow, Amasa died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai went in pursuit of Sheba, son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stood beside Amasa's body and cried out, "Whoever is for Joab and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab!"

Now Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that all the people were stopping, he dragged Amasa off the road into a field and threw a garment over him, for everyone who passed by stopped at the sight of him.
Once Amasa had been removed from the road, everyone went on behind Joab, in pursuit of Sheba, son of Bichri.
Joab passed through all the tribes of Israel as far as Abel-beth-maacah; all the picked men gathered and followed him.
They came and besieged Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah; they raised a siege ramp against the city, reaching the rampart, and all the people with Joab were battering the wall to bring it down.
Then a wise woman called out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab: Come near here, I want to speak with you."
He came near her, and the woman asked, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." She said, "Listen to the words of your servant." He said, "I am listening."
She said, "In the old days people used to say: Let them go and inquire at Abel, and so the matter was settled.
I am one of the peaceful and faithful cities of Israel; you are seeking to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel! Why do you want to swallow up the Lord's inheritance?"
Joab answered, "Far, far be it from me to swallow up or destroy!

That is not so. But a man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba, son of Bichri, has lifted his hand against King David. Hand him over, him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." The woman said to Joab, "His head shall be thrown to you over the wall."

Then the woman went to all the people with her wisdom; they cut off the head of Sheba, son of Bichri, and threw it to Joab. So he sounded the ram's horn, and they dispersed from the city, each to his own tent; and Joab returned to Jerusalem, to the king.
Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, commanded the Cherethites and the Pelethites;
Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder;
Sheva was the secretary; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;
and Ira the Jairite was also in David's personal service.

In the time of David there was a famine that lasted three years running. David sought the face of the Lord, and the Lord said, "It is because of Saul and his house stained with blood, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

The king summoned the Gibeonites to speak with them. The Gibeonites were not sons of Israel but a remnant of the Amorites; the sons of Israel had bound themselves to them by oath, and yet Saul, in his zeal for the sons of Israel and Judah, had tried to wipe them out.
So David said to the Gibeonites, "What can I do for you, and with what reparation will you bless the Lord's inheritance?"

The Gibeonites answered him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house, and it is not for us to put anyone in Israel to death." David said, "Then what do you want me to do for you?"
They answered the king, "The man who decimated us and who plotted to destroy us, so that we should have no place anywhere in the territory of Israel,
let seven of his descendants be handed over to us, and we will hang them before the Lord at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen one of the Lord." The king said, "I will hand them over to you."
But the king spared Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath sworn before the Lord between David and Jonathan, son of Saul.

The king took the two sons whom Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, along with the five sons whom Merab, daughter of Saul, had borne to Adriel, son of Barzillai, from Meholah,

and he handed them over to the Gibeonites, who hanged them on the mountain before the Lord. All seven perished together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock, from the beginning of the harvest until the rain fell from heaven upon them; she kept the birds of the sky from settling on the bodies by day, and the wild beasts by night.
David was told what Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done.

David went to take the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them the day they defeated Saul at Gilboa.
He brought up from there the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan; the bones of those who had been hanged were also gathered up.

They buried the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin, at Zela, in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father; they did everything the king had ordered. After that, God let himself be moved to mercy for the land.
War broke out again between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his servants to fight the Philistines, and David grew exhausted.
Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of Rapha, whose spear weighed about three and a half kilograms of bronze and who was girded with a new sword, was set on killing David.

But Abishai, son of Zeruiah, came to David's rescue: he struck down the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore this oath to him, "You shall never again go out with us to battle, so that you may not put out the lamp of Israel."
After this, there was another battle with the Philistines, at Gob. It was then that Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, one of the descendants of Rapha.
There was yet another battle with the Philistines at Gob; Elhanan, son of Jair, from Bethlehem, struck down Lahmi, the brother of Goliath of Gath, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam.
There was still another battle at Gath. There was a man of great stature there, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all; he too was descended from Rapha.
He defied Israel, and Jonathan, son of Shimeah, David's brother, struck him down.
These four were descended from Rapha at Gath; they fell at the hand of David and his servants.
David spoke to the Lord the words of this song, on the day the Lord had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
He said: The Lord is my rock, my fortress, the one who delivers me;
God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge. My Savior, you save me from violence.
I call on the Lord, who is worthy of praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
The waves of death engulfed me, the torrents of destruction terrified me;
the cords of the realm of the dead entangled me, the snares of death caught me unawares.
In my distress I called on the Lord, I cried out to my God; from his temple he heard my voice, and my cry reached his ears.
The earth reeled and quaked, the foundations of the heavens shook, trembling because he was angry.
Smoke rose from his nostrils, from his mouth a devouring fire, burning coals blazed out of it.
He bent the heavens and came down, a dark cloud beneath his feet.
He mounted a cherub and flew, he soared on the wings of the wind.
He wrapped himself in darkness as in a tent, in a mass of waters and thick clouds.
From the brightness before him blazed coals of fire.
The Lord thundered from the heavens, the Most High made his voice resound.
He shot his arrows and scattered my enemies, his lightning bolts, and he routed them.
The bed of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were laid bare, at the Lord's rebuke, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
From on high he reached out his hand and seized me, he drew me out of the mighty waters;
he delivered me from my powerful enemy, from those who hated me and were stronger than I.
They had surprised me on the day of my calamity, but the Lord was my support.
He brought me out into open ground, he delivered me, because he delighted in me.
The Lord dealt with me according to my righteousness, he repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands,
for I have kept the ways of the Lord and have not turned away from my God to do evil.
All his ordinances were before me, and I did not depart from his laws.
I was blameless before him, keeping myself from all sin.
The Lord repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in his eyes.
With the faithful you are faithful, with the man of integrity you are upright;
with the pure you are pure, but with the crooked you show yourself shrewd.
You save the humble people, but your gaze brings down the proud.
Yes, you are my lamp, O Lord; the Lord lights up my darkness.
With you I charge against an armed troop, with my God I leap over a wall.
God, his way is perfect; the word of the Lord is tested. He is a shield to all who take refuge in him.
For who is God but the Lord? Who is the Rock but our God?
It is God who is my strong stronghold and who makes my way perfect;
he makes my feet like the feet of deer and sets me firm on the heights;
he trains my hands for battle, and my arms bend a bow of bronze.
You give me your shield that saves, and your kindness keeps making me great.
You widen the path beneath my steps, and my ankles do not give way.
I pursue my enemies and destroy them, I do not turn back until I have finished them off.
I finish them off, I crush them, they rise no more, they fall beneath my feet.
You gird me with strength for battle, you make my adversaries bow beneath me.
You make my enemies turn their backs to me, and I destroy those who hate me.
They look, but no one saves them; they cry out to the Lord, but he does not answer.
I grind them like the dust of the earth, I trample them, I tread them down like the mire of the streets.
You deliver me from the strife of my people, you keep me at the head of the nations; a people I did not know serves me.
Foreigners come cringing to me; as soon as they hear of me, they obey me.
Foreigners lose heart; they come trembling out of their strongholds.
The Lord lives! Blessed be my Rock! Exalted be God, the Rock of my salvation,
the God who avenges me and subdues peoples under me,
who snatches me from my enemies! Yes, you lift me above my adversaries, you deliver me from the man of violence.
Therefore I will praise you among the nations, O Lord, and sing to your name.
He gives great victories to his king, he shows faithful love to his anointed, to David and his descendants forever.
These are the last words of David. Oracle of David, son of Jesse, oracle of the man raised on high, of the anointed of the God of Jacob, of the sweet singer of Israel:
The Spirit of the Lord has spoken through me, his word is on my tongue.
The God of Israel has spoken, the Rock of Israel has said to me: The one who rules over men with justice, who rules in the fear of God,
is like the light of morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds: by its brightness, after the rain, the grass springs from the earth.

Is it not so with my house before God? He has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and kept secure. Is he not all my salvation and all my desire? Will he not make them flourish?
But scoundrels are all like thorns that are cast away: no one takes them up with his hand;
whoever would touch them arms himself with iron or a spear shaft, and they are burned on the spot, in the fire.
These are the names of David's mighty men. Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite, chief of the officers: he brandished his spear over eight hundred men whom he struck down at one time.
After him, Eleazar, son of Dodo, son of Ahohi, one of the three mighty men who were with David when they defied the Philistines gathered there for battle. When the men of Israel had withdrawn,

he stood his ground and struck down the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck fast to his sword. The Lord granted a great victory that day, and the people came back behind Eleazar only to strip the slain.
After him, Shammah, son of Agee, the Hararite. The Philistines had gathered into a single band; there was there a plot of ground full of lentils, and the people were fleeing before the Philistines.
But Shammah took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines; and the Lord granted a great victory.
Three of the thirty chiefs went down, at harvest time, to join David at the cave of Adullam, while a band of Philistines was camped in the Valley of Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold, and there was a Philistine garrison at Bethlehem.
David had a longing and said, "Who will bring me water to drink from the cistern that is at the gate of Bethlehem?"

The three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines, drew water from the cistern at the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it to David. But he would not drink it; he poured it out as a libation to the Lord,
saying, "Far be it from me, Lord, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" And he would not drink it. Such were the deeds of these three mighty men.
Abishai, brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Thirty. He brandished his spear over three hundred men whom he killed, and he won a name among the Three.
He was the most honored of the Thirty and became their chief, but he did not equal the first Three.
Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, a valiant man rich in exploits, from Kabzeel, struck down the two champions of Moab; he also went down and struck down a lion in the bottom of a cistern on a snowy day.

He also struck down an Egyptian of great stature: the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff, wrenched the spear from the Egyptian's hand, and killed him with his own spear.
Such were the deeds of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, and he won a name among the three mighty men.
He was more honored than the Thirty, but he did not equal the Three; and David put him in charge of his bodyguard.
Asahel, brother of Joab, was one of the Thirty; then Elhanan, son of Dodo, from Bethlehem;
Shammah from Harod; Elika from Harod;
Helez from Peleth; Ira, son of Ikkesh, from Tekoa;
Abiezer from Anathoth; Sibbecai the Hushathite;
Zalmon the Ahohite; Maharai from Netophah;
Heled, son of Baanah, from Netophah; Ittai, son of Ribai, from Gibeah of the sons of Benjamin;
Benaiah from Pirathon; Hiddai from the wadis of Gaash;
Abi-albon from Arabah; Azmaveth from Barhum;
Eliahba from Shaalbon; the sons of Jashen; Jonathan,
son of Shammah the Hararite; Ahiam, son of Sharar the Hararite;
Eliphelet, son of Ahasbai, son of the Maacathite; Eliam, son of Ahithophel, from Giloh;
Hezrai from Carmel; Paarai the Arbite;
Igal, son of Nathan, from Zobah; Bani from Gad;
Zelek the Ammonite; Naharai from Beeroth, armor-bearer of Joab, son of Zeruiah;
Ira from Jether; Gareb from Jether;
Uriah the Hittite. Thirty-seven in all.
The anger of the Lord blazed out again against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, take a census of Israel and Judah."
The king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, "Go throughout all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba; number the people, so that I may know how many there are."
Joab answered the king, "May the Lord your God multiply the people a hundredfold, and may the eyes of my lord the king see it! But why does my lord the king want to do this?"
But the king's word prevailed over Joab and over the commanders of the army; they left the king to go and number the people of Israel.
Having crossed the Jordan, they camped at Aroer, south of the city that is in the middle of the valley, on the way to Gad and then toward Jazer.
They came into Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi; they came to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon;
they reached the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites, then ended up in the Negeb of Judah, at Beersheba.
After going through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
Joab handed the king the figure of the census: there were in Israel eight hundred thousand fighting men who drew the sword, and in Judah five hundred thousand men.

But after he had numbered the people, David's heart smote him, and he said to the Lord, "I have sinned gravely in doing this. Now, Lord, take away, I pray, the guilt of your servant, for I have acted like a fool."
The next morning, when David got up, the word of the Lord had come to the prophet Gad, David's seer, in these words:
"Go and say to David: Thus says the Lord: I offer you three things; choose one of them, and I will do it to you."

So Gad came to David and reported this word to him: "Will you have seven years of famine in your land, or three months of flight before your enemies as they pursue you, or three days of plague in your land? Consider now and see what answer I am to give to the one who sent me."
David answered Gad, "I am in great distress! Let us fall rather into the hands of the Lord, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hands of men!"
So the Lord sent a plague on Israel, from that morning until the appointed time; from Dan to Beersheba, seventy thousand of the people died.

The angel was already stretching out his hand over Jerusalem to destroy it, when the Lord relented of this disaster and said to the angel who was ravaging the people, "Enough! Now stay your hand." The angel of the Lord was then near the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When he saw the angel who was striking the people, David said to the Lord, "It is I who have sinned, it is I who am guilty; but these sheep, what have they done? Let your hand be against me, then, and against my father's house!"
That day, Gad came to David and said to him, "Go up and set up an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
David went up, according to Gad's word, as the Lord had commanded.
Araunah, looking out, saw the king and his servants coming toward him; he went out and prostrated himself before the king, his face to the ground.
Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David answered, "To buy this threshing floor from you and build an altar to the Lord, so that the plague may be lifted from the people."
Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take it and offer what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the oxen's yokes for the wood.
All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah added, "May the Lord your God receive you with favor!"

But the king said to Araunah, "No! I will buy it from you at its price; I will not offer to the Lord my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty pieces of silver.
David built there an altar to the Lord and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the Lord let himself be moved to mercy for the land, and the plague was lifted from Israel.
King David was old, advanced in years; however much they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.
His servants said to him, "Let a young virgin be sought for our lord the king, to wait on the king and care for him; let her lie against his chest, and our lord the king will be warm."
So they searched throughout the territory of Israel for a beautiful young woman, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very beautiful; she cared for the king and served him, but the king had no relations with her.
Now Adonijah son of Haggith set his heart on the throne, saying, "I will be king." He got himself a chariot, horsemen, and fifty men to run ahead of him.
Never in his life had his father crossed him by asking, 'Why are you doing this?' Adonijah too was very handsome; he had been born after Absalom.
He came to an understanding with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, who rallied to him and supported him.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's warriors were not with Adonijah.
Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves near the stone of Zoheleth, beside En-rogel; he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the men of Judah in the king's service.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, or Benaiah, or the warriors, or his brother Solomon.
Then Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, "Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has made himself king, and our lord David does not know it?
Come now, let me give you a piece of advice, so that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.

Go to King David and say to him, 'My lord the king, did you not yourself swear to your servant: Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne? Why then has Adonijah become king?'
And while you are still speaking there with the king, I will come in after you and confirm your words."
So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending to him.
Bathsheba bowed low and prostrated herself before the king, who asked her, "What do you want?"
She answered him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the Lord your God: Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.
But now Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, know nothing of it!

He has sacrificed oxen, fattened calves, and sheep in abundance; he has invited all the king's sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but he has not invited your servant Solomon.
Now the eyes of all Israel are turned toward you, my lord the king, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
Otherwise, when my lord the king lies down with his fathers, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals."
She was still speaking with the king when Nathan the prophet arrived.
The king was told, "Here is Nathan the prophet." He came in before the king and prostrated himself with his face to the ground.
Nathan said, "My lord the king, is it you who have declared, 'Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne'?

For today he has gone down and sacrificed oxen, fattened calves, and sheep in abundance; he has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. There they are, eating and drinking before him and shouting, 'Long live King Adonijah!'
But me, your servant, he did not invite, nor Zadok the priest, nor Benaiah son of Jehoiada, nor your servant Solomon.
Has this really been done by my lord the king, without your letting your servants know who is to sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"
King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." She came in and stood before the king.
Then the king swore this oath: "As the Lord lives, who has delivered me from every distress,
I swear to you: as I swore to you by the Lord, the God of Israel, saying, Solomon your son shall reign after me and he shall sit on my throne in my place, so will I do this very day."
Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground, prostrated herself before the king, and said, "May my lord King David live forever!"
King David said, "Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada to me." They came in before the king,
and the king said to them, "Take with you the servants of your lord, mount my son Solomon on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet shall anoint him king over Israel. You shall blow the horn and shout, 'Long live King Solomon!'
Then you shall go up after him; he shall come and sit on my throne and reign in my place, for it is he whom I appoint ruler over Israel and over Judah."
Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the Lord, the God of my lord the king, confirm it so!
As the Lord has been with my lord the king, so may he be with Solomon, and may he make his throne even greater than the throne of my lord King David!"
So Zadok the priest went down with Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites; they mounted Solomon on King David's mule and led him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. They blew the horn, and all the people shouted, "Long live King Solomon!"
Then all the people went up after him, playing flutes and rejoicing with such great joy that the earth seemed to split with the noise of their shouting.
Adonijah and all his guests heard the noise just as they were finishing their feast. When Joab heard the sound of the horn, he asked, "Why this uproar in the city in commotion?"
He was still speaking when Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said to him, "Come, for you are a worthy man; surely you bring good news."
Jonathan answered Adonijah, "Not at all! Our lord King David has made Solomon king.
The king sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and they mounted him on the king's mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon. From there they have gone up rejoicing, and the city is in an uproar: that is the noise you heard.
What is more, Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne,

and the king's servants have come to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May your God make Solomon's name even more glorious than yours, and his throne greater than yours!' And the king bowed low on his bed;
he even said, 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who has granted me today a successor on my throne and let me see it with my own eyes!'"
Then, seized with terror, all of Adonijah's guests rose and went their separate ways.
Adonijah, in fear of Solomon, rose and ran to take hold of the horns of the altar.

Solomon was told, "Adonijah is afraid of King Solomon; he has taken hold of the horns of the altar and said, 'Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not put his servant to death by the sword.'"
Solomon declared, "If he behaves as a loyal man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the ground; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die."
King Solomon sent men to bring him down from the altar. Adonijah came and prostrated himself before King Solomon, who said to him, "Go to your house."
As the time of his death drew near, David gave his orders to his son Solomon:
"I am going the way of all the earth. Be strong and show yourself a man.

Keep the charge of the Lord your God, walking in his ways, observing his statutes, his precepts, his rules, and his ordinances, as it is written in the law of Moses. Then you will succeed in all that you do and wherever you turn,

and the Lord will fulfill the word he spoke concerning me: If your sons watch over their conduct, walking before me in faithfulness with all their heart and all their soul, you will never lack a descendant on the throne of Israel.

You yourself know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of Israel's armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether: he killed them, shedding the blood of war in a time of peace, staining with it the belt around his waist and the sandals on his feet.
Act according to your wisdom, and do not let his gray head go down to the realm of the dead in peace.
As for the sons of Barzillai of Gilead, treat them kindly: let them be among those who eat at your table, for they stood by me in the same way when I was fleeing from your brother Absalom.

You still have near you Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim. He hurled a violent curse at me the day I set out for Mahanaim; but he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the Lord that I would not put him to death by the sword.
Now do not let him go unpunished. You are a wise man, and you will know how to deal with him: you shall bring his gray head down to the realm of the dead in blood."
David lay down with his fathers and was buried in the city of David.
He had reigned forty years over Israel: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his reign was firmly established.
Adonijah son of Haggith came to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. She asked him, "Do you come as a friend?" He answered, "As a friend."
Then he added, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Speak."
He went on, "You know that the kingship was mine, and all Israel expected me to reign. But the kingship slipped away from me and passed to my brother: it came to him from the Lord.
Now I have one request to make of you: do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak."
He said, "Please tell King Solomon, for he will not refuse you, to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."
Bathsheba answered, "Very well! I will speak to the king on your behalf."

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. The king rose to meet her, bowed before her, then sat down on his throne. He had a seat placed for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand.
She said, "I have one small request to make of you: do not refuse me." The king answered her, "Ask, my mother, for I will not refuse you."
She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given as a wife to your brother Adonijah."

King Solomon answered his mother, "Why do you ask for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask the kingship for him as well, since he is my older brother, for him and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah!"
And King Solomon swore by the Lord, "May God deal with me in the harshest way if Adonijah has not made this request at the cost of his life!
As surely as the Lord lives, who established me, seated me on the throne of David my father, and built me a house as he promised, this very day Adonijah shall be put to death."
King Solomon gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck down Adonijah, and he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your own lands, for you deserve death; but today I will not put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord God before David my father and shared in all his hardships."
So Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood of the Lord, fulfilling the word the Lord had spoken against the house of Eli at Shiloh.
The news reached Joab, who had sided with Adonijah though he had not followed Absalom. Joab fled to the tent of the Lord and took hold of the horns of the altar.
King Solomon was told that Joab had fled to the tent of the Lord and was beside the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada with this order: "Go, strike him down."

Benaiah came to the tent of the Lord and said to Joab, "Thus says the king: Come out." But he answered, "No, I will die here." Benaiah brought the reply back to the king: "This is what Joab said, this is how he answered me."
The king said to him, "Do as he said: strike him down and bury him. In this way you will remove from me and from my father's house the blood that Joab shed without cause.

The Lord will bring that blood back on his own head, for he struck down two men more righteous and better than himself and killed them with the sword without my father David's knowledge: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah's army.
Their blood will come back forever on the head of Joab and his descendants; but on David, on his descendants, on his house, and on his throne, there will be the peace of the Lord forever."
Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck down Joab, and put him to death; he was buried at his home in the wilderness.
In his place the king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army, and he put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
The king summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem; you shall live there and shall not leave it to go anywhere.
Know this well: the day you go out and cross the Kidron, you shall surely die, and your blood will be on your own head."
Shimei answered the king, "Very well. Your servant will do as my lord the king has said." And Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.
But after three years, two of his servants fled to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei was told, "Your servants are in Gath."
Shimei rose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath, to Achish, to look for his servants. He set out and brought his servants back from Gath.
Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned.

The king summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the Lord, solemnly warning you: On the day you go out to go anywhere at all, know for certain that you shall surely die? And you answered me, 'Very well, I have heard.'
Why then did you not keep the oath sworn to the Lord and the order I gave you?"
The king added, "You yourself know, your heart knows, all the evil you did to David my father; the Lord brings your wickedness back on your own head.
But King Solomon will be blessed, and the throne of David will be firmly established before the Lord forever."
The king gave his orders to Benaiah son of Jehoiada; he went out, struck down Shimei, and he died. Thus the kingship was firmly established in Solomon's hands.

titres.titre: The Egyptian marriage and the high places

versets.t: Solomon allied himself by marriage with Pharaoh, king of Egypt: he married Pharaoh's daughter and settled her in the city of David until he had finished building his palace, the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem.
Only, the people were offering sacrifices at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the Lord up to that time.
Solomon loved the Lord and followed the precepts of David his father; only, he too offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the greatest of the high places; Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
At Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream during the night. God said to him, "Ask what you want me to give you."

Solomon answered, "You have shown great kindness to your servant David, my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart; and you have kept this great kindness for him by giving him a son who sits on his throne today.
Now, Lord my God, it is you who have made your servant king in place of David my father. But I am only a very young man, who does not know how to conduct himself.
Your servant is in the midst of your people, the one you have chosen, a vast people too numerous to be counted or numbered.
Give your servant, then, an attentive heart to govern your people and to discern good from evil; for otherwise, who could govern this people of yours, so numerous?"
It pleased the Lord that Solomon had made this request.
God said to him, "Because you have asked for this, and have not asked for yourself long life, or riches, or the death of your enemies, but understanding to discern what is right,
I now grant your request: I give you a wise and understanding heart, such as no one has had before you and no one will have after you.
And even what you did not ask for, I give you: riches and glory, so that in all your days no king will equal you.
And if you walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments as David your father did, I will lengthen your days."
Solomon awoke: it had been a dream. Returning to Jerusalem, he stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and gave a feast for all his servants.
One day two prostitutes came and presented themselves before the king.
One of them said, "Please, my lord! This woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth while she was there in the house.
Three days after my delivery, this woman also gave birth. We were alone; there was no one else with us in the house, only the two of us.
Now this woman's son died in the night, because she had lain on top of him.
In the middle of the night she got up, took my son from my side while your servant was asleep, and laid him against her chest; then she laid her dead son against my chest.
In the morning, when I got up to nurse my son, I found him dead; but when I looked at him closely in the daylight, I saw clearly that he was not the son I had borne."

The other woman said, "No! My son is the living one, and yours is the dead one." But the first kept saying, "Not at all! Your son is the dead one, and mine is the living one." And they argued before the king.
The king said, "One says, 'This living one is my son, and the dead one is yours'; and the other says, 'No, the dead one is your son, and the living one is mine.'"
Then the king ordered, "Bring me a sword." They brought the sword before the king,
and the king said, "Cut the living child in two, and give half to one and half to the other."

Then the woman whose son was the living one, her heart yearning for her child, cried out to the king, "Please, my lord! Give her the living child; do not kill him!" But the other said, "Let him be neither mine nor yours: divide him!"
The king spoke up, "Give the living child to the first woman; do not kill him: she is his mother."
All Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, and they held him in reverent awe, for they saw that there was in him a divine wisdom to administer justice.
King Solomon reigned over all Israel.
These were his high officials. Azariah son of Zadok was priest;
Elihoreph and Ahijah, sons of Shisha, were secretaries; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder;
Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;
Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the district governors; Zabud son of Nathan, a priest, was the king's friend;
Ahishar was in charge of the palace; Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon had twelve district governors over all Israel; they provided for the king and his household, each having to provide for one month of the year.
These are their names. Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;
Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan;
Ben-hesed, in Arubboth: he had Socoh and all the land of Hepher;
Ben-abinadab, who had all the plateau of Dor; his wife was Taphath, Solomon's daughter;
Baana son of Ahilud, who had Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean, near Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah and beyond Jokmeam;
Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead: he had the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead, as well as the region of Argob in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars;
Ahinadab son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;
Ahimaaz, in Naphtali: he too had married a daughter of Solomon, Basemath;
Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and in Bealoth;
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar;
Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin;
Geber son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the former land of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. There was a single governor over all this region.
Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore; they ate, drank, and lived in joy.

titres.titre: The alliance with Hiram of Tyre
The forced labor for the temple

versets.t: Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. These peoples brought their tribute and were subject to Solomon all the days of his life.
Each day Solomon consumed about six thousand six hundred liters of fine flour and thirteen thousand two hundred liters of ordinary flour,
ten fattened oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.
For he ruled over all the region west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings of that region; and he had peace on every side with his neighbors.
Judah and Israel lived in safety, each under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls for his chariot horses and twelve thousand cavalry horses.
Those district governors provided for King Solomon and for all who were admitted to his table, each in his month; they let nothing be lacking.
They also brought the barley and straw for the workhorses and the steeds to the proper place, each according to the instructions he had received.
God gave Solomon wisdom, very great understanding, and a mind as vast as the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom surpassed that of all the people of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than anyone, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, than Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol; and his fame spread among all the surrounding nations.
He spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five.
He spoke about trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; he also spoke about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.
People came from all nations to hear the wisdom of Solomon, sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.
Hiram, king of Tyre, sent his servants to Solomon, for he had heard that he had been anointed king in place of his father; and Hiram had always been David's friend.
Solomon sent word to Hiram:
"You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the Lord his God, because of the wars that surrounded him with enemies, until the Lord put them under the soles of his feet.
But now the Lord my God has given me rest on every side: no adversary, no threat.

So I intend to build a house for the name of the Lord my God, as the Lord declared to David my father: It is your son, whom I will set in your place on your throne, who will build the house for my name.

So give orders that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. My servants will work with yours, and I will pay you the wages of your servants according to whatever you say; for you know that there is no one among us who can fell timber like the Sidonians."
When Hiram heard Solomon's words, he was greatly overjoyed and said, "Blessed be the Lord today, who has given David a wise son to reign over this great people!"
And Hiram sent word to Solomon: "I have received your message. I will do all you desire concerning the cedar timber and the cypress timber.

My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea; I will float them by sea to the place you tell me, where I will have them untied, and you will take them. For your part, you will grant my wish by providing food for my household."
So Hiram supplied Solomon with as much cedar and cypress timber as he wanted,

and Solomon gave Hiram, for the upkeep of his household, about four million four hundred thousand liters of wheat and four thousand four hundred liters of pure olive oil. This is what Solomon delivered to Hiram each year.
The Lord gave Solomon wisdom, as he had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
King Solomon raised a labor force from all Israel: it numbered thirty thousand men.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand, taking turns: they spent one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon also had seventy thousand porters and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountains,
besides the site foremen, three thousand three hundred in number, who directed the people engaged in the work.
At the king's command, they quarried great stones, choice stones, to lay the foundations of the temple with dressed stone.
Solomon's workers and Hiram's, together with the men of Gebal, cut and prepared the timber and the stones for building the temple.

It was in the four hundred and eightieth year after the sons of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, the second month, that Solomon began to build the house of the Lord.
The temple that King Solomon built for the Lord was thirty meters long, ten meters wide, and fifteen meters high.
The vestibule in front of the great hall of the temple was ten meters long, across the width of the temple, and five meters deep at the front of the temple.
Solomon made latticed windows for the temple, fitted with gratings.
Against the wall of the temple he built a tiered annex, all around the walls, around the great hall and the sanctuary; in this way he made side chambers all around.

The lower story was two and a half meters wide, the middle one three meters, and the third three and a half meters; for offsets had been made on the outside all around the temple, so that the beams would not be set into the walls.
When the temple was built, only stones dressed beforehand at the quarry were used; so during construction no hammer, pick, or any iron tool was heard in the temple.
The entrance to the lower chambers was on the right side of the temple; one went up by a spiral staircase to the middle story, and from there to the third.
Solomon built the temple and finished it; he roofed it with paneling and beams of cedar.
He built the tiered annex against the whole temple; each story was two and a half meters high, and the whole was fastened to the temple with cedar beams.
The word of the Lord came to Solomon:

"This house you are building: if you walk according to my statutes, if you observe my rules and keep all my commandments to guide your conduct by them, I will fulfill for you the word I spoke to David your father:
I will dwell among the sons of Israel and I will not forsake my people Israel."
So Solomon built the temple and finished it.
He lined the interior walls with cedar boards, from floor to ceiling, covering the whole interior with wood; and he covered the floor of the temple with cypress boards.
He lined the last ten meters, at the back of the temple, with cedar boards, from floor to ceiling, and so set apart for himself an inner sanctuary, the Holy of Holies.
The great hall, in front of the sanctuary, was twenty meters long.
Inside, the cedar of the temple was carved with gourds and open flowers; everything was cedar, and no stone could be seen.
At the back of the temple Solomon prepared the sanctuary to place there the ark of the covenant of the Lord.
The sanctuary was ten meters long, ten meters wide, and ten meters high; Solomon overlaid it with pure gold, and he overlaid the altar with cedar.
Solomon overlaid the interior of the temple with pure gold, and he stretched gold chains across the front of the sanctuary, which he overlaid with gold.
He overlaid the entire temple with gold, absolutely all of it; he also overlaid with gold the whole altar that belonged to the sanctuary.
In the sanctuary he made two cherubim of wild olive wood, five meters high.
Each wing of the cherub was two and a half meters; from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was five meters.
The second cherub also measured five meters: the two cherubim were of the same size and the same form.
The height of one was five meters, and the same for the other.

Solomon placed the cherubim in the middle of the sanctuary, their wings spread out: the wing of one touched one wall, the wing of the other touched the opposite wall, and their inner wings met in the middle of the sanctuary.
And he overlaid the cherubim with gold.
On all the walls of the temple, all around, both inside and outside, he had carved in relief cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
He overlaid the floor of the temple with gold, both inside and outside.
At the entrance of the sanctuary he made a double door of wild olive wood; the lintel and the doorposts took up a fifth of the wall.
On these two doors of wild olive wood he carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, which he overlaid with gold, applying the gold over the cherubim and the palm trees.
In the same way, for the entrance of the great hall, he made doorposts of wild olive wood, taking up a fourth of the wall,
and two doors of cypress wood: each door was made of two panels that turned on hinges.
On them he carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, which he overlaid with gold, evenly fitted to the carving.
He built the inner courtyard with three courses of dressed stone and one course of cedar beams.
In the fourth year, in the month of Ziv, the foundations of the house of the Lord were laid;
and in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, the eighth month, the temple was finished in all its details and according to all its specifications. Solomon took seven years to build it.
As for his own palace, Solomon took thirteen years to build it, and he completed it entirely.
He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon: fifty meters long, twenty-five meters wide, fifteen meters high, on four rows of cedar columns topped with cedar beams.
A cedar ceiling covered the chambers that rested on the columns, forty-five in number, fifteen per row.
There were three rows of windows, facing one another three by three.
All the doors and doorposts had square frames, and the windows faced one another three by three.
He made the Hall of Columns: twenty-five meters long and fifteen meters wide, with, at the front, a porch borne by columns.
He made the Hall of the Throne, where he administered justice, the Hall of Judgment, which he paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling.
His own living quarters, in a second court, set back from the hall, were built in the same way. Solomon also built, similar to this hall, a palace for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had married.
All these buildings were of choice stone, cut to measure, sawn with the saw on all faces, from the foundations to the cornices, and on the outside as far as the great court.
The foundations were of choice stone, great stones of five meters and of four meters.
Above them were more choice stones, cut to measure, and cedar.
The great court was surrounded by three courses of dressed stone and one course of cedar beams, like the inner courtyard of the house of the Lord and like the vestibule of the temple.
King Solomon sent to Tyre and brought Hiram.

He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father, a man of Tyre, had been a bronzeworker. Filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill for all work in bronze, he came to King Solomon and carried out all his work.
He cast the two bronze columns: one was nine meters high, and a cord of six meters measured its circumference; and the same for the second.
He made two capitals of cast bronze to crown the tops of the columns; each was two and a half meters high.
Latticework in the form of netting and festoons in the form of little chains adorned the capitals at the tops of the columns, seven for one and seven for the other.
He made the pomegranates: two rows around each lattice, to cover the capitals at the tops of the columns; and he did the same for the second capital.
The capitals on top of the columns of the porch were shaped like lilies, two meters high.
On the two columns, at the very top, above the rounded part that projects beyond the lattice, there were two hundred pomegranates, arranged in rows around each capital.
He set up the columns in front of the vestibule of the temple: the one on the right, which he named Jachin, and the one on the left, which he named Boaz.
At the top of the columns lilies bloomed. So the work of the columns was completed.
He made the Sea of cast bronze: five meters from one edge to the other, perfectly round, two and a half meters high; a cord of fifteen meters measured its circumference.
Under the rim, all around, gourds encircled it, ten for each half meter, going all the way around the Sea in two rows, cast in one piece with it.
It rested on twelve oxen: three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, three facing east; the Sea was set on them, and all their hindquarters were turned inward.
Its thickness was about eight centimeters; its rim, shaped like the rim of a cup, flared out like a lily blossom. It held about forty-four thousand liters.
He also made ten bronze stands: each was two meters long, two meters wide, and one and a half meters high.
This is how they were made: they were formed of panels set into frames;
on the panels, between the frames, there were lions, bulls, and cherubim; and likewise on the frames. Above and below the lions and the bulls hung wreaths in relief.
Each stand had four bronze wheels and bronze axles; its four feet had cast supports, placed under the basin, beyond the wreaths.

The opening for the basin was inside the crown, projecting fifty centimeters; this opening was round, in the form of a pedestal, and seventy-five centimeters wide; it too was carved. The panels themselves were square, not round.
The four wheels were under the panels, and their axles fixed to the stand; each wheel was seventy-five centimeters high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels: axles, rims, spokes, and hubs, all were cast.
At the four corners of each stand were four supports, of one piece with the stand.
At the top of the stand was a circular rim twenty-five centimeters high; and the braces and the panels were of one piece with it.
On the plates of the braces and on the panels he engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space available, with wreaths all around.
This is how he made the ten stands: same casting, same measure, same form for all of them.
He made ten bronze basins: each held about eight hundred eighty liters and measured two meters in diameter; there was one basin on each of the ten stands.
He set the stands, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left; and he placed the Sea on the right side, toward the southeast.
Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the sprinkling bowls. So he finished all the work he was doing for King Solomon in the house of the Lord:
the two columns, the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the columns, the two lattices to cover these two bowls,
the four hundred pomegranates for the two lattices, two rows of pomegranates per lattice, to cover the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the columns;
the ten stands and the ten basins they carried;
the Sea, single, and the twelve oxen that supported it;
the pots, the shovels, and the sprinkling bowls. All these objects that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of polished bronze.
The king had them cast in the plain of the Jordan, in clayey ground, between Succoth and Zarethan.
