versets.t: When the sons of Israel who lived in the land of Judah heard of these things, they were seized with fear at the approach of Holofernes.
Dread and horror took hold of them at the thought that he might treat Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord as he had treated the other cities and their temples.
They sent messengers throughout all Samaria and its surroundings, as far as Jericho, and occupied in advance all the mountain summits.
They surrounded their villages with walls and laid up stores of grain, in view of the coming battle.
The high priest Joakim also wrote to all who lived opposite Esdraelon, facing the great plain near Dothan, and to all whose territory commanded the passes,
instructing them to hold the mountain slopes by which one could climb up to Jerusalem, and to guard the narrow passages that offered a way between the mountains.
The sons of Israel carried out the orders of Joakim, the priest of the Lord.
All the people called upon the Lord with great fervor; they humbled themselves in fasting and prayer, they and their wives.
The priests clothed themselves in sackcloth, the children prostrated themselves before the temple of the Lord, and the altar of the Lord was covered with sackcloth.

With one heart they cried out to the Lord, the God of Israel, that he would not let their children become prey, their wives spoil, their cities a ruin, their sanctuary a profanation, and themselves a mockery to the nations.
Then Joakim, the high priest of the Lord, went through all the land of Israel and spoke to the people:
"Know that the Lord will hear your supplications, if you persevere in fasting and prayer before him.

Remember Moses, the servant of the Lord: Amalek trusted in his strength, his power, his army, his shields, his chariots and his horsemen; Moses defeated him, not by the sword, but by holy prayers addressed to God.
So it will be with all the enemies of Israel, if you persevere in the work you have begun."
After this exhortation, they entreated the Lord, standing in his presence.
Even those who offered the burnt offerings offered them to the Lord clothed in sackcloth, with ashes on their heads.
And all prayed to God with all their heart, that he would visit his people Israel.
It was reported to Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, that the sons of Israel were preparing to resist and had closed the mountain passes.
Beside himself with fury and burning with anger, he summoned all the princes of Moab and the commanders of Ammon,

and said to them: "Tell me who these people are who occupy the mountains; what their cities are, what their strength and importance is; what their military power is, what their number, and what leader commands them.
Why, alone of all the peoples of the West, have they scorned us and not come out to meet us and receive us in peace?"

Then Achior, leader of all the sons of Ammon, answered him: "If you will deign to listen to me, my lord, I will tell you the truth before you about this people who live in the mountains, and no lie will come from my mouth.
This people is of the race of the Chaldeans.
They first went to live in Mesopotamia, because they refused to follow the gods of their fathers, who were in the land of the Chaldeans.
Having abandoned the rites of their ancestors, who honored a multitude of gods,

they worshiped the one God of heaven, who commanded them to leave their country and go to live in Canaan. When famine spread over all the earth, they went down into Egypt, and there, in four hundred years, they multiplied until they became a countless multitude.
Treated harshly by the king of Egypt, forced to build his cities with mortar and brick, they cried out to the Lord their God, who struck the whole land of Egypt with various plagues.
The Egyptians drove them out of their land, and the plague ceased to strike them; but they wanted to enslave them again.
Then the Israelites fled, and God opened the sea before them: the waters rose up, solid like a wall on either side, and they passed on dry ground across the bottom of the sea.
The countless army of the Egyptians pursued them there, but it was swallowed up beneath the waters, and not one of them was left to pass on the story to later generations.
When they had come out of the Red Sea, the Israelites occupied the deserts of Mount Sinai, where no one had ever been able to live or settle.
There the bitter springs turned into sweet water to quench their thirst, and for forty years they received their food from heaven.
Wherever they advanced, without bow or arrow, without shield or sword, their God fought for them and won the victory.
No one has ever overcome this people, except when they turned away from the service of the Lord their God.
Whenever they worshiped a god other than him, they were handed over to plunder, to the sword and to shame.
And whenever they repented of having abandoned their God, the God of heaven gave them the strength to withstand their enemies.

So they defeated the kings of the Canaanites, the Jebusites, the Perizzites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Amorites, and all the mighty men of Heshbon, and they took possession of their lands and their cities.
As long as they did not sin against their God, prosperity was with them, for their God hates iniquity.
But even in recent years, having turned aside from the way that God had marked out for them, they were cut to pieces in battle by several nations, and many were carried off captive to a foreign land.
Lately, having returned to the Lord their God, they have gathered again after this dispersion, they have occupied all these mountains, and they possess Jerusalem once more, where their sanctuary is.

Now therefore, my lord, find out: if they have committed some fault against their God, let us march up against them, for their God will hand them over to you, and they will be brought under the yoke of your power.
But if they have not offended their God, we will not be able to stand against them, for their God will defend them, and we will become the laughingstock of all the earth."
When Achior had finished speaking, all the nobles of Holofernes, full of anger, wanted to kill him, saying to one another:
"Who is this man who dares to claim that the sons of Israel can resist King Nebuchadnezzar and his armies, they, a people without weapons, without strength, ignorant of the art of war?
To show Achior that he is deceiving us, let us climb these mountains; and when the strongest among them have fallen into our hands, we will put him to the sword along with them,
so that all the nations may know that Nebuchadnezzar is the god of the earth, and that there is no other but him."
When they had finished speaking, Holofernes, beside himself with fury, said to Achior:
"Since, playing the prophet, you announce to us that the people of Israel will be defended by their God, I am going to show you that there is no other god but Nebuchadnezzar.
When we have struck them all down as one man, you yourself will perish by the sword of the Assyrians, and all Israel will be wiped out with you.

Then you will know that Nebuchadnezzar is master of all the earth. The sword of my soldiers will run you through, you will fall among the wounded of Israel, and you will breathe no more until you are destroyed together with them.
If you believe your prophecy true, do not let your face fall; let the pallor that covers it leave you, if you imagine that my words will not come to pass.

But so that you may know full well that you will perish with them, from now on you will be joined to this people: when my sword inflicts on them the punishment they deserve, you will fall with them under my vengeance."
Then Holofernes ordered his servants to seize Achior, to lead him to Bethulia, and to hand him over into the hands of the sons of Israel.
The servants of Holofernes took hold of him and crossed the plain; but near the mountain the slingers came out against them.
The Assyrians then turned aside, went along the mountain, bound Achior to a tree by his hands and feet, and left him there before returning to their master.

Then the sons of Israel came down from Bethulia, came to him, untied him, and led him to Bethulia; then they brought him before the people and asked him why the Assyrians had left him bound like that.
At that time Uzziah, son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon, and Charmi, also called Gothoniel, were in command of the city.
So Achior recounted, before the elders and all the people, everything he had answered to the questions of Holofernes, how the men of Holofernes had wanted to kill him for these words,

and how Holofernes, in his anger, had ordered that he be handed over to the Israelites for this, so that after his victory over Israel he might put Achior to death by various tortures, for having said that the God of heaven was their defender.

When Achior had finished his account, all the people fell down, their faces to the ground, worshiping the Lord; and, mingling groans and tears, with one heart they poured out their prayers before the Lord:

"Lord, God of heaven and earth, see their pride, consider our lowliness; turn your eyes to the face of your faithful ones, and show that you do not abandon those who trust in you, but that you humble those who presume upon themselves and glory in their own power."
When the people had ceased weeping and had spent the whole day in prayer, they comforted Achior:
"The God of our fathers, whose power you have proclaimed, will reward you by letting you see their ruin instead.
And when the Lord our God has granted this deliverance to his servants, may God be with you also among us, so that you may live with us, as you please, you and all who belong to you."
When the assembly had dispersed, Uzziah received Achior into his house and gave him a great banquet.
He invited the elders to it, and, the fast being over, they ate together.
Then all the people gathered again, and they prayed all night in their meeting place, imploring the help of the God of Israel.

titres.titre: The people at the end of their strength; the reprieve of Uzziah

versets.t: The next day, Holofernes ordered his troops to march up against Bethulia.

His army numbered one hundred and twenty thousand foot soldiers and twenty-two thousand horsemen, not counting the men of war he had taken prisoner and the young men brought from the provinces and cities.

All together they prepared for battle against the sons of Israel and, going along the mountain to the summit that faces Dothan, they camped from the place called Belma as far as Kelmon, opposite Esdraelon.
When the sons of Israel saw this multitude, they fell to the ground, covered their heads with ashes, and all together prayed to the God of Israel to show his mercy to his people.
Then, taking up their weapons, they occupied the places where narrow paths passed between the mountains, and they kept watch there day and night.
As he went about the surroundings, Holofernes discovered, outside the city to the south, a spring that supplied it with water through an aqueduct, and he had this aqueduct cut off.
There were, however, not far from the walls, other springs where the besieged came to draw a little water in secret, more to relieve their thirst than to quench it.

But the sons of Ammon and of Moab came to Holofernes: "The sons of Israel trust neither in their spears nor in their arrows; it is these mountains that protect them, these hills hanging over the precipices that make their strength.

To defeat them without giving battle, post guards near the springs, so that they cannot draw water there; thus you will make them perish without a fight, or else, exhausted by thirst, they will surrender their city, which they think impregnable because it stands on the mountains."
This advice pleased Holofernes and his officers, and he posted a hundred men around each spring.

After twenty days of this watch, all the cisterns and reservoirs ran dry for the inhabitants of Bethulia; there was not enough left in the city to quench their thirst for a single day, for water was distributed to the people by ration.
Then all of them, men and women, young men and children, gathered around Uzziah, and with one voice
they said to him: "Let God be judge between you and us: you have brought about our misfortune by refusing to make peace with the Assyrians, and that is why God has handed us over into their hands.
That is why no one comes to our aid, while thirst and great misery make us faint before their eyes.
Gather now all the inhabitants of the city, so that we may all surrender, of our own accord, to the men of Holofernes.
For it is better, keeping our lives, to bless God in captivity than to die and be a reproach to all people, after seeing our wives and our children perish before our eyes.

We call to witness today heaven and earth, and the God of our fathers, who chastises us according to our sins: surrender the city without delay to the soldiers of Holofernes, so that we may find a swift death by the sword, rather than a slow agony in the burning of thirst."
At these words, there was lamentation and great outcry throughout the whole assembly; and all, with one voice, for many hours, cried out to God:
"We have sinned with our fathers, we have been unfaithful, we have committed iniquity.
You who are merciful, have pity on us; or else take vengeance on our crimes by chastising us yourself, but do not hand over those who praise you to a people that does not know you,
lest they say among the nations: Where is their God?"
Worn out from so much crying and weeping, they fell silent.
Then Uzziah stood up, bathed in tears, and said: "Take courage, my brothers! Let us wait five more days for the mercy of the Lord.
Perhaps he will put an end to his anger and give glory to his name.
If, when these five days have passed, help has not come, we will do what you have proposed."

These words were reported to Judith, a widow, daughter of Merari, son of Ox, son of Joseph, son of Oziel, son of Elkiah, son of Ananias, son of Gideon, son of Raphaim, son of Ahitub, son of Malchiah, son of Enan, son of Nethaniah, son of Salathiel, son of Simeon, son of Israel.
Her husband, whose name was Manasseh, had died at the time of the barley harvest.
As he was supervising the reapers who bound the sheaves in the fields, the heat of the sun struck him on the head; he died in Bethulia, his city, and was buried there beside his fathers.
Judith had already been a widow for three years and six months.
She had made for herself, on the roof of her house, a secluded room, where she lived in seclusion with her maidservants.
With sackcloth about her waist, she fasted every day of her life, except on the sabbaths, the new moons, and the feasts of the house of Israel.
She was very beautiful, and her husband had left her great riches, many servants, and estates full of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep.
She enjoyed the esteem of all, for she feared the Lord greatly, and no one could say a word of blame against her.
So when she learned that Uzziah had promised to surrender the city after the fifth day, she sent for Chabris and Charmi, two of the elders of the people.
They came to her, and she said to them: "How could Uzziah have said that he would surrender the city to the Assyrians, if within five days help did not come to you?
And who are you to put the Lord to the test like this?
This is no word that draws down mercy, but one that rather stirs up anger and kindles fury.
You have set the Lord a deadline for exercising his mercy, and you have appointed him a day at your own pleasure!
But since the Lord is patient, let us do penance for this fault and beg his pardon with tears.
For God does not threaten as a human does, and he does not blaze up in anger like a mortal.
Let us therefore humble our souls before him, and keep a spirit of humility, as befits his servants.

Let us pray to the Lord with tears to make us feel, in his own way, the effects of his mercy; so that, as the pride of our enemies has troubled our hearts, our humility may become for us a cause of glory.
For we have not imitated the sins of our fathers, who abandoned their God to worship foreign gods.
It was for this crime that they were handed over to the sword, to plunder and to the mockery of their enemies; but we, we know no other God but him.
Let us humbly await his consolation: he will avenge our blood on our enemies who oppress us, he will humble all the nations that rise up against us and cover them with shame, he, the Lord our God.

And now, my brothers, since you are the elders of the people of God and their life depends on you, lift up their hearts with your words, so that they may remember that our fathers were tested, so that it might be known whether they truly served their God.
Let them recall how Abraham our father was tempted and how, tried by many trials, he became the friend of God.
So too Isaac, so too Jacob, so too Moses and all who pleased God: they passed through many afflictions while remaining faithful.
But those who did not accept these trials with the fear of the Lord, who gave free rein to their impatience and murmured against the Lord, insulting him,
those the destroyer struck dead, and the serpents made them perish.
Let us therefore not give in to impatience because of the sufferings we endure,

but let us regard these torments, less than our sins, as the rods with which the Lord corrects us, as his servants, to amend us; let us believe that they are sent to us, not for our destruction, but for our correction."
Uzziah and the elders answered her: "Everything you have said is true, and there is nothing to reproach in your words.
Now therefore pray to God for us, for you are a holy woman and one who fears God."
Judith said to them: "Since you acknowledge that whatever I have been able to say comes from God,
see whether what I have resolved to do also comes from him, and pray that God may give me the strength to accomplish my purpose.
This night you will stand at the gate, and I will go out with my maidservant; pray that, within five days, as you have said, the Lord may look upon his people Israel.
But I do not want you to try to find out what I am undertaking; until my return, when I will bring you news of it, do nothing else but pray to the Lord our God for me."
Uzziah, the ruler of Judah, said to her: "Go in peace, and may the Lord be with you to take vengeance on our enemies!" And leaving her, they went away.
When they had gone, Judith went into her place of prayer; clothed in sackcloth, her head covered with ashes, she prostrated herself before the Lord and called upon him:
"Lord, God of my father Simeon, to whom you gave a sword to punish the strangers who, carried away by lust, had dishonored a virgin by stripping her to her shame;
you who handed over their wives to plunder, their daughters to slavery, and all their spoils to be shared among your servants who burned with zeal for you: come to my aid, Lord my God, help a widow.
It is you who accomplished the wonders of ancient times, you who conceived the events that followed, and they came to pass because you willed it.
All your ways are marked out beforehand, and you have ordered your judgments by your foresight.

Look now upon the camp of the Assyrians, as you once deigned to look upon the camp of the Egyptians who pursued, weapons in hand, your servants, trusting in their chariots, their horsemen, and their multitude of fighters.
But you looked upon their camp, and the darkness stripped them of their strength.
The deep held their feet fast, and the waters swallowed them up.
Let it be so, Lord, with these men, who trust in their multitude, in their chariots, their javelins, their shields and their arrows, and glory in their spears.
They do not know that it is you who are our God, you who, from the beginning, shatter armies, and whose name is the Lord.

Raise your arm, as in ages past; break their power by your power; let their strength collapse under your anger, they who promise themselves to violate your sanctuary, to profane the Dwelling of your name, and to strike down the horns of your altar with their sword.
Grant, Lord, that this man's pride may be brought down by his own sword.
Let him be caught in the snare of his own eyes gazing on me, and strike him down by the sweet words of my lips.
Put in my heart enough firmness to despise him, enough strength to bring him down.
It will be a memorable glory for your name that he should fall by the hand of a woman.

For your power, Lord, is not in numbers, and your will does not depend on the strength of horses; from the beginning the proud have not pleased you, but you have always accepted the prayer of the humble and the gentle.
God of heaven, Creator of the waters and Lord of all creation, hear me, wretched as I am, who beg you and put my trust in your mercy.
Remember, Lord, your covenant; put the word on my lips, strengthen in my heart the purpose it holds, so that your house may keep the holiness with which you have clothed it,
and that all the nations may acknowledge that you are God, and that there is no other but you."

titres.titre: Judith goes to the Assyrian camp

versets.t: When she had finished her prayer to the Lord, Judith rose from the place where she had prostrated herself to the ground before the Lord.
She called her maidservant and, going down into her house, took off her sackcloth and laid aside her widow's garments.

She washed her body, anointed herself with precious myrrh, arranged her hair, put a turban on her head, put on her festive clothes, fastened her sandals, took her bracelets, her necklace, her earrings and her rings: in short, she adorned herself with all her ornaments.

And the Lord heightened her splendor still more; for this adornment sprang not from sensuality but from virtue, and the Lord increased her beauty so that she shone in the eyes of all with an incomparable radiance.
Then she had her maidservant carry a skin of wine, a jar of oil, roasted grain, dried fruit, bread and cheese, and she set out.
When she and her maidservant reached the gate of the city, she found Uzziah and the elders waiting for her.
When they saw her, they were struck with admiration at her beauty.

Without asking her any question, they let her pass, saying: "May the God of our fathers grant you his favor, may he strengthen by his power all the designs of your heart, so that Jerusalem may be glorified by you and your name may be counted among those of the saints and the just!"
All who were present answered with one voice: "Amen! Amen!"
And Judith passed through the gates, she and her maidservant, praying to the Lord.
As she was going down the mountain at daybreak, the Assyrian outposts met her and stopped her: "Where do you come from, and where are you going?"

She answered: "I am a daughter of the Hebrews, and I have fled from them, because I understood that they will be handed over to you as prey, for having scorned you and for not being willing to surrender to you of their own accord, so as to find favor before you.

That is why I said to myself: I will present myself before the prince Holofernes, to reveal to him their secrets and to show him by which way he can take them without losing a single man of his army."
As they heard her words, these men gazed at her face, their eyes filled with astonishment, so greatly did they marvel at her great beauty.
"You have saved your life," they said to her, "by resolving to come down to our lord.
Be assured that when you appear before him, he will treat you well and you will be very pleasing to his heart." Then they led her to the tent of Holofernes and announced her.
As soon as she came into his presence, Holofernes was at once captivated by her eyes.
His officers said to him: "Who could despise the people of the Hebrews, who have such beautiful women? Do they not deserve that, to possess them, we should make war on them?"
Judith saw Holofernes seated under his canopy, whose fabric of purple and gold was adorned with emeralds and precious stones.
Having fixed her eyes on his face, she prostrated herself to the ground to do him homage; and, at their master's command, the servants of Holofernes raised her up.
Then Holofernes said to her: "Take heart, banish fear from your heart; I have never done harm to anyone who was willing to serve King Nebuchadnezzar.
If your people had not scorned me, I would not have raised my spear against them.
Now, tell me why you have withdrawn from them and chosen to come to us."
Judith answered him: "Receive the words of your servant; for if you follow the words of your servant, the Lord will accomplish through you a perfect work.

As surely as Nebuchadnezzar lives, king of the earth, and as his power lives, of which you are the steward for punishing all who go astray: through you not only do men serve him, but the very beasts of the field obey him.
For the wisdom of your mind is famous among all the nations; everyone knows that in all your kingdom you alone are good and powerful, and your governance is praised in all the provinces.
It is also known what Achior said, and no one is unaware how you ordered him to be treated.

For it is certain that our God is so offended by the sins of his people that he has had it announced to them through his prophets that he was going to hand them over to their enemies because of their unfaithfulness.
And because the sons of Israel know that they have offended their God, they tremble with fear before you.
Moreover, famine presses hard on them, and, with their water reservoirs dry, they are already to be counted among the dead.
They have even resolved to kill their cattle and drink their blood.

And the things consecrated to the Lord their God, which he has forbidden them to touch, the grain, the wine and the oil of the tithes and the firstfruits, they have decided to use, daring to feed on what they are not even permitted to touch with the hand. Since they act like this, it is certain that they are rushing to their ruin.
This is what I know, I, your servant; that is why I have fled far from them, and the Lord has sent me to inform you of it.
For I, your servant, serve God even here with you; and your servant will go out of the camp to pray to God.

He will let me know when he will punish them for their sin, and I will come and tell you. Then I will lead you through Judea as far as Jerusalem, and you will find all the people of Israel like sheep without a shepherd: not even a dog will bark against you.
It is the foreknowledge of God that has revealed this to me;
and, since he is angry with them, I have received the mission to inform you of it."
This speech pleased Holofernes and his servants; they marveled at the wisdom of Judith and said to one another:
"There is no woman like her on the earth for bearing, beauty and wisdom of speech." Holofernes said to her:
"God has done well to send you ahead of this people, to hand it over to us.
And if your God does this for me, as your word is good, he will also be my God; you will be great in the house of Nebuchadnezzar, and your name will become famous throughout all the earth."
Then Holofernes had Judith led into the tent where his treasures were kept, that she might stay there, and he arranged what should be served to her from his own table.
Judith answered him: "I cannot eat what you order to be given to me, for fear of committing a fault; I will feed on what I have brought for myself."
Holofernes said to her: "When the provisions you have brought are used up, what shall we do for you?"

"By your life, my lord," answered Judith, "your servant will not have used up all these provisions before God has accomplished by my hand the purpose I have formed." And his servants brought her into the tent that had been assigned.
As she entered, she asked to be allowed to go out, at night and before dawn, to pray and call upon the Lord.
Holofernes ordered his servants to let her come and go as she pleased, for three days, to worship her God.
So each night she went out into the valley of Bethulia and washed herself at a spring.
When she came back up, she prayed to the Lord, the God of Israel, to direct her way for the deliverance of his people.
Then, returning to her tent, she remained pure until evening, when she took her food.
On the fourth day, Holofernes gave a banquet for his servants, and he said to Bagoas, his eunuch: "Go and persuade this Jewish woman to consent willingly to stay with me.
It would be a disgrace, among the Assyrians, for a woman to trifle with a man and leave him without having yielded to his desires."
So Bagoas went in to Judith and said to her: "Let this beautiful young woman not be afraid to come to my lord, to be honored in his presence, to eat with him and to drink wine in joy."
"Who am I," answered Judith, "to resist my lord?
Whatever will be good and excellent in his eyes, I will do; and what pleases him will be the best for me, all the days of my life."
She rose, adorned herself with her ornaments, went in and presented herself before Holofernes.
The heart of Holofernes was overwhelmed, for he burned with desire for her. He said to her:
"Drink, then, and eat in joy, for you have found favor before me."
Judith answered: "I will drink, my lord, for my soul is more honored today than it has been in all the days of my life."
And, taking what her maidservant had prepared for her, she ate and drank before him.
Holofernes, carried away with joy because of her, drank wine to excess, more than he had ever drunk in his life.
When evening came, the servants of Holofernes hurried back to their tents; Bagoas closed the door of the chamber and went away.
All were heavy with wine,
and Judith was left alone in the chamber.
Holofernes lay stretched out on his bed, sunk in the sleep of a deep drunkenness.
Judith had told her maidservant to stand outside, in front of the chamber, and to keep watch.
Standing before the bed, Judith prayed for a while with tears, moving her lips in silence:

"Lord, God of Israel," she said, "strengthen me; cast in this moment a favorable look on the work of my hands, so that, according to your promise, you may raise up your city of Jerusalem, and that I may accomplish what I have believed possible with your help."
When these words were said, she went up to the pillar at the head of Holofernes' bed, took down the sword that hung there,
drew it from its sheath, seized Holofernes by the hair and said: "Lord God, strengthen me at this hour!"
And with two blows to the neck, she cut off his head. Then she took down the drapery from the pillars and rolled the beheaded body to the ground.
Going out without delay, she handed the head of Holofernes to her maidservant, ordering her to put it in her bag.
Then the two of them went out, as was their custom, as if to go and pray; having crossed the camp and gone around the valley, they came to the gate of the city.
From afar, Judith called to the guards on the walls: "Open the gate, for God is with us, and he has shown his power on behalf of Israel."
When they heard her voice, the guards called the elders of the city.
At once all ran toward her, from the least to the greatest, for they had despaired of her return.
They lit torches and gathered around her. Standing on a raised place, Judith called for silence; and when all had fallen quiet,
she said to them: "Praise the Lord our God, who has not abandoned those who hoped in him.
Through me, his servant, he has kept his promises of mercy toward the house of Israel, and this night, by my hand, he has killed the enemy of his people."

Then, drawing the head of Holofernes from the bag, she showed it to them: "Here is the head of Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, and here is the drapery under which he lay in his drunkenness, when the Lord our God struck him down by the hand of a woman.

As surely as the Lord lives, his angel guarded me at my departure, during my stay among them and at my return; the Lord did not allow his servant to be defiled, but he has restored me to you without stain of sin, wholly rejoicing in his victory, in my safety, and in your deliverance.
Celebrate him, all of you, for he is good, for his faithful love is everlasting!"
All, worshiping the Lord, said to Judith: "The Lord has blessed you in his strength, for through you he has reduced all our enemies to nothing."
Uzziah, the ruler of the people of Israel, said to her: "You are blessed, my daughter, by the Lord, the Most High God, above all the women of the earth.
Blessed be the Lord, creator of heaven and earth, who has guided your hand to cut off the head of the greatest of our enemies!

He has made your name so glorious today that your praise will not leave the mouths of people, who will remember forever the power of the Lord; for you did not spare your own life in the face of the sufferings and distress of your race, but you saved us from ruin by walking in uprightness before our God."
And all the people answered: "Amen! Amen!"

Then Achior was brought in, and Judith said to him: "The God of Israel, whom you testified takes vengeance on his enemies, has himself this night, by my hand, cut off the head of the chief of all the unbelievers.

To convince you of it, here is the head of Holofernes who, in the insolence of his pride, despised the God of Israel and threatened you with death, saying: When the people of Israel are defeated, I will put you to the sword."
At the sight of the head of Holofernes, Achior shuddered with horror; he fell face to the ground and fainted.
When he came to himself, he prostrated himself at the feet of Judith and said to her:
"Be blessed by your God in all the tents of Jacob! Among all the peoples who hear your name, the God of Israel will be glorified because of you."
Then Judith said to all the people: "Listen to me, my brothers: hang this head on the top of our walls.
Then, at sunrise, let each one take up his weapons and go out with force, not merely to go down into the valley, but as if to launch a full assault.
The outposts will then run to their general to rouse him for battle.
And when their commanders rush to the tent of Holofernes and find him beheaded, bathed in his blood, terror will seize them.
As soon as you see them flee, throw yourselves boldly in pursuit of them, for the Lord will crush them under your feet."

Then Achior, seeing the power displayed by the God of Israel, abandoned the worship of the nations; he believed in God, had himself circumcised, and was joined to the people of Israel, he and all his descendants, to this day.
As soon as day appeared, the inhabitants of Bethulia hung the head of Holofernes on the walls, and, each having taken up his weapons, they went out of the city with a great uproar and loud shouts.
The outposts, seeing this, ran to the tent of Holofernes.

Those who were there drew near and made noise at the door of the chamber to wake him, deliberately increasing the din, so that Holofernes might be roused from his sleep by this racket, without any of his men having to wake him.
For no one dared, either by knocking or by entering, to open the door of the chamber of the greatest of the Assyrians.
But when his generals, his commanders and all the officers of the army of the king of the Assyrians had arrived, they said to the chamberlains:
"Go in and wake him, for these rats have come out of their holes and dare to challenge us to battle!"
Then Bagoas went into the chamber, stopped before the drapery, and clapped his hands, thinking that his master was sleeping with Judith.

But, straining his ear without hearing the slightest movement of a sleeper, he approached the drapery, lifted it, and saw the corpse of Holofernes stretched on the ground, headless and bathed in his blood. He gave a great cry, burst into tears, and tore his garments.
He went into the tent of Judith and did not find her there; he then rushed out toward the people
and cried out: "A single Jewish woman has brought shame upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar! Here is Holofernes stretched on the ground, and his head is no longer on his body!"
When they heard these words, all the princes of the Assyrian army tore their garments; an immense fear and dread seized them, and their minds were thrown into confusion.
An indescribable outcry rang out in the midst of their camp.
When the whole army learned that Holofernes had been beheaded, it lost all sense and all judgment; heeding only fear and dread, they sought their safety in flight.

Without a word to one another, with heads bowed, abandoning everything, eager to escape the Hebrews whom they heard rushing upon them weapons in hand, they fled across the fields and by the mountain paths.
Seeing the Assyrians in flight, the sons of Israel set out in pursuit of them; they came down sounding the trumpet and raising loud shouts behind them.
As the Assyrians fled in disorder, in all haste, the sons of Israel, pursuing them as one body, cut to pieces all whom they overtook.
At the same time, Uzziah sent messengers to all the cities and countryside of Israel.
So each village and each city, having armed the pick of its young men, sent them in pursuit of the Assyrians; and they hunted them down by the sword as far as their most distant border.
Those who had remained in Bethulia entered the camp of the Assyrians, carried off the plunder abandoned in the flight, and came back from it laden with spoils.

And those who, after the victory, returned to Bethulia, brought back everything that had belonged to the Assyrians: countless cattle, draft animals, and all their baggage; so that all, from the least to the greatest, grew rich from these spoils.
Joakim, the high priest, came from Jerusalem to Bethulia with all his elders, to see Judith.
When she came out to meet him, they all blessed her with one voice: "You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the joy of Israel, you are the honor of our people!

For you have shown a manly heart, and your soul has been full of valor. Because you have loved chastity and, after the loss of your husband, were not willing to know another, the hand of the Lord has clothed you with strength, and you will be blessed forever."
All the people answered: "Amen! Amen!"
Thirty days were scarcely enough for the people of Israel to gather the spoils of the Assyrians.
Everything recognized as having belonged to Holofernes, the gold, the silver, the garments, the precious stones and all the objects, was given to Judith, and the people made it over to her.
And all the people rejoiced, with the women, the young girls and the young men, to the sound of harps and lyres.

titres.titre: The thanksgiving; the end of Judith

versets.t: Then Judith sang this song to the Lord:
"Celebrate the Lord to the sound of tambourines, sing to the Lord with cymbals, compose for him a new song, exalt and acclaim his name.
The Lord puts an end to wars; the Lord, such is his name!
He has pitched his camp in the midst of his people, to deliver us from the hand of all our enemies.
Assyria came from the mountains, from the north, with the myriads of his warriors; their multitude choked the wadis, and their horses covered the valleys.
He promised himself to set fire to my land, to slaughter my young men by the sword, to make my children a spoil and my virgins captives.
But the Lord Almighty covered him with shame; he handed him over into the hands of a woman, and she brought him down.

Their hero did not fall under the blows of young men, the sons of the giants did not strike him, the towering colossi did not measure themselves against him: it was Judith, the daughter of Merari, who felled him by the beauty of her face.
She had laid aside the garments of her widowhood and put on her festive clothes, for the triumph of the sons of Israel;
she poured perfumed oil over her face, arranged the curls of her hair beneath the turban, and put on a new robe to entice him.
The gleam of her sandal dazzled his eyes, her beauty took his soul captive, and with the sword she cut off his head.
The Persians shuddered at her boldness, the Medes at her daring;
the camp of the Assyrians rang with howling, when my people appeared, worn out and parched with thirst.
The sons of young women ran them through, killed them like fleeing children: they perished in battle, before the face of the Lord my God.
Let us sing a song to the Lord, let us sing to the Lord a new song:
Sovereign Master, Lord, you are great and magnificent in your power, and no one can surpass you.
Let all your creatures serve you, for you spoke, and all was made; you sent your breath, and all was created, and no one can resist your voice.
The mountains and the waters are shaken to their foundations, the rocks melt like wax before your face;
but those who fear you are great before you in all things.
Woe to the nation that rises up against my people! For the Lord Almighty will take vengeance on it, he will visit it on the day of judgment,
he will give their flesh to fire and worms, and they will burn, and they will weep in pain forever."
After this victory, all the people went up to Jerusalem to worship the Lord; as soon as they were purified, they all offered their burnt offerings and fulfilled their vows and their promises.
Judith offered all the weapons of Holofernes, which the people had given her, together with the drapery she herself had taken from his bed, as an offering vowed to the Lord.
All the people were in exultation before the sanctuary, and the joy of this victory was celebrated with Judith for three months.
When these days of feasting had passed, each returned home; Judith was honored in Bethulia, and her renown shone throughout all the land of Israel.
Joining chastity to her courage, she knew no man for the rest of her life, from the death of Manasseh, her husband.
On feast days, she appeared magnificently adorned.
After living one hundred and five years in the house of her husband and setting her maidservant free, she died and was buried at Bethulia beside her husband;
and all the people mourned her for seven days.
Throughout her life, and after her death, there was no one, for long years, to trouble the peace of Israel.
The feast day instituted in memory of this victory is counted, among the Hebrews, as one of the holy days, and it has been celebrated by the Jews from that time until today.
This was in the days of Ahasuerus, the one who reigned over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia.
In those days King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa.

In the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and his servants; the commanders of the army of the Persians and the Medes, the nobles and the governors of the provinces gathered before him.
For many days, a hundred and eighty days, he displayed the wealth and glory of his kingdom and the dazzling splendour of his majesty.

When those days were over, the king gave a feast lasting seven days for all the people present in the citadel of Susa, from the greatest to the least, in the courtyard of the garden of the royal palace.

White, green and blue hangings were fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and marble columns; couches of gold and silver rested on a pavement of porphyry, white marble, mother-of-pearl and black marble.
Drinks were served in golden cups of many shapes, and the royal wine flowed freely, with a generosity worthy of the king.
By the king's decree no one was compelled to drink, for the king had ordered all the stewards of his palace to serve each guest as he wished.
Queen Vashti too gave a feast for the women, in the royal palace of King Ahasuerus.
On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he ordered Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served him,
to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing the royal crown, to display her beauty to the peoples and the nobles; for she was very beautiful.
But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. The king was greatly enraged, and his anger burned within him.
So the king consulted the wise men who knew the customs, for the king's business was always laid before all who knew law and justice.
His closest advisers were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king's face and held the highest rank in the kingdom.
"According to the law," he asked, "what is to be done with Queen Vashti, for not obeying the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"
Memucan answered before the king and the princes: "Queen Vashti has done wrong not only to the king, but to all the princes and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.
For the queen's conduct will spread among all the women and make them despise their husbands; they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.'
This very day the princesses of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's conduct will say the same to all the king's princes, and there will be no end of contempt and anger.

If it pleases the king, let a royal edict go out from him, written among the irrevocable laws of the Persians and the Medes: that Vashti shall never again appear before King Ahasuerus, and that the king shall give her royal rank to another woman, better than she.
When the king's edict is proclaimed throughout his vast kingdom, all the women will honour their husbands, from the greatest to the least."
This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king acted on Memucan's word.

He sent letters to all the provinces of the kingdom, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, that every husband should be master in his own house and speak the language of his own people.
After these events, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had subsided, he remembered Vashti, what she had done and the decision that had been made about her.
Then the king's attendants who served him said: "Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king;

let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to the citadel of Susa, into the harem, under the care of Hegai, the king's eunuch, keeper of the women, who will provide for their beauty treatments;
and let the young woman who pleases the king reign in place of Vashti." This advice pleased the king, and he acted on it.
Now in the citadel of Susa there was a Jew named Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin,
who had been carried into exile from Jerusalem among the captives taken away with Jeconiah king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.

He was bringing up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was shapely and beautiful; and when her parents died, Mordecai had adopted her as his own daughter.

When the king's command and edict were proclaimed and many young women were gathered to the citadel of Susa under the care of Hegai, Esther too was taken and brought to the king's palace, under the care of Hegai, keeper of the women.

The young woman pleased him and won his favour; he made haste to provide her with her beauty treatments and her portion of food, gave her seven chosen maids from the king's palace, and settled her and her maids in the finest quarters of the harem.
Esther revealed neither her people nor her family, for Mordecai had forbidden her to do so.
Every day Mordecai would walk in front of the court of the harem, to learn how Esther was and what was being done to her.

When the turn came for each young woman to go to King Ahasuerus, at the end of the twelve months prescribed for the women, that is, six months of treatment with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and the cosmetics used by women,
the young woman would go to the king in this way: she was allowed to take whatever she wished when she went from the harem to the king's palace.

She went in the evening, and in the morning she returned to a second harem, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, keeper of the concubines; she did not go back to the king unless he desired her and she was summoned by name.

When the turn came for Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai who had adopted her, to go to the king, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai, the king's eunuch, keeper of the women, suggested; and Esther won the favour of all who saw her.
Esther was brought to King Ahasuerus in his royal palace in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth (about December to January), in the seventh year of his reign.
The king loved Esther more than all the other women; she found grace and favour with him more than all the rest. He set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.
Then the king gave a great feast for all his princes and his servants, the feast of Esther; he granted the provinces a remission of taxes and gave gifts with royal generosity.
When the young women were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther had revealed neither her family nor her people, as Mordecai had ordered her; for she obeyed Mordecai's commands as when he was bringing her up.
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold, grew angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
Mordecai learned of it and informed Queen Esther, who told the king on Mordecai's behalf.
An inquiry was made, the matter was confirmed, and the two eunuchs were hanged on a gallows; then it was recorded in the book of the Chronicles, in the king's presence.

titres.titre: Haman and the decree of extermination

versets.t: After these events, King Ahasuerus advanced Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, to high rank; he raised him above all the princes of his court.
All the king's servants at his gate knelt and bowed down before Haman, for so the king had commanded; but Mordecai would not kneel or bow down.
The king's servants at his gate said to Mordecai: "Why do you disobey the king's command?"
When they said this to him day after day and he would not listen, they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's words would hold, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not kneel or bow down before him, he was filled with fury.
But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone, for they had told him of what people he was; and Haman resolved to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus.

In the first month, the month of Nisan (about March to April), in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, the pur, that is, the lot, was cast before Haman for each day and each month, and the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar (about February to March).

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus: "There is a certain people scattered among the peoples, in all the provinces of your kingdom, a people set apart, whose laws differ from those of every other people and who do not keep the king's laws: it is not in the king's interest to leave them in peace.
If it pleases the king, let an order be written to destroy them; and I will pay about three hundred and forty tonnes of silver into the hands of the officials, for the king's treasury."
The king took the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews.
And the king said to Haman: "The silver is yours, and the people too: do with them as you see fit."

The king's secretaries were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and everything Haman commanded was written to the king's satraps, to the governors of each province and the officials of each people, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language; it was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the royal signet ring.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces, ordering that all the Jews, young and old, children and women, be destroyed, slaughtered and exterminated in a single day, the thirteenth of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, and that their goods be plundered.
A copy of the edict, to be promulgated as law in every province, was made known openly to all the peoples, so that they would be ready on that day.
The couriers set out in all haste at the king's command, and the edict was promulgated in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, while the city of Susa was in dismay.

titres.titre: The mourning of the Jews; Mordecai urges Esther

versets.t: When Mordecai learned all that had happened, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went through the city crying out with a loud and bitter cry;
he came up to the very gate of the king, for no one could pass through that gate clothed in sackcloth.
In every province, wherever the king's command and edict reached, there was great mourning among the Jews: fasting, weeping and lamentation; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
Esther's maids and eunuchs came and told her, and the queen was deeply shaken. She sent clothes to Mordecai so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he refused them.
Then Esther summoned Hathach, one of the eunuchs the king had appointed to attend her, and charged him to ask Mordecai what was happening and why he was in mourning.
Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square, in front of the king's gate;
and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the sum of money Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasury for the slaughter of the Jews.

He also gave him a copy of the edict of extermination promulgated at Susa, to show to Esther, to inform her of everything, and to charge her to go and plead with the king and beg his mercy for her people.
Hathach came back and reported Mordecai's words to Esther.
Esther charged Hathach to answer Mordecai:

"All the king's servants and the people of his provinces know that if anyone, man or woman, enters the inner court of the king without being summoned, there is one law: he is put to death, unless the king holds out to him his golden sceptre to spare his life. And I have not been summoned to the king these thirty days."
When Esther's words were reported to Mordecai,
he sent back this answer: "Do not imagine that in the king's palace you alone of all the Jews will escape.

For if you keep silent at this time, help and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another quarter, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether it is not for a time like this that you have come to royal rank?"
Esther sent back this answer to Mordecai:

"Go, gather all the Jews of Susa, and fast for me: neither eat nor drink for three days, night or day. I too will fast in the same way with my maids; then I will go to the king in defiance of the law, and if I must perish, I will perish!"
Mordecai went away and did all that Esther had ordered him.

titres.titre: Esther before the king; the first banquet

versets.t: On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, facing the king's apartment. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the apartment, facing the entrance.
When he saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she found grace in his eyes, and he held out to her the golden sceptre he was holding; Esther came forward and touched its tip.
The king said to her: "What is it, Queen Esther? What do you ask? Were it half the kingdom, it would be given to you."
Esther answered: "If it pleases the king, let the king come today, with Haman, to the banquet I have prepared for him."
The king said: "Call Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has said." And the king came with Haman to the banquet Esther had prepared.
At the banquet, over the wine, the king said to Esther: "What is your request? It will be granted. What do you desire? Were it half the kingdom, it would be yours."
Esther answered: "This is my request and my desire:

if I have found grace in the king's eyes, and if it pleases the king to grant my request and fulfil my desire, let the king come, with Haman, to the banquet I will prepare for them; and tomorrow I will answer the king's question."
That day Haman went out joyful and glad at heart; but when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, neither rising nor stirring before him, he was filled with fury against him.
Yet Haman restrained himself and went home. Then he sent for his friends and Zeresh his wife,
and boasted to them of the splendour of his wealth, the great number of his sons, and all the honours with which the king had exalted him above the princes and the servants of the king.
"What is more," he added, "Queen Esther invited no one but me to the banquet she gave with the king; and tomorrow too I am invited by her, together with the king.
But all this means nothing to me, as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."

Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him: "Let a gallows be set up, twenty-five metres high, and in the morning ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it; then go joyfully with the king to the banquet." This advice pleased Haman, and he had the gallows set up.
That night the king could not sleep, so he had the book of records, the Chronicles, brought and read to him.
There was found the account of how Mordecai had denounced Bigthan and Teresh, the two eunuchs of the king who guarded the threshold, who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The king asked: "What mark of honour and distinction has been given to Mordecai for this?" "He has received none," answered the king's attendants who served him.
The king said: "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on the gallows he had set up for him.
The king's attendants answered: "It is Haman, standing in the court." "Let him come in!" said the king.
Haman came in, and the king said to him: "What should be done for the man the king wishes to honour?" Haman said to himself: "Whom would the king wish to honour more than me?"
So Haman answered the king: "For the man the king wishes to honour,
let a royal robe be brought that the king himself has worn, and a horse the king himself has ridden, with a royal crown set on its head;

let the robe and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble princes, let him robe the man the king wishes to honour, lead him on horseback through the city square, and proclaim before him: 'This is what is done for the man the king wishes to honour!'"
The king said to Haman: "Quick, take the robe and the horse, as you have said, and do so for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate; leave out nothing of all you have described."
Haman took the robe and the horse, robed Mordecai, led him on horseback through the city square, and proclaimed before him: "This is what is done for the man the king wishes to honour!"
Mordecai returned to the king's gate, but Haman hurried home, crushed, with his head covered.

He told Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him: "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him: you will only go on falling before him."
While they were still speaking, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman away to the banquet Esther had prepared.

titres.titre: The second banquet; the fall of Haman

versets.t: The king and Haman came to the banquet of Queen Esther.

On this second day, at the banquet, over the wine, the king again said to Esther: "What is your request, Queen Esther? It will be granted. What do you desire? Were it half the kingdom, it would be yours."
Queen Esther answered: "If I have found grace in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases the king, grant me my life, that is my request, and the life of my people, that is my desire.

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, slaughtered and wiped out. Had we only been sold as slaves and servants, I would have kept silent; but the harm done to the king is such that the oppressor could never make it good."
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther: "Who is he, and where is he, the man whose heart has driven him to act like this?"
Esther answered: "The oppressor, the enemy, is this wicked Haman!" Haman was seized with terror before the king and the queen.
In his anger the king rose and left the banquet for the palace garden; Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw clearly that the king had already decided his doom.

When the king came back from the garden to the banquet hall, he saw Haman collapsed on the couch where Esther was reclining. "What!" he said, "will he even assault the queen, here, in my own palace?" No sooner had the words left his mouth than Haman's face was covered.

Harbona, one of the eunuchs, said before the king: "There, in Haman's house, stands the very gallows, twenty-five metres high, that he set up for Mordecai, the man who spoke for the good of the king." The king said: "Hang him on it!"
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had set up for Mordecai. Then the king's anger subsided.

titres.titre: The decree in favour of the Jews

versets.t: That same day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews; and Mordecai was presented to the king, for Esther had revealed what he was to her.
The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai; and Esther put Mordecai in charge of the house of Haman.
Then Esther spoke again before the king; throwing herself at his feet, she pleaded with him in tears to avert the wickedness of Haman the Agagite and the plot he had devised against the Jews.
The king held out to Esther the golden sceptre; she rose and stood before him.

"If it pleases the king," she said, "and if I have found grace before him, if the matter seems right to him and I am pleasing in his sight, let an order be written to revoke the letters that Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, devised and had written to exterminate the Jews in all the king's provinces.
For how could I bear to see disaster fall upon my people, and how could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew: "See, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and he has been hanged on the gallows for laying hands on the Jews.
Now you, write in favour of the Jews as it pleases you, in the king's name, and seal it with the royal signet ring; for a letter written in the king's name and sealed with his ring is irrevocable."

The king's secretaries were then summoned, on the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan (about May to June), and everything Mordecai commanded was written to the Jews, to the satraps, the governors and the officials of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, to each province in its own script, to each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language.

It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus, sealed with the royal signet ring, and the letters were dispatched by mounted couriers, riding on the swift horses of the royal service, bred in the king's stables.

By these letters the king granted the Jews in every city the right to assemble and defend their lives, to destroy, kill and exterminate any armed force of a people or province that might attack them, with its children and women, and to plunder their goods;
and this on a single day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the edict, to be promulgated as law in every province, was made known openly to all the peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to avenge themselves on their enemies.
At once the couriers, mounted on the swift horses of the royal service, set out in all haste, driven on by the king's command; and the edict was promulgated in the citadel of Susa.
Mordecai went out from the king's presence in a royal robe of blue and white, a great crown of gold and a mantle of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa broke into rejoicing.
For the Jews there was nothing but happiness and joy, gladness and honour.

In every province and every city, wherever the king's command and edict reached, there was joy and gladness among the Jews, feasting and holidays. And many among the peoples of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.

On the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day, when the king's command and edict were to be carried out, the very day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, the reverse happened: the Jews overpowered those who hated them.

The Jews assembled in their cities, throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, to strike down those who sought their ruin; no one could withstand them, for the fear of them had come upon all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors and the king's administrators supported the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had come upon them;
for Mordecai was powerful in the king's palace, and his fame spread through all the provinces: this man Mordecai grew greater and greater.
So the Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword: it was a slaughter, an extermination; they dealt as they pleased with those who hated them.
In the citadel of Susa the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men;
they also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman, son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews; but they did not touch the plunder.
That day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

And the king said to Queen Esther: "In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman; what must they have done in the rest of the king's provinces? What is your request? It will be granted. What more do you desire? It will be done."
Esther answered: "If it pleases the king, let the Jews of Susa be permitted to act tomorrow also according to today's edict, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."
The king commanded that this be done; the edict was promulgated at Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
The Jews of Susa assembled again on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa; but they did not touch the plunder.

The rest of the Jews, in the king's provinces, assembled to defend their lives and rid themselves of their enemies; they killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but did not touch the plunder.
This took place on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar; on the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
The Jews of Susa, however, having assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth day, rested on the fifteenth and made it a day of feasting and joy.

That is why the Jews of the countryside, who live in towns without walls, make the fourteenth day of the month of Adar a day of joy, feasting and celebration, when they send portions of food to one another.
Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to all the Jews in the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far,
to require them to celebrate every year the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar,

as the days on which the Jews had gained rest from their enemies, and the month in which their sorrow had turned to joy and their mourning into celebration: days of feasting and joy, when they send portions of food to one another and give gifts to the poor.
So the Jews adopted as a custom what they had begun to do and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them and had cast the pur, that is, the lot, to wipe them out and destroy them;
but when Esther came before the king, he ordered in writing that the wicked plot Haman had devised against the Jews should recoil on his own head, and he and his sons were hanged on the gallows.
That is why these days were called Purim, from the word pur. So, in keeping with all the words of this letter, with what they had seen and what had happened to them,

the Jews established and adopted, for themselves, for their descendants and for all who should join them, the irrevocable custom of celebrating every year these two days, according to the appointed rite and at the appointed time.

These days were to be remembered and celebrated from generation to generation, in every family, every province and every city; and these days of Purim were never to fall into disuse among the Jews, nor their memory fade among their descendants.
Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote a second time, with full authority, to confirm this letter about Purim.
Letters were sent to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and faithfulness,

to establish these days of Purim at their appointed time, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had ordained them, and as the Jews had ordained them for themselves and their descendants, with their fasts and their lamentations.
So the command of Esther fixed these regulations of Purim, and it was recorded in the book.
King Ahasuerus imposed a tribute on the mainland and on the islands of the sea.
All the acts of his power and his valour, and the full account of the greatness to which the king raised Mordecai, are they not written in the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Ahasuerus; great among the Jews, beloved by the multitude of his brothers, he sought the good of his people and spoke for the welfare of all his kindred.
Then Mordecai said: "All this comes from God!
I remember the dream I had about these things: not one detail of that vision has failed to come true.
The little spring that became a river, the light that shone out, the sun and the abundance of waters: this river is Esther, whom the king married and made queen.
The two dragons are myself and Haman.
The nations are those who banded together to blot out the name of the Jews;

and my people, this is Israel, who cried out to God and was saved. The Lord has saved his people, he has delivered us from all these evils; God has worked signs and great wonders, such as have never happened among the nations.
For this he prepared two lots: one for the people of God, the other for all the nations;
and these two lots came at the hour, the time and the day of judgement that God had appointed for all the nations.
Then God remembered his people and did justice to his heritage.
And these days of the month of Adar, the fourteenth and the fifteenth, will be for them days of assembly, joy and gladness before God, from generation to generation, for ever, in Israel, his people."

titres.titre: The colophon; the dream of Mordecai

versets.t: In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought the present letter about Purim, which they declared authentic and translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, a resident of Jerusalem.
In the second year of the reign of Ahasuerus the great king, on the first day of the month of Nisan, Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, had a dream.
He was a Jew who lived in the city of Susa, a man of high standing, attached to the king's service.
He was one of the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried into exile from Jerusalem with Jeconiah king of Judah.
This was his dream: suddenly there were shouts, a great uproar, thunderclaps; the earth trembled and was thrown into turmoil.
Then two great dragons came forward, both ready for battle;
they gave a great roar, and at their voice all the nations made ready for war, to fight against the people of the righteous.
It was a day of darkness and gloom, of anguish, distress, torment and great terror upon the earth.
All the people of the righteous, dreading the disasters that threatened them, were in turmoil and expected to perish;
they cried out to God, and at their cry, from a little spring there gushed a great river, an abundance of waters.
Light and the sun appeared; the lowly were lifted up, and they devoured the mighty.
When Mordecai awoke, having seen in the dream what God had resolved to do, he kept it fixed in his mind and tried, until nightfall, to understand it by every means.
Mordecai was then resting at the court, together with Bigthan and Teresh, the two eunuchs of the king who guarded the palace.
Having caught their thoughts and seen into their plans, he discovered that they were preparing to lay hands on King Ahasuerus, and he warned the king.
The king had the two eunuchs questioned and, on their confession, sent them to their execution.
The king recorded these events in the Chronicles, and Mordecai too kept a written record of them.
The king ordered that Mordecai should hold an office at the court, and he rewarded him for his denunciation.
But Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, stood high in the king's favour; and because of the two eunuchs he sought to destroy Mordecai and his people.

This is a copy of that letter: "Ahasuerus, the great king, to the satraps and governors of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia, who are under his authority, makes this known.

Although I rule over a great many nations and have brought the whole earth under my sway, I have chosen not to abuse my power in pride, but always to govern with mildness and gentleness, to secure a peaceful life for my subjects, to give my kingdom calm and safety to its farthest borders, and to restore the peace that all people cherish.

When I asked my counsellors how this might be achieved, one of them, Haman, who surpasses us all in wisdom, remarkable for his unshakeable devotion and constant loyalty, and who holds the second rank in the kingdom,

revealed to me that a certain people, ill-disposed and mingled among all the nations of the earth, sets itself by its laws against every other people, ceaselessly despises the commands of kings, and so prevents the perfect harmony of our empire.

Considering, then, that this people, alone in perpetual opposition to the whole human race, holding itself apart by the strangeness of its laws, hostile to our interests, commits the worst excesses and endangers the prosperity of the kingdom,

we command that all those pointed out to you in the letters of Haman, our chancellor honoured as a second father, be, together with their wives and children, utterly exterminated by the sword of their enemies, without pity or mercy, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, of this present year;
so that these people, our enemies both in the past and now, cast down in a single day by a violent death into the realm of the dead, may at last leave our affairs in perfect peace and tranquillity."
And Mordecai prayed to the Lord, calling to mind all his works.
He said: "Lord, Lord, almighty King, all things are subject to your power, and no one can withstand you, if you have resolved to save Israel.
It is you who made heaven and earth, and all the wonders that are under heaven.
You are the Lord of all things, and no one can resist you, the Lord!
You know all things, and you know that it was neither from insolence, nor from pride, nor from any desire for glory that I refused to bow down before the proud Haman;
for the salvation of Israel I would gladly have kissed the very soles of his feet.
But I did this so as not to set the honour of a man above the honour due to my God; and I will bow down before no one but you, my Lord, and this is not out of pride.
Now therefore, Lord my God and my King, God of Abraham, have pity on your people; for our enemies have eyes only for our ruin and long to destroy your ancient heritage.
Do not despise your portion, which you redeemed for yourself out of the land of Egypt. Hear my prayer,
be favourable to your heritage, turn our mourning into joy, so that we may live to praise your name, Lord, and do not silence the mouths of those who praise you."
All Israel too cried out to the Lord with all their strength, for death was before their eyes.
Queen Esther too, seeing herself in extreme danger of death, took refuge with the Lord.

Taking off her sumptuous garments, she put on the clothes of anguish and mourning; instead of her precious perfumes she covered her head with ashes and dust, harshly mortified her body, and covered with her torn hair the places she once adorned in joy.
Then she made this prayer to the Lord, the God of Israel: "My Lord, you who are our only King, come to the help of one who is forsaken and has no other helper but you;
for danger is already at hand, reaching out for me.

From my childhood I have heard, in my father's tribe, that you, Lord, chose Israel out of all the nations, and our fathers out of all their forebears, as an everlasting heritage, and that you kept toward them all your promises.
But now we have sinned before you, and you have handed us over to our enemies,
because we worshipped their gods. You are just, Lord!
And now, not content with imposing a bitter servitude on us, they have sworn, by the hands of their idols,
to abolish what your mouth has decreed, to destroy your heritage, to silence the mouths of those who praise you, to extinguish the glory of your temple and your altar,
and to open the mouths of the nations to praise the power of idols and to exalt a king of flesh for ever.

Do not surrender your sceptre, Lord, to what is nothing; let them not laugh at our downfall, but turn their plot back on themselves, and make an example of the man who first raised his fury against us.
Remember us, Lord, reveal yourself in the time of our distress, and give me courage, King of gods and ruler of all power!
Put skilful words on my lips before the lion, and turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, for his ruin and that of his accomplices.
As for us, deliver us by your hand, and come to my help, to me who am alone and have no one but you, Lord! You who know all things,
you know that I hate the glory of the wicked, that I loathe the bed of the uncircumcised and of any foreigner.

You know the constraint I am under, and that I loathe the emblem of my rank set upon my head on the days when I must appear; I loathe it like a filthy rag, and I do not wear it on the days when I keep to myself.
Your servant has never eaten at Haman's table, nor prized the king's banquets, nor drunk the wine of the libations.
From the day I came here until now, your servant has found no joy except in you, Lord God, God of Abraham.
O God, whose power surpasses all, hear the voice of the despairing, deliver us from the hand of the wicked, and rescue me from my anguish!"
Mordecai sent word to her to go in to the king, to plead with him for her people and her homeland.
"Remember," he said, "the days of your lowly condition, when you were fed from my hand; for Haman, the first after the king, has spoken against us to bring about our ruin.
You, call upon the Lord and speak for us to the king: rescue us from death!"
On the third day, when her prayer was ended, Esther took off her clothes of penitence and put on the ornaments of her rank.
Radiant in her adornment, after calling upon God, the arbiter and saviour of all, she took with her two maids.
On one she leaned, as though scarcely able to support her delicate frame;
