the other followed, carrying her mistress's long train.
She herself, blushing in all the radiance of her beauty, her face bright and gracious, yet had her heart gripped with fear.

When she had passed through all the doors, she stood before the king. Ahasuerus was sitting on his royal throne, clothed in all the insignia of his majesty, all resplendent with gold and precious stones; his aspect was fearsome.
Lifting his face, radiant with glory, he cast a glance blazing with anger; the queen fainted, changed colour, and sank against the shoulder of the maid who went before her.
But God changed the king's anger into gentleness: alarmed, he sprang from his throne, held her in his arms until she came to herself, and calmed her with kindly words:
"What is it, Esther?" he said to her; "I am your brother, take courage;
you shall not die, for our decree applies only to our ordinary subjects.
Come near!"
And lifting the golden sceptre, he laid it on her neck, embraced her and said: "Speak to me."
She answered: "I saw you, my lord, like an angel of God, and my heart was troubled before your fearsome majesty;
for you are wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of grace."
As she was speaking, she fainted again, on the point of collapse.
The king was deeply shaken, and all his servants tried to revive her.

titres.titre: The second edict, in favour of the Jews

versets.t: This is a copy of that letter: "Ahasuerus, the great king, to the satraps and officials of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia, and to all who have our interests at heart: greetings!
Many, showered with honours by the boundless kindness of their benefactors, grow arrogant because of it.
Not content with oppressing our subjects, unable to bear the weight of their honours, they plot against their very benefactors.
Banishing gratitude from among men, and puffed up by the insolent glitter of an unexpected fortune, they imagine they can escape the avenging justice of God, who always sees all things.

Often too, the crafty speech of men entrusted, through the friendship of princes, with the administration of affairs, has drawn their rulers into irreparable evils, making them accomplices in the shedding of innocent blood,
the treacherous lies of malice thus deceiving the kindly honesty of those in charge.

And it is not only in ancient tales, as we have just recalled, that you will see such crimes born of the baneful influence of those who abuse their power; look rather at what is happening before your own eyes.
We must therefore provide for the future, to ensure for all a peaceful life and the peace of the kingdom,
by making the necessary changes and by judging with discernment the matters that come before us.
Thus Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian, truly a stranger to Persian blood and far removed from our kindness, welcomed by our hospitality,
had known the goodwill we show to all peoples, to the point of being proclaimed our father and of having everyone bow down before him, in the rank nearest the royal throne.
But unable to bear such greatness with dignity, he set out to rob us of our throne and our life;
by all manner of tricks and lies he sought to destroy Mordecai, our saviour and constant benefactor, and Esther, the blameless partner of our royal dignity, together with their whole people.
By this he hoped to leave us isolated and to hand over the empire of the Persians to the Macedonians.
But these Jews, condemned to death by the most wicked of men, we have found to be not guilty, but faithful to the most just of laws,
and sons of the Most High God, most great and living, who, for us as for our ancestors, keeps our kingdom in prosperity.
You will therefore do well to disregard the letters sent by Haman, son of Hammedatha,
for their author has been hanged on the gallows, with all his household, before the gates of Susa: God, sovereign master of all things, has visited on him without delay the punishment he deserved.
Post up, then, in every place a copy of this letter, let the Jews freely follow their own laws,
and give them your support, so that they may repel those who would attack them in the day of distress, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on that very day.
For God, master of all things, has turned for the people he has chosen this day of ruin into a day of gladness.
You too, therefore, among your solemn feasts, celebrate this great day with every kind of rejoicing, so that now and in time to come
it may be, for us and for the Persians of good will, a pledge of deliverance, and, for those who plot against us, a reminder of ruin.

Any city, and in general any region, that does not observe these prescriptions will be laid waste with fire and sword in fury, made for ever not only unfit for human habitation, but hateful even to wild beasts and birds." Let copies of this decree be posted throughout the empire, and let all the Jews hold themselves ready, on that day, to fight their enemies.
Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian, set out from the land of Kittim and defeated Darius, king of the Persians and the Medes, reigning in his place after having first reigned over Greece.
He fought many wars, captured many fortresses, and put the kings of the earth to death.
He advanced to the ends of the earth and carried off the spoils of a multitude of nations, and the earth fell silent before him.
His heart was lifted up and swelled with pride; he gathered a very powerful army,
and subdued countries, nations, and princes, who became his tributaries.
After this he fell sick and knew that he was about to die.
He summoned his highest officers, the companions of his youth, and while still alive divided his empire among them.
Alexander had reigned twelve years when he died.
His officers took power, each in his own domain.
They all put on the royal crown after his death, and their sons after them, for many years, and they multiplied evils upon the earth.
From these kings there came a wicked offshoot, Antiochus Epiphanes, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome; he became king around 175 before Jesus Christ.

In those days there arose in Israel unfaithful sons who led many astray, saying, "Come, let us make a covenant with the nations around us, for ever since we set ourselves apart from them, many evils have overtaken us."
This proposal seemed good in their eyes,
and some of the people eagerly went to the king, who authorized them to follow the customs of the nations.
So they built a gymnasium in Jerusalem, in the manner of the nations;
they removed the marks of their circumcision, and thus, renouncing the holy covenant, they allied themselves with the nations and sold themselves to do evil.
When his power seemed to him secure, Antiochus resolved to reign over Egypt, so as to be master of the two kingdoms.
He entered Egypt with a powerful army, with chariots, elephants, cavalry, and a great fleet.
He attacked Ptolemy, king of Egypt, who took fright before him and fled; many fell, struck down and slain.
The Syrians captured the fortified cities of Egypt, and Antiochus carried off their spoils.
After defeating Egypt, around 169 before Jesus Christ, Antiochus turned back and marched against Israel.
Going up to Jerusalem with a powerful army,

he entered the sanctuary with insolent boldness and carried off the golden altar, the lampstand with all its utensils, the table for the bread of the offering, the cups, the bowls, and the golden censers, the veil, the crowns, and the golden ornament on the front of the temple, stripping off all its overlay.
He also took the silver, the gold, and the precious vessels, as well as the hidden treasures he could find; and carrying it all off, he returned to his own land,
after slaughtering many people and speaking with great insolence.
There was deep mourning in Israel, everywhere it dwelt.
Rulers and elders groaned; young women and young men lost their vigor, and the beauty of the women faded.
The bridegroom took up the lament; seated in her bridal chamber, the bride wept.
The land trembled for its inhabitants, and the whole house of Jacob was clothed with shame.
Two years later, the king sent a chief collector of tribute to the towns of Judah. He arrived at Jerusalem with a large force;
he addressed the inhabitants with friendly words, by deceit, and they received him without suspicion;
then, suddenly, he fell upon the city, struck it a heavy blow, and destroyed many of the people of Israel.
He plundered the city, set fire to it, tore down its houses, and demolished its walls.
The women and children were led away captive, and the livestock was seized.
Then the Syrians surrounded the City of David with a great and strong wall and with sturdy towers, and it became their citadel.
There they settled a wicked brood, lawless men, and they entrenched themselves;
they stored up weapons and provisions, and gathering the spoils of Jerusalem, they deposited them there; and so they became a great menace to the city.
This citadel was like an ambush set against the sanctuary, a relentless and formidable adversary for Israel.
They shed innocent blood around the temple and defiled the sanctuary.
Because of them the inhabitants fled from Jerusalem, which became a dwelling of strangers, a stranger to her own children, forsaken by her own.
Her sanctuary was left desolate like a wilderness, her feasts were turned into mourning, her sabbaths into reproach, and her honor into contempt.
As great as her glory had been, so great was her humiliation, and her greatness was turned into mourning.
King Antiochus published throughout his kingdom an edict ordering that all should become one single people and that each should abandon his own law.
All the nations bowed to the king's command,
and many of the people of Israel too adopted his worship: they sacrificed to idols and profaned the sabbath.
The king sent messengers with letters to Jerusalem and to the towns of Judah, ordering them to follow customs foreign to the land,
to put a stop in the temple to the burnt offerings, the sacrifices, and the libations,
to profane the sabbaths and the feasts,
to defile the sanctuary and everything holy,
to build altars, sacred precincts, and temples for idols, to sacrifice swine and other unclean animals,
to leave their sons uncircumcised, and to defile themselves with every kind of uncleanness and profanation, so as to make them forget the law and change all its precepts.
And whoever did not obey the command of King Antiochus was to be put to death.
Such were the letters he published throughout his kingdom; he appointed overseers over all the people
and commanded the towns of Judah to offer sacrifices, town by town.
Many of the people rallied to them, all those who forsook the law, and they did evil in the land;
they forced the faithful of Israel to take refuge in every kind of hiding place.

On the fifteenth day of the month of Chislev (around December), around 167 before Jesus Christ, they set up the abomination of desolation on the altar of burnt offerings. They also built altars in the surrounding towns of Judah,
and burned incense at the doors of the houses and in the squares.
The books of the law that were found, they tore up and burned.
Anyone found with a book of the covenant, or showing attachment to the law, was put to death according to the king's edict.
With such violence they acted month after month, in the towns, against any of the people of Israel caught in a fault.
On the twenty-fifth day of the month they offered a sacrifice on the altar that had been built on top of the altar of burnt offerings.
They also put to death, according to the edict, the women who had had their children circumcised,
hanging the infants around their necks; and they plundered their houses and killed those who had performed the circumcision.
Yet many in Israel stood firm and resolved not to eat anything unclean. They chose to die rather than defile themselves with food
and profane the holy covenant; and they died.
It was an immense wrath that fell upon Israel.
In those days there appeared Mattathias, son of John, son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib, from Jerusalem, who lived at Modein.
He had five sons: John, called Gaddi;
Simon, called Thassi;
Judas, called Maccabeus;
Eleazar, called Avaran; and Jonathan, called Apphus.
Seeing the sacrileges being committed in Judah and Jerusalem,
Mattathias said, "Alas! Why was I born to see the ruin of my people and the ruin of the holy city, and to sit here while she is handed over into the hands of enemies,
and her sanctuary into the power of strangers? Her temple has become like a man without honor;
the precious objects that were her glory have been carried off as plunder; her little children have been slaughtered in her streets, her young men have fallen by the enemy's sword.
What nation has not inherited her royalty and seized a share of her spoils?
All her adornment has been torn from her; from free she has become a slave.
See how all that made our holiness, our beauty, and our glory is laid waste, profaned by the nations.
Why should we go on living?"
Then Mattathias and his sons tore their garments, put on sackcloth, and mourned deeply.
The king's officers charged with enforcing the apostasy came to the town of Modein to organize the sacrifices.
Many of the people of Israel joined them; but Mattathias and his sons kept apart.
The envoys of Antiochus addressed Mattathias, "You are the foremost man of this town, the most respected and the most influential, surrounded by sons and brothers.

Come forward, then, first of all, and carry out the king's command, as all the nations have done, and the men of Judah, and those who have remained in Jerusalem; then you and your sons will be among the king's friends, and you and your sons will be showered with gold, silver, and many gifts."
Mattathias answered in a loud voice, "Even if all the nations in King Antiochus's realm obey him, each one forsaking the worship of its fathers to submit to his commands,
I, my sons, and my brothers will follow the covenant of our fathers.
Heaven forbid that we should forsake the law and its precepts!
We will not obey the king's commands, and we will not turn aside from our worship to the right or to the left."
He had scarcely finished speaking when a Jew came forward, in full view of all, to sacrifice on the altar at Modein, according to the king's order.
At the sight, Mattathias shuddered; his heart was stirred, and letting the just anger rise within him, he rushed forward and killed the man on the altar.
At the same time he killed the king's officer who was forcing them to sacrifice, and he tore down the altar.
Thus he burned with zeal for the law, after the example of Phinehas, who killed Zimri, son of Salu.
Then Mattathias went through the town shouting in a loud voice, "Let everyone who has zeal for the law and upholds the covenant come out and follow me!"
And he fled into the hills with his sons, leaving behind everything they owned in the town.
Then many who sought justice and right went down into the wilderness to settle there,
they and their children, their wives, and their livestock, for the evils that pressed upon them had reached their height.
It was reported to the king's officers and to the troops in Jerusalem, in the City of David, that men who had rejected the king's command had gone down into the wilderness, into hidden retreats.
At once many soldiers pursued them; having overtaken them, they camped opposite them and prepared to attack them on the sabbath day.
They said to them, "Enough resistance! Come out, carry out the king's command, and you will live!"
The Jews answered, "We will not come out, and we will not obey the king's command: that would be to violate the sabbath day."
The Syrians immediately joined battle against them.
But they did not fight back, nor throw a single stone at them, nor barricade their hiding places,
saying, "Let us all die in our innocence! Heaven and earth are our witnesses that you are putting us to death unjustly."
Attacked in this way on the sabbath day, they died, they and their wives, their children, and their livestock: about a thousand people.
When Mattathias and his friends learned of it, they were deeply grieved.
They said to one another, "If we all do as our brothers have done, and do not fight the nations for our lives and our customs, they will soon wipe us off the earth."
That day they made this resolve: "Whoever comes to fight us on the sabbath day, we will fight him, so that we do not all die as our brothers did in their hiding places."
Then a company of Hasideans joined them, valiant men of Israel, all wholeheartedly devoted to the law;
and all who were fleeing the present evils came to swell their ranks and add to their strength.
Having thus formed an army, they struck down the sinners in their anger and the wicked in their indignation; the rest fled to the nations for refuge.
Mattathias and his sons went through the land; they tore down the altars,
forcibly circumcised all the uncircumcised boys they found within the territory of Israel,
and hunted down the arrogant. The enterprise prospered in their hands;
they defended the law against the power of the pagans and the kings, and did not let the sinner triumph.
As the days of Mattathias drew to a close, he said to his sons, "Now is the time when pride reigns and chastisement rages, a time of ruin and burning anger.
Now, my sons, show your zeal for the law and give your lives for the covenant of our fathers.
Remember the deeds accomplished by our fathers in their day, and you will win great glory and an everlasting name.
Was not Abraham found faithful in trial, and was this not counted to him as righteousness?
Joseph, in the time of his trial, kept the commandments and became lord of Egypt.
Phinehas, our father, because he burned with zeal, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.
Joshua, because he fulfilled the word, became a judge in Israel.
Caleb, because he bore witness in the assembly, received a portion of the land.
David, for his devotion, obtained a royal throne forever.
Elijah, because he burned with zeal for the law, was taken up into heaven.
Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, because they believed, were saved from the flames.
Daniel, for his innocence, was delivered from the mouth of the lions.
Consider thus, from age to age, that all who hope in him do not fail.
Do not fear the threats of a sinful man, for his glory goes to rot and worms.
Today he is exalted, and tomorrow he will be gone, for he will have returned to his dust and his schemes will have vanished.
You, then, my sons, be strong and valiant for the law, for by it you will be glorified.
Here is Simon, your brother; I know that he is a man of counsel: listen to him always, and he will be a father to you.
Let Judas Maccabeus, valiant from his youth, be the commander of your army and lead the war against the peoples.
Rally to yourselves all who observe the law, and avenge your people.
Repay the nations for what they have done to Israel, and keep the commandments of the law."
Then he blessed them and was gathered to his fathers.
He died around 166 before Jesus Christ; his sons buried him in the tomb of their fathers at Modein, and all Israel mourned deeply for him.

titres.titre: Judas gathers the people at Mizpah

versets.t: Judas, his son, called Maccabeus, rose up in his place.
All his brothers and all who had joined his father supported him, and they waged Israel's battles with joy.
He extended his people's glory far and wide; he put on the breastplate like a hero, girded on his weapons, and gave battle, protecting the camp of Israel with his sword.
In action he was like a lion, like a young lion roaring over its prey.
He tracked down the wicked in their lairs and gave to the flames those who troubled his people.
The wicked drew back, gripped by dread; all the workers of iniquity trembled, and deliverance prospered in his hand.
By his exploits he brought bitterness to many kings and joy to Jacob; his memory is blessed forever.
He went through the towns of Judah to root out the wicked from them, and he turned wrath away from Israel.
His name reached to the ends of the earth, and he gathered those who were about to perish.
Apollonius mustered the pagans, a large army drawn from Samaria, to fight against Israel.
As soon as he learned of it, Judas marched against him, defeated him, and killed him; many of the enemy fell, and the rest fled.
The Jews took their spoils, and Judas seized the sword of Apollonius, which he used from then on in all his battles.
Seron, commander of the Syrian army, heard that Judas had gathered around him a company of the faithful, a band of fighters;
he said, "I will make a name and a reputation for myself in the kingdom: I will fight Judas and his men, who despise the king's commands."
So he in turn marched up, and with him a powerful army of the wicked, to help him take vengeance on the sons of Israel.
As he approached the ascent of Beth-horon, Judas went out to meet him with a small band.
At the sight of the army advancing against them, they said to Judas, "How can we, so few, fight such a multitude, exhausted as we are by today's fasting?"
Judas answered, "It is easy for a multitude to be handed over into the hands of a few; for Heaven it makes no difference to save by many or by few.
For victory in war does not depend on the size of the army: strength comes from Heaven.
They march against us, full of pride and impiety, to destroy us, our wives, and our children, and to plunder us;
but we fight for our lives and for our laws.
Heaven will crush them before us; so do not fear them."
He had scarcely finished speaking when he fell upon them by surprise: Seron was defeated and saw his army crushed before his eyes.
Judas pursued him down the descent of Beth-horon as far as the plain; eight hundred of their men fell, and the rest fled to the land of the Philistines.
Then the fear of Judas and his brothers, and the terror of them, fell upon the surrounding nations.
His name reached even the king, and all the peoples talked of Judas's battles.
When King Antiochus heard this news, he was seized with rage; he ordered all the forces of his kingdom to be assembled, a very powerful army.
He opened his treasury, gave his troops a year's pay, and ordered them to be ready for anything.

But he found that the money in his coffers was running low, and that the tributes of the country were bringing in little, because of the disorder and the evils he had unleashed by seeking to abolish the customs that had prevailed from ancient times.
He feared that he might not be able, as before, to meet the expenses and the largesses he had once lavished more freely than all the kings before him.
In this extreme difficulty, he resolved to go to Persia to collect the tributes of those provinces and to amass a great deal of money.
He left Lysias, a distinguished man of royal blood, in charge of the affairs of the kingdom, from the Euphrates to the frontiers of Egypt,
and charged with watching over his son Antiochus until his return.
He entrusted to him half of his troops and the elephants, and gave him orders for the execution of all his plans, in particular concerning the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem:
Lysias was to send an army against them to break and destroy the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem, and to blot out their memory from the place,
then to settle foreigners throughout their country and distribute their lands to them by lot.
Taking the other half of his troops with him, the king set out from Antioch, his capital, around 165 before Jesus Christ, crossed the Euphrates, and traversed the provinces of the upper country.
Lysias chose Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, Nicanor, and Gorgias, able commanders and friends of the king,
and sent with them forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry to invade the land of Judah and ravage it, according to the king's order.
They set out with all their forces and, arriving in Judea, camped near Emmaus in the plain.

At the news of their arrival, the merchants of the country, provided with a great deal of silver and gold, and with fetters, came to the camp to buy the sons of Israel as slaves; and the forces of Syria and of the land of the Philistines joined them.
Judas and his brothers, seeing the evils growing worse and the enemy armies camped on their frontiers, informed too of the king's order to destroy and exterminate their people,
said to one another, "Let us raise up the ruins of our people, and fight for our people and our sanctuary!"
So the assembly gathered to prepare for battle, and to pray and implore pity and mercy.

Now Jerusalem was abandoned like a wilderness; none of her children went in or out, the sanctuary was trampled underfoot, the sons of foreigners held the citadel, a lair of the nations; joy had vanished from Jacob, and the flute and the harp had fallen silent.
So they gathered and came to Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem, for there had once been a place of prayer for Israel at Mizpah.
That day they fasted, put on sackcloth, sprinkled ashes on their heads, and tore their garments.
They unrolled the book of the law, in which the nations sought to portray the images of their idols.
They brought the priestly vestments, the firstfruits, and the tithes, and summoned the Nazirites who had completed the time of their vow;
and they cried aloud to Heaven, "What shall we do with these men, and where shall we take them?
Your sanctuary has been trampled underfoot and profaned, your priests are in mourning and humiliation.
And now the nations have banded together against us to destroy us! You know their designs against us.
How shall we be able to stand before them, if you do not come to our aid?"
Then they sounded the trumpets and raised a great shout.
After this, Judas appointed leaders of the people: commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens;
and he told those who had just built a house, or married, or planted a vineyard, and those who were afraid, to return, each to his own home, according to the law.
Then the army set out and camped to the south of Emmaus.
There Judas said to them, "Take up your weapons and be valiant; be ready by morning to fight these nations that have banded together to destroy us and our sanctuary.
For it is better for us to die in battle than to see the misfortunes of our people and of our sanctuary.
But whatever be the will of Heaven, may it be done!"
Gorgias took with him five thousand infantry and a thousand picked cavalry, and they set out by night
to surprise the camp of the Jews and strike them unawares; the men of the citadel served as their guides.
When Judas learned of it, he set out with his valiant men to strike the king's army at Emmaus,
while the troops were still scattered outside the camp.
Gorgias reached Judas's camp by night, but found no one there; he searched for them in the mountains, saying, "They are fleeing from us!"
At daybreak, Judas appeared in the plain with three thousand men; but they did not have the armor and swords they would have wished.
At the sight of the fortified camp of the nations, of the mailed soldiers and the cavalry patrolling around it, all battle-hardened,
Judas said to his men, "Do not fear their numbers or dread their charge.
Remember how our fathers were saved at the Red Sea, when Pharaoh pursued them with his army.
Let us now cry out to Heaven: perhaps he will have mercy on us, remember his covenant with our fathers, and crush this army before our eyes today.
Then all the nations will know that there is One who redeems and saves Israel."
The foreigners lifted up their eyes and saw them marching against them;
they came out of the camp to give battle, while Judas's men sounded the trumpet.
They engaged, and the nations were defeated and fled into the plain.
The whole rear guard fell by the sword. The Jews pursued them as far as Gazara, and into the plains of Idumea, Azotus, and Jamnia, and killed about three thousand of their men.
Then Judas and his army turned back and broke off the pursuit,
Judas saying to the people, "Do not be greedy for plunder, for another battle awaits us:
Gorgias and his troops are near us, in the mountains. Stand firm now against our enemies, defeat them, and afterward you will take their spoils without fear."
Judas was still speaking when an advance guard of Gorgias appeared, coming out of the mountains.
They saw their own men in flight and the camp in flames, for the smoke they saw revealed what had happened.
At the sight they were seized with great fear; and seeing at the same time the army of Judas drawn up in the plain, ready for battle,
they all fled to the land of the Philistines.
Judas came back to plunder the camp; they carried off much gold and silver, cloth dyed violet and scarlet, and great riches.
As they returned, they sang, raising up to Heaven praises to the Lord: "For he is good, for his faithful love endures forever."
That day a great deliverance was granted to Israel.
Those of the foreigners who had escaped came and told Lysias all that had happened.
At the news he was dismayed and downcast, for his designs against Israel had failed and the king's orders had not been carried out.
The following year, Lysias assembled sixty thousand picked infantry and five thousand cavalry to make an end of the Jews.
They advanced toward Judea and camped near Beth-zur. Judas marched against them with ten thousand men.

At the sight of that formidable army, he prayed, "Blessed are you, deliverer of Israel, you who broke the onslaught of the giant by the hand of your servant David, and handed over the camp of the Philistines into the hands of Jonathan, son of Saul, and of his armor-bearer.
Shut up this army in the hand of your people Israel; let them be put to shame with their infantry and their cavalry.
Strike them with terror, break down their presumptuous boldness, and let them be shaken by their defeat.
Bring them down by the sword of those who love you, and let all who know your name sing hymns of praise to you."
They joined battle, and five thousand men of Lysias's army fell, cut down before the Jews.

Seeing the rout of his army and the fearlessness of Judas's soldiers, ready to live or to die valiantly, Lysias returned to Antioch and recruited mercenaries, resolving to come back to Judea with increased forces.
Then Judas and his brothers said, "Now that our enemies are defeated, let us go up to purify and rededicate the sanctuary."
The whole army assembled and went up to Mount Zion.
Seeing the sanctuary laid waste, the altar profaned, the gates burned, brushwood growing in the courts as in a thicket or on the mountains, and the chambers destroyed,
they tore their garments, mourned deeply, sprinkled ashes on their heads,
prostrated themselves with their faces to the ground, and, while the trumpets sounded the alarm, cried out to Heaven.
Then Judas detailed men to hold off the garrison of the citadel while the sanctuary was being purified.
He chose blameless priests, devoted to the law of God,
and they purified the sanctuary, carrying the defiled stones to an unclean place.
They deliberated on what to do with the altar of burnt offerings, which had been profaned;
and the happy thought came to them to tear it down, lest it be a reproach to them, having been defiled by the nations. So they demolished the altar
and stored its stones on the mountain of the temple, in a suitable place, until a prophet should come to decide about them.
They took unhewn stones, according to the law, and built a new altar on the pattern of the old one.
They rebuilt the sanctuary and the interior of the temple, and consecrated the courts.
They made new sacred utensils, and brought back into the temple the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table.
They burned incense on the altar, lit the lamps of the lampstand, which gave light in the temple,
set out the bread on the table, and hung up the veils. Having finished all the work they had undertaken,
they rose early in the morning, on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, the month of Chislev (around December), around 164 before Jesus Christ,
and offered a sacrifice, according to the law, on the new altar of burnt offerings they had built.
On the very day and in the very month when the nations had profaned it, the altar was consecrated anew, with the singing of psalms, with harps, lyres, and cymbals.
All the people fell prostrate and worshiped, and, lifting up their eyes to Heaven, blessed the One who had brought them to this happy outcome.
They celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days, offering burnt offerings with joy and sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise.
They adorned the front of the temple with golden crowns and small shields, repaired the entrances and the chambers, and fitted them with doors.
There was very great joy among the people, and the reproach inflicted by the nations was wiped away.

Judas, with his brothers and the whole assembly of Israel, decreed that the days of the dedication of the altar should be observed in their season, year by year, for eight days, from the twenty-fifth of Chislev, with joy and gladness.
At that same time they surrounded Mount Zion with high walls and strong towers, so that the nations might not come, as before, to trample the holy places underfoot.
Judas stationed a garrison there to guard it, and fortified Beth-zur, so that the people might have a stronghold facing Idumea.

titres.titre: The campaigns in Gilead and Galilee
The appeal of the Jews of Gilead
The failure of Joseph and Azariah

versets.t: When the surrounding nations heard that the altar had been rebuilt and the sanctuary restored as before, they fell into a great fury
and resolved to exterminate the descendants of Jacob who lived among them; they began to slaughter and hunt them down.
Judas made war on the sons of Esau, in Idumea, in the region of Acrabattene, because they were harassing Israel; he inflicted a great defeat on them, humbled them, and took their spoils.
He also remembered the wickedness of the sons of Baean, who were a snare and a trap for the people through the ambushes they set on the roads.
He shut them up in their towers, laid siege to them, put them under the ban, and burned their towers with all who were in them.
Then he crossed over to the Ammonites, where he found a strong army and a numerous people commanded by Timothy.
He fought many battles with them; they were crushed before him, and he cut them to pieces.
He took Jazer and its dependent villages, and returned to Judea.
The nations of Gilead banded together against the people of Israel settled in their territory, to exterminate them; and these took refuge in the stronghold of Dathema
and sent letters to Judas and his brothers, saying, "The nations around us have banded together against us to destroy us;
they are preparing to come and take the stronghold where we have taken refuge, and Timothy commands their army.
Come, then, now and rescue us from their hands, for many of us have already fallen.
All our brothers in the land of Tob have been put to death; their wives and children have been led away captive, their goods have been taken, and about a thousand men have been killed there."
These letters were still being read when other messengers arrived from Galilee, their garments torn, bringing this news:
"The people of Ptolemais, of Tyre, of Sidon, and of all Galilee of the nations have banded together to annihilate us."
At these accounts, Judas and the people held a great assembly to deliberate on what they should do for their brothers in distress, under attack from these enemies.
Judas said to his brother Simon, "Choose men for yourself and go deliver your brothers in Galilee; my brother Jonathan and I will go to Gilead."
He left in Judea Joseph son of Zechariah, and Azariah, leaders of the people, with the rest of the army to stand guard,
and he gave them this order, "Govern this people, but do not engage in battle with the nations before our return."
Three thousand men were assigned to Simon for Galilee, and eight thousand to Judas for Gilead.
Simon set out for Galilee and fought many battles with the nations, who were crushed before him; he pursued them to the gate of Ptolemais.
About three thousand men of the nations fell, and he took their spoils.
He gathered up the Jews of Galilee and of Arbatta, with their wives, their children, and all their goods, and brought them to Judea with great rejoicing.
For their part, Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan crossed the Jordan and marched three days through the wilderness.
They met the Nabateans, who received them in a friendly manner and told them all that had happened to their brothers in Gilead:
"A great number of them," they said, "are shut up in Bozrah, in Bosor, in Alema, in Casphor, in Maked, and in Carnaim, all of them large and fortified cities;
others are shut up in the other cities of Gilead, and their enemies are preparing to attack these strongholds tomorrow, to seize them and put them all to death in a single day."

Judas, changing his route, took the way through the wilderness toward Bozrah and appeared suddenly before the city; he captured it, put every male to the sword, took all its spoils, and gave it to the flames.
He set out from there by night and marched to the stronghold of Dathema.
In the morning they lifted up their eyes and saw an innumerable multitude raising ladders and siege engines to take the stronghold, and pressing hard on the besieged.
Seeing that the battle was joined and that the outcry of the city was rising to heaven, mingled with the sound of trumpets,
Judas said to his men, "Fight today for your brothers!"
He advanced in three columns on the enemy's rear; they sounded the trumpets and cried out their prayer.
As soon as Timothy's army recognized that it was Maccabeus, it fled before him, and he inflicted a great defeat on it: about eight thousand men fell that day.
From there Judas turned toward Mizpah; he attacked it, captured it, killed every male, took its spoils, and gave it to the flames.
Pushing on, he captured Casphor, Maked, Bosor, and the other cities of Gilead.
After this, Timothy assembled another army and camped opposite Raphon, beyond the wadi.
Judas sent men to reconnoiter this army; the report came back to him, "All the nations around us have joined the forces of Timothy, forming an immense army;
they have hired Arabs as auxiliaries and are camped beyond the wadi, ready to give you battle." And Judas marched to meet them.
Timothy said to the commanders of his army, "When Judas and his troops approach the watercourse, if he crosses over to us first, we will not be able to withstand him, he will prevail against us;
but if he is afraid and camps beyond the river, let us cross over to him and we will prevail."
When he reached the watercourse, Judas posted the scribes of the army on the bank and gave them this order, "Let no one halt; let all march to battle!"
Marching against the enemy, he crossed the water first, followed by all the people. All the nations were crushed before him; they threw down their weapons and fled to the temple at Carnaim.
The Jews took the city and burned the temple with all who were in it. Carnaim was overthrown, and the enemy could no longer stand before Judas.

Then Judas gathered all the people of Israel in Gilead, from the least to the greatest, with their wives, their children, and their goods, an immense multitude, to bring them back to the land of Judah.
They came to Ephron, a large and heavily fortified city commanding the pass; it could not be bypassed to the right or to the left, one had to go through it.
But the inhabitants shut themselves in and blocked the gates with stones. Judas sent them words of peace:
"Let us pass through your territory to reach our own country; no one will do you any harm, we ask only to pass through." But they refused to open to him.
Then Judas had it proclaimed through his army that each man should camp where he was,
and the men took up their positions; then he assaulted the city all that day and all that night, and the city fell into his hands.
He put every male to the sword, razed the city, carried off its spoils, and passed through it over the dead bodies.
Then, crossing the Jordan, they arrived in the great plain, opposite Beth-shan.
Judas stayed at the rear guard, rallying the stragglers and encouraging the people all along the road, until they reached the land of Judah.
They went up to Mount Zion with joy and gladness, and offered burnt offerings, glad to have returned safe and sound, without the loss of a single one of their own.
While Judas and Jonathan were in the land of Gilead, and Simon, their brother, in Galilee before Ptolemais,
Joseph son of Zechariah, and Azariah, commanders of the army, heard of their exploits and of the battles they had fought;
and they said, "Let us make a name for ourselves too, and go fight the nations around us!"
So they gave orders to their men and marched against Jamnia.
Gorgias came out of the city with his men and advanced to meet them in battle.
Joseph and Azariah were defeated and pursued to the frontier of Judea; two thousand men of the people of Israel perished that day. This great reverse fell upon the people
because they had not listened to Judas and his brothers, imagining they could prove their valor.
But they were not of the family of those men into whose hands the deliverance of Israel had been entrusted.
The valiant Judas and his brothers won great glory before all Israel and before all the nations where their name was spoken;
people gathered around them to acclaim them.

After this, Judas set out with his brothers to fight the sons of Esau in the land to the south; he took Hebron and its dependent villages, destroyed its fortifications, and burned the towers of its wall.
He broke camp and made for the land of the Philistines, passing through Maresha.
On that day several priests fell in battle who had wished to prove their bravery by rashly taking part in the fighting.
Then Judas turned toward Azotus, in Philistine territory; he tore down their altars, burned the carved idols of their gods, and, after plundering the towns, returned to the land of Judah.

titres.titre: Antiochus Eupator; the siege of the citadel
The battle of Beth-zechariah; the death of Eleazar
The siege of the sanctuary; the peace

versets.t: Meanwhile King Antiochus was traversing the provinces of the upper country. He heard that in Persia, at Elymais, there was a city famous for its riches in silver and gold,
with a very rich temple containing golden armor, breastplates, and weapons that had been left there by Alexander, son of Philip, king of Macedonia, the first to reign over the Greeks.
He went there and sought to take and plunder the city; but he did not succeed, for the inhabitants got wind of his plan.
They rose up to fight him, and he fled; it was with great sorrow that he set out again for Babylon.
Then, in Persia, a messenger came to tell him of the defeat of the troops that had entered the land of Judah:
Lysias, who had set out with a very strong army, had been forced to flee before the Jews, who had grown in strength through the weapons, soldiers, and spoils taken from the vanquished;
they had destroyed the abomination he had set up on the altar in Jerusalem, surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as before, and likewise fortified Beth-zur, one of his towns.
At this news the king was struck with astonishment; deeply shaken, he threw himself on his bed and fell sick from grief, because his desires had not been fulfilled.
He lay there for many days, seized again and again by deep melancholy; and feeling that he was near death,
he summoned his friends and said to them, "Sleep has fled from my eyes, and anxiety weighs my heart down.
I say to myself: To what distress am I reduced, into what abyss have I now fallen, I who was kind and beloved in the time of my power!
But now I remember the evils I did at Jerusalem: I carried off all its vessels of gold and silver, and I sent, without cause, an army to exterminate the inhabitants of Judea.
I acknowledge that it is for this that these misfortunes have overtaken me, and here I am dying of grief in a foreign land."
He summoned Philip, one of his friends, and set him over his whole kingdom.
He gave him his crown, his robe, and the royal seal, charging him to bring up his son Antiochus and train him for kingship.
And King Antiochus died there, around 163 before Jesus Christ.
When Lysias learned of the king's death, he set up in his place his son Antiochus, whom he had brought up from childhood, and gave him the name Eupator.
Meanwhile the garrison of the citadel kept Israel penned in around the sanctuary, constantly seeking to harm it and supporting the nations.
Judas resolved to destroy it and gathered all the people to lay siege to it.
They came together and besieged it around 162 before Jesus Christ, raising against it siege towers and engines.
But some of the besieged escaped, and several of the wicked of Israel joined them.
They went to the king and said, "How long will you delay to do us justice and to avenge our brothers?
We willingly served your father, followed his orders, and carried out his wishes;
for this, the sons of our own people have become our enemies: they have killed all of us they could catch and plundered our inheritances.
It is not against us alone that they have raised their hand, but against all the neighboring countries.
Even now they are camped before the citadel of Jerusalem to take it, and they have fortified the sanctuary and Beth-zur.
If you do not hurry to forestall them, they will do worse still, and you will no longer be able to stop them."
At these words the king was seized with anger; he summoned all his friends, the commanders of his army, and the officers of his cavalry.
Mercenaries also came to him from other kingdoms and from the islands of the sea.
His army numbered a hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for war.
They advanced through Idumea and camped before Beth-zur; they attacked it for a long time and built engines, but the Jews made a sortie and burned them, showing great valor.
Then Judas left the citadel and went to camp at Beth-zechariah, facing the king's camp.
The king rose early in the morning and suddenly launched his army along the road to Beth-zechariah; the troops arrayed themselves for battle and sounded the trumpets.
They showed the elephants the juice of grapes and mulberries, to rouse them for battle.

They distributed the beasts among the phalanxes: each elephant was escorted by a thousand men clad in coats of iron mail, with bronze helmets on their heads, and five hundred picked cavalry were stationed beside it.
These cavalry went ahead of the beast wherever it went: where it went, they went, never leaving it.
On each elephant rose a sturdy wooden tower, strapped around it, and each carried thirty-two warriors on the tower, besides its driver.
They placed the rest of the cavalry on the two flanks of the army, to harass the enemy and cover the phalanxes.
When the rays of the sun fell on the shields of gold and bronze, the mountains blazed with their brilliance and shone like torches of fire.
One part of the king's army deployed on the heights, the other in the valleys, and they advanced with a firm step and in good order.
All trembled at the din of that multitude, at the noise of its march and the clashing of its weapons: it was an immense and powerful army.
Judas advanced with his army to give battle, and six hundred men of the king's army fell.
Eleazar, called Avaran, noticed one of the elephants covered with royal harness and taller than all the others; believing that the king was on it,
he gave himself up to deliver his people and to win himself an everlasting name.
He ran boldly toward the beast through the phalanx, striking to the right and to the left, and the enemy drew back on either side before him.
Slipping under the elephant, he drove his sword into it and killed it; but the beast collapsed on top of him, and Eleazar died there.
Seeing the strength of the kingdom and the fury of its troops, the Jews withdrew before them.
The king's army went up to Jerusalem to meet the Jews, and the king camped against Judea and Mount Zion.
He made peace with the people of Beth-zur, who came out of the city, for they had no provisions to withstand a siege there, since it was the year of the land's rest.
So the king took Beth-zur and left a garrison there.
He camped before the holy place for many days, and set up against it siege towers, war engines, catapults for hurling fire and stones, scorpions for shooting arrows, and slings.
The besieged likewise set up engines against those of the besiegers and held out for a long time.
But the storehouses were empty, for it was the seventh year, and the people of Israel who had taken refuge in Judea before the nations had consumed the last of the reserves.
Only a small number of Jews remained in the holy place, so severe was the famine; the rest scattered, each to his own home.
Meanwhile Philip, whom King Antiochus, while still alive, had designated to bring up his son Antiochus and make him king,
had returned from Persia and Media with the troops that had accompanied the king, and he was seeking to take the affairs of the kingdom into his own hands.

At this news, Lysias hastened to depart; he said to the king, to the commanders of the army, and to the troops, "We are growing weaker here day by day; we are short of provisions, the place we are besieging is strongly fortified, and the affairs of the state demand our attention.
Now therefore let us extend our hand to these men, make peace with them and with their whole nation,
and grant them the right to live according to their laws, as before; for it is for these laws, which we sought to abolish, that they rose up and did all this."
This proposal pleased the king and the commanders; he sent to offer peace to the Jews, who accepted it.
The king and the commanders confirmed the treaty by oath, and the besieged came out of the stronghold.
But the king, having entered the enclosure of Mount Zion and seen the fortifications, broke his oath and ordered the walls all around to be razed.
Then he departed in haste and returned to Antioch, where he found Philip master of the city; he fought him and took the city by storm.

titres.titre: The defeat and death of Nicanor

versets.t: Around 161 before Jesus Christ, Demetrius son of Seleucus escaped from the city of Rome and landed, with a few men, in a coastal city, where he proclaimed himself king.
As soon as he entered the kingdom of his fathers, the army seized Antiochus and Lysias to bring them to him.
When he was informed, he said, "Do not let me see their faces."
The army killed them, and Demetrius sat on the throne of his kingdom.
Then all the lawless and wicked men of Israel came to him, led by Alcimus, who wanted to become high priest.
They accused the people before the king, saying, "Judas and his brothers have destroyed all your friends and driven us out of our land.
Now send a man you trust, to see all the ruin they have brought upon us and upon the king's provinces, and to punish them and all their supporters."
The king chose from among his friends Bacchides, governor of the province Beyond the River, a man of high standing in the kingdom and loyal to the king;
he sent him with the wicked Alcimus, on whom he conferred the high priesthood, with orders to take vengeance on the sons of Israel.
They set out and came with a large army to the land of Judah; they sent to Judas and his brothers messengers with words of peace, to deceive them.
But these men, seeing that they had come with a large army, paid no heed to their words.
Yet a group of scribes went to Alcimus and Bacchides to seek a just settlement;
and the Hasideans, who were foremost among the sons of Israel, asked them for peace,
for they said, "A priest of the line of Aaron has come with the army; he will do us no harm."
He spoke to them words of peace and swore this oath to them, "We intend no harm to you or to your friends."
They believed him; but he seized sixty of them and had them massacred on the same day, according to the word of Scripture:
"They have scattered the flesh of your faithful ones and shed their blood around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them."
Then fear and dread seized the whole people: "There is among them," they said, "neither truth nor justice, for they have broken their pledge and the oath they had sworn."

Bacchides set out from Jerusalem and camped at Beth-zaith; there he seized a great number of those who had deserted his party, along with some of the people, and, having killed them, he threw their bodies into the great cistern.
Then, having entrusted the country to Alcimus and left him troops to defend it, Bacchides returned to the king.
Alcimus fought to secure the high priesthood for himself;
all who troubled their people rallied to him, made themselves masters of the land of Judah, and caused great harm in Israel.
Seeing all the evil that Alcimus and his supporters were doing to the sons of Israel, worse than the nations,
Judas went through the whole territory of Judea, punishing the traitors and preventing them from moving about the countryside.
When Alcimus saw that Judas and his men had grown powerful and that he could not stand against them, he returned to the king and accused them of the worst crimes.
The king sent Nicanor, one of his most distinguished generals, full of hatred for Israel, with orders to exterminate the people.
Arriving at Jerusalem with a strong army, Nicanor sent to Judas and his brothers words of peace, to deceive them:
"Let there be no war between us," he said; "I wish to come with a few men to see your faces in friendship."
So he came to Judas, and they greeted one another as friends; but the enemy stood ready to carry Judas off.
Warned that Nicanor was coming to him with a treacherous intent, Judas took fright and refused to see him again.
Nicanor realized that his plan was discovered, and he came to blows with Judas near Capharsalama.
About five thousand men of Nicanor's army fell, and the rest fled into the City of David.
After this, Nicanor went up to Mount Zion; some of the priests came out of the sanctuary, with elders of the people, to greet him amiably and to show him the burnt offerings offered for the king.
But he mocked them, despised them, defiled them, and spoke insolent words;
and in his anger he swore, "If Judas and his army are not delivered up to me at once, then as soon as I return victorious, I will burn this building." And he went out in a fury.
Then the priests went back in and, standing before the altar and the sanctuary, said, weeping:
"It is you, Lord, who chose this house that your name might dwell in it, that it might be for your people a house of prayer and supplication.
Take vengeance on this man and on his army; let them fall by the sword! Remember their blasphemies, and do not let them survive!"
Nicanor left Jerusalem and camped near Beth-horon, where a corps of Syrians came to reinforce him.
Judas, for his part, camped near Adasa with three thousand men, and he prayed:
"When the envoys of the king of the Assyrians blasphemed you, Lord, your angel went out and killed a hundred and eighty-five thousand of them.
Crush this army in the same way today before our eyes, so that all the rest may recognize that he has spoken impiously against your sanctuary; and judge him according to his wickedness."
The armies came to blows on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar (around February to March); Nicanor's troops were cut to pieces, and he himself was the first to fall in the battle.
Seeing Nicanor fallen, his troops threw down their weapons and fled.
The Jews pursued them a day's march, from Adasa to the approaches of Gazara, sounding the alarm trumpets behind them.
From all the villages of Judea round about, men came out to hem in the fugitives, who turned back one against another; all fell by the sword, and not one of them escaped.
The Jews took their spoils and their plunder; they cut off Nicanor's head and the right hand he had insolently stretched out, and went and hung them up in sight of Jerusalem.
The people were filled with joy and kept that day as a day of great gladness.
It was decided to celebrate it every year, on the thirteenth of the month of Adar.
And the land of Judah was at peace for a while.
Now Judas heard of the Romans: they are, he was told, mighty in war, well disposed toward all who attach themselves to them, making friends with anyone who comes to them, and formidable in battle.
He was told of their wars and their exploits among the Galatians, whom they had subdued and made their tributaries;
all they had done in the land of Spain to seize the mines of gold and silver, and how they had subdued that whole country by their shrewdness and their persistence,
far off though it was. Likewise the kings who had come to attack them from the ends of the earth: they had defeated them and struck them hard, and the others paid them an annual tribute.
They had defeated in war Philip and Perseus, king of the Kittim, and all who had taken up arms against them, and had subdued them.
Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, who had advanced against them with a hundred and twenty elephants, cavalry, chariots, and a very powerful army, had been defeated by them;
they had taken him alive and imposed on him and on his successors a heavy tribute, the surrender of hostages, and the cession of a part of his kingdom,
namely India, Media, Lydia, and some of his finest provinces; having received them from him, they had given them to King Eumenes.
When the Greeks formed the plan of coming to destroy them, the Romans learned of it

and sent a single general against them: they made war on them, killed many of them, led away captive their wives and children, plundered their goods, subdued their country, razed their strongholds, and reduced them to servitude to this day.
All the other kingdoms and islands that had resisted them, they had destroyed and enslaved.
But to their friends and to those who rely on them, they keep their friendship. They have made themselves masters of the kingdoms near and far, and all who hear their name are afraid of them.
All those they wish to help and to make reign, do reign; and those they wish, they depose: it is a very powerful nation.
Yet with all this, none of them puts on the royal crown or wears purple to exalt himself.
They have set up a senate, where three hundred and twenty members deliberate each day, constantly attending to the good of the people for its prosperity.
Each year they entrust to a single man the power to govern their whole country; all obey that one man, and there is among them neither envy nor jealousy.
Judas chose Eupolemus son of John, son of Accos, and Jason son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to make friendship and alliance,
and to obtain freedom from the yoke; for they saw that the kingdom of the Greeks was reducing Israel to servitude.
So they went to Rome, after a very long journey, and, entering the senate, they spoke up:
"Judas Maccabeus, his brothers, and the Jewish people have sent us to you to conclude a treaty of alliance and peace, and to be enrolled among your allies and your friends."
This request was granted.
And here is the copy of the letter that the Romans engraved on tablets of bronze and sent to Jerusalem, to remain there as a memorial of peace and alliance:
"May the Romans and the Jewish nation prosper on sea and on land forever! Far from them the sword and the enemy!
If war first befalls Rome, or any of its allies throughout the whole extent of its dominion,
the Jewish nation will fight at its side wholeheartedly, as the circumstances allow;
and to the enemy it will neither supply nor provide grain, weapons, money, or ships: such is the will of Rome, and the Jews will keep their commitments, receiving nothing in return.
Likewise, if war first befalls the Jewish nation, the Romans will fight at its side with all their soul, as the circumstances allow;
and to the enemy they will supply neither grain, weapons, money, nor ships: such is the will of Rome, and they will keep their commitments without deceit.
These are the terms of the treaty concluded by the Romans with the Jewish people.
If, in time to come, either party wishes to add to them or subtract from them, they may do so at their discretion, and whatever is added or subtracted will have the force of law."
"As for the evils that King Demetrius has done them, we have written to him thus: Why have you made your yoke heavy upon the Jews, our friends and allies?
If they lodge a further complaint against you before us, we will uphold their right and make war on you by sea and by land."
When Demetrius learned that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, he sent Bacchides and Alcimus into Judea once again, with the right wing of his army.
They took the road to Gilgal and pitched camp at Mesaloth, in the territory of Arbela; they seized that town and killed many of its people.
In the first month (about March-April), around 160 before Jesus Christ, they drew up their forces before Jerusalem.
Then they broke camp and marched to Berea with twenty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand horsemen.
Judas had pitched camp at Eleasa, with three thousand picked warriors.
At the sight of so vast an enemy host they were struck with terror, and many slipped secretly out of the camp, until only eight hundred remained.
Judas saw that his army had melted away just as the battle was about to be joined; his heart broke, for there was no time to gather his men, and he felt his strength failing.
Yet he said to those who remained: "Up! Let us march against our foes, if only we can face them!"
But they tried to dissuade him: "We cannot. Let us rather save our lives and go back to our brothers; then we will return to fight them. We are far too few."
Judas answered: "Far be it from me to act so, to flee before them! If our hour has come, let us die bravely for our brothers, and leave no stain upon our honor!"
The Syrian army marched out of the camp to meet them: the cavalry in two divisions, the slingers and archers in front, and the bravest men in the first rank.
Bacchides was on the right wing; the phalanx advanced from both sides to the sound of the trumpet.
The men of Judas also sounded the trumpet, and the earth shook with the din of the two armies. The battle was joined and lasted from morning until evening.
Seeing that Bacchides and the main body of his forces were on the right wing, Judas rallied around him all the stout-hearted men;
he crushed the right wing and pursued it as far as Mount Azotus.
But those on the left wing, seeing the right wing beaten, wheeled about and followed close behind Judas and his men;
the fighting grew fierce, and there were many killed on both sides.
Judas too fell, and the rest took flight.
Jonathan and Simon carried off their brother Judas and buried him in the tomb of their fathers at Modein.
All Israel wept for him and made great lamentation over him; they mourned for many days,
and they said: "How is the hero fallen, the savior of Israel!"
The rest of the story of Judas, his other wars, his exploits and his titles of glory, have not been written down, for they are too many.
After the death of Judas, the godless reappeared throughout the territory of Israel, and all the workers of iniquity raised their heads again.
In those days a very great famine came upon the land, and the country itself went over to their side.
Bacchides picked out godless men and set them to govern the country.
They hunted down the friends of Judas and, whenever they found them, brought them before Bacchides, who punished them and made sport of them.
Israel suffered a distress such as had not been since the day when prophets ceased to appear among them.
Then all the friends of Judas gathered together and said to Jonathan:
"Since your brother Judas died, there is no one like him to march against our enemies, against Bacchides and those who hate our nation.
So today we choose you to be our leader in his place, to lead us in battle."
Jonathan then took up the command and rose up in the place of his brother Judas.
As soon as Bacchides learned of Jonathan's election, he sought to kill him.
Warned of this plan, Jonathan, his brother Simon and all their followers fled into the wilderness of Tekoa and settled by the waters of the cistern of Asphar.
Bacchides learned of it on a sabbath day and moved with all his army beyond the Jordan.
Jonathan had sent his brother John, as leader of the company, to the Nabateans, his friends, to ask them to store his baggage, which was considerable, in safekeeping.
But the sons of Jambri, coming out from Medaba, seized John and all his baggage and made off with the spoil.

Some time later, word came to Jonathan and his brother Simon that the sons of Jambri were celebrating a great wedding and were bringing the bride from Nadabath in a grand procession, the daughter of one of the powerful princes of Canaan.
Remembering their brother John, they went up and hid in the shelter of the mountain.

Raising their eyes, they saw a great commotion and an imposing train: the bridegroom, with his friends and his brothers, was coming out to meet them, with tambourines, music and a great deal of equipment.
Then the companions of Jonathan sprang from their ambush and fell upon them; many were killed, the rest fled to the mountain, and the Jews took their spoils.
So the wedding was turned into mourning, and the festive music into lamentation.
Having avenged the murder of their brother, Jonathan and Simon withdrew to the marshes of the Jordan.
Bacchides learned of it and came, on a sabbath day, to the banks of the Jordan with a powerful army.
Then Jonathan said to his companions: "Up! Let us fight for our lives, for today is not like yesterday and the day before.
See, the enemy is before us and behind us in arms, and on every side the water of the Jordan, the marsh and the thicket: there is no way to escape.
Cry out now to Heaven, that you may be delivered from the hand of your enemies!" And the battle was joined.
Jonathan reached out his hand to strike Bacchides, but he dodged by throwing himself back.
Then Jonathan and his companions leaped into the Jordan and swam across; the Syrians did not cross after them in pursuit.
That day a thousand men fell on the side of Bacchides.
He returned to Jerusalem and built fortified towns in Judea: the stronghold near Jericho, Emmaus, Beth-horon, Bethel, Timnath, Pharathon and Tephon, with high walls, gates and bars;
and he placed garrisons in them to harass Israel.
He also fortified Beth-zur, Gazara and the citadel, stationing troops and stores of provisions there,
and he took as hostages the sons of the country's leading men, holding them in the citadel of Jerusalem.

Around 159 before Jesus Christ, in the second month (about April-May), Alcimus ordered the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary to be torn down, thus destroying the work of the prophets; he began the demolition.
At that time Alcimus was struck down by God, and his undertakings were halted: his mouth was stopped, he was paralyzed, and he could no longer say a word or give any order concerning his household.
And Alcimus died then in great torment.
Seeing that Alcimus was dead, Bacchides returned to the king, and the land of Judah was at peace for two years.
Then all the faithless Jews conspired together: "See," they said, "Jonathan and his men are living in peace and security; let us bring Bacchides, and he will seize them all in a single night."
They went and came to an agreement with him.
Bacchides set out with a large army and secretly sent letters to all his supporters in Judea, telling them to seize Jonathan and his men; but they failed, for their plan got wind.
What is more, the Jews seized about fifty of the men of the country who were leaders of the plot and put them to death.
Then Jonathan, with Simon and their men, withdrew to Bethbasi in the wilderness; he rebuilt its ruins and fortified it.
Bacchides learned of it, mustered all his troops and called on his supporters in Judea.
He came and camped near Bethbasi, besieged it for many days and built siege engines.
But Jonathan, leaving his brother Simon in the town, went out into the countryside and returned with a small band.
He struck Odomera, his brothers and the sons of Phasiron in their tents, and began to harass the besiegers and to attack them in force.
Simon, for his part, made a sortie with his men and burned the siege engines.
The two of them fought Bacchides, routed him and threw him into deep dismay, for his plan and his campaign had utterly failed.
Furious with the godless men who had advised him to come into the country, he put many of them to death and resolved to return home.
Jonathan learned of it and sent messengers to him to negotiate peace and secure the release of the prisoners.
Bacchides received them, accepted their proposals and swore to Jonathan that he would do him no harm as long as he lived.
He gave back the prisoners he had earlier taken in the land of Judah, then returned home and no longer set foot in the territory of the Jews.
The sword came to rest in Israel. Jonathan settled at Michmash; he began to judge the people and made the godless vanish from among Israel.

titres.titre: The fall of Demetrius; Jonathan honored
Demetrius II; the victory over Apollonius

versets.t: Around 152 before Jesus Christ, Alexander, son of Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, set out and seized Ptolemais; its people welcomed him, and he became king.
When King Demetrius heard this, he assembled a very strong army and marched against him to give battle.
At the same time, Demetrius sent Jonathan a letter full of peaceful words, promising to raise him in rank;
"Let us hurry," he said, "to make peace with him, before he makes peace with Alexander against us;
for he will remember all the harm we have done to him, to his brother and to his nation."
He authorized him to raise troops, to manufacture arms and to call himself his ally, and ordered that the hostages in the citadel be handed over to him.
Jonathan at once went to Jerusalem and read the letter aloud before all the people and before those in the citadel.
They were seized with great fear when they heard that the king had given Jonathan the power to raise an army.
Those in the citadel handed the hostages over to Jonathan, who returned them to their parents.
Jonathan settled in Jerusalem and began to rebuild and restore the city.
He ordered the workers to rebuild the walls and to surround Mount Zion with dressed stone, to fortify it; and it was done.
Then the foreigners who were in the fortresses built by Bacchides fled,
each one leaving his post to return home.
Only a few renegades from the law and the commandments remained at Beth-zur, which served them as a refuge.

Meanwhile King Alexander learned of the offers that Demetrius had made to Jonathan; he was also told of the battles and the exploits of Jonathan and his brothers, and of the hardships they had endured.
And he said: "Shall we ever find another man like him? Let us make him our friend and ally."
He wrote him a letter in these terms:
"King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings!
We have heard about you, that you are a powerful man and worthy to be our friend.

So today we appoint you high priest of your nation and give you the title of friend of the king (and he sent him at the same time a purple robe and a golden crown); take our interests to heart and keep your friendship with us."

Jonathan put on the sacred vestments in the seventh month (about September-October), around 152 before Jesus Christ, at the feast of Booths; he raised an army and manufactured a great deal of weaponry.
When Demetrius heard this, he was deeply distressed:
"What have we done," he said, "that Alexander has outstripped us in gaining the friendship of the Jews to strengthen his power?
I too will address persuasive words to them and offer them honors and gifts, so that they may support me."
So he sent them this letter: "King Demetrius to the Jewish nation, greetings!
You have faithfully kept the alliance made with us, persevering in our friendship without joining our enemies: we have heard of it and have rejoiced.
So continue to keep faith with us, and we will reward with benefits what you do for us.
We will grant you many exemptions and favors.
From this day I release and remit to all the Jews the tributes, the salt tax and the crown levies.

The third of the produce of the soil and the half of the fruit of the trees that are due to me, I remit to you today; and I will no longer exact anything, at any time, from the land of Judah or from the three districts detached from Samaria and Galilee and annexed to it.
I will that Jerusalem be holy and exempt, together with its territory, its tithes and its tributes.
I also give up my authority over the citadel of Jerusalem, and I hand it over to the high priest, that he may station there, as a garrison, the men he chooses.
All the Jews carried off as captives from the land of Judah anywhere in my kingdom, I set free without ransom; and I will that all remit their tributes, even on their livestock.
Let all the feasts, the sabbaths, the new moons, the appointed days, and the three days before and after a solemn feast, all be days of immunity and exemption for all the Jews of my kingdom.
In those days no one shall have the right to prosecute or trouble any of them over any matter whatsoever.
Up to thirty thousand Jews shall be enrolled in the king's army, at the same pay as all the king's troops; some of them shall be placed in the great royal fortresses,

and several admitted to the positions of trust in the kingdom; their officers shall be taken from their own ranks, and they shall live by their own laws, as the king has ordered for the land of Judah.
The three districts detached from Samaria and annexed to Judea shall be incorporated into it and reckoned as one with it, obeying no other authority than that of the high priest.
I give Ptolemais and its territory to the sanctuary at Jerusalem, for the expenses of worship.
And I myself give each year about 170 kilograms of silver, drawn from the royal revenues in the appropriate places.
All the arrears that the tax officials have not paid, as in past years, they shall henceforth apply to the work of the temple.
Moreover, the some 57 kilograms of silver that the officers used to levy each year on the revenues of the sanctuary shall now be remitted, for they belong to the priests who perform the service.
Whoever, owing the royal taxes or any other debt, takes refuge in the sanctuary at Jerusalem or within its precincts, shall be free, along with all the goods he owns in my kingdom.
The cost of building and restoring the sanctuary shall be drawn from the king's revenues;
likewise, for rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem and fortifying its precincts, and for restoring the walls of the towns of Judea, the cost shall be met from the king's revenues."
At these words, Jonathan and the people did not believe them and refused to consent, remembering the great evils that Demetrius had done to Israel and the distress he had brought upon them.
They preferred Alexander, whose peace proposals pleased them, and they remained his steadfast allies.
King Alexander gathered a great army and marched against Demetrius.
The two kings gave battle; the army of Demetrius fled, Alexander pursued it and prevailed over them.
He fought very bravely until sunset, and Demetrius was killed that day.
Alexander sent ambassadors to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, charged to say to him:
"See, I have returned to my kingdom, seated on the throne of my fathers; I have taken back power by my victory over Demetrius and taken possession of our country.
I gave him battle, and he was defeated, he and his army, and I have ascended the throne of his kingship.
Let us therefore make friendship together: give me your daughter in marriage, I will be your son-in-law, and I will give you, both you and her, gifts worthy of you."
King Ptolemy replied: "Happy the day when you returned to the land of your fathers and sat on their throne!
I will do for you what you have written; but come to meet me at Ptolemais, that we may see each other, and I will make you my son-in-law, as you have asked."
Ptolemy set out from Egypt, with his daughter Cleopatra, and came to Ptolemais, around 150 before Jesus Christ.
King Alexander came out to meet him; Ptolemy gave him his daughter Cleopatra, and he celebrated the wedding at Ptolemais with great magnificence, in the manner of kings.
King Alexander also wrote to Jonathan to come and meet him.
Jonathan went in great pomp to Ptolemais, where he met the two kings; he offered them, and their courtiers, silver, gold and many gifts, and won their favor.
Then wicked men of Israel, godless men, banded together against him to accuse him; but the king would not listen to them.
What is more, he ordered that Jonathan's garments be removed and that he be clothed in purple; it was done, and the king had him sit beside him.

He said to the nobles of his court: "Go out with him into the middle of the city, and proclaim that no one is to bring any complaint against him on any matter, and that no one is to trouble him on any pretext."
At the sight of these public honors and of the purple in which he was clothed, his accusers all took flight.
Adding to these honors, the king enrolled him among his first friends and made him a general and a provincial governor.
And Jonathan returned to Jerusalem in peace and joy.
Around 147 before Jesus Christ, Demetrius, son of Demetrius, came from Crete to the land of his fathers.
When King Alexander heard this, he was deeply distressed and returned to Antioch.
Demetrius took as his general Apollonius, governor of Coele-Syria; he assembled a great army and came and camped near Jamnia. From there he sent word to Jonathan, the high priest:
"You alone rise up against us, and because of you I have become an object of derision and reproach! How do you dare to lord it over us in your mountains?
If you trust in your strength, come down to us in the plain, and there let us measure ourselves, for the strong cities of the coast are on my side.
Inquire and learn who I am and who those are who support me. They say you cannot stand against us, since twice your fathers were put to flight in their own land.
Now you will not be able to withstand the charge of cavalry and so great an army, in a plain where there is neither stone, nor rock, nor place to flee."
At these words of Apollonius, Jonathan was indignant; he chose ten thousand men, set out from Jerusalem, and his brother Simon came to join him and support him.
They camped near Joppa; the town shut its gates against them, for a garrison of Apollonius held it, and they began the siege of it.
In fear, the townspeople opened the gates, and Jonathan became master of Joppa.
When Apollonius heard this, he drew up three thousand horsemen and a large army, and headed toward Azotus as though withdrawing;
but at the same time he was making for the plain, trusting in his numerous cavalry. Jonathan followed him toward Azotus, and the two armies came to blows.
Apollonius had left a thousand horsemen behind in ambush;
Jonathan learned that an ambush lay behind him. The horsemen surrounded his force and shot arrows at his men from morning until evening;
