but his men held firm, as Jonathan had instructed, while the enemy horses wore themselves out.
Then Simon brought his force forward and attacked the phalanx, the cavalry being spent; the Syrians were beaten and fled.
The cavalry scattered across the plain, and the fugitives reached Azotus, entering Beth-dagon, their idol's temple, to seek asylum there.
Jonathan burned Azotus and the surrounding towns after plundering them, and set fire to the temple of Dagon along with those who had taken refuge in it.
Those who fell by the sword or by fire were about eight thousand.
Setting out from there, Jonathan came and camped near Ascalon, whose people came out to meet him, paying him great honors.
Then Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his men, laden with rich spoil.
When King Alexander heard of these events, he granted Jonathan new honors:
he sent him a golden brooch, such as is customarily given to the kinsmen of kings, and gave him Ekron and its territory as a possession.

titres.titre: The death of Ptolemy and of Alexander

versets.t: The king of Egypt assembled an army as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and a considerable fleet, seeking to take Alexander's kingdom by cunning and annex it to his own.
He advanced toward Syria with peaceful words; the people of the towns opened their gates to him and came out to meet him, for King Alexander had so ordered, Ptolemy being his father-in-law.
But as soon as he entered a town, Ptolemy left some of his troops there as a garrison.
As he approached Azotus, they showed him the temple of Dagon burned down, the town and its surroundings in ruins, the corpses scattered and the charred remains of the war heaped along his path.
They told the king what Jonathan had done, to make him hateful; but the king said nothing.
Jonathan came to meet the king at Joppa with splendor; they greeted each other and spent the night there.
Jonathan accompanied the king as far as the river called Eleutherus, then returned to Jerusalem.
King Ptolemy made himself master of the coastal towns as far as Seleucia-by-the-Sea, plotting evil designs against Alexander.
He sent ambassadors to say to King Demetrius: "Come, let us make an alliance; I will give you my daughter, whom Alexander married, and you will reign in your father's kingdom.
I regret having given him my daughter, for he has sought to kill me."
He slandered him thus because he coveted his kingdom.
Having taken back his daughter, he gave her to Demetrius; he then broke with Alexander, and their hostility became public.
Ptolemy entered Antioch and put on the crown of Asia, thus setting two crowns on his head, that of Egypt and that of Asia.
At that time Alexander was in Cilicia, whose people had revolted.
Learning of his father-in-law's treachery, Alexander marched against him; King Ptolemy deployed his army, met him with great forces and put him to flight.
Alexander fled to Arabia to seek asylum there, and King Ptolemy was triumphant.
Zabdiel the Arab cut off Alexander's head and sent it to Ptolemy.
But King Ptolemy died three days later, and the Egyptians in the fortresses were killed by the local people.
And Demetrius became king, around 145 before Jesus Christ.
In those days Jonathan gathered the men of Judea to seize the citadel of Jerusalem, and he set up many siege engines against it.
Then some godless men, who hated their own nation, went to King Demetrius and reported that Jonathan was besieging the citadel.
Angered by this news, Demetrius hurried at once to Ptolemais and wrote to Jonathan to lift the siege and come immediately to confer with him at Ptolemais.
On receiving this letter, Jonathan ordered the siege to continue and, surrounding himself with some elders of Israel and priests, put himself in danger:
taking with him gold, silver, garments and many other gifts, he went to the king at Ptolemais, where he was well received.
Some wicked men of the nation brought charges against him;
but the king treated him as his predecessors had done: he heaped honors on him before all his friends,
confirmed him in the high priesthood and in all his former distinctions, and ranked him among his first friends.
Jonathan asked the king to exempt Judea and the three districts of Samaria from all tribute, promising him in return about ten tonnes of silver.
The king consented and wrote Jonathan a letter in these terms:
"King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan and to the nation of the Jews, greetings!
We send you a copy of the letter we have written about you to Lasthenes, our kinsman, that you may take note of it:
King Demetrius to Lasthenes, his father, greetings!
We have resolved to do good to the nation of the Jews, our friends, who deal justly with us, on account of the goodwill they show us.

We confirm to them the territory of Judea and the three districts detached from Samaria to be joined to it, namely Ephraim, Lydda and Ramathaim, with their dependencies; to all who go to sacrifice in Jerusalem we grant this concession, in place of the dues that the king used to collect each year, formerly, on the produce of the soil and the fruit of the trees.
And all the other dues that henceforth belong to us, the tithes and taxes, the salt pans and the crowns owed to us,
we remit to them completely; there shall be no revocation of this at any time.
See to it, then, that a copy of this decree is made; let it be given to Jonathan and placed on the holy mountain, in a conspicuous place."

King Demetrius, seeing the land at peace and offering no resistance, sent all his troops home, except the mercenaries recruited from the islands of the nations; and so all the armies of his fathers turned hostile to him.
Tryphon, once a supporter of Alexander, seeing the whole army murmuring against Demetrius, went to Imalkue the Arab, who was raising the young Antiochus, son of Alexander.
He pressed him to hand the boy over to him, to make him reign in his father's place; he told him of Demetrius's doings and of the hatred of his troops; and he stayed there many days.
Jonathan sent to King Demetrius, asking him to withdraw the troops from the citadel of Jerusalem and from the fortresses of Judea, for they were making war on Israel.
Demetrius sent back word to Jonathan: "Not only will I do this for you and your nation, but I will heap honors on you, as soon as circumstances permit.
For now, you would do well to send me men to my aid, for my whole army has deserted."
Jonathan sent him to Antioch three thousand of his bravest men; their arrival gladdened the king.
Now the people of the city, numbering a hundred and twenty thousand, gathered in the middle of the city to kill the king.
The king took refuge in the palace; the people occupied the streets and joined battle.
Then the king called the Jews to his aid; they all rallied around him, then spread through the city and killed about a hundred thousand men there that day.
They set fire to the city, took a considerable spoil that day and saved the king.
Seeing the Jews masters of the city, the people lost heart and begged the king with loud cries:
"Make peace with us, and let the Jews stop fighting us and the city!"
They threw down their weapons and made peace. The Jews gained great glory before the king and before all his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with rich spoils.
King Demetrius was able to sit on his throne, and the land was at peace before him;
but he went back on all his promises, turned away from Jonathan, did not keep the kindnesses he had promised, and afflicted him greatly.
After this, Tryphon returned, bringing the young Antiochus; he proclaimed him king and set the crown on his head.
All the troops that Demetrius had disbanded gathered around him; they fought Demetrius, who took flight and was defeated.
Tryphon seized the elephants and occupied Antioch.
Then the young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan: "I confirm you in the priesthood, I set you over the four districts and give you the rank of friend of the king."
He sent him at the same time gold vessels and a table service, with permission to drink from a golden cup, to wear purple and to wear a golden brooch.
He appointed his brother Simon governor of the region from the Ladder of Tyre to the frontier of Egypt.

Jonathan then set out to travel through the country beyond the River and its towns; all the troops of Syria rallied to him to fight at his side. He came to Ascalon, whose people came out to meet him with great honors.
From there he passed on to Gaza. When its people shut their gates against him, he besieged the town and burned and plundered its surroundings.
Then the people of Gaza implored Jonathan; he granted them peace, but took the sons of their leaders as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. Then he traveled through the region as far as Damascus.
Jonathan learned that the generals of Demetrius were at Kedesh in Galilee with a large army, intending to draw him away from his undertaking.
He marched against them, leaving his brother Simon in the country.
Simon advanced against Beth-zur, besieged it for many days and hemmed it in.
The besieged asked him for peace; he granted it, made them leave the town, took possession of it and placed a garrison there.
Jonathan and his army camped near the waters of Gennesaret, and the next day, at dawn, they made for the plain of Hazor.
Now foreign troops were advancing to meet him in the plain, having set an ambush against him in the mountains, while they marched straight toward him.
Suddenly the men of the ambush sprang from their hiding place and joined battle; and all of Jonathan's men took flight.
No one remained except Mattathias, son of Absalom, and Judas, son of Chalphi, generals of the troops.
Then Jonathan tore his garments, put dust on his head and prayed;
then he returned to the battle against them, drove them back and put them to flight.
Seeing this, those of his men who were fleeing came back to him, and all together they pursued the enemy as far as his camp at Kedesh, where they themselves encamped.
That day three thousand men of the foreign troops fell, and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.

titres.titre: The embassies to Rome and to Sparta
Fresh campaigns; the works at Jerusalem
The treachery of Tryphon; Jonathan captured

versets.t: Seeing that circumstances were favorable, Jonathan chose men and sent them to Rome to confirm and renew the friendship of the Jews with the Romans.
He also sent letters to the same effect to the Spartans and to other places.
The envoys went to Rome, entered the senate and said: "Jonathan, the high priest, and the nation of the Jews have sent us to renew the friendship and alliance that existed before."
And the senate gave them letters for the authorities of each place, directing them to see to their safe return to the land of Judah.
Here is a copy of the letter that Jonathan wrote to the Spartans:
"Jonathan, high priest, the council of elders of the nation, the priests and the rest of the Jewish people, to the Spartans, their brothers, greetings!
Long ago a letter was sent to the high priest Onias from Areus, who reigned over you, testifying that you are our brothers, as the copy below attests.
Onias received the envoy with honor and accepted the letter, which spoke clearly of alliance and friendship.
For our part, though we have no need of this, having for our consolation the holy books that are in our hands,
we have undertaken to send to you to renew the brotherhood and friendship that unite us, so as not to become strangers to you; for many years have passed since your last message to us.
We, at all times, without ceasing, remember you, in our feasts and our other holy days, in the sacrifices we offer and in our prayers, as it is right and fitting to remember one's brothers.
We rejoice in your glory.
As for us, many troubles and unceasing wars beset us, for the kings around us make war on us.
We have not wished, on the occasion of these wars, to be a burden to you or to our other allies and friends,
for we have the help of Heaven to sustain us: we have been delivered, and our enemies have been humbled.
So we have chosen Numenius, son of Antiochus, and Antipater, son of Jason, and have sent them to the Romans to renew with them the ancient friendship and alliance.
We have instructed them to pass by you as well, to greet you and to deliver our letter concerning the renewal of our brotherhood.
You will do well, then, to send us a reply on this matter."
Here is a copy of the letter that had been sent to Onias:
"Areus, king of the Spartans, to the high priest Onias, greetings!
It has been found in a document concerning the Spartans and the Jews that they are brothers and of the race of Abraham.
Now that we know this, you will do well to write to us about your prosperity.
For our part, we write to you: your flocks and your goods are ours, and ours are yours. The bearers of this letter have orders to make declarations to you to this effect."
Informed that the generals of Demetrius had come back to attack him with an army stronger than before,
Jonathan set out from Jerusalem and marched to meet them as far as the country of Hamath, giving them no time to invade his land.
He sent spies into their camp; on their return, they reported that the Syrians had resolved to fall upon him by night.
At sunset, Jonathan ordered his men to keep watch and to stay under arms all night, ready for battle, and he posted sentries around the camp.
But the enemy, learning that Jonathan and his men were ready, were seized with fear; with trembling hearts, they lit fires in their camp and fled.
Jonathan and his men did not notice their departure until morning, for they saw the fires burning.
Then Jonathan set off in pursuit of them, but did not overtake them, for they had crossed the river Eleutherus.
Jonathan then turned against the Arabs called Zabadeans; he defeated them and took their spoils.
From there he made for Damascus and traveled through the whole region.
Simon, for his part, advanced as far as Ascalon and the neighboring fortresses; then he turned toward Joppa and occupied it,
for he had learned that the population was thinking of handing the place over to Demetrius; he placed a garrison there to guard the town.
On his return to Jerusalem, Jonathan convened the elders of the people and decided with them to build fortresses in Judea,
to raise the walls of Jerusalem higher and to erect a high wall between the citadel and the city, to separate them, so that the citadel would be isolated and no one could buy or sell there.
Workers were assembled to rebuild the city; the wall overlooking the Kidron valley on the east side was falling, and they repaired the quarter called Chaphenatha.
Simon, for his part, built Adida in the Shephelah, with gates and bars.
Meanwhile Tryphon aspired to become king of Asia, to put on the crown and to lay hands on King Antiochus.
Fearing that Jonathan would prevent him and fight him, he sought to seize his person and put him to death. He set out and came to Beth-shan.
Jonathan advanced to meet him with forty thousand picked warriors and marched on Beth-shan.
Seeing Jonathan come with a large army, Tryphon dared not lay a hand on him.
He received him with honor, commended him to all his friends, offered him gifts and ordered his troops to obey him as they would himself.
Then he said to Jonathan: "Why have you wearied all these people, since there is no war between us?

Send them home, choose a few men to accompany you, and come with me to Ptolemais: I will hand over to you that city, the other fortresses, the other troops and all the royal officers, then I will return to Antioch; for that is why I have come."
Jonathan believed him, did as he said and sent his army away, and it returned to Judea.
He kept with him three thousand men, of whom he detached two thousand in Galilee; only a thousand accompanied him.
But as soon as Jonathan had entered Ptolemais, the people shut the gates, seized him and put to the sword all who had entered with him.
At the same time, Tryphon sent an army and horsemen into Galilee and the great plain, to massacre all of Jonathan's men.
But these, learning that Jonathan had been captured and put to death with his companions, encouraged one another and set out, in close ranks, ready for battle.
Their pursuers, seeing them resolved to defend their lives, turned back;
and they all returned safely to the land of Judah. They wept for Jonathan and his companions; a great fear seized them, and all Israel made great mourning.
Then all the surrounding nations sought to destroy them, saying:
"They have no more leader or support; let us attack them now and blot out their memory from among men."

titres.titre: Simon takes the lead of the people

versets.t: Simon learned that Tryphon had assembled a considerable army to come and ravage the land of Judah.
Seeing the people gripped by fear and dread, he went up to Jerusalem and gathered the crowd.

He exhorted them in these words: "You know all that my brothers and I, and all my father's house, have done for our laws and for the sanctuary, the battles we have fought and the trials we have endured.
It is for this that all my brothers have perished for Israel, and that I alone am left.
And now, far be it from me to spare my own life in a time of distress, for I am no better than my brothers!
But I mean to avenge my people, the sanctuary, our wives and our children, for all the nations have banded together to destroy us out of hatred."
At these words, the spirit of the people was rekindled;
and they answered with a loud voice: "You are our leader, in the place of Judas and Jonathan your brother.
Fight our battles, and whatever you tell us, we will do."
Then Simon assembled all the men able to bear arms, hastened the completion of the walls of Jerusalem and fortified the city all around.
He sent Jonathan, son of Absalom, to Joppa with a strong force; he drove out its inhabitants and settled there.
Tryphon set out from Ptolemais with a large army to invade the land of Judah, taking with him Jonathan in chains.
Simon pitched his camp at Adida, facing the plain.
When Tryphon learned that Simon had taken command in place of his brother Jonathan and was preparing to fight him, he sent messengers to say to him:
"It is on account of the money your brother Jonathan owes the royal treasury, for the offices he held, that we are holding him prisoner.
So send about three and a half tonnes of silver and two of his sons as hostages, lest once free he turn against us, and we will release him."

Simon understood that they were speaking to him with cunning; nevertheless he sent for the silver and the two boys, so as not to draw upon himself the hatred of the people of Israel, who might have said:
"It is because Simon did not send the silver and the children that Jonathan perished."
So he sent the children and the silver; but Tryphon broke his word and did not release Jonathan.
After this Tryphon set out to invade and ravage the country; he made a detour by the road to Adora, but Simon and his army followed him step by step, wherever he went.
Those in the citadel of Jerusalem sent messengers to Tryphon, urging him to come in haste through the wilderness and bring them provisions.
Tryphon arranged all his cavalry to arrive that night; but such a heavy snow fell that he could not reach Jerusalem. He set out and made for the country of Gilead.
When he came near Bascama, he killed Jonathan, who was buried in that place.
Then Tryphon turned back and went to his own country.
Simon sent to gather up the remains of his brother Jonathan and buried them at Modein, the town of his fathers.
All Israel made great mourning over him and wept for him for many days.
Over the tomb of his father and his brothers, Simon raised a monument high enough to be seen from afar, in polished stone front and back.
He set up seven pyramids facing one another two by two, for his father, his mother and his four brothers.
He surrounded them with tall columns crowned with trophies of arms, for an everlasting memorial; and beside the trophies he had ships carved, visible to all who sail the sea.
Such is the tomb he made at Modein, and it stands to this day.
As for Tryphon, dealing treacherously with the young king Antiochus, he put him to death.
He reigned in his place, put on the crown of Asia and did much evil in the land.
Simon, for his part, rebuilt the fortresses of Judea, provided them with high towers, great walls, gates and bars, and stored provisions in them.
Then he chose men and sent them to King Demetrius to obtain a remission of taxes for the country, for all of Tryphon's acts were nothing but plunder.
King Demetrius answered him favorably and wrote him this letter:
"King Demetrius to Simon, high priest and friend of kings, to the elders and to the nation of the Jews, greetings!
We have received the golden crown and the palm that you sent us, and we are disposed to conclude with you a full peace and to write to our officers to grant you remissions.
All that we have decided in your regard stands firm; the fortresses you have built, keep them.
We remit to you the errors and faults committed to this day, as well as the crown tax you owed us; and if any other tax was being levied in Jerusalem, let it be levied no longer.
If any of you are fit to enter our guard, let them enroll, and let there be peace between us."
So, around 142 before Jesus Christ, the yoke of the nations was lifted from Israel.
And the people began to write in their deeds and contracts: "In the first year of Simon, eminent high priest, general and leader of the nation of the Jews."
In those days Simon marched against Gaza and invested it with his troops; he built a siege tower, pushed it up against the town, attacked one of the towers and captured it.
The men in the siege tower leaped into the town, where they caused great confusion.
The inhabitants, with their wives and children, went up on the walls, their garments torn, and begged Simon with loud cries to make peace with them:
"Do not treat us according to our wickedness," they said, "but according to your mercy!"

Simon let himself be moved and stopped fighting them; but he drove them out of the town, purified the houses where there were idols, and made his entry into it with the singing of hymns and thanksgiving.
After removing all impurity from it, he settled there men faithful to the law; he fortified it and built himself a dwelling there.
Meanwhile those in the citadel of Jerusalem, prevented from going out, from going into the country, from buying and selling, suffered cruelly from hunger, and many of them died.
They begged Simon with loud cries to make peace with them; he granted it, but drove them out of there and purified the citadel of all defilement.

He made his entry into it on the twenty-third day of the second month (about April-May), around 141 before Jesus Christ, with songs of praise, palm branches, lyres, cymbals, harps, hymns and canticles, because a great enemy of Israel had been crushed.
He ordered that this day of gladness be celebrated every year.
He fortified the temple mount on the side of the citadel, and dwelt there, he and his men.
Seeing that his son John was a man of worth, Simon entrusted to him the command of all the troops, with Gazara for his residence.

titres.titre: The decree in honor of Simon

versets.t: Around 140 before Jesus Christ, King Demetrius assembled his armies and set out for Media, to recruit reinforcements there to fight Tryphon.
But Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, learning that Demetrius had entered his territory, sent one of his generals to take him alive.
This man set out, defeated the army of Demetrius, seized his person and brought him to Arsaces, who threw him into prison.
The land of Judah was at peace all the days of Simon. He sought the good of his people; his authority and his glory were pleasing to all, throughout those days.
To all his glory he added the capture of Joppa, which he made into a harbor opening access to the islands of the sea.
He enlarged the borders of his nation and became master of the country.
He gathered a great number of freed captives; he became master of Gazara, Beth-zur and the citadel, from which he removed all defilement, and no one could resist him.
Each cultivated his land in peace; the land gave its harvests and the trees of the fields their fruit.
The old men, seated in the squares, all spoke of the country's prosperity, while the young men put on the dress and the array of the warrior.
Simon supplied provisions to the towns and equipped them with all that was needed for their defense, so that his name was renowned to the ends of the earth.
He gave peace to the country, and Israel knew great joy.
Each sat under his vine and his fig tree, and no one troubled them:
there was no one left in the country to fight them, and the kings themselves were brought low in those days.
He was the support of all the lowly of his people; zealous for the law, he made all the godless and the wicked vanish.
He restored the splendor of the sanctuary and increased its sacred vessels.
When the death of Jonathan was learned at Rome, and as far as Sparta, they were deeply grieved.
But when they learned that his brother Simon had succeeded him as high priest and was governing all the country and its towns,
they wrote to him on bronze tablets to renew with him the friendship and alliance concluded formerly with his brothers Judas and Jonathan.
These letters were read before the assembly at Jerusalem. Here is a copy of the one the Spartans sent:
"The magistrates and the city of Sparta to Simon, high priest, to the elders, the priests and the rest of the Jewish people, their brothers, greetings!
The ambassadors you sent to our people have spoken to us of your glory and your honor, and we rejoiced at their coming.
We have recorded their words in the public registers: Numenius, son of Antiochus, and Antipater, son of Jason, ambassadors of the Jews, came to renew their friendship with us.

It pleased the people to receive these men with honor and to deposit a copy of their speeches in the public archives, so that the people of Sparta might keep the memory of them. We have had a copy of it made for Simon, the high priest."
After this, Simon sent Numenius to Rome with a great golden shield weighing about 500 kilograms, to confirm the alliance with the Romans.
On learning these things, the people said: "How shall we show our gratitude to Simon and his sons?

For he has proved steadfast, he, his brothers and his father's house; they have fought and driven back the enemies of Israel, and won for it its freedom." So they engraved these things on bronze tablets, which they fixed to columns on Mount Zion.
Here is a copy of it: "On the eighteenth day of the month of Elul (about August-September), around 140 before Jesus Christ, in the third year of Simon, eminent high priest, at Saramel,
in the great assembly of the priests, the people, the leaders of the nation and the elders of the country, this was proclaimed: In the many wars that have broken out over our country,

Simon, son of Mattathias, of the line of Joarib, and his brothers, exposed themselves to danger and stood up to the enemies of their nation, to keep their sanctuary and the law standing; and they won their nation great glory.
Jonathan gathered his nation and became its high priest, then was gathered to his fathers.
Their enemies sought to invade and ravage their country, and to lay hands on their sanctuary.
Then Simon rose up and fought for his nation; he spent large sums of his own goods, armed the valiant men of his nation and paid them wages.
He fortified the towns of Judea, as well as Beth-zur on the frontier, where the enemy's arms had formerly been, and he placed there a garrison of Jews.
He fortified Joppa on the sea, and Gazara on the borders of Azotus, once inhabited by the enemy; he settled Jews there and provided them with all that was needed for their recovery.

The people saw the faithfulness of Simon and the glory he wished to bring to his nation; they made him their leader and their high priest, on account of all these services, of his justice and of the faithfulness he kept toward his nation, and because he sought by every means to raise up his people.

In his days, all prospered in his hands, so that he drove the nations out of the country, and in particular those who occupied the city of David at Jerusalem, where they had made themselves a citadel from which they sallied out, defiling the surroundings of the sanctuary and doing grave harm to its holiness.
He settled Jewish fighters there, fortified it for the safety of the country and the city, and raised the walls of Jerusalem higher.
In consequence, King Demetrius confirmed him in the high priesthood,
counted him among his friends and heaped honors on him.
For he had heard that the Romans called the Jews their friends, their allies and their brothers, and that they had received the ambassadors of Simon with honor.
The Jews and the priests therefore decided that Simon should be their leader and their high priest forever, until a trustworthy prophet should arise;
that he should command their armies, have charge of the sanctuary, appoint the officers for the public works, the administration of the country, the armament and the guarding of the fortresses;
that he should have charge of the sanctuary, be obeyed by all, that all the public acts of the country should be written in his name, and that he should be clothed in purple and gold.

It shall be permitted to no one, whether of the people or of the priests, to abolish any of these points, to contradict his orders, to convene an assembly in the country without his permission, or to wear the purple or the golden brooch.
Whoever acts against these decisions or violates any article of them shall be liable to punishment.
All the people approved granting Simon the power to act according to these provisions.
Simon accepted: he consented to exercise the office of high priest, of general and of leader of the Jews and the priests, and to preside over all."
It was decided to engrave this text on bronze tablets and to place them within the precincts of the temple, in a conspicuous place,
and to deposit a copy of it in the treasury, at the disposal of Simon and his sons.
King Antiochus, son of Demetrius, sent from the islands of the sea a letter to Simon, high priest and leader of the Jews, and to the whole nation.
Its contents were as follows: "King Antiochus to Simon, high priest and leader of the nation, and to the people of the Jews, greetings!
Wretched men have seized the kingdom of our fathers; I mean to claim it back and restore it as it was before. I have raised numerous troops and fitted out many warships;
I intend to land in the country to take vengeance on those who have ruined it and laid waste many towns of my kingdom.
So I confirm to you all the remissions of taxes that the kings before me granted you, and all the other exemptions they conceded to you.
I permit you to strike your own coinage for your country.
Let Jerusalem and the sanctuary be free; let all the arms you have made and the fortresses you have built and hold remain yours.
Every debt to the royal treasury, present or to come, is remitted to you from now and forever.
And when we have recovered our kingdom, we will heap honors on you, on your nation and on the sanctuary, so that your glory will shine out over all the earth."
Around 138 before Jesus Christ, Antiochus set out for the land of his fathers, and all the troops rallied to him, so that few were left with Tryphon.
King Antiochus pursued him, and Tryphon fled to Dora, on the sea,
for he saw the disasters piling up against him and his army abandoning him.
Antiochus came and camped before Dora with a hundred and twenty thousand foot soldiers and eight thousand horsemen.
He invested the town, and as his fleet drew near by sea, he pressed it hard by land and sea, letting no one enter or leave.
Meanwhile Numenius and his companions returned from Rome, with letters addressed to the kings and the countries. Their contents were as follows:
"Lucius, consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy, greetings!
The ambassadors of the Jews have come to us, as our friends and allies, to renew the ancient friendship and alliance; they were sent by the high priest Simon and by the Jewish people.
They have brought a golden shield weighing about 500 kilograms.

It has therefore seemed good to us to write to the kings and the countries to do them no wrong, to attack neither them, nor their towns, nor their country, and to lend no aid to those who would make war on them.
We have judged it right to accept this shield from them.
If, then, any troublemakers have fled from their country to you, hand them over to the high priest Simon, that he may punish them according to their law."
The same letter was sent to King Demetrius, to Attalus, to Ariarathes and to Arsaces,

as well as to all the countries: to Lampsacus, to the Spartans, to Delos, to Myndos, to Sicyon, to Caria, to Samos, to Pamphylia, to Lycia, to Halicarnassus, to Rhodes, to Phaselis, to Cos, to Side, to Aradus, to Gortyna, to Cnidus, to Cyprus and to Cyrene.
A copy of it was made for Simon, the high priest.

Meanwhile King Antiochus came to attack Dora a second time, pressing his assaults without let-up and setting up siege engines, and he blockaded Tryphon, so that no one could any longer enter or leave.
Simon sent him as reinforcement two thousand picked men, along with silver, gold and considerable equipment.
But the king refused to receive them; he revoked all the commitments he had made to Simon and broke with him.
He dispatched to him Athenobius, one of his friends, to confer with him and to say: "You occupy Joppa, Gazara and the citadel of Jerusalem, which are towns of my kingdom.
You have ravaged their territories, done great damage to the country and seized many places of my kingdom.
So now give back the towns you have taken and the taxes of the places you have made yourselves masters of outside the borders of Judea.
Otherwise, give in their place about seventeen tonnes of silver, and, for the ravages committed and the taxes of the towns, seventeen tonnes more; failing which we will come and make war on you."

Athenobius arrived at Jerusalem; he saw the magnificence of Simon, a sideboard loaded with gold and silver vessels, and great splendor around him. Struck with amazement, he reported to him the words of the king.
Simon answered him: "We have taken neither foreign land nor the goods of others; it is the inheritance of our fathers, which our enemies had for a time unjustly possessed.
We, seizing the opportunity, are reclaiming the inheritance of our fathers.

As for Joppa and Gazara, which you demand, these towns were doing great harm to our people and our country; for them we will give about three and a half tonnes of silver." Athenobius answered not a word;
he returned in anger to the king and reported to him Simon's answer, his magnificence and all he had seen; and the king flew into a great fury.
Meanwhile Tryphon embarked and fled to Orthosia.
The king appointed Cendebeus commander of the coast and gave him an army of foot soldiers and horsemen.
He ordered him to camp facing Judea, to fortify Gedor, to strengthen its gates and to make war on the people; as for himself, he was pursuing Tryphon.
Cendebeus reached Jamnia and began to provoke the people, to invade Judea, to take prisoners and to massacre.
He fortified Gedor, stationed there horsemen and foot soldiers to make sorties and watch the roads of Judea, as the king had ordered him.

titres.titre: The victory of John over Cendebeus

versets.t: John went up from Gazara and came to tell his father the doings of Cendebeus.

Then Simon called his two eldest sons, Judas and John, and said to them: "My brothers and I, and my father's house, have fought the enemies of Israel from our youth to this day, and by our hands Israel has often been saved.
I am old now; but you, by the favor of Heaven, are in the prime of life: take my place and that of my brother, go out to fight for our nation, and may the help of Heaven be with you!"
He chose from the country twenty thousand fighting men and horsemen; they marched against Cendebeus and spent the night at Modein.
Rising in the morning, they advanced toward the plain; and behold, a large army of foot soldiers and horsemen was coming to meet them, separated from them by the bed of a wadi.
John drew up his camp facing the enemy. Seeing his men hesitate to cross the wadi, he crossed it first; at the sight of him, his warriors crossed after him.
He divided his army into two divisions and placed the horsemen between the foot soldiers, for the enemy cavalry was very numerous.
The trumpets were sounded, and Cendebeus was routed with his army; many fell mortally wounded, and the rest fled into the fortress.
It was then that Judas, John's brother, was wounded; but John pursued the fugitives as far as Gedor, which Cendebeus had fortified.
The defeated took refuge even in the towers of the fields of Azotus; John set fire to the town. About two thousand of them perished, and he returned safe and sound to Judea.
Now Ptolemy, son of Abubus, had been made governor of the plain of Jericho; he possessed much gold and silver,
for he was the son-in-law of the high priest.
His heart swelled with pride; he resolved to make himself master of the country and formed treacherous designs against Simon and his sons, to put them to death.

Now Simon, who was going about the towns of Judea to see to their needs, went down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, in the eleventh month, the month of Shebat (about January-February), around 135 before Jesus Christ.
The son of Abubus received them by cunning in a small fortress called Dok, which he had built; he offered them a great banquet, but he had posted men there in ambush.
When Simon and his sons had grown drunk, Ptolemy and his men rose up, seized their arms, fell upon Simon in the banquet hall and slew him with his two sons and some of his servants.
Thus he committed a great act of treachery and rendered evil for good.
At once Ptolemy wrote to the king to inform him of the event and to ask him to send troops to his aid, promising to hand over to him the country and the towns of the Jews.
He sent other agents to Gazara to kill John, and dispatched to the officers letters summoning them to his side, to give them silver, gold and gifts.
He sent still others to occupy Jerusalem and the temple mount.
But someone, getting there ahead, came and told John, in Gazara, that his father and his brothers had perished, and he added: "He has also sent men to kill you."
At this news, John was overwhelmed; he seized those who were coming to kill him and put them to death, for he had recognized that they meant to take his life.
The rest of the story of John, of his wars, of the exploits he accomplished, of the walls he raised and of all his deeds,
behold, all this is written in the chronicles of his high priesthood, from the day he became high priest after his father.

titres.titre: First letter to the Jews of Egypt
Second letter: the death of Antiochus
The sacred fire recovered by Nehemiah

versets.t: To their brothers, the Jews of Egypt, greetings! Your brothers, the Jews of Jerusalem and the land of Judea, wish you true peace.
May God shower his blessings upon you and remember the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May he give you all a heart able to worship him and to carry out his will wholeheartedly and willingly.
May he open your heart to his law and his commandments, and grant you peace within.
May he hear your prayers, be reconciled to you, and never forsake you in the day of trouble.
For now, we are here praying for you.

In the reign of Demetrius, around 143 before Jesus Christ, we Jews already wrote to you at the height of the distress that struck us from the time Jason and his followers betrayed the Holy Land and the kingdom.

The gate of the temple had been set on fire and innocent blood had been shed. Then we prayed to the Lord, and he heard us: once again we offered sacrifice and fine flour, lit the lamps, and set out the loaves.
Now we write to you again, so that you may keep the days of the feast of Booths in the month of Kislev (about December).

Around 124 before Jesus Christ. The people of Jerusalem and Judea, the council of elders, and Judas, to Aristobulus, counselor of King Ptolemy and member of a family of consecrated priests, and to the Jews of Egypt: greetings and good health!
Having been saved by God from grave dangers, we give him heartfelt thanks, we who were ready to fight against the king.
For God himself drove out those who had marched under arms against the holy city.

Indeed, their leader had gone to Persia at the head of an army that seemed invincible; but they were cut to pieces in the temple of the goddess Nanaea, victims of a trick devised by the priests of that temple.
On the pretext of marrying the goddess, Antiochus had come there with his friends to seize her treasures as a dowry.
The priests of Nanaea had displayed them, and Antiochus entered the sacred precinct with a small escort.

As soon as he had entered, the priests shut the temple, opened a hidden trapdoor in the ceiling, and struck him down with a hail of stones, him and his retinue; then they cut them in pieces and threw their heads to those who had remained outside.
Blessed in all things be our God, who has handed the impious over to death!

As we are about to celebrate, on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev (about December), the purification of the temple, we thought it right to inform you, so that you too may keep this feast, in the manner of the feast of Booths, as well as the day the fire reappeared, when Nehemiah, after rebuilding the temple and the altar, offered sacrifices.

For when our ancestors were deported to Persia, the devout priests of that time took some of the fire from the altar and secretly hid it at the bottom of a dry well, so that the place remained unknown to everyone.

Many years later, when God so willed, Nehemiah, sent back to Judea by the king of Persia, charged the descendants of the priests who had hidden it to recover this fire. But they reported that they had found no fire, only a thick liquid.

Nehemiah ordered them to draw some of it and bring it to him. Then, when what was needed for the sacrifice had been arranged on the altar, he had this liquid sprinkled over the wood and the offerings.
Once this was done, and the moment came when the sun, until then veiled by clouds, shone out again, a great fire blazed up, to the amazement of all.
While the offerings were being consumed, the priests said a prayer, and all who were present with them; Jonathan began it, and the others, Nehemiah among them, joined their voices to his.
This was the prayer: "Lord, Lord God, creator of all things, awesome and mighty, just and compassionate, you alone are king, you alone are good,
you alone are generous, you alone are just, almighty and eternal, you who deliver Israel from every evil, who chose our ancestors and made them holy,
accept this sacrifice on behalf of all your people Israel; guard your heritage and make it holy.
Gather those of us who are scattered, set free those who live in slavery among the nations, look with favor on those who are despised and rejected: so the nations will know that you are our God.
Punish those who oppress us and insult us in their arrogance.
Plant your people in your holy place, as Moses promised."
The priests, for their part, sang the hymns.
When the sacrifice was completed, Nehemiah had the rest of the liquid poured over some large stones.
Then a flame rose up from them and went out, absorbed by the brightness that shone from the altar.

When word of this spread, it was reported to the king of Persia that at the spot where the deported priests had hidden the fire, the liquid had been found which Nehemiah and his companions had used to consecrate the sacrifices.
The king had the place fenced off and declared it sacred, thus confirming the wonder.
To those he wished to favor, he distributed many gifts of every kind.
Nehemiah and his companions called this place Nephthar, which means "purification"; but most people call it Nephthai.

titres.titre: Jeremiah hides the tent and the ark
The library of Nehemiah and of Judas
An invitation to celebrate the purification of the temple

versets.t: It is found in the records that the prophet Jeremiah ordered the exiles to take some of that sacred fire, as has been related,
and that he gave them a copy of the Law, urging them not to forget the commandments of the Lord and not to let their hearts be led astray at the sight of idols of gold and silver and their ornaments.
With other words of the same kind, he pressed them never to let the Law depart from their hearts.
The same writings told how the prophet, warned by an oracle of God, had the tent and the ark carried after him to the mountain that Moses had climbed to behold the heritage of God.
When he arrived there, Jeremiah found a cave; in it he placed the tent, the ark, and the altar of incense, and then blocked up the entrance.
Some of his companions came back later to mark out the way, but they could not find it again.
When Jeremiah learned of this, he rebuked them: "This place," he said, "is to remain hidden until God gathers his people together and shows them mercy.
Then the Lord will reveal these sacred objects; the glory of the Lord and the cloud will appear, as in the days of Moses and when Solomon prayed that the temple might be gloriously consecrated."
These writings also told how Solomon, in his wisdom, offered the sacrifice of dedication at the completion of the sanctuary.
Just as Moses had prayed and fire had come down from heaven to consume the sacrifice, so Solomon prayed, and fire came down to consume the offerings.
Moses had said: "The victim offered for sin was not eaten: that is why it was consumed."
In the same way, Solomon kept the dedication for eight days.

All this is recorded in the archives and in the memoirs of Nehemiah, where we also read how he founded a library and gathered into it the books of the kings and the prophets, those of David, and the letters of the kings of Persia concerning their offerings.
In the same way, Judas has collected all the books scattered during the war we had to wage, and they are now in our hands.
So if you need any of them, send messengers to bring you copies.
Since we are about to celebrate the purification of the temple, we write you this letter; you will do well to keep these days with us.
God, who has saved all his people and restored to all of them the heritage, the kingship, the priesthood, and the sanctuary,
as he promised through the Law, will soon have pity on us, we hope, and gather us from every corner of the world into the holy place;
for he has rescued us from great misfortunes and has purified the temple.
This is the story of Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, of the purification of the great temple and the dedication of the altar,
as well as of the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator,
and of the striking interventions of Heaven on behalf of those who fought bravely for Judaism: though few in number, they reconquered the whole country, put to flight a multitude of enemies,
recovered the sanctuary famous throughout the world, freed the city, and restored the laws that were to be abolished, the Lord having favored them with all his kindness.
All these events, set out by Jason of Cyrene in five books, we shall try to condense into one.
For faced with the mass of figures and the difficulty that anyone meets, because of the abundance of material, who wishes to enter into the details of this account,
we have sought to make the work pleasant for those content with a simple reading, convenient for those who wish to commit it to memory, and useful to all without exception.
For us who have undertaken this abridgment, the task is not an easy one: it is a labor of sweat and sleepless nights,
as hard as the work of one who prepares a banquet and tries to satisfy others. Yet, to be useful to as many as possible, we gladly take on this heavy burden.
We leave to the original author the care of setting out each event in detail, and hold ourselves, for our part, to the rules of the summary.
For just as the architect of a new house must keep the whole construction in view, while the painter charged with decorating it cares only for the ornament, so it is, I believe, with us.
To dig into the subject, to review everything, to linger over every detail: that is the duty of the one who composes a history.
But the one who only wants an abridgment of it should be allowed to seek brevity and to give up setting everything out.
Let us begin our account, then, without adding anything more to this preamble: it would be absurd to be long before the history and brief in the history itself.

titres.titre: Heliodorus tries to plunder the temple treasury
The distress and prayer of the city

versets.t: As long as the holy city enjoyed perfect peace and the laws were faithfully observed there, thanks to the piety of the high priest Onias and his hatred of evil,
the kings themselves honored the holy place and enriched the temple with magnificent gifts,
so that Seleucus, king of Asia, met from his own revenues all the expenses of the sacrificial service.
But a certain Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, who had been appointed administrator of the temple, came into conflict with the high priest over the regulation of the city market.
Unable to get the better of Onias, he went to Apollonius, son of Thraseas, who was then military governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

He told him that the treasury of the temple in Jerusalem was overflowing with enormous sums, with untold riches out of all proportion to the cost of the sacrifices, and that all of this could be brought into the king's hands.
When Apollonius was received by the king, he pointed out these riches to him. The king then chose Heliodorus, his minister, and sent him with orders to confiscate them.
Heliodorus set out at once, on the pretext of inspecting the cities of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, but in reality to carry out the king's plan.
When he reached Jerusalem, he was welcomed warmly by the high priest. He explained the information he had received, declared the purpose of his coming, and asked whether things were really so.
The high priest explained to him that these were deposits entrusted by widows and orphans,
and that part of the money belonged to Hyrcanus, son of Tobias, a man of high rank; far from what the impious Simon claimed, it all amounted to about ten tons of silver and five tons of gold.
He added that it was impossible to wrong those who had trusted in the holiness of the place, in the inviolable majesty of a temple revered throughout the world.
But Heliodorus, by virtue of the king's orders, absolutely insisted that this money must be turned over to the royal treasury.
On the appointed day, he was preparing to enter and inspect the riches. The whole city was thrown into turmoil:

the priests, in their priestly vestments, prostrated themselves before the altar and, facing heaven, begged him who had established the law about deposits to keep these goods intact for those who had entrusted them.
To see the face of the high priest was to be wounded to the depths of the soul: his features and his changed color betrayed the anguish that was tearing at him.
Everything about him, the fear written on his face, the trembling of his body, revealed to all the pain of his heart.
The inhabitants came pouring out of their houses and prayed all together that the holy place might not be profaned.
The women, with sackcloth tied over their breasts, filled the streets; the young girls, normally kept secluded, ran, some to the gates, some to the walls, and some leaned out of the windows,
all with their hands stretched out to heaven in supplication.
It was a pitiful sight: this frantic crowd and the high priest waiting in agony.
While the Jews were begging the Sovereign Lord to keep the deposits perfectly safe for those who had entrusted them,
Heliodorus was carrying out his plan. Already he was there, with his guard, close to the treasury.
But just as he arrived, the Lord of spirits, the master of all power, manifested himself with such splendor that all who had dared to enter, struck by the might of God, collapsed in terror.
A horse appeared to them, ridden by a terrifying and richly harnessed rider; it charged at Heliodorus and struck him with its front hooves. The rider seemed to be wearing golden armor.

At the same moment two other young men appeared, full of vigor, of dazzling beauty, and magnificently dressed; taking their places on either side of Heliodorus, they scourged him without pause, overwhelming him with blows.
Heliodorus suddenly collapsed, plunged into thick darkness. They lifted him up and placed him on a stretcher:
this man who had just entered the treasury with a large armed escort was carried away helpless, having just plainly experienced the power of God.
While he lay there, laid low by the divine power, speechless and without any further hope of help,

the Jews blessed the Lord for having glorified his holy place: the temple, which a moment before had been full of terror and confusion, was filled with joy and gladness by this manifestation of the Sovereign Lord.
At once some of Heliodorus's companions came to beg Onias to pray to the Most High to grant life to the man who lay there gasping for breath.
Fearing that the king might suspect the Jews of an attempt on Heliodorus's life, the high priest offered a sacrifice for his recovery.

As he was offering this sacrifice of atonement, the same two young men appeared again to Heliodorus, in the same clothing, and standing before him they said: "Give great thanks to the high priest Onias: it is for his sake that the Lord grants you your life.
And you, having been chastised by Heaven in this way, proclaim everywhere the great power of God." With these words they vanished.
Heliodorus then offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made great vows to him who had spared his life; then, having assured Onias of his friendship, he returned to the king with his troops.
Before everyone he testified to the works of the great God that he had seen with his own eyes.
When the king asked him whom he thought it good to send to Jerusalem once again, Heliodorus replied:
"If you have an enemy or an opponent of your rule, send him there: he will come back to you flogged, if he survives at all, for there is truly a divine power in that place.
He who dwells in heaven watches over that place and protects it; those who approach it with evil intentions he strikes down and destroys."
This is how the affair of Heliodorus and the safeguarding of the sacred treasury came to an end.

titres.titre: Simon's intrigues against the high priest Onias
Jason buys the priesthood and Hellenizes Jerusalem
The murder of the high priest Onias
The riot against Lysimachus; the impunity of Menelaus

versets.t: This Simon, the informer who had betrayed the treasury and his homeland, now slandered Onias: it was he, Simon claimed, who had put Heliodorus up to it and caused all the trouble.
The benefactor of the city, the protector of his countrymen, the faithful guardian of the laws, he dared to pass off as an enemy of the state.
This hatred went so far that one of Simon's followers committed murders.
Seeing the danger of these divisions, and knowing that Apollonius, the military governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, was encouraging Simon's malice, Onias went to the king.
It was not to accuse his countrymen, but to serve the interests of his whole people, in general and in particular.
He saw clearly that without the king's intervention peace was impossible, and that Simon would not give up his criminal schemes.
But Seleucus died, and Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes succeeded him. Then Jason, the brother of Onias, set about seizing the high priesthood.
In an interview with the king, he promised him about nine tons of silver, and two tons more drawn from other revenues.

He further undertook in writing to pay another four tons of silver or so, if he were allowed on his own authority to open a gymnasium and a training ground for young men, and to enroll the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch.
The king agreed to everything. As soon as he had the power, Jason began to impose Greek ways on his countrymen.

He abolished the privileges the kings had graciously granted to the Jews, obtained long before through the embassy of John, father of that Eupolemus who later negotiated the treaty of alliance and friendship with the Romans; destroying the lawful institutions, he introduced practices contrary to the Law.
He took pleasure in founding a gymnasium at the very foot of the citadel, and he trained the finest of the young men to wear the Greek hat.
The craze for Greek ways and foreign customs then grew to such a pitch, through the wickedness of that impious Jason, who was no high priest at all,

that the priests no longer showed any zeal for the service of the altar: despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the games of the gymnasium, forbidden by the Law, as soon as the signal was given for the throwing of the discus.
Scorning the honors of their own country, they prized the Greek distinctions above all.
This is why grave misfortunes fell upon them: those whose way of life they imitated and whom they wished to resemble in everything became their enemies and their tormentors.
For one does not violate the laws of God with impunity, as the course of events will show.
While the games, held every five years, were being celebrated at Tyre in the king's presence,

the vile Jason sent from Jerusalem some delegates, citizens of Antioch, carrying about a kilo and a half of silver for the sacrifice in honor of Heracles. But those who carried this money themselves asked that it be used, not for a sacrifice that was unfitting, but for other expenses.
So this money, intended by the sender for the sacrifice in honor of Heracles, was in fact used, at the request of those who carried it, to build warships.

Apollonius, son of Menestheus, was sent to Egypt for the enthronement of King Ptolemy Philometor. Learning that this king had become hostile to him, Antiochus wanted to secure his own position: he went to Joppa and then to Jerusalem.
Received magnificently by Jason and the whole city, he made his entrance by torchlight, amid acclamations; then he led his army into Phoenicia.
Three years later, Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the Simon already mentioned, to carry the money to the king and settle important matters.
But Menelaus gained access to the king, flattered him with the airs of an important person, and got the high priesthood assigned to himself, offering about eight tons of silver more than Jason.
Armed with his letters of appointment, he came back to Jerusalem with nothing worthy of the priesthood, bringing only the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a wild beast.
So Jason, who had supplanted his own brother, was in turn supplanted by another and had to flee to the land of the Ammonites.
Menelaus held on to power; but he did not pay the king the sum he had promised, despite the demands of Sostratus, the commander of the citadel,
who was in charge of collecting the taxes. So both of them were summoned before the king.
Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus to take his place as high priest, and Sostratus left Crates, the governor of Cyprus.
At this juncture, the people of Tarsus and Mallus revolted, because these two cities had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king's concubine.
So the king set off in haste to quell the revolt, leaving Andronicus, one of his high officials, to take his place.
Judging the moment favorable, Menelaus stole some gold objects from the temple: he gave part of them to Andronicus and managed to sell the rest at Tyre and in the neighboring towns.
When Onias had clear proof of this, he denounced the crime to Menelaus, from the place of asylum where he had withdrawn, at Daphne, near Antioch.

Menelaus then took Andronicus aside and urged him to kill Onias. So Andronicus came to Onias, offered him his right hand with an oath, and though he inspired distrust, persuaded him to leave his sanctuary; then he put him to death at once, in contempt of all justice.
For this reason not only the Jews but many people of other nations were outraged at this unjust murder.
When the king returned from Cilicia, the Jews of Antioch, together with Greeks who were revolted by this violence, came to him about the wicked murder of Onias.
Antiochus was grieved to the depths of his soul; moved to pity, he wept as he thought of the wisdom and self-control of the dead man.

Blazing with anger, he immediately had the purple stripped from Andronicus, tore his garments, and, after having him led through the whole city, had him executed at the very place where he had committed his crime against Onias: thus the Lord struck him with a just punishment.

Meanwhile Lysimachus, in agreement with Menelaus, had committed many sacrilegious thefts in the city. When the news spread, and many gold objects had already been dispersed, the people rose up against him.
Faced with this angry crowd in revolt, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and resorted to violence, under the command of a certain Tyrannus, as advanced in years as in wickedness.

Seeing Lysimachus's attack, the people snatched up whatever they could, some stones, some heavy clubs, and some handfuls of the ashes lying about, and hurled them all in confusion at Lysimachus's men.
In this way they wounded many of his men, killed several, put the rest to flight, and slaughtered the sacrilegious man himself near the temple treasury.
Legal proceedings were opened against Menelaus over these events.
When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the council of elders laid before him the justice of their cause.
Seeing himself doomed, Menelaus promised a large sum to Ptolemy, son of Dorymenes, to bring the king around in his favor.
Ptolemy drew the king aside into the colonnade, as if to take the air, and made him change his mind.
The king acquitted Menelaus, though guilty of all these crimes, and condemned to death the unfortunate accused, who would have been declared innocent even before Scythians.
So those who had defended the city, the people, and the sacred objects at once suffered this unjust penalty.
The people of Tyre themselves were outraged at this and gave these victims a magnificent funeral.
As for Menelaus, thanks to the greed of those in power, he kept his position, growing ever more wicked, a true scourge to his fellow citizens.

titres.titre: The massacre on the sabbath day
Judas Maccabeus withdraws to the wilderness

versets.t: About this time, Antiochus launched his second campaign against Egypt.
Now throughout the whole city of Jerusalem, for nearly forty days, there appeared, galloping through the air, horsemen clothed in gold, armed with lances like troops in formation,
squadrons drawn up for battle, charges launched from both sides, shields waving, a forest of spears, swords drawn, missiles flying, the gleam of golden armor and breastplates of every kind.
So everyone prayed that these apparitions might be a good omen.

A false rumor spread that Antiochus was dead. Jason then gathered at least a thousand men and attacked the city by surprise. The inhabitants ran to the walls, but the city finally fell, and Menelaus took refuge in the citadel.

Jason slaughtered his own countrymen without mercy, not realizing that a victory over one's own people is the worst of defeats: he thought he was triumphing over enemies, not over people of his own nation.
Yet he did not manage to seize power, and, his intrigues turning to his own shame, he had to flee once more to the land of the Ammonites.

His criminal life came to a wretched end. Hunted by Aretas, king of the Arabs, fleeing from city to city, pursued by all, hated as a renegade, loathed as the executioner of his homeland and his countrymen, he was driven all the way to Egypt.
He who had banished so many people from their homeland died in a foreign land: he had gone to Sparta, hoping to find refuge there on the grounds of an ancient kinship.
He who had left so many men unburied was mourned by no one and given no funeral rites; he had no place in the tomb of his ancestors.
When these events reached the king, he thought Judea was in revolt. So he left Egypt, raging like a wild beast, and took the city by storm.
He ordered the soldiers to kill without mercy everyone they met and to cut down those who took refuge on the rooftops.
So young men and old were slaughtered, men, women, and children; even young girls and infants were put to death.
In three days there were eighty thousand victims: forty thousand killed in the carnage, and as many sold into slavery.
Not content with these atrocities, Antiochus dared to enter the temple, the holiest in all the earth, guided by Menelaus, that traitor to the Law and to his homeland.
With his defiled hands he seized the sacred objects and swept up the offerings that other kings had placed there to enhance the glory and honor of the place, handing them over to profane hands.

Antiochus swelled with pride, not understanding that the Lord was angered only for a time, because of the sins of the city's inhabitants, and that this was why he was turning his gaze away from the holy place for a moment.

Otherwise, had they not been burdened with so many sins, Antiochus, like Heliodorus sent by King Seleucus to inspect the treasury, would have been flogged and stopped in his audacity the moment he arrived.
But God did not choose his people for the sake of the holy place: he chose the place for the sake of the people.

That is why the place itself shared the misfortunes of the people, before later sharing its blessings: abandoned in the wrath of the Almighty, it recovered all its glory when the Sovereign Lord was reconciled with his people.
After carrying off from the temple about forty-five tons of gold and silver, Antiochus hurried back to Antioch, so drunk with pride that he believed he could make dry land sail and walk on the sea.
He left behind officials to torment the people: at Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian even crueler than the one who had appointed him;
at Mount Gerizim, Andronicus; and, worst of all, Menelaus, who set himself insolently above his countrymen and hated them.
Antiochus also sent the odious Apollonius at the head of twenty-two thousand men, with orders to kill all the men of fighting age and to sell the women and children.
When he reached Jerusalem, Apollonius pretended to have peaceful intentions and waited for the holy sabbath day; then, seeing the Jews at rest, he ordered his troops to take up arms.
He had all those who had come out to watch the parade massacred, then, ranging through the city under arms, he killed a great crowd of people.
As for Judas Maccabeus, he withdrew to the wilderness with nine companions; they lived in the mountains like wild beasts, feeding only on plants so as not to defile themselves.

titres.titre: The persecution: the temple profaned, the faith outlawed
The martyrdom of the aged Eleazar

versets.t: Not long afterward, the king sent an aged Athenian to force the Jews to renounce the faith of their ancestors and to give up living according to the laws of God,
and to profane the temple in Jerusalem by dedicating it to Olympian Zeus, and the one on Mount Gerizim to Zeus the Protector of Strangers, as the inhabitants of the place wished.
This flood of evils was, even for ordinary people, crushing and unbearable.
For the temple was filled with the revels and debaucheries of dissolute pagans, who dallied with prostitutes in the sacred courts and brought forbidden things into them.
The altar itself was covered with unclean victims, forbidden by the Law.
It was no longer possible to keep the sabbath or the ancestral feasts, or even to admit that one was a Jew.

A cruel compulsion drove the Jews, each month, to the sacrifice offered on the king's birthday; and at the feasts of Dionysus they were forced to march through the streets, crowned with ivy in his honor.
At the instigation of Ptolemy, an edict ordered that the same measures be applied to the Jews of the neighboring Greek cities, that they be forced to take part in these sacrifices,
and that those who refused to adopt Greek customs be put to death. So misfortune was everywhere before their eyes.
Thus two women who had had their children circumcised were dragged publicly through the city, their infants hanging at their breasts, and then thrown down from the top of the walls.
Others, who had gathered in nearby caves to keep the sabbath in secret, were denounced to Philip and burned alive, not daring to defend themselves out of reverence for the holiness of that day.
I beg those who read this book not to be discouraged by these misfortunes, but to understand that these trials were meant not for the ruin but for the correction of our people.
Not to leave sinners long unpunished, but to send them a prompt chastisement, is a mark of great goodness.
Toward the other nations the Sovereign Master waits patiently, in order to punish them, until they have filled up the measure of their sins. With us it is otherwise:
he does not want to have to take vengeance on us later, when our sins have reached their full measure.
So he never withdraws his mercy from us: he corrects his people by trials, but he does not abandon them.
Let this reminder suffice; after these few words, let us return to the account.
Eleazar, one of the foremost teachers of the Law, a man already advanced in years and of noble bearing, was having his mouth forced open to make him eat pork.
But he, preferring a glorious death to a dishonored life, walked willingly to his torment.
He spat out the meat, showing how anyone should come forward to torment who has the courage to refuse what it is not lawful to eat, even to save his own life.

Those in charge of that unlawful meal, who had long been friends with Eleazar, took him aside and pressed him to bring meat that was permitted, prepared by himself, and only to pretend to eat the meat of the sacrifice ordered by the king,
so that in this way he might escape death and enjoy this favor owed to their old friendship.

But he, reasoning with the wisdom of his years, thinking of the authority that his old age and gray hair gave him, of the blameless life he had led from childhood, and above all of the holy laws established by God, answered without hesitation that they should send him without delay to the realm of the dead.
"At my age," he said, "it is not fitting to pretend. Many young men would think that Eleazar, at ninety years old, had gone over to the foreign ways;
and because of my playacting, for the sake of a wretched scrap of life, I would lead them astray and cover my old age with shame and disgrace.
Even if for the moment I escaped the punishment of men, I would not escape, living or dead, the hands of the Almighty.
That is why, in leaving this life courageously, I will show myself worthy of my old age,
and I will leave to the young the noble example of a death freely and generously accepted for the venerable and holy laws." With these words, he walked straight to his torment.
Those who were leading him, kindly a moment before, turned harsh: his words seemed to them sheer madness.

As he was about to die under the blows, he groaned and said: "The Lord, who possesses holy knowledge, knows well that, though I could have escaped death, I endure in my body cruel pains under the rods, but that in my soul I suffer them with joy, out of reverence for him."
So he died, leaving by his death, for the young and for the whole people, an example of courage and a memorial of virtue.

titres.titre: The martyrdom of the seven brothers
The youngest son, then the mother

versets.t: Seven brothers were also arrested along with their mother. The king wanted to force them, with whips and lashes, to eat pork, which is forbidden by the Law.
One of them, speaking for all, declared: "What do you mean to ask of us, what do you want from us? We are ready to die rather than break the law of our ancestors."
Beside himself with rage, the king ordered pans and cauldrons to be heated white-hot.

As soon as they were red-hot, he had the tongue cut out of the one who had spoken for all, the skin of his head torn off, and his hands and feet cut off, before the eyes of his brothers and his mother.

When he was thus completely mutilated, the king had him brought to the fire, still alive, and roasted in the pan. As the smoke spread far and wide, his brothers and their mother encouraged one another to die with courage.
"The Lord God sees us," they said, "and he truly has pity on us, as Moses declared in his song that warns Israel: He will have pity on his servants."

When the first had died in this way, they brought the second forward for torture. After tearing the skin of his head off along with the hair, they asked him whether he would eat pork before being tortured limb by limb.
He answered in the language of his ancestors: "No!" So he underwent the same torments as the first.
With his last breath he said: "You scoundrel, you take from us this present life; but the King of the universe will raise us up to eternal life, we who die for his laws."
After him, the third was tortured. Ordered to put out his tongue, he did so at once and held out his hands without trembling.
With noble courage he said: "It is from Heaven that I received these limbs; for the sake of his laws I count them as nothing, and it is from him that I hope to receive them again."
The king himself and those around him were struck by the courage of this young man, who counted his suffering as nothing.
When he was dead, they inflicted the same torments on the fourth.
About to expire, he said: "It is good to die at the hands of men when one looks to God for the hope of being raised up by him. For you, there will be no resurrection to life."
Then they brought the fifth forward and tortured him. But he, fixing his eyes on the king,
said to him: "You are mortal, and yet you have power over men and you do as you please. But do not think that God has abandoned our people.
Wait a little, and you will see his great power, when he torments you and your offspring."

After him, they brought the sixth forward. About to die, he said: "Have no illusions: it is we ourselves who have brought these evils upon us, by sinning against our God; that is why such strange things are happening to us.
But you, do not imagine you will go unpunished after daring to fight against God."
The mother, admirable above all and worthy of glorious remembrance, saw her seven sons perish in a single day and bore it with courage, sustained by her hope in the Lord.
She encouraged each of them in the language of her ancestors; full of nobility of soul, she reinforced her mother's tenderness with a manly courage.
She said to them: "I do not know how you appeared in my womb; it was not I who gave you breath and life, nor I who arranged the elements of your body.

So it is the Creator of the world, who shapes each person at birth and presides over the origin of all things, who in his mercy will give you back breath and life, since you now sacrifice yourselves for the love of his laws."

Antiochus thought himself insulted and suspected an affront in these words. Since the youngest was still alive, he did not stop at urging him: he promised him under oath to make him rich and happy if he would give up the faith of his ancestors, to make him his friend and entrust him with high offices.
When the young man paid no attention to this, the king called for the mother and urged her to advise the boy to save himself.
After he had pressed her at length, she agreed to persuade her son.

But bending over him, she mocked the cruel tyrant and said to him in the language of her ancestors: "My son, have pity on me who carried you nine months in my womb, nursed you three years, and raised and fed you until the age you have now reached.
I beg you, my child, look at heaven and earth and all that is in them, and know that God made them out of nothing, and that the human race came into being in the same way.
Do not fear this executioner: show yourself worthy of your brothers and accept death, so that I may find you again with them at the time of mercy."
She was still speaking when the young man said: "What are you all waiting for? I do not obey the king's order, but the commandments of the Law given by Moses to our ancestors.
And you, the author of all the miseries unleashed on the Hebrews, you will not escape the hand of God.
As for us, it is for our own sins that we suffer.
If the Lord, who is living, has shown us his anger for a moment to correct and instruct us, he will be reconciled again with his servants.
But you, impious man, most villainous of all men, do not swell with mad pride or vain hopes as you raise your hand against the servants of Heaven:
you have not yet escaped the judgment of the almighty God, who sees all things.
Our brothers, after a passing suffering, have received, under God's covenant, eternal life; but you, by the judgment of God, will bear the just punishment of your pride.

Like my brothers, I give up my body and my life for the laws of our ancestors. I beg God to have pity on his people soon, and to force you, through trials and blows, to acknowledge that he is the only God.
May the wrath of the Almighty, justly unleashed on our whole people, come to rest at last on me and on my brothers!"
Beside himself, the king turned on this last one even more cruelly than on the others, unable to bear being defied in this way.
So this young man died, without having defiled himself with any idolatry, entrusting himself entirely to the Lord.
Last of all, the mother died, after her sons.
But let this be enough about the forced sacrifices and the boundless cruelties of Antiochus.

titres.titre: Nicanor is sent to sell the Jews as slaves
Judas routs the army of Nicanor

versets.t: Meanwhile Judas Maccabeus and his companions slipped secretly into the villages, gathering their relatives and all who had remained faithful to Judaism; in this way they assembled a force of about six thousand men.
They begged the Lord to look upon his people, trampled underfoot by all, to have pity on his temple profaned by the impious,
to take pity on the devastated city, about to be leveled, and to listen to the blood that cried out to him,
to remember the criminal massacre of innocent little children and the blasphemies hurled against his name, and to show his hatred of evil.
Once at the head of a large force, Maccabeus became invincible to the nations, for the Lord's anger had turned to mercy.
Falling suddenly on the towns and villages, he burned them; occupying the best positions, he inflicted defeat after defeat on his enemies.
He chose the night above all for these expeditions, and the report of his valor spread everywhere.
Seeing this man's rapid progress and his ever more frequent successes, Philip wrote to Ptolemy, the military governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, to come to the aid of the king's cause.
