Without delay, Ptolemy sent Nicanor, son of Patroclus, one of the king's chief favorites, at the head of at least twenty thousand men of various nations, to exterminate the whole Jewish people. He assigned to him Gorgias, a very experienced general.
Nicanor counted on raising from the sale of the captives of Judea the some fifty tons of silver that the king owed to the Romans as tribute.

He hastened to invite the coastal cities to come and buy Jewish slaves, promising to hand over ninety of them for about twenty-five kilos of silver. He gave no thought to the punishment of the Almighty that was about to fall upon him.
As soon as he learned of Nicanor's advance, Judas warned his companions of the army's approach.
Some, seized with fear and lacking faith in the justice of God, fled and made for other places;
the others sold all that they had left, while praying the Lord to deliver them from the impious Nicanor, who had sold them even before the battle,
if not for their own sake, at least for the sake of the covenant made with their ancestors, and because his holy and glorious name had been invoked over them.
Maccabeus assembled his six thousand men and urged them not to dread the enemy or be frightened by the multitude of nations marching unjustly against them, but to fight with courage,
keeping before their eyes the outrageous profanation of the holy place, the affront done to the ravaged city, and the ruin of the customs of their forebears.
"They," he said, "rely on their weapons and their daring; we put our trust in God, the master of all things, who can with a single sign strike down our attackers, and the whole universe with them."
He reminded them of the help God had granted in the past, in particular how, in the time of Sennacherib, a hundred and eighty thousand men had perished,

and how, in the battle fought against the Galatians in Babylonia, eight thousand fighters, along with four thousand Macedonians, though in great difficulty, had wiped out a hundred and twenty thousand enemies thanks to the help that came from heaven, and had won a great booty.
These memories filled them with confidence and made them ready to die for the laws and for their homeland. Judas then divided his army into four corps.
He gave the command to his brothers Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan, with fifteen hundred men each.
He also charged Eleazar to read aloud from the holy Book and then, having given as the watchword "The help of God!", he himself took the lead of the first corps and attacked Nicanor.
With the help of the Almighty, they killed more than nine thousand of the enemy, wounded and maimed most of Nicanor's soldiers, and put them all to flight.
They also seized the money of those who had come to buy them. After pursuing the fugitives quite a long way,
they had to stop, for lack of time: it was the eve of the sabbath, and so they did not continue the pursuit.
Having gathered the weapons and the spoils of the enemy, they kept the sabbath, blessing and praising the Lord without ceasing, who had saved them that day and thus gave them a first pledge of mercy.
After the sabbath, they distributed a share of the booty to the victims of the persecution, to the widows and orphans, and then divided the rest among themselves and their children.
When this was done, they all prayed together, begging the merciful Lord to be fully reconciled with his servants.

They also killed more than twenty thousand men of the forces of Timothy and Bacchides, seized high fortresses, and divided their vast booty into two equal parts, one for themselves, the other for the persecuted, the orphans, the widows, and the aged.
They carefully collected all the weapons and stored them in suitable places, and then brought the rest of the booty to Jerusalem.
They put to death Phylarches, a man of Timothy's entourage, as perverse as he was harmful to the Jews.

While they were celebrating their victory in the city, they burned, in the small house where they had taken refuge, Callisthenes and a few others who had set fire to the sacred gates of the temple: a just reward for their sacrilege.
As for that triple villain Nicanor, who had brought in the thousand merchants to sell the Jews to them,

humbled with the Lord's help by those he thought the weakest, he took off his fine garments and, fleeing alone across the countryside, without escort, made his way back to Antioch, in despair at having lost his army.

He who had promised to pay the Romans their tribute with the price of the captives of Jerusalem now proclaimed that the Jews had God as their defender and that they were invincible because they obeyed the laws he had given them.

titres.titre: The illness and punishment of Antiochus
The letter of Antiochus to the Jews

versets.t: About that time, Antiochus was returning, covered with shame, from the regions of Persia.

He had entered the city of Persepolis to plunder its temple and oppress the city, but the people had risen up in arms, and he had been forced to flee, routed by the inhabitants and driven back in disgrace.
When he reached the region of Ecbatana, he learned what had happened to Nicanor and to the army of Timothy.

Wild with rage, he meant to make the Jews pay for the affront of those who had forced him to flee. So he ordered his driver to press the chariot on without stopping and hasten the journey. But the judgment of heaven was already upon him, for in his pride he had said, 'The moment I reach Jerusalem, I will make that city a graveyard for the Jews.'

Then the Lord, the all-seeing God of Israel, struck him with an incurable and horrible affliction. No sooner had he spoken these words than a searing pain seized his bowels, with cruel inner torments.
It was only just, for he had torn open the bowels of others with countless unheard-of tortures. Yet he abated nothing of his arrogance;

still swollen with pride, he poured out the fire of his fury on the Jews and pressed the march, when suddenly he fell from his chariot as it sped along, and his fall was so violent that every limb of his body was broken.

He who, a moment before, in his more-than-human pride, thought he could command the waves of the sea and weigh the height of the mountains on a scale, now lay on the ground, carried on a stretcher: the power of God was plain for all to see.
From the body of this godless man worms swarmed out; his flesh fell away in strips while he was still alive, in agonizing pain, and the stench of his rottenness sickened the whole army.
The man who a little before had seemed to touch the stars could now be carried by no one, so unbearable was the smell.
Then, broken, he began to come down from his immense pride and to know himself, under the lash of God, whose torments never ceased to grow worse.
Unable to endure his own stench any longer, he said, 'It is right to submit to God, and not to think oneself, a mere mortal, the equal of the divine.'
But this wretch went on praying to the Sovereign Lord, who would no longer have mercy on him.
He promised to declare free the holy city, toward which he was rushing to raze it and make it a mass grave;
to treat all the Jews as citizens equal to the Athenians, those Jews he had lately judged unworthy even of burial, dooming them and their children to be devoured by birds of prey and wild beasts;
to adorn with the finest offerings the holy Temple he had plundered, to restore a hundredfold all its sacred vessels, and to meet the cost of the sacrifices from his own revenues;
and, more than that, to become a Jew himself and to travel through the whole inhabited world proclaiming the power of God.
But his sufferings did not cease, for the just judgment of God had reached him. Seeing his condition hopeless, he then wrote to the Jews the following letter, in the form of a plea:
'To the Jews, his most excellent fellow citizens, the king and general Antiochus sends greeting and his best wishes for their health and happiness.
If you and your children are well, and if your affairs go as you wish, I give thanks to God and set my hope in heaven.

As for me, I lie ill and without strength, but I keep an affectionate memory of your esteem and goodwill. On my way back from Persia I fell gravely ill, and I judged it necessary to see to the good of all.
Not that I despair of myself: on the contrary, I have great hope of recovery.
But I remember that my father, whenever he set out on campaign in the distant provinces, would name his successor,
so that, if some unexpected misfortune or alarming rumor should arise, the people of the kingdom, knowing to whom the government had been entrusted, would not be troubled.

Bearing in mind, too, that the neighboring kings and the princes on our borders are watching for their chance and waiting to see what will happen, I have named as king my son Antiochus, whom I have often commended and entrusted to most of you during my tours through the upper provinces. I have written to him what follows.
I ask you, then, and I beg you, to remember my benefits, both public and private, and each of you to keep your goodwill toward me and toward my son.
For I am convinced that, full of gentleness and kindness, he will follow my intentions and deal well with you.'
So this murderer and blasphemer, in the grip of horrible sufferings such as he had inflicted on others, died in a foreign land, in the mountains, a wretched death.
Philip, his boyhood companion, brought his body home; but, fearing the son of Antiochus, he withdrew to Egypt, to Ptolemy Philometor.

titres.titre: The purification of the Temple and the feast of the Dedication
The defeat and death of Timothy

versets.t: Meanwhile, Maccabeus and his companions, with the help of the Lord, recovered the Temple and the city.
They tore down the altars that the foreigners had set up in the public square, as well as the pagan places of worship.

After purifying the Temple, they built a new altar and then, having struck fire from flint, they used it to offer a sacrifice, after an interruption of two years; they burned incense again, lit the lamps, and set out the bread of the offering.

When this was done, they prostrated themselves on the ground and implored the Lord never again to let them fall into such misfortunes; and if they should sin again, that he himself would correct them with moderation, without handing them over once more to godless and barbarous nations.
The Temple had been profaned by the foreigners on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Chislev (around December); it was on the very same day that it was purified.
They kept a feast of eight days, in the manner of the feast of Booths, remembering that a short time before they had spent that feast in the mountains and the caves, like wild beasts.
So, holding decorated branches, green boughs, and palms, they sang hymns to the glory of the one who had brought them safely through to the purification of his Temple.
And they decreed, by a public edict, that the whole Jewish nation should celebrate these same days every year.
Such was the end of Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes.
We shall now tell the story of Antiochus Eupator, the son of that godless man, summarizing the calamities caused by his wars.
On coming to the throne, he entrusted the government to a certain Lysias, whom he also appointed commander in chief of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.
For Ptolemy, surnamed Macron, had been the first to treat the Jews justly, because of the wrongs they had suffered, and to seek to govern them in peace.

For this very reason, friends of the king denounced him to Eupator. Constantly called a traitor for having abandoned Cyprus, which Philometor had entrusted to him, and for having gone over to Antiochus Epiphanes, he was stripped of all honor, lost heart, and poisoned himself.
Now Gorgias, having become military governor of the region, was hiring mercenaries and seizing every occasion to make war on the Jews.
At the same time the Idumeans, masters of strong fortresses, were harassing the Jews; they welcomed those banished from Jerusalem and sought to keep the war going.
Maccabeus and his men, after praying and asking for God's help, launched an attack against the strongholds of the Idumeans.
They assaulted them vigorously, seized them, drove back the defenders of the ramparts, and killed all who fell into their hands: at least twenty thousand men.
At least nine thousand had taken refuge in two very strong towers, supplied with everything needed to withstand a siege.
Maccabeus left Simon, Joseph, and Zacchaeus, with their men, in sufficient numbers to reduce them, and set off himself to where his presence was urgently needed.
But Simon's men, greedy for money, let themselves be bribed by some of the besieged: for about three hundred kilograms of silver, they let a number of them escape.

When this was reported to Maccabeus, he called together the leaders of the people and accused these men of having sold their brothers for silver, by letting enemies slip away who were now armed against them.
He put these traitors to death and at once seized the two towers.
Succeeding in all his operations, he killed in these two fortresses more than twenty thousand men.
Meanwhile Timothy, already beaten by the Jews, gathered a large army of mercenaries, assembled a strong cavalry force from Asia, and advanced to conquer Judea by force of arms.
As he drew near, Maccabeus and his men began to pray to God, their heads covered with dust and their waists girded with sackcloth.
Prostrate at the foot of the altar, they asked the Lord to be favorable to them, to be the enemy of their enemies and the adversary of their adversaries, as the Law promises.
When their prayer was ended, they took up their arms, went some distance from the city, and halted near the enemy.
At the first light of day the two armies engaged: the one had, besides their courage, the recourse to the Lord as their pledge of victory; the other had nothing to guide them but their fury.
At the height of the battle, five splendid figures appeared from heaven to the enemy, mounted on horses with golden bridles, and they placed themselves at the head of the Jews.

Two of them, flanking Maccabeus, shielded him with their weapons and kept him unharmed, while they hurled darts and lightning bolts at the enemy, who, blinded and seized with panic, were thrown into rout.
Twenty thousand five hundred foot soldiers and six hundred horsemen perished in this way.
Timothy fled to a very strong place, Gazara, which was commanded by Chaereas.
Full of ardor, Maccabeus and his men besieged it for four days.
Confident in the strength of the place, the besieged poured out blasphemies and impious words.
At dawn on the fifth day, twenty young men from Maccabeus' troop, their anger inflamed by these blasphemies, bravely rushed the wall and, with the fury of lions, cut down all who came before them.

Others climbed to the assault on the opposite side, set fire to the towers, and lit pyres in which they burned the blasphemers alive; still others broke down the gates and opened a way for the rest of the army, which took the city.
Finding Timothy hidden in a cistern, they put him to death, along with his brother Chaereas and Apollophanes.
When these exploits were accomplished, they blessed with hymns and songs of praise the Lord, who had done great things for Israel and given them the victory.

titres.titre: The campaign of Lysias against the Jews

versets.t: A very short time later, Lysias, guardian and kinsman of the king, regent of the kingdom, took ill what had just happened.
He gathered about eighty thousand men and all his cavalry, and marched against the Jews. He fully intended to people the holy city with Greeks,
to subject the Temple to a tax, like the other sanctuaries of the nations, and to sell the office of high priest year by year,
taking no account at all of the power of God, proud as he was of his hosts of foot soldiers, his thousands of horsemen, and his eighty elephants.
Entering Judea, he came up to Beth-zur, a fortress of difficult access about thirty kilometers from Jerusalem, and pressed it hard.
When Maccabeus and his men learned that Lysias was besieging the fortresses, they, together with the people, implored the Lord, with groans and tears, to send a good angel to save Israel.
Maccabeus, taking up his arms first, urged the others to face the danger with him to rescue their brothers. All rushed forward with ardor.
They were still in sight of Jerusalem when a horseman clothed in white appeared at their head, brandishing weapons of gold.
Then all together they blessed the merciful God, and their courage was strengthened: they were ready to face not only men, but the fiercest of beasts, and to pierce walls of iron.
They advanced in battle order, with an ally come from heaven, for the Lord had pity on them.
Falling like lions on the enemy, they struck down eleven thousand foot soldiers and sixteen hundred horsemen, and put all the rest to flight.
Most escaped wounded and stripped of their weapons, and Lysias himself owed his life only to a shameful flight.
But, being a man of sense, he reflected on his defeat; understanding that the Hebrews were invincible because the almighty God fought for them, he sent to them
and proposed peace on just terms, even undertaking to persuade the king to become their friend.
Concerned only for the common good, Maccabeus accepted all of Lysias' proposals; and the king consented to all the terms that Maccabeus sent in writing to Lysias concerning the Jews.
Here is the letter that Lysias wrote to the Jews: 'Lysias, to the Jewish people, greeting.
John and Absalom, your envoys, have handed me the document signed by you and have asked me to carry out its terms.
Everything that had to be submitted to the king I have laid before him, and he has granted what was acceptable.
If, then, you remain well disposed toward the government, I will strive in the future to contribute to your welfare.
As for the details, I have instructed your envoys and mine to confer with you about them.
Farewell. Around 164 before Jesus Christ, the twenty-fourth of the month of Dioscorinthius (around March).'
Here is the letter of the king: 'King Antiochus, to his brother Lysias, greeting.
Since our father has been received among the gods, we wish our subjects to go about their affairs undisturbed.
Having learned that the Jews refuse, contrary to our father's wish, to adopt Greek customs, that they prefer their own ways and ask to be allowed to live according to their laws,
and desiring that this nation too remain at peace, we decree that the Temple be restored to them and that they live according to the customs of their ancestors.
You will therefore do well to send to them and offer them your hand, so that, knowing our intentions, they may take heart again and devote themselves gladly to their own affairs.'
Here, finally, is the king's letter to the Jewish nation: 'King Antiochus, to the council of the elders of the Jews and to all the other Jews, greeting.
If you are well, our wishes are fulfilled; we ourselves are in good health.
Menelaus has made known to us your desire to return home and go about your affairs.
Those who set out from now until the thirtieth of the month of Xanthicus (around April) will enjoy peace and security.
The Jews may use their own food and follow their laws as before, and no one will be troubled for offenses committed in ignorance.
I have sent Menelaus to reassure you.
Farewell. Around 164 before Jesus Christ, the fifteenth of the month of Xanthicus (around April).'
The Romans too addressed a letter to the Jews, worded as follows: 'Quintus Memmius and Titus Manlius, ambassadors of the Romans, to the Jewish people, greeting.
What Lysias, the kinsman of the king, has granted you, we too grant you.

As for the matters he judged should be submitted to the king, send us someone without delay, once you have examined the question carefully, so that we may lay it before the king as befits your cause; for we are on our way to Antioch.
So hasten to send your delegates, that we too may know your intentions.
Farewell. Around 164 before Jesus Christ, the fifteenth of the month of Xanthicus (around April).'

titres.titre: The crime of Joppa and the response of Judas
The campaigns of Judas beyond the Jordan
The prayer and sacrifice for the dead

versets.t: When this treaty was concluded, Lysias returned to the king, and the Jews went back to cultivating their fields.
But the governors of the region, Timothy and Apollonius son of Gennaeus, as well as Hieronymus and Demophon, not to mention Nicanor, the governor of Cyprus, left them neither in peace nor at rest.

The people of Joppa then committed an abominable crime. They invited the Jews living among them to embark, with their wives and children, on boats they had prepared, as though they bore them no hostility at all.
It was a decision made by the whole city. The Jews accepted, as people who desire peace and suspect nothing. But once they were out at sea, they were drowned: more than two hundred persons.
As soon as Judas learned of this crime committed against his own people, he gave his orders to his men and, after calling on God,
the just judge, he marched against the murderers of his brothers. By night he set fire to the harbor installations, burned the ships, and put to the sword those who had taken refuge there.
The town being closed, he withdrew, but with the intention of returning to raze the whole city of Joppa.
Learning that the people of Jamnia meant to do the same to the Jews settled among them,
Judas attacked Jamnia by night and set fire to the harbor along with its ships; the glow of the blaze was seen as far as Jerusalem, about forty-five kilometers away.
They had gone about a kilometer and a half, marching against Timothy, when some Arabs fell upon Judas, at least five thousand foot soldiers and five hundred horsemen.
The battle was fierce, but with God's help Judas and his men prevailed. Defeated, the nomads asked Judas for peace, promising to hand over livestock and to be useful to him.
Convinced that they could indeed render many services, Judas granted them peace; they shook hands, and the nomads returned to their tents.
Judas next attacked a fortified town, ringed with ramparts and drawbridges, inhabited by people of various nations: it was called Caspin.
Confident in their walls and well supplied, the besieged behaved coarsely, insulting Judas and his men and uttering blasphemies.

But Judas and his men, after calling on the Sovereign Lord of the world, who in the time of Joshua had thrown down the walls of Jericho without ram or siege engine, hurled themselves at the wall like lions.
By the will of the Lord they took the city and made such slaughter there that the nearby pool, about four hundred meters wide, seemed filled with the blood that was shed.
From there, after a march of about a hundred and forty kilometers, they reached the Charax, where the Jews called Toubiani live.
There they did not find Timothy: having been able to do nothing in the region, he had gone off, leaving only a strong garrison in one particular place.
But two of Maccabeus' generals, Dositheus and Sosipater, went and attacked that fortress and killed the men Timothy had left there, more than ten thousand.

For his part, Maccabeus divided his army into cohorts, put commanders over them, and marched against Timothy, who had a hundred and twenty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand five hundred horsemen.
Informed of Judas' approach, Timothy sent the women, the children, and the baggage to Carnion, a place impregnable and hard to reach because of the narrow passes throughout the whole region.

As soon as the first cohort of Judas appeared, terror seized the enemy, for the power of the One who sees all was manifesting itself fearfully to them. They fled in all directions, wounding one another and running themselves through with their own swords.
Judas pursued them relentlessly, striking down these criminals: he cut down as many as thirty thousand.

Timothy himself fell into the hands of the men of Dositheus and Sosipater. With great cunning, he begged them to release him safe and sound, for he held in his power, he said, the parents and brothers of many of them, who would suffer the worst if he were to die.
With long speeches he assured them that he would give these people back without doing them any harm; and so the Jews released him to save their brothers.
Judas then marched on Carnion and the temple of the goddess Atargatis, where he killed twenty-five thousand men.

After routing and destroying these enemies, Judas led his army against Ephron, a fortified city inhabited by people of various nations; sturdy young men defended it before the ramparts, and it had many engines and missiles.
But the Jews called on the Almighty, who by his power shatters the strength of the enemy: they took the city and struck down twenty-five thousand of its inhabitants.
From there they marched against the city of the Scythians, about a hundred and ten kilometers from Jerusalem.
But the Jews who lived there testified that the inhabitants had treated them kindly and had helped them in the days of misfortune.
So Judas and his men thanked them and urged them to remain kindly toward their people in the future. Then they returned to Jerusalem, as the feast of Weeks drew near.
After Pentecost, they marched against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.
He came out with three thousand foot soldiers and four hundred horsemen.
They joined battle, and a few of the Jews fell.

A certain Dositheus, a horseman of Bacenor's troop, a valiant man, seized Gorgias and, pulling him by his cloak, was dragging him off by force, meaning to take this accursed man alive; but a Thracian horseman charged Dositheus and cut off his arm at the shoulder, so that Gorgias managed to escape to Marisa.
Meanwhile the men of Esdris had been fighting for a long time and were worn out. Judas then implored the Lord to be their ally and their leader in the battle.
Then, raising at the top of his voice, in the language of his fathers, the war cry mingled with hymns, he fell unexpectedly on the troops of Gorgias and put them to rout.
Judas then rallied his army and led it to the town of Adullam. When the seventh day came, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the sabbath there.
The next day, as had to be done, Judas and his men came to gather up the bodies of the dead, to bury them with their kinsmen in the tombs of their fathers.
But under the tunic of each of the dead they found objects consecrated to the idols of Jamnia, which the Law forbids to the Jews. It became clear to all that this was the cause of their death.
So all blessed the Lord, the just judge who brings hidden things to light.

Then they turned to prayer, imploring that the sin committed might be wholly blotted out. And the valiant Judas urged the people to keep themselves from sin, having before their eyes what had happened because of the fault of those who had fallen.

He then took up a collection, gathered about nine kilograms of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sacrifice of atonement. A beautiful and noble deed, inspired by the thought of the resurrection!
For if he had not hoped that the fallen soldiers would rise again, it would have been vain and foolish to pray for the dead.
But he was mindful of the magnificent reward laid up for those who fall asleep in godliness.
This is a holy and pious thought. This is why he had this sacrifice of atonement offered for the dead, so that they might be freed from their sin.

titres.titre: The invasion of Antiochus Eupator and the death of Menelaus
The siege of Beth-zur and the peace

versets.t: Around 163 before Jesus Christ, Judas and his men learned that Antiochus Eupator was marching against Judea with numerous troops,

accompanied by Lysias, his guardian and regent. Each of them commanded a Greek army: a hundred and ten thousand foot soldiers, five thousand three hundred horsemen, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots fitted with scythes.
Menelaus joined them and, with great treachery, kept urging Antiochus on, not for the good of his country, but in the hope of being restored to his office.

But the King of kings stirred up against this scoundrel the anger of Antiochus. When Lysias had shown the king that Menelaus was the cause of all the troubles, Antiochus ordered him to be taken to Beroea and put to death there according to the custom of the place.
At Beroea there was a tower about twenty-two meters high, full of ashes, fitted with a revolving machine that on every side hurls a man down into the ashes.
It is there that the people of Beroea throw, to make him perish, anyone guilty of sacrilegious theft or of some other great crime.
So died Menelaus, that violator of the Law, deprived of burial in the open ground, which was only just:
he who had sinned so many times against the altar, whose fire and ashes were pure, met his death in the ashes.
The king, then, came on with his mind full of barbarous designs, resolved to treat the Jews even more cruelly than his father.
As soon as Judas heard of it, he ordered the people to call upon the Lord night and day, that once again he might come to the help of those
who were about to be deprived of the Law, their homeland, and the holy Temple, and that he might not let this people, barely allowed to breathe again, fall back under the yoke of the godless nations.
After they had all prayed together and implored the merciful Lord, with tears and fasting, prostrate for three days, Judas exhorted them and commanded them to hold themselves ready.

Then, having conferred privately with the elders, he decided not to wait until the king had brought his army into Judea and taken Jerusalem, but to set out at once and settle everything with the help of the Lord.

Leaving the outcome of the battle to the Creator of the world, he urged his companions to fight valiantly to the death for the laws, the Temple, the holy city, their homeland, and their institutions, and then he pitched his camp near Modein.

Having given his men the watchword 'Victory through God!', he chose the bravest of the young warriors and attacked the king's tent by night. In the camp he killed four thousand men, as well as the largest of the elephants together with its tower and its crew.
At last, having filled the camp with terror and confusion, they withdrew in complete success.
Day was scarcely breaking when all was accomplished, thanks to the protection with which the Lord shielded Judas.
Having thus tested the boldness of the Jews, the king tried to take the strongholds by cunning.
He marched against Beth-zur, a strong Jewish fortress; but he was repulsed, met with setbacks, and got the worst of it.
Judas got the necessary supplies through to the besieged.
Meanwhile a certain Rhodocus, of the Jewish army, was betraying the secrets to the enemy; an inquiry was made, he was unmasked and imprisoned.
The king negotiated a second time with the besieged of Beth-zur, offered his hand, took theirs, and then withdrew;

he attacked the men of Judas and was beaten. But, having learned that Philip, left by Epiphanes in charge of affairs, had revolted in Antioch, he was dismayed: he spoke kindly to the Jews, submitted, swore to fair terms, was reconciled, offered a sacrifice, honored the Temple, and treated the holy place with goodwill.
He received Maccabeus warmly and appointed him military governor from Ptolemais to the country of the Gerrhenians.
But when he came to Ptolemais, the inhabitants, displeased with the treaty, were indignant and refused to carry out its terms.
Lysias mounted the platform, defended the agreement as best he could, won the people over, calmed them, and then set out for Antioch. Such was the course of the king's attack and retreat.

titres.titre: The friendship between Nicanor and Judas

versets.t: Three years later, Judas and his men learned that Demetrius, son of Seleucus, had sailed from Tripolis with a strong army and a fleet,
had seized the country, and had put to death Antiochus and his guardian Lysias.
A certain Alcimus, who had once become high priest but had willingly defiled himself in the time of the troubles, realized that he no longer had any hope of safety or of access to the holy altar.

So he went to King Demetrius around 162 before Jesus Christ, offering him a crown of gold with a palm and some olive branches, such as it is customary to present at the Temple; that day he did no more than this.
But he found the occasion to serve his own wickedness when Demetrius, having summoned him to his council, questioned him about the dispositions and plans of the Jews.
He answered, 'The Jews who are called Hasideans, led by Judas Maccabeus, keep up war and rebellion and prevent the kingdom from enjoying peace.
That is why, stripped of the dignity of my fathers, I mean of the high priesthood, I have come here,
first out of sincere concern for the king's interests, and second for the good of my fellow citizens, for the recklessness of these people plunges our whole nation into misery.
You, then, O king, when you have learned all this, provide for the safety of our country and of our oppressed nation, with the kindness that makes you gracious to all.
For as long as Judas lives, peace will be impossible in the state.'
He had scarcely spoken when the other friends of the king, who hated Judas, inflamed Demetrius still further.
He at once summoned Nicanor, the former commander of the elephant corps, appointed him general in Judea, and sent him off
with written orders to kill Judas, to scatter his companions, and to install Alcimus as high priest of the great Temple.
The pagans who had fled Judea before Judas gathered in crowds around Nicanor, counting on the misfortune of the Jews turning to their own advantage.

When the Jews learned of Nicanor's advance and the rallying of the nations, they covered themselves with dust and implored the One who established his people forever and had never ceased to protect his heritage by striking signs.
At the order of their leader, they set out at once and confronted the enemy at the village of Dessau.
Simon, the brother of Judas, had engaged Nicanor in battle; but, taken by surprise by the enemy's sudden onset, he suffered a slight reverse.
Nevertheless, hearing what valor Judas and his men had, and with what fearlessness they fought for their homeland, Nicanor shrank from deciding the matter by bloodshed.
He sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to offer their hand to the Jews and receive theirs.
After a long examination of the proposals, the general laid them before his troops and, agreement being reached, they consented to make terms.
A day was fixed on which the two leaders would meet face to face. Judas came, and a seat of honor was set out for each.
As a precaution, fearing some sudden treachery, Judas had posted armed men at favorable spots. The meeting went off properly.
Nicanor stayed some time in Jerusalem without committing any injustice, and he dismissed the crowds that had gathered.
He kept Judas near him, feeling a true affection for him.
He urged him to marry and have children; Judas married, lived happily, and enjoyed life.

Seeing their friendship, Alcimus procured a copy of the treaty and went to Demetrius: he told him that Nicanor was betraying the interests of the state, since he had designated as his successor Judas, an enemy of the kingdom.

Beside himself, stirred up by the slanders of this scoundrel, the king wrote to Nicanor of his keen displeasure at the agreement that had been made, and ordered him to send Maccabeus to Antioch in chains, without delay.
On reading this letter, Nicanor was dismayed: it grieved him to break a lawful agreement when Judas had done nothing wrong.
But, unable to oppose the king, he looked for a way to carry out this order by some ruse.

For his part, Maccabeus, noticing that Nicanor was becoming more distant and less friendly, understood that this coolness boded no good; he gathered a good number of his men and slipped away from Nicanor.

Seeing that he had been outdone by Judas' cleverness, Nicanor went to the great and holy Temple, while the priests were offering the customary sacrifices, and ordered them to hand the man over to him.
When they swore that they did not know where the man he was looking for might be, Nicanor raised his hand toward the Temple
and swore, 'If you do not hand Judas over to me in chains, I will raze this sanctuary of God, destroy the altar, and erect here a splendid temple to Dionysus.'
With these words he withdrew. The priests, lifting up their hands toward heaven, called on the One who has always fought for our people:
'You, Lord, who need nothing, were pleased that the Temple where you dwell should be in our midst.
Now therefore, Lord, holy above all that is holy, keep forever undefiled this dwelling so recently purified.'
Now a certain Razis, one of the elders of Jerusalem, was denounced to Nicanor. He was a man who loved his fellow citizens, of very good repute, called the father of the Jews because of his kindness.
In earlier times, when all contact with the pagans had to be avoided, he had been accused of Judaism and had, with unshakable steadfastness, risked his body and his life for Judaism.
Wishing to show his hatred of the Jews, Nicanor sent more than five hundred soldiers to arrest him,
convinced that his capture would deal a great blow to the Jews.

This troop was about to seize the tower and force the entrance of the courtyard; already the order had been given to set it on fire and burn the gates. On the point of being taken, Razis threw himself on his sword,
preferring a noble death to the shame of falling into the hands of these criminals and suffering outrages unworthy of his dignity.
But in his haste he had not struck himself in the right place. Seeing the crowd rushing through the gates, he ran bravely to the top of the wall and threw himself down on the crowd with courage.
They all drew back at once, and he fell into the space thus left empty.
Still breathing, his soul on fire, he rose up all streaming with blood and, despite his terrible wounds, ran through the crowd; standing on a steep rock,
by now drained of his blood, he tore out his entrails and hurled them with both hands at the crowd, praying the Master of life and breath to give them back to him one day. And so he died.

titres.titre: Nicanor plans to attack on a sabbath day
The dream of Judas: Onias and Jeremiah
The defeat and death of Nicanor
The feast of Nicanor and the conclusion of the book

versets.t: Meanwhile, Nicanor learned that Judas and his men were in the region of Samaria, and he decided to attack them in complete safety on the sabbath day.
The Jews who followed him under compulsion said to him, 'Do not slaughter them in so savage and barbarous a way; respect the day that the One who governs all has honored and hallowed.'
This thrice-accursed man then asked whether there was in heaven a sovereign who had commanded the sabbath day to be kept.
They answered, 'It is the Lord, the living God, the Sovereign Lord in heaven, who has commanded the seventh day to be kept holy.'
'And I,' he retorted, 'am sovereign on the earth, and I command that arms be taken up for the king's service.' Yet he did not manage to carry out his evil design.
While Nicanor, in his arrogant self-assurance, was planning to raise a trophy from the spoils of Judas and his men,
Maccabeus kept full confidence, sure of obtaining the help of the Lord.
He urged his men not to fear the assault of the nations, but to remember the help that Heaven had already given them and to hope that the Almighty would grant them the victory once more.
He strengthened them by quoting the Law and the prophets, reminded them of the battles already fought, and filled them with great ardor.
Having thus raised their courage, he gave them his orders, pointing out to them the treachery of the nations and their violation of oaths.
He armed each of them less with the security of shields and spears than with the confidence born of good words; then he told them a trustworthy dream, a vision that gladdened them all.

This is what he had seen: the high priest Onias, that good man, modest in bearing and gentle in manner, refined in speech, trained from childhood in every virtue, had appeared to him with hands outstretched, praying for the whole Jewish nation.
Then there had appeared to him, in the same way, a man of venerable great age, of imposing look, surrounded by a wonderful majesty.
Speaking up, Onias had said, 'Here is the friend of his brothers, who prays much for the people and for the holy city: Jeremiah, the prophet of God.'
Then Jeremiah, stretching out his right hand, had given Judas a sword of gold, saying,
'Take this holy sword, a gift from God; with it you will shatter your enemies.'

Heartened by these fine words of Judas, able to rouse valor and to steady young hearts, they decided not to make camp, but to fall boldly on the enemy and to decide everything in a fierce battle, since the city, their religion, and the Temple were in peril.
For they were less anxious about their wives, their children, their brothers, and their kinsmen: their greatest and first concern was for the holy Temple.
Those who had remained in the city were no less distressed, anxious about the outcome of the battle that was about to be fought outside.
While all were awaiting the coming decision, and the enemy were already massing in battle order, the elephants placed in the right position and the cavalry on the wings,

Maccabeus, seeing this immense multitude, the variety of their weaponry, and the fierce appearance of the elephants, raised his hands to heaven and called on the Lord who works wonders; for he knew that victory does not come from arms, but that God grants it to those who are worthy of it.
This was his prayer: 'You, Sovereign Lord, who sent your angel in the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed a hundred and eighty-five thousand men of the camp of Sennacherib,
now too, Sovereign of the heavens, send your good angel before us to spread fear and dread.
By the power of your arm strike down those who have come, blasphemy on their lips, against your holy people!' Such were his words.
Nicanor and his army advanced to the sound of trumpets and war songs.
Judas and his men engaged in battle with invocation and prayer.
Fighting with their hands and praying to God in their hearts, they struck down at least thirty-five thousand men, filled with joy at this manifest help of God.
When the battle was over, as they were dispersing in gladness, they recognized Nicanor, fallen in his armor.
Then, amid shouting and deep emotion, they blessed the Sovereign Lord in the language of their fathers.

And Judas, the man who had given himself wholly, body and soul, to the defense of his fellow citizens, and who had kept for his people the affection of his youth, ordered Nicanor's head to be cut off, along with his arm up to the shoulder, and carried to Jerusalem.
He went there himself, gathered his compatriots and the priests, and, standing before the altar, he summoned the garrison of the citadel.
He showed them the head of the infamous Nicanor and the hand that this blasphemer had raised with such insolence against the holy dwelling of the Almighty.
Then, having cut out the tongue of the godless Nicanor, he ordered it to be given piece by piece as food to the birds, and the wages of his folly to be hung up facing the Temple.
All raised up blessings to heaven to the glorious Lord: 'Blessed be the One who has kept his dwelling undefiled!'
Judas had Nicanor's head fastened to the citadel, a clear sign, visible to all, of the help of the Lord.
By common consent, they decreed by a public edict never to let this day pass without celebrating it,
but to solemnize the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar in Syriac (around March), the day before Mordecai's day.
So ended the affair of Nicanor. And since from that time the city remained in the hands of the Hebrews, I too will end my account here.
If it is well composed and well handled, that is what I wanted; if it is mediocre and imperfect, it is all I could do.

For just as it is harmful to drink wine alone or water alone, while wine mixed with water is pleasant and enjoyable, so it is the art of shaping the story that delights the ear of those who read the history. Here I make an end.

titres.titre: Job, the blameless man of the land of Uz
Job loses his possessions and his children

versets.t: In the land of Uz there was a man named Job. He was a blameless and upright man, who feared God and turned away from evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters.
He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred donkeys, along with a great many servants; this man was the greatest of all the sons of the East.
His sons used to go and feast in one another's houses, each on his own day, and they would invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the round of feasting was over, Job would send for them to purify them; he would rise early in the morning and offer a burnt offering for each of them, for he thought, "Perhaps my sons have sinned and offended God in their hearts." This is what Job did, every time.
Now one day the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and the Accuser also came among them.
The Lord said to the Accuser, "Where have you come from?" The Accuser answered him, "From roaming the earth and prowling about on it."
The Lord said again, "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil."
The Accuser answered, "Is it for nothing that Job fears God?
Have you not put a hedge of protection around him, around his house and all that he owns? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his herds spread across the land.
But just stretch out your hand and touch all that he owns: I swear he will curse you to your face!"
The Lord said to the Accuser, "So be it! All that he owns is in your power; only, do not lay a hand on the man himself." And the Accuser withdrew from the presence of the Lord.
Now on the day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,
a messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them,
when the Sabeans swept down on them and carried them off. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone escaped to tell you."
He was still speaking when another arrived and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven; it burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone escaped to tell you."
He was still speaking when another arrived and said, "The Chaldeans, in three bands, fell upon the camels and carried them off. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone escaped to tell you."
He was still speaking when another arrived and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,
when a great wind rose from the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people, and they died; I alone escaped to tell you."
Then Job rose, tore his robe and shaved his head; then he fell to the ground and bowed low.
He said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I shall return there. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away: blessed be the name of the Lord!"
In all this, Job did not sin, and he said nothing foolish against God.

titres.titre: The arrival of the three friends

versets.t: On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and the Accuser also came among them to present himself before him.
The Lord said to the Accuser, "Where have you come from?" The Accuser answered, "From roaming the earth and prowling about on it."

The Lord said again, "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil. He still holds firm to his integrity, though you incited me to strike him down without cause."
The Accuser answered him, "Skin for skin! A man will give all he owns to save his life.
But just stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh: I swear he will curse you to your face!"
The Lord said to the Accuser, "So be it! He is in your power; only, spare his life."
The Accuser withdrew from the presence of the Lord, and he struck Job with malignant sores, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.
Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself, and he sat down among the ashes.
His wife said to him, "Do you still hold firm to your integrity? Curse God, and die!"
He answered her, "You speak like a foolish woman. We accept good fortune from God: should we not accept misfortune as well?" In all this, Job did not sin with his lips.

Three friends of Job heard of all the misfortunes that had come upon him: Eliphaz of Teman, Bildad of Shuah and Zophar of Naamah. Each set out from his own land, and they agreed to go together to console and comfort him.
Looking up from a distance, they did not recognize him. Then they broke into sobs, tore their robes and threw dust toward heaven, onto their heads.
Then they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw how great his suffering was.

titres.titre: Job curses the day of his birth
Why did I not die at birth?

versets.t: Then Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.
He spoke and said:
Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, "A boy is conceived!"
That day, let it become darkness! Let God on high take no care for it, let no light shine upon it!
Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it back, let a cloud settle over it, let an eclipse fill it with terror!
That night, let deep gloom seize it! Let it not be joined to the days of the year, let it not enter the count of the months!
Yes, let that night be barren, let no cry of joy be raised in it!
Let them curse it, those who curse the days, those who know how to rouse Leviathan!
Let the stars of its dawn go dark, let it wait in vain for the light and never see the eyelids of the morning,
for it did not close against me the doors of the womb nor hide sorrow from my eyes.
Why did I not die at birth? Why did I not perish as I came from the womb?
Why were there two knees to receive me, and two breasts to nurse me?
For now I would be lying in peace, I would be asleep and at rest
with the kings and the great ones of the earth, who built for themselves palaces now deserted,
with the princes who possessed gold and filled their houses with silver.
Or, like a stillborn child that is buried, I would not exist, like the little ones who never saw the light.
There the wicked cease their raging; there the weary are at rest.
The prisoners there are all at peace, they no longer hear the voice of their oppressor.
There the small and the great are found together, and the slave is free of his master.
Why give light to the wretched, and life to those whose souls are full of bitterness,
who long for death, and it does not come, who search for it more eagerly than for treasure,
who would be overjoyed and exult if only they found the grave?
Why give life to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in on every side?
My sighs have become my bread, and my groans pour out like water.
What I dread, that is what befalls me; what I fear falls upon me.
No more peace, no more calm, no more rest: torment has come.

titres.titre: Eliphaz's first speech: no just man perishes
The night vision: no mortal is pure before God

versets.t: Then Eliphaz of Teman spoke and said:
If one ventures a word, will you bear it? Yet who could hold back his words?
See: you have instructed many, you have strengthened failing hands;
your words have lifted up those who were stumbling, you have steadied the knees that were giving way.
And now that misfortune reaches you, you falter; it touches you, and you are dismayed.
Was not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your life your hope?
Remember: what innocent man ever perished? Where were upright men ever seen to perish?
For my part, I have seen it: those who plow evil and sow trouble also reap its harvest.
At the breath of God they perish; at the wind of his anger they are swept away.
The lion may roar and growl, yet the fangs of the young lion are broken;
the great beast perishes for lack of prey, and the lioness's cubs are scattered.
A word came stealing to me, my ear caught its whisper.
Amid the troubling visions of the night, when deep sleep weighs upon men,
dread seized me, and terror set all my bones trembling.
A breath glided over my face, and the hair of my flesh bristled.
Someone was standing there, whose features I could not make out; a form was before my eyes. There was silence, then I heard a voice:
"Can a man be just before God? Can a mortal be pure before his Maker?
See, God does not even trust his servants, and he finds fault in his angels:
how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust, who are crushed sooner than a moth!
From morning to evening they are broken to pieces; unnoticed by anyone, they vanish forever.
The cord of their tent is pulled up: they die, and it is without having gained wisdom."

titres.titre: Happy the man whom God corrects

versets.t: Call out, then! Will anyone answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
Resentment kills the fool, and passion is the death of the simpleton.
I have seen the fool take root, and suddenly his dwelling was cursed.
His sons are far from any help, they are trampled at the city gate, and no one delivers them.
His harvest, the hungry devour, taking it even from among the thorns, and the thirsty crave his wealth.
For trouble does not come from the dust, and hardship does not sprout from the ground:
it is man who breeds his own hardship, as the sparks fly upward.
If I were you, I would turn to God, it is to him that I would commit my cause.
He does great things, beyond fathoming, wonders past counting.
He pours rain upon the earth and sends water over the fields;
he raises up those who are brought low, and lifts the mourners to safety.
He foils the schemes of the crafty, so that their hands achieve nothing.
He catches the clever in their own cunning, and brings down the plans of the devious.
In broad daylight they meet with darkness, at noon they grope as in the night.
But God saves the poor from the sword of their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty.
So hope is reborn for the weak, and injustice shuts its mouth.
Happy the man whom God corrects! So do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.
For he wounds, but he binds up; he strikes, but his hands heal.
Six times he will deliver you from distress, and the seventh, evil will not touch you.
In famine he will ransom you from death; in war, from the edge of the sword.
You will be sheltered from the lash of the tongue, and unafraid before the devastation that comes.
At devastation and famine you will laugh; the wild beasts you will not fear.
For you will have a pact with the stones of the field, and the wild beasts will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is secure; you will visit your estate, and find nothing missing.
You will see your offspring numerous, and your descendants like the grass of the fields.
You will go down to the grave still full of vigor, like a sheaf gathered in its season.
This is what we have observed: it is the truth. Listen to it, and take it to heart for yourself.

titres.titre: Job replies: if only my grief were weighed
Friends as disappointing as a dried-up torrent
Show me where I have failed

versets.t: Then Job spoke and said:
Ah, if only my grief could be weighed, and all my misfortune set on the scales!
It would be heavier than the sand of the seas; that is why my words run wild.
For the arrows of the Almighty are lodged in me, and my spirit drinks their venom; the terrors of God are drawn up in battle against me.
Does the wild donkey bray when it has grass? Does the ox low over its fodder?
Is tasteless food eaten without salt? Is there any flavor in the white of an egg?
What I once refused even to touch is now my pitiful food.
Ah, who will grant my request, that God would give me what I hope for!
That God would consent to crush me, that he would let his hand loose and cut me off!
At least I would have this comfort, this joy in a pain that shows no pity: that I have never denied the words of the Holy One.
What strength have I left, to keep hoping? What future, to hold on?
Is my strength the strength of stone? Is my flesh made of bronze?
No, there is no help left in me at all, and every means of rescue is torn from me.
To a man in despair his friend owes compassion, even if he should forsake the fear of the Almighty.
But my brothers have betrayed me like a torrent, like the bed of streams that overflow:
dark when the ice swells them, when the snow melts into them,
they dry up in the heat, and at the first blaze their bed vanishes.
The caravans turn aside from their course, wander into the desert and are lost.
The caravans of Tema looked for them, the travelers of Sheba counted on them:
they are dismayed in their hope; arriving at the bank, they stand confounded.
That is what you are to me: you see the terror, and you take fright.
Did I say to you, "Give me something, offer for me a share of your wealth,
snatch me from the hand of the enemy, deliver me from the power of the violent"?
Instruct me, and I will be silent; make me see where I have gone wrong.
How straight upright words strike home! But what do your rebukes prove?
Do you mean to correct with mere words, when the sayings of a desperate man are so much wind?
You would even cast lots for an orphan, and bargain over your friend!
Now, be so good as to look at me: would I lie to your face?
Turn back, I beg you, let there be no injustice! Turn back: my good cause is at stake.
Is there any falsehood on my tongue? Can my palate no longer tell what is evil?

titres.titre: Remember, my life is but a breath
What is man, that you watch him?

versets.t: Is not the life of man on earth a drudgery? Are his days not those of a hired laborer?
As the slave longs for the shade, as the worker waits for his wages,
so I have received as my portion months of emptiness, and nights of suffering have been counted out to me.
Scarcely lying down, I say, "When will I be able to rise?" But the evening drags on, and I toss with sleeplessness until dawn.
My flesh is covered with worms and crusts of dirt; my skin cracks and festers.
My days have passed, swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and they come to an end for lack of thread.
Remember, O God: my life is but a breath, and my eyes will never again see happiness.
The eye that saw me will see me no more; your eyes will look for me, and I will not be there.
As the cloud dissolves and is gone, so the one who goes down to the realm of the dead does not come back up;
he returns no more to his house, and the place where he lived knows him no longer.
So I will not hold back my mouth: I will speak in the anguish of my spirit, I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the Sea, or the Monster of the deep, that you set a guard over me?
If I say, "My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,"
then you terrify me with dreams, you frighten me with visions.
I would rather be strangled: better death than this wasted body!
I waste away; I will not live forever. Leave me be, for my days are but a breath.
What is man, that you make so much of him, that you fix your attention on him,
that you inspect him every morning and test him at every moment?
When will you turn your gaze from me? Will you not leave me long enough to swallow my spit?
If I have sinned, what have I done to you, O watcher of men? Why have you made me your target? Why have I become a burden to myself?
Why do you not pardon my offense, why do you not blot out my sin? For soon I will lie down in the dust; you will look for me, and I will be no more.

titres.titre: Bildad's reply: God does not pervert justice
The lesson of the ancients: the hope of the godless fades
God does not reject the blameless man

versets.t: Then Bildad of Shuah spoke and said:
How long will you go on talking like this? Your words are a stormy wind!
Would God pervert justice? Would the Almighty overturn what is right?
If your children sinned against him, he handed them over to the power of their guilt.
But as for you, if you turn to God, if you plead with the Almighty,
if you are pure and upright, then, without delay, he will watch over you and restore the home of your righteousness.
Your past will seem a small thing, so great will your future be.
Ask the past generations, then, and give heed to the experience of the fathers;
for we, born only yesterday, know nothing, and our days on earth are but a shadow.
Will they not instruct you and speak to you, and out of their hearts bring forth these sayings?
"Does the papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Does the reed flourish without water?
Still green, before it is cut, it withers faster than any grass.
Such is the fate of all who forget God: the hope of the godless fades away.
His confidence is but a slender thread, his assurance a spider's web.
He leans on his house: it does not hold. He clings to it: it does not stand.
There he is, full of sap in the sunshine, his branches spreading over his garden,
his roots entwined around the stone heap, gripping among the rocks.
But let him be torn from his place, and it disowns him: I have never seen you.
See, that is all the joy of his way! And from the same soil others will spring up after him."
No, God does not reject the blameless man, nor does he uphold the hand of the wicked.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more.

titres.titre: Job replies: how can a man be just before God?
The elusive God who cannot be summoned
If only there were an arbiter between us

versets.t: Then Job spoke and said:
Yes, I know well that it is so: how could a man be in the right against God?
If he chose to argue with him, of a thousand charges he could not answer one.
God is wise of heart and mighty in strength: who has defied him and come away unharmed?
He moves the mountains without their knowing it, he overturns them in his anger.
He shakes the earth from its foundations, and its pillars tremble.
He commands the sun, and the sun does not rise; he sets a seal upon the stars.
He alone spreads out the heavens, he treads upon the waves of the sea.
He made the Great Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the southern sky.
He does great things, beyond fathoming, wonders past counting.
See, he passes close by me, and I do not see him; he glides by, and I do not perceive him.
If he snatches away a prey, who will stop him? Who will dare say to him, "What are you doing?"
God does not hold back his anger; beneath him the allies of Rahab already bowed low.
And I, would I presume to answer him, to choose my words to argue with him?
Even in the right, I would not answer; I could only implore the mercy of my judge.
And if I called and he answered me, I would not believe that he had listened to my voice,
he who crushes me in the storm and multiplies my wounds without cause,
who does not let me catch my breath and fills me with bitterness.
Is it a matter of strength? He is the stronger. Is it a matter of justice? "Who then will summon me?"
Were I in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; were I blameless, it would declare me guilty.
Blameless I am! But I no longer care about myself, I despise my life.
It all comes to the same thing; that is why I say it: he destroys the blameless man and the wicked alike.
When a sudden scourge spreads death, he mocks the despair of the innocent.
The earth is handed over to the power of the wicked, and he veils the faces of its judges. If it is not he, then who is it?
My days have run faster than a runner; they have fled without seeing happiness.
They have slipped by like boats of reeds, like the eagle swooping on its prey.
If I say, "I will forget my complaint, put off my gloomy face and be glad,"
dread seizes me again before all my sufferings, for I know you will not hold me innocent.
Since I will be guilty no matter what, why should I wear myself out in vain?
Though I washed myself in snow and cleansed my hands with lye,
you would plunge me into the pit, and my own clothes would loathe me.
For he is not a man like me, whom I could answer, that we might come to trial together.
There is no arbiter between us who could lay his hand on us both.
Let him take his rod away from me, let his terror cease to frighten me:
then I would speak without fear of him. But as I am, I cannot.

titres.titre: Job pleads: why did you form me?
Your hands shaped me, and would you destroy me?
Leave me a moment before the darkness

versets.t: I am sick of life! I will give free rein to my complaint, I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.
I will say to God: Do not condemn me! Let me know why you contend with me.
Do you find it good to oppress, to spurn the work of your hands, and to favor the designs of the wicked?
Do you have eyes of flesh? Do you see as men see?
Are your days like the days of a mortal, your years like those of a man,
that you should search out my fault and probe after my sin,
when you know that I am not guilty, and that no one can wrench me from your hand?
Your hands formed me and shaped me whole, and would you destroy me?
Remember that you molded me like clay, and would you return me to the dust?
Did you not pour me out like milk, then curdle me like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh, you wove me together with bones and sinews;
you gave me life and favor, and your providence watched over my breath.
But this is what you were hiding in your heart; I know well what you were plotting:
to watch me if I sinned, and not to absolve me of my fault.
Am I guilty, woe to me! Am I innocent, I dare not lift my head, sated with shame, drenched in my misery.
And if I raise it, you hunt me like a lion, you strike me again with your astounding blows;
you bring up fresh witnesses against me, you kindle your fury, and new troops assail me.
Why, then, did you draw me from the womb? I would have died, and no eye would have seen me.
I would be as though I had never been, carried from my mother's womb to the grave.
Are my days not so few? Let him leave me, then, let him turn away from me, that I may breathe a moment,
before I go, never to return, to the land of darkness and the shadow of death,
a land of gloom and chaos, where the shadow of death serves for light, and even the brightness is darkness.

titres.titre: Zophar's reply: the unfathomable depths of God
Return to God, and peace will return

versets.t: Then Zophar of Naamah spoke and said:
Will this flood of words go unanswered? Is it enough to talk much to be in the right?
Will your chatter reduce men to silence? Will you mock without anyone confounding you?
You have said, "My teaching is pure, and I am blameless in your eyes."
Ah, if only God would speak, if he would open his lips to answer you!
He would unveil to you the secrets of wisdom, for his designs go beyond our understanding; and you would know that God overlooks part of your guilt.
Do you claim to fathom the depths of God, to reach the limit of the Almighty?
It is higher than the heavens: what will you do? Deeper than the realm of the dead: what will you know of it?
Its measure is longer than the earth, wider than the sea.
If he comes to seize a man and summon him to trial, who will stop him?
For he sees through liars, he beholds evil and takes note of it.
But will the dull-witted man come to his senses when the wild donkey is born tame?
As for you, if you set your heart right and stretch out your hands to God,
if you put away the evil in your hand and banish injustice from your tent,
then you will lift up a face unstained, you will stand firm and unafraid.
You will forget your troubles, you will remember them like water that has flowed away.
Your life will rise brighter than noon, and the darkness itself will become like the dawn.
You will live in confidence, for there is hope; you will look about you and lie down in peace.
You will lie down with no one to trouble you, and many will seek your favor.
But the eyes of the wicked will fail; every refuge will be lost to them, and their only hope will be to breathe their last.

titres.titre: Job replies: I too have understanding
All creation knows the hand of God
God undoes the wise and the mighty

versets.t: Then Job spoke and said:
Truly, you are a whole people all by yourselves, and wisdom will die with you!
But I have understanding as much as you, I am in no way inferior to you: who does not know the things you are saying?
I have become the laughingstock of my friends, I who called on God and to whom he answered! The just, the innocent, is mocked!
"Contempt for misfortune!" thinks the man at ease; a further kick for the one who staggers.
Yet peace reigns in the tents of raiders, and security among those who provoke God and rely only on their own arm.
Ask the beasts, then, and they will instruct you; the birds of the sky, and they will tell you;
speak to the earth, and it will teach you; the fish of the sea will recount it to you.
Who among all these beings does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all this?
In his hand is the life of every living thing, the breath of every human being.
Does not the ear weigh words, as the palate tastes food?
Wisdom is with the aged, they say, and understanding comes with length of years.
But it is in God that wisdom and power reside; his are counsel and understanding.
What he tears down, no one rebuilds; the man he shuts in, no one sets free.
If he holds back the waters, everything dries up; if he lets them loose, they ravage the earth.
His are strength and clear sight; his are the deceived and the deceiver.
He leads counselors away stripped, and strikes judges with madness.
He undoes the belt of kings and ties a rope around their waists.
He leads priests away barefoot and overturns the powers long established.
He takes speech from those sure of their eloquence and removes discernment from the elders.
He pours contempt on nobles and loosens the belt of the strong.
He uncovers the secrets hidden in the darkness and brings to light the shadow of death.
He raises up nations, then destroys them; he spreads them out, then scatters them.
He takes away the reason of the chiefs of peoples and makes them wander in a trackless chaos;
they grope in the dark without light, he makes them stagger like drunkards.

titres.titre: Job would plead with God, not with you
Though he slay me, I will defend my cause

versets.t: All this my eye has seen, my ear has heard and understood.
What you know, I know too; I am in no way inferior to you.
But as for me, it is to the Almighty that I want to speak, it is with God that I long to plead.
For you are only plasterers of lies, all of you physicians of no worth.
Ah, if only you would keep silent: that would be your wisdom!
Listen, then, to my defense, give heed to the pleading of my lips.
Is it for God that you will speak lies? For him that you will utter deceit?
Will you take his side out of favor, and make yourselves God's advocates?
Would it go well for you if he examined you? Will you deceive him as one deceives a man?
No, he would sternly rebuke you, if in secret you showed partiality.
Does his majesty not terrify you? Does his terror not fall upon you?
Your maxims are sentences of ash, your defenses are defenses of clay.
Be silent, let me speak, and let come upon me what may!
Yes, I take my flesh in my teeth, I hold my life in my hand.
Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will defend my conduct before him.
And this very thing will be my salvation: a godless man would not dare appear before him.
Listen, listen to my words, let my declarations enter your ears.
See, I have prepared my case, I know that I will be vindicated.
Who, then, will bring a charge against me? Then I would fall silent and die.
Only spare me two things, O God, and I will no longer hide from your presence:
withdraw your hand that weighs on me, and let your terror cease to frighten me.
Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you will answer me.
How many faults and sins have I committed? Make known to me my offense and my sin.
Why do you hide your face and treat me as an enemy?
Would you frighten a leaf driven by the wind, chase a dry wisp of straw?
For you write bitter sentences against me, you make me pay for the faults of my youth;
you put my feet in shackles, you watch all my ways, you trace a boundary at the soles of my feet.
And a man wastes away like rotten wood, like a garment eaten by moths.

titres.titre: The tree sprouts again, but man?
If only you would hide me until you remembered me

versets.t: Man, born of woman, lives but a few days, and he is sated with troubles.
Like a flower, he opens, then fades; he flees like a shadow, without stopping.
And it is on such a being that you keep your eyes open, it is he whom you drag to trial before you!
Who can bring the pure out of the impure? No one.
Since the days of man are numbered, since the number of his months depends on you, since you have fixed a limit he will not pass,
turn your gaze from him and leave him in peace, until he savors, like a hired worker, the end of his day.
For a tree, there is still hope: cut down, it can turn green again, and its shoots will not fail.
Though its root grows old in the ground, though its stump dies in the dust,
at the scent of water it buds and puts out branches like a young plant.
But a man dies, and there he lies powerless; he breathes his last, and where is he?
Water goes from the sea, the river runs dry and is parched:
so a man lies down and rises no more. As long as the heavens last, he will not awake, nor be roused from his sleep.
Ah, if only you would hide me in the realm of the dead, keep me safe there until your anger has passed, set me a limit and then remember me!
If a man dies, will he live again? Then, all the time of my drudgery, I would wait for my relief to come.
You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands.
But now you count my steps, you watch endlessly for my fault;
my rebellion is sealed up in a bag, and you plaster over my fault.
The mountain in the end crumbles, the rock leaves its place,
water in the end wears away the stones, and its flooding sweeps off the soil's dust: so you ruin the hope of man.
You overpower him forever, and he goes; you disfigure his face and drive him away.
Are his children honored, he knows nothing of it; are they brought low, he does not notice.
He feels only the pain of his own flesh, he mourns only for himself.

titres.titre: Eliphaz's second speech: your mouth condemns you
No mortal is pure before God

versets.t: Then Eliphaz of Teman spoke and said:
Does a wise man answer with hollow knowledge and fill his belly with wind?
Does he defend himself with useless talk, with speeches that serve no purpose?
You go so far as to ruin the fear of God and to discourage prayer before him.
It is your guilt that prompts your mouth, and you take up the language of the crafty.
It is not I, it is your own mouth that condemns you; your lips testify against you.
Were you the firstborn of mankind? Were you brought forth before the hills?
Have you listened in the council of God? Have you seized wisdom for yourself alone?
What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that escapes us?
Among us are gray heads, old men more laden with years than your father.
Are the consolations of God too little for you, and the word spoken to you so gently?
Where is your heart carrying you? What is the meaning of this rolling of your eyes,
that you turn your fury against God and let such words escape you?
What is man, that he should be pure, the son of woman, that he should be just?
See, God does not even trust his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his eyes;
how much less man, that corrupt and vile being, who drinks injustice like water!
I will instruct you; listen to me. What I have seen, I will recount to you,
what the wise hand down, hiding nothing, having received it from their fathers,
to whom alone the land was given, with no stranger passing through their midst.
All his days the wicked man is gnawed by anguish; the count of his years is reserved for the tyrant.
Sounds of terror fill his ears; in the midst of peace the raider falls upon him.
He no longer hopes to escape the darkness, he knows he is marked for the sword.
He wanders in search of his bread: where to find it? He knows that the day of darkness is at hand, close by.
Distress and anguish terrify him, they assail him like a king ready to attack.
For he raised his hand against God, he defied the Almighty,
he charged at him, head down, behind the thickness of his shields.
His face was bloated with fat, his loins heavy with flesh;
he had settled in ruined cities, in deserted houses, doomed to be nothing but rubble.
He will grow rich no more, his fortune will not hold, his goods will spread no further over the land.
He will not escape the darkness; a flame will wither his shoots, and the breath of God will sweep him away.
Let him not trust in emptiness: he is deceived, for emptiness will be his wage.
It will be fulfilled before its time, and his branch will not turn green.
Like a vine, he will lose his grapes while still unripe; like the olive tree, he will drop his blossom.
Yes, the house of the godless is barren, and fire devours the tents of those who take bribes.
They conceive trouble and give birth to crime, their womb ripens nothing but deceit.

titres.titre: God has handed me over and broken me

versets.t: Then Job spoke and said:
Speeches like these I have heard many! You are all comforters who crush.
Will these empty words never end? What still drives you to keep answering?
I too could speak like you, if you were in my place; I would string fine phrases against you, I would shake my head over you.
But I would give you comfort with my mouth, and the trembling of my lips would ease your pain.
If I speak, my pain does not yield; if I keep silent, is it any better?
Now, God has worn me out. You have laid waste my whole house;
you have seized me, and that is a witness against me; my gauntness rises up and accuses me to my face.
His anger tears me and rages on, he gnashes his teeth against me; my adversary fixes his glare on me.
They open their gaping mouths against me, they slap me in contempt, all together they band against me.
God has handed me over to the unjust, he has thrown me into the power of the wicked.
I was at peace, and he shattered me; he seized me by the neck and broke me to pieces, he made me his target.
His arrows surround me; without pity he pierces my kidneys and spills my gall on the ground.
He breaches me, breach upon breach, he charges at me like a warrior.
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin, I have thrust my brow into the dust.
My face is inflamed with weeping, and over my eyelids lies the shadow of death,
though there is no violence in my hands, and though my prayer is pure.
O earth, do not cover my blood, and let my cry find no place to rest!
Even now, though, I have my witness in heaven, my defender is on high.
My friends mock me? It is toward God that my eyes weep:
