It is the Lord who directs a man's steps; how then can a man understand his own road?
It is a snare to dedicate an offering rashly and to reflect only after making the vow.
A wise king scatters the wicked and drives the wheel over them.
The breath of man is a lamp of the Lord, searching the depths of his being.
Kindness and faithfulness guard the king, and by kindness he makes his throne secure.
Strength is the glory of the young, and grey hair the honour of the old.
Wounds and bruises purge away evil, and blows reach the depths of one's being.
The king's heart is a stream in the hand of the Lord: he turns it wherever he pleases.
All a man's ways seem right in his own eyes, but it is the Lord who weighs hearts.
To practise righteousness and justice pleases the Lord more than sacrifice.
Haughty eyes and a proud heart, that lamp of the wicked, are nothing but sin.
The plans of the diligent lead only to abundance, but whoever is hasty rushes into want.
Treasures gained by a lying tongue are a fleeting breath, for men who seek death.
The violence of the wicked sweeps them away, because they refuse to practise justice.
The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.
Better to live in a corner of the roof than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.
The wicked man desires only evil; even his neighbour finds no mercy in his eyes.
When the mocker is punished, the simple becomes wise; when the wise is instructed, he gains knowledge.
The Righteous One watches the house of the wicked and casts the wicked down into ruin.
Whoever shuts his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard.
A gift given in secret soothes anger, a present slipped under the cloak calms fury.
To practise justice is a joy for the righteous, but a terror for evildoers.
The man who strays from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the shades.
Whoever loves pleasure will know poverty; whoever loves wine and perfumed oil will not grow rich.
The wicked serves as ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright.
Better to live in the desert than with a quarrelsome and fretful wife.
Precious treasures and fine oil are in the house of the wise, but a fool devours them.
Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness and glory.
The wise man scales the city of warriors and tears down the rampart in which it trusted.
Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps himself from distress.
The proud man, swollen with self-importance, is called a mocker; he acts with excessive arrogance.
The sluggard's cravings kill him, for his hands refuse to work.
All day long he does nothing but crave, but the righteous gives without holding back.
The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, all the more when offered with criminal intent.
A false witness will perish, but the man who listens well may speak forever.
The wicked man puts on a bold front, but the upright makes his conduct sure.
There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can stand against the Lord.
The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the Lord.
A good name is worth more than great riches, and esteem more than silver and gold.
The rich and the poor meet together: it is the Lord who made them both.
A prudent man sees danger coming and takes shelter, but the simple pass on and pay for it.
The fruit of humility and the fear of the Lord is riches, glory and life.
Thorns and snares line the way of the perverse; whoever would guard his life keeps far from them.
Bring up a child in the way he should go, and even when old he will not depart from it.
The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower becomes the slave of the lender.
Whoever sows injustice reaps disaster, and the rod of his fury will be broken.
A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
Drive out the mocker, and the quarrel will depart; disputes and insults will cease.
Whoever loves purity of heart and has grace on his lips will have the king for a friend.
The eyes of the Lord watch over knowledge, but he overturns the words of the traitor.
The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I would be killed in the streets!"
The mouth of adulterous women is a deep pit; the one with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it.
Folly is bound up in the heart of a child; the rod of correction will drive it far from him.
Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself, or giving to the rich: both lead to poverty.
Turn your ear and listen to the sayings of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge;
it will be pleasant to keep them within you, to have them all ready on your lips.
So that your trust may rest in the Lord, it is you I want to teach today.
Have I not already written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge,
to teach you what is true and reliable, so that you may give a right answer to the one who sends you?
Do not rob the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the gate,
for the Lord will take up their cause and rob of life those who have robbed them.
Do not associate with a hot-tempered man, and do not go with one given to anger,
lest you learn his ways and set a snare for your own life.
Do not be one of those who strike hands in pledge, who put up security for debts:
if you have nothing to pay, why should your very bed be taken from under you?
Do not move the ancient boundary stone that your fathers set up.
Do you see a man skilled at his work? He will serve kings; he will not remain in the service of obscure men.
When you sit down to dine with a ruler, note well who is before you,
and put a knife to your throat if you have a big appetite.
Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.
Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to hold back.
No sooner have you set your eyes on wealth than it is gone: it sprouts wings and, like an eagle, flies off toward the sky.
Do not eat the bread of a grudging man, and do not crave his fine dishes,
for he is like someone doing sums in his mind. "Eat and drink," he says to you, but his heart is not with you.
The morsel you have swallowed you will vomit up, and you will have wasted your pleasant words.
Do not speak in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words.
Do not move the ancient boundary stone, and do not encroach on the fields of orphans,
for their defender is strong: he will plead their cause against you.
Open your heart to correction and your ears to words of knowledge.
Do not withhold correction from a child: if you strike him with the rod, he will not die;
by striking him with the rod, you save his life from the realm of the dead.
My son, if your heart becomes wise, my own heart too will rejoice;
my whole being will exult when your lips speak what is right.
Do not let your heart envy sinners, but stay all day long in the fear of the Lord;
for there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
Listen, my son, and become wise, and set your heart on the right road.
Do not join the drinkers of wine, the gluttons who gorge on meat,
for the drunkard and the glutton grow poor, and drowsiness clothes a man in rags.
Listen to your father, who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.
Buy the truth and do not sell it, nor wisdom, correction and understanding.
The father of the righteous rejoices greatly; whoever fathers a wise son will delight in him.
May your father and mother rejoice, may the woman who bore you be glad!
My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes delight in my ways;
for a prostitute is a deep pit, and the wayward woman a narrow well:
like a bandit she lies in wait and multiplies the faithless among men.
Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has quarrels, complaints, needless wounds, bloodshot eyes?
Those who linger over wine, who go to sample the spiced wine.
Do not gaze at the wine: how red it is, how it sparkles in the cup, how smoothly it goes down!
In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like a viper.
Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart will utter incoherent words.
You will be like a man lying out at sea, like one asleep at the top of a mast:
"They struck me, but I felt no pain! They beat me, but I felt nothing! When will I wake up? I want more!"
Do not envy wicked men, and do not seek their company,
for their hearts brood only on violence, and their lips speak only of trouble.
By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is made firm;
by knowledge its rooms are filled with all things precious and pleasant.
A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge increases his power;
for it is with wise counsel that you will wage war, and victory lies in many advisers.
For a fool, wisdom is too high; at the city gate he does not open his mouth.
Whoever plans only to do evil is called a master of intrigue.
The schemes of folly are sin, and the mocker is detestable to all.
If you let yourself grow faint on the day of trouble, your strength is very small.
Rescue those being dragged to death, hold back those staggering toward slaughter!
Will you say, "But we did not know"? Does not the one who weighs hearts see it? Does not the one who watches over your life know it? He will repay each according to his deeds.
My son, eat honey, for it is good; the honeycomb is sweet to your palate.
Know that wisdom is likewise for your soul: if you find it, there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
Do not lie in wait, you wicked man, around the home of the righteous, and do not ravage the place where he rests,
for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble into ruin.
If your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and if you see him stumble, do not let your heart exult,
lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn his anger away from him.
Do not be angered by the wicked, and do not envy the perverse,
for the wicked has no future, and the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out.
My son, fear the Lord and the king, and do not join the rebels,
for their ruin will rise up suddenly, and who knows what disaster the two of them can send?
These also are sayings of the wise. To show partiality in judgment is not good.
Whoever says to the guilty, "You are innocent," the peoples will curse him, the nations will loathe him;
but those who condemn him will fare well, and a rich blessing will come upon them.
To give an honest answer is like a kiss on the lips.
Put your outdoor work in order, get your fields ready, then build your house.
Do not testify against your neighbour without cause: would you deceive with your lips?
Do not say, "I will do to him as he did to me, I will repay him according to his deeds."
I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man without judgment:
thorns had grown up everywhere, weeds covered the ground, and the stone wall was broken down.
I looked and reflected; I saw and drew the lesson:
"A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the arms on the bed,"
and poverty will come upon you like a prowler, and want like an armed man.

titres.titre: Further proverbs of Solomon (the Hezekiah collection)

versets.t: These also are proverbs of Solomon, collected by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah.
It is the glory of God to conceal things, and the glory of kings to search them out.
The height of the heavens, the depth of the earth, and the heart of kings are unsearchable.
Remove the dross from silver, and a vessel comes forth for the smith;
remove the wicked from before the king, and his throne will be made secure in righteousness.
Do not put yourself forward before the king, and do not take the place of the great,
for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be brought low before a prince. What your eyes have seen,
do not rush into court over it, for what will you do in the end if your neighbour puts you to shame?
Argue your case with your neighbour, but do not betray another's secret,
lest whoever hears it shame you, and the disgrace never leave you.
Like apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken at the right time.
Like a ring of gold, a jewel of fine gold, is a wise rebuke to a listening ear.
Like the coolness of snow at harvest time is a faithful messenger to those who send him: he refreshes the heart of his master.
Clouds and wind but no rain: such is the one who boasts of gifts he does not give.
With patience a judge is won over, and a gentle tongue can break bones.
Have you found honey? Eat only what you need, lest you be gorged with it and vomit it up.
Rarely set foot in your neighbour's house, lest he grow tired of you and come to hate you.
Like a club, a sword, a sharp arrow is the man who gives false testimony against his neighbour.
Like a bad tooth or a slipping foot is reliance on a traitor in the day of trouble.
Like taking off a cloak on a cold day, or pouring vinegar on a wound, is one who sings songs to a grieving heart.
If your enemy is hungry, give him food; if he is thirsty, give him drink:
in doing so you heap coals on his head, and the Lord will reward you.
The north wind brings forth rain, and a tongue that slanders in secret, an angry face.
Better to live in a corner of the roof than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.
Like cold water to a parched throat is good news from a distant land.
Like a trampled spring or a polluted fountain is the righteous who gives way before the wicked.
Eating too much honey is not good; likewise, searching out the divine glory crushes whoever attempts it.
Like a city breached and left without walls is a man who cannot control himself.
Like snow in summer or rain at harvest, honour is not fitting for a fool.
Like a fleeing sparrow or a darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not reach its mark.
A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the backs of fools.
Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself;
answer a fool according to his folly, or he will think himself wise.
Cutting off one's own feet and drinking down bitterness: so does whoever sends a message by a fool.
Like the useless dangling legs of a lame man is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
Like tying a stone in a sling is giving honour to a fool.
Like a thorn that pierces the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a fool or any passerby.
As a dog returns to its vomit, a fool repeats his folly.
Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
The sluggard says, "There is a wild beast on the road, a lion in the streets!"
As a door turns on its hinges, so the sluggard on his bed.
The sluggard plunges his hand into the dish and can hardly bring it back to his mouth.
The sluggard thinks himself wiser than seven men who give sound counsel.
Like grabbing a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own.
Like a madman shooting firebrands, arrows and death,
is the man who deceives his neighbour and says, "I was only joking!"
For lack of wood the fire goes out; without a gossip the quarrel dies down.
Charcoal makes embers and wood makes fire; a quarrelsome man stirs up strife.
The words of a talebearer are choice morsels that go down to the depths of the belly.
Like a glaze of silver on an earthen pot are fervent lips over an evil heart.
Whoever hates disguises it with his words, but within he nurses deceit.
When he speaks graciously, do not trust him, for there are seven abominations in his heart.
Though he masks his hatred with cunning, his wickedness will be exposed before the assembly.
Whoever digs a pit falls into it, and the stone rolls back on the one who pushes it.
A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth brings ruin.
Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.
Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
A stone is heavy and sand a burden, but a fool's provocation weighs more than both.
Fury is cruel and anger overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?
Better an open rebuke than a friendship that stays silent.
The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
A full stomach tramples on honey, but to the hungry every bitter thing is sweet.
Like a bird that flees its nest is a man who wanders far from home.
Oil and incense gladden the heart, and the sweetness of a friend is better than self-serving counsel.
Do not forsake your friend or your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your trouble: better a neighbour nearby than a brother far off.
Become wise, my son, and gladden my heart, so that I can answer whoever insults me.
A prudent man sees danger coming and takes shelter; the simple pass on and pay for it.
Take the garment of one who has pledged himself for a stranger; hold it as security for the foreign woman.
Whoever loudly blesses his neighbour early in the morning, it will be counted as a curse.
A leaking roof on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike;
to restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's hand.
Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.
Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever looks after his master will be honoured.
As water reflects the face, so a man's heart reflects the man.
The realm of the dead and the abyss are never satisfied, and the eyes of man are never satisfied.
The crucible tests silver and the furnace gold, and a man is judged by the praise he receives.
Though you pound a fool in a mortar, among the grain, with a pestle, his folly will not leave him.
Know well the state of your flocks, take care of your herds,
for riches do not last forever, nor a crown from age to age.
When the grass has grown back, when the greenery appears, when the hay of the mountains is gathered in,
the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats the price of a field;
the goats' milk will be enough for your food, for your household, and for the keep of your maidservants.
The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion.
A rebellious land multiplies its rulers, but a man of understanding and knowledge maintains order for a long time.
A poor man who crushes the weak is like a driving rain that ruins the harvest.
Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep it resist them.
Evil men understand nothing of justice, but those who seek the Lord understand everything.
Better a poor man who walks in integrity than one whose ways are crooked, though he be rich.
Whoever keeps the law is a discerning son, but a companion of profligates shames his father.
Whoever increases his wealth by interest and usury gathers it for one who will be kind to the poor.
Whoever turns his ear away from listening to the law, even his prayer is detestable.
Whoever leads the upright astray onto an evil path will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will receive good things as their portion.
The rich man thinks himself wise, but a discerning poor man sees through him.
When the righteous triumph, there is great celebration; when the wicked rise, everyone hides.
Whoever conceals his faults will not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.
Blessed is the man who always fears the Lord! But whoever hardens his heart will fall into misfortune.
Like a roaring lion or a starving bear is a wicked man ruling over a defenceless people.
A prince without understanding multiplies abuses, but whoever hates dishonest gain will live long.
A man burdened with another's blood flees to the grave: let no one hold him back.
Whoever walks in integrity will be saved, but whoever follows crooked ways will fall all at once.
Whoever works his land will have bread to spare, but whoever chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.
A faithful man will be showered with blessings, but whoever rushes to get rich will not go unpunished.
It is not good to show favouritism, yet for a piece of bread a man will do wrong.
A grudging man rushes after wealth, not seeing that poverty is about to overtake him.
Whoever rebukes another will in the end win more favour than the flatterer.
Whoever robs his father and mother and says, "It is no sin," is the companion of a bandit.
A greedy man kindles quarrels, but whoever trusts in the Lord will prosper.
Whoever trusts his own judgment is a fool, but whoever walks in wisdom will be saved.
Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing, but whoever shuts his eyes will be heaped with curses.
When the wicked rise, everyone hides; when they perish, the righteous multiply.
A man who stiffens his neck after many rebukes will be broken suddenly, beyond remedy.
When the righteous multiply, the people rejoice; when the wicked govern, the people groan.
Whoever loves wisdom gladdens his father, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
By justice a king makes his land firm, but a man greedy for taxes ruins it.
Whoever flatters his neighbour spreads a net for his feet.
An evil man is caught in the snare of his own sin, but the righteous sings and rejoices.
The righteous cares about the cause of the poor, but the wicked understands nothing of it.
Mockers set a city in turmoil, but the wise turn away anger.
When a wise man goes to court with a fool, whether the fool rages or jokes, there is no rest.
Bloodthirsty men hate a man of integrity, but the upright watch over his life.
A fool gives full vent to his anger, but the wise holds it back and calms it.
When a ruler listens to lies, all his officials become wicked.
The poor man and the oppressor meet together: it is the Lord who gives light to the eyes of both.
A king who judges the weak with fairness will see his throne made secure forever.
The rod and correction give wisdom, but a child left to himself shames his mother.
When the wicked multiply, crime abounds, but the righteous will witness their downfall.
Correct your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.
Without vision the people run wild; blessed is the one who keeps the law!
A servant is not corrected by words alone: he understands, but does not obey.
Do you see a man too quick to speak? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him acting like a son.
A hot-tempered man kindles quarrels, and one given to anger multiplies wrongdoing.
Pride brings a man low, but the humble of heart receives glory.
Whoever shares with a thief hates himself: he hears the curse but says nothing.
The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is safe.
Many seek the favour of a ruler, but justice for each comes from the Lord.
An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and the upright is detestable to the wicked.
The words of Agur son of Jakeh, of Massa. This man declares: I am worn out, O God, I am worn out, O God, and I am spent.
Truly, I am the most stupid of men; I do not have human understanding;
I have not learned wisdom, and I do not know the knowledge of the Most Holy One.

Who has gone up to heaven and come down again? Who has gathered the wind in his hands? Who has wrapped up the waters in his cloak? Who has fixed all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know?
Every word of God is tested in the fire: he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.
Add nothing to his words, lest he rebuke you and prove you a liar.
Two things I ask of you; do not refuse me before I die:
keep falsehood and lies far from me; give me neither poverty nor riches, grant me only the bread I need,
lest, being full, I disown you and say, "Who is the Lord?", or lest, in poverty, I steal and dishonour the name of my God.
Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you and you bear the guilt of it.
There are those who curse their father and do not bless their mother;
those who think themselves pure though not washed of their filth;
those with haughty eyes and disdainful eyelids;
those whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, to devour the lowly of the land and the poor among men.
The leech has two daughters: "Give! Give!" Three things are never satisfied, four never say, "Enough!":
the realm of the dead, the barren womb, land that water never satisfies, and fire that never says, "Enough!"
The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience owed to a mother, the ravens of the wadi will pluck it out and the young eagles will devour it.
There are three things too wonderful for me, and even four that I do not understand:
the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a young woman.
This is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, "I have done nothing wrong."
Under three things the earth trembles, and there is a fourth it cannot bear:
a slave who becomes king, a fool gorged with food,
an unloved woman who finally finds a husband, and a maidservant who supplants her mistress.
There are four things on earth that are small, yet full of wisdom:
the ants, a people without strength, who store up their food in summer;
the rock badgers, a people without power, who make their homes in the crags;
the locusts, who have no king, yet go out in close ranks;
the lizard, which you can catch in your hand, yet lives in the palaces of kings.
There are three things stately in their stride, and even four graceful in their walk:
the lion, bravest of animals, who retreats before nothing;
the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and the king at the head of his army.
If you have been fool enough to boast, or if you have merely thought of it, put your hand over your mouth;
for churning milk produces butter, twisting the nose draws blood, and stirring up anger produces strife.
The words of Lemuel, king of Massa, which his mother taught him.
What, my son? What, son of my womb? What, son of my vows?
Do not give your strength to women, nor your life to those who ruin kings.
It is not for kings, Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, nor for princes to crave strong drink,
lest by drinking they forget the law and pervert the rights of all the afflicted.
Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those whose soul is bitter:
let him drink and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.
Open your mouth for the one who cannot speak, for the cause of all the forsaken;
open your mouth, judge with justice, and defend the rights of the poor and needy.
A woman of worth, who can find? She is worth far more than pearls.
Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he will lack no gain.
She does him good and never harm, all the days of her life.
She obtains wool and flax and works with eager hands.
Like the merchant ships, she brings her provisions from afar.
She rises while it is still night, gives food to her household and their tasks to her maidservants.
She considers a field and buys it; from the fruit of her labour she plants a vineyard.
She girds her waist with strength and makes her arms strong.
She knows that her trading goes well, and her lamp does not go out at night.
She lays her hand to the distaff, and her fingers hold the spindle.
She reaches out her hand to the afflicted and opens it to the needy.
She does not fear the snow for her household, for all her house is warmly clothed.
She makes her own coverings; her garments are of fine linen and purple.
Her husband is known at the city gates, when he sits among the elders of the land.
She weaves cloth and sells it, and supplies the merchant with sashes.
Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the days to come.
She opens her mouth with wisdom, and kindly teaching is on her tongue.
She watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.
Her sons rise up and call her blessed; her husband too praises her:
"Many women have shown their worth, but you surpass them all."
Charm is deceptive and beauty fleeting; the woman who fears the Lord is the one to be praised.
Give her the fruit of her labour, and let her works praise her at the city gates.

titres.titre: Prologue: a breath, a mere breath

versets.t: The words of Qoheleth, son of David, king in Jerusalem.
A breath, a mere breath, says Qoheleth, a breath, a mere breath: everything is a breath.
What profit does anyone gain from all the toil at which they labor under the sun?
One generation goes, another comes, but the earth remains forever.
The sun rises, the sun sets, then hurries back to the place where it rises again.
The wind blows toward the south, then turns toward the north; round and round it goes, ever returning on its circuit.
All the rivers run to the sea, yet the sea is never full; to the place where the rivers flow, there they flow again.
All things are wearisome, more than anyone can say; the eye is never satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done: there is nothing new under the sun.
If someone says of something, 'Look, this is new!', in truth it already existed in the ages that came before us.
No one remembers the days of old; and those still to come will not be remembered either by those who follow.
I, Qoheleth, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I set my heart to study and explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven. What a heavy task God has laid on humankind!
I looked at all that is done under the sun: and behold, all is breath and a chasing after the wind.
What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted.
I said to myself, 'I have gained greater wisdom than all who were before me over Jerusalem, and my heart has known wisdom and knowledge in abundance.'
I set my heart to know wisdom, and also madness and folly. And I came to see that this too is a chasing after the wind.
For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and whoever increases knowledge increases grief.

titres.titre: The test of pleasure and great works
The wise and the fool, one same fate
Leaving to others the fruit of one's labor

versets.t: I said to myself, 'Come now, I will test you with pleasure: enjoy what is good!' But behold, this too is a breath.
Of laughter I said, 'It is madness!'; and of pleasure, 'What does it accomplish?'
I resolved to give my body to wine, while still guiding my heart with wisdom, and to lay hold of folly, until I might see what is good for people to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
I undertook great works: I built myself houses and planted vineyards;
I made myself gardens and orchards, and planted in them fruit trees of every kind;
I dug myself pools of water to irrigate a grove of flourishing trees.
I bought male and female servants, and had others born in my house; I also owned herds and flocks, more than all who were before me in Jerusalem.
I amassed silver and gold, the treasures of kings and provinces; I acquired male and female singers, and what delights the hearts of men: women in abundance.
I became great, greater than all who were before me in Jerusalem; and still my wisdom remained with me.
Whatever my eyes desired, I did not refuse them; I withheld from my heart no joy. Indeed, my heart found joy in all my toil, and this was the reward of all my toil.
Then I turned to all that my hands had done, and to all the toil I had spent in doing it: and behold, all was breath and a chasing after the wind; there is no profit under the sun.
Then I turned to consider wisdom, as well as madness and folly. For what can the one who comes after the king do? Only what has already been done.
I saw that wisdom surpasses folly as much as light surpasses darkness.
The wise have their eyes open, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I understood that one same fate awaits them both.
So I said to myself, 'The fate of the fool will be mine as well. Why then have I been so wise?' And I said to myself that this too is a breath.
For the wise will not be remembered any more than the fool: in the days to come both will be alike forgotten. The wise die just like the fool!
So I hated life, because all that is done under the sun seemed evil to me: all is breath and a chasing after the wind.
I hated too all the toil at which I had labored under the sun, since I must leave its fruit to the one who comes after me.
And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will have mastery over all the work at which I labored with wisdom under the sun. This too is a breath.
So I gave my heart over to despair over all the toil at which I had labored under the sun.
Here is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge, and skill: and he must leave his portion to another who has not labored for it! This too is a breath, and a great evil.
What then does a man gain from all his toil and from the striving of his heart with which he wears himself out under the sun?
All his days are but pain, his tasks but sorrow; even at night his heart finds no rest. This too is a breath.
There is nothing better for a person than to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in their work. Yet I saw that this too comes from the hand of God;
for apart from him, who can eat or find enjoyment in anything?

To the one who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he gives the task of gathering and heaping up, only to leave it all to the one who pleases God. This too is breath and a chasing after the wind.
There is a moment for everything, and a time for every matter under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to uproot what is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to tear down, and a time to build;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to scatter stones, and a time to gather them; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to throw away;
a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to be silent, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
What profit does the worker gain from the toil at which he labors?
I have seen the task that God lays on humankind to keep them occupied.
God has made everything beautiful in its time; he has also set eternity in their hearts, yet without allowing anyone to grasp, from beginning to end, the work that God does.
I understood that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and find enjoyment during their life;
and that if anyone eats, drinks, and finds enjoyment in all their toil, this is a gift of God.
I understood that all God does endures forever: nothing can be added to it, nothing taken from it; and God acts so that people may fear him.
What is has already been, and what will be has already existed; and God brings back what has passed away.
I saw again, under the sun, that in the seat of judgment sits wickedness, and in the place of justice, injustice.
I said to myself, 'The just and the wicked, God will judge, for there is a time for every matter and every deed.'
I said to myself, concerning human beings, 'God wants to test them and show them that by themselves they are but beasts.'

For the fate of humans and the fate of beasts is one and the same fate: as one dies, so dies the other; the same breath of life is in them all. Humans have no advantage over beasts, for all is breath.
All go to one same place: all come from the dust, and all return to the dust.
Who knows whether the breath of humans rises upward, and whether the breath of beasts descends downward, to the earth?
So I saw that there is nothing better for a person than to find joy in what they do: this is their portion. For who will bring them to see what will come after them?

titres.titre: Listening, in the house of God

versets.t: I turned and saw all the oppression that is committed under the sun. Here are the tears of the oppressed, with no one to comfort them; power is on the side of their oppressors, with no one to comfort them.
So I counted the dead, already dead, more fortunate than the living, still alive;
and more fortunate than both, the one who has not yet come to be, who has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.
I saw that all labor and all success in work are but the rivalry of one against another. This too is breath and a chasing after the wind.
The fool folds his arms and ends up consuming himself.
Better one handful with rest than two handfuls gained through toil and a chasing after the wind.
I turned and saw another breath under the sun:

a man alone, with no one beside him, no son or brother, and yet his toil has no end, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches. 'For whom then am I toiling, depriving myself of all enjoyment?' This too is a breath, a sorry business.
Better two than one, for the two gain a good reward from their labor:
if one falls, the other lifts him up. But woe to the one who is alone: if he falls, he has no one to lift him up!
So too, if two lie down together, they keep warm; but the one who is alone, how can he keep warm?
And where one alone would be overpowered, two will stand their ground: a cord of three strands is not easily broken.
Better a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to heed a warning.
For this youth came out of prison to reign, even though he was born poor in the other's kingdom.
I saw all the living who move about under the sun rally behind the youth, the second, the one who takes the king's place.
All that crowd, all that people at its head, was without number; and yet those who come after will take no joy in him. This too is breath and a chasing after the wind.
Watch your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near and listen is better than the sacrifice offered by fools, who do not even know they are doing wrong.

titres.titre: Weighing one's words and vows before God
Receiving from God one's portion and joy

versets.t: Do not be quick to open your mouth, and let your heart not be hasty to utter a word before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth: so let your words be few.
For from too many concerns come dreams, and from too many words, the talk of a fool.
When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, for God takes no pleasure in fools: the vow you have made, fulfill it.
Better not to make a vow than to make one and not fulfill it.
Do not let your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger of God, 'It was a mistake.' Why should God be angry at your words and destroy the work of your hands?
Where dreams and words abound, breath abounds as well. As for you, fear God.
If you see in a province the poor oppressed, and justice and right violated, do not be astonished: for one high official is watched by a higher, and over them are higher still.
And in every respect, the advantage of a land is a king who watches over its cultivated fields.
Whoever loves money is never satisfied with money; whoever loves abundance gains nothing from it. This too is a breath.
When goods increase, those who consume them increase as well; and what profit has the owner, except to feast his eyes on them?
Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he has eaten little or much; but the abundance of the rich will not let him sleep.
There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: riches hoarded by their owner to his own harm.
These riches are lost in some bad venture; he has a son, and nothing is left in his hands.
As he came naked from his mother's womb, so he will return as he came, taking nothing from his toil that he can carry in his hand.
This too is a grievous evil: he departs exactly as he came. What profit does he gain from having toiled for the wind?
And on top of all this, his whole life he eats in darkness, weighed down with sorrow, suffering, and bitterness.

Here then is what I have found to be good: it is fitting for a person to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in all the toil at which they labor under the sun during the days of life God gives them, for this is their portion.
And if God gives someone riches, possessions, and the power to enjoy them, to take their portion and find joy in their toil, this is a gift of God.
For then such a person hardly dwells on the days of their life, because God fills their heart with joy.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavy on humankind:

a man to whom God has given riches, treasures, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires; but God does not let him enjoy them, for a stranger enjoys them instead. This is a breath, a grievous evil.

Though a man have a hundred children and live many years, however many they be, if his heart is not satisfied with good things and he has no burial, then I say: the stillborn child is more fortunate than he.
For that child comes for nothing, departs into darkness, and its name is covered with darkness;
it has never even seen the sun or known anything; it has more rest than the other.
And even if he lived two thousand years without tasting happiness, do not all go to one same place?
All human toil is for the mouth, and yet the appetite is never filled.
What advantage has the wise over the fool? And what does the poor gain from knowing how to conduct themselves before the living?
Better what the eyes see than the wandering of desire. This too is breath and a chasing after the wind.
Whatever exists has already been named; it is known what man is, and he cannot contend with one stronger than himself.
The more words there are, the greater the breath: what profit is there for anyone?
For who knows what is good for a person in life, throughout the few days of their fleeting life, which they pass like a shadow? And who can tell anyone what will come after them under the sun?

titres.titre: Wisdom in the face of death and suffering
Receiving good and ill from God
Neither too righteous, nor too wicked
The strength of wisdom, the weakness of all

versets.t: A good name is better than precious perfume, and the day of death better than the day of birth.
Better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, for there the end of everyone is seen, and the living take it to heart.
Better sorrow than laughter, for a grave face makes the heart better.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools in the house of mirth.
Better to heed the rebuke of the wise than to listen to the song of fools.
For the laughter of fools is like the crackling of thorns under the pot: this too is a breath.
For oppression drives the wise to folly, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
Better the end of a matter than its beginning; better a patient spirit than a proud one.
Do not be too quickly seized by anger, for anger lodges in the heart of fools.
Do not say, 'How is it that the past was better than today?' For it is not wisdom that prompts you to ask this.
Wisdom is as good as an inheritance, and profits those who see the sun.
For wisdom offers protection as money does; but the advantage of knowledge is this: wisdom gives life to the one who possesses it.
Consider the work of God: who can straighten what he has bent?
In the day of prosperity, be happy; in the day of adversity, reflect: God has made the one as well as the other, so that no one can discover anything of their future.
In my fleeting life I have seen it all: a righteous man who perishes despite his righteousness, a wicked man who prolongs his days despite his wickedness.
Do not be righteous to excess, nor make yourself wise beyond measure: why should you destroy yourself?
Do not be wicked to excess, and do not be a fool: why die before your time?
It is good to hold to the one without letting go of the other: whoever fears God will avoid both extremes.
Wisdom makes the wise stronger than ten rulers in a city.
Yet there is no one on earth so righteous as to do good and never sin.
Do not pay attention either to everything that is said, lest you hear your servant curse you;
for your heart knows well that you too have often cursed others.
All this I tested by wisdom. I said, 'I want to become wise!' But wisdom stayed far from me.
What exists is far off, deep, so very deep: who can reach it?
I applied my whole heart to know, to explore, to seek wisdom and the meaning of things, and to recognize that wickedness is folly, and stupidity is madness.
And I found something more bitter than death: the woman who is nothing but a snare, whose heart is a net and whose arms are chains. Whoever pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is caught by her.
See what I have found, says Qoheleth, weighing things one by one to grasp their meaning.
What my heart long sought without finding: one man among a thousand I have found; but a woman, among them all, I have not found.
See only what I have found: God made humankind upright, but people go seeking many devious ways.

titres.titre: The wise before the king's authority
The riddle of the wicked who prosper

versets.t: Who is like the wise? Who knows, as they do, how to explain things? Wisdom lights up a person's face and softens its harshness.
I say to you: keep the king's command, because of the oath sworn before God.
Do not be hasty to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he does whatever he pleases.
For the word of the king is sovereign, and who would dare say to him, 'What are you doing?'
Whoever keeps the commandment will know no harm, and the heart of the wise knows there is a time and a judgment.
For there is a time and a judgment for every matter; but the misery of humankind weighs heavy upon them,
since they do not know what is to come: who can tell them how it will happen?
No one has power over the breath so as to hold it back; no one has power over the day of their death. No one is released from that struggle, and wickedness will not save those who practice it.
All this I saw as I applied my heart to all that is done under the sun, in a time when one person lords it over another to their harm.
And then I saw the wicked brought to burial and laid to rest; but those who had done right had to leave the holy place and were forgotten in the city. This too is a breath.
Because the sentence against evil deeds is not carried out at once, the hearts of people grow bold to do evil.
Yet even if a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his days, I know this: it will go well with those who fear God, who live in reverence before him.
But there is no happiness for the wicked: like a shadow, he will not prolong his days, because he does not fear God.
There is another breath upon the earth: the righteous treated as the wicked deserve, and the wicked treated as the righteous deserve. I say that this too is a breath.

So I commended joy, for there is nothing good for a person under the sun but to eat, drink, and rejoice; this is what accompanies them in their toil during the days of life God gives them under the sun.
When I applied my heart to know wisdom and to observe all the activity that unfolds on the earth, day and night without the eyes finding sleep,

then I looked at all the work of God, and I saw that no one can grasp what is done under the sun: however hard they toil to search it out, they do not find it; and even if the wise claim to know, they cannot reach it.

titres.titre: Time and chance foil the strong
The wisdom of the poor, despised

versets.t: Yes, I took all this to heart, and I saw clearly that the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. No one knows whether love or hatred awaits them: everything before them remains uncertain.

The same fate awaits everyone: the righteous and the wicked, the good and pure and the impure, the one who offers sacrifices and the one who does not. It is the same for the good as for the sinner, for the one who takes an oath as for the one who fears to do so.

This is the evil in all that is done under the sun: one same fate for all. And so the hearts of people are full of wickedness, and folly dwells in their hearts throughout their life; then they go to join the dead.
Whoever is still among the living keeps some hope: a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing more; there is no more reward for them, and even their memory fades away.
Their love, their hatred, their jealousy have already vanished, and never again will they have a share in all that is done under the sun.
Go, eat your bread with joy, drink your wine with a glad heart, for God already looks with favor on your deeds.
Let your garments be white at all times, and let your head never lack perfume.

Enjoy life with the woman you love, throughout all the fleeting days God grants you under the sun, all these passing days; for this is your portion in life and in the toil at which you labor under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength; for there is no work, no thought, no knowledge, no wisdom in the realm of the dead, where you are going.

I saw again, under the sun, that the race does not belong to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; that bread does not go to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to the learned: time and chance overtake them all.
For no more than the fish caught in the fatal net, or the birds taken in the snare, does anyone know their hour: like them, people are caught by misfortune when it falls on them suddenly.
I saw yet another example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.
There was a small town, with few inhabitants. A mighty king came to attack it, laid siege to it, and raised great siege works against it.
Now there was found in it a poor but wise man, who saved the town by his wisdom. And yet no one remembered that poor man.
Then I said to myself, 'Wisdom is better than strength.' Yet the wisdom of the poor is despised, and their words go unheeded.
The words of the wise, spoken in calm, are better heard than the shouting of a ruler among fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war; but a single sinner destroys much good.

titres.titre: The words of the wise and the fool

versets.t: Dead flies spoil and sour the perfumer's oil; so too, a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
The heart of the wise turns them toward good, that of the fool toward evil.
Even along the road, the fool lacks sense, and shows everyone that he is a fool.
If the ruler's anger rises against you, do not leave your post, for composure prevents great faults.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, like an error that comes from the one who governs:
folly is placed in the highest posts, while men of worth occupy the lowest ranks.
I have seen slaves on horseback, and princes walking on foot like slaves.
Whoever digs a pit may fall into it; whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
Whoever quarries stones may be hurt by them; whoever splits wood is put at risk.
If the axe is blunt and its edge is not sharpened, one must redouble the effort; but wisdom has the advantage of bringing success.
If the snake bites for lack of being charmed, the charmer gains no advantage.
The words of the wise win them favor, but the lips of the fool devour him.
His words begin in foolishness and end in raving madness.
The fool multiplies words. Yet no one knows what is to come; and what will be after them, who can tell?
The fool's toil wears him out: he does not even know the way to town.
Woe to you, land whose king is a child, and whose princes feast in the morning!
Happy are you, land whose king is of noble birth, and whose princes eat at the proper time, to gain strength and not to get drunk.
When the arms are lazy, the rafters sag; when the hands stay idle, the roof begins to leak.
Feasts are made for enjoyment, wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
Even in thought, do not curse the king; even in your bedroom, do not curse the powerful: for a bird of the sky might carry off your word, and the winged creature repeat what you have said.

titres.titre: The light of life, the joy of youth

versets.t: Cast your bread upon the surface of the water: after many days, you will find it again.
Divide it into seven or eight portions, for you do not know what disaster may strike the land.
When the clouds are full, they pour out rain on the earth; and where the tree falls, to the south or to the north, there it stays where it has fallen.
Whoever watches the wind will never sow; whoever scans the clouds will never reap.
You do not know the way of the wind, nor how the bones are formed in the womb of a pregnant woman; so too you cannot understand the work of God, who makes all things.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand rest; for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.
Sweet is the light, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
If someone lives many years, let them rejoice in them all; but let them also remember the dark days, for they will be many. All that comes is but a breath.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth; let your heart bring you happiness in the days of your youth! Follow the ways of your heart and what your eyes see; but know that for all this God will bring you to judgment.
Banish sorrow from your heart, and put away suffering from your body; for youth and the dawn of life quickly pass.

titres.titre: Remembering your Creator before old age

versets.t: Remember your Creators in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, 'I find no pleasure in them';
before the sun and the light, the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;
in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, when the strong men stoop, when the women grinding cease, too few in number, when those who look through the windows grow dim;
when the two doors close upon the street, as the sound of the mill fades; when one wakes at the song of a bird, when all the singing voices fall silent;

when one dreads the climb, when the journey is filled with terrors, when the almond tree blossoms, when the grasshopper drags itself along, when the caper loses its effect. For man goes to his eternal home, and already the mourners prowl the streets;
before the silver cord is snapped, the golden lamp is shattered, the pitcher is broken at the spring, the pulley is broken over the well;
and the dust returns to the earth, where it came from, and the breath of life returns to God who had given it.
A breath, a mere breath, says Qoheleth, everything is a breath.
Not only was Qoheleth a wise man, but he also taught the people knowledge; he weighed, examined, and set in order a great number of proverbs.
Qoheleth sought to find pleasing words, and to write with uprightness words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads, and their collected sayings like well-driven nails: they all come from one Shepherd.
For the rest, my son, be on your guard: of making many books there is no end, and too much study wearies the body.
End of the discourse; all has been said: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of humankind.
For God will bring into judgment every deed, even the hidden, whether good or evil.
The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is more delightful than wine;
the scent of your perfumes is sweet, your name is oil poured out; that is why the maidens love you.
Draw me after you, let us run! The king has brought me into his chambers. We will exult and rejoice in you, we will praise your love more than wine. How rightly they love you!
I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the pavilions of Solomon.
Do not look down on me because I am black: it is the sun that has burned me. My mother's sons were angry with me, they set me to guard the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not guarded.
Tell me, you whom my heart loves, where you pasture your flock, where you let it rest at noon, that I may not go wandering after the flocks of your companions.
If you do not know, O fairest of women, then follow the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
To my mare among Pharaoh's chariots I compare you, my love.
Your cheeks are lovely amid the pendants, your neck amid strings of pearls.
We will make you pendants of gold, studded with points of silver.
While the king is at his table, my nard gives forth its fragrance.
My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts;
my beloved is to me a cluster of henna in the vineyards of En-gedi.
How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves.
How beautiful you are, my beloved, how lovely! Our couch is all greenery;
the beams of our house are cedars, our rafters are cypresses.
I am the narcissus of Sharon, the lily of the valleys.
Like a lily among thorns, so is my love among the maidens.
Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. I longed to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste.
He brought me to the house of wine, and the banner he raises over me is love.
Sustain me with raisin cakes, revive me with apples, for I am sick with love.
His left arm is beneath my head, and his right hand embraces me.
I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the does of the field: do not stir, do not awaken love until it please.
The voice of my beloved! Here he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.
My beloved is like a gazelle, like a young stag. There he stands behind our wall: he gazes through the window, he peers through the lattice.
My beloved spoke and said to me: "Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away!
For behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.
The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.
The fig tree forms its first fruits, the blossoming vine gives its fragrance. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away!
My dove, hidden in the cleft of the rock, in the secret of the steep places, show me your face, let me hear your voice: for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that ravage the vineyards, for our vineyards are in bloom."
My beloved is mine, and I am his; he pastures his flock among the lilies.
Before the day breathes and the shadows flee, return! Be, my beloved, like a gazelle, like a young stag upon the rugged mountains.
Upon my bed at night I sought him whom my heart loves; I sought him, but did not find him.
"I will rise now," I said, "and go about the city, through the streets and the squares; I will seek him whom my heart loves." I sought him, but did not find him.
The watchmen found me, those who make their rounds in the city: "Him whom my heart loves, have you seen him?"
Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my heart loves. I held him fast and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me.
I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the does of the field: do not stir, do not awaken love until it please.
Who is this coming up from the wilderness, like a column of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of the merchant?
Behold, it is the litter of Solomon: sixty warriors surround it, among the mighty men of Israel,
all of them armed with the sword, trained for war; each has his sword at his side, against the terrors of the night.
King Solomon made himself a palanquin from the wood of Lebanon:
he made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior lovingly inlaid by the daughters of Jerusalem.
Come out, daughters of Zion, and gaze upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.
How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down the slopes of Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes coming up from the washing: each one has its twin, and not one is missing.
Your lips are a ribbon of scarlet, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheek, behind your veil, is like a half of pomegranate.
Your neck is like the tower of David, built as an armory: a thousand shields hang upon it, all the shields of warriors.
Your two breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.
Before the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go to the mountain of myrrh, to the hill of frankincense.
You are all beautiful, my love, and there is no flaw in you!
With me from Lebanon, my bride, with me, come from Lebanon! Come down from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride, you have ravished my heart with a single one of your glances, with a single strand of your necklace.
How charming is your love, my sister, my bride! Your love is better than wine, and the scent of your perfumes than all spices.
Your lips drip honey, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.
You are a garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.
Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, with the choicest fruits, henna and nard,
nard and saffron, cinnamon and cassia, with all the trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all the finest balsams.
You are the fountain of the gardens, a well of living waters, a stream flowing down from Lebanon.
Awake, north wind! Come, south wind! Blow upon my garden, that its fragrances may stream forth! Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits.
I come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I gather my myrrh and my balm, I eat my honeycomb and my honey, I drink my wine and my milk. Eat, my friends, drink, be drunk with love!

I sleep, but my heart is awake. It is the voice of my beloved, knocking: "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one! For my head is drenched with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
"I have taken off my tunic, how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet, how shall I soil them?"
My beloved put his hand through the opening of the door, and for him my whole being trembled.
I rose to open to my beloved, and from my hands dripped myrrh, from my fingers flowing myrrh, upon the handle of the bolt.
I open to my beloved, but my beloved had turned away and was gone. I fainted at the sound of his word. I sought him, but did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer.
The watchmen found me, those who make their rounds in the city; they struck me, they wounded me, they tore away my cloak, the keepers of the walls.
I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am sick with love.
What is your beloved more than another, O fairest of women? What is your beloved more than another, that you charge us so?
My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand.
His head is purest gold, his locks, supple as palm fronds, are black as the raven.
His eyes are doves beside the streams of water, bathing in milk, perched beside a brimming pool.
His cheeks are beds of balsam, banks of fragrant herbs; his lips are lilies, dripping flowing myrrh.
His hands are rings of gold, set with gems of Tarshish; his body a work of ivory, inlaid with sapphires.
His legs are pillars of alabaster, set on bases of pure gold. His bearing is like Lebanon, majestic as the cedars.
His mouth is all sweetness, and everything about him is delight. Such is my beloved, such is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.
Where has your beloved gone, O fairest of women? Which way has he turned, that we may seek him with you?
My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of balsam, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine; he pastures his flock among the lilies.
You are beautiful, my love, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army in battle array.
Turn your eyes away from me, for they overwhelm me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down the slopes of Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of ewes coming up from the washing: each one has its twin, and not one is missing.
Your cheek, behind your veil, is like a half of pomegranate.
There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number:
but unique is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the favorite of her who bore her. The maidens saw her and called her blessed, the queens and the concubines praised her:
"Who is this that rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, radiant as the sun, awesome as an army in battle array?"
I had gone down to the walnut orchard to see the fresh shoots of the valley, to see whether the vine had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.
And before I knew it, my longing had set me upon the princely chariots of my people.
Return, return, O Shulammite! Return, return, that we may gaze upon you! Why do you gaze upon the Shulammite, as upon the dance of the two camps?
How beautiful are your feet in their sandals, O prince's daughter! The curve of your hips is like a necklace, the work of a craftsman's hands.
Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks spiced wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat encircled with lilies.
Your two breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle.
Your neck is like a tower of ivory; your eyes, the pools of Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim; your nose, like the tower of Lebanon that looks toward Damascus.
Your head rises like Carmel, and your flowing hair is like purple: a king is held captive in its tresses.
How beautiful you are, how lovely, O love, among all delights!
Your stature is like the palm tree, and your breasts like its clusters.
I said: I will climb the palm tree, I will grasp its branches. May your breasts be like clusters of the vine, the fragrance of your breath like apples,
and your mouth like the finest wine that flows straight to my beloved, gliding over the lips of those who slumber.
I am my beloved's, and for me is his longing.
Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields, let us spend the night among the villages;
early we will go to the vineyards, we will see whether the vine has budded, whether its blossoms have opened, whether the pomegranates are in flower. There I will give you my love.
The mandrakes give their fragrance, and at our doors are all the choicest fruits, the new as well as the old: my beloved, I have kept them for you.
Oh, that you were to me like a brother, nursed at my mother's breast! Finding you outside, I could kiss you, and no one would despise me.
I would lead you, I would bring you into my mother's house, you who would teach me; I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranates.
His left arm is beneath my head, and his right hand embraces me.
I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem: do not stir, do not awaken love until it please.
Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother conceived you, there she who bore you brought you forth.
Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, its passion relentless as the realm of the dead. Its flames are flames of fire, a flame of the Lord.
Great waters cannot quench love, nor can the rivers sweep it away. Were a man to give for love all the wealth of his house, he would reap only contempt.
We have a little sister, who has no breasts yet: what shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?
If she is a wall, we will build upon her battlements of silver; if she is a door, we will barricade her with boards of cedar.
I am a wall, and my breasts are its towers; in his eyes I have become one who has found peace.
Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he entrusted it to keepers, and each was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver.
My own vineyard is before me: yours, Solomon, the thousand pieces, and two hundred for the keepers of its fruit!
You who dwell in the gardens, companions are listening for your voice: let me hear it!
Flee, my beloved! Be like a gazelle, like a young stag, upon the mountains of spices!
Love righteousness, you who govern the earth; think of the Lord with uprightness, and seek him with a sincere heart.
For he lets himself be found by those who do not put him to the test, and he reveals himself to those who do not refuse to believe in him.
Crooked thoughts separate people from God, and his power, when it is tested, confounds the foolish.
Wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sin;
for the holy spirit of instruction flees deceit, withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding, and is repelled when injustice draws near.

Wisdom is a spirit that loves humankind, yet she will not leave the blasphemer's words unpunished; for God is the witness of his inmost self, the true guardian of his heart, and he hears what his tongue says.
For the Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world, and he who holds all things together knows every word.
So no one who speaks unjustly can hide, and the justice that punishes will not pass him by.
For there will be an inquiry into the schemes of the ungodly, and the sound of his words will reach the Lord to denounce his sins.
A jealous ear hears everything, and the murmur of complaints does not escape it.
Guard yourselves, then, from useless grumbling, and keep your tongue from slander; for a word spoken in secret does not go without effect, and a lying mouth destroys the soul.
Do not court death by the errors of your life, nor draw ruin upon yourselves by the work of your hands;
for God did not make death, and he takes no pleasure in the destruction of the living.
He created all things that they might exist: the creatures that come into the world are life-bearing, there is in them no destructive poison, and the realm of the dead has no dominion on earth;
for righteousness is immortal.
But the ungodly, by their deeds and their words, call death to themselves; taking it for a friend, they pine away for it, they make a covenant with it, and it is fitting that they belong to it.
They say to one another, reasoning falsely: "Our life is short and full of trouble, there is no remedy when a person's end comes, and no one is known to have returned from the realm of the dead.
We were born by chance, and after this life it will be as though we had never been. The breath in our nostrils is only a smoke, and thought a spark struck from the beating of our heart;
let it go out, and the body will fall to ashes, and the spirit will dissolve like thin air.

Our name will sink little by little into oblivion, and no one will remember our works. Our life will pass like the trace of a cloud, it will scatter like a mist chased away by the rays of the sun and beaten down by its heat.
Our existence is the passing of a shadow, and our end has no return: the seal is set, and no one comes back.
Come then, let us enjoy the good things at hand, let us make use of created things with the eagerness of youth!
Let us drink our fill of fine wines and perfumes, and let no flower of spring pass us by;
let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wither;
let none of us miss his share of our pleasures, let us leave the marks of our joy everywhere, for this is our portion, this is our lot.
Let us oppress the righteous man who is poor, let us not spare the widow nor respect the gray hairs of the aged;
let our strength be the measure of right, for what is weak is shown to be useless.
Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, since he stands in our way, opposes what we do, reproaches us for breaking the law, and accuses us of betraying our upbringing.
He claims to possess the knowledge of God, and calls himself a son of the Lord;
he is a living reproach to our thoughts, and the very sight of him weighs on us,
for his manner of life is unlike any other, and his ways are strange.
He regards us as counterfeit coin, and shuns our ways as defilements; he calls the final lot of the righteous blessed, and boasts that God is his father.
Let us see, then, whether his words are true, and test what will happen at his death;
for if the righteous man is God's son, God will help him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries.
Let us test him with insult and torture, to learn his gentleness and prove his patience.
Let us condemn him to a shameful death, since, by his own account, he will be protected."
So they reason, but they are mistaken: their malice has blinded them.
They do not know the secret purposes of God, they hope for no reward for holiness, and they do not believe in the recompense of pure souls.
Yet God created man for incorruption, and made him in the image of his own eternity;
but through the envy of the devil death entered the world,
and those who belong to his party experience it.

titres.titre: The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God

versets.t: The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will touch them.
In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; their departure was thought a disaster,
and their leaving us an annihilation; but they are at peace.
Though in the sight of others they were punished, their hope was full of immortality;
after a brief chastening they will receive great blessings, for God tested them and found them worthy of himself:
he tried them like gold in the furnace, and accepted them like a perfect sacrifice.
On the day of their visitation they will shine out, and will run like sparks through the stubble;
they will judge nations and rule over peoples, and the Lord will reign over them forever.
Those who trust in him will understand the truth, and the faithful will abide with him in love; for grace and mercy are for his chosen ones.
But the ungodly will be punished according to their thoughts, they who scorned the righteous man and turned away from the Lord;
for whoever rejects wisdom and discipline is wretched: their hope is empty, their labors fruitless, their works useless.
Their wives are foolish, their children wicked, and their offspring accursed.
Blessed is the barren woman who has kept herself pure, whose bed has known no transgression: she will have her fruit on the day when God visits the souls.

Blessed too is the eunuch whose hand has done nothing wrong, who has harbored no evil thoughts against the Lord: a choice grace will reward his faithfulness, and he will have a most desirable place in the temple of the Lord.
For the fruit of good deeds is glorious, and the root of wisdom never withers.
But the children of adulterers will come to nothing, and the offspring of an unlawful union will disappear.
Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing, and their old age at the last will be without honor;
and if they die early, they will have neither hope nor consolation on the day of judgment,
for the end of an unrighteous race is always cruel.

titres.titre: The righteous man who dies before his time
The righteous man condemns the ungodly

versets.t: Better to have no children and to possess virtue: its memory is immortal, for it is known both to God and to men.
When present, it is imitated; when absent, it is longed for; and in eternity it marches crowned in triumph, having won victory in unsullied contests.
But the many children of the ungodly are of no use: sprung from illegitimate shoots, they will not put down deep roots or establish a firm foundation.
Even if for a time their branches grow green, standing insecure they will be shaken by the wind and uprooted by the fury of the storm.
Their boughs will be broken before their time, their fruit worthless, too unripe to eat, good for nothing.
For children born of unlawful unions are witnesses, on the day of reckoning, against their parents' sin.
The righteous man, even if he dies before his time, will be at rest.
For honored old age does not consist in length of years, nor is it measured by the number of days:
wisdom is a man's gray hair, and a blameless life is the true old age.
Having become pleasing to God, he was loved by him; and since he was living among sinners, he was taken up.
He was carried off lest evil corrupt his understanding or deceit beguile his soul;
for the fascination of vice obscures the good, and the whirl of desire perverts an innocent heart.
Coming quickly to perfection, he fulfilled long years;
for his soul was pleasing to the Lord, and so the Lord hastened to take him from the midst of evil.
The peoples see this without understanding, without taking to heart that the grace of God and his mercy are for his chosen ones, and that he watches over his holy ones.
The righteous man who dies condemns the ungodly who survive, and youth soon brought to perfection condemns the long old age of the unrighteous.
They will see the wise man's end without understanding the Lord's purpose for him, or why he set him in safety.
They will see and despise, but the Lord will laugh at them.

After this they will become a dishonored corpse, an object of shame among the dead forever; he will dash them down speechless, headlong, he will shake them to their foundations, they will be utterly laid waste, given over to anguish, and their memory will perish.
They will come trembling to the reckoning of their sins, and their crimes, standing up before them, will accuse them.

titres.titre: The remorse of the ungodly at the judgment

versets.t: Then the righteous man will stand with great confidence before those who persecuted him and made light of his sufferings.
At the sight of him they will be shaken with terrible fear, astounded at his unexpected salvation.
Full of remorse, they will say to themselves, groaning with anguished hearts: "This is the man we once made our laughingstock and byword of scorn!
Fools that we were, we thought his life madness and his death a disgrace.
How then was he numbered among the sons of God? How is his lot among the holy ones?
So we strayed from the way of truth: the light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise upon us.
We took our fill of the paths of iniquity and ruin, we crossed trackless deserts, and we did not know the way of the Lord.
What good did our pride do us? What has the wealth we boasted of brought us?
All those things have passed like a shadow, like a rumor hurrying by,
like a ship cutting through the churning water, leaving no trace of its passage nor any furrow of its keel in the waves;

or like a bird flying through the air, leaving no sign of its path: it beats the light air with its wings, cuts through it with a mighty rush, forces a way with the stroke of its wings, and afterward no mark of its passing can be found;
or again, when an arrow is shot at the target, the divided air closes at once, and no one can tell where it went.
So it is with us: scarcely born, we ceased to be, with no trace of virtue to show; we were consumed in our own malice."

Yes, the hope of the ungodly is like chaff carried off by the wind, like light frost scattered by the storm, like smoke dispersed by a breath; it fades like the memory of a guest who stays a single day.
But the righteous live forever; their reward is with the Lord, and the Most High takes care of them.
Therefore they will receive from the Lord's hand the glorious kingdom and the splendid diadem, for he will shelter them with his right hand and shield them with his arm.
He will take his zeal as armor and arm creation to punish his enemies;
