he will put on righteousness as a breastplate and wear as a helmet an unwavering judgment;
he will take holiness as an invincible shield;
of his relentless wrath he will make a sharp sword, and the universe will fight with him against the foolish.
Well-aimed bolts of lightning will fly, and from the clouds, as from a well-drawn bow, they will speed to their mark.
His anger, like a catapult, will hurl dense hailstones; the waters of the sea will rise up against them, and the rivers will overwhelm them without mercy;
a mighty wind will rise against them and sweep them away like a hurricane. So lawlessness will lay the whole earth waste, and evildoing will overthrow the thrones of the mighty.
Listen then, you kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth;
give ear, you who rule over the multitudes and pride yourselves on governing many peoples.
Your power was given you by the Lord, and your sovereignty by the Most High; it is he who will examine your deeds and scrutinize your intentions.
For, as servants of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law, nor follow the will of God.
Terrible and swift he will come upon you, for stern judgment awaits those in high places.
The lowly are pardoned in mercy, but the mighty will be mightily punished.
The Master of all shrinks before no one, and no greatness overawes him: small and great alike, he made them all, and he cares for all equally;
but it is for the mighty that the most rigorous scrutiny is reserved.
To you then, O kings, my words are addressed, that you may learn wisdom and not fall away;
for those who keep holy things in holiness will be held holy, and those who have learned them will find a defense.
Desire my words, then, long for them, and you will be instructed.
Wisdom is radiant and unfading; those who love her see her easily, and those who seek her find her.
She hastens to make herself known to those who desire her, coming to them first.
Whoever rises early for her will have no trouble: he will find her sitting at his door.
To fix one's thought on her is perfect understanding; whoever keeps watch for her will soon be free from care,
for she herself goes about seeking those worthy of her, graciously showing herself to them along their paths and meeting them in their every thought.
Her true beginning is the desire for instruction, and concern for instruction is love;
love is the keeping of her laws, and attention to her laws is the assurance of incorruption,
and incorruption brings one near to God.
So the desire for wisdom leads to a kingdom.
If then, you rulers of the peoples, you delight in thrones and scepters, honor wisdom, and you will reign forever.

What Wisdom is and how she came to be I will tell you, and I will hide no mysteries from you; I will trace her back to the very origins of creation, bring the knowledge of her to light, and not stray from the truth.
I will not travel in the company of devouring envy, for it has nothing in common with Wisdom.
A multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world, and a sensible king the stability of his people.
So let yourselves be instructed by my words: you will profit from them.

titres.titre: Solomon, a man like all others
He preferred Wisdom to all things

versets.t: I too am mortal like everyone else, a descendant of the first man, formed from the earth.
In my mother's womb my flesh was shaped, taking form over ten months in the blood, from a man's seed and the pleasure that comes with sleep.
At my birth I too breathed the common air, I fell upon the same earth, and my first cry, like everyone's, was a wail.
I was brought up in swaddling clothes and with constant care;
no king had any other beginning of existence:
there is for all one single entrance into life, and one way out.
This is why I prayed, and understanding was given me; I pleaded, and the spirit of Wisdom came to me.
I preferred her to scepters and thrones, and I counted riches as nothing beside her;
I compared no precious stone to her, for beside her all gold is but a little sand, and silver counts as clay.
I loved her more than health and beauty, and preferred her to the light of day, for the radiance that comes from her never goes out.
With her there came to me all good things, and in her hands was untold wealth;
and I rejoiced in all of it, because Wisdom leads them; yet I did not know that she was their mother.
I learned her without guile, and I share her without envy; I do not hide her riches;
for she is to men an inexhaustible treasure: those who gain her win the friendship of God, commended by the gifts that come from instruction.
May God grant me to speak of her as I wish and to think in a manner worthy of his gifts, for it is he who guides wisdom and sets the wise right;
we are in his hand, we and our words, all our knowledge and our skill.
It is he who gave me true knowledge of the things that are: to know how the world is made and the force of the elements,
the beginning, the end, and the middle of times, the turning of the solstices and the change of the seasons,
the cycle of the years and the position of the stars,
the nature of animals and the instincts of beasts, the power of spirits and the thoughts of men, the varieties of plants and the virtues of roots.
All that is hidden or visible I learned,

for Wisdom, the maker of all things, taught me. In her there is a spirit that is intelligent, holy, unique yet manifold, subtle, agile, penetrating, unstained, clear, invulnerable, loving the good, keen, unhindered,
beneficent, loving humankind, steadfast, sure, serene, all-powerful, watching over all things and penetrating all spirits, the intelligent, the pure, and the most subtle.
For Wisdom is more mobile than any motion; in her purity she passes through and penetrates all things.
She is a breath of the power of God, a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled can steal into her.
She is the reflection of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the working of God, and the image of his goodness.
Though she is but one, she can do all things; abiding in herself, she renews all things; age after age, passing into holy souls, she makes them friends of God and prophets.
For God loves none but the one who dwells with Wisdom;
she is more beautiful than the sun, surpassing every constellation; compared with the light, she is found to excel it,
for the light gives way to night, but against Wisdom no evil can prevail.

titres.titre: She must be asked of God

versets.t: She reaches from one end of the world to the other with her strength, and orders all things with gentleness.
I loved her and sought her out from my youth, and I resolved to take her for my bride, in love with her beauty.
She magnifies her noble birth by living with God, and the Master of all things loves her;
for she is initiated into the knowledge of God, and it is she who chooses his works.
If riches are a desirable possession in life, what is richer than Wisdom, who makes all things?
If understanding is at work, who more than she is the maker of all that exists?
Does one love righteousness? Her labors are the virtues: she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage, the most useful things for people in life.
Does one desire wide knowledge? She knows the past and divines the future, she grasps subtle arguments and unravels riddles, she foresees signs and wonders, and the outcome of times and seasons.
So I resolved to take her to share my life, knowing that she would be my counselor for good, a comfort in cares and sorrow.
Through her I will have glory in the assembly and, though young, honor among the elders;
my keenness in judgment will be recognized, and the great will admire me.
If I am silent, they will wait for me to speak; if I speak, they will pay attention; and if I speak at length, they will lay their hand upon their mouth.
Through her I will gain immortality and leave to posterity an everlasting memory.
I will govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me;
at the mere sound of my name dread rulers will fear me. I will show myself good among the people and valiant in war.
Returning home, I will find rest beside her, for her company brings no bitterness, and life with her no vexation, but contentment and joy.
Pondering all this within myself, and reflecting in my heart that immortality is found in union with Wisdom,

that in her friendship there is pure delight, in the work of her hands inexhaustible wealth, in intimacy with her understanding, and in her conversation renown, I went about seeking a way to take her for my own.
I was a child of happy nature, and a good soul fell to my lot;
or rather, being good, I entered an undefiled body.

But realizing that I could not possess Wisdom unless God gave her to me, and it was already an act of wisdom to know from whom this gift comes, I turned to the Lord and pleaded with him, saying from the depths of my heart:
"God of my fathers, Lord of mercy, you who made the universe by your word,
and by your wisdom formed man to rule over the creatures you have made,
to govern the world in holiness and righteousness and pronounce judgment with an upright heart:
give me Wisdom, who sits beside your throne, and do not reject me from among your children.
For I am your servant, the son of your handmaid, a frail man, short-lived, too small to understand justice and the laws.
Even one who is perfect among the sons of men, without the wisdom that comes from you, would count for nothing.
You chose me to be king of your people and judge of your sons and daughters;
you told me to build a temple on your holy mountain and an altar in the city where you dwell, on the model of the holy Dwelling that you prepared from the beginning.
With you is Wisdom, who knows your works and was present when you made the world; she knows what is pleasing in your eyes and what is right according to your commandments.
Send her forth from the most holy heavens, dispatch her from the throne of your glory, that she may labor at my side and I may know what pleases you;
for she knows and understands all things, and will guide me prudently in what I do and protect me with her glory.
Then my works will be pleasing to you, I will govern your people justly, and I will be worthy of my father's throne.
For what man can know the purpose of God? Who can conceive what the Lord wills?
The reasonings of mortals are timid, and our calculations uncertain;
for the perishable body weighs down the soul, and this tent of clay burdens the mind teeming with thoughts.
We can barely guess at what is on earth, and only with toil find what lies within our reach; who then has traced out what is in the heavens?
And who could have known your will, if you had not given Wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high?
So it was that the paths of those on earth were set straight, that people were taught what pleases you, and that they were saved by Wisdom."
It was Wisdom who protected the first-formed father of the world, created alone and shaped by God;
she raised him up from his fall and gave him the strength to master all things.
But when an unrighteous man in his anger turned away from her, he perished through the fury that drove him to kill his brother.
When, because of him, the earth was flooded, Wisdom again saved it, steering the righteous man by a mere piece of wood.
When the nations, united in wickedness, were confounded, she knew how to recognize the righteous man, kept him blameless before God, and held him firm despite his tenderness for his child.
It was she who, in the destruction of the ungodly, delivered the righteous man as he fled the fire falling on the Five Cities.
As witnesses to their wickedness, a desolate land still smokes, trees bear fruit that does not ripen, and a pillar of salt stands as a memorial to an unbelieving soul.
For, having neglected wisdom, they not only lost the knowledge of the good but also left the living a monument of their folly, so that their sins could not remain hidden.
But Wisdom delivered from their troubles those who served her.

It was she who led by straight paths the righteous man fleeing his brother's anger; she showed him the kingdom of God and gave him knowledge of holy things, made him prosper in his hard labors and multiplied the fruit of his toil.
Against the greed of his oppressors she stood by him and made him rich;
she guarded him from his enemies, protected him from ambushes, and gave him victory in a hard contest, that he might know that piety is more powerful than all things.
She did not forsake the righteous man when he was sold, but preserved him from sin;

she went down with him into the pit and did not leave him in his chains, until she brought him the royal scepter and power over those who oppressed him; she exposed as liars those who had accused him and granted him everlasting glory.
It was she who delivered a holy people, a blameless race, from the nations that oppressed them.
She entered the soul of a servant of the Lord and withstood dread kings with signs and wonders.
She gave the holy ones the reward of their labors, led them by a marvelous road, and became a shelter for them by day and a starry light by night;
she brought them across the Red Sea and led them through deep waters,
while she engulfed their enemies and then cast them up from the depths of the abyss.
So the righteous plundered the ungodly; they sang, O Lord, your holy name, and with one heart praised your defending hand;
for Wisdom opened the mouths of the mute and made the tongues of infants speak clearly.

titres.titre: The wilderness: water from the rock
Punishment through the very thing by which one has sinned

versets.t: She made their undertakings prosper by the hand of a holy prophet.
They crossed an uninhabited wilderness and pitched their tents in trackless places;
they stood against their enemies and drove off their foes.
When they were thirsty and called upon you, water was given them from a sheer rock, and from hard stone, relief for their thirst.
For the very thing that had punished their enemies became, in their need, a benefit to them.
Where a perennial river had been fouled with corrupted blood,
as a punishment for the decree that killed the newborn, you gave your people, beyond all hope, abundant water,
showing them, by the thirst they felt then, how you had struck their adversaries.
For when they were tested, though in mercy, they understood how the ungodly, judged in wrath, were tormented;
for the one group you tested like a father who admonishes, but the others you punished like a stern king who condemns.
Absent or present, they were equally distressed,
seized by a twofold grief, groaning at the memory of the past.
For when they learned that their own punishment was benefiting those they had driven out, they recognized the Lord;
and the man they had once exposed and then rejected with scorn, they came to admire at the end of events, after suffering a thirst quite unlike that of the righteous.
For the foolish thoughts of their wickedness, which led them astray to worship senseless reptiles and vile creatures, you sent upon them a swarm of dumb animals as a punishment,
that they might learn that one is punished by the very things through which one sins.
It was not hard for your all-powerful hand, which created the world out of formless matter, to unleash against them a horde of bears or fierce lions,
or beasts unknown, newly created, full of rage, breathing out fiery breath, exhaling a foul smoke, or flashing terrible sparks from their eyes,
able not only to tear them apart but to destroy them with terror by their mere appearance.
And even without these, a single breath could have laid them low, pursued by justice and swept away by the breath of your power. But you have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight;
for your great strength is always at your service, and who could resist the might of your arm?
The whole world before you is like the grain that tips the scales, like the drop of morning dew that falls upon the earth.
But you have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook people's sins so that they may repent;
for you love all that exists, and loathe nothing you have made: if you had hated anything, you would not have formed it.
How could anything endure if you had not willed it? How could anything be preserved that you had not called forth?
But you spare all things, because they are yours, O Lord, lover of life.
For your incorruptible breath is in all beings.
This is why you correct little by little those who fall, and admonish them by reminding them of their sins, so that, freed from evil, they may believe in you, O Lord.
So too the ancient inhabitants of your holy land,
you had come to abhor for their detestable practices, their sorceries and unholy rites,
their pitiless slaughter of children, their feasts of human flesh and blood, those initiates of secret brotherhoods,
those parents who murdered defenseless lives: you willed to destroy them by the hands of our fathers,
that the land dearest of all to you might receive a worthy colony of God's children.
Yet, because they were human, you dealt gently with them: you sent hornets ahead of your army to destroy them little by little.
Not that you were unable to hand these ungodly over to the righteous in pitched battle, or to wipe them out at a stroke by fierce beasts or a stern word;
but by carrying out your judgment by stages, you gave them a chance to repent, though you knew well that their origin was evil, their malice inborn, and that their way of thinking would never change,
for they were an accursed race from the beginning. Nor was it out of fear of anyone that you overlooked their sins;

for who could say to you, "What have you done?" Who could oppose your sentence? Who could bring a charge against you for destroying nations that you had made? Who could stand up to plead against you the cause of the guilty?
There is no other God but you, who care for all; you need prove to no one that your judgments are just.
Neither king nor tyrant can confront you on behalf of those you have punished.
Being righteous, you govern all things justly, and you count it unworthy of your power to condemn one who does not deserve to be punished.
For your strength is the source of your justice, and it is because you are Master of all that you spare all.
You show your strength to those who doubt the fullness of your power, and confound the boldness of those who know it;
but you, master of your strength, judge with gentleness and govern us with great forbearance, for your power is at your service whenever you will.
By acting thus you taught your people that the righteous must love humankind, and you gave your children the good hope that after sin you grant repentance.
For if you punished the enemies of your servants, though they deserved death, with such patience and indulgence, giving them time and opportunity to renounce their evil,
with what care do you judge your sons, to whose fathers you gave the gift of oaths and covenants full of noble promises!
So, while you correct us, you strike our enemies a thousand times harder, to teach us, when we judge, to think of your goodness, and, when we are judged, to hope for your mercy.
This is why those who had led senseless lives in unrighteousness you tormented by their own abominations.
For they had strayed far along the paths of error, taking for gods the vilest of animals, deceived like foolish children.
So, as to unreasoning children, you first sent them a ludicrous punishment;
but those whom this mocking correction did not bring back will undergo a judgment worthy of God.

Justly punished by the very creatures they took for gods, and exasperated by their sufferings, they saw at last and acknowledged as the true God the one they had once refused to know; and so the ultimate condemnation fell upon them.
Foolish by nature are all who were ignorant of God and could not, from the good things seen, recognize the One who is, nor discern the Artisan by considering his works.
Fire, wind, the light air, the circling stars, rushing water, the lights of heaven, these they took for the gods that govern the world.
If, charmed by their beauty, they took these things for gods, let them know how far their Master surpasses them, for it is the very Author of beauty who created them.
And if it was their power and activity that struck them, let them infer from these how much mightier is the one who formed them;
for from the greatness and beauty of created things their Creator is seen by analogy.
Yet these deserve the lesser blame, for perhaps they only go astray while seeking God and longing to find him:
immersed in his works, they search them out, and they let themselves be captivated by appearances, so beautiful is what they see.
But even these are not to be pardoned:
if they were able to know enough to grasp the universe, how did they not more quickly find its Master?

But wretched indeed are those who set their hope on dead things and call gods the works of human hands: gold and silver skillfully wrought, figures of animals, or a worthless stone, the work of an ancient hand.
Consider a woodcutter: he saws down a tree that is easy to work, carefully strips off all its bark and, with skill, makes from it a handy piece of furniture for daily use;
the shavings from his work he burns to cook his food and eat his fill.
But the leftover piece, good for nothing, a crooked and knotted length of wood, he takes up and carves in his idle moments, shaping it with care and giving it the form of a man,
or the image of some vile animal; he coats it with vermilion, reddens it with paint, and covers over every flaw.
Then he makes for it a fitting dwelling, sets it in the wall, and fastens it with iron.
He takes care that it does not fall, knowing well that this god cannot help itself: it is only an image, and it needs support.
Yet he prays to it for his goods, his marriage, and his children, unashamed to speak to a lifeless thing; for health he appeals to what is weak,
for life he asks of what is dead; for help he implores what is utterly helpless, for a good journey what cannot even walk;
for gain, for his work, for success in what he does, he begs strength from what has the most powerless hands of all.

titres.titre: The wood that saves, the wood that is worshiped

versets.t: Here is another: about to put out to sea and cross the raging waves, he calls upon a piece of wood more fragile even than the ship that carries him.
That ship was invented by the craving for gain and built by the craftsman's skill;
but it is your providence, O Father, that steers it, you who opened a way in the sea and a safe path through the waves,
showing that you can save from every danger, so that even the untrained may go to sea. You do not wish the works of your wisdom to be barren: so people entrust their lives to a frail piece of wood,
crossing the swell on a raft, and they arrive safe and sound.
Long ago too, when the proud giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge on a raft and, guided by your hand, left the world the seed of a new generation;
for blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes about.
But the idol made by hand is accursed, both it and its maker: he for having made it, and it because, though perishable, it was called a god.
For God hates equally the ungodly man and his ungodliness,
and the work will be punished together with the workman.
This is why the idols of the nations will be visited with punishment: creatures of God, they have become an abomination, a stumbling block to human souls, and a snare for the feet of the foolish.
The invention of idols was the beginning of debauchery, and their discovery the corruption of life.
They did not exist at the beginning, and they will not last forever:
it was the vain pride of men that brought them into the world, and so their end has already been decreed.
A father, crushed by untimely grief, made an image of the child so suddenly taken from him; this dead thing he then began to honor as a god, and handed down to his household rites and ceremonies.
Then this ungodly custom, strengthened over time, was kept as a law; and by command of rulers, worship was paid to statues.

When people could not honor a sovereign in person because he dwelt far off, they imagined his distant face and made a visible image of the king they revered, so as to flatter the absent one as zealously as if he were present.
The advance of this worship, even among those who did not know him, was furthered by the ambition of the artist;
for, wishing to please the powerful, he strained his art to make the likeness more beautiful,
and the crowd, drawn by the beauty of the work, took for a god the one whom only yesterday they had honored as a man.
And this became a snare for life: people, enslaved by misfortune or by power, gave to stone and wood the incommunicable Name.
Then it was not enough for them to be in error about the knowledge of God: living in a great conflict born of their ignorance, they give to such evils the name of peace.
With their child-sacrifices, their secret mysteries, and their frenzied revels with strange rites,
they keep nothing pure any longer, neither their lives nor their marriages: one kills another by treachery or wrongs him through adultery.
Everywhere, all mingled together, blood and murder, theft and fraud, corruption and betrayal, disorder and perjury,
the harassing of good people, ingratitude for kindness, the defiling of souls, the confusion of roles, the disorder of unions, adultery and debauchery.
For the worship of nameless idols is the beginning, the cause, and the end of every evil.
Their festivals are frenzies, their oracles lies; they live in unrighteousness and perjure themselves without scruple.
Because they trust in lifeless idols, they fear no harm for their false oaths;
but a just punishment will overtake them on both counts: because they thought wrongly of God by clinging to idols, and because they swore falsely out of deceit, scorning holiness.
It is not the power of the things they swear by, but the punishment due to sinners, that always pursues the transgression of the ungodly.
But you, our God, are good and faithful, patient, and you govern all things with mercy.
Even when we sin, we are yours, for we know your power; but we do not wish to sin, knowing that we are counted as yours.
To know you is perfect righteousness, and to know your power is the root of immortality.
We have not been led astray by the perverse invention of human art, nor by the futile work of a painter, a shape smeared with colors,
the sight of which stirs up the passion of the fool, who longs for the lifeless form of a dead image.
Lovers of evil, they deserve such hopes, those who make them, those who desire them, and those who worship them.

Consider a potter: he laboriously kneads the soft clay and shapes each vessel for our use. From the same clay he molds both the vessels meant for noble purposes and those that will serve the opposite; and of each object it is the potter who decides the use.

Then, by a sinful labor, from this same clay he molds an illusory god, he who, himself lately born from the earth, will soon return to the earth from which he was taken, when the soul lent to him is demanded back.
Yet he cares nothing for his failing strength or his brief life; he vies with goldsmiths and bronze-founders, and takes pride in fashioning frauds.
His heart is ashes, his hope cheaper than dirt, and his life of less worth than clay,
for he has failed to know the one who fashioned him, who breathed into him an active soul and inspired a living spirit.
He counts our existence a game and life a lucrative fair: "One must," he says, "make a profit by any means, even by evil."
This man, more than any other, knows that he sins, he who from the same earth makes both fragile vessels and idols.
But they are all utterly foolish, more to be pitied than a little child, these enemies who have oppressed your people;
for they took for gods all the idols of the nations, which have no eyes to see, no nostrils to breathe, no ears to hear, no fingers to touch, and whose feet cannot walk.
It was a man who made them, a borrowed being who molded them; no one can fashion a god that resembles himself.
Mortal, with his unholy hands he produces only a dead thing; he is worth more than the idols he worships, for he at least has life, and they never had it.
They worship even the most repulsive of beasts, more stupid than all the rest,
lacking even the beauty that in other animals stirs desire: they received neither God's praise nor his blessing.

titres.titre: Beasts against Egypt, quails for Israel
Fire in the heart of the hail

versets.t: This is why they were justly punished by creatures like their own and tormented by a swarm of beasts.
But to your people, instead of this punishment, you granted a kindness: to satisfy their appetite you prepared for them an astonishing food, quails;
so that the one group, despite their hunger, lost their very appetite at the repulsive sight of the beasts loosed against them, while the others, after a brief want, tasted a delicious food.
For it was fitting that an inescapable famine should fall upon the oppressors, and that to the others it should only be shown how their enemies were tormented.
When the fury of cruel beasts fell upon your people and they were dying under the bite of writhing serpents, your anger did not last to the end:
troubled for a moment, for their correction, they received a token of salvation to remind them of the commandments of your law;
for whoever turned toward that sign was saved, not by what he looked upon, but by you, the Savior of all.
In this way too you showed our enemies that it is you who deliver from every evil;
for them, the bites of locusts and flies brought death, and no remedy was found to save their lives, for they deserved such a punishment;
but your children were not overcome even by the fangs of venomous serpents, for your mercy came to their aid and healed them.
They were stung so as to remember your words, then quickly healed, lest, sinking into deep forgetfulness, they should be cut off from your kindness.
It was neither herb nor poultice that healed them, but your word, O Lord, which heals all things;
for you have power over life and death, you bring down to the gates of the realm of the dead, and you bring back up again.
A man in his malice may kill, but he cannot bring back the departed breath, nor set free the soul the realm of the dead has received.
From your hand it is impossible to escape.
The ungodly, who refused to know you, were scourged by the strength of your arm: unheard-of rains, hail, and relentless downpours overwhelmed them, and fire devoured them.
And here was the strangest thing: in the water that quenches all things, the fire burned all the more fiercely, for the universe fights on behalf of the righteous.
At times the flame would die down, so as not to consume the beasts sent against the ungodly, that at this sight they might understand that a judgment of God was pursuing them;
at other times it blazed even in the midst of the water, hotter than natural fire, to destroy the crops of a guilty land.
By contrast, you fed your people with the food of angels: from heaven you gave them without toil a bread ready to eat, offering every taste and suited to every palate.
This food revealed your sweetness toward your children: yielding to the desire of the one who ate it, it changed into whatever he wished.
Snow and ice held out against the fire without melting, that your people might know that the same fire, blazing in the hail and flashing in the rain, was destroying the crops of their enemies,
and that afterward, to feed the righteous, it forgot its own force.
For creation, serving you its Creator, strains its power to punish the wicked and relaxes to do good to those who trust in you.
So, adapting itself then to all these changes, it obeyed your grace, which nourishes all, according to the will of those in need,
that your beloved children might learn, O Lord, that it is not the crops that feed man, but that your word sustains those who believe in you.
Indeed, what withstood the destroying fire melted at the least warmth of a ray of sun,
to teach all that one must rise before the sun to give you thanks and pray to you at the break of day;
for the hope of the ungrateful will melt like winter frost and drain away like water running to waste.
Your judgments, indeed, are great and hard to express; this is why untaught souls have gone astray.

Convinced that they could oppress the holy nation, the wicked were chained by darkness, prisoners of a long night; shut in under their roofs, they lay there, exiled from your ever-watchful providence.
Thinking to stay hidden with their secret sins under the thick veil of oblivion, they were scattered, seized with horrible fear, terrified by phantoms.
The recess where they shut themselves did not keep them from fear: terrifying noises rumbled around them, and grim-faced specters appeared to them.
No fire had the power to give them light, and the bright blaze of the stars could not pierce that horrid night.
Only from time to time there appeared to them a mass of self-kindled fire, full of terror; and, dismayed by this vision whose cause they could not see, they judged it more dreadful still.
The laughable arts of the magicians failed, and their pretension to wisdom was shamefully exposed;
those who claimed to drive away terror and turmoil from sick souls were themselves sick with a ridiculous fear.
Even when nothing frightening was there, the passing of a beast or the hiss of a serpent set them trembling;
they died of fright, refusing even to look at that air from which no one can escape.
For wickedness is cowardly, condemned by its own testimony; pressed by conscience, it always magnifies its troubles;
fear is nothing other than the surrender of the help that reflection would give:
the less hope one has within, the more one dreads not knowing the cause of one's torment.
As for them, that night, truly powerless, rising from the depths of a powerless realm of the dead, they lay sunk in the same sleep,
harried now by terrifying specters, now paralyzed by the failing of their courage, for a sudden and unforeseen terror had fallen upon them.
And each one, wherever he collapsed helpless, found himself held as in a prison without bars:
farmer, shepherd, or laborer toiling in the fields, all, caught by the plague, endured the same inescapable constraint,
bound by a single chain of darkness. The whistling wind, the melodious song of birds among the branches, the roar of a torrent tumbling down,
the crash of falling rocks, the unseen rush of bounding animals, the howling of savage beasts, the echo thrown back from the hollows of the mountains, all made them faint with terror.
For while the whole world shone with pure light and went about its work unhindered,
over them alone lay a heavy night, an image of the darkness that was to receive them; yet they were to themselves a heavier burden than the darkness.

titres.titre: The Word comes down from heaven
The intercession that halts the plague

versets.t: Meanwhile a great light was shining for your holy ones. The Egyptians, hearing their voices but not seeing their faces, called them blessed for not suffering as they did,
and, because your people, though ill-treated, did not take revenge, they thanked them and begged their pardon for their hostility.
In place of that darkness you gave your people a pillar of fire, a guide on an unknown road, a harmless sun for their glorious pilgrimage.
They well deserved to be deprived of light and imprisoned in darkness, those who had held captive your children, through whom the incorruptible light of the law was to be given to the world.

They had resolved to kill the children of the holy ones, and one child, exposed, had been saved; to punish them, you took from them their multitude of sons and engulfed them all together in the raging waters.
That night was announced beforehand to our fathers, that they might take courage, knowing with sure faith the oaths in which they had believed.
So your people awaited the salvation of the righteous and the ruin of their enemies;
for by the same stroke with which you punished our adversaries, you glorified us by calling us to yourself.

The devout children of the holy ones offered their sacrifice in secret and agreed together upon this divine law: that the holy ones would share alike in blessings and dangers, already raising the hymns of their fathers.
In answer there echoed back the discordant cries of their enemies, and one heard the wailing of those who mourned their children.
One and the same penalty struck slave and master, and the common man suffered the same fate as the king;
all together, by a single kind of death, they had countless dead, and the living were not enough to bury them, for in one stroke their noblest offspring had been destroyed.
They who, because of their sorceries, had refused to believe, at the death of the firstborn acknowledged that this people was God's son.
While a peaceful silence enveloped all things and night was in the middle of its course,
your all-powerful Word, from the heavens, from the royal throne, leaped down like a relentless warrior into the midst of a land doomed to destruction,
carrying as a sharp sword your irrevocable decree; standing, it filled all things with death, touching heaven while treading the earth.
At once visions in terrible dreams overwhelmed them, and unforeseen terrors fell upon them;
flung here and there, half dead, they told why they were dying,
for the dreams that had troubled them had shown it to them, so that they might not perish without knowing the cause of their misfortune.
The trial of death touched the righteous too, and in the wilderness a multitude perished; but your anger did not last long.

For a blameless man hastened to defend them: taking up the weapons of his ministry, prayer and the incense of atonement, he stood against the wrath and put an end to the plague, showing that he was your servant.
He overcame the fury, not by strength of body nor force of arms, but by his word he prevailed on the one who was punishing, recalling the oaths and covenants made to the fathers.
When the dead were already piled one upon another, he stepped between them, halted the wrath, and barred the Destroyer's path to the living;
for on his long robe was the whole universe, the glorious names of the fathers engraved on the four rows of stones, and your majesty on the diadem of his head.
Before this the Destroyer drew back, seized with fear, for it was enough to have felt this one outburst of wrath.

titres.titre: The crossing of the Red Sea

versets.t: But upon the ungodly there fell a merciless wrath to the very end, for God knew beforehand what they would do:
after letting the righteous depart and even hastening their going, they would change their minds and pursue them.

Indeed, their mourning was not yet over, they were still weeping at the graves of their dead, when they conceived another senseless plan: those whom they had begged to leave, they now pursued as fugitives.
A just doom was drawing them to this end and making them forget what had just happened, so that they might fill up the punishment their torments still lacked,
and that, while your people made their marvelous crossing, they themselves might meet a strange death.
For the whole creation, in its very nature, was fashioned anew, obeying your special commands, so that your children might be kept unharmed.
The cloud was seen overshadowing the camp; where there had been water, dry land appeared; the Red Sea became an open passage, and the raging waves a green plain,
through which the whole nation passed, sheltered by your hand, gazing at prodigious wonders.
Like horses at pasture, like frolicking lambs, they glorified you, O Lord, their deliverer;
for they still remembered their sojourn in a foreign land: how the ground had brought forth gnats instead of animals, and the river had thrown up frogs instead of fish.
Later they saw also a strange birth of birds when, driven by craving, they demanded delicate food:
to appease them, quails came up from the sea.
But upon the sinners the punishments fell, foretold by violent flashes of lightning; they suffered justly for their crimes, for they had carried to the extreme their hatred of the stranger.
Others had refused to welcome strangers who came to them; these enslaved guests who had done them good.
And there is more: the first will have their judgment, for they had received these strangers as enemies;
but the latter, after welcoming with festivities and admitting to their rights those who already shared their life, crushed them with terrible sufferings.
So they were struck with blindness, like those who, at the door of the righteous man, wrapped in thick darkness, each groped for the entrance.
The elements exchanged their properties with one another, as on the harp the notes vary in rhythm while keeping the same pitch; this can be seen clearly by considering what happened.
Land animals became water creatures, and those that swim moved onto the land;
fire kept its force in water, and water forgot its power to quench;
conversely, the flames did not consume the flesh of the frail creatures that ventured into them, nor melt that heavenly food, like frost and as easily melted as it.
In everything, O Lord, you magnified your people and glorified them; you did not neglect them, but stood by them at all times and in every place.

titres.titre: All wisdom comes from the Lord

versets.t: All wisdom comes from the Lord, and it is with him forever.
The sand of the sea, the drops of rain, the days of eternity, who can count them?
The height of the sky, the breadth of the earth, the deep, and wisdom, who can fathom them?
Before all things wisdom was created, and prudent understanding is from eternity.
The source of wisdom is the word of God in the highest heavens, and her ways are the eternal commandments.
To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed? Who has known her hidden designs?
To whom has the knowledge of wisdom been shown? Who has grasped the richness of her ways?
One alone is wise, most fearsome of all, seated on his throne: the Lord.
It is he who created her; he saw her and measured her, he poured her out on all his works,
on all flesh, according to his generosity, he lavished her on those who love him.
The fear of the Lord is glory and pride, joy and a crown of gladness.
The fear of the Lord gladdens the heart, it gives cheer, joy, and long life.
Whoever fears the Lord will come to a good end; he will be blessed on the day of his death.
The beginning of wisdom is to fear the Lord; she is formed together with the faithful in the mother's womb.
Among human beings she has built herself an eternal home, and she will stay faithful to their descendants.
The fullness of wisdom is to fear the Lord; she makes her own drunk with her fruits.
She fills their whole house with precious things, and their storerooms with her produce.
The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; it makes peace and health blossom.
The Lord saw her and measured her; he rained down knowledge and understanding, and he exalted the glory of those who possess her.
The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and her branches are long life.
The fear of the Lord drives away sin; whoever holds fast to it turns away wrath.
An unjust and hot-tempered man cannot be justified, for the surge of his fury brings about his ruin.
The patient man holds firm until the right moment, and then joy returns to him.
Until the right moment he keeps his words to himself, and many will praise his wisdom.
In the treasures of wisdom are the maxims of knowledge, but piety is loathsome to the sinner.
Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you;
for wisdom and instruction are the fear of the Lord, and what pleases him is faithfulness and gentleness.
Do not resist the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a divided heart.
Do not be a hypocrite before others, and keep watch over your lips.

Do not exalt yourself, or you may fall and bring shame upon yourself; for the Lord will lay bare your secrets and cast you down in the midst of the assembly, because you did not come to the fear of the Lord and your heart is full of deceit.
My son, if you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for testing.
Steady your heart and stand firm, do not be shaken in the time of misfortune.
Cling to him and do not leave him, so that you may grow to the end of your days.
Accept whatever happens to you, and in the reverses of your humiliation be patient;
for gold is tested in the fire, and those pleasing to God in the furnace of humiliation.
Trust in him, and he will help you; make your paths straight and hope in him.
You who fear the Lord, wait for his mercy; do not turn away, or you may fall.
You who fear the Lord, trust in him, and your reward will not be lost.
You who fear the Lord, hope for good things, for everlasting joy and mercy.
Look at the generations of old and see: who ever hoped in the Lord and was disappointed? Who remained in his fear and was forsaken? Who called upon him and was despised?
For the Lord is tenderness and compassion; he forgives sins and saves in the day of distress.
Woe to faint hearts, to powerless hands, and to the sinner who walks on two paths!
Woe to the weak heart that does not believe: it will have no protection.
Woe to you who have lost heart! What will you do when the Lord comes to visit?
Those who fear the Lord do not disobey his words, and those who love him keep his ways.
Those who fear the Lord seek to please him, and those who love him are filled with his law.
Those who fear the Lord set their hearts in order and humble themselves before him,
saying: "Let us fall into the hands of the Lord, not into the hands of men, for his greatness equals his mercy."
Listen to me, my children, for I am your father, and act accordingly, so that you may be saved;
for the Lord wills that a father be honored by his children, and he has confirmed the mother's right over them.
Whoever honors his father atones for his faults,
and whoever respects his mother stores up a treasure.
Whoever honors his father will find his joy in his own children, and he will be heard on the day of his prayer.
Whoever honors his father will have long life; whoever obeys the Lord brings comfort to his mother.
Whoever fears the Lord honors his father and mother, and serves those who gave him life as if they were his masters.
In deed and in word, honor your father, so that his blessing may come upon you;
for a father's blessing makes the house of his children secure, but a mother's curse tears out its foundations.
Do not glory in your father's disgrace: his disgrace is no glory to you;
for a man's glory comes from the honor of his father, and it is a shame for children to have a mother who is despised.
My son, come to your father's aid in his old age, and do not grieve him during his life;
and if his mind fails, be patient, do not despise him, you who are in your full strength.
For kindness to a father will not be forgotten: it will be credited to you in reparation for your sins.
In the day of your distress the Lord will remember you; as ice melts in fair weather, your sins will dissolve.
Whoever abandons his father is like a blasphemer; whoever provokes his mother is cursed by the Lord.
My son, carry out your affairs with gentleness, and you will be loved more than a generous man.
The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord;
for great is the power of the Lord, yet he is glorified by the humble.
Do not seek what is too high for you, do not probe what is beyond your strength;
what has been prescribed for you, that is what you must ponder; you have no need to concern yourself with hidden things.
Do not meddle in what is beyond you: you have already been shown more than the human mind can grasp.
Many have gone astray in their speculations, and evil notions have warped their judgment.
Whoever loves danger will perish by it; the stubborn heart ends in misfortune.
A stubborn heart will be weighed down with troubles, and the sinner heaps sin upon sin.
For the misfortune of the proud there is no remedy, for the evil plant has taken root in him.
The intelligent heart ponders the sayings of the wise, and an attentive ear is the wise man's dream.
Water quenches a blazing fire, and almsgiving atones for sins.
Whoever repays the good done to him prepares for the future, and in the day of misfortune he will find support.
My son, do not deny the poor their livelihood, and do not keep the eyes of the needy waiting.
Do not afflict the hungry, do not exasperate a man in his distress.
Do not further embitter an angry heart, and do not keep the needy waiting for your gift.
Do not turn away the suppliant in his misery, do not turn your face from the poor.
Do not turn your eyes from the needy, do not give him cause to curse you;
for if he curses you in the bitterness of his soul, the one who made him will hear his prayer.
Make yourself beloved in the assembly, and bow your head before a great man.
Lend your ear to the poor, and answer him with gentleness and kindness.
Rescue the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor, and do not be timid when you render justice.
Be a father to orphans and a support to their mother: then you will be like a son of the Most High, and he will love you more than your own mother does.
Wisdom raises up her children and takes care of those who seek her.
Whoever loves her loves life, and whoever seeks her early will be filled with joy.
Whoever possesses her will inherit glory; wherever he goes, the Lord blesses him.
To serve her is to serve the Holy One; those who love her are loved by the Lord.
Whoever listens to her will judge the nations, and whoever holds fast to her will dwell in safety.
If he trusts in her, he will have her as his inheritance, and his descendants will keep her.
For at first she leads him by winding paths, she brings fear and dread upon him, she puts him to torment with her discipline, until she can trust him and has tested him by her demands;
then she comes back to him by the straight path, she gladdens him and reveals her secrets to him.
But if he strays, she abandons him and hands him over to his ruin.
Watch the circumstances and guard yourself against evil, and do not be ashamed of yourself;
for there is a shame that leads to sin, and a shame that brings glory and grace.
Do not show favoritism to your own harm, do not blush to your own downfall.
Do not hold back a word when it can help, do not hide your wisdom;
for wisdom is known by speech, and instruction shows itself in words.
Do not contradict the truth, but blush for your ignorance.
Do not be ashamed to confess your faults, and do not fight against the current of the river.
Do not lie down beneath a fool, do not flatter the power of a great man.
Fight for the truth to the death, and the Lord God will fight for you.
Do not be bold in words and slack in your deeds.
Do not be a lion at home and a coward with your servants.
Do not let your hand be stretched out to receive and closed when it is time to give.
Do not rely on your riches, do not say: "I have enough to live on."
Do not follow your impulses and your strength, indulging the desires of your heart;
do not say: "Who has power over me?", for the Lord will surely punish you.
Do not say: "I have sinned, and what has happened to me?", for the Lord is patient.
Do not be so sure of forgiveness that you heap sin upon sin;
do not say: "His pity is great, he will forgive the mass of my sins"; for with him are mercy and wrath, and his anger falls upon sinners.
Do not delay in returning to the Lord, do not put it off from day to day; for suddenly his wrath will break out, and at the time of punishment you will perish.
Do not rely on ill-gotten riches: they will be of no use in the day of misfortune.
Do not winnow with every wind, do not set out on every path: that is what the double-tongued sinner does.
Be firm in your conviction, and let your word be one.
Be quick to listen, but slow to answer.
If you know something, answer your neighbor; if not, put your hand over your mouth.
Glory and shame lie in the power of speech, and a man's tongue can cause his downfall.
Do not earn a reputation as a slanderer, do not set traps with your tongue; for shame awaits the thief, and a harsh sentence, the double-tongued man.
Whether the fault be small or great, guard against it,
and do not become an enemy instead of a friend; for a bad name brings shame and disgrace: such is the double-tongued sinner.
Do not let yourself be carried away by the heat of your desires, or it may tear you apart like a bull;
you would devour your own foliage, lose your fruit, and leave nothing of yourself but dry wood.
An evil soul destroys the one who bears it and makes him the laughingstock of his enemies.
A gentle word multiplies friends, and a kindly tongue draws kind responses.
Let many be on good terms with you, but let your counselor be one in a thousand.
If you make a friend, make him through testing, and do not trust him too quickly;
for there is the friend of a moment who will not stay in the day of your distress;
there is the friend who turns into an enemy and, to shame you, reveals your quarrels;
there is the friend who shares your table but disappears in the day of misfortune.
In your prosperity he will be another self and give orders to your servants;
in your downfall he will turn against you and hide himself from you.
Keep away from your enemies, and be wary of your friends.
A faithful friend is a sure shelter: whoever has found one has found a treasure.
A faithful friend is beyond price, nothing can weigh his worth.
A faithful friend is a balm of life; those who fear the Lord find one.
Whoever fears the Lord guides his friendship well, for as a man is, so will his friend be.
My son, from your youth welcome instruction, and until your hair turns white you will keep finding wisdom.
Approach her like the plowman and the sower, and wait for her good fruits; a little toil in cultivating her, and soon you will eat of her produce.
How harsh she is to the ignorant! The senseless do not hold fast to her:
she weighs on him like a heavy stone, and he is quick to throw her off;
for wisdom deserves her name: she does not show herself to all.
Listen, my son, welcome my thought, do not reject my counsel.
Put your feet into her fetters, your neck into her collar;
offer your shoulder and carry her, do not chafe at her bonds.
Come to her with all your heart, keep her ways with all your strength;
seek her, follow her trail, and she will make herself known; once you have seized her, do not let her go.
For in the end you will find rest in her, and she will turn into joy for you;
her fetters will become a strong shelter for you, her collar a robe of glory.
She wears an ornament of gold, and her bonds are of violet purple;
you will put her on like a robe of state, you will wear her like a festal crown.
If you are willing, my son, you will become wise, and if you set your heart to it, you will become skilled.
If you love to listen, you will learn; if you lend your ear, you will be wise.
Stand in the assembly of the elders; is someone wise? Attach yourself to him.
Gladly listen to every word of God, and do not let profound proverbs escape you.
If you see a man of good sense, go to him early, and let your foot wear down the threshold of his door.
Meditate on the commandments of the Lord, apply yourself constantly to his precepts; it is he who will make your heart firm, and the wisdom you desire will be given to you.

titres.titre: God, the priests, and the poor

versets.t: Do no evil, and evil will not seize you;
turn away from injustice, and it will turn away from you.
My son, do not sow in the furrows of injustice, or you may reap it sevenfold.
Do not ask the Lord for power, nor the king for a place of honor.
Do not make yourself out to be righteous before the Lord, nor wise before the king.
Do not seek to become a judge, or you may be unable to root out injustice, may yield before a powerful man, and so compromise your integrity.
Do not set a whole city against you, do not throw yourself into the crowd.
Do not bind sin twice, for even for one you will not go unpunished.
Do not say: "God will look at the multitude of my offerings; when I present them to the Most High God, he will accept them."
Do not be timid in your prayer, and do not neglect to give alms.
Do not mock the man whose heart is grieved, for there is One who both humbles and exalts.
Do not forge a lie against your brother, and do the same to no friend.
Refuse to tell any lie, for it leads to nothing good.
Do not chatter in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat yourself over and over in your prayer.
Do not hate hard work or the labor of the fields, which the Most High has appointed.
Do not count yourself among the crowd of sinners; remember that wrath will not delay.
Humble your soul deeply, for the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms.
Do not exchange a friend for money, nor a true brother for the gold of Ophir.
Do not part with a wise and good wife, for her charm is worth more than gold.
Do not mistreat the servant who works faithfully, nor the laborer who gives himself to your task.
Love an intelligent servant, do not deny him his freedom.
Do you have livestock? Take care of it; if it profits you, keep it.
Do you have sons? Instruct them, and bend their necks from childhood.
Do you have daughters? Watch over their purity, and do not show them too indulgent a face.
Marry off your daughter: it will be a great matter settled; give her to a sensible man.
Do you have a wife after your own heart? Do not send her away.
With all your heart honor your father, and do not forget the pains of your mother;
remember that through them you came into the world: what can you give them in return for what they gave you?
Fear the Lord with all your soul, and venerate his priests.
With all your strength love the One who made you, and do not abandon his ministers.
Fear the Lord and honor the priest; give him his share, as it is prescribed for you: the guilt offering, the offering of the shoulders, the holy portion, and the firstfruits.
Stretch out your hand also to the poor, so that your blessing may be complete.
Give generously to all the living, and do not withhold your kindness even from the dead.
Do not turn away from those who weep, but mourn with those who mourn.
Do not neglect to visit the sick: it is by such deeds that you will make yourself loved.
In all that you do, remember your end, and you will never sin.
Do not enter into conflict with a powerful man, or you may fall into his hands.
Do not pick a quarrel with a rich man, or he may tip the scales against you with his gold; for gold has ruined many and led the hearts of kings astray.
Do not argue with a big talker, and do not add wood to his fire.
Do not joke with an ill-bred man, or your ancestors may be dishonored by it.
Do not shame the one who turns away from sin; remember that we all deserve punishment.
Do not despise a man in his old age, for we too will grow old.
Do not rejoice over anyone's death; remember that we will all die.
Do not disdain the discourse of the wise, but ponder their maxims: from them you will learn instruction and the art of serving the great.
Do not let the stories of the elders slip away, for they themselves received them from their fathers: from them you will learn understanding and how to answer at the right moment.
Do not fan the embers of the sinner, or you may be burned by his flame.
Do not give way before the insolent, or he may lay a trap for your words.
Do not lend to one more powerful than you; if you lend to him, consider it lost.
Do not go surety beyond your means; if you have done so, be ready to pay.
Do not go to court against a judge, for they will judge in his favor, given his rank.
Do not travel with a reckless man, or he may bring trouble on you; he does as he pleases, and his folly will destroy you along with him.
Do not quarrel with a hot-tempered man, do not cross the desert with him: blood is nothing in his eyes, and where no one can help you, he will strike you down.
Do not take counsel with a fool, for he will not be able to keep anything to himself.
In the presence of a stranger, do nothing that should remain secret, for you do not know what he will do with it.
Do not open your heart to just anyone: he might hold it against you.
Do not be jealous of the wife who rests on your heart, or you will teach her to do you harm.
Do not give yourself over to your wife's power to the point where she dominates your authority.
Do not go to meet a woman of loose life, or you may fall into her snares.
Do not linger with a singing girl, or you may be caught by her wiles.
Do not fix your gaze on a young woman, or you may be punished on her account.
Do not give yourself to prostitutes, or you may lose your inheritance.
Do not let your eyes rove through the streets of the city, do not prowl its deserted corners.
Turn your eyes from a beautiful woman, do not stare at a beauty that is not yours; through a woman's beauty many have been ruined, and love flares up over it like a fire.
Never sit beside a married woman, do not sit at table to drink with her, or your heart may turn toward her and passion may drag you to your ruin.
Do not abandon an old friend, for the new one will not be his equal: new friend, new wine; let it age, and you will drink it with pleasure.
Do not envy the glory of the sinner, for you do not know how he will end.
Do not take pleasure in what pleases the ungodly; remember that they will not go unpunished until the realm of the dead.

Keep far from the man who has power to kill, and you will not know the fear of death; if you approach him, commit no fault, or he may take your life: know that you are walking amid traps and treading on the city rampart.
As much as you can, seek to know your neighbor, and take counsel from the wise.
Let your conversation be with intelligent people, and all your discussions about the law of the Most High.
Let the righteous be your table companions, and let your pride be in the fear of God.
A work is praised for the artist's hand, and the leader of the people for the wisdom of his speech.
The big talker is feared in his city, and the braggart is hated for his words.
A wise magistrate educates his people, and the government of a sensible man is well ordered.
As the leader of the people, so his officers; as the governor of a city, so its inhabitants.
A king without instruction ruins his people, but a city grows rich through the good sense of its leaders.
Power over the earth is in the hand of the Lord; in due time he raises up over it the right man.
A man's success is in the hand of the Lord, and it is he who confers authority on the magistrate.
Do not hold any wrong against your neighbor, and do nothing by violence.
Pride is hateful to the Lord and to human beings, and injustice revolts them both.
Sovereignty passes from one people to another because of injustice, violence, and greed for riches.
Why be proud, you who are only dust and ashes? Even while you live, your inward parts decay.
A long illness baffles the physician; today's king will die tomorrow.
When a man dies, his inheritance is vermin, beasts, and worms.
The beginning of pride is to move away from the Lord and to turn one's heart from the One who made him;
for the beginning of pride is sin, and whoever clings to it pours out abomination. That is why the Lord inflicts terrible punishments on him and reduces him to nothing.
The Lord overturns the thrones of the mighty and sets the humble in their place.
The Lord tears out the roots of nations and plants the humble in their place.
The Lord upheaves the lands of the nations and destroys them to the very foundations of the earth;
he sweeps several of them away, exterminates them, and blots out their memory from the earth.
Pride was not made for man, nor insolent fury for one born of woman.
Which race deserves honor? The human race. Which one? Those who fear the Lord. Which race deserves contempt? The human race. Which one? Those who break the commandments.
Among his brothers the leader is honored, but in the eyes of the Lord it is those who fear him.
Rich, noble, or poor, their pride is the fear of the Lord.
It is not right to despise a poor man who is intelligent, and it is not fitting to honor a sinner.
The great, the judge, and the powerful are honored, but none is greater than the one who fears the Lord.
Free men will serve a prudent servant, and the sensible man will not complain of it.
Do not play the expert in carrying out your task, and do not boast in the time of hardship.
Better the man who works and lives in plenty than the one who parades himself and lacks bread.
My son, honor yourself with modesty, and value yourself at your true worth.
Who will vindicate the man who harms himself? Who will honor one who dishonors himself?
The poor man is honored for his knowledge, and the rich man for his fortune.
Honored in poverty, how much more would he be in wealth! Despised in wealth, how much more in poverty!
The wisdom of the humble man lifts up his head and seats him among the great.
Do not praise a man for his beauty, and do not loathe anyone for his appearance.
The bee is small among winged creatures, but its fruit is the sweetest of all.
Do not glory in the clothes that cover you, do not swell with pride in the day of glory; for the works of the Lord are wonderful, and his action remains hidden from human beings.
Many kings have found themselves on the ground, and one no one expected has worn the crown.
Many powerful men have been covered with shame, and illustrious men handed over into the hands of others.
Before you inquire, do not blame; examine first, then reprove.
Do not answer before you have listened, and do not interrupt others while they speak.
Do not argue about a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit with sinners to judge.
My son, do not scatter yourself over a thousand occupations: by taking on too much, you will not be without fault; by chasing after everything, you will attain nothing and will not come out clear.
One man wears himself out, struggles and hurries, and is only further behind.
Another is weak, begging for help, short of strength and overwhelmed with misery; but the eyes of the Lord look on him with kindness, he raises him from his lowliness,
and makes him lift up his head, to the astonishment of many.
Good and evil, life and death, poverty and wealth, all come from the Lord.
The gifts of the Lord remain with the devout, and his favor makes them prosper forever.
One man grows rich by economy and calculation, and here is the reward he draws from it:
he says to himself: "I have found rest, now I will enjoy my goods"; but he does not know how much time will pass: he will leave everything to others and die.
Stay faithful to your duty, live by it, and grow old in your work.
Do not be astonished at the successes of the sinner; trust in the Lord and persevere in your labor; for it is easy for the Lord to enrich the poor man in an instant.
The blessing of the Lord rewards the devout man: in a moment he makes his blessing flourish.
Do not say: "What do I need? What good can I still expect?"
Nor say: "I have all I need, what harm could reach me?"
In the day of good fortune, misfortune is forgotten; in the day of misfortune, good fortune is no longer remembered;
for it is easy for the Lord, on the day of death, to repay each one according to his conduct.
A moment of misfortune makes well-being forgotten, and at a man's end his deeds are revealed.
Call no one happy before his death: it is at his end that a man is judged.
Do not bring just anyone into your home, for many are the traps of the deceiver.
Like the partridge trapped in its cage, so is the heart of the proud: like a spy, he watches for your fall.
Turning good into evil, he lays snares, and casts a stain on what is purest.
A spark kindles a great blaze; so the sinner, lying in wait, seeks to shed blood.
Beware of the wicked man, for he plots evil, or he may put an indelible stain on you.
Take a stranger into your home, and he will turn everything upside down and set you at odds with your own people.

titres.titre: To whom good should be done

versets.t: If you do good, know to whom you do it, and you will be thanked for your kindnesses.
Do good to the devout man, and you will be rewarded, if not by him, then by the Most High.
No kindness for the one who persists in evil or for the one who refuses to give alms.
Give to the devout man, but do not help the sinner.
Do good to the humble, give nothing to the ungodly; refuse him bread, or he may become stronger than you through it; for all the good you would do him would come back to you doubled in evil.
The Most High himself hates sinners, and he will take vengeance on the ungodly.
Give to the good man, and do not help the sinner.
It is not in prosperity that a friend is tested, nor in adversity that an enemy is hidden.
When a man is fortunate, his enemies are grieved; when he is unfortunate, even his friend keeps away from him.
Never trust your enemy, for his malice is like bronze that gathers rust;
even if he plays the humble man and walks bowed down, be on your guard and beware of him; treat him like one polishing a mirror, and you will see that his rust keeps coming back.

Do not set him at your side, or he may overturn you and take your place; do not seat him at your right hand, or he may covet your seat; in the end you would understand my words, and my warnings would grieve you.
Who will pity the snake charmer bitten by the serpent, or all those who approach wild beasts?
So too whoever associates with a sinner and gets mixed up in his faults.
He stays an hour with you; but if you falter, he will hold on no longer.
The enemy has sweetness on his lips, but in his heart he plots to throw you into the pit; he has tears in his eyes, but if he finds the chance, he will not have his fill of your blood.
If misfortune reaches you, you will find him there ahead of you, and, pretending to help you, he will trip you up;
then he will shake his head, clap his hands, whisper endlessly, and change his expression.
Whoever touches pitch is smeared by it, and whoever keeps company with the proud becomes like him.

Do not load your shoulders with a burden too heavy, do not bind yourself to one stronger and richer than you. What accord is there between the clay pot and the cauldron? The cauldron will strike the pot, and the pot will shatter.
The rich man does a wrong, and it is he who is indignant; the poor man is wronged, and it is he who must apologize.
As long as you are useful to him, he exploits you; when you have nothing left, he drops you.
Do you have wealth? He will live with you, he will strip you bare without the slightest remorse.
Does he need you? He will flatter you, smile at you, make you promises, say fine things to you: "What do you need?"
He will lavish banquets on you until he has stripped you two or three times over; in the end he will mock you, then look at you and forsake you, shaking his head.
Take care not to let yourself be deceived and so be humiliated in your fine self-assurance.
If a great man invites you, hold back, and he will invite you all the more insistently.
Do not press too eagerly toward him, or you may be pushed away; do not keep too far off, or you may be forgotten.
Do not presume to speak with him as an equal, do not trust his flood of words; for by all that chatter he is testing you, and, with a smile, he is sounding you out.
Without pity he will not keep your words to himself, and he will spare you neither blows nor chains.
Take care, be very attentive, for you are walking on the edge of your ruin.
Every living thing loves its own kind, and every man his neighbor.
All flesh unites according to its kind, and every man attaches himself to one like himself.
What accord is there between the wolf and the lamb? No more between the sinner and the devout man.
What peace is there between the hyena and the dog? What peace between the rich man and the poor man?
Wild donkeys are the prey of lions in the desert; so the poor are the food of the rich.
The proud man loathes the humble; so the rich man loathes the poor.
Does the rich man stumble? His friends hold him up. Does the humble man fall? His friends push him further down.
The rich man slips: many come to his aid; he talks nonsense, and they say he is right. The humble man slips: they blame him into the bargain; he speaks with good sense, and they make no room for him.
The rich man speaks: all fall silent and extol his discourse to the skies. The poor man speaks: they say "Who is this?", and if he stumbles, they finish him off.
Wealth is good when it is without sin, and poverty is only wicked on the lips of the ungodly.
A man's heart changes his face, for good or for evil;
the sign of a happy heart is a radiant face, but finding wise maxims costs reflection.

titres.titre: The good and bad use of goods
The happiness of the seeker of wisdom

versets.t: Happy the man who has not failed in his words and is not tormented by remorse for sin!
Happy the one whose conscience does not condemn him and who has not fallen away from his hope!
To the mean-spirited man wealth does not suit; what good are goods to the envious?
Whoever hoards by depriving himself hoards for others, and it is strangers who will feast on his goods.
Whoever is harsh with himself, to whom will he be good? He does not even enjoy what he possesses.
There is nothing worse than the man who is harsh with himself: this is the wage of his wickedness.
If he does a little good, it is by mistake, and in the end he lets his malice show.
He is wicked, the man with the envious eye, who turns his eyes away and despises others.
The eye of the greedy is not content with its share, and his evil covetousness withers his soul.
The eye of the miser scrimps on bread, and want is at his own table.
My son, according to your means, treat yourself well, and present worthy offerings to the Lord.
Remember that death does not delay and that the pact of the realm of the dead is not revealed to you.
Before you die, do good to your friend; according to your means, open your hand and give to him.
Do not deprive yourself of a day of happiness, do not let slip any share of a good pleasure.
Will you not leave to others the fruit of your labors, and what you have earned to be divided by lot?
Give and receive, and refresh your soul, for in the realm of the dead there is no pleasure to be sought.
All flesh grows old like a garment, for the law of all time is: you will surely die.
Like foliage on a leafy tree, of which some fall and others grow, so are the generations of flesh and blood: one dies out, another is born.
Every corruptible work passes away, and its maker goes with it.
Happy the man who meditates on wisdom and reasons with understanding,
who reflects in his heart on the ways of wisdom and penetrates her secrets!
He pursues her like a hunter and lies in wait at her entrances;
he leans in at her windows and listens at her door;
he camps close to her dwelling and drives his stake into her walls;
he pitches his tent beside her and settles in a home of happiness;
he shelters his children under her foliage and rests beneath her branches;
in her shade he is protected from the heat, and he dwells in her glory.

titres.titre: Wisdom and the gift of freedom
God drives no one to sin

versets.t: So acts the one who fears the Lord; whoever holds fast to the law will obtain wisdom.
She comes to meet him like a mother, she welcomes him like a young bride;
she feeds him with the bread of understanding and gives him the water of wisdom to drink.
He leans on her and does not stumble; he clings to her and is not put to shame.
She raises him above his companions and opens his mouth in the midst of the assembly;
she gives him as his portion joy, a crown of gladness, and an everlasting name.
Fools will not reach her, and sinners will not even see her;
she keeps far from the proud, and liars will not think of her.
Praise ill suits the mouth of the sinner, for it does not come to him from the Lord;
praise is born of wisdom, and the Lord makes it prosper.
Do not say: "It is the Lord who made me sin," for he does not do what he hates.
Do not say: "It is he who led me astray," for he has no use for the sinner.
The Lord hates every abomination, and those who fear him do not love it either.
In the beginning he created man and left him in the power of his own choice.
If you are willing, you will keep the commandments, and remaining faithful depends on your good will;
he has set before you fire and water: you stretch out your hand toward whichever you choose.
Before man are life and death: whichever he prefers will be given to him.
Great is the wisdom of the Lord; strong and almighty, he sees all things;
his eyes are on those who fear him, and he knows every deed of man.
He has commanded no one to be ungodly, and he has given no one permission to sin.
Do not wish for a crowd of good-for-nothing children, do not set your joy in ungodly sons.
If they multiply, do not rejoice in them if they do not have the fear of the Lord;
do not hope for a long life for them, do not count on their number: one is better than a thousand, and it is better to die childless than to have ungodly children.
Through one sensible man a city is peopled, but the race of the wicked will be destroyed.
I have seen many examples with my own eyes, and my ear has heard of even graver ones.
Fire is kindled over the assembly of sinners, and wrath blazes up against a rebellious people.
The Lord did not forgive the giants of old, who rebelled in their strength;
he did not spare the city where Lot lived, held in horror for its pride;
he had no pity on the people doomed to destruction, wiped out for their sins;
and likewise the six hundred thousand foot soldiers, gathered together in the hardness of their heart.
Were there even a single stiff-necked man, it would be a wonder if he went unpunished; for with the Lord are mercy and wrath: mighty to forgive, he also pours out his anger.
As great as his mercy is, so great is his severity; he judges each one according to his works.
The sinner will not escape with his plunder, and the hope of the devout will not be disappointed.
Every act of almsgiving will find its place, and each one will be treated according to his works.
Do not say: "I will hide myself from the Lord; up there, who will think of me? In the crowd I will be forgotten; what am I in the immensity of creation?"
See: the heavens, the highest heavens, the deep and the earth tremble when he visits them;
the mountains and the foundations of the earth quake together when he looks upon them.
But the heart of man does not reflect on this; who then ponders his ways?
The hurricane itself escapes the eyes of man, and most of the works of God are hidden.
"Who will announce the works of his justice, who will wait for them? The covenant of judgment is so far off!"
So thinks the man without understanding; the fool who goes astray dreams of nothing but follies.
Listen to me, my son, learn wisdom, and make your heart attentive to my words.
I will set out for you a well-weighed teaching and make known to you an exact knowledge.
