The works of the Lord have endured from the beginning as he arranged them; from their creation he fixed their domains.
He ordered his works forever, and their dominion through the ages: they feel no hunger and no weariness and never interrupt their task;
none collides with its neighbor, and they never disobey his word.
After that, the Lord looked at the earth and filled it with his good things;
with living beings of every kind he covered its surface, and it is to it that they must return.

titres.titre: The creation of man and the covenant

versets.t: The Lord created man from the earth and makes him return to it.
He set for him a number of days and a fixed span of time, and gave him power over all that is on the earth.
He clothed him with a strength suited to himself and made him in his own image;
he set the fear of man on all flesh, so that he might rule over beasts and birds.
He gave them discernment, a tongue, eyes, ears, and a heart to think with.
He filled them with knowledge and understanding, and showed them good and evil.
He set his own eye in their hearts to make them see the greatness of his works,
so that they might praise his holy name and proclaim the wonders he has done.
He gave them knowledge as well and put them in possession of the law of life;
he made an everlasting covenant with them and revealed his commandments to them.
Their eyes saw the splendor of his glory, and their ears heard the majesty of his voice.
He said to them: "Guard yourselves against all injustice," and he laid down for each one his duties toward his neighbor.
Their ways are always before him, nothing escapes his gaze.
To each people he gave a leader, but Israel is the Lord's portion.
All their works are before him like the sun, and his eyes are constantly on their paths.
Their injustices are not hidden from him, and all their sins are before the Lord.
A man's almsgiving is like a seal to him, and he keeps a man's good deeds like the apple of his eye.
One day he will rise up and repay them according to their deeds, bringing down on their heads what is due to them.
But to those who repent he opens the way back, and he comforts those who had lost hope.
Return to the Lord and give up your sins; pray before his face and lessen your offenses.
Turn back to the Most High, turn away from injustice, and deeply hate what is abominable.
Who will praise the Most High in the realm of the dead, in place of the living who give him thanks?
With the dead, as though he no longer existed, praise dies away; it is the living, those in good health, who praise the Lord.
How great is the mercy of the Lord, and his forgiveness for those who return to him!
For not everything can be found among human beings, since the son of man is not immortal.
What is brighter than the sun? Yet it is eclipsed; so flesh and blood think only of evil.
The sun watches over the army of the stars in the heights of the sky, but all human beings are only dust and ashes.

titres.titre: The greatness of God and his patience

versets.t: He who lives forever created all things without exception;
the Lord alone will be found righteous.
To no one has he granted the power to recount his works, and who will discover his mighty deeds?
Who will measure the might of his majesty, and who will retell his acts of mercy?
Nothing to take away, nothing to add: one cannot fathom the wonders of the Lord.
When a man has finished, he is only beginning; when he stops, he is left perplexed.
What is man, and what use is he? What is his good, and what is his evil?
The span of his life is a hundred years, at most;
like a drop of water in the sea, like a grain of sand, so are his few years against eternity.
That is why the Lord is patient with human beings and pours out his mercy on them.
He sees and knows that their end is wretched; so he multiplies his forgiveness.
Man's pity goes to his neighbor, but the mercy of the Lord extends to all flesh: he rebukes, corrects, teaches, and brings back, as a shepherd does his flock.
He has pity on those who accept correction and are eager to keep his precepts.
My son, do not add reproach to your kindness, nor hurtful words to your gifts.
Does not the dew relieve the heat? So a good word is worth more than a gift.
See: does not a word surpass a gift? The gracious man joins both.
The fool reproaches without restraint, and the gift of the envious dries up the eyes.
Before you speak, learn; before illness, take care of yourself.
Before judgment, examine yourself, and at the hour of inquiry you will find favor.
Before you fall ill, humble yourself, and in the time of fault, show your conversion.
Let nothing prevent you from fulfilling your vow in time; do not wait for death to discharge it.
Before making a vow, prepare yourself, and do not be like one who puts the Lord to the test.
Think of the wrath of the last days, of the time of punishment, when he will turn away his face.
In the time of plenty, think of hunger; in the days of wealth, of poverty and want.
From morning to evening the times change: everything moves swiftly before the Lord.
The wise man is on his guard in all things; in the days of sin, he guards himself against fault.
Every sensible man recognizes wisdom and pays homage to the one who has found her.
Those who know how to savor the words of the wise are wise themselves and rain down just maxims.
Do not let yourself be led by your cravings, and rein in your desires.
If you grant your soul all its whims, it will make you the laughingstock of your enemies.
Do not set your joy in the pleasures of good food, do not tie yourself to its expense;
do not impoverish yourself by banqueting with borrowed money, when your purse is empty.
The workman who drinks will not grow rich; whoever neglects the little he has will soon fall into ruin.
Wine and women lead sensible men astray, and whoever consorts with prostitutes loses all restraint:
rot and worms will make him their prey, and the reckless soul will be cut off.
Whoever believes too quickly is light of heart, and whoever sins this way harms himself.
Whoever delights in wicked talk will be condemned,
and whoever hates gossip escapes evil.
Never repeat what is said, and you will lose nothing by it;
whether to friend or enemy, do not repeat it, and, unless it is a fault not to, do not disclose it;
for people would listen to you, would grow wary of you, and in time would hate you.
Have you heard something? Let it die with you! Take heart, it will not make you burst.
Over a piece of news the fool suffers like a woman in labor;
like an arrow lodged in the thigh, so is a word in the heart of the fool.
Question your friend: perhaps he has done nothing; and if he has done something, let him not do it again.
Question your friend: perhaps he has said nothing; and if he has said it, let him not repeat it.
Question your friend, for often there is slander: do not believe everything that is reported.
One man may slip without setting his heart on it; and who has never sinned with his tongue?
Reprove your friend before coming to threats, and make room for the law of the Most High.
All wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom there is the fulfillment of the law.
The knowledge of evil is not wisdom, and the counsel of sinners is not prudence.
There is a cleverness that is hateful, and there is a naivety that is only a lack of wisdom.
Better a little understanding with the fear of God than much knowledge with contempt for the law.
There is a shrewdness that is cunning but unjust, and one man twists things to make his cause prevail.
One man walks bent over, with a downcast air, but his heart is full of deceit;
he bows his head, turns a deaf ear, and, as soon as no one is watching, he gets the better of you.
And if weakness keeps him from sinning, he will do evil as soon as he finds the chance.
A man is known by his appearance, and the wise man by his face when you meet him;
a man's dress, his laugh, his gait reveal what he is.
There are reproofs that come at the wrong moment, and one who keeps silent is the wiser.
Better to reprove than to hold a grudge, and whoever admits his fault escapes harm.
Like the eunuch who claims to deflower a young girl, so is the one who tries to render justice by force.
One man keeps silent and passes for wise, another makes himself hateful by his chatter.
One man keeps silent for lack of anything to answer, another keeps silent because he knows the right moment.
The wise man keeps silent until the favorable moment, but the braggart and the fool let it pass.
Whoever talks too much makes himself hated, and whoever claims every right makes himself odious.
There are misfortunes that make a man's happiness, and windfalls that turn to his ruin.
One gift brings you nothing in return, and another is repaid double.
There are humiliations that follow glory, and one man has lifted his head after being brought low.
One man buys much at a low price and pays for it seven times its worth.
The wise man, by his words, makes himself loved, but the flatteries of fools are wasted.
The gift of the fool will do you no good, for he expects in return far more than he gave;
he gives little and reproaches much, he opens his mouth like a town crier; he lends today and demands repayment tomorrow: such is a hateful man.
The fool says: "I have no friend, no one is grateful for my kindnesses; those who eat my bread have wicked tongues."
How many times, and by how many people, will he be made a laughingstock!
Better a slip on the ground than a slip of the tongue: so the ruin of the wicked comes quickly.
A graceless man is like a tale told out of place, forever on the lips of the ill-bred.
A maxim spoken by a fool is rejected, for he does not say it at the right time.
One man cannot sin, for lack of means, and in his repose he has no remorse.
One man ruins himself through false shame and falls because of a fool's look;
another, through false shame, promises too much to his friend and needlessly makes an enemy of him.
Lying is a shameful stain in a man, forever on the lips of the ignorant.
Better a thief than an inveterate liar, but both are rushing to their ruin.
The liar has no honor, and his shame follows him without respite.
The wise man, by his words, gains in esteem, and the prudent man pleases the great.
Whoever cultivates his land increases his harvest, and whoever pleases the great is forgiven his faults.
Gifts and presents blind the eyes of the wise and, like a muzzle, stop the mouth from reproving.
Hidden wisdom, invisible treasure: what use are either of them?
Better the man who hides his folly than the one who hides his wisdom.
My son, have you sinned? Do it no more, and pray for your past faults.
Flee from sin as from a serpent; if you approach it, it will bite you: its teeth are the teeth of a lion, which put men to death.
Every fault is like a two-edged sword: the wound it makes is incurable.
Terror and violence lay wealth waste: so the house of the proud will be laid waste.
The prayer of the poor rises from his mouth to the ear of God, and judgment on his oppressor comes down very quickly.
Whoever hates reproof follows the track of the sinner, but whoever fears God is converted with all his heart.
The smooth talker is noticed from afar, but the sensible man knows when he is failing.
To build one's house with another's money is to gather stones for one's own tomb.
A gathering of the ungodly is a heap of tow: it will end in flames.
The path of sinners is paved with flagstones, but it leads to the pit of the realm of the dead.
Whoever keeps the law masters his thoughts, and the fruit of the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
Whoever has no sense will not be taught, but there is a cleverness that breeds bitterness.
The knowledge of the wise man overflows like a river, and his counsel is a spring of life.
The inside of the fool is like a cracked jar: it holds no knowledge.
Let the intelligent man hear a wise word, and he approves it and adds to it; let the debauched man hear it, and it displeases him and he throws it behind his back.
The discourse of the fool weighs like a burden on a journey, but on the lips of the intelligent man is found grace.
In the assembly the word of the prudent man is sought, and his sayings are pondered in the heart.
For the fool, wisdom is a house in ruins, and the knowledge of the senseless, mere babble.
Instruction is for the senseless man like fetters on the feet, handcuffs on the right hand.
The fool laughs at the top of his voice, but the shrewd man barely smiles, quietly.
Instruction is for the sensible man an ornament of gold, a bracelet on the right arm.
The fool enters your home with hurried step, but the man of experience stops, discreet, on the threshold.
The senseless man leans in at the door to look into the house, but the well-bred man stays outside.
It is coarse to eavesdrop at doors; the sensible man would be ashamed of it.
The lips of chatterers repeat the words of others, but the words of the wise are weighed in the balance.
The heart of fools is in their mouth, but the mouth of the wise is in their heart.
When the ungodly curses his adversary, it is himself he curses.
The slanderer defiles himself and makes himself hated by those around him.
The sluggard is like a filthy stone, and everyone hisses at his disgrace.
The sluggard is like a lump of dung: whoever picks it up shakes his hand.
A badly raised son is the shame of his father, and a daughter like him is born to his misfortune.
A sensible daughter will find a husband, but one who brings shame is her father's grief.
The brazen woman dishonors father and husband, and both will despise her.
A speech out of season is like music in the midst of mourning; but blows and correction are wisdom at all times.
To instruct a fool is to glue a broken pot back together, to wake a man from a deep sleep;
to speak to a fool is to speak to a sleeper: at the end of your speech, he will say: "What was that?"
Weep for the dead, he has lost the light; weep for the fool, he has lost his sense. Weep less for the dead, for he has found rest, but the life of the fool is worse than death.
Mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but for the fool and the ungodly, all their life.

Do not talk much with the senseless, do not go about with the fool; guard yourself against him, and you will have no trouble and will not be defiled by contact with him; keep away from him, and you will find rest and will not have to grieve over his folly.
What is heavier than lead? And what other name to give it than "fool"?
Sand, salt, a mass of iron are more easily borne than a man without understanding.
A well-built framework does not come apart in an earthquake: so a heart steadied by well-considered decision does not give way at the critical moment.
A heart resting on thoughtful reflection is like a smooth coating on a polished wall:
a fence on a height does not stand against the wind; so a fearful heart, with its foolish resolves, does not withstand fear.
Whoever hurts an eye brings tears; whoever hurts a heart awakens pain.
Whoever throws a stone at birds scatters them; whoever insults his friend breaks the friendship.
Have you drawn your sword against your friend? Do not despair, a return is possible.

Have you opened your mouth against him? Do not be afraid, reconciliation is possible; but insult, arrogance, the betrayal of a secret, a treacherous stab of the tongue: these are what put every friend to flight.
Stay faithful to your neighbor in his poverty, and you will share in his prosperity; remain with him in trial, and you will have a part in his goods.
Before the fire come the steam and smoke of the furnace; so, before bloodshed, come insults.
I will not be ashamed to protect a friend, and I will not hide myself from him;
if some harm comes to me through him, all who hear of it will beware of him.
Who will set a guard over my mouth and on my lips a prudent seal, so that I may not fall because of them and my tongue may not destroy me?
Lord, Father and Master of my life, do not abandon me to the whim of my lips, do not let me fall because of them.
Who will apply the whip to my thoughts, and to my heart the discipline of wisdom, so that they may not spare me in my errors and may not let my faults pass,
lest my errors multiply, lest my sins abound, lest I fall before my adversaries and my enemy rejoice over me?
Lord, Father and God of my life, do not give me haughty eyes,
and turn covetousness away from me;
let the craving of the senses and the desire of the flesh not take hold of me, and do not hand me over to a shameless soul.
Listen, my children, to the discipline of the mouth: whoever observes it will not be caught in the snare.
The sinner is trapped by his own lips, and the slanderer and the proud man find their downfall there.
Do not accustom your mouth to oaths, and do not make a habit of naming the Holy One;
for, as the slave who is constantly whipped is never without bruises, so the one who swears and invokes the Name at every turn will not be clean of sin.

The man of many oaths multiplies iniquity, and the scourge will not leave his house: if he breaks his oath, his fault is upon him; if he pays no heed, he sins doubly; if he has sworn falsely, he will not be justified, and his house will be filled with misfortunes.
There is a way of speaking that calls down death: may it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob! All this remains far from the devout, who do not wallow in these sins.
Do not accustom your mouth to coarse impurity, for it leads to sinful words.

Remember your father and mother when you sit among the great, lest by force of habit you make a fool of yourself before them and come to wish you had never been born and to curse the day of your birth.
Whoever grows used to insulting speech will never correct himself as long as he lives.

Two kinds of men multiply sins, and the third draws down wrath: passion burning like a blazing fire will not be quenched until it has consumed itself; the man given over to his own flesh will not stop until the fire devours him.
To the debauched man all bread is sweet; he will not tire of it until his death.
The man who betrays his marriage bed says in his heart: "Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, the walls hide me, no one sees me: what should I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins."
He fears only the eyes of men, and he does not know that the eyes of the Lord are a thousand times brighter than the sun, that they observe all the ways of man and penetrate the most hidden corners.
Before they were even created, all things were known to him, and so they are after they are finished.
This man will be punished in the streets of the city; where he least expected it, he will be seized.
So too the woman who has been unfaithful to her husband and given him an heir by another:
first she disobeyed the law of the Most High, then she sinned against her husband, and finally she defiled herself by adultery and bore children of another's blood.
She will be brought before the assembly, and the punishment will reach her children;
her children will not take root, and her branches will bear no fruit;
she will leave behind a cursed memory, and her shame will never be blotted out.
And those who survive will understand that there is nothing better than the fear of the Lord, nothing sweeter than to observe his commandments.
Wisdom sings her own praise, she glories in the midst of her people;
she opens her mouth in the assembly of the Most High, she glories before his Power:
"I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, and like a mist I covered the earth;
I dwelt in the heights, and my throne was on a pillar of cloud;
alone I circled the vault of heaven and walked the depths of the abyss;
over the waves of the sea, over all the earth, over every people and nation, I held sway.
Among all of them I sought a place of rest, a domain in which to dwell.
Then the Creator of all things gave me a command, the one who created me fixed my tent, and he said: 'Dwell in Jacob, take your inheritance in Israel.'
Before the ages, from the beginning, he created me, and never, to all eternity, will I cease to be.
Before him I ministered in the holy Dwelling, and so I gained a foothold in Zion.
In the beloved city he gave me rest, and Jerusalem is the seat of my power.
I took root in a glorious people, in the portion of the Lord, in his inheritance.
I rose up like the cedar of Lebanon, like the cypress on the heights of Hermon;
I rose up like the palm of En-gedi, like the rosebushes of Jericho, like a fair olive tree in the plain; I rose up like a plane tree.
I breathed out my perfume like cinnamon and fragrant balm, like choice myrrh I spread my scent, like galbanum, onyx, and stacte, like a cloud of incense in the Dwelling.
I stretched out my branches like the terebinth, and my boughs are boughs of glory and grace;
like the vine, I put forth lovely shoots, and my flowers gave fruit of glory and wealth.
Come to me, you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits;
for the memory of me is sweeter than honey, and to possess me sweeter than the honeycomb.
Those who eat me will hunger still, those who drink me will thirst still;
whoever obeys me will never be put to shame, and those who act through me will not sin."
All this is none other than the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law that Moses prescribed for us as an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.
It makes wisdom overflow like the Pishon, like the Tigris in the season of the first fruits;
it pours out understanding like the Euphrates, like the Jordan in the time of harvest;
it makes knowledge gush forth like the Nile, like the Gihon in the season of the vintage.
The first who studied her did not finish knowing her, nor did the last penetrate her fully;
for her thought is vaster than the sea, and her counsel deeper than the great abyss.
And I, like a channel drawn off from a river, like a watercourse leading into a garden,
I said: "I will water my garden, I will drench my flowerbed"; and behold, my channel became a river, and my river a sea.
I will make instruction shine like the dawn, I will make it gleam far and wide;
I will pour out teaching once more like prophecy, and I will leave it to future generations.
See: I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek wisdom.
Three things please me, beautiful in the sight of the Lord and of men: harmony among brothers, friendship between neighbors, and a husband and wife who suit each other well.
Three kinds of people fill me with disgust, and their way of life is hateful to me: a proud pauper, a wealthy liar, and an old man who is an adulterer and a fool.
You gathered nothing in your youth: how then could you have anything in your old age?
How fine it is for gray hair to know how to judge, and for the elders to know how to give counsel!
How well wisdom becomes the aged, and reflection and counsel those in high position!
The crown of the aged is long experience, and their pride is the fear of the Lord.
There are nine things my heart counts as happy, and a tenth my tongue proclaims: the man who finds joy in his children, the one who lives to see the downfall of his enemies;
happy is the man who lives with a sensible wife, who does not sin with his tongue, who does not serve a master unworthy of him;
happy is the man who has found prudence and can teach it to an attentive ear!
How great is the man who has found wisdom! Yet no one is above the one who fears the Lord.
The fear of the Lord surpasses everything: to whom can we compare the one who possesses it?
Any wound, but not a wound of the heart; any wickedness, but not the wickedness of a wife.
Any harm, but not the harm done by adversaries; any revenge, but not the revenge of enemies.
There is no venom worse than the venom of a serpent, and no anger worse than the anger of a wife.
I would rather live with a lion and a dragon than share a house with a wicked wife.
The wickedness of a wife alters her face and darkens it like sackcloth;
among his friends her husband sits, and in spite of himself he sighs bitterly.
Any wickedness is slight beside the wickedness of a wife: may the fate of sinners fall upon her!
Like a sandy climb for the feet of an old man, so is a nagging wife to a peaceable husband.
Do not be caught by a woman's beauty, and do not covet her.
It is anger, shame, and great dishonor when a wife supports her husband.
A downcast heart, a mournful face, a wounded soul: this is what a wicked wife brings about; slack hands and failing knees: such is the one who does not make her husband happy.
It was through a woman that sin began, and it is because of her that we all die.
Give water no outlet, and a wicked wife no freedom of speech.
If she will not go as your hand directs, cut her off from your flesh.
Happy is the husband of an excellent wife: the number of his days will be doubled.
A valiant wife brings joy to her husband, who will live out his years in peace.
A good wife is a fine portion, reserved for those who fear the Lord;
rich or poor, her husband's heart is content, and his face is always cheerful.
Three things frighten my heart, and before a fourth I plead with the Lord: the slander of a whole town, the gathering of a mob, and a lying accusation, all harder for me to bear than death;
but grief of heart and pain is a wife jealous of another, and the lash of a tongue that spreads her complaints to all.
A wicked wife is an ill-fitted yoke: to master her is to seize a scorpion.
A drunken wife stirs great anger: she will not even hide her shame.
A wife's misconduct is read in the boldness of her glance and the fluttering of her eyelids.
Over a headstrong daughter keep close watch, lest, seeing you slack, she give herself over.
Beware of a shameless eye, and do not be surprised if it draws you into evil.
As a thirsty traveler opens his mouth and drinks any water he finds, so she sits down before every post and opens her quiver to the first arrow.
A wife's grace brings joy to her husband, and her wisdom restores his strength.
A silent wife is a gift from the Lord, and nothing is worth as much as a well-bred wife;
grace upon grace is a modest wife, and no treasure equals a chaste soul.
As the sun rises over the heights of the Lord, so is the beauty of a good wife in a well-ordered home;
as the lamp shining on the sacred lampstand, so is the beauty of a face upon a straight and upright stature;
as columns of gold on bases of silver, so are shapely legs on firm heels.

Two things sadden my heart, and a third rouses my anger: a warrior brought to poverty, intelligent men treated with contempt, and the one who turns from justice to sin, whom the Lord dooms to the sword.
Hardly will the trader avoid wrongdoing, and the merchant will not be free of sin.
Many have sinned for love of gain, and whoever seeks to grow rich turns a blind eye.
As a stake is driven between two joined stones, so sin slips in between selling and buying.
If you do not hold fast to the fear of the Lord, your house will soon be destroyed.
When the sieve is shaken, the refuse remains; so a man's faults appear in his talk.
The furnace tests the potter's vessels, and the test of a man is in his conversation.
The cultivated tree is judged by its fruit; so speech reveals the depths of the heart.
Praise no one before he has spoken, for that is the test of a man.
Pursue justice and you will attain it, and you will put it on like a robe of honor.
Birds settle among their own kind; so truth returns to those who practice it.
The lion lies in wait for its prey; so sin lies in wait for those who commit injustice.
The talk of a devout man is always wisdom, but the fool changes like the moon.
Among fools, measure out your time, but among thoughtful people, stay on and on.
The conversation of fools is offensive, and their laughter bursts out only in sin.
The speech of a man given to oaths makes the hair stand on end, and his quarreling makes one stop the ears.
The quarrels of the proud make blood flow, and their insults are painful to hear.
Whoever betrays secrets loses trust and will never find a friend after his own heart.
Love your friend and be faithful to him; but if you have disclosed his secrets, do not run after him,
for, as one kills an enemy, so you have killed the friendship of your neighbor;
as one lets a bird slip from the hand, so you have let your friend go, and you will not catch him again.
Do not chase after him, he is far off, fled like a gazelle escaped from the snare;
for a wound can be bound up, an insult can be forgiven, but whoever betrays a secret is without hope.
Whoever winks the eye is plotting evil, and no one will turn him from it;
to your face his mouth is all sweetness, he admires your words; but afterward he will change his tone and give a spiteful twist to your remarks.
There are many things I hate, but nothing as much as him, and the Lord hates him too.
Whoever throws a stone into the air brings it down on his own head, and a treacherous blow wounds the one who deals it.
Whoever digs a pit falls into it, and whoever sets a snare is caught in it.
Whoever does evil sees it come back upon him, without knowing where it came from.
Sarcasm and insult are in the mouth of the proud, but vengeance lies in wait for him like a lion.
Those who rejoice at the misfortune of the devout will fall into the trap, and pain will gnaw at them before they die.
Rancor and anger, these too are detestable things, and the sinner holds them fast.
Whoever takes revenge will feel the vengeance of the Lord, who will keep an exact account of his sins.
Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be pardoned.
If a man nurses anger against another, how can he dare ask the Lord for healing?
He has no mercy on a man like himself, yet he pleads for his own sins!
He who is only flesh holds on to his wrath: who then will win pardon for his sins?
Remember your end and stop hating; think of death and decay, and keep the commandments;
remember the commandments and do not nurse anger against your neighbor; think of the covenant of the Most High, and overlook the offense.
Keep clear of quarrels and you will sin less, for a hot-tempered man kindles strife,
and a sinner troubles friends and sows discord among people who were living in peace.
Fire burns according to its fuel; so a man's anger flares up according to his power: as his wealth grows, so his fury mounts, and it is fanned according to the fierceness of the quarrel.
A headlong quarrel kindles a fire, and a reckless dispute makes blood flow.
Blow on a spark and it bursts into flame; spit on it and it goes out: and both come from your own mouth.
Curse the gossip and the double-tongued, for they have ruined many who were living in peace.
The slanderous tongue has shaken many and driven them from nation to nation; it has overthrown strong cities and torn down the palaces of the great;
the slanderous tongue has caused valiant wives to be divorced and stripped them of the fruit of their labors.
Whoever listens to it will never find rest and will no longer dwell in peace.
A stroke of the whip raises a welt, but a stroke of the tongue breaks the bones.
Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but far more by the tongue.
Happy is the one who is sheltered from it, who has not suffered its fury, who has not dragged its yoke or been bound with its chains;
for its yoke is a yoke of iron, and its chains are chains of bronze.
The death it gives is a dreadful death, and the realm of the dead is better than it.
But it will have no hold on the devout: they will not be burned by its flame.
Those who forsake the Lord will fall into it, and it will consume them without going out.
See: hedge your property about with thorns, put your silver and gold under lock and key,
and for your words make a balance and weights, and for your mouth a door and a bolt.
Take care not to stumble by the tongue, lest you fall before the one who lies in wait for you.
Whoever practices mercy lends to his neighbor, and whoever supports him with his hand keeps the commandments.
Lend to your neighbor when he is in need, and repay in turn, when the time comes, what you have been lent.
Keep your word, deal honestly with him, and at all times you will find what you need.
Many treat a loan as a windfall and cause trouble for those who have helped them:

until they have received it, they kiss the lender's hand and speak in hushed tones of his wealth; but when the time comes to repay, they drag their feet, offer nothing but complaints, and blame hard times.

Can he pay? The lender will scarcely receive back half, and will count himself fortunate; if not, the other cheats him of his money and gains an enemy for nothing, one who repays him with curses and insults and, instead of honor, gives him only abuse.
Many, out of spite, refuse to lend, afraid of being cheated for nothing.
Yet be patient with the unfortunate, and do not keep him waiting for your charity;
help the poor for the sake of the commandment, and in his distress do not send him away empty-handed.
Lose your money for a brother and a friend: do not let it rust uselessly under a stone.
Lay up your treasure according to the precepts of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold;
store almsgiving in your granaries, and it will deliver you from every misfortune:
better than a stout shield, better than a heavy spear, it will fight for you against the enemy.
A good man goes surety for his neighbor, but only the one who has lost all shame abandons him.
Do not forget the kindness of your guarantor, for he pledged himself for you.
The sinner ruins the goods of his guarantor, and the ungrateful man abandons his rescuer.
Going surety has ruined many prosperous people and tossed them about like the waves of the sea;
it has driven powerful men into exile, so that they had to wander among foreign nations.
The sinner rushes to go surety, and whoever chases after gain will fall into lawsuits.
Help your neighbor according to your means, but take care not to fall yourself.
The essentials of life are water, bread, clothing, and a roof to cover one's nakedness.
Better the life of a poor man under a roof of planks than sumptuous feasts in a stranger's house.
Whether you have little or much, be content with it.
It is a wretched life to go from house to house: where you are received as a stranger, you dare not open your mouth.
You give lodging and drink to ungrateful people, and on top of it you hear bitter words:
"Come here, stranger, set the table, and if you have anything, give me something to eat.
Away with you, stranger, make room for a worthier guest: my brother is coming to stay, I need my house."
It is hard, for a man of feeling, to be reproached for his lodging and insulted by his creditor.
Whoever loves his son plies him with the rod, so as to find joy in him later on.
Whoever brings up his son well will profit from him and will glory in him among his relatives.
Whoever instructs his son makes his enemy jealous and will rejoice over him before his friends.
Does his father die? It is as though he had not died, for he leaves behind another self.
In his lifetime he sees him and rejoices; at his death he has no regret:
he leaves behind an avenger against his enemies and a grateful friend.
Whoever spoils his son will bind up his wounds, and at every cry his heart will tremble.
An untrained horse turns stubborn; a son left to himself turns insolent.
Pamper your child and he will make you tremble; play with him and he will bring you grief.
Do not laugh with him, lest you have to suffer for it and end up gnashing your teeth.
Do not give him free rein in his youth, and do not close your eyes to his follies.
Make him bow his head while he is young, correct him while he is a child, lest he grow stubborn, defy you, and break your heart.
Correct your son and give him work to do, lest his misconduct bring you dishonor.
Better a poor man sound and vigorous than a rich man burdened with illness in his body.
Health and a sound constitution are worth more than all the gold, and a robust body more than an immense fortune.
There is no wealth preferable to health of body, and no joy greater than gladness of heart.
Better death than a bitter life, and eternal rest than unending suffering.
Dainties poured out on a closed mouth are like offerings laid on a grave:
what use is an offering to an idol? It can neither eat it nor smell it; so it is with the one whom the Lord afflicts:
he looks on with his eyes and sighs, as a eunuch sighs when he embraces a young woman.
Do not give your soul over to sadness, and do not torment yourself with gloomy thoughts.
Gladness of heart is the life of a man, and cheerfulness prolongs his days.
Love your soul, comfort your heart, drive sadness far from you; for sadness has killed many, and it is of no use at all.
Envy and anger shorten one's days, and worry brings on old age before its time.
A generous and contented heart takes care of its food.
The rich man's sleepless nights waste his flesh, and worry robs him of sleep;
constant worry keeps him from sleeping, as a serious illness drives sleep away.
The rich man toils to amass, and when he rests, he enjoys his pleasures;
the poor man toils for lack of means, and when he rests, he remains in need.
Whoever loves gold will not go blameless, and whoever chases after profit will be led astray by it.
Many have rushed to their ruin because of gold, and their downfall stood before them.
Gold is a snare for those who are mad for it: every fool is caught by it.
Happy is the rich man found without blemish, who has not chased after gold!
Who is he, that we may call him happy? For he has done a marvelous thing among his people.
Who has undergone this test and come through it without reproach? It will be a title of glory for him. Who could have transgressed and did not, could have done evil and refrained?
His fortune will be made secure, and the assembly will proclaim his good deeds.
Are you at a well-laden table? Do not open your mouth wide, and do not say, "What a spread!"
Remember that a greedy eye is an evil thing: nothing worse has been created than the eye, and over everything it weeps.
Where your host is looking, do not reach out your hand, and do not collide with him in the dish.
Judge your neighbor's desires by your own, and in everything act with thought.
Eat like a man what is set before you, and do not chew noisily, lest you disgust others.
Out of good manners, be the first to stop, and do not be greedy, lest you give offense.
If you are at table in a large company, do not help yourself before the others.
How little suffices for a well-bred man! And so he does not gasp for breath on his bed.
Sound sleep comes from a sober stomach: one rises early, the mind refreshed; but insomnia, nausea, and colic are the lot of the intemperate.
If you have been forced to eat too much, get up, go and vomit aside, and you will feel relieved.
Listen to me, my son, do not despise me, and in the end you will recognize the truth of my words: in everything be moderate, and no illness will overtake you.
People bless the one who gives generously, and the testimony to his generosity is well founded;
the town murmurs against the stingy host, and the testimony to his meanness is exact.
Do not play the hero with wine, for wine has ruined many.
The furnace tests the temper of steel; wine tests hearts in the quarrels of the proud.
Wine is like life to a man, if you drink it in moderation. What life does one lead without wine? It was created for the joy of men.
Gladness of heart and joy of soul, such is wine drunk at the right time and in moderation;
bitterness of soul, such is wine drunk to excess, in irritation and dispute.
Drunkenness inflames the fury of the fool and makes him fall, it saps his strength and earns him blows.
At a banquet, do not rebuke your neighbor, do not despise him in his joy, do not say wounding words to him, and do not harass him by demanding what he owes you.

titres.titre: At table and in the assembly
The fear of the Lord and prudence

versets.t: Have they made you master of the feast? Do not put on airs; be among them as one of them; take care of them first, then sit down.
Once all your duties are done, take your place to rejoice with them and to receive the crown for the good ordering of the banquet.
Speak, old man, for it befits you, but with sound judgment and knowledge, and do not disturb the music.
Where there is listening, do not pour out your words, and do not parade your wisdom at the wrong moment.
A ruby seal on a golden ornament, such is a concert in the midst of a banquet.
An emerald seal set in gold, such is a melody over a delicious wine.
Speak, young man, if it is necessary, twice at most, and only if you are asked;
be brief, say much in few words, be like one who knows and yet knows how to keep silent.
Among the great, do not put yourself forward, and where there are elders, speak little.
Before the thunder runs the lightning, and before a modest young man goes favor.
When the time comes, rise from table without lingering, go home and do not delay;
there amuse yourself and do as you please, but without sinning by insolent talk.
And for all this, bless the One who created you and fills you with his good things.
Whoever fears the Lord welcomes correction, and those who seek him at dawn will find his favor.
Whoever seeks the law is satisfied by it, but for the hypocrite it is a stumbling block.
Those who fear the Lord will find right judgment and will make just verdicts shine like a torch.
The sinner shuns reproof and finds excuses to suit himself.
A sensible man overlooks no advice, but the insolent and the proud stop at nothing and, afterward, act without thought.
Do nothing without reflection, and you will not have to repent after the deed.
Do not walk on a broken road, and you will not strike against the stones.
Do not trust a road too smooth, and be wary even of your own children.
In everything you do, watch over yourself, for this too is keeping the commandments.
Whoever trusts the law observes its precepts, and whoever relies on the Lord will suffer no harm.
To the one who fears the Lord, no misfortune comes; though tested, he will be delivered from it.
A wise man does not hate the law, but the hypocrite toward it is like a boat in a storm.
An intelligent man trusts the law, sure for him as a consultation of the Urim.
Prepare your speech and you will be heard; gather your knowledge, then answer.
The inner life of a fool is like a chariot wheel, and his thinking like a turning axle.
A mocking friend is like a stallion that neighs under any rider.
Why does one day surpass another, since all the days of the year receive their light from the sun?
It is the wisdom of the Lord that set them apart: he established the seasons and the feasts;
he raised up and sanctified certain days, and made others ordinary days.
In the same way, all people come from the dust, from the earth from which Adam was formed;
but in his great wisdom the Lord set them apart and traced out for them different paths:
some he blessed and exalted, some he sanctified and drew near to himself; others he cursed and brought low, overthrowing them from their place.
As clay in the potter's hand, who disposes of it as he pleases, so are people in the hand of their Creator, who treats them according to his judgment.
Facing evil, the good; facing death, life; so, facing the just man, the sinner.
Look likewise at all the works of the Most High: they go in pairs, each one set against the other.
And I, who came last, kept watch over wisdom, like one who gleans after the grape-pickers;
by the blessing of the Lord I got ahead and, like a grape-picker, filled the winepress.
See: I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek wisdom; listen to me, leaders of the people, and you who preside over the assembly, give ear.
To your son, your wife, your brother, or your friend, give no power over you while you live, and do not hand your goods over to another, lest you regret it and have to beg them back.
As long as you live and have breath in you, submit yourself to no one.
Better that your children should ask of you than that you should have to hold out your hand to them.
In everything you do, remain the master, and let no stain fall on your reputation.
When the last days of your life come, at the hour of death, distribute your inheritance.
For the donkey, fodder, the stick, and the load; for the slave, bread, correction, and work.
Keep your servant at work, and you will have rest; leave his hands idle, and he will seek his freedom.
The yoke and the strap bend the neck; for a wicked slave, torture and fetters.
Put him to work so that he does not stay idle, for idleness teaches many kinds of evil;
give him his task, it suits him; if he does not obey, weigh down his fetters; but do not go beyond measure with anyone, and do nothing against justice.
Do you have a servant? Let him be like yourself, for you acquired him with blood.
Do you have a servant? Treat him as a brother, and you will bind him to you as to your own soul.
If you mistreat him and he runs away, on what road will you go to look for him?
The fool lulls himself with empty and deceptive hopes, and dreams give wings to fools.
To rely on dreams is to grasp a shadow and chase the wind.
A dream is only a reflection, the image of a face facing a face.
From the unclean, what pure thing can come? From falsehood, what true thing can come?
Divinations, omens, and dreams are empty things, images of a fevered heart.
Unless they are a visitation from the Most High, do not set your heart on them;
for dreams have led many astray, and those who put their hope in them have fallen.
The law, however, is fulfilled without falsehood, and wisdom is perfect on faithful lips.
An educated man knows much, and a man of experience speaks with sense;
one who has been through nothing knows little, but one who has traveled abounds in skill.
I have seen much in my travels, and I have learned more than I could say;
often I have brushed against death, but through all of it I was saved.
The spirit of those who fear the Lord will live, for their hope is in the one who saves them.
Whoever fears the Lord dreads nothing, he does not tremble, for God is his hope.
Happy is the soul of the one who fears the Lord! On whom does he lean, and who is his support?
The eyes of the Lord are on those who love him: a mighty shield, a firm support, shelter from the scorching wind, shade from the noonday heat, a guard against stumbling, a help against falling.
He lifts up the soul, gives light to the eyes, grants health, life, and blessing.
To sacrifice ill-gotten goods is to make a paltry offering, and the gifts of the godless cannot please.
The Most High does not accept the offerings of the godless, and it is not by a multitude of victims that he pardons sins.
To slaughter a son before his father's eyes, such is the one who offers a sacrifice taken from the goods of the poor.
The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; to deprive them of it is murder.
To kill your neighbor is to take away his livelihood; to shed blood is to rob the worker of his wages.
One builds, another tears down: what do they gain but toil?
One prays, another curses: to whose voice will the Master listen?
Whoever purifies himself from the touch of a corpse and touches it again, what has washing profited him?
So it is with the man who fasts for his sins and then goes and repeats them: who will listen to his prayer, and what will humbling himself have profited him?
To keep the law is to multiply offerings;
to hold fast to the precepts is to offer a peace offering.
To give thanks is to present the fine flour;
to give alms is to offer a sacrifice of praise.
What pleases the Lord is to turn away from evil; what wins his pardon is to flee from injustice.
Yet do not appear before the Lord empty-handed,
for all this is required by the commandment.
The offering of the just man makes the altar rich, and its fragrance rises before the Most High;
the sacrifice of the just man is accepted, and the memory of it will not be forgotten.
Glorify the Lord with a generous heart, and do not skimp on the firstfruits of your hands;
at every offering, keep a cheerful face, and consecrate your tithe with gladness.
Give to the Most High according to what he has given you, generously, according to your means;
for the Lord repays, he will give you back sevenfold.
Do not try to bribe him with gifts, for he would not accept them;
do not rely on an unjust sacrifice. For the Lord is judge, and he shows no favoritism.
He shows no partiality to the harm of the poor, and he hears the prayer of the oppressed;
he does not despise the plea of the orphan, nor the complaint of the widow.
Do not the widow's tears run down her cheeks,
and does her cry not rise against the one who makes them flow?
Whoever serves God as he approves will be well received, and his prayer will reach the clouds.
The prayer of the humble passes through the clouds; it is not consoled until it reaches its goal, and does not stop until the Most High has looked down, has judged the just and rendered his sentence.
The Lord will not delay, he will no longer be patient, until he has broken the loins of the merciless
and taken vengeance on the nations, until he has destroyed the host of the proud and broken the scepters of the unjust,
until he has repaid each one according to his deeds and rewarded the works of men according to their thoughts,
until he has judged the cause of his people and gladdened them with his mercy.
His mercy is welcome in time of distress, like rain clouds in time of drought.

titres.titre: Prayer for the deliverance of Israel

versets.t: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all, and look upon us;
spread your terror over all the nations.
Raise your hand against the foreign peoples, that they may feel your power!
As you have shown your holiness before them in punishing us, show your greatness before us in chastising them,
and let them learn, as we have learned, that there is no God but you, O Lord.
Renew the signs, work the wonders again,
glorify your hand and your right arm.
Rouse your anger and pour out your fury,
strike down the adversary and crush the enemy.
Hasten the time, remember the oath, and let people tell of your mighty deeds!
Let a raging fire devour the survivor, and let those who mistreat your people meet their ruin.
Crush the heads of the enemy leaders, who say, "There is no one but us!"
Gather all the tribes of Jacob, and restore to them their inheritance as in the beginning.
Have mercy, O Lord, on the people that bears your name, on Israel, whom you have treated as a firstborn.
Take pity on the city of your sanctuary, Jerusalem, the place of your rest;
fill Zion with your praise, and your people with your glory.
Bear witness to those you created at the beginning, and fulfill the promises made in your name.
Reward those who hope in you, and let your prophets be found truthful. Hear, O Lord, the prayer of your servants,
according to the blessing of Aaron on your people, and let all the inhabitants of the earth acknowledge that you are the Lord, the God of the ages.
The stomach takes in any food, but one dish is better than another;
the palate distinguishes game by its taste, and the sensible heart recognizes a lying word.
A perverse heart causes grief, but a man of experience guards against it.
A woman will accept any husband, but one daughter is better than another.
A wife's beauty gladdens the face and surpasses all a man's desires;
and if kindness and gentleness are also on her tongue, her husband is no longer a mere mortal.
Whoever takes a wife makes the best of acquisitions: a help like himself, a pillar of support.
Without a fence, an estate is plundered; without a wife, a man wanders about groaning.
Who would trust a nimble bandit who runs from town to town? So too the man without a home, who lodges wherever night overtakes him.
Every friend says, "I am your friend too," but some are friends in name only.
Is it not a deadly grief when a companion, a friend, turns into an enemy?
O evil inclination, from where did you come, to cover the earth with deceit?
The companion rejoices in his friend's good fortune, but in the day of trouble he turns against him;
the companion shares his friend's toil for his own gain, but in the face of battle he takes up his shield for himself.
Do not forget your friend in your heart, and do not lose sight of him in the midst of plenty.
Every counselor gives advice, but some think only of themselves.
Beware of the counselor: first find out where his interest lies, for he will advise for himself, and he might cast the lot against you
and say to you, "Your way is good," then stand aside to see what happens to you.
Do not consult one who looks at you askance, and hide your plans from one who envies you;

do not consult a woman about her rival, a coward about war, a merchant about a trade, a buyer about a sale, an envious man about gratitude, a heartless man about a kindness, a lazy man about work, a seasonal laborer about finishing a task, or an idle slave about a heavy job: rely on none of them for advice.
Rather, keep company with a devout man whom you know to be faithful to the commandments, whose heart is like your own and who will suffer with you if you fall.
Then hold to the counsel of your own heart, for no one is more faithful to you;
for a man's soul sometimes sees farther than seven sentinels posted on a height.
And above all, pray to the Most High to guide your way in the truth.
Before any action, the word; before any undertaking, reflection.
As a root of the heart's decisions, four things spring up:
good and evil, life and death, and it is the tongue that rules over them.
One man is clever at teaching others yet remains useless to himself;
another plays the scholar in words and makes himself hated: he will end up without bread,
for the Lord has not granted him his grace: he is devoid of all wisdom.
One man is wise for himself, and the fruits of his knowledge are sure on his lips;
the wise man instructs his people, and the fruits of his knowledge are sure.
The wise man is filled with blessings, and all who see him call him happy.
A man's life is counted in days, but the days of Israel are without number.
The wise man wins the trust of his people, and his name will live forever.
My son, in your way of living, test yourself; see what harms you and do not allow it to yourself;
for not everything is good for everyone, and not everyone takes pleasure in everything.
Do not be insatiable for delicacies, and do not fall upon your food,
for eating too much brings on illness, and gluttony leads to colic:
intemperance has killed many, but whoever watches himself prolongs his life.
Honor the physician for the services he renders, for he too was created by the Lord;
healing comes from the Most High, and the physician receives his gifts from the king.
The physician's knowledge lets him hold his head high, and he is admired by the great.
The Lord has brought forth remedies from the earth, and the sensible man does not disdain them.
Did not a piece of wood sweeten the bitter water, to reveal its power to all?
The Lord has given knowledge to men, to be glorified through his marvelous works:
by them the physician heals and puts an end to pain,
and the pharmacist prepares his remedies; thus the works of the Lord do not cease, and from him comes well-being upon the earth.
My son, if you are ill, do not neglect anything, but pray to the Lord, and he will heal you;
give up your faults, set your conduct right, and cleanse your heart of every sin;
offer the incense and the memorial of fine flour, present rich offerings according to your means,
then let the physician do his work, for he too was created by the Lord; let him not leave your side, you have need of him.
There are cases where success is in their hands,
for they too pray to the Lord to grant them the power to relieve and to heal, so as to prolong life.
Whoever sins before his Creator, let him fall into the hands of the physician!
My son, shed tears over a dead man, take up the lament like one who suffers cruelly; bury his body with the honors due, and do not neglect his grave.
Weep bitterly, mourn fervently, keep the mourning according to his worth, a day or two, to avoid gossip, then console yourself for your grief;
for grief can bring on death, and sorrow of heart saps one's strength.
In misfortune, the pain lingers; a life of poverty weighs on the heart.
Do not give your heart over to sadness; drive it away by thinking of your end.
Do not forget: there is no coming back; you will do the dead no good and will harm yourself.
Remember my fate, for it will be yours as well: mine yesterday, yours today.
When the dead man is at rest, let his memory rest, and console yourself once his soul has departed.
The scribe's wisdom is gained in leisure, and whoever is free of affairs will grow wise.
How could he grow wise who holds the plow, whose pride is to wield the goad, who drives his oxen, is absorbed in their labors, and talks of nothing but cattle?
He sets his whole heart on tracing furrows, and his vigilance on giving fodder to his heifers.

So too every craftsman and master workman, who spends his days and nights at his task; the seal engraver, intent on varying the designs, sets his heart on reproducing the drawing and his vigilance on perfecting the work.

So too the blacksmith seated by the anvil, his eye on the raw iron; the heat of the fire melts his flesh, he battles against the heat of the furnace, the hammer deafens his ear, his gaze is fixed on the model; he sets his heart on completing his work and his vigilance on polishing it to perfection.
So too the potter seated at his work, turning the wheel with his foot, forever anxious over his task, counting the number of vessels to be made;
with his arm he shapes the clay, with his foot he softens it; he sets his heart on perfecting the glaze and his vigilance on cleaning out his kiln.
All these people rely on their hands, and each is expert in his own trade;
without them no city would be built, no one would settle or travel.

But they are not sought out in the council of the people, they do not shine in the assembly; they do not sit on the judge's bench and do not know the decrees of the law; they set forth neither instruction nor judgment, and they are not found among the makers of maxims;
yet they sustain the life of the world, and their prayer is about their trade.

titres.titre: Hymn to the works of God

versets.t: It is otherwise with the one who devotes himself to meditating on the law of the Most High! He searches out the wisdom of all the ancients and gives himself to the prophecies;
he retains the sayings of famous men and penetrates the twists of maxims;
he searches out the hidden meaning of proverbs and delights in riddles;
he serves among the great and appears before princes; he travels in foreign lands, having tested good and evil among men.
From early morning he turns his heart to the Lord who made him, he prays before the Most High, he opens his mouth in supplication and asks pardon for his sins.
If the Lord, who is great, so wills, he will be filled with the spirit of understanding: he will pour out words of wisdom and give thanks to the Lord in his prayer;
he will direct his counsel and knowledge well, and will meditate on the secrets of God;
he will make his teaching known and will glory in the law of the Lord's covenant.
Many will praise his understanding; it will never be forgotten, his memory will not fade, and his name will live from age to age;
the peoples will tell of his wisdom, and the assembly will speak his praise.
If he lives, his name outweighs a thousand; and if he goes to his rest, his glory grows still greater.
I still wish to pour out the fruit of my thoughts, for I am full as the moon at its height.
Listen to me, devout children, and grow up like the rose beside a stream;
send out your fragrance like incense; blossom like the lily, spread your scent and sing a song; bless the Lord for all his works.
Give glory to his name, proclaim his praise with your songs and your harps, and say as you celebrate him:
All the works of the Lord are very good, and everything he commands is accomplished in its time.

One must not say, "What is this? What is it for?" for everything has its reason in its time. At his word the water stood up like a wall, and at a word from his mouth the reservoirs of the waters were formed.
At his command, all that he wills comes to pass, and no one can hold back the salvation he sends.
The deeds of all flesh are before him, and nothing escapes his eyes;
his gaze reaches from eternity to eternity, and nothing amazes him.
One must not say, "What is this? What is it for?" for each thing was created for its use.
His blessing overflows like a river and, like a flood, waters the earth;
so too he gives his anger as a portion to the nations, as he turned a well-watered land into a desert of salt.
His ways are straight for the holy, but for the godless they are stumbling blocks.
Good things were created from the beginning for the good, and likewise evils for the wicked.
The first necessities of human life are water, fire, iron, and salt, wheat flour, honey and milk, the juice of the grape, oil and clothing:
all these are a good thing for the devout, but turn to evil for sinners.
There are winds created for punishment, which in their fury unleash their scourges; on the day of destruction they deploy their force and appease the anger of their Creator.
Fire and hail, famine and plague, all these are created for punishment,
like the fangs of wild beasts, the scorpions, the vipers, and the avenging sword that exterminates the godless:
all rejoice in the command of the Lord, stand ready on the earth for the appointed moment, and at the fixed hour do not disobey his word.
This is why, from the outset, I was firm in my convictions; after reflection, I set them down in writing:
All the works of the Lord are good, and he provides for every need in its time.
One must not say, "This is worse than that," for each thing, in its time, proves to be good.
Now therefore sing with all your heart, at the top of your voice, and bless the name of the Lord.
A great burden is the lot of every man, a heavy yoke weighs on the sons of Adam, from the day they come out of their mother's womb until the day they return to the mother of us all.
What troubles their thoughts and makes their hearts pound is anxious expectation, the fear of death.
From the one who sits enthroned in glory to the wretch seated in dust and ashes,
from the one who wears purple and crown to the poor man clothed in coarse cloth:
anger, envy, turmoil, agitation, fear of death, rancor and quarrels, this is the lot of all; and during his rest, at night, sleep throws his thoughts into confusion.
Scarcely has he fallen asleep for a moment when dreams disturb him; he imagines himself on watch in broad daylight, terrified by the visions of his mind, like a man fleeing before battle;
at the moment of being rescued, he wakes, astonished at his groundless fear.
So it is with all flesh, from man to beast, and for sinners, seven times more:
plague and bloodshed, strife and sword, calamities, famine and destruction,
all these are created for the wicked, and it was because of them that the flood came.
Everything that comes from the earth returns to the earth, as the waters return to the sea.
Every bribe and every unjust gain will perish, but good faith will endure forever.
The wealth of the unjust will run dry like a torrent, like the great clap of thunder in a downpour;
whoever knows how to open his hand will rejoice, but cheats will end in ruin.
The offspring of the godless do not multiply their branches, and their impure roots are on a jagged crag;
the reeds by the water, on the bank of a river, are torn up before any other grass.
Kindness is like a blessed garden, and almsgiving endures forever.
Sweet is the life of the self-sufficient, and of the laborer; but more than both, of the one who finds a treasure.
Children and the founding of a city perpetuate a name; but more than both, a blameless wife is esteemed.
Wine and music gladden the heart; but more than both, the love of wisdom.
The flute and the harp make sweet melodies; but more than both, a kindly tongue.
Grace and beauty charm the eyes; but more than both, the green of the fields.
Friend and companion meet as occasion allows; but more than both, a wife with her husband.
Brothers and help are for the day of distress; but more than both, almsgiving delivers.
Gold and silver steady the step; but more than both, good counsel is prized.
Wealth and strength give assurance; but more than both, the fear of the Lord. With the fear of the Lord, one lacks nothing, and one need seek no other support.
The fear of the Lord is like a blessed garden, and the Lord clothes it with a glory beyond compare.
My son, do not lead the life of a beggar: better to die than to beg.
Whoever must look to another's table, his life does not count as a life; he defiles his soul with another's food, which the educated and well-bred man will guard against.
In the mouth of the shameless, begging is sweet, but in his belly it burns like a fire.
O death, how bitter is the thought of you to the man who lives at ease among his goods, free of care, prosperous in all things, and still able to enjoy the pleasures of the table!
O death, your sentence is welcome to the needy man whose strength is spent, to the old man burdened with years and cares, rebelling against his lot and without hope.
Do not dread the sentence of death: remember those who came before you and those who will come after you.

This is the decree of the Lord over all flesh; why rebel against the good pleasure of the Most High? Whether you have lived ten years, a hundred, or a thousand, in the realm of the dead no one disputes the length of a life.
They are abominable children, the children of sinners, who haunt the dwellings of the godless:
the inheritance of the children of sinners comes to ruin, and dishonor clings to their offspring.
Children reproach their godless father as the cause of their shame.
Woe to you, godless men, who have forsaken the law of God Most High!
If you are born, it is for a curse; if you die, the curse will be your portion.
Everything that comes from the earth returns to the earth; so the godless go from the curse to ruin.
People mourn their bodies, but the accursed name of sinners will be blotted out.
Take care of your name, for it will stay with you more surely than a thousand treasures of gold;
the days of a good life are numbered, but a good name endures forever.
My children, keep my teaching in peace. Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure, what use are either of them?
Better the man who hides his foolishness than the one who hides his wisdom.
So then, be ashamed of what I am about to tell you; for not all shame is good to keep, and not everything is equally valued by all.
Be ashamed of misconduct before your father and mother, of lying before the prince and the powerful,
of wrongdoing before the judge and the magistrate, of transgression before the assembly and the people, of injustice before your companion and your friend,
of theft before your neighbors. Before the truth of God and his covenant, be ashamed of leaning your elbow on the bread, of the contempt you bring on yourself in taking and giving,
of silence before those who greet you, of the look cast on a woman of loose life,
of rebuffing a relative, of taking his share and his gift, of ogling a married woman,
of familiarities with your maidservant, do not approach her bed; of wounding words before your friends, do not follow up a gift with reproaches.

titres.titre: The shame one ought to have
The glory of God in creation

versets.t: Be ashamed of repeating what you have heard and of betraying secrets: then you will have true shame and will find favor with all. But do not blush at these things, and do not sin out of human respect:
at the law of the Most High and his covenant, at the sentence that acquits the godless,
at settling accounts with your partner or your traveling companions, at sharing the inheritance with your friends,
at a just balance and exact weights, at earning little or much,
at the profit of trade, at correcting your children strictly, at drawing blood from the back of a bad servant.
With a wicked wife, a seal is good; where many hands pass, put things under lock and key;
whatever you hand over, count it and weigh it, and put in writing what you give and receive.
Do not be ashamed to correct the foolish and the senseless, nor the old man who quarrels with the young; thus you will be truly instructed and approved by all.
A daughter is for her father a hidden worry, and the anxiety she brings robs him of sleep: while young, lest she pass the flower of her age; married, lest she be disliked;
while a virgin, lest she be seduced and conceive in her father's house; with a husband, lest she be unfaithful, or remain barren.
Over a headstrong daughter keep close watch, lest she make you the laughingstock of your enemies, the talk of the town and the subject of public rumor, and disgrace you before all.
Do not dwell on anyone's beauty, and do not sit among women;
for from clothing comes the moth, and from a woman, feminine malice.
Better the harshness of a man than the caresses of a woman, for a woman can lead to shame and dishonor.
I will call to mind the works of the Lord and tell what I have seen: it is by the word of the Lord that his works exist.
The shining sun looks on all things, and the work of the Lord is full of his glory.
The Lord has not allowed his holy ones to recount all his wonders, which he has firmly established so that the universe may stand fast in his glory.
He fathoms the abyss and the heart of men and sees through their schemes; for the Most High possesses all knowledge and sees the signs of the times.
He announces the past and the future and uncovers the traces of hidden things;
no thought escapes him, no word is hidden from him.
He has ordered the marvels of his wisdom, he who is before the ages and forever; nothing has been added to him or taken away, and he has needed no counselor.
How beautiful are all his works, and of them we see but a spark!
All this lives and endures forever, ready for every use, and everything obeys his word.
Everything goes in pairs, one facing the other, and he has made nothing imperfect;
each enhances the good of the other. Who could ever tire of contemplating his glory?
The pride of the heights is the firmament in its pure brightness; the sight of the sky is a vision of glory.
The sun, at its rising, proclaims as it appears: what a marvel, this work of the Most High!
At noon it parches the earth; who can stand before its blazing heat?
One stokes the furnace for work at the fire; the sun burns the mountains three times more: it breathes out fiery vapors and, darting its rays, dazzles the eyes.
Great is the Lord who made it, and at his command it hastens on its course.
The moon too returns always at its hour, to mark the seasons and signal the feasts;
from it comes the signal for the festivals, and its light wanes once it is full.
From it the month takes its name; it grows marvelously through its phases, an ensign of the host of heaven, shining in the firmament.
The beauty of the sky is the brilliance of the stars, a luminous adornment in the heights of the Lord;
at the command of the Holy One they hold their posts and do not slacken in their watch.
Look at the rainbow and bless the One who made it, so beautiful is it in its splendor!
It encircles the sky with its glorious ring, stretched out by the hands of the Most High.
At his command the snow hurries down, and the lightning flashes, executors of his judgments;
for this his storehouses are opened, and the clouds fly out like birds.
By his power he thickens the clouds, and the hailstones shatter into pieces;
the voice of his thunder makes the earth tremble, and at the sight of him the mountains totter.
At his will the south wind blows, the hurricane from the north and the tempest; he scatters the snow like birds swooping down, it descends like locusts settling.
The eye marvels at its whiteness, and the heart wonders at its falling.
He pours the frost on the earth like salt, which, once frozen, bristles with sharp points;
the cold north wind rises, and the water sets into ice; it covers every expanse of water and clothes it as with a breastplate.
The Lord consumes the mountains, scorches the desert, and devours the greenery like a fire;
the remedy for all this is the cloud that comes rushing, and the dew that comes to relieve the burning heat.
According to his design, he has subdued the abyss and planted islands in it;
those who sail it tell of its perils, and their accounts leave us astonished:
there are strange and marvelous creatures, animals of every kind and the race of sea monsters.
Thanks to him, all reaches its proper end, and everything holds together by his word.
We could say much and never be done; the last word is this: he is the all.
Where would we find the strength to praise him? He is the Almighty, above all his works.
The Lord is fearsome and supremely great, and his power is wonderful.
In praising the Lord, exalt him as much as you can, he will still be beyond you; to exalt him, gather all your strength, do not grow weary, for you will never succeed.
Who has seen him, to speak of him? Who could praise him as he truly is?
Many hidden wonders surpass him still, for we see only a little of his works:
the Lord has made all things, and to the devout he gives wisdom.
Let us now praise famous men, our ancestors, generation by generation.
The Lord brought forth great glory in them, his greatness from the beginning:
rulers in their kingdoms, men renowned for their power, counselors full of wisdom, prophets foretelling the future;
leaders who guided the people by their counsel and their knowledge of the Scriptures, teachers of wise discourse;
composers of melodies, authors of narratives set down in writing;
rich and powerful men, living in peace in their homes. All were honored in their own time,
each was the glory of his age.
Some have left behind a name, whose praise is still repeated;
others have left no memory: they have vanished as though they had never existed, as though they had never been born, they and their children after them.
But here are men of goodness, whose merits have not been forgotten;
their prosperity remains attached to their descendants, and their inheritance to their children;
their posterity remains faithful to the covenants, and their children as well, thanks to them;
their descendants endure forever, and their glory will not be blotted out.
Their bodies were buried in peace, and their name lives from age to age;
the peoples tell of their wisdom, and the assembly proclaims their praise.
Enoch pleased the Lord and was taken up, a model of conversion for the generations.
Noah was found perfect and just; in the time of wrath he was the ransom of the world; therefore a remnant remained on the earth when the flood came.
An everlasting covenant was made with him, that never again should a flood destroy all flesh.
Abraham was the glorious father of a multitude of nations, and no one has equaled him in glory:
he kept the law of the Most High and entered into covenant with him; he inscribed the covenant in his flesh, and in trial he was found faithful.

So God promised him with an oath to bless the nations in his offspring, to multiply them like the dust of the earth, to raise up his posterity like the stars, and to give them an inheritance from sea to sea, from the River to the ends of the earth.
To Isaac too, for the sake of Abraham his father, he confirmed the blessing of all the peoples and the covenant;
he made it rest on the head of Jacob, he acknowledged him in his blessings, gave him the land as an inheritance and divided it into twelve portions for the twelve tribes.
From Jacob he brought forth a man of goodness, who found favor in the sight of all, beloved of God and of men, Moses, whose memory is a blessing.
He gave him a glory equal to that of the holy ones and made him great by the terrors he inspired in his enemies;
by his word he worked wonders, and glorified him before kings; he gave him commandments for his people and let him see a ray of his glory.
For his faithfulness and his meekness, he consecrated him, choosing him out of all mortals;

he let him hear his voice, led him into the cloud, and handed over to him face to face the commandments, the law of life and knowledge, that he might teach Jacob his covenant and his decrees to Israel.
He raised up Aaron, a holy man like him, his brother, of the tribe of Levi.
He made with him an everlasting covenant and gave him the priesthood of the people; he adorned him with splendid attire and clothed him in the robe of glory;
he covered him with sovereign magnificence and assigned him the garments of honor: the breeches, the long tunic, and the ephod;
he surrounded him with pomegranates and many golden bells, which were to ring at his step and make their sound heard in the temple, a memorial for the sons of his people;

with the sacred vestment woven of gold, of violet and scarlet purple, the work of the embroiderer; with the breastpiece of judgment, with the Urim and the Thummim, in crimson thread, the work of an artist;
with precious stones engraved like seals, set in gold, the work of the lapidary, bearing the names of the tribes of Israel, as a memorial.
He set upon his turban the crown of gold, engraved with the seal of consecration, "Holy to the Lord," a mark of honor, a masterpiece, a delight to the eyes, a magnificent adornment.
Before him nothing like it, and never after; no stranger shall wear it, but only his sons and his descendants forever.
His sacrifices shall be wholly consumed, twice a day, without ceasing.

Moses consecrated him and anointed him with the holy oil: this was for him an everlasting covenant, and for his race, as long as the heavens endure, to serve the Lord, to exercise the priesthood, and to bless the people in his name.
The Lord chose him out of all the living to offer the sacrifice, the incense and the fragrance as a memorial, and to make atonement for his people.
He entrusted to him his commandments, authority over the precepts of the law, to teach his decrees to Jacob and his law to Israel.
Strangers banded together against him, jealous of him in the wilderness: the followers of Dathan and Abiram, and the company of Korah, furious and enraged.
The Lord saw it and was indignant; they were destroyed in the heat of his anger; he worked wonders against them and consumed them by the flame of his fire.
He increased Aaron's glory still further, and gave him an inheritance: the firstfruits of the harvest, and first of all bread in abundance;
for they feed on the sacrifices of the Lord, which he gave to Aaron and his descendants.
But he has no inheritance in the land of the people, no portion among the nation, for the Lord himself is his portion and his inheritance.
Phinehas, son of Eleazar, is third in glory, for having shown his zeal in the fear of the Lord: in the defection of the people, he stood firm, courageous in soul, and made atonement for Israel.
So a covenant of peace was made with him, making him head of the sanctuary and of the people, that the dignity of the priesthood should belong to him and to his descendants forever.
