So the whole portion set aside will form a square about thirteen kilometers by thirteen; you will reserve a quarter of it for the property of the city.

The rest will be for the prince, on both sides of the holy portion and of the property of the city: on the east, along the thirteen kilometers to the eastern border; on the west, along the thirteen kilometers to the western border, parallel to the tribal portions. This will be for the prince, and the holy portion, with the sanctuary of the temple, will be in its center.

So, apart from the domain of the Levites and the domain of the city, which lie in the middle of the prince's domain, everything between the border of Judah and the border of Benjamin will belong to the prince.
For the rest of the tribes. From east to west: Benjamin, one portion.
Alongside Benjamin, from east to west: Simeon, one portion.
Alongside Simeon, from east to west: Issachar, one portion.
Alongside Issachar, from east to west: Zebulun, one portion.
Alongside Zebulun, from east to west: Gad, one portion.
Alongside Gad, on the south, toward the Negev, the border will run from Tamar to the waters of Meribah, at Kadesh, then along the Wadi to the Great Sea.
This is the land that you will allot as an inheritance among the tribes of Israel, and these will be their portions, oracle of the Lord God.
These are the exits of the city. On the north side, which measures about two and a half kilometers,
the gates will bear the names of the tribes of Israel. Three gates on the north: the gate of Reuben, the gate of Judah, the gate of Levi.
On the east side, about two and a half kilometers, three gates: the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, the gate of Dan.
On the south side, about two and a half kilometers, three gates: the gate of Simeon, the gate of Issachar, the gate of Zebulun.
On the west side, about two and a half kilometers, three gates: the gate of Gad, the gate of Asher, the gate of Naphtali.
The circuit of the city will measure about nine and a half kilometers. And from now on the name of the city will be: "The Lord is there."

titres.titre: Daniel and his companions at Babylon

versets.t: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, marched against Jerusalem and laid siege to it.

The Lord delivered into his hands Jehoiakim, king of Judah, along with some of the vessels of the house of God; Nebuchadnezzar carried them off to the land of Shinar, into the temple of his god, and placed these vessels in the treasury of his god.
The king ordered Ashpenaz, the chief of his eunuchs, to bring him some of the sons of Israel of royal blood or of noble family,

young men without blemish, handsome, gifted for every kind of knowledge, well taught, intelligent, and full of vigour, fit to serve in the king's palace; they were to be taught the writing and the language of the Chaldeans.
The king assigned them, for each day, a portion of the food from his table and of the wine that he drank. They were to be trained for three years, after which they would enter his service.
Among them, from the sons of Judah, were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
The chief of the eunuchs gave them new names: he called Daniel Belteshazzar, Hananiah Shadrach, Mishael Meshach, and Azariah Abednego.
But Daniel resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king's food and the wine that he drank; so he asked the chief of the eunuchs not to force him to defile himself.
God granted Daniel kindness and favour in the eyes of the chief of the eunuchs.

But the man said to Daniel: "I fear the king, my master: it is he who has fixed your food and your drink. Why should he see your faces looking more wasted than those of the young men your age? You would put my head at risk before the king."
Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief of the eunuchs had put in charge of him, of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
"Please test your servants for ten days: let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink.
Then compare our faces with those of the young men who eat the king's food, and deal with your servants according to what you see."
He agreed to this proposal and put them to the test for ten days.
At the end of ten days, they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who ate the king's food.
From then on, the steward took away the food and the wine they were to have, and gave them vegetables.
To these four young men God gave knowledge and skill in all literature and wisdom; and Daniel understood all visions and dreams.
At the time the king had set for them to be brought in, the chief of the eunuchs presented them to Nebuchadnezzar.
The king spoke with them, and among them all none was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah; so they entered his service.
On every question of wisdom and understanding that he put to them, the king found them ten times better than all the diviners and magicians in his kingdom.
And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.

titres.titre: Daniel asks for time and prays
Daniel reveals the dream to the king
The statue and the four kingdoms

versets.t: In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and sleep left him.
The king summoned the diviners, the magicians, the enchanters, and the Chaldeans, to explain his dreams to him. They came and stood before the king.
The king said to them: "I have had a dream, and my spirit is troubled with the desire to understand it."
The Chaldeans answered the king in Aramaic: "O king, live forever! Tell the dream to your servants, and we will give you its interpretation."
The king answered the Chaldeans: "My decision is firm: if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will be torn limb from limb and your houses reduced to a heap of rubble.
But if you reveal to me the dream and its interpretation, you will receive from me gifts, rewards, and great honours. So make known to me the dream and its interpretation."
They answered a second time: "Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will give its interpretation."
The king replied: "I can see that you are trying to gain time, because you know my decision is firm.

If you do not make the dream known to me, one sentence alone awaits you. You have agreed together to feed me lies and falsehoods, waiting for the times to change. So tell me the dream, and I will know that you are able to give me its interpretation."

The Chaldeans answered before the king: "There is no one on earth who can tell what the king asks. No king, however great and powerful, has ever demanded such a thing of any diviner, magician, or Chaldean.
What the king asks is too hard; no one can reveal it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not among mortals."
At this the king flew into a violent rage and ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be put to death.
The decree was published, and the killing of the wise men had begun; Daniel and his companions were also sought, to be put to death.
Then Daniel spoke with prudence and wisdom to Arioch, the chief of the king's guard, who was about to execute the wise men of Babylon.
He asked Arioch, the king's officer: "Why has the king issued so harsh a sentence?" And Arioch explained the matter to him.
Then Daniel went to the king and asked him to grant him some time, so that he might give him the interpretation.
Then Daniel went home and told the matter to his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,
urging them to implore the mercy of the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that he and his companions would not be put to death with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision during the night; and Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
Daniel spoke and said: "Blessed be the name of God from everlasting to everlasting, for to him belong wisdom and might!
It is he who changes times and seasons, who removes kings and sets them up, who gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding.
It is he who uncovers deep and hidden things, who knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with him.
It is you, God of my fathers, whom I thank and praise: you have given me wisdom and might, and now you have made known to me what we asked of you, you have revealed to us the king's matter."

Then Daniel went to Arioch, whom the king had charged with putting the wise men of Babylon to death, and said to him: "Do not put the wise men of Babylon to death. Take me to the king, and I will give him the interpretation."
At once Arioch brought Daniel before the king and said: "I have found among the captives of Judah a man who will give the king the interpretation."
The king said to Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar: "Are you able to make known to me the dream I had and its interpretation?"
Daniel answered before the king: "The mystery that the king seeks to fathom, no wise men, magicians, diviners, or astrologers can reveal to him.

But there is a God in heaven who uncovers mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen at the end of days. Here is your dream and the visions that passed through your mind as you lay in bed.
As for you, O king, as you lay in bed your thoughts turned to the future, and he who uncovers mysteries has made known to you what will happen.
And if this mystery has been revealed to me, it is not because I am wiser than anyone else alive, but so that the king may receive its interpretation and understand the thoughts of his heart.
You, O king, were looking, and behold: an immense statue. This statue was enormous, of extraordinary brilliance; it stood before you, terrifying to behold.
Its head was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze,
its legs of iron, its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.
You were watching, when a stone broke away, with no hand to throw it, struck the statue at its feet of iron and clay, and shattered them.

Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold all shattered together; they became like chaff on the threshing floor in summer, which the wind sweeps away without a trace. But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
That is the dream; now we will give its interpretation before the king.
You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given kingship, power, might, and glory;
wherever men dwell, with the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky, he has handed them into your hands and made you master of them all. You are the head of gold.
After you will arise another kingdom, lesser than yours, then a third kingdom, of bronze, which will rule over the whole earth.
A fourth kingdom will be as hard as iron: just as iron crushes and shatters everything, it will crush and grind all the others.
If you saw the feet and toes partly of clay and partly of iron, it means this kingdom will be divided; it will keep something of the hardness of iron, since you saw the iron mixed with clay.
But as the toes were partly of iron and partly of clay, this kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle.
If you saw the iron mixed with clay, it means they will mingle through human alliances, without holding together, just as iron does not bond with clay.

In the time of these kings, the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and whose sovereignty will pass to no other people. It will shatter and bring to an end all these kingdoms, but it will itself endure forever.

This is the meaning of the stone that you saw break away from the mountain with no hand to throw it, and shatter the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. The great God has made known to the king what will happen hereafter. The dream is true, and its interpretation certain."
Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and bowed down before Daniel; he ordered that offerings and incense be presented to him.
The king said to Daniel: "Truly, your God is the God of gods, the Lord of kings, the one who uncovers mysteries, since you have been able to fathom this mystery."
The king loaded Daniel with honours and rich gifts; he made him governor of the whole province of Babylon and chief over all the wise men of Babylon.
At Daniel's request, the king entrusted the administration of the province of Babylon to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; and Daniel remained at the king's court.

titres.titre: The golden statue and the command to worship
The song of the three young men
The king acknowledges the living God

versets.t: King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, about thirty metres high and about three metres wide, and he set it up on the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.

Then he summoned the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the counsellors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all the authorities of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the statue he had set up.

So the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the counsellors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all the authorities of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the statue, and they stood before it.
A herald cried out with a loud voice: "To you, peoples, nations, and languages, this is the command:

as soon as you hear the sound of the horn, the flute, the zither, the harp, the lyre, the bagpipe, and every kind of instrument, you shall fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.
Whoever does not fall down and worship it will at once be thrown into the blazing furnace."

So, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, the flute, the zither, the harp, the lyre, the bagpipe, and every kind of instrument, all the peoples, nations, and languages fell down and worshipped the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
Thereupon, at once, some Chaldeans came forward to accuse the Jews.
They said to King Nebuchadnezzar: "O king, live forever!

You, O king, have given this command: whoever hears the sound of the horn, the flute, the zither, the harp, the lyre, the bagpipe, and every kind of instrument shall fall down and worship the golden statue,
and whoever does not fall down and worship it will be thrown into the blazing furnace.

Now there are some Jews whom you have set over the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: these men pay no heed to you, O king; they do not serve your gods, and they do not worship the golden statue you have set up."
Then Nebuchadnezzar, in a fit of rage, ordered Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to be brought; and they were brought before the king.
Nebuchadnezzar said to them: "Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods and do not worship the golden statue I have set up?

Now be ready: as soon as you hear the sound of the horn, the flute, the zither, the harp, the lyre, the bagpipe, and every kind of instrument, fall down and worship the statue I have made. If you do not worship it, you will at once be thrown into the blazing furnace; and what god will deliver you from my hand?"
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king: "Nebuchadnezzar, on this matter we have no need to answer you.
If our God, whom we serve, wishes to deliver us, he will deliver us from the blazing furnace and from your hand, O king.
And even if he does not, know this well, O king: we will not serve your gods, and we will not worship the golden statue you have set up."
Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and the look of his face changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace to be heated seven times hotter than usual,
and he commanded the strongest men of his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and to throw them into the blazing furnace.
So they were bound, in their tunics, their robes, their cloaks, and their other garments, and thrown into the blazing furnace.
Since the king's order was urgent and the furnace heated to the extreme, the flame killed the men who had thrown in Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
As for these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, they fell, still bound, into the midst of the blazing furnace.
And they walked in the midst of the flames, praising God and blessing the Lord.
Then Azariah stood up and began to pray; opening his mouth in the midst of the fire, he said:
"Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and may your name be praised and glorified forever!
For you are just in all that you have done for us; all your works are true, your ways are right, and all your judgments are fair.
You have passed just sentences in all that you have brought upon us and upon Jerusalem, the holy city of our fathers: it is by a just judgment that you have dealt with us thus, because of our sins.
For we have sinned and done evil by turning away from you; we have gravely failed, we have disobeyed your commandments.
We have not kept them, we have not done what you commanded us for our own good.
All that you have brought upon us, all that you have done to us, you have done by a just judgment.
You have handed us over to lawless enemies, to hateful apostates, and to an unjust king, the most wicked in all the earth.
Today we no longer dare to open our mouths: shame and disgrace weigh upon your servants and those who worship you.
Do not abandon us forever, for the sake of your name, do not break your covenant.
Do not withdraw your mercy from us, for the sake of Abraham your friend, Isaac your servant, and Israel your holy one,
to whom you promised to multiply their descendants like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore.
For here we are, Lord, smaller than all the nations; here we are humbled today throughout the earth, because of our sins.
In this time we no longer have prince, or leader, or prophet, or burnt offering, or sacrifice, or offering, or incense, or any place to bring you our firstfruits and find favour.
But may a broken soul and a humbled spirit find a good welcome with you,

like burnt offerings of rams and bulls, like thousands of fat lambs! May such be our sacrifice before you today, and may it please you that we follow you to the end; for those who trust in you know no shame.
Now, with all our heart we follow you, we fear you, and we seek your face.
Do not cover us with shame, but deal with us according to your gentleness and your great mercy.
Deliver us by your wonders, and bring glory to your name, Lord.
Let them be confounded, all who mistreat your servants; let them be covered with shame, stripped of all their power, and let their strength be broken.
Let them know that you alone are the Lord God, glorious over all the earth."
Meanwhile, the king's servants who had thrown them into the fire kept stoking the furnace with naphtha, tow, pitch, and brushwood.
The flame rose about twenty-five metres above the furnace;
and as it shot up, it burned the Chaldeans it reached around the furnace.
But the angel of the Lord came down into the furnace beside Azariah and his companions; he drove the flame out of the furnace
and made a fresh, dew-laden breeze blow in the midst of the fire. The fire did not touch them at all, did not harm them, did them no injury.
Then all three, with one voice, praised, glorified, and blessed God in the furnace, saying:
"Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, praised and exalted forever! Blessed is your holy and glorious name, praised and exalted forever!
Blessed are you in the temple of your holy glory, praised and exalted forever!
Blessed are you on the throne of your kingdom, praised and exalted forever!
Blessed are you, you whose gaze searches the depths and who are enthroned above the cherubim, praised and exalted forever!
Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven, praised and exalted forever!
All you works of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
You angels of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
You heavens, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
All you waters above the heavens, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
All you powers of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Sun and moon, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Stars of heaven, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Rain and dew, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Winds unleashed by God, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Fire and heat, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Cold and heat, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Dews and frosts, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Frost and cold, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Ice and snow, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Nights and days, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Light and darkness, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Lightning and clouds, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Let the earth bless the Lord: let it praise and exalt him forever!
Mountains and hills, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
All you plants of the earth, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
You springs, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Seas and rivers, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Sea monsters and all that lives in the waters, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
All you birds of the sky, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
All you wild beasts and cattle, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
You children of men, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Let Israel bless the Lord: let it praise and exalt him forever!
You priests of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
You servants of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!
Holy and humble of heart, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever!

Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him forever! For he has snatched us from the realm of the dead, saved us from the hand of death; he has drawn us out of the burning furnace, snatched us from the midst of the fire.
Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his love endures forever!
All you who are devout, bless the Lord, the God of gods; praise him and give him thanks, for his love endures forever!"
Then King Nebuchadnezzar, astonished, rose in haste and said to his counsellors: "Did we not throw three men, bound, into the fire?" They answered: "Certainly, O king!"
He went on: "Well, I see four men, unbound, walking in the midst of the fire without any harm, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods."

Nebuchadnezzar approached the opening of the blazing furnace and said: "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out and come here!" And Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the midst of the fire.

The satraps, the prefects, the governors, and the king's counsellors gathered and saw that the fire had had no power over the bodies of these men: not a hair of their heads was singed, their cloaks were untouched, and the smell of fire had not even come near them.

Nebuchadnezzar spoke: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel to deliver his servants! They trusted in him, they disobeyed the king's order and gave up their bodies rather than serve or worship any god but their own God.

So here is my decree: any man, of whatever people, nation, or language, who speaks ill of the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego will be torn limb from limb and his house reduced to a heap of rubble; for there is no other god who can save in this way."
And the king made Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego prosper in the province of Babylon.
King Nebuchadnezzar, to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell throughout the earth: may peace be given to you in abundance!
It has seemed good to me to make known the signs and wonders that the Most High God has worked for me.
How great are his signs, how mighty his wonders! His reign is an everlasting reign, and his dominion endures from age to age.

titres.titre: The dream of the great tree
The king regains his reason and praises God

versets.t: I, Nebuchadnezzar, was living at peace in my house, prosperous in my palace.
I had a dream that terrified me; as I lay in bed, my thoughts and the visions of my mind filled me with dread.
I ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be brought before me to give me its interpretation.
Then the diviners, the magicians, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers came; I told them the dream, but they could not give me its interpretation.
At last Daniel came before me, called Belteshazzar after the name of my god, in whom dwells the spirit of the holy gods; and I told him the dream:
"Belteshazzar, chief of the diviners, I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you. Here are the visions I had in my dream: tell me their interpretation.
These were the visions of my mind as I lay in bed. I was looking: in the middle of the earth stood a tree of great height.
The tree grew and became strong; its top reached the sky, it could be seen from the ends of all the earth.
Its foliage was beautiful, its fruit abundant; it bore food for all. Under its shade the beasts of the field found shelter, in its branches the birds of the sky dwelt, and every creature fed from it.
In the visions of my mind, as I lay in bed, I was looking: behold, a watcher, a holy one, was coming down from heaven.
He cried out with force: Cut down the tree, lop off its branches, shake off its foliage, scatter its fruit! Let the beasts flee from beneath it, and the birds from its branches!
But leave in the ground the stump and its roots, in bands of iron and bronze, amid the grass of the field. Let it be drenched with the dew of heaven and share the grass of the earth with the beasts.
Let his human heart be taken from him, let a beast's heart be given to him, and let seven times pass over him.

Such is the sentence of the watchers, such is the decree of the holy ones, so that the living may know that the Most High rules over the kingship of men: he gives it to whom he wills, and raises up over it the lowliest of them.

This is the dream I had, I, King Nebuchadnezzar. It is for you, Belteshazzar, to give its interpretation, since none of the wise men of my kingdom can; but you can, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you."

Then Daniel, called Belteshazzar, sat stunned for a moment, overwhelmed by his thoughts. The king said: "Belteshazzar, do not let the dream and its interpretation trouble you!" Belteshazzar answered: "My lord, may this dream be for your enemies, and its meaning for your foes!
The tree that you saw, which grew and became strong, whose top reached the sky and which could be seen from all the earth,
with its splendid foliage, its abundant fruit, which bore food for all, under which the beasts of the field found shelter and in whose branches the birds of the sky dwelt,
that tree is you, O king: you have become great and strong, your greatness has grown until it touches the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth.

The king also saw a watcher, a holy one, come down from heaven and order the tree to be cut down and destroyed, but its stump and roots to be left in the ground, in bands of iron and bronze, amid the grass of the field, drenched with the dew of heaven and sharing the lot of the beasts, until seven times have passed over him.
This is its meaning, O king; it is a decree of the Most High that will be fulfilled upon my lord the king:

you will be driven from among men, you will live among the beasts of the field; you will be fed grass like oxen, you will be drenched with the dew of heaven, and seven times will pass over you, until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingship of men and gives it to whom he wills.
And if it was ordered that the stump and roots of the tree be left, it means that your kingship will be restored to you, as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven is the true master.
Therefore, O king, listen to my counsel: redeem your sins by justice, and your faults by mercy toward the poor; perhaps your prosperity will yet endure."
All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar.
Twelve months later, as he was walking on the terrace of the royal palace of Babylon,
the king exclaimed: "Is this not Babylon the great, which I have built as a royal residence, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?"
The word was still in his mouth when a voice fell from heaven: "To you, King Nebuchadnezzar, it is declared: the kingship is taken from you.

You will be driven from among men, you will live among the beasts of the field; you will be fed grass like oxen, and seven times will pass over you, until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingship of men and gives it to whom he wills."

At that very moment, the word was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: he was driven from among men, he ate grass like oxen, his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like eagle's feathers and his nails like bird's claws.

At the end of that time, I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me. I blessed the Most High, I praised and glorified him who lives forever: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, his reign endures from age to age.

All the inhabitants of the earth count for nothing before him; he acts as he pleases with the host of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth, and no one can stay his hand or say to him: "What are you doing?"

At the moment my reason returned, for the glory of my kingship, my majesty and my splendour were restored to me; my counsellors and my nobles sought me out, I was reestablished in my kingship, and my power grew even greater.
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, exalt, and glorify the King of heaven, all of whose works are true and whose ways are just, and who can humble those who walk in pride.
King Belshazzar gave a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and before them all he drank wine.

Under the influence of the wine, Belshazzar ordered the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar, his father, had taken from the Temple of Jerusalem to be brought, so that he, his nobles, his wives, and his concubines might drink from them.
So they brought the gold vessels taken from the Temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king, his nobles, his wives, and his concubines drank from them.
They drank wine and praised their gods of gold and silver, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone.
At that moment the fingers of a human hand appeared, and began to write, opposite the lampstand, on the whitewashed wall of the royal palace; and the king saw the hand that was writing.
Then the king's face changed colour, overwhelmed by his thoughts; his limbs went weak and his knees knocked together.

He cried out for the magicians, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers to be brought, and he said to the wise men of Babylon: "Whoever reads this inscription and gives me its meaning will be clothed in purple, will wear a gold chain around his neck, and will rule as third in the kingdom."
All the king's wise men came in, but none could read the inscription or give its meaning to the king.
Then King Belshazzar was seized with terror, his face changed colour, and his nobles were in dismay.
Hearing of what was troubling the king and his nobles, the queen came into the banquet hall and said: "O king, live forever! Do not let your thoughts trouble you, do not let your face change colour.

There is in your kingdom a man in whom dwells the spirit of the holy gods. In the days of your father, there was found in him insight, understanding, and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods; so King Nebuchadnezzar, your father, made him chief of the diviners, the magicians, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers.

For there was found in this man, Daniel, to whom the king had given the name Belteshazzar, a superior spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, solve riddles, and untangle hard questions. So let Daniel be called, and he will give you the meaning of the inscription."
Daniel was brought before the king, and the king said to him: "Are you that Daniel, one of the captives of Judah whom the king, my father, brought from Judea?
I have heard that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that insight, understanding, and extraordinary wisdom are found in you.
The wise men and the magicians have just been brought before me to read this inscription and give me its meaning, but they could not.

I have heard that you know how to give interpretations and untangle hard questions. So if you can read this inscription and give me its meaning, you will be clothed in purple, you will wear a gold chain around your neck, and you will rule as third in the kingdom."
Daniel answered before the king: "Keep your gifts for yourself, and give your rewards to another; even so, I will read the king the inscription and give him its meaning.
O king, the Most High God had given Nebuchadnezzar, your father, kingship, greatness, glory, and majesty.

Because of this greatness, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled with fear before him: he put to death whom he wished and let live whom he wished, he raised up whom he wished and brought low whom he wished.
But when his heart swelled and his spirit grew hard to the point of arrogance, he was cast down from his royal throne and stripped of his glory.

He was driven from among men, his heart became like that of the beasts, he lived among the wild asses, he was fed grass like oxen, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingship of men and raises up over it whom he wills.
And you, Belshazzar, his son, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.

You have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven: the vessels of his house were brought before you, and you, your nobles, your wives, and your concubines drank wine from them; you praised gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which see nothing, hear nothing, and know nothing. But the God who holds your breath in his hand and on whom all your ways depend, him you have not glorified.
That is why he sent this hand, which traced the inscription.
And this is what was traced: Mene, Mene, Tekel, Peres.
This is its meaning. Mene: God has counted the days of your reign and brought it to an end.
Tekel: you have been weighed in the balance and found wanting.
Peres: your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and the Persians."
Then, by order of Belshazzar, Daniel was clothed in purple, a gold chain was put around his neck, and it was proclaimed that he would rule as third in the kingdom.
That very night, Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed.

titres.titre: The deliverance and the edict of Darius

versets.t: Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.
He saw fit to set over the kingdom a hundred and twenty satraps, distributed throughout the land,
and to place over them three ministers, of whom Daniel was one; the satraps were to give account to them, so that the king would suffer no harm.
Now Daniel surpassed the ministers and the satraps, for there was in him an extraordinary spirit, and the king was thinking of setting him over the whole kingdom.

Then the ministers and the satraps sought grounds for an accusation against Daniel in the affairs of the kingdom; but they found none, no fault, for he was faithful, and no negligence or fault could be found in him.
So these men said to themselves: "We will find no grounds against this Daniel, except in the law of his God."
Then these ministers and satraps rushed to the king and said to him: "King Darius, live forever!

All the ministers of the kingdom, the prefects, the satraps, the counsellors, and the governors have agreed that the king should issue an edict and a strict ban: whoever, for thirty days, addresses a prayer to any god or man, except to you, O king, shall be thrown into the lions' den.
Now, O king, issue this ban and sign the decree, so that it cannot be changed, in accordance with the law of the Medes and the Persians, which is irrevocable."
Accordingly, King Darius signed the decree and the ban.
When Daniel learned that the decree was signed, he went home. His upper room had windows open toward Jerusalem; three times a day he knelt down, praying and praising his God, as he had always done.
Then these men rushed in and found Daniel praying and imploring his God.

They went to the king and reminded him of his ban: "Have you not signed a ban: that whoever, for thirty days, prays to any god or man, except you, O king, would be thrown into the lions' den?" The king answered: "The matter stands firm, in accordance with the law of the Medes and the Persians, which is irrevocable."
Then they said before the king: "Daniel, one of the captives of Judah, has paid no heed to you, O king, nor to the ban you signed: three times a day he says his prayer."
At these words, the king was deeply distressed; he set his heart on saving Daniel and, until sunset, sought a way to deliver him.
But these men rushed again to the king and said: "Know, O king, that according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, no ban or decree issued by the king can be changed."
Then the king ordered Daniel to be brought and thrown into the lions' den. He said to Daniel: "May your God, whom you serve with constancy, deliver you himself!"
A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den; the king sealed it with his own signet and that of his nobles, so that nothing might be changed in Daniel's fate.
Then the king returned to his palace; he spent the night fasting, allowed no entertainment to be brought, and sleep fled from him.
At dawn, at first light, the king rose and ran to the lions' den.
As he drew near the den, he called out to Daniel in an anguished voice: "Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve with constancy, been able to deliver you from the lions?"
Daniel answered the king: "O king, live forever!
My God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths: they have done me no harm, for I was found innocent before him; and before you too, O king, I have committed no wrong."
The king was filled with joy and ordered Daniel to be lifted out of the den. He was lifted out, and no injury was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

By order of the king, the men who had accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the lions' den, they, their wives, and their children; they had not reached the bottom before the lions seized them and crushed all their bones.
Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell throughout the earth: "May peace be given to you in abundance!

This is my decree: throughout the whole extent of my kingdom, let all tremble with fear before the God of Daniel. For he is the living God, who endures forever; his kingdom will never be destroyed, and his dominion will have no end.
He delivers and he saves, he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth: it is he who has delivered Daniel from the lions' claws."
And this Daniel prospered under the reign of Darius and under the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

titres.titre: The vision of the four beasts
The Ancient of Days and the judgment
The one who comes on the clouds

versets.t: In the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon, Daniel, as he lay in bed, had a dream and visions. Then he wrote the dream down and set out its main points.
Daniel said: In my night vision I was looking: behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea,
and four huge beasts came up out of the sea, each different from the others.
The first was like a lion and had eagle's wings. I was watching: its wings were torn off, it was lifted up from the ground and set on its feet like a man, and a human heart was given to it.
Then behold a second beast, like a bear; it was raised up on one side, holding three ribs between the teeth of its mouth, and it was told: "Arise, devour much flesh!"
After this, I was watching: behold another beast, like a leopard, with four bird's wings on its back; it had four heads, and dominion was given to it.

Then, in my night visions, I was watching: behold a fourth beast, terrible, frightening, of extraordinary strength, with great iron teeth. It devoured, crushed, and trampled underfoot whatever was left; different from all the beasts before it, it had ten horns.

I was considering these horns, when another, a little one, rose up among them; three of the first horns were torn out before it. And this horn had eyes like human eyes and a mouth that uttered great words.

I was watching, until thrones were set up and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His garment was white as snow, the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was flames of fire, with wheels of blazing fire.
A river of fire streamed out before him; thousands upon thousands served him, myriads upon myriads stood before him. The court took its seat, and books were opened.
I was watching, because of the great words the horn was uttering; I watched until the beast was killed, its body destroyed and given over to the fire.
As for the other beasts, their dominion too was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a time and a season.
I was watching, in my night visions: behold, on the clouds of heaven came one like a son of man; he advanced as far as the Ancient of Days, and was brought before him.

To him were given dominion, glory, and kingship; all peoples, nations, and languages served him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his reign will never be destroyed.
I, Daniel, was troubled deep within me, and the visions of my mind terrified me.
I approached one of those who were standing there and asked him the truth about all this; he answered me and gave me its explanation:
"These four huge beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth;
but the holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and they will possess it forever, for ages upon ages."

Then I wanted to be sure about the fourth beast, different from all the others, most terrible of all, with iron teeth and bronze claws, which devoured, crushed, and trampled underfoot whatever was left;

and about the ten horns on its head, and about the other horn that had risen up and before which three had fallen, that horn with eyes and a mouth full of arrogance, which seemed greater than the others.
I was watching, and this horn was making war on the holy ones and prevailing over them,
until the Ancient of Days came, judgment was given in favour of the holy ones of the Most High, and the time came when the holy ones possessed the kingdom.
He spoke to me thus: "The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will arise on the earth, different from all the others; it will devour the whole earth, trample it, and grind it to dust.
The ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom; another will rise after them, different from the first, and he will bring down three kings.

He will utter words against the Most High, he will oppress the holy ones of the Most High and claim to change the times and the law; the holy ones will be handed over to his power for a time, times, and half a time.
Then the court will sit in judgment, and his dominion will be taken from him, to destroy and annihilate it forever.

Then the kingship, the dominion, and the greatness of all the kingdoms under heaven will be given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High; their reign is an everlasting reign, and all powers will serve and obey them."
Here the account ends. I, Daniel, was terrified by my thoughts, my face changed colour; but I kept the matter in my heart.

titres.titre: The vision of the ram and the goat
The little horn and the profaned sanctuary

versets.t: In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar, a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after the one I had already had.
I was looking in this vision, and it seemed to me that I was at Susa, the fortress of the province of Elam; I was looking, and I stood by the river Ulai.
I lifted my eyes and saw: a ram stood before the river. It had two horns, both tall, but one taller than the other, and the taller had grown up last.
I saw the ram charging with its horns toward the west, the north, and the south; no beast could withstand it, none could deliver from its power; it did as it pleased and grew strong.
I was watching, and behold a goat came from the west, crossing the whole earth without touching the ground; this goat had a prominent horn between its eyes.
It came up to the two-horned ram that I had seen before the river, and rushed at it with all the fury of its strength.

I saw it reach the ram; furious against it, it struck it and broke both its horns, and the ram had no strength to resist; it threw the ram to the ground and trampled it underfoot, and no one could deliver the ram from its power.
The goat grew exceedingly strong; but at the height of its strength, its great horn was broken, and four horns rose up in its place, toward the four winds of heaven.
From one of them came out a little horn, which grew immensely toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land.
It rose up to the host of heaven, cast down to the earth some of that host and some of the stars, and trampled them underfoot.
It even rose up to the Prince of the host: it took away from him the perpetual sacrifice and overthrew the place of his sanctuary.
Through a revolt, the host was handed over, together with the perpetual sacrifice; the horn threw truth to the ground, and everything it undertook succeeded.

Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one asked him: "How long will what the vision announces last: the perpetual sacrifice abolished, the revolt that devastates, the sanctuary and the host handed over and trampled?"
He answered me: "For two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be purified."
While I, Daniel, was contemplating this vision and trying to understand it, behold, there stood before me a figure like a man.
And I heard a human voice come from the river Ulai; it cried out: "Gabriel, explain the vision to him."
He came near to where I was standing; at his approach, seized with dread, I fell on my face. He said to me: "Understand, son of man: this vision concerns the time of the end."
While he was speaking to me, I lost consciousness, my face to the ground; but he touched me and set me on my feet again.
Then he said: "Behold, I will teach you what will happen at the end of the wrath, for this vision concerns the time of the end.
The two-horned ram that you saw, these are the kings of Media and Persia.
The goat is the king of Greece, and the great horn between its eyes is the first king.
This horn was broken, and four others rose up in its place: four kingdoms will arise from this nation, but without having the same strength.
At the end of their reign, when the unfaithful have filled up the measure, a king of harsh countenance, expert in intrigue, will arise.
His power will grow, but not by his own strength; he will cause unheard-of ruin, will succeed in his undertakings, and will destroy the mighty and the people of the holy ones.

Through his cunning, he will make deceit prosper; he will grow proud in his heart, and in the midst of peace he will destroy a multitude. He will rise up against the Prince of princes, but he will be broken with no human hand touching him.
The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been revealed to you is true; but keep it secret, for it concerns a distant time."
Then I, Daniel, was overcome and lay ill for several days; then I got up and resumed my service to the king. I was overwhelmed by this vision, which no one understood.

titres.titre: Daniel understands the prophecy of Jeremiah

versets.t: In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the race of the Medes, who was made king over the kingdom of the Chaldeans,

in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years that, according to the word of the Lord addressed to the prophet Jeremiah, were to pass over the ruins of Jerusalem: seventy years.
I turned my face toward the Lord God, to seek him in prayer and supplication, by fasting, in sackcloth and ashes.
I prayed to the Lord my God and made this confession: "Ah, Lord, great and awesome God, who keep your covenant and your kindness toward those who love you and observe your commandments:
we have sinned, we have done evil, we have been guilty and rebellious, we have turned away from your commandments and your laws.
We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our leaders, our fathers, and all the people of the land.

To you, Lord, belongs justice; to us, shame on our faces, as is seen today, to us, the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and all Israel, near and far, in all the lands where you have scattered us because of our unfaithfulness to you.
Lord, to us belongs shame on our faces, to our kings, our leaders, and our fathers, for we have sinned against you.
To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him.
We have not obeyed the voice of the Lord our God, to follow the laws he set before us through his servants the prophets.

All Israel has transgressed your law and turned away, refusing to listen to your voice. Then the curse and the imprecation written in the law of Moses, the servant of God, were poured out upon us, for we had sinned against him.
He has carried out the word he had spoken against us and against our judges: he brought upon us so great a calamity that nothing like what happened to Jerusalem has ever happened under heaven.
As it is written in the law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; and we have not sought to appease the Lord our God, by turning away from our faults and becoming attentive to your truth.
The Lord has kept watch over this calamity and brought it upon us; for the Lord our God is just in all that he does, and we have not listened to his voice.
And now, Lord our God, you who brought your people out of the land of Egypt by your mighty hand and made a name for yourself, as is seen today: we have sinned, we have done evil.

Lord, in keeping with all your justice, let your anger and your indignation turn away from your city of Jerusalem, your holy mountain; for it is because of our sins and the faults of our fathers that Jerusalem and your people are an object of shame to all our neighbours.
Now, listen, O our God, to the prayer of your servant and his supplications; make your face shine upon your desolate sanctuary, for your own sake, Lord.

My God, incline your ear and listen, open your eyes and see our ruins and the city that bears your name. For it is not on account of our merits that we lay our supplications before you, but because of your great mercy.
Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, be attentive and act without delay, for your own sake, O my God; for your name is invoked over your city and over your people!"
I was still speaking, praying and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and laying my supplication before the Lord my God for the holy mountain of my God;
I was still speaking in prayer, when Gabriel, the man I had seen in the earlier vision, came to me in swift flight, at the hour of the evening offering.
He instructed me and said: "Daniel, I have now come to open your understanding.
At the very beginning of your prayer a word went out, and I have come to announce it to you, for you are a man beloved of God. So be attentive to the word and understand the vision.

Seventy weeks have been fixed for your people and your holy city, to put an end to the revolt, to make an end of sin, to atone for guilt, to establish everlasting justice, to seal vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Holy of Holies.

Know this, then, and understand: from the order to rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed one, a leader, there will be seven weeks; then, for sixty-two weeks, it will be rebuilt, squares and ramparts, but in the distress of the times.

After the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one will be cut off, and he will have no one for him. The people of a leader who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary; his end will come in a flood, and to the very end there will be war, with the devastations decreed.

He will impose a covenant on many for one week; at the middle of the week he will put a stop to sacrifice and offering, and upon the wing of the Temple will come the desolating abomination, until the ruin decreed falls upon the devastator."

In the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia, a word was revealed to Daniel, surnamed Belteshazzar. This word is true and announces a great conflict. Daniel grasped its meaning and understood the vision.
In those days, I, Daniel, mourned for three full weeks.
I ate no fine food, no meat or wine passed my lips, and I did not anoint myself, until the end of those three weeks.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month (around March-April), I was on the bank of the great river, the Tigris.
I lifted my eyes and looked: behold a man clothed in linen, his waist girded with a belt of fine gold.

His body was like beryl, his face shone like lightning, his eyes were like torches of fire, his arms and feet had the gleam of polished bronze, and the sound of his voice was like the roar of a crowd.
I, Daniel, alone saw this apparition; the men who were with me did not see it, but a great terror seized them and they fled to hide.
I was left alone to behold this great apparition; all my strength left me, my face fell, and I was left without vigour.
I heard the sound of his words, and at that sound I fell in a faint, my face to the ground.
Then a hand touched me and raised me onto my knees and onto the palms of my hands.
He said to me: "Daniel, man beloved of God, be attentive to the words I am about to say to you and stand up, for I am now sent to you." At these words, I stood up, trembling.

He said to me: "Do not be afraid, Daniel. From the very first day you set your heart to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and it is because of them that I have come.
But the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to my help, and I remained there beside the kings of Persia.
I have come to make you understand what will happen to your people at the end of days, for this vision concerns days still far off."
While he was speaking to me thus, I kept my face bowed toward the ground, unable to say a word.

And behold: someone with the likeness of a man touched my lips. I opened my mouth and spoke; I said to the one standing before me: "My lord, at this apparition anguish has seized me and all my strength has left me.
How could I, my lord's servant, speak with my lord? Already all my strength is leaving me, and no breath is left in me."
Again, the one with the likeness of a man touched me and gave me back my strength.

He said to me: "Do not be afraid, man beloved of God! Peace be with you! Take courage, take courage!" While he was speaking to me, I regained my strength and said: "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."
He said to me: Do you know why I have come to you? I am now going to return to fight the prince of Persia, and when I leave, behold, the prince of Greece will come.
But I will announce to you what is written in the book of truth. No one supports me against these princes except Michael, your prince.

titres.titre: The kings of Persia and Greece
The wars of the south and the north
The king's pride and his end

versets.t: And I, in the first year of Darius the Mede, stood beside him to support and strengthen him.

Now I will announce the truth to you. Behold: three more kings will arise for Persia, and the fourth will amass more wealth than all the others; strong in his wealth, he will rouse everyone against the kingdom of Greece.
Then a valiant king will arise, who will exercise great dominion and do as he pleases.

But no sooner is he established than his kingdom will be shattered and divided toward the four winds of heaven; it will not pass to his descendants and will no longer have the power it had, for his kingdom will be dismembered and given to others.
The king of the south will grow powerful; but one of his generals will become even more powerful than he and will rule: his dominion will be great.

After some years, they will form an alliance: the daughter of the king of the south will come to the king of the north to seal an agreement. But she will not keep her strength, and he too will not endure: she will be handed over, along with those who had brought her, with her father and the one who had supported her.
A shoot from her roots will arise in her place; he will march against the army, enter the fortress of the king of the north, deal with them as he pleases, and prevail.
He will even carry off to Egypt their gods, their metal statues, and their precious vessels of silver and gold; then, for some years, he will keep away from the king of the north.
The latter will invade the kingdom of the south, then return to his own land.
His sons will prepare for war and gather an immense army; one of them will advance, sweep on, invade, then come back to carry the war as far as the fortress.
Furious, the king of the south will go out to fight the king of the north; the latter will raise a great army, but it will be handed over into the hands of his adversary.
When this army is scattered, the heart of the king of the south will swell; he will bring down tens of thousands of men, but without gaining any lasting advantage.
For the king of the north will again raise an army more numerous than the first and, after some years, he will return with a great army and immense equipment.
In that time, many will rise up against the king of the south; and among your people, violent men will rise up to fulfill the vision, but they will fail.
The king of the north will come, throw up siege ramps, and take a fortified city; the forces of the south will not hold, not even their best troops: there will be no strength to resist.
The invader will do as he pleases, and no one will stand before him; he will settle in the glorious land, destruction in his hand.
He will resolve to come with the full strength of his kingdom; he will conclude an agreement and give him a young woman in marriage to ruin him, but the plan will fail and not profit him.
He will then turn toward the islands and take many of them; but a commander will put an end to his arrogance and turn it back upon him.
He will withdraw toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble, he will fall, and he will be found no more.
In his place will arise another, who will send a tax collector into the jewel of his kingdom; but in a few days he will be broken, without anger or battle.
In his place will arise a contemptible man, to whom royal dignity was not destined: he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingship by intrigue.
Before him, the flooding armies will be swept away and broken, and even the leader of the covenant.
Despite the agreement made with him, he will act by deceit: he will rise and prevail with few people.

In a time of peace, he will invade the richest provinces and do what neither his fathers nor his fathers' fathers had done: he will distribute to his followers plunder, spoil, and wealth, and he will form plans against the fortresses, for a time.

He will muster his strength and his courage against the king of the south, at the head of a great army. The king of the south will engage in war with a numerous and powerful army, but he will not hold, for plots will be woven against him.
Those who eat at his table will break him; his army will be swept away, and many will fall, struck down.
The two kings, their hearts bent on evil, will tell each other lies at the same table; but nothing will come of it, for the end will come only at the appointed time.
The king of the north will return to his own land with great wealth, his heart set against the holy covenant; he will act, then return home.
At the appointed time, he will come back toward the south; but this campaign will not be like the first.

Ships from Kittim will come against him, and he will lose heart. He will turn back and vent his fury against the holy covenant; and he will again come to terms with those who have abandoned the holy covenant.
Troops sent by him will rise up, profane the sanctuary and its fortress, put a stop to the perpetual sacrifice, and set up the desolating abomination.
By flattery, he will seduce those who betray the covenant; but the people of those who know their God will stand firm and act.
The wise among the people will instruct many; but, for a time, they will fall by sword and fire, by captivity and plunder.
In their fall, they will receive a little help, and many will join them, but out of hypocrisy.
Some of these wise ones will fall, so that they may be tested, purified, and made white until the time of the end; for the appointed term has not yet come.

The king will do as he pleases; he will rise up and magnify himself above every god, he will utter unheard-of things against the God of gods, and he will prosper until the wrath reaches its peak; for what is decreed must be fulfilled.
He will have no regard for the gods of his fathers, nor for the god cherished by women, nor for any god, for he will magnify himself above them all.
In their place, he will honour the god of fortresses; a god his fathers did not know, he will honour with gold, silver, precious stones, and jewels.

Against the best-defended fortresses, he will act with this foreign god: those who acknowledge it, he will load with honours, give authority over the multitude, and distribute land to them as a reward.

At the time of the end, the king of the south will clash with him. The king of the north will fall upon him with chariots, horsemen, and many ships; he will invade the lands, sweep on, and pass through.
He will enter the glorious land, and many lands will fall; but Edom, Moab, and the elite of the sons of Ammon will escape his hand.
He will stretch out his hand against the lands, and Egypt will not escape.
He will gain control of the treasures of gold and silver and all the riches of Egypt; the Libyans and the Ethiopians will follow in his train.
But news from the east and the north will trouble him, and he will set out, in great fury, to destroy and exterminate a multitude.
He will pitch the tents of his palace between the sea and the holy and glorious mountain; then he will come to his end, and no one will help him.

In that time Michael will arise, the great prince, the one who watches over the sons of your people. It will be a time of distress such as there has never been since nations came into being until this day. But in that time, your people will be saved, all those who are found written in the book.
And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to eternal life, others to everlasting shame and horror.
Those who have been wise will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have led the multitude to justice will shine like the stars, forever and ever.
And you, Daniel, keep these words secret and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will search it, and knowledge will grow.
Then I, Daniel, looked: behold, two other men were standing, one on one bank of the river, the other on the other bank.
One of them said to the man clothed in linen who stood above the waters of the river: "How long until these wonders, before they are fulfilled?"

And I heard the man clothed in linen who stood above the waters: raising his right hand and his left hand toward heaven, he swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time; and when the strength of the holy people has finished being broken, then all this will be fulfilled.
I heard, but without understanding, and I said: "My lord, what will be the outcome of all this?"
He answered: "Go, Daniel, for these words remain secret and sealed until the time of the end.
Many will be purified, made white, and tested; the wicked will do evil, and no wicked person will understand, but the wise will understand.
From the moment the perpetual sacrifice is abolished and the abomination of desolation set up, there will be one thousand two hundred and ninety days.
Happy the one who waits and reaches one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days!
And you, go toward your end and rest; you will rise to receive your inheritance, at the end of days."
There was in Babylon a man named Joakim.
He had married a woman named Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, very beautiful and God-fearing;
her parents, who were righteous, had raised their daughter according to the law of Moses.
Joakim was very wealthy; he had a garden adjoining his house, and the Jews gathered at his home, for he was the most respected of all.

That year, two elders of the people had been appointed as judges, of those about whom the Lord had said: "Iniquity has come out of Babylon through elders who were judges and claimed to guide the people."
They frequented the house of Joakim, and all who had a dispute came to them.
Around midday, when the people had withdrawn, Susanna would go in to walk in her husband's garden.
The two elders saw her going in and walking each day, and they began to burn with desire for her.
They corrupted their judgment and turned away their eyes, so as no longer to look to heaven or remember the just judgments of God.
Both were wounded with love for her, but they hid their torment from each other,
for they were ashamed to confess the desire that drove them toward her.
Each day they watched her eagerly to see her. One day, they said to each other:
"Let us go home, it is time for the meal." And they went out, each his own way.

But, retracing their steps, they met again; questioned by each other about the reason for their return, they confessed their passion to one another, and agreed together on a moment when they could catch her alone.
As they were watching for the right day, Susanna came into the garden, as on the day before and the day before that, with only two maidservants; she wished to bathe, for it was hot.
There was no one there but the two elders, hidden, spying on her.
She said to the maidservants: "Bring me scented oil and ointments, and shut the garden gates, so that I may bathe."
They did as she asked, shut the garden gates, and went out by a back door to fetch what she wanted, unaware that the elders were hidden.
As soon as the maidservants had gone out, the two elders rose, ran to Susanna,
and said to her: "Look: the garden gates are shut, no one sees us, and we burn with desire for you. Yield to us and be ours.
Otherwise, we will testify against you: we will say that a young man was with you, and that this is why you sent away your maidservants."
Susanna groaned and said: "On every side, anguish grips me. If I yield, it is death for me; if I refuse, I will not escape your hands.
But it is better for me to fall into your hands without having acted, than to sin before the Lord."
Then Susanna cried out with a loud voice; the two elders also cried out against her,
and one of them ran to open the garden gates.
Hearing these cries in the garden, the servants of the house rushed in by the back door to see what was happening to Susanna.
When the elders had spoken, the servants were filled with shame, for nothing of the kind had ever been said about Susanna.
The next day, when the people gathered at the house of Joakim, her husband, the two elders came as well, full of their criminal designs to have her condemned to death.
They said before the people: "Send for Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, wife of Joakim." And they sent for her.
She came, with her parents, her children, and all her relatives.
Susanna was of great delicacy and great beauty.
Since she was veiled, these perverse judges ordered her to be unveiled, to feast on her beauty.
But all her own people and all who knew her wept.
The two elders stood up in the midst of the people and laid their hands on Susanna's head.
She, weeping, lifted her eyes to heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord.
The elders said: "As we were walking alone in the garden, this woman came in with two maidservants; she had the gates shut and sent the maidservants away.
A young man, who was hidden, came to her and sinned with her.
We were in a corner of the garden; seeing this crime, we ran toward them and caught them together.
We could not hold the young man, who was stronger than we: he opened the gate and fled.
But her we seized, and we asked her who the young man was; she would not tell us. This is what we testify."
The assembly believed them, because they were elders and judges of the people, and it condemned Susanna to death.
Then Susanna cried out with a loud voice: "Eternal God, you who know hidden things and who know all before it happens,
you know that they have borne false witness against me. And behold, I die, though I have done none of the things they have wickedly invented against me!"
The Lord heard her voice.
As she was being led to death, God stirred up the holy spirit of a young boy named Daniel,
who cried out with a loud voice: "I am innocent of this woman's blood!"
All the people turned toward him: "What do you mean by that?"
Standing in their midst, Daniel said: "Are you so foolish, sons of Israel, as to condemn a daughter of Israel without inquiry and without proof?
Return to the court, for these men have borne false witness against her."
The people returned in haste, and the elders said to Daniel: "Come, take your place among us and instruct us, for God has given you the authority of an elder."
Daniel said to the people: "Separate them from each other, and I will question them."
When they were separated, Daniel called the first and said to him: "Man grown old in evil, now the sins you committed long ago catch up with you,
you who passed unjust judgments, condemning the innocent and releasing the guilty, though the Lord has said not to put to death the innocent and the just.
Now then, if you truly saw her, tell me under what tree you caught them together." He answered: "Under a mastic tree."
Daniel said: "You lie, and this lie will be your ruin: for the angel of God has already received from him the order to cut you in two."
He sent him away and had the other brought, to whom he said: "Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has led you astray and desire has corrupted your heart.
This is how you treated the daughters of Israel, and they, out of fear, yielded to your advances; but a daughter of Judah did not endure your infamy.
So tell me under what tree you caught them together." He answered: "Under an oak."
Daniel said to him: "You too lie, and this lie will be your ruin: for the angel of God waits, sword in hand, to cut you in two, to destroy you both."
Then the whole assembly cried out with a loud voice and blessed God, who saves those who hope in him.
Then they rose up against the two elders, whom Daniel had convicted of false witness by their own mouths, and they did to them the evil they themselves had meant to do to their neighbour:
to fulfill the law of Moses, they put them to death. And innocent blood was saved that day.
Hilkiah and his wife gave thanks to God for their daughter Susanna, with Joakim her husband and all her relatives, because nothing shameful had been found in her.
And Daniel, from that day on, was great in the eyes of the people.
King Astyages was gathered to his fathers, and Cyrus the Persian received the kingdom.

titres.titre: The deliverance and the king's faith

versets.t: Daniel ate at the king's table, and he was honoured more than all his friends.
The Babylonians had an idol named Bel; every day about six hundred litres of flour, forty sheep, and about two hundred and forty litres of wine were spent on it.
The king venerated it and went every day to worship it; but Daniel worshipped his God.

The king said to him: "Why do you not worship Bel?" He answered: "Because I do not venerate idols made by human hands, but the living God, who made heaven and earth and who has power over every creature."
The king went on: "Does Bel not seem to you a living god? Do you not see all that he eats and drinks each day?"
Daniel answered with a smile: "Do not be deceived, O king: this Bel is clay within and bronze without, he has never eaten anything."
The king, angered, summoned the priests of Bel and said to them: "If you do not tell me who eats all these offerings, you will die;
but if you prove that it is Bel who eats them, Daniel will die, for having blasphemed against Bel."
There were seventy priests of Bel, not counting their wives and children. The king went with Daniel to the temple of Bel.
The priests of Bel said: "We are going to go out; you, O king, have the food set out and the wine poured, then shut the door and seal it with your signet.
Tomorrow morning, when you come in, if you do not find that Bel has eaten everything, we will die; otherwise, it will be Daniel, who has lied against us."
They were unconcerned, for they had arranged a secret entrance beneath the table by which they always came to consume the offerings.

When they had gone out and the king had had the food set out before Bel, Daniel had ashes brought by his servants and scattered them throughout the temple, in the presence of the king alone; then they went out, shut the door, sealed it with the king's signet, and departed.
During the night, the priests came as usual, with their wives and children, and they ate and drank everything.
The king rose at dawn, and Daniel with him.
The king asked: "Are the seals intact, Daniel?" He answered: "Intact, O king."
As soon as he had opened the door and looked at the table, the king exclaimed: "You are great, O Bel, and there is no deceit in you!"
Daniel began to laugh; holding the king back to stop him from going forward, he said to him: "Look at the floor: whose footprints are these?"
The king answered: "I see footprints of men, women, and children!" And he flew into a great rage.
He had the priests seized, with their wives and children; they showed him the secret doors by which they came to consume what was on the table.
The king had them put to death and handed Bel over to Daniel, who destroyed it along with its temple.
There was also a great dragon, which the Babylonians venerated.
The king said to Daniel: "Will you still say that this one is bronze? See: it lives, it eats and drinks; you can no longer say it is not a living god."
Daniel answered: "I worship the Lord, my God, for he is the living God; but this one is not a living god.
Give me leave, O king, and I will kill this dragon without sword or club." The king said: "I give it to you."

Then Daniel took pitch, fat, and hair, boiled them together, and formed them into balls that he threw into the dragon's mouth; the dragon swallowed them and burst. And Daniel said: "So this is what you venerated!"

At this news, the Babylonians were filled with fierce indignation; they rose up against the king, saying: "The king has become a Jew: he has destroyed Bel, killed the dragon, and slaughtered the priests."
They went to the king and said to him: "Hand Daniel over to us; otherwise, we will destroy you and your household."
Seeing that they were pressing him violently, the king, under constraint, handed Daniel over to them.
They threw him into the lions' den, where he stayed six days.
There were seven lions in the den, to whom two carcasses and two sheep were given each day; but now they were given nothing, so that they would devour Daniel.
Now the prophet Habakkuk was in Judea; he had just prepared a stew and crumbled bread into a basket, and he was going to carry it to the reapers in the fields.
The angel of the Lord said to Habakkuk: "Carry to Babylon the meal you are holding, for Daniel, who is in the lions' den."
Habakkuk answered: "Lord, I have never seen Babylon and I do not know this den."
Then the angel seized him by the top of his head and, holding him by the hair, set him down in Babylon, above the den, with all the swiftness of his nature.
Habakkuk cried out: "Daniel, servant of God, take the meal that God sends you!"
Daniel said: "You have remembered me, O God, and you have not forsaken those who love you!"
Daniel rose and ate, while the angel of God at once put Habakkuk back in his place.
On the seventh day, the king came to mourn Daniel; arriving at the den, he looked, and behold, Daniel was sitting in the midst of the lions.
He cried out with a loud voice: "You are great, Lord, God of Daniel, and there is no other but you!" And he had him lifted out of the den.
Then he had those who had sought to destroy him thrown into the den, and they were devoured before his eyes, in an instant.

Then the king declared: "Let all the inhabitants of the earth fear the God of Daniel! For it is he who is the Saviour, who works signs and wonders on the earth, he who has delivered Daniel from the lions' den."

titres.titre: Hosea's marriage and the symbolic children

versets.t: The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.

When the Lord first spoke through Hosea, he said to him: "Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution and have children of prostitution, for the land keeps prostituting itself by forsaking the Lord."
So Hosea went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; she conceived and bore him a son.
The Lord said to him: "Name him Jezreel, for soon I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood shed at Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingship of the house of Israel.
On that day I will break Israel's bow in the Valley of Jezreel."
She conceived again and bore a daughter. The Lord said to Hosea: "Name her Not-loved, for I will no longer show my love to the house of Israel, nor forgive them anymore.
But I will have pity on the house of Judah; I will save them by the Lord their God, and not by bow or sword or war, nor by horses and horsemen."
After she had weaned Not-loved, Gomer conceived and bore a son.
The Lord said: "Name him Not-my-people, for you are not my people, and I am not your God."

titres.titre: The case against the unfaithful wife

versets.t: The number of the children of Israel will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. And instead of being told, 'Not-my-people,' they will be called 'children of the living God.'
The children of Judah and the children of Israel will gather together, appoint for themselves a single head, and come up out of the land; for great will be the day of Jezreel.
Say to your brothers, 'My-people!' and to your sisters, 'Loved!'

Bring a case against your mother, bring your case! For she is no longer my wife, and I am no longer her husband. Let her remove her prostitutions from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts;
otherwise I will strip her naked and leave her as on the day she was born; I will make her like the desert, turn her into parched land, and let her die of thirst.
I will have no pity on her children, for they are children of prostitution.

Yes, their mother has prostituted herself; she who conceived them has covered herself with shame. She said, 'I will run after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my linen, my oil and my drink.'
