Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?" Taking him for the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if it is you who have carried him off, tell me where you have put him, and I will go and take him."
Jesus said to her, "Mary!" She turned and said to him in Hebrew, "Rabbouni!", that is, Master.
Jesus said to her, "Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God."
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord!", and she reported what he had said to her.

On the evening of that same day, the first of the week, while the doors of the place where the disciples were had been locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them. He said to them, "Peace be with you!"
As he said this, he showed them his hands and his side. When they saw the Lord, the disciples were filled with joy.
Again Jesus said to them, "Peace be with you! As the Father has sent me, so I send you."
After saying this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit.
Those whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; those whose sins you retain, they are retained."
Now Thomas, one of the Twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus had come.

The other disciples kept telling him, "We have seen the Lord!" But he answered them, "Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger where the nails were, and my hand into his side, I will not believe."
Eight days later, the disciples were again gathered together, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, though the doors were locked, stood among them, and said, "Peace be with you!"
Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and look at my hands; reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting: believe."
Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
Jesus said to him, "Because you have seen me, you believe. Blessed are those who believe without having seen!"
Jesus performed, in the presence of his disciples, many other signs as well that are not written in this book.
But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that through believing you may have life in his name.

titres.titre: Simon, do you love me? The mission entrusted to Peter

versets.t: After this, Jesus revealed himself again to his disciples, by the Sea of Tiberias. This is how it happened.
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They answered him, "We are coming with you." They went out and got into the boat; but that night they caught nothing.
At daybreak Jesus was standing on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was he.
Jesus said to them, "My children, have you caught any fish?" They answered, "No."
He said to them, "Cast the net to the right of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and they could no longer haul it in, there were so many fish.
Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put back on the garment he had taken off for work and threw himself into the water.
The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish; they were not far from shore, about a hundred meters.
Once they had come ashore, they saw a charcoal fire, with fish laid on it, and bread.
Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught."
Simon Peter went back into the boat and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish: there were a hundred and fifty-three of them. And despite this number, the net did not tear.
Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." None of the disciples dared to ask him, "Who are you?", for they knew it was the Lord.
Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them; he did the same with the fish.
This was now the third time that Jesus revealed himself to his disciples since he had risen from the dead.

After the meal, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these do?" He answered him, "Yes, Lord, you know that I am your friend." Jesus said to him, "Take care of my lambs."
He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter answered him, "Yes, Lord, you know that I am your friend." Jesus said to him, "Be the shepherd of my sheep."

He said to him a third time, "Simon, son of John, are you my friend?" Peter was hurt at being questioned a third time in this way, and he answered him, "Lord, you who know everything, you know that I am your friend." Jesus said to him, "Take care of my sheep.

Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were young, you tied your own belt and went where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will tie your belt and lead you where you would rather not go."
Jesus said this to show by what kind of death Peter was going to glorify God. Then he added, "Follow me."
Turning around, Peter saw behind him the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one who during the meal had leaned close against him to ask, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
Seeing him, Peter said to Jesus, "Lord, and what about him?"
Jesus answered him, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You, follow me."
So the report spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. Yet Jesus had not said that he would not die, but, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?"
It is this disciple who bears witness to all this and who has written it; and we know that his witness is true.
Jesus did many other things as well. If they were told one by one, I suppose that the whole world could not contain the books that would have to be written.
In my first book, Theophilus, I told of all that Jesus did and taught from the beginning,
up to the day when he was taken up to heaven, after he had given his instructions, through the Holy Spirit, to the apostles he had chosen.
To them he showed himself alive after his passion, proving it by many appearances: over forty days he appeared to them and spoke of the kingdom of God.
One day, as he was sharing a meal with them, he told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for what the Father had promised: "You have heard me speak of it:
John baptized with water, but you, in a few days from now, will be baptized in the Holy Spirit."
So when they were gathered together, they asked him, "Lord, is this the time when you are going to restore the kingdom to Israel?"
He answered them, "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth."
When he had said this, as they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him from their sight.
As they were still gazing at the sky where Jesus was going, suddenly two men in white robes stood beside them
and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking at the sky? This Jesus who has been taken up to heaven from among you will come back in the same way as you have seen him go up to heaven."
Then, from the hill called the Mount of Olives, they returned to Jerusalem, which is close by, a sabbath day's walk away.

When they arrived, they went up to the upper room where they usually stayed. They were Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Jude son of James.
All of them, with one heart, were constant in prayer, together with some women, with Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.
In those days Peter stood up among the brothers, who were gathered, about a hundred and twenty in number, and said,
"Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled in which the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of David, spoke in advance of Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus.
He was one of us and had received his share in our ministry.
Now, with the wages of his crime, this man had bought himself a field; then he fell headlong, his body burst open down the middle, and all his entrails spilled out.
All the people of Jerusalem came to know of it, so that this field was called in their language Hakeldama, that is, the Field of Blood.
For it is written in the book of Psalms: May his dwelling become deserted, and may no one live in it! And again: May another take over his office!
So one of the men who accompanied us the whole time the Lord Jesus lived among us,
from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up from us, must become with us a witness to his resurrection."
They put forward two: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias.
Then they prayed: "Lord, you who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen
to take, in this apostolic ministry, the place that Judas left to go to the place that was his own."
They drew lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, who was added to the eleven apostles.

titres.titre: The life of the first community

versets.t: When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in the same place.
Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.
Then there appeared to them tongues that seemed to be of fire; they separated, and one came to rest on each of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them to speak.
Now there were staying in Jerusalem devout Jews from every nation under heaven.
At this sound the crowd gathered, bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language.
Amazed and astonished, they said, "Are not all these people who are speaking Galileans?
How is it that each of us hears them in his own native language?
Parthians, Medes and Elamites, inhabitants of Mesopotamia, of Judea and Cappadocia, of Pontus and Asia,
of Phrygia and Pamphylia, of Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, visitors from Rome,
Jews and converts to Judaism, Cretans and Arabs, we hear them proclaiming in our own languages the marvels of God."
All of them, bewildered and perplexed, said to one another, "What does this mean?"
But others sneered, "They are full of new wine."
Then Peter, standing with the Eleven, raised his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea, and all you who are staying in Jerusalem, understand this well, and listen carefully to my words.
No, these people are not drunk, as you suppose; it is only nine in the morning.
Rather, this is what the prophet Joel foretold:
In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh: your sons and your daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your elders will dream dreams.
Yes, in those days, on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy.
I will work wonders up in the sky and signs down here on the earth: blood, fire, and a column of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the coming of the day of the Lord, that great and glorious day.
Then everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
Men of Israel, listen to these words. Jesus of Nazareth, this man whom God accredited to you by the miracles, wonders, and signs that God worked through him among you, as you yourselves know,
this man, handed over according to the set purpose and foreknowledge of God, you put to death by nailing him to the cross by the hand of the wicked.
But God raised him up, freeing him from the pangs of death, for it was impossible for death to keep him in its power.
It is of him that David says: I kept the Lord before me without ceasing; he is at my right hand, so that I will not be shaken.
That is why my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my flesh, too, will rest in hope,
for you will not abandon my soul to the realm of the dead, nor let your faithful one see corruption.
You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence.
Brothers, let me say to you plainly: the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is still among us to this day.
But he was a prophet, and he knew that God had sworn to him that he would seat one of his own descendants on his throne.
Seeing in advance the resurrection of the Christ, he said that he would not be abandoned to the realm of the dead and that his flesh would not see corruption.
This Jesus, God raised him up, and of this we are all witnesses.
Raised up by the right hand of God, he received from the Father the Holy Spirit that was promised, and he has poured him out: this is what you see and hear.
For David did not go up to heaven; yet he himself says: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.
So let the whole house of Israel know for certain: God has made him Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
At these words, cut to the heart, they said to Peter and the other apostles, "Brothers, what must we do?"
Peter answered them, "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins; then you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
For the promise is for you, for your children, and for all who are far off, all whom the Lord our God will call."
And with many other words he urged and exhorted them: "Turn away from this corrupt generation, and be saved."
Those who welcomed his word were baptized, and that day about three thousand people joined the disciples.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship of the brothers, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.
A sense of awe was in every heart, and many wonders and signs were worked by the apostles.
All the believers lived united and held everything in common;
they would sell their property and possessions and share the proceeds among all, according to each one's need.
Each day, with one heart, they were faithful in attending the Temple; they broke bread in their homes and shared their food with gladness and simplicity of heart,
praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And each day the Lord added to the community those who were being saved.

titres.titre: The healing of the crippled man

versets.t: Peter and John were going up to the Temple for the prayer at three in the afternoon.
A man was being carried there who had been crippled from birth. Each day he was set down near the Temple gate called the Beautiful Gate, to beg for alms from those who were going in.
Seeing Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for alms.
Peter, together with John, fixed his eyes on him and said, "Look at us."
The man watched them, expecting to receive something.
But Peter said to him, "I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk."
He took him by the right hand and lifted him up. At once his feet and ankles grew strong:
with a leap he was on his feet and began to walk. He entered the Temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
All the people saw him walking and praising God.
They recognized him as the beggar who used to sit at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple, and they were filled with astonishment and awe at what had happened to him.
As he clung to Peter and John, all the people, in amazement, ran toward them at the portico called Solomon's Portico.

Seeing this, Peter said to the people, "Men of Israel, why are you astonished at what has happened? Why do you fix your eyes on us, as if it were by our own power or piety that we had made this man walk?
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus, whom you handed over and disowned before Pilate, even though he had decided to release him.
You disowned the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for the pardon of a murderer.
You put to death the author of life, whom God raised from the dead: of this we are witnesses.
It is by faith in his name that this name has given strength to the man you see and know; and the faith that comes through Jesus has given him, before you all, this complete healing.
Now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders.
But in this way God fulfilled what he had foretold through the mouth of all the prophets: that his Christ would suffer.
So repent and turn back to God, that your sins may be wiped away,
so that the Lord may bring the times of rest and send the Christ who was appointed for you, Jesus,
whom heaven must receive until the times when all things are restored, of which God spoke from of old through the mouth of his holy prophets.
Moses said: The Lord your God will raise up for you, from among your brothers, a prophet like me; you will listen to him in everything he says to you.
And whoever does not listen to that prophet will be cut off from the people.
All the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who followed, also foretold these days.
You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, when he said to Abraham: In your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.
It is for you first that God raised up his servant, and he sent him to bless you, turning each of you away from your sins."

titres.titre: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin

versets.t: Peter and John were still speaking to the people when the priests, the captain of the Temple, and the Sadducees came upon them,
annoyed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming, in the person of Jesus, the resurrection from the dead.
They seized them and threw them in prison until the next day, for it was already evening.
But many of those who had heard the word came to believe, and the number of the men reached about five thousand.
The next day the rulers, the elders, and the scribes assembled in Jerusalem,
with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who belonged to the high priestly family.
They had Peter and John brought before them and questioned them: "By what power or in whose name have you done this?"
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders,
since we are being questioned today about a good deed done to a crippled man and how he was healed,

let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: it is in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, the one you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, it is by him that this man stands here before you, healed.
This Jesus is the stone that you, the builders, rejected, and which has become the cornerstone.
In no one else is there salvation; for under heaven no other name has been given to men by which we must be saved."
Seeing the boldness of Peter and John, and realizing that they were uneducated, ordinary men, they were amazed; and they recognized them as companions of Jesus.
But since they saw the man who had been healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in reply.
They ordered them to leave the Sanhedrin and conferred among themselves:
"What are we to do with these men? They have worked a clear miracle, known to everyone living in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.
But to keep it from spreading further among the people, let us warn them, under threat of punishment, not to speak in this name to anyone again."
They called them back and strictly forbade them to speak or teach in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, "Is it right, before God, to obey you rather than God? Judge for yourselves.
As for us, we cannot keep silent about what we have seen and heard."
After further threats they let them go, finding no way to punish them because of the people, for everyone was glorifying God for what had happened;
the man healed by this miracle was, in fact, more than forty years old.
Once released, Peter and John went back to their own people and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
At this, with one heart, they raised their voices to God: "Sovereign Master, it is you who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them.
It is you who said, through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our father David, your servant: Why this raging of the nations, these vain plots of the peoples?
The kings of the earth rose up, the princes banded together against the Lord and against his Christ.
Yes, truly, in this city there banded together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate along with the pagan nations and the peoples of Israel,
to carry out all that your hand and your will had decided in advance.
And now, Lord, consider their threats and grant your servants to proclaim your word with all boldness,
as you stretch out your hand to bring about healings, miracles, and wonders through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
When they had prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken; they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and proclaimed the word of God with boldness.
The whole company of believers was of one heart and one soul; no one claimed as his own what belonged to him, but they held everything in common.
With great power the apostles bore witness to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace rested on all of them.
None of them was in need: all who owned lands or houses would sell them, bring the proceeds of the sale,
and lay them at the apostles' feet; the money was then distributed to each according to his needs.
So Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles surnamed Barnabas, which means son of encouragement,
sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet.

titres.titre: The apostles arrested and set free

versets.t: Now a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property
and, in collusion with her, kept back part of the price; he brought the rest and laid it at the apostles' feet.
Peter said to him, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so as to make you lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of the field?
Before it was sold, was it not yours? And once sold, was its price not at your disposal? How could you conceive such a scheme? It is not to men that you have lied, but to God."
On hearing these words, Ananias collapsed and died. Great fear seized all who heard of it.
The young men rose, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.
About three hours later, his wife came in, not knowing what had happened.
Peter asked her, "Tell me, is this the price at which you sold the field?" She answered, "Yes, that price."
Then Peter said to her, "How could the two of you agree to put the Spirit of the Lord to the test? Look: those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out too."
At once she collapsed at his feet and died. When the young men came in, they found her dead; they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
Great fear then seized the whole Church and all who heard of these events.
Many miracles and wonders were done among the people by the hands of the apostles. They all met together with one heart at Solomon's Portico.
No one else dared to join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
More and more, believers were being drawn to the Lord, a great number of both men and women.
People even carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on beds and mats, so that when Peter passed by, at least his shadow might fall on one of them.
Crowds also came flocking from the towns near Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
Then the high priest and all his circle, the party of the Sadducees, rose up, filled with fury.
They seized the apostles and threw them into the public prison.
But during the night the angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and said,
"Go, take your stand in the Temple, and proclaim to the people all the words of this life."

On hearing this, they entered the Temple at daybreak and began to teach. Meanwhile the high priest and his circle convened the Sanhedrin and the whole council of the elders of Israel, and they sent to the prison to have the apostles brought.
But when the guards got there, they did not find them in the prison. They came back and reported,
"We found the prison securely locked and the sentries on duty at the doors; but when we opened up, we found no one inside."
On hearing these words, the captain of the Temple and the chief priests were perplexed: what could have happened?
Just then someone came and told them, "The men you put in prison, they are standing in the Temple, teaching the people!"
The captain went off with his guards and brought them back, but without force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people.
They brought them in and made them stand before the Sanhedrin. The high priest questioned them:
"We strictly forbade you to teach in that name! And here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you want to bring this man's blood down on us."
Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you put to death by hanging him on a tree.
It is he whom God has exalted at his right hand as Prince and Savior, to give Israel repentance and the forgiveness of sins.
Of this we are witnesses, we and the Holy Spirit whom God has given to those who obey him."
On hearing this, they were furious and wanted to put them to death.
But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the Law respected by all the people, stood up in the Sanhedrin and ordered the apostles to be put outside for a moment.
Then he said, "Men of Israel, be careful what you are about to do to these men.
Not long ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be someone important; about four hundred men rallied to him. He was killed, all who had followed him scattered, and nothing came of it.
After him, at the time of the census, Judas the Galilean rose up and drew people after him. He too perished, and all his followers were scattered.
So in the present case, here is my advice: have nothing more to do with these men, and leave them alone. For if their plan or their work is of human origin, it will destroy itself;
but if it is from God, you will not be able to destroy them. Take care that you do not find yourselves at war with God!" They accepted his advice.
They called the apostles back, had them flogged, forbade them to speak in the name of Jesus, and then released them.
As for the apostles, they left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the Name.
And every day, in the Temple and in their homes, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the Good News: the Christ is Jesus.
In those days, as the number of disciples was growing, the Greek-speaking believers complained about the Hebrew-speaking ones: their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution.
So the Twelve called together the whole body of disciples and said, "It would not be right for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.
So look, brothers, among yourselves for seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, and we will entrust this task to them;
as for us, we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the service of the word."
The proposal pleased the whole assembly. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, along with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch.
They presented them to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
The word of God spread, the number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly, and a large group of priests became obedient to the faith.
Stephen, full of grace and power, was working great wonders and signs among the people.
Then some men from the synagogue known as the Synagogue of the Freedmen intervened, together with Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and Jews from Cilicia and Asia; they began to argue with Stephen,
but they were unable to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit that inspired him.
So they bribed some men to say, "We have heard him utter blasphemies against Moses and against God."
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, rushed at him, seized him, and brought him before the Sanhedrin.
They produced false witnesses, who declared, "This man never stops speaking against the holy Place and against the Law.
We have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this Place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us."
All who sat in the Sanhedrin had their eyes fixed on him, and his face appeared to them like the face of an angel.
The high priest asked, "Is this really so?"
Stephen answered, "Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran,
and said to him: Leave your country and your kindred, and go to the land I will show you.
So he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. From there, after his father's death, God brought him into this land where you now live.
He gave him no property there, not even a foot of ground; but he promised to give it into his possession, and to his descendants after him, even though he had no child.
God spoke thus: His descendants will live in a foreign land; they will be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.
But the nation whose slaves they will be, I myself will judge, says God; after that they will come out and worship me in this place.
Then he gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; Isaac did the same for Jacob, and Jacob for the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. But God was with him:
he rescued him from all his troubles and gave him grace and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who put him in charge of Egypt and of all his household.
Then a famine came over all Egypt and Canaan; the distress was great, and our fathers could find nothing to eat.
Hearing that there was grain in Egypt, Jacob sent our fathers there a first time.
On the second visit, Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned of his family.
Joseph then sent for his father Jacob and all his kindred, seventy-five people.
Jacob went down to Egypt, where he died, as did our fathers;
they were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor at Shechem.
As the time drew near for the promise that God had made to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until there arose over Egypt another king, who had not known Joseph.
Dealing craftily with our race, this king mistreated our fathers, forcing them to abandon their newborns so that they would not survive.
It was at this time that Moses was born, beautiful in the sight of God. For three months he was brought up in his father's house;
then, when he was abandoned, Pharaoh's daughter took him in and raised him as her own son.
Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in words and deeds.
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel.
Seeing one of them being mistreated, he came to his defense and avenged the oppressed man by killing the Egyptian.
He thought his brothers would understand that God was bringing them deliverance through his hand; but they did not understand.
The next day he came upon two of them fighting and tried to reconcile them: Men, you are brothers; why do you mistreat each other?
But the one who was mistreating his neighbor pushed him away: Who made you ruler and judge over us?
Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?
At these words Moses fled and lived as a stranger in the land of Midian, where he had two sons.
Forty years later, in the desert of Mount Sinai, an angel appeared to him in the flame of a burning bush.
At this sight Moses was filled with amazement; and as he drew near to look, the voice of the Lord was heard:
I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Trembling all over, Moses did not dare to look.
The Lord said to him: Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.
Indeed, I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. Come now, let me send you to Egypt.
This Moses whom they had disowned, saying: Who made you ruler and judge? him God sent as ruler and deliverer, with the help of the angel who had appeared to him in the bush.
It was he who led them out, working wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the desert for forty years.
It is this Moses who said to the sons of Israel: God will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me.
It is he who, in the assembly in the desert, was with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers; he received words of life to pass on to us.
But our fathers refused to obey him; they pushed him aside and, in their hearts, turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron: Make us gods to go before us; for this Moses who brought us out of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.
Then they made a calf, offered a sacrifice to that idol, and rejoiced in the work of their own hands.

But God turned away and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: Did you offer me victims and sacrifices for forty years in the desert, house of Israel?
You carried the tent of Molech and the star of the god Rephan, those images you made to worship them! So I will deport you beyond Babylon.
Our fathers in the desert had the tent of the Testimony, as the one who spoke to Moses had directed, commanding him to make it on the pattern he had seen.
Having received it, our fathers, under Joshua's leadership, brought it into the land taken from the nations that God drove out before them; and so it remained until the days of David.
David found favor before God and asked to find a dwelling for the house of Jacob.
But it was Solomon who built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says:
Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build me, says the Lord, and what will be the place of my rest?
Was it not my hand that made all this?
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; you are just like your fathers.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, the one you have just betrayed and murdered,
you who received the Law through the ministry of angels, and did not keep it!"
On hearing this, they were furious in their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him.
But Stephen, filled with the Holy Spirit, gazed at the sky: he saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
He said, "Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
Crying out loudly, they covered their ears and rushed at him all together.
They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.
As they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
Then he fell to his knees and cried out in a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." With these words, he fell asleep.

Saul, for his part, approved of this killing. That day a violent persecution broke out against the Church in Jerusalem, and everyone except the apostles was scattered through the countryside of Judea and Samaria.
Devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him.
As for Saul, he was ravaging the Church: entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and had them thrown into prison.
Those who had been scattered traveled through the country, proclaiming the Good News of the word.
Philip went down to a city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ there.
The crowds, with one heart, paid attention to what Philip was saying, as they listened to him and saw the signs he was performing.
For unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed, shrieking loudly, and many paralyzed and lame people were healed;
there was great joy in that city.
Now there was already there a man named Simon, who practiced magic and amazed the people of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.
Everyone, from the least to the greatest, was devoted to him: This man, they said, is the Power of God, the one called the Great Power.
They were devoted to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
But when they believed Philip, who was proclaiming to them the Good News of the kingdom of God and of the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptized.
Simon himself believed and, once baptized, stayed close to Philip: at the sight of the signs and the great wonders that were taking place, he was amazed.
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
On their arrival, these two prayed for the Samaritans, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;
for he had not yet come down on any of them: they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
Seeing that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, Simon offered them money:
"Give me this power too, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
But Peter said to him, "May your money perish with you, since you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!
You have no part or share in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.
So repent of your wickedness and pray to the Lord: perhaps he will forgive you this thought of your heart.
For I see that you are full of bitter gall and a prisoner of sin."
Simon answered, "Pray to the Lord for me yourselves, so that nothing you have said may happen to me."
After bearing witness and proclaiming the word of the Lord, Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, proclaiming the Good News in many villages of Samaria.
The angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Get up and go south, on the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza; it is a desert road."
He got up and set out. Now an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of Ethiopia, and in charge of all her treasury, had come to Jerusalem to worship.
He was on his way back, seated in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
Philip ran up to it and heard the man reading the prophet Isaiah. He said to him, "Do you understand what you are reading?"
The man replied, "How could I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to climb up and sit beside him.
The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter; like a lamb silent before its shearer, he does not open his mouth.
In his humiliation, justice was denied him. His descendants, who will tell of them? For his life is cut off from the earth.
The eunuch said to Philip, "Please, tell me, of whom is the prophet speaking? Of himself, or of someone else?"
Then Philip spoke, and beginning from this passage of Scripture, he proclaimed to him the Good News of Jesus.
As they went along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "Look, here is water: what is to prevent me from being baptized?"
Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, it is possible." The eunuch answered, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
He ordered the chariot to stop; the two of them went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and Philip baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more; but he went on his way rejoicing.
Philip, for his part, found himself at Azotus, and he proclaimed the Good News in every town he passed through, until he reached Caesarea.

titres.titre: Ananias and the baptism of Saul

versets.t: Saul, meanwhile, was still breathing nothing but threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord. He went to the high priest
and asked him for letters to the synagogues of Damascus, so that he might bring in chains to Jerusalem any followers of the Way that he found, whether men or women.
On the way, as he was approaching Damascus, suddenly a light from the sky flashed all around him.
Falling to the ground, he heard a voice say to him, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?"
He asked, "Who are you, Lord?" The Lord answered, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up, go into the city, and you will be told what you must do."
His traveling companions had stopped, speechless with amazement: they heard the voice but saw no one.
Saul got up from the ground; but although his eyes were open, he could see nothing. They took him by the hand to lead him to Damascus,
where he stayed three days without sight, without eating or drinking.
Now there was in Damascus a disciple named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias!" He answered, "Here I am, Lord."
The Lord went on, "Get up, go to the street called Straight, and look, in the house of Judas, for a man named Saul of Tarsus. He is there praying,
and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him to restore his sight."
Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many people about this man, about all the harm he has done to your faithful in Jerusalem.
And here he has authority, received from the chief priests, to put in chains all who call on your name."
But the Lord said to him, "Go! For this man is the instrument I have chosen to carry my name before the nations, the kings, and the sons of Israel.
And I myself will show him how much he must suffer for my name."

Ananias went off, entered the house, and laid his hands on Saul: "Saul, my brother, the one who sends me is the Lord, this Jesus who appeared to you on the road you were traveling; so you will regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit."
At once something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he regained his sight. He got up and was baptized;
then he took some food and regained his strength. Saul spent a few days with the disciples in Damascus,
and at once he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues: He is the Son of God.
All who heard him were amazed: "Is this not the man who in Jerusalem was hunting down those who call on this name? And has he not come here to take them in chains to the chief priests?"
But Saul grew ever stronger and confounded the Jews of Damascus, proving that Jesus is the Christ.
After some time, the Jews plotted to kill him,
but Saul got wind of their plot. They were even watching the gates day and night to put him to death.
So the disciples took him by night and lowered him down the wall in a basket.
When Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

Then Barnabas took him along, brought him to the apostles, and told them how, on the road, Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and with what boldness he had preached in Damascus in the name of Jesus.
From then on, he came and went with them in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He also spoke to the Greek-speaking Jews and argued with them; but they were trying to do away with him.
When the brothers learned of it, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
The Church, then, was at peace throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria; it was being built up and walked in the fear of the Lord, and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit caused it to grow.
Now Peter, who was traveling all over the region, also came down to visit the faithful who lived in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years: he was paralyzed.
Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you: get up and make your own bed." At once he got up.
All the inhabitants of Lydda and the plain of Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
In Joppa there was among the disciples a woman named Tabitha, which means Dorcas, the Gazelle. She was rich in the good works and acts of charity that she did.
Now in those days she fell ill and died. After washing her, they laid her in an upper room.
Since Lydda is near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him to urge him, "Come to us without delay."

Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows gathered around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and cloaks that Dorcas used to make when she was with them.
Peter sent everyone outside, knelt down, and prayed; then, turning to the body, he said, "Tabitha, get up." She opened her eyes and, seeing Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand and helped her to her feet. Then he called the faithful and the widows and presented her to them alive.
The news spread throughout Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
Peter stayed for some time in Joppa, at the house of a tanner named Simon.

titres.titre: Peter at the house of Cornelius
The Holy Spirit upon the Gentiles

versets.t: In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort known as the Italian Cohort.
He was religious and God-fearing, together with his whole household; he gave generous alms to the people and prayed to God constantly.
One day, about three in the afternoon, he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come to him and say, "Cornelius!"
Staring at the angel, filled with fear, he said, "What is it, Lord?" The angel answered, "Your prayers and your alms have gone up before God, who has remembered them.
Now send men to Joppa and have a certain Simon, also called Peter, brought here:
he is lodging with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the sea."
When the angel who was speaking to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among his men;
he told them everything and sent them to Joppa.
The next day, as they were on their way and approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof, around noon, to pray.
He grew hungry and wanted something to eat. While the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance:
he saw the sky opened and an object coming down, like a great sheet held by its four corners and being lowered to the earth;
inside it were all the four-footed animals, the reptiles of the earth, and the birds of the sky.
A voice said to him, "Get up, Peter, kill and eat."
Peter answered, "Certainly not, Lord! Never have I eaten anything defiled or unclean."
The voice spoke again, a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call unclean."
This happened three times, and then at once the object was taken back up into the sky.
As Peter was wondering, perplexed, what the vision he had seen might mean, the men sent by Cornelius, having asked the way to Simon's house, presented themselves at the gate.
They called out and asked whether Simon, also called Peter, was lodging there.
Peter was still thinking about the vision when the Spirit said to him, "Look, three men are looking for you.
Get up, go down, and go with them without hesitation, for it is I who have sent them."
Peter went down to the men: "Here I am, I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?"

They answered, "The centurion Cornelius, a righteous and God-fearing man, well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, has been directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and hear what you have to say."
Peter invited them in and gave them lodging. The next day he got up and went off with them; some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
The following day he arrived in Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them, having gathered his relatives and close friends.
As Peter was entering, Cornelius went to meet him and threw himself at his feet in worship.
But Peter raised him up: "Get up! I too am only a man."
And as he talked with him, he went in and found many people gathered.
He said to them, "You know that it is forbidden for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or to enter his house; but God has shown me that I must call no one defiled or unclean.
That is why I came without objection as soon as you sent for me. So I ask: for what reason have you sent for me?"
Cornelius answered, "Four days ago now, I was praying at home at three in the afternoon, when suddenly a man in dazzling clothing stood before me.
He said: Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and God has remembered your alms.
So send to Joppa and summon Simon, also called Peter; he is lodging in the house of Simon the tanner, by the sea.
So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now, here we all are before God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you to say."
Then Peter spoke: "Truly, I now understand: God shows no partiality among people;
rather, in every nation, whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.
He sent his word to the sons of Israel, proclaiming to them the Good News of peace through Jesus Christ: he is the Lord of all.
You know what happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee, after the baptism that John proclaimed:
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power; he went about doing good and healing all who were under the power of the devil, for God was with him.
And we are witnesses of all that he did in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree;
but God raised him up on the third day and granted that he be seen,
not by all the people, but by the witnesses whom God had chosen in advance: by us, who ate and drank with him after his resurrection from the dead.
And he commanded us to proclaim to the people and to testify that it is he whom God has appointed judge of the living and the dead.
It is of him that all the prophets bear this witness: everyone who believes in him receives through his name the forgiveness of sins."
Peter was still speaking when the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening to the word.
The faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were amazed that the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles;
for they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God. Then Peter said,
"Can anyone refuse the water of baptism to these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?"
And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for a few days.

titres.titre: Peter defends the baptism of the Gentiles

versets.t: The apostles and the brothers in Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.
So when Peter went back up to Jerusalem, the faithful of the circumcision took issue with him:
"You went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them!"
Then Peter began to explain to them, point by point, what had happened:
"I was praying in the city of Joppa when, in a trance, I had a vision: an object, like a great sheet held by its four corners, was coming down from the sky and reaching all the way to me.
Looking closely at it, I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the reptiles, and the birds of the sky.
I also heard a voice say to me: Get up, Peter, kill and eat.
I answered: Certainly not, Lord! Never has anything defiled or unclean entered my mouth.
A second time the voice spoke from the sky: What God has made clean, do not call unclean.
This happened three times, and then everything was taken back up into the sky.
At that very moment, three men presented themselves at the house where we were: they had been sent to me from Caesarea.
The Spirit told me to go with them without hesitation. These six brothers came with me, and we entered the man's house.
He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying to him: Send to Joppa for Simon, also called Peter;
he will speak to you words by which you and your whole household will be saved.
I had barely begun to speak when the Holy Spirit came down on them, as on us at the beginning.
Then I remembered the word of the Lord, when he said: John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.
So if God gave them the same gift as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to stand in God's way?"
On hearing this, they were calmed and gave glory to God: "So to the Gentiles too God has granted the repentance that leads to life."
Those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over the death of Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, proclaiming the word to no one but Jews.
But some of them, natives of Cyprus and Cyrene, on reaching Antioch, spoke also to the Greeks, proclaiming to them the Good News of the Lord Jesus.
The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great many people believed and turned to the Lord.
News of this reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, which sent Barnabas as far as Antioch.
On his arrival, seeing the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to remain firmly devoted to the Lord;
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a considerable crowd was added to the Lord.
Then Barnabas went off to Tarsus to look for Saul;

when he found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they took part in the meetings of the church and taught a great many people. It was at Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
In those days some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and foretold through the Spirit that a great famine would strike the whole world; it did in fact come under Claudius.
The disciples decided to send, each according to his means, relief to the brothers living in Judea;
and this they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

titres.titre: The martyrdom of James and the arrest of Peter

versets.t: Around that time King Herod began to mistreat some members of the Church.
He put James, the brother of John, to death by the sword.
Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well. It was during the days of Unleavened Bread.
Once Peter was seized, he threw him in prison and put him under the guard of four squads of four soldiers each, intending to bring him before the people after Passover.
So Peter was kept in prison, but the Church prayed to God for him without ceasing.
On the very night when Herod was going to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while sentries kept guard at the prison door.
Suddenly the angel of the Lord appeared, and a light shone in the cell. Striking Peter on the side, the angel woke him: "Get up quickly." And the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, "Put on your belt and your sandals." He did so. The angel added, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me."
Peter went out and followed him; he did not realize that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.

They passed the first guard post, then the second, and came to the iron gate leading into the city: it opened for them of its own accord. They went out, went along one street, and at once the angel left him.
Then Peter, coming to himself, said, "Now I know for certain that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from Herod's hand and from all that the Jewish people were expecting."
After thinking it over, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John also called Mark, where many people were gathered in prayer.
As he knocked at the door of the entryway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to listen.
Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy, instead of opening the door, she ran to announce that Peter was standing at the door.
They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she insisted that it was true. Then they said, "It is his angel."
Peter, meanwhile, kept on knocking. When they opened the door and saw him, they were astonished.

With his hand he motioned for them to be quiet, then told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison, and he added, "Report this to James and to the brothers." Then he left and went off to another place.
At daybreak there was great commotion among the soldiers: what had become of Peter?
Herod had him searched for and, not finding him, questioned the guards and ordered them to be executed. Then he left Judea for Caesarea, where he stayed.

Herod was in open conflict with the people of Tyre and Sidon. By common agreement they came to him and, having won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, for their country depended on the king's for its food.
On the appointed day, Herod, dressed in his royal robes and seated on the platform, was addressing them.
And the people were shouting, "This is the voice of a god, not of a man!"
At that very moment the angel of the Lord struck him down, because he had not given glory to God; eaten by worms, he died.
Meanwhile the word of God kept growing and spreading.
Barnabas and Saul, their task accomplished, returned from Jerusalem, taking with them John also called Mark.

titres.titre: The sending of Barnabas and Saul
Paul's sermon at Antioch in Pisidia
The refusal of the Jews, the call to the Gentiles

versets.t: In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, a childhood companion of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
One day, as they were celebrating the worship of the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
Then, after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and let them go.
So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, Barnabas and Saul went down to Seleucia, from which they sailed to Cyprus.
On reaching Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews; they had John as their helper.
Having crossed the whole island as far as Paphos, they found a magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a shrewd man. The proconsul sent for Barnabas and Saul, eager to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the magician, for that is what his name means, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
Then Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked straight at him
and said, "You who are full of every trick and every fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, will you never stop twisting the straight paths of the Lord?

Now look, the hand of the Lord is upon you: you will be blind, deprived for a time of the light of the sun." At once a thick darkness came over him, and he groped about looking for someone to lead him by the hand.
Seeing what had happened, the proconsul believed, struck by the teaching of the Lord.
From Paphos, Paul and his companions set sail and came to Perga in Pamphylia. But John left them and went back to Jerusalem.
They themselves went on from Perga to Antioch in Pisidia and, on the sabbath day, went into the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the leaders of the synagogue sent word to them, "Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, speak."
Paul stood up, made a gesture with his hand, and said, "Israelites, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers. He made this people great during their stay in Egypt and brought them out of it with outstretched arm.
For about forty years he bore with them in the desert.
Then, having overthrown seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them its territory as an inheritance.
All this lasted about four hundred and fifty years. After that, he gave them judges, until the prophet Samuel.
They then asked for a king, and God gave them Saul, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
Then, having set him aside, he raised up David as their king, to whom he gave this testimony: I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will carry out all my wishes.
From his descendants, according to his promise, God brought forth for Israel a Savior, Jesus.
Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance for all the people of Israel.
As he was completing his course, John would say: What you think I am, I am not; but look, there comes after me one whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.
Brothers, sons of the race of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, it is to us that this word of salvation has been sent.
The inhabitants of Jerusalem and their leaders, because they failed to recognize Jesus and the words of the prophets that are read every sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him.
Though they found in him nothing deserving death, they demanded of Pilate his execution.
And when they had carried out everything that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, and who are now his witnesses to the people.
And we announce this Good News to you: the promise made to our fathers,
God has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising Jesus, as it is written in the second psalm: You are my Son, today I have begotten you.
That he raised him from the dead, never again to return to corruption, God said in these words: I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.
That is why he says again elsewhere: You will not let your Holy One see corruption.
Now David, after serving God's purpose in his own time, fell asleep, was gathered to his fathers, and saw corruption.
But the one whom God raised did not see corruption.
So know this, brothers: it is through him that the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. From everything that the law of Moses could not justify you,
everyone who believes is justified through him.
So take care that what is said in the Prophets does not happen to you:
Look, you scoffers, be struck with amazement and vanish! For in your days I am going to do a work, a work that you would not believe if someone told you of it."
As they were leaving, the people begged them to speak on the same subject the following sabbath.
When the assembly dispersed, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them and urged them to remain in the grace of God.
The following sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
Seeing this crowd, the Jews were filled with jealousy and, with their insults, contradicted what Paul was saying.

Then Paul and Barnabas declared boldly, "It was to you first that the word of God had to be proclaimed. But since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, we are now turning to the Gentiles.
For this is the command the Lord has given us: I have made you a light for the nations, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth."
On hearing this, the Gentiles rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed to eternal life became believers.
And the word of the Lord spread throughout the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, launched a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their territory.
Shaking off against them the dust of their feet, these two went to Iconium.
As for the disciples, they were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

titres.titre: In Lystra: the healing and the misunderstanding

versets.t: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went in the same way into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great crowd of both Jews and Greeks became believers.
But the Jews who remained unbelieving stirred up and poisoned the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers.
Paul and Barnabas nevertheless prolonged their stay, speaking boldly, relying on the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting them to work signs and wonders.
The population of the city was divided: some sided with the Jews, others with the apostles.
When the Gentiles and the Jews, along with their leaders, were preparing to mistreat and stone them,
the apostles, having learned of it, took refuge in the towns of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and in the surrounding region, where they proclaimed the Good News.
In Lystra there was a man with crippled legs, disabled from birth, who had never walked.
He was listening to Paul speak. Paul, looking straight at him and seeing that he had the faith to be healed,
said in a loud voice, "Stand up straight on your feet." The man sprang up and began to walk.
Seeing what Paul had just done, the crowds cried out in Lycaonian, "The gods, in human form, have come down to us!"
They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the one who did the speaking.
The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood at the entrance to the city, brought bulls decked with garlands to the gates and, together with the crowd, wanted to offer a sacrifice.
On learning of it, the apostles Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting,

"Friends, why are you doing this? We too are men, of the same nature as you! We proclaim to you that you must turn away from these empty idols to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them.
In past generations he let all the nations follow their own ways;
yet he never stopped bearing witness to himself by his benefits: from the sky he gives you rain and fruitful seasons, he fills you with food and your hearts with joy."
Even with these words, they could barely keep the crowd from offering a sacrifice to them.
Then some Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium, won over the crowds, stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, thinking he was dead.
But when the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. The next day he left for Derbe with Barnabas.
After proclaiming the Good News to that city and making a good number of disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch.
They strengthened the hearts of the disciples and encouraged them to persevere in the faith, saying that it is through many trials that we must enter the kingdom of God.
In each Church they appointed elders for them and, after praying and fasting, entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had put their faith.
They passed through Pisidia and reached Pamphylia;
after proclaiming the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, from which they had set out, entrusted to the grace of God for the work they had just accomplished.
On their arrival, they gathered the Church and reported all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they stayed for some time with the disciples.
Some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved."

This led to a sharp dispute and heated debate between Paul and Barnabas and these men; it was decided that Paul, Barnabas, and a few others should go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and the elders about this question.
Sent on their way by the church, they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, telling how the Gentiles had been converted, and this brought great joy to all the brothers.
When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church, the apostles, and the elders, and they reported everything God had done through them.
But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared that the Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.
The apostles and the elders met to consider the question.

After much discussion, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that from the early days God chose me from among you, so that through my mouth the Gentiles might hear the word of the Good News and come to believe.
And God, who knows the heart, bore witness in their favor by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us;
he made no distinction between them and us, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Why, then, do you now put God to the test by laying on the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have had the strength to bear?
No! It is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we believe we are saved, exactly as they are."
The whole assembly fell silent, then listened to Barnabas and Paul as they told of all the signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles.
When they had finished, James spoke up, "Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has told how God first showed his care by taking from among the Gentiles a people to bear his name.
This agrees with the words of the prophets, for it is written:
After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will repair its ruins and set it up again,
so that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, along with all the nations over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who does these things
known from of old.
Therefore my judgment is that we should not burden those of the Gentiles who turn to God;
we should only write to them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from unlawful unions, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.
For from ancient generations Moses has had those who proclaim him in every town, since he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath day."

Then the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, decided to choose some of their own to send to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: they chose Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, men who were highly regarded among the brothers.
They sent this letter with them: "The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers of Gentile origin in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings!
We have heard that some of our number, without any authorization from us, have disturbed you with their words and unsettled your minds.
So we have decided, by common accord, to choose delegates and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We are therefore sending Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to lay on you any burden beyond these necessary requirements:
that you abstain from meat offered to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from unlawful unions. You will do well to keep yourselves from these. Farewell."
So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, where they gathered the assembly and delivered the letter.
When it was read, everyone rejoiced at the encouragement it brought.
Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, spoke at length to the brothers to encourage and strengthen them.
After spending some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.
Silas, however, thought it good to remain there.
Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the word of the Lord along with many others.
Some time later, Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing."
Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark, with them;
but Paul thought it best not to take along someone who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not shared in their work.
The disagreement was so sharp that they parted from each other. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus;
Paul, for his part, chose Silas and set out, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
Paul then went on to Derbe, and then to Lystra. There was a disciple there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father;
the brothers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.
Paul wanted to take him along; so he took him and circumcised him, because of the Jews in those parts, for they all knew that his father was Greek.
As they traveled through the towns, they passed on to the faithful the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to observe.
So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew in number day by day.
They traveled through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, since the Holy Spirit had prevented them from preaching the word in the province of Asia.
When they came to the borders of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them.
So passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.
There, one night, Paul had a vision: a Macedonian was standing and pleading with him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us."
As soon as he had seen the vision, we sought to leave for Macedonia, convinced that God was calling us to proclaim the Good News there.
Setting sail from Troas, we made a straight run to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis;
from there to Philippi, the leading city of that district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We spent several days in this city.
On the Sabbath day we went out through the gate to the riverside, where we thought there would be a place of prayer. We sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered there.
One of them, named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, was a woman who feared God; she listened, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.
After she had been baptized, together with her household, she urged us, "Since you have judged me faithful to the Lord, come and stay at my house." And she pressed us until we agreed.
One day, as we were going to the place of prayer, we met a young slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination, who brought her masters a great profit by her fortune-telling.
She began to follow us, Paul and the rest of us, shouting, "These men are servants of the Most High God; they are proclaiming to you the way of salvation."
She did this for many days. Finally Paul, worn out, turned and said to the spirit, "In the name of Jesus Christ I command you: come out of her." And it came out at that very moment.
When her masters saw that their hope of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the public square before the authorities.
They brought them before the magistrates and said, "These men are throwing our city into turmoil. They are Jews,
and they are advocating customs that we Romans are not allowed to accept or practice."
The crowd, too, rose up against them, and the magistrates ordered their clothes to be torn off and had them beaten with rods.
After they had been severely flogged, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was ordered to keep them under close guard.
Having received these orders, he put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.
Around midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns of praise to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a violent earthquake: the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up and saw the prison doors open; thinking the prisoners had escaped, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself.
But Paul shouted in a loud voice, "Do yourself no harm, we are all here."
The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and trembling, fell down before Paul and Silas;
then he brought them out and said, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"
They answered, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all those in his house.
At that hour of the night the jailer took them, washed their wounds, and was baptized at once, he and all his family.
Then he brought them up into his house, set food before them, and rejoiced with his whole household that he had come to believe in God.
When day came, the magistrates sent the lictors with the order, "Release those men."
The jailer reported these words to Paul, "The magistrates have sent word to release you; so come out now and go in peace."

But Paul said to the lictors, "They beat us with rods in public, without a trial, though we are Roman citizens, and they threw us into prison; and now they want to send us away secretly? Certainly not! Let them come themselves and bring us out."
The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, who were alarmed when they learned that they were Roman citizens.
They came and apologized to them, brought them out, and asked them to leave the city.
On leaving the prison, Paul and Silas went to Lydia's house; they saw the brothers, encouraged them, and then departed.
Passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, Paul and Silas came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
As was his custom, Paul went in, and for three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures;
he explained and proved that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, "And this Christ," he said, "is this Jesus whom I proclaim to you."
Some of them were convinced and joined Paul and Silas, along with a great many God-fearing Greeks and quite a few prominent women.

But the Jews, jealous, recruited some worthless men from the streets, stirred up the crowd, and threw the city into an uproar. They went to Jason's house, looking for Paul and Silas to bring them out to the people.
When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some brothers before the city magistrates, shouting, "These men who have turned the whole world upside down are now here,
and Jason has welcomed them! They all act against the decrees of the emperor, claiming that there is another king, Jesus."
These words threw the crowd and the magistrates into confusion,
and they released Jason and the others only after taking bail from them.
Without delay, the brothers sent Paul and Silas off by night to Berea. On their arrival, they went to the synagogue of the Jews.
These Jews were more open-minded than those of Thessalonica: they received the word with great eagerness, examining the Scriptures every day to check the accuracy of what they were told.
Many of them came to believe, and among the Greeks, women of standing and a good number of men.
But when the Jews of Thessalonica learned that Paul was also proclaiming the word of God in Berea, they came to stir up trouble among the crowd there.
At once the brothers sent Paul off toward the sea; Silas and Timothy stayed behind.
Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, then went back with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was stirred within him at the sight of this city full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing, and every day in the public square with those he happened to meet.

Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers took issue with him. Some said, "What can this babbler be trying to say?" Others, hearing him proclaim Jesus and the resurrection, said, "He seems to be preaching foreign deities."
They took him and led him to the Areopagus: "May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
For you are bringing strange things to our ears, and we would like to know what they mean."
Now all the Athenians, as well as the foreigners staying there, spent their time doing nothing but telling or listening to the latest novelty.
Then Paul stood up in the middle of the Areopagus and said, "Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.
