For as I walked through your sanctuaries, I even found an altar with this inscription: To an unknown god. What you worship without knowing it, I now proclaim to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by human hands.
Nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything: it is he who gives to everyone life and breath and everything else.
From one man he made the whole human race to live over all the face of the earth, fixing for each people the times and the boundaries of their place,
so that they would seek God, and perhaps grope for him and find him; and indeed he is not far from any one of us.
For in him we live and move and have our being; as some of your own poets have also said: We are his offspring.
Since, then, we are God's offspring, we should not think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, shaped by human skill and imagination.
Now, overlooking the times of that ignorance, God commands all people everywhere to repent;
for he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world with justice, through a man he has appointed, giving assurance to all by raising him from the dead."
At these words about the resurrection of the dead, some sneered, while others said, "We will hear you on this some other time."
And so Paul left them.
A few, however, joined him and came to believe, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul joined them;
and since he had the same trade, he stayed and worked with them: they were tentmakers.
Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue and tried to convince both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself entirely to the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ is Jesus.
But when they opposed and insulted him, he shook out his clothes and said to them, "Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it; from now on I will go to the Gentiles."
He left there and went to the house of a certain Titius Justus, a man who feared God, whose house adjoined the synagogue.
Now Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, came to believe in the Lord together with his whole household; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul came to believe and were baptized.
One night the Lord said to Paul in a vision, "Do not be afraid; speak, and do not be silent.
For I am with you, and no one will lay a hand on you to harm you; I have many people in this city."
So Paul stayed there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews united in an attack on Paul and dragged him before the tribunal:
"This man," they said, "is inciting people to worship God in a way contrary to the Law."
Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, "If this were a crime or a serious wrongdoing, I would have good reason to hear you out, O Jews.
But since it is a matter of arguments over words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves; I refuse to be a judge of such things."
And he dismissed them from the tribunal.
Then they all seized Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal; but Gallio paid no attention to it.
Paul stayed on for a good while longer, then took leave of the brothers and sailed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had his head shaved, because of a vow.
They arrived at Ephesus, where Paul left his companions. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
They asked him to stay longer, but he declined
and took his leave, saying, "I will come back to you, if God wills." Then he set sail from Ephesus.
Landing at Caesarea, he went up to greet the church, then went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he set out again and traveled from place to place through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man well versed in the Scriptures, arrived at Ephesus.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and with a burning heart he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

When he wanted to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him warmly. On his arrival, he was a great help to those who through grace had become believers;
for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, proving from the Scriptures that the Christ is Jesus.

titres.titre: The disciples of John at Ephesus
The riot of the silversmiths of Artemis

versets.t: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul, after traveling through the interior highlands, arrived at Ephesus. There he found some disciples
and asked them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?" They answered, "We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit."
"What baptism did you receive, then?" Paul asked. They said, "The baptism of John."
Paul replied, "John gave a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was coming after him, that is, in Jesus."
On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus;
and when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them: they began to speak in tongues and to prophesy.
There were about twelve men in all.
Paul went to the synagogue and for three months spoke there boldly, reasoning persuasively about the kingdom of God.
But when some grew stubborn and refused to believe, disparaging the way of the Lord before the assembly, he withdrew from them, took the disciples aside, and taught daily in the school of Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so that all the inhabitants of the province of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord.
And God worked extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul:
handkerchiefs and cloths that had touched his skin were applied to the sick, and their illnesses left them, and the evil spirits departed.
Some itinerant Jewish exorcists tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, "I adjure you by this Jesus whom Paul proclaims!"
It was the seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish high priest, who were doing this.
But the evil spirit answered them, "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?"
And the man possessed by the evil spirit threw himself on them, overpowered them all, and handled them so roughly that they fled from the house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the inhabitants of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks; fear seized them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was glorified.
Many of those who had become believers came to confess and disclose their practices.
A good number of those who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone; the value was reckoned at fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So, with power, the word of the Lord kept growing and gaining strength.
After these events, Paul resolved to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia: "Once I have been there," he said to himself, "I must also see Rome."
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed on for a time in the province of Asia.
It was at that time that a great disturbance arose concerning the way of the Lord.
A silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver miniature shrines of Artemis, brought considerable profit to his craftsmen.
He gathered them, along with the workers in the same trade, and said, "My friends, you know that our prosperity comes from this business.
Now you see and hear that this Paul, not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia, has convinced and led astray a great many people, saying that gods made by human hands are not gods at all.

So we are in danger not only of seeing our trade discredited, but also of seeing the temple of the great goddess Artemis counted as nothing, and soon of seeing stripped of her greatness the one whom all Asia and the whole world revere."
At these words, seized with fury, they began to shout, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
The whole city was filled with confusion. With one impulse they rushed into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's traveling companions.
Paul wanted to appear before the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some officials of the province of Asia, who were his friends, sent word to him not to risk going into the theater.
Some were shouting one thing, some another; the assembly was in complete confusion, and most did not even know why they had come together.
Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews pushed forward. Motioning with his hand, he wanted to make a defense before the people;
but when they realized he was a Jew, they all shouted with one voice for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

Finally, the city secretary calmed the crowd, "Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of Ephesus is the guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her statue that fell from heaven?
Since this is undeniable, you must keep calm and do nothing rash.
These men you have brought here are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
If, then, Demetrius and his craftsmen have a grievance against anyone, there are court days and there are proconsuls: let them bring charges against one another.
And if you have any other matter, it will be settled in the regular assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today's gathering, with no reason to justify it." With these words, he dismissed the assembly.

titres.titre: Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus

versets.t: When the uproar had ceased, Paul summoned the disciples, encouraged them, then said goodbye and left for Macedonia.
He traveled through that region, giving the faithful much encouragement, and came to Greece,
where he spent three months. As he was about to sail for Syria, the Jews laid a plot against him; so he decided to go back through Macedonia.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Berea; the Thessalonians Aristarchus and Secundus; Gaius from Derbe and Timothy; and the Asians Tychicus and Trophimus.
These went ahead and waited for us at Troas.
We ourselves, after the days of Unleavened Bread, sailed from Philippi and, five days later, joined them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, we were gathered to break bread. Paul, who was to leave the next day, was speaking with the brothers and prolonged his talk until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the windowsill. Overcome by a deep sleep during Paul's long talk, he fell from the third floor, and was picked up dead.
Paul went down, bent over him, took him in his arms, and said, "Do not be alarmed: his life is in him."
Then he went back up, broke bread, and ate; he went on speaking for a long time, until daybreak, and then left.
As for the young man, they took him home alive, to the great comfort of all.
We went ahead by sea and sailed to Assos, where we were to take Paul on board; he had arranged it this way, since he wanted to make the journey on foot.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene.
From there, continuing by sea, we arrived the next day opposite Chios; the following day we touched at Samos, and the day after that we reached Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so as not to linger in Asia; he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church.
When they came to him, he said to them, "You know how, from the first day I set foot in Asia, I have always conducted myself among you:
I served the Lord in all humility, with tears and trials that came to me through the plots of the Jews;
I kept back nothing that was helpful to you, preaching and teaching you in public and from house to house,
testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about conversion to God and faith in our Lord Jesus.
And now, bound by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there,
except that, from city to city, the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and trials await me.
But I place no value on my own life, as long as I may finish my course and the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to bear witness to the Good News of the grace of God.
And now, I know that none of you, among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom, will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,
for I have proclaimed to you, keeping nothing back, the whole plan of God.
Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock among which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to be shepherds of the Church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.
I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock.
And even from among your own selves men will rise up, speaking perverse things to draw the disciples after them.
So be on your guard, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you with tears.
And now I commit you to God and to the word of his grace, which has the power to build up the edifice and to give you the inheritance among all the sanctified.
I have coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands provided for my own needs and those of my companions.
In everything I showed you that it is by working hard like this that we must help the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, who himself said: It is more blessed to give than to receive."
With these words, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
They all wept, and throwing their arms around Paul's neck, they kissed him,
grieving most of all over the words: You will not see my face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship.

titres.titre: The arrest of Paul in the Temple

versets.t: After we had torn ourselves away from them, we put out to sea and sailed a straight course to Cos; the next day to Rhodes, then to Patara.
Finding a ship there bound for Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.
Coming in sight of Cyprus, we passed it on our left and sailed to Syria, and put in at Tyre, where the ship was to unload its cargo.
Having found the disciples, we stayed there seven days; prompted by the Spirit, they urged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
When those days were over, we set out again. All of them, with their wives and children, escorted us out of the city, and kneeling on the shore, we prayed.
After saying goodbye to one another, we boarded the ship, while they returned home.
Finishing our voyage, we went from Tyre to Ptolemais; we greeted the brothers and spent a day with them.
The next day we set out again and arrived at Caesarea. Entering the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven, we stayed with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
As we were there for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, tied up his own feet and hands, and said, "Here is what the Holy Spirit declares: The man to whom this belt belongs, the Jews will bind like this in Jerusalem and hand over into the hands of the Gentiles."
At these words, both we and the local people begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
But he answered, "What are you doing, weeping like this and breaking my heart? For my part, I am ready not only to be bound, but to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
Since he would not be moved, we stopped urging him and said, "The will of the Lord be done!"
After these days, our preparations complete, we went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea came with us and brought us to stay with a certain Mnason, a Cypriot, a disciple of long standing.
On our arrival in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us with joy.
The next day, Paul went with us to see James, and all the elders gathered.
After greeting them, he described in detail what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
On hearing this, they gave glory to God. Then they said to him, "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews have become believers, and all of them are zealous for the Law.
Now they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews living among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or to follow the customs.
What, then, is to be done? They are sure to hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have here four men who are under a vow;

take them with you, purify yourself along with them, and pay the expenses for them so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing to what they have been told about you, and that you yourself keep the Law.
As for the Gentiles who have become believers, we have written to them our decision: that they abstain from meat offered to idols, from blood, from strangled animals, and from unlawful unions."

The next day, Paul took the men with him, purified himself along with them, and entered the Temple to give notice of when, at the completion of the purification, the offering would be presented for each of them.
As the seven days were drawing to a close, the Jews from Asia, having seen Paul in the Temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him,

shouting, "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, against the Law, and against this place; on top of that, he has brought Greeks into the Temple and defiled this holy place."
For they had previously seen Trophimus of Ephesus with him in the city, and they thought Paul had brought him into the Temple.
The whole city was in an uproar, and the people came running from every direction; they seized Paul and dragged him out of the Temple, whose doors were immediately shut.
They were trying to kill him when word reached the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in complete confusion.
At once he took soldiers and centurions and rushed down to them. At the sight of the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came up, took hold of him, and ordered him bound with two chains; then he asked who he was and what he had done.
But in the crowd some were shouting one thing, some another. Unable to learn anything certain because of the uproar, he ordered Paul to be taken to the fortress.
When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him, so violent was the crowd;
for the people followed in a mass, screaming, "Away with him!"
Just as he was about to be taken into the fortress, Paul said to the commander, "May I say something to you?" The man replied, "You know Greek?
So you are not that Egyptian who recently stirred up and led out into the desert the four thousand armed rebels?"
Paul answered, "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people."
The commander gave him permission. Standing on the steps, Paul motioned with his hand to the people. A great silence fell, and he addressed them in the Hebrew language:
"Brothers and fathers, listen to what I now have to say to you in my defense."
When they heard him speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. Paul continued:
"I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, trained at the feet of Gamaliel in the strict observance of the Law of our fathers, zealous for God as all of you are today.
I persecuted to the death those of this Way, chaining and throwing into prison both men and women;

the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. I even received letters from them for the brothers; I was setting out for Damascus to bring those who were there back to Jerusalem in chains, to be punished.
I was on the road, close to Damascus, when about noon, suddenly, a bright light from heaven flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice say to me, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?
I answered, Who are you, Lord? He said to me, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.
Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me.
Then I said, What am I to do, Lord? The Lord answered me, Get up, go to Damascus, and there you will be told all that you are appointed to do.
Since I could no longer see, because of the brightness of that light, my companions took me by the hand, and I came to Damascus.
A certain Ananias, a devout man according to the Law and well spoken of by all the Jews of the city,
came to me and, standing beside me, said, Saul, my brother, receive your sight. And at that very moment I saw him.
Then he said, The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear the voice from his mouth;
for you will be his witness before all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why delay? Get up, be baptized, and have your sins washed away, calling on his name.
When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the Temple, I fell into a trance
and saw the Lord saying to me, Hurry, leave Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me.
I answered, Lord, they know well that from synagogue to synagogue I used to imprison and flog those who believe in you;
and when the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I too was there, approving of the killing and guarding the clothes of those who put him to death.
Then he said to me, Go, for I am going to send you far away, to the nations."
They had listened to him up to this word; then they raised their voices, "Away with such a man from the earth! He does not deserve to live!"
As they were shouting, throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,
the commander ordered Paul to be brought into the fortress and to be examined under the lash, to find out why they were shouting against him like this.
When they had tied him up with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there, "Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen, and one who has not even been tried?"
At these words, the centurion went to warn the commander, "What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen."
The commander came and asked Paul, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" "Yes," he replied.
The commander said, "It cost me a large sum to acquire this citizenship." "And I," said Paul, "was born with it."
At once, those who were about to examine him drew back, and the commander himself was alarmed to learn that he had put a Roman citizen in chains.

The next day, wanting to know exactly what the Jews were accusing him of, he had his chains removed and ordered the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to assemble; then he brought Paul down and placed him before them.
Looking intently at the Sanhedrin, Paul said, "Brothers, to this day I have lived before God in all good conscience."
The high priest Ananias ordered his attendants to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit to judge me according to the Law, and in defiance of the Law you order me to be struck!"
Those standing by said, "You insult God's high priest!"
Paul replied, "I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest; for it is written: You shall not curse a ruler of your people."

Knowing that part of the assembly was Sadducee and the other Pharisee, Paul cried out in the middle of the Sanhedrin, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; it is for our hope, the resurrection of the dead, that I am on trial."
As soon as he said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.
For the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, no angel, and no spirit, while the Pharisees affirm them all.
There was a great outcry. Some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and protested vigorously, "We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?"
As the quarrel grew violent, the commander, fearing that Paul would be torn to pieces, ordered the troops to go down, pull him out from among them, and bring him back to the fortress.
The following night, the Lord stood near Paul and said, "Take courage! Just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also bear witness in Rome."
At daybreak, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves with an oath, under a curse, not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty who had bound themselves in this way.
They went to the chief priests and the elders and said, "We have bound ourselves with an oath, under a curse, to take nothing until we have killed Paul.
So now you, together with the Sanhedrin, ask the commander to bring him down to you, on the pretext of examining his case more closely; and we are ready to do away with him before he arrives."
But the son of Paul's sister got wind of the ambush; he went to the fortress, entered, and warned Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the commander, for he has something to report to him."
The centurion took him, led him to the commander, and said, "The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring you this young man, who has something to tell you."
The commander took him by the hand, drew aside, and asked him, "What do you have to report to me?"
He answered, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the Sanhedrin tomorrow, on the pretext of examining his case more closely.

Do not believe them: more than forty of them are lying in ambush for him, having sworn under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are ready now and are only waiting for your consent."
The commander sent the young man away, warning him, "Do not tell anyone that you have informed me of this."
Then he called two centurions and said, "Have two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen ready to march to Caesarea by nine o'clock tonight.
Provide mounts as well, to take Paul safely to Felix the governor."
And he wrote a letter in these terms:
"Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.
This man had been seized by the Jews and was about to be killed, when I stepped in with the troops and rescued him from their hands, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.
Wanting to know the reason for their accusation, I brought him down before their Sanhedrin.
I found that he was accused over questions relating to their law, without any charge against him deserving death or imprisonment.
When I was informed that a plot was being hatched against this man, I sent him to you without delay, instructing his accusers to state their case against him before you."
Following their orders, the soldiers took Paul and brought him by night as far as Antipatris.
The next day, leaving the horsemen to go on with him, they returned to the fortress.
On arriving at Caesarea, the horsemen delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul to him.
After reading it, the governor asked what province he was from; learning that he was from Cilicia,
he said, "I will hear you when your accusers arrive." And he ordered him to be kept under guard in Herod's praetorium.
Five days later, the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer, a certain Tertullus; they brought charges against Paul before the governor.
When Paul was called in, Tertullus began his prosecution, "Thanks to you, we enjoy a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought reforms to this nation;
in every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we welcome this with all gratitude.
But, so as not to detain you further, I beg you to hear us briefly with your usual kindness.
We have found this man to be a plague: he stirs up trouble among all the Jews throughout the world, as a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes;
he even tried to profane the Temple, and that is when we arrested him, meaning to judge him according to our Law.
But the commander Lysias came and, with great violence, tore him from our hands,
ordering his accusers to appear before you. By questioning him yourself, you will be able to learn from him all the things of which we accuse him."
The Jews joined in the accusation, maintaining that this was indeed so.
At a signal from the governor, Paul answered, "Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I make my defense with confidence.
You can verify that it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
And they did not find me arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the Temple, or in the synagogues, or in the city.
They cannot prove to you any of the things of which they now accuse me.
Yet I confess this to you: it is according to the Way, which they call a sect, that I serve the God of our fathers, believing everything that is written in the Law and the Prophets,
and having in God this hope, which they themselves share: that there will be a resurrection of the just and the unjust.
That is why I too always strive to keep a clear conscience before God and before men.
After several years, I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings.
It was thus that they found me in the Temple, once I had been purified, with no crowd and no disturbance.
But some Jews from Asia were there: it was for them to appear before you and accuse me, if they had any grievance against me.
Or else, let these men themselves say what offense they found when I appeared before the Sanhedrin,
unless it is this one thing I shouted in their midst: It is for the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today."
Felix, who was well informed about the Way, adjourned the case, "When the commander Lysias comes down," he said, "I will examine your case."
And he ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard, while allowing him some freedom and not preventing any of his own people from attending to him.
Some days later, Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
But as Paul went on to speak of justice, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix, alarmed, said to him, "For now, go away; I will call you back when I find the time."
He was also hoping that Paul would give him money; that is why he sent for him fairly often to talk with him.
Two years passed in this way, and then Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and wanting to please the Jews, he left Paul in prison.
Three days after his arrival in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the leading men of the Jews brought charges against Paul before him. Insistently,
they asked him as a favor, to Paul's detriment, to have him transferred to Jerusalem; they were preparing an ambush to kill him on the way.
Festus replied that Paul was being held at Caesarea and that he himself would be returning there shortly.
"Let those among you who have the authority," he added, "come down with me, and if this man has done anything wrong, let them accuse him."
After spending eight or ten days at most among them, he went down to Caesarea. The next day he took his seat at the tribunal and had Paul brought in.
As soon as he appeared, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem surrounded him, bringing many serious charges against him that they could not prove.
Paul defended himself, "I have done nothing wrong, neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the Temple, nor against the emperor."
Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asked Paul, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to be tried there on these charges in my presence?"
Paul replied, "I am standing before the emperor's tribunal: this is where I must be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.
If I am guilty and have committed some crime deserving death, I do not refuse to die; but if there is nothing to their accusations, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar."
Then Festus, after conferring with his council, replied, "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go."
A few days later, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
As their stay went on, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, "There is a man here whom Felix left as a prisoner.
During my stay in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews brought charges against him, demanding his condemnation.
I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to hand over a man before the accused has been confronted with his accusers and given the chance to defend himself against the charge.
So they came here, and without delay I took my seat at the tribunal the next day and had the man brought in.
When his accusers stood up, they charged him with none of the crimes I had supposed;
they only had certain disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died, whom Paul claimed to be alive.
At a loss how to investigate such matters, I asked him whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem to be tried there on these charges.
But since Paul appealed to have his case reserved for the emperor's decision, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar."
Agrippa said to Festus, "I would have liked to hear this man myself." "Tomorrow," Festus replied, "you will hear him."
The next day, Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall with the commanders and the leading men of the city. At Festus's order, Paul was brought in.

Festus said, "King Agrippa, and all of you here present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish community appealed to me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.
For my part, I found that he had done nothing deserving death; but since he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to send him.
Having nothing definite to write to my lord about him, I have brought him before you, and above all before you, King Agrippa, so that after this examination I may have something to write.
For it seems absurd to me to send a prisoner without indicating the charges against him."
Agrippa said to Paul, "You have permission to speak in your defense." Then Paul, stretching out his hand, made his defense:
"Of all the accusations brought against me by the Jews, I count myself fortunate, King Agrippa, to be defending myself today before you,
especially since you are thoroughly acquainted with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. I beg you, then, to listen to me patiently.
My life, from my youth, as it unfolded from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known to all the Jews.
They have known me for a long time and can testify, if they are willing, that I lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest current of our religion.
And now, if I am on trial, it is for the hope of the promise God made to our fathers,
the promise whose fulfillment our twelve tribes, serving God earnestly night and day, hope to see. It is for this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews!
Why is it judged incredible among you that God raises the dead?
For my part, I had thought it my duty to fight by every means against the name of Jesus of Nazareth;
and that is what I did in Jerusalem. Armed with full authority from the chief priests, I threw many of the faithful into prison, and when they were put to death, I cast my vote against them.
In all the synagogues, again and again, I punished them to force them to blaspheme; and in my growing fury I pursued them even to foreign cities.
It was on such a journey that one day I was going to Damascus, armed with full authority and a commission from the chief priests.
On the way, O king, about noon, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blaze around me and my traveling companions.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice say to me in the Hebrew language, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.
I said, Who are you, Lord? The Lord replied, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and stand on your feet: if I have appeared to you, it is to make you a servant and a witness of what you have seen and of what I will yet show you.
I am rescuing you from your people and from the nations to whom I am sending you,

to open their eyes, to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive, through faith in me, the forgiveness of sins and a share in the inheritance among the sanctified.
From then on, King Agrippa, I did not disobey the heavenly vision;
but to the people of Damascus first, then to those of Jerusalem and all Judea, and to the nations, I proclaimed that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds that express this conversion.
That is why the Jews seized me in the Temple and tried to kill me.
But with God's help I have stood firm to this day, bearing witness to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses foretold would happen:
that the Christ would suffer, and that, being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light to his people and to the nations."
As he was making his defense in this way, Festus said in a loud voice, "You are out of your mind, Paul! Your great learning is driving you insane."
Paul replied, "I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words that are true and reasonable.
The king knows about all this, and it is to him that I speak with confidence: none of it, I am sure, escapes him, for this was not done in a corner.
Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you do."
Agrippa said to Paul, "A little more, and you would persuade me to become a Christian."
Paul replied, "Whether it takes little or much, I pray to God that not only you, but all who are listening to me today, may become such as I am, except for these chains."
Then the king rose, and so did the governor, Bernice, and their whole retinue.
As they withdrew, they said to one another, "This man has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment."
And Agrippa said to Festus, "He could have been set free, if he had not appealed to Caesar."
When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion of the Imperial Cohort named Julius.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was to sail along the coast of the province of Asia, and we put out to sea; Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon. Julius, who treated Paul kindly, allowed him to go to his friends to be cared for.
Setting out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us;
then, after crossing the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we arrived at Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy and put us aboard.
For several days we sailed slowly and reached the vicinity of Cnidus with great difficulty. Since the wind would not let us go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete, off Salmone,
and coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
A considerable time had passed, and sailing had become dangerous, for even the time of the great Fast was now over. Paul warned them,
"My friends, I can see that this voyage will end in serious loss, not only to the cargo and the ship, but to our lives as well."
But the centurion trusted the pilot and the ship's owner more than what Paul said.

Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, most were of the opinion that they should put out to sea and try to reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest, to spend the winter there.
When a gentle south wind came up, they thought they had gained their purpose; they weighed anchor and sailed close along the coast of Crete.
But before long a hurricane-force wind, the one called the Northeaster, swept down from the island.
The ship was caught and could not head into the wind; so we gave way and let ourselves be driven along.
As we passed under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed only with great difficulty to secure the ship's boat.
After hoisting it aboard, they used cables to undergird the ship; then, fearing they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the sail and let themselves be carried along.
As the storm battered us violently, the next day they threw the cargo overboard,
and on the third day, with our own hands, we threw the ship's tackle overboard.
For several days neither sun nor stars appeared, and the storm still raged; all hope of being saved was slipping away.

No one had eaten for a long time when Paul stood up among them and said, "My friends, you should have listened to me and not set sail from Crete; you would have spared yourselves this danger and loss.
But now I urge you to keep up your courage: not one of you will lose his life; only the ship will be lost.
This very night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me
and said, Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar, and behold, God has granted you the lives of all who are sailing with you.
So keep up your courage, my friends: I trust in God that it will be exactly as I was told.
We are to run aground on some island."
On the fourteenth night, as we were drifting across the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors sensed that land was near.
They took a sounding and found a depth of about thirty-seven meters; a little farther on, they took another sounding and found twenty-eight.
Fearing that we would strike the reefs, they threw out four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak.
When the sailors tried to escape from the ship and had let the boat down into the sea, on the pretext of laying out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these men stay with the ship, you cannot be saved."
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall.
While waiting for daylight, Paul urged them all to take some food, "For fourteen days now," he said, "you have been in suspense, going hungry and taking nothing.
So I urge you to eat: your survival depends on it; not one of you will lose a single hair from his head."
With these words, he took bread, gave thanks to God before them all, broke it, and began to eat.
Then they all took courage and ate as well.
In all, there were two hundred and seventy-six of us on the ship.
When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the coast, but they noticed a bay with a beach and resolved to run the ship aground there, if they could.
They cast off the anchors, leaving them in the sea, and at the same time loosened the ropes of the rudders, hoisted the foresail to the wind, and headed for the beach.
But striking a sandbar between two currents, they ran the ship aground: the bow stuck fast and stayed immovable, while the stern was being broken up by the pounding of the waves.
The soldiers were of a mind to kill the prisoners, for fear that any might swim away and escape;
but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and reach the land,
and the rest to follow on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that they all reached the shore safely.

titres.titre: Paul and the Jews of Rome

versets.t: Once we were safe, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The local people showed us unusual kindness: they lit a large fire and welcomed us all, because of the rain that was falling and the cold.
Paul had gathered an armful of dead wood; as he was throwing it on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened onto his hand.
When the local people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, "This man must be a murderer: he escaped the sea, but divine Justice will not let him live."
He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.
They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead; but after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and began to say that he was a god.
Nearby were lands belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius; he received us and hospitably entertained us for three days.
Now the father of Publius was lying in bed, burning with fever and suffering from dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After this, the other sick people of the island came as well and were healed.
They showered honors on us, and when we departed, they provided us with what we needed.
Three months later, we set sail on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island; it had the Dioscuri as its figurehead.
We put in at Syracuse, where we stayed three days;
from there, coasting along, we reached Rhegium. The next day, when a south wind came up, we reached Puteoli in two days.
There we found brothers, who invited us to stay a week with them. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers there, informed of our coming, came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.
On our arrival in Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

Three days later, Paul summoned the leading men of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, "Brothers, though I have done nothing against our people or against the customs of our fathers, I was handed over as a prisoner in Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
After examining me, they wanted to release me, since there was no ground in me for a death sentence.
But when the Jews objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar, without meaning to bring any accusation against my nation.
This is why I asked to see you and speak with you: it is because of the hope of Israel that I wear this chain."
They answered him, "We have received no letter from Judea about you, and none of the brothers who have come from there has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we would like to hear you set out your own thinking; for as regards this sect, we know that it meets with opposition everywhere."

They set a day with him and came in large numbers to where he was staying. From morning till evening, Paul laid out for them the kingdom of God, trying to convince them about Jesus, from the law of Moses and the prophets.
Some were convinced by his words, while others refused to believe.
As they were leaving in disagreement, Paul added one final word, "Rightly did the Holy Spirit speak to your fathers through the prophet Isaiah:
Go to this people and say to them: You will hear and hear, but never understand; you will look and look, but never see.

For the heart of this people has grown dull: they have become hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, lest their eyes should see, their ears should hear, their heart should understand, and they should turn back, and I should heal them.
So know this: it is to the nations that this salvation of God has been sent; and they, they will listen."
At these words, the Jews left, arguing sharply among themselves.
Paul stayed for two full years in the lodging he had rented, and he welcomed all who came to him,
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ, with complete freedom and without hindrance.

titres.titre: The righteousness of God through faith
The wrath of God against the pagans

versets.t: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Good News of God
that Good News which God had promised long ago through his prophets in the holy Scriptures,
concerning his Son, born of the line of David according to the flesh,
established as Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.
Through him we have received grace and the office of apostle, to bring all the nations, for the sake of his name, to the obedience of faith,
and you are among them, you too, called by Jesus Christ.
To all God's beloved who are in Rome, called to be saints: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First of all, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is spoken of throughout the whole world.
God, whom I serve in my spirit by proclaiming the Good News of his Son, is my witness that I remember you constantly,
always asking in my prayers that by his will I may at last have the happy chance to come to you.
For I long to see you, so that I may share with you some spiritual gift to strengthen you,
or rather, so that we may be encouraged together, among you, by the faith we hold in common, both you and I.
I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you, in order to reap some harvest among you as among the other nations; but until now I have been prevented.
I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the learned and to the ignorant;
hence my eagerness to proclaim the Good News to you also who are in Rome.
For I am not ashamed of the Good News: it is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes, the Jew first and then the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed, from faith to faith, as it is written: The righteous shall live by faith.
For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and injustice of those who by their injustice hold the truth captive;
since what can be known of God is plain to them: God has made it plain to them.
For ever since the creation of the world his invisible perfections, his eternal power and his divinity, have been perceived by the mind through the things he has made. So they are without excuse:
though they knew God, they did not give him the glory and thanks that are due to God; instead, they became lost in their empty reasonings, and their senseless hearts were darkened.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools;
they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for images representing corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles.
So God gave them up, in the cravings of their hearts, to an impurity in which they degrade their own bodies,
they who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature instead of the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.
That is why God gave them up to degrading passions: their women exchanged natural relations for those that are against nature;
in the same way the men, giving up natural relations with women, burned with desire for one another, men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the fitting wage of their error.
And since they did not see fit to keep the true knowledge of God, God gave them up to their undiscerning minds, so that they did what is not fitting:
filled with every kind of injustice, wickedness, greed, and malice, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and spite, slanderers,
backbiters, enemies of God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventive in evil, rebellious toward their parents,
without understanding, without loyalty, without heart, without mercy.
And though they know the decree of God, which declares that those who do such things deserve death, they not only do them but also approve of those who do them.

titres.titre: The judgment of God and the Law

versets.t: So you are without excuse, whoever you are, you who pass judgment. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the very same things, you who judge.
Now we know that God's judgment against those who do such things is in keeping with the truth.
And do you suppose, you who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape God's judgment?
Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, his patience, and his forbearance, failing to recognize that this kindness of God is meant to lead you to conversion?
By your stubbornness, by your heart that refuses to turn, you are storing up for yourself a treasure of wrath for the day of wrath, when the just judgment of God will be revealed,
for he will repay each one according to his works:
eternal life to those who, by perseverance in doing good, seek glory, honor, and incorruptibility;
but wrath and indignation to those who, out of a spirit of rivalry, rebel against the truth and submit to injustice.
Distress and anguish for every human being who does evil, for the Jew first and then the Greek;
glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, for the Jew first and then the Greek.
For God shows no partiality.
All who have sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law; and all who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law.
For it is not those who hear the Law who are righteous before God, but those who put it into practice who will be justified.
When pagans, who do not have the Law, do by nature what the Law prescribes, they, who do not have the Law, are a law to themselves;
they show that the work required by the Law is written on their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts by turns accusing or defending them.
So it will be on the day when, according to the Good News that I proclaim, God will judge the secrets of hearts through Christ Jesus.
But if you call yourself a Jew, if you rely on the Law, if you take pride in God,
if you know his will and can discern what is best, instructed by the Law,
if you are convinced that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of little children, because in the Law you possess the very expression of knowledge and truth,
you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?
You who say one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you plunder their temples?
You who take pride in the Law, do you dishonor God by transgressing that Law?
For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you, as it is written.
Circumcision is indeed of value if you keep the Law; but if you transgress the Law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision.
So if an uncircumcised man keeps the requirements of the Law, will his uncircumcision not count as circumcision?
And the one who is physically uncircumcised yet fulfills the Law will judge you who, with the letter and circumcision, transgress the Law.
For the true Jew is not the one who is so outwardly, and true circumcision is not what is visible in the flesh;
rather, the true Jew is the one who is so inwardly, and true circumcision is of the heart, according to the Spirit and not the letter. Such a person receives his praise not from men but from God.
What then is the advantage of the Jew, or what is the value of circumcision?
Great in every respect! First of all, it is to them that the words of God were entrusted.
What then? If some were unfaithful, will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not!
Let God be shown to be truthful, and every man a liar, as it is written: So you are proved right in your words, and you prevail when you are judged.
But if our injustice brings out the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Would God be unjust to let his wrath break out? (I am speaking in a human way.)
Certainly not! Otherwise, how could God judge the world?
But if by my falsehood the truth of God has stood out all the more for his glory, why am I still being judged as a sinner?
And why not do evil so that good may come of it, as some, who slander us, claim that we teach? Their condemnation is just.
What then? Are we any better? Not at all. For we have just charged that all people, Jews and Greeks alike, are under the power of sin,
as it is written: There is no one righteous, not even one;
no one who understands, no one who seeks God.
All have turned aside, together they have become corrupt; there is no one who does good, no, not even one.
Their throat is an open grave, their tongues weave deceit; the venom of vipers is under their lips,
their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness;
their feet are swift to shed blood,
ruin and misery mark their paths,
and the way of peace they have not known.
There is no fear of God before their eyes.
Now we know that whatever the Law says, it says to those who are under the Law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable before God.
For no one will be justified before him by the works of the Law: the Law does nothing more than give the knowledge of sin.
But now, apart from the Law, the righteousness of God has been made known, attested by the Law and the Prophets:
the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
all have sinned and are deprived of the glory of God,
and they are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption accomplished in Christ Jesus.

It is he whom God appointed to be, by his blood, the means of atonement received through faith. In this way he displayed his righteousness, since in his patience he had left unpunished the sins of the past;
he displayed his righteousness in the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who lives by faith in Jesus.
Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? That of works? No, by the law of faith.
For we hold that a person is justified by faith, apart from the works of the Law.
Or is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the nations? Yes, he is the God of the nations too,
since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised on the basis of faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
Do we then nullify the Law through faith? Certainly not! On the contrary, we uphold it firmly.
What then shall we say about Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? What did he obtain?
If Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about; but not before God.
For what does Scripture say? Abraham had faith in God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
To one who does a work, the wage is not credited as a gift but as something owed;
but to one who, without doing any work, puts his faith in the One who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.
So too David calls blessed the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works:
Blessed are those whose faults are forgiven and whose sins are covered!
Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not credit his sin!
Is this blessing then for the circumcised only, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say: faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness.
How then was it credited to him? When he was circumcised, or uncircumcised? Not circumcised, but uncircumcised.

And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while still uncircumcised. So he is the father of all who believe without being circumcised, that righteousness might also be credited to them,
and the father of the circumcised, of those who are not only circumcised but who also follow in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while he was still uncircumcised.
It was not through the Law that the promise of inheriting the world was made to Abraham and his descendants, but through the righteousness of faith.
For if the inheritance belongs to those who depend on the Law, then faith is emptied of meaning and the promise abolished;
for the Law produces wrath, and where there is no law there is no transgression either.

That is why it is through faith: so that all may be by grace, and the promise held secure for all his descendants, not only for those who depend on the Law but also for those who share the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all,
as it is written: I have made you the father of many nations. He is our father before the One in whom he believed, God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence what does not exist.
Hoping against all hope, he believed and so became the father of many nations, according to the word: So shall your descendants be.
Without weakening in faith, he considered his own body, already as good as dead (he was about a hundred years old), and Sarah's womb, dead as well;
yet in the face of God's promise he did not waver in unbelief; on the contrary, he was strengthened by faith and gave glory to God,
fully convinced that God has the power to do what he has promised.
That is why it was credited to him as righteousness.
But it was not for his sake alone that it is written that it was credited to him;
it is also for our sake, to whom it is to be credited, we who believe in the One who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,
who was handed over for our faults and raised for our justification.
So then, justified by faith, we are at peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
through him we have gained access, in faith, to this grace in which we stand; and we take pride in the hope of the glory of God.
More than that, we take pride even in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance,
perseverance a tested virtue, and tested virtue hope;
and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
Yes, while we were still without strength, Christ, at the appointed time, died for the ungodly.
One would hardly die for a righteous person; for a good person, perhaps someone might have the courage to die.
But God proves his love for us: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
How much more, then, now that we are justified by his blood, will we be saved through him from the wrath.
For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, how much more, now that we are reconciled, will we be saved by his life.
More than that, we take pride in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
So then, just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, so death spread to all men, because all sinned.
For until the Law, sin was in the world; but sin is not charged when there is no law.
Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned by a transgression like Adam's, who is a figure of the one who was to come.

But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if by the trespass of one man the many died, how much more have the grace of God and the gift given by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, overflowed to the many.
And the gift is not like the consequences of the one man's sin: the judgment, from a single trespass, led to condemnation, whereas the free gift, from many trespasses, leads to justification.

For if, by the trespass of one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
So then, just as one man's trespass brought condemnation on all men, so one man's act of righteousness brings to all men the justification that gives life.
For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous.
The Law came in so that the trespass might increase; but where sin increased, grace overflowed all the more,
so that, just as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through righteousness for eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

titres.titre: Dead to sin, alive to God

versets.t: What then shall we say? Are we to remain in sin so that grace may abound?
Certainly not! We who died to sin, how could we still live in it?
Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
Through baptism into his death we were therefore buried with him, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
For if we have been grafted onto him by a death like his, we shall also be so by a resurrection like his;
we know this: our old self was crucified with him, so that this body of sin might be reduced to nothing, and thus we might no longer be slaves of sin.
For anyone who has died is set free from sin.
And if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him,
knowing that Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more: death no longer has dominion over him.
His death was a death to sin, once for all; his life is a life for God.
In the same way, you too, consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, making you obey its cravings.
Do not offer your members to sin as weapons of injustice; instead, offer yourselves to God as those brought back from death to life, and offer him your members as weapons of righteousness.
For sin will no longer have dominion over you: you are not under the Law but under grace.
What then? Are we to sin because we are not under the Law but under grace? Certainly not!
Do you not know this? If you offer yourselves to someone as slaves to obey him, you are slaves of the one you obey: either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness.
But thanks be to God: you who were slaves of sin have obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were entrusted,
and, set free from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness.

I am speaking in a human way, because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you offered your members as slaves to impurity and to disorder, leading to more disorder, so now offer your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.
For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.
What fruit did you then bear? Deeds that now make you blush, for they end in death.
But now, set free from sin and become slaves of God, you bear fruit for holiness, and your end is eternal life.
For the wage of sin is death; but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Do you not know, brothers (I am speaking to people who know the law), that the law has authority over a person only during his lifetime?
So a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law that bound her to him.
So while her husband lives she would be called an adulteress if she belonged to another man; but if the husband dies, she is free from the law, and she is not an adulteress if she belongs to another.

In the same way, my brothers, you too were put to death with regard to the Law, through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, to the one who was raised from the dead, so that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions, awakened by the Law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
But now, having died to what held us captive, we have been released from the Law, so that we serve God under the new regime of the Spirit and not the old regime of the letter.
What then shall we say? Is the Law sin? Certainly not! Yet I would not have known sin except through the Law. For I would not have known covetousness if the Law had not said: You shall not covet.
Seizing the opportunity through the commandment, sin produced in me every kind of covetousness; for apart from the Law, sin is dead.
Once, apart from the Law, I was alive; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life,
and I died; and the commandment that was meant to lead to life turned out, for me, to lead to death.
For sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and, through it, put me to death.
So the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.

Did what is good, then, become a cause of death for me? Certainly not! Rather, it was sin that, in order to show itself as sin, put me to death through what is good; so that sin, through the commandment, might be revealed as sinful beyond measure.
For we know that the Law is spiritual; but I am fleshly, sold into the power of sin.
For I do not understand what I do: I do not do what I want, and what I hate, that is what I do.
Now if I do what I do not want, I thereby acknowledge that the Law is good.
But then it is no longer I who act, but sin that dwells in me.
For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh; for the willing of good is within my reach, but not the doing of it.
I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that is what I do.
Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who act, but sin that dwells in me.
So I discover this law: when I want to do good, it is evil that is within my reach.
For I delight in the law of God, according to the inner self;
but I see in my members another law, which fights against the law of my reason and makes me a captive to the law of sin present in my members.
Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?
Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself, with my reason, am a slave to the law of God, and with my flesh, a slave to the law of sin.
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
For the law of the Spirit who gives life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death.
For what was impossible for the Law, powerless because of the flesh, God has done: sending his own Son in flesh like that of sin and to deal with sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,
so that the righteousness required by the Law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.
Those who live according to the flesh are set on what is of the flesh; those who live according to the Spirit, on what is of the Spirit.
Now the craving of the flesh is death, whereas the aspiration of the Spirit is life and peace;
for the craving of the flesh is hostility toward God: it does not submit to the law of God, indeed it cannot;
and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
But you are not in the flesh, you are in the Spirit, since the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.
But if Christ is in you, your body, it is true, is destined for death because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.
And if the Spirit of the One who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, the One who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, through his Spirit who dwells in you.
So then, brothers, we have a debt, but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.
For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God, they are the children of God.
You did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear; you received a Spirit who makes you adopted children, and through him we cry out: Abba, Father!
It is the Spirit himself who bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.
Children, and therefore heirs: heirs of God, coheirs with Christ, since we suffer with him so as also to be glorified with him.
For I consider that there is no comparison between the sufferings of the present time and the glory that is to be revealed in us.
For creation waits with eager longing for the revelation of the children of God.
Creation was subjected to futility, not of its own will, but because of the one who subjected it; yet it keeps hope,
for creation itself will also be set free from slavery to corruption, to enter into the freedom and glory of the children of God.
For we know that the whole of creation is groaning even now in the pains of childbirth.
And it is not alone: we too, who possess the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait for our adoption as children, the redemption of our body.
For we have been saved, but it is in hope. Now to see what one hopes for is no longer to hope: what one sees, how can one still hope for it?
But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with perseverance.
In the same way, the Spirit comes to the aid of our weakness, for we do not know how to pray as we ought; but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.
And the One who searches hearts knows what is the aspiration of the Spirit: it is according to God that he intercedes for the saints.
Moreover, we know that with those who love him, God works together in everything for their good, with those whom he has called according to his purpose.
Those whom he knew beforehand, he also predestined to become conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among a multitude of brothers.
Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.
What then shall we say after this? If God is for us, who can be against us?
He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not give us everything, along with him?
Who will accuse God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies!
Who will condemn? Christ Jesus died; more than that, he was raised, he is at the right hand of God, and he intercedes for us!
Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Distress, anguish, persecution, hunger, destitution, danger, the sword?
It is written: For your sake we are put to death all day long, we are treated as sheep for the slaughter.
But in all this we are more than conquerors through the One who loved us.
Yes, I am certain of this: neither death nor life, neither angels nor powers, neither the present nor the future, nor any forces,
neither height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God shown in Christ Jesus our Lord.

titres.titre: Israel and the righteousness of faith

versets.t: I speak the truth in Christ, I am not lying, my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit:
I have great sorrow in my heart, an unceasing grief.
Indeed, I could wish to be accursed myself, cut off from Christ, for the sake of my brothers, my own people according to the flesh,
the Israelites, to whom belong the adoption as children, the glory, the covenants, the gift of the Law, the worship, the promises;
to them belong the patriarchs, and from them comes the Christ according to the flesh, he who is above all, God blessed for ever. Amen.
It is not that the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel,
and not all are children of Abraham merely because they are his descendants; but: It is through Isaac that you will have descendants who will bear your name.
In other words, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God; it is the children of the promise who count as descendants.
For these are the terms of the promise: At this time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.
More than that, when Rebekah had conceived by one man, our father Isaac,
while the twins were not yet born and had done nothing, either good or evil (so that God's purpose, which chooses freely,
depending not on works but on the One who calls, might stand), it was said to Rebekah: The elder will serve the younger,
as it is written: Jacob I loved, and Esau I rejected.
What then shall we say? Is there injustice in God? Certainly not!
For he says to Moses: I show mercy to whom I show mercy, and I take pity on whom I take pity.
So it depends not on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.
For Scripture says to Pharaoh: This is why I raised you up: to show my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.
So he shows mercy to whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.
You will say to me: Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist his will?
But who are you, O man, to argue with God? Will what is made say to the one who molded it: Why did you make me this way?
Is the potter not master of his clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for a noble use and another for an ordinary one?
And what if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, bore with great patience vessels of wrath, ready for destruction,
in order to make known the riches of his glory toward vessels of mercy that he had prepared beforehand for glory?
These vessels are us, whom he has called not only from among the Jews but also from among the nations.
This is what he says in Hosea: The one who was not my people I will call 'My people,' and her who was not loved, 'Beloved';
and in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' they will be called children of the living God.
And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: Though the number of the sons of Israel were like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved;
for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, fully and without delay.
And as Isaiah had foretold: If the Lord of hosts had not left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, made like Gomorrah.
What then shall we say? The nations, who were not seeking righteousness, have attained righteousness, the righteousness that comes from faith;
while Israel, who sought a law of righteousness, did not reach that law.
Why? Because they sought it not by faith but as if it came from works. They stumbled over the stone of stumbling,
as it is written: See, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling, a rock that makes them fall; but whoever puts his faith in him will not be put to shame.
Brothers, the desire of my heart and my prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
For I testify to them: they have zeal for God, but a zeal without true knowledge.
Failing to recognize the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.
For the end of the Law is Christ, so that everyone who believes may be justified.
Moses writes about the righteousness that comes from the Law: The man who does these precepts will live by them.
But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks like this: Do not say in your heart: Who will go up to heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down)
or: Who will go down into the abyss? (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.)
So what does it say? The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart. This word is the word of faith that we proclaim.
If with your mouth you confess that Jesus is Lord, and if in your heart you believe that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
For it is by believing with the heart that one becomes righteous, and by confessing with the mouth that one attains salvation.
For Scripture says: Whoever puts his faith in him will not be put to shame.
There is no distinction between the Jew and the Greek: all have the same Lord, generous toward all who call on him.
For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
But how are they to call on him without having believed in him? How are they to believe in him without having heard of him? How are they to hear without a preacher?
And how are they to preach unless they are sent? So it is written: how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!
But not all have obeyed the Good News. Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our message?
So faith is born of the message that is heard, and this message comes through the word of Christ.
